text: The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two nitro groups, one at a position adjacent to the carbon carrying a CH2 linker and one at the para-like position relative to that linker, giving a 2,4-dinitro substitution pattern. A methylene bridge connects this dinitrobenzene ring to a pyridine ring attached through its carbon at position 2, so the scaffold is a diaryl-methane type of two separate aromatic rings joined by a single flexible sp3 carbon. The two rings are not fused, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the nitro groups occupy different positions. Both nitro groups act as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, the pyridine nitrogen is an additional acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central CH2 gives the structure some rotational flexibility, while the two aromatic rings remain planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on an aniline-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a primary amino group on one carbon, with a piperidine ring attached through its nitrogen to the adjacent (ortho) carbon. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, while the piperidine is a fully saturated six-membered ring that adopts a flexible chair conformation. The two rings are connected by a single C–N bond, so they are not fused but joined directly, and the ortho substitution pattern places the two nitrogen substituents next to each other. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two rings differ in character. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the primary amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its two N–H bonds) and an acceptor, while the tertiary piperidine nitrogen serves mainly as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3. Attached at the 2-position, between the two ring nitrogens, is a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring with nitrogens at opposite positions. The piperazine is linked to the aromatic ring through one of its nitrogens, which is therefore fully substituted, while the other piperazine nitrogen carries a free secondary amine hydrogen. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted elsewhere, and the saturated ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The pyrimidine nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the free piperazine N–H provides a hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a piperazine ring attached through a nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The six-membered piperazine ring is saturated and contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 relationship; only the nitrogen bonded to the aryl ring is substituted, while the distal nitrogen bears a free hydrogen. The phenol hydroxyl and the secondary amine N-H can both act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen and both nitrogen atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Ring fusion is absent, as the two rings are joined by a single C–N bond, which allows rotation and gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The piperazine ring can adopt chair conformations, and the overall structure has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local symmetry of the piperazine ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexene, with one carbon-carbon double bond located within the ring. Attached to one of the sp2 ring carbons is a two-carbon ethyl chain that terminates in a primary amine group. The ring itself is unfused and carries no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local mirror plane of the ring. The ring provides moderate rigidity around the alkene, while the saturated ethyl linker gives the amine end conformational freedom. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, whose ring nitrogen is capped by a tert-butoxycarbonyl carbamate group, which carries a bulky tert-butyl ester-like unit. At the 4-position of the ring sits an ether oxygen linking to a flexible CH2 bridge that ends in a secondary amide, with an N-methyl substituent on the amide nitrogen. The ring is non-fused and fully saturated, so it adopts a chair-like conformation, though the side chains add conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks a symmetry axis because the two ends differ, and it contains one amide N-H as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygens of the amide and carbamate, the ether oxygen, and the carbamate ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, which is not fused to any other ring. The nitrogen is capped by a tert-butyl carbamate group, with a bulky tert-butyl ester-type oxygen attached to a carbonyl bonded to the ring nitrogen. At the opposite (4-) position of the ring, an ether oxygen links to a CH2 that leads into an amide, where the amide nitrogen carries a cyclopropyl group. The substitution pattern is therefore symmetric about the ring axis, but the two ends carry different chains, so the overall molecule lacks symmetry. The saturated ring and flexible linkers give moderate conformational freedom, while the carbamate and amide groups add some rigidity. The amide N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, which serves as the central scaffold. The ring nitrogen is capped by a tert-butoxycarbonyl carbamate group, a bulky, lipophilic protecting-group motif that adds steric bulk. At the 4-position of the piperidine, an ether oxygen links the ring to a two-carbon chain ending in an N,N-dimethyl amide, giving a tertiary amide carbonyl. The substitution pattern is therefore symmetric about the piperidine ring axis at the 1 and 4 positions, while the flexible ether-acetamide side chain and the rotatable carbamate bond add conformational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all nitrogens are fully substituted, and the carbonyl oxygens and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic organosilane built around a single silicon atom bearing three methyl groups and one propynyl chain. The alkyne unit, a carbon-carbon triple bond, sits directly next to the silicon and is terminated by a methyl group, giving a linear, rigid segment with no rings and no ring fusion. There are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. The arrangement around the silicon is nearly tetrahedral and the three methyl substituents are equivalent, giving the silicon center local threefold symmetry, while the linear alkyne makes the overall shape elongated and fairly rigid.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered carbocycle that contains a ketone. The aromatic ring is ortho-fused to the saturated ring, so the two rings share one edge of two adjacent carbons. The ketone carbonyl sits on the non-aromatic ring, adjacent to the fused aromatic carbon, while the three remaining saturated carbons form a flexible chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, rather flat framework, with the aromatic portion rigid and the saturated portion able to pucker. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a polycyclic aromatic aldehyde built on a fused four-ring carbon framework, which is a pyrene-type scaffold (four rings sharing edges in a compact, roughly planar arrangement). A single formyl group (–CHO) is attached to one peripheral carbon of the aromatic core, and no other substituents are present, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the molecule has no true rotational symmetry beyond its planar framework. The fused rings make the structure rigid and flat, with the aldehyde carbonyl able to rotate only slightly about its single bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

CCCO is a straight, saturated three-carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems, so its scaffold is simply an acyclic propyl backbone. A single hydroxyl group sits on the terminal carbon, making the molecule a primary alcohol with a polar end and a nonpolar hydrocarbon tail. The structure has no substitution pattern beyond that one terminal substitution, and it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry in a meaningful sense because the hydroxyl breaks the chain's otherwise linear arrangement. The molecule is highly flexible, since all carbon-carbon and carbon-oxygen bonds are single bonds that rotate freely. The oxygen atom can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is built on a cyclopropane ring, a three-membered carbocycle, with two substituents on one carbon: a phenyl group and a carboxylic acid group. The phenyl ring is a simple benzene ring with no further substitution, so it is unsubstituted and carries no additional functional groups. The carboxylic acid (–COOH) is attached directly to the quaternary ring carbon, and it provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The cyclopropane ring and the attached phenyl ring give the scaffold considerable rigidity, while the single bond to the carboxyl group allows some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond a local pseudo-mirror arrangement, because the two ring-carbon substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring that bears a phenyl group and a hydroxyl group on the same carbon, making that carbon a tertiary alcohol center. The six-membered saturated ring is non-aromatic and adopts flexible chair-like conformations, while the attached benzene ring is planar and aromatic. The two ring systems are joined by a single C–C bond with no fusion between them, so the structure is a 1-substituted cyclohexanol scaffold with a pendant aryl group. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local rotational freedom around the single bond to the phenyl ring. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs, while the aromatic and aliphatic carbons contribute only nonpolar surface.

The molecule is built on a five-membered pyrazolidinone scaffold: a saturated ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which bears a carbonyl group forming a cyclic amide (lactam). The other nitrogen carries a phenyl ring attached directly to it, so the N-aryl group is a simple monosubstituted benzene with no further substitution on the ring. There is no ring fusion, and the two ring systems are joined by a single nitrogen-carbon bond. The compound offers one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen and one hydrogen-bond donor at the amide nitrogen position, though the latter nitrogen is substituted, so the N-H donor is present only if a hydrogen remains on that nitrogen. The five-membered ring is fairly compact and conformationally limited, while the phenyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring nitrogen.

The molecule is built around a five-membered saturated lactam ring, a pyrrolidin-2-one, in which a carbonyl carbon sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen. That nitrogen is bonded directly to a phenyl ring, so the two ring systems are connected by a single N–C bond rather than being fused. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, carrying only hydrogens, which gives it a simple, symmetric monosubstituted pattern with a mirror plane through the attachment point. The lactam's amide-type carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen carries no hydrogen. The five-membered ring is fairly compact and the N-aryl bond allows some rotation, so the overall shape is moderately rigid.

The molecule is built on a two-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring, specifically a 1,2-diol motif: a phenyl group bearing a CH(OH) carbon that is bonded to a CH2OH group. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings and no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. The molecule contains two secondary and primary hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, giving it two hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptors. The side chain has a stereogenic center at the benzylic carbon, and the molecule is fairly flexible because of the rotatable single bonds in the side chain, while the aromatic ring remains rigid and planar.

This molecule is a straight-chain four-carbon alkyne, with a carbon-carbon triple bond located at one terminus of the chain, so it is a terminal alkyne. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or other functional groups beyond the alkyne itself. Because the backbone is linear and carries no substituents, the molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond its simple chain. The triple bond makes the terminal carbon-hydrogen bond relatively acidic compared with alkane C–H bonds, and the terminal alkyne C–H can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the pi system offers only weak acceptor character. The chain itself is fairly flexible through its sp3 carbons, while the alkyne end remains rigid and linear.

This molecule is a straight-chain primary alcohol built on an unbranched saturated skeleton of fifteen carbon atoms, with no rings and no fused ring systems. The terminal carbon bears a single hydroxyl group, which is the only functional group present, and there are no other substituents or substitution patterns along the chain. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the mirror-like equivalence of its two ends, and the long methylene chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many rotational conformations. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar.

This molecule is an acyclic primary aliphatic amine built on a straight, unbranched eight-carbon chain, with the nitrogen bonded to a terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups or substituents, so its scaffold is simply a linear alkyl chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror relationship of the chain, and the flexible saturated chain allows many rotational conformations. The amine group carries two N–H bonds, giving it two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and its lone pair makes the nitrogen a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a straight-chain, acyclic alkene: a single eight-carbon backbone with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or fused scaffold to describe. Its only functional group is a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at one end of the chain, where the first two carbons are joined by a double bond and the rest are saturated single-bonded methylene units. The molecule has no substituents branching off the chain and no heteroatoms, so it is a simple hydrocarbon with no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its linear, unbranched backbone gives it a high degree of conformational flexibility, since the saturated segments can rotate freely about their single bonds. Overall the structure is symmetric only in a loose sense, as it lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because of the terminal double bond.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol: a linear eight-carbon saturated chain with no rings, double bonds, or branching. The terminal carbon at one end carries a sulfur atom bearing a single hydrogen, which makes it a thiol (sulfhydryl) functional group. The rest of the skeleton is composed only of sp3 methylene units, so the structure is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a rough mirror relationship of the carbon chain about its midpoint in idealized conformations, and it lacks any stereocenters. The thiol sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H group and as a weak acceptor through its lone pairs, though it is far less polar than an alcohol.

This molecule is an acyclic alkanesulfonyl chloride built on a straight eight-carbon chain, with no rings and no branching. At one end of the chain sits a sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms, which is in turn bonded to a chlorine atom. The sulfur center is tetrahedral in geometry, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the free rotation of its flexible alkyl chain. The sulfonyl chloride is the sole functional group, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two sulfonyl oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic primary aliphatic amine built on a straight, unbranched chain of nine carbon atoms, so it has no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic character. The only functional group is a terminal primary amine (–NH2) bonded to the first carbon of the chain, with no other substituents or branch points along the backbone. Because the carbon chain is saturated and can rotate freely about its single bonds, the molecule is highly flexible and lacks any rigid core. Its symmetry is low: the polar amine end contrasts sharply with the long nonpolar hydrocarbon tail, giving the structure a strongly amphiphilic character. The amine nitrogen carries two hydrogen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and its lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the alkyl chain offers no additional hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built from a three-carbon straight chain: a terminal methyl, a central methylene, and a methylene attached to the heteroatom. Attached to the end of this chain is a nitro group, in which a nitrogen atom bears a positive formal charge and is bonded to two oxygen atoms, one double-bonded and one single-bonded to a negative charge, giving a planar, polarized N(=O)O arrangement. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so the scaffold is a simple linear alkyl chain carrying a single terminal functional group. The molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single C–C and C–N bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the nitro group. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a straight-chain propyl group on one carbon and a nitro group on the opposite carbon. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The nitro group, with its formally charged nitrogen and two oxygens, is strongly electron-withdrawing and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The para arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry about its long axis, and the aromatic ring is rigid, whereas the propyl chain adds conformational flexibility at one end.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold. It carries two substituents placed para to each other, specifically a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and two oxygens, one negatively charged) and a trifluoromethoxy group (an oxygen bridging the ring to a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms). The ring itself is planar and rigid, while the trifluoromethoxy linkage offers some rotational freedom around the aryl-oxygen bond. Because the two substituents sit opposite one another, the overall arrangement has a high degree of symmetry about the ring axis. The nitro group contributes oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a linear, rod-like diarylalkyne built from a hexyl-substituted benzene ring joined to a para-methyl-substituted benzene ring through a carbon-carbon triple bond. Both aromatic rings are simple monocyclic benzene rings with no fused ring systems, and each carries a single substituent in the para position relative to the alkyne linkage. The alkyne unit forces the two rings into a collinear arrangement, giving the scaffold a long, stiff, extended shape, while the hexyl chain adds a flexible aliphatic tail at one end. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either. Its only polar-character features are the aromatic and alkyne pi systems, and the overall structure is essentially nonpolar and hydrocarbon in nature.

This molecule is a diarylalkyne: two para-butyl-substituted benzene rings joined end to end through a carbon-carbon triple bond. The scaffold is fully linear and rigid, since the alkyne holds the two aromatic rings collinear, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold (C2h-like) symmetry through its center. Each ring carries a single n-butyl chain at the position opposite the alkyne, giving a symmetric para substitution pattern. The four aliphatic butyl chains are flexible and add conformational freedom at the periphery. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor or donor capability.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with an acetic acid side chain attached at the 1-position of the naphthalene ring system. The side chain consists of a methylene group linking the aromatic core to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the carboxyl group is the only functional group present. The fused bicyclic aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the CH2-COOH arm adds some conformational flexibility around its single bonds. Because the substitution is asymmetric, the molecule lacks any overall symmetry axis or plane. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a planar, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A hydroxyl group (–OH) is attached to one of the carbon atoms adjacent to the ring-fusion position, placing it at the alpha position of the naphthalene core. The rest of the framework is unsubstituted, so there is only this single substituent and no symmetry-breaking additional groups beyond it. The fused aromatic rings make the structure rigid and flat, with the hydroxyl oxygen able to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Attached to one of the alpha positions (carbon 1) is a carbohydrazide group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon bonded to an NH-NH2 unit, so the substitution pattern is a single substituent on the naphthalene ring. The carbonyl is conjugated with the aromatic system, while the terminal hydrazide nitrogens are sp3-like and rotatable, adding modest flexibility to the otherwise planar framework. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituent breaks the symmetry of the naphthalene core. The hydrazide unit provides multiple hydrogen-bond donors (the NH and NH2 groups) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs).

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. Attached to one of the fused-ring positions adjacent to the ring junction is a formyl group, an aldehyde carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to the aromatic ring. The substitution pattern is therefore a single carbonyl substituent on the naphthalene core, which breaks any mirror symmetry the bare ring system would otherwise have. The rigid aromatic framework is largely planar, with the aldehyde group capable of limited rotation about its bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methylsulfonyl group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a methyl carbon. The other is a nitro group, in which a nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens, one of which carries a formal negative charge while the nitrogen carries a formal positive charge. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no stereocenters, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through both substituents. Both electron-withdrawing groups contribute strong hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through their oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, with the nitrogen bearing a methyl group, so there is no N-H hydrogen-bond donor on the ring. A carboxylic acid group (-C(=O)OH) is attached to a ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, which places it at the 2-position of the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen contributes only weak acceptor character because its lone pair is part of the aromatic system.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, which is the defining scaffold of a piperidine. The ring carries no fused partners and no other rings, so the core is a simple monocyclic heterocycle. The only substituent is a methyl group attached directly to the nitrogen, making it a tertiary amine with no additional functional groups present. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a chair-like conformation, giving it moderate conformational flexibility rather than rigidity. The nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen carries no N–H bond.

This molecule is N-methylisatin, built on an indole-type scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The nitrogen carries a methyl group, so it is a tertiary amide-type nitrogen with no N-H. The five-membered ring contains an amide carbonyl adjacent to the nitrogen and a second, adjacent ketone carbonyl, making the ring a 1,2-dicarbonyl system fused directly to the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, with four aromatic C-H positions and no additional substituents. The fused bicyclic core is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds apart from the N-methyl group. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic aromatic scaffold, a naphthalene-like skeleton in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a pyridine ring, forming an isoquinoline core. The nitrogen sits in the six-membered heteroaromatic ring, adjacent to the fusion region, and that ring is fully aromatic and planar. A single methyl group is attached to the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, giving a one-substituent pattern with no symmetry elements beyond the planar framework. The rigid, flat fused system has essentially no rotatable bonds, so the structure is conformationally fixed. The pyridine-type nitrogen has a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a 2-aryloxypropanoic acid, built from a propanoic acid backbone whose alpha carbon carries a methyl group and an ether oxygen linking to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single benzene with two chlorine substituents at the 2 and 4 positions relative to the ether oxygen, giving a 2,4-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid group provides one hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens, while the ether oxygen and the chlorine atoms serve as additional, weaker acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, whereas the saturated side chain between the ring and the carboxyl group retains rotational freedom around its single bonds. The stereocenter at the alpha carbon is unspecified in the input.

The molecule is a 2-aryloxypropanoic acid: a three-carbon chain whose carboxylic acid terminus sits beside a stereogenic carbon bearing a methyl group and an ether oxygen linked to a benzene ring. That benzene ring is a single unfused aromatic ring carrying three chlorine substituents at the 2, 4, and 5 positions relative to the ether oxygen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ether oxygen and the chlorine atoms act only as weak acceptors. The molecule has a moderately flexible aliphatic linker connecting its rigid aromatic core to the polar acid end.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at the ortho positions, giving a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a pivalamide group, where a tertiary-butyl carbon (three methyl groups attached to a quaternary carbon) is bonded to a carbonyl that links through an amide nitrogen to the ring. The neighboring substituent is a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups. The amide N-H and the two boronic acid O-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygens serve as acceptors. The bulky tert-butyl group gives the amide side chain considerable steric bulk, while the rest of the framework is fairly rigid. The molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the three methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzoic acid bearing a pyrrole ring attached at the ortho position relative to the carboxyl group. A benzene ring carries a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) on one carbon and a five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring linked through its nitrogen atom on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit next to each other on the benzene ring. The pyrrole nitrogen is part of the aromatic system and carries no hydrogen, since it is bonded to the benzene ring. The molecule has two separate aromatic rings joined by a single N–C bond, which allows some rotation and gives it moderate rather than rigid flexibility. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyrrole nitrogen provides no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a pyrrolidine nitrogen on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-substituted aromatic scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, while the attached pyrrolidine is a saturated five-membered ring containing a tertiary amine nitrogen that bonds directly to the phenyl carbon, so the two ring systems are linked by a single N-aryl bond rather than being fused. The phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the tertiary nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor only, since it carries no hydrogen. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents sit in different environments, and the pyrrolidine ring is conformationally flexible, while the aromatic core remains rigid.

The molecule is built around a five-membered thiazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom. Attached to the ring is a formyl group, an aldehyde carbonyl (C=O bonded to a hydrogen), which serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. At the position between the sulfur and the nitrogen sits a piperidine ring bonded through its nitrogen atom, making that nitrogen a tertiary amine whose lone pair is conjugated into the thiazole. The piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring, adopting a flexible chair-like conformation, while the thiazole-aldehyde portion is essentially planar and rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis and a single substitution pattern across the ring positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its acceptors are the aldehyde oxygen and the thiazole nitrogen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a phenol group and a piperidine ring attached through nitrogen. The benzene ring is monosubstituted in an ortho pattern: a hydroxyl group sits on one carbon and the saturated six-membered piperidine nitrogen is bonded to the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents are next to each other. The piperidine is a fully saturated, non-aromatic ring with one nitrogen and five methylene carbons, adopting a flexible chair-like conformation. The nitrogen is a tertiary amine that is bonded to the aromatic ring, giving it an aniline-type character, and it can accept a hydrogen bond. The phenolic hydroxyl can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two rings are joined asymmetrically.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), which is linear and electron-withdrawing and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other is a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one tertiary nitrogen directly attached to the benzene. The piperidine ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the planar aromatic core remains rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ring geometry, and the tertiary amine nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate one, since it has no hydrogen attached.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing two nitrogen-containing groups on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a primary aromatic amine (an aniline-type NH2 group), and the other is a piperazine ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms, forming an N-aryl bond. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens at opposite positions, and its free secondary amine nitrogen remains unsubstituted. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the piperazine ring is flexible and adopts non-planar chair-like conformations. The primary amine and the secondary piperazine NH each can donate hydrogen bonds, and the nitrogen atoms in both groups can accept them.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with a 2-hydroxyethyl group attached at the 1-position of one ring. The fused bicyclic aromatic system is planar and rigid, while the saturated two-carbon chain attached to it adds limited rotational flexibility. The only functional group is a primary alcohol, whose hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the aromatic rings, because the substituent breaks the mirror relationship of the naphthalene framework.

The molecule is built on a 1,3-benzodioxole scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a five-membered dioxole ring through two adjacent carbons, with the methylene bridge (OCH2O) completing the heterocycle. Attached to the benzene ring, at a position adjacent to one of the ring oxygens' carbons, is a piperazine ring connected through a carbon atom of that ring, so the piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 arrangement. The benzodioxole portion is largely planar and rigid, while the piperazine ring is flexible and can adopt chair-like conformations. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the piperazine attaches at a single carbon, making one side of the ring system distinct. The two secondary amine nitrogens in the piperazine can each donate a hydrogen bond, and together with the two ether oxygens of the dioxole they provide several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is an unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, built from a terminal alkyne at one end and a fully saturated run of methylene units at the other. The triple bond sits at the very end of the chain, so the carbon bearing the terminal hydrogen is sp-hybridized and the molecule has a linear, rod-like geometry. Apart from the single terminal C–H on the alkyne, there are no heteroatoms or other functional groups, and no substituents branch off the backbone. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the trivial one, since the two ends differ in saturation. It is highly flexible because of the many freely rotating single bonds along the chain, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, apart from the weakly acidic terminal alkyne hydrogen.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated-except-for-one-site hydrocarbon chain: a terminal alkene (vinyl group) at one end of a straight carbon backbone of ten carbons in total. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups other than the single carbon-carbon double bond at the chain terminus. Because there are no substituents branching off the chain, the substitution pattern is simply linear, and the molecule has no symmetry beyond the trivial one. The flexible, freely rotating sigma bonds make it highly conformationally flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated aliphatic chain of eleven carbon atoms with a primary alcohol group at one terminus. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic or unsaturated bonds, so the scaffold is a simple linear alkane backbone with a single hydroxyl substituent on the terminal carbon. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond a mirror-like arrangement of its two ends, and its long carbon chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the remainder of the chain contributes only nonpolar, hydrophobic character.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary sp3 carbon bearing three phenyl rings and one imidazol-1-yl group, giving a propeller-like, three-dimensionally crowded scaffold. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the ring positions carry only hydrogens and the overall pattern is highly symmetric around the central carbon. The imidazole ring is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle attached through one of its ring nitrogens, leaving the other nitrogen free to act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H sites are absent. The core is fairly rigid because the bulky aryl groups restrict rotation about the central carbon, though the single bonds to the imidazole and phenyls still allow some conformational motion.

The molecule is built around a three-membered cyclopropane ring, a strained carbocycle with no fused or additional rings. One carbon of this ring carries two substituents: a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) and a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3), making it a quaternary ring carbon. The remaining two ring carbons are unsubstituted CH2 units, so the substitution pattern is geminal on a single atom. The ring is rigid, and the only rotational freedom comes from the bonds linking the carboxyl and trifluoromethyl groups to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the substituted carbon. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkene, with a single carbon-carbon double bond at one end of an otherwise saturated twelve-carbon backbone. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the terminal vinyl group. The chain is unbranched and substituted nowhere along its length, so the molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any meaningful internal symmetry. Its long, unbranched chain makes it highly flexible, with many accessible rotational conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, as only carbon and hydrogen are present.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered pyranose-type ring containing one oxygen atom, bearing a thiol group at the anomeric carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which makes it a thiosugar. Four acetyl ester groups are attached to the ring carbons and the exocyclic CH2, so every free hydroxyl of the parent sugar has been capped by an acetate, giving a fully acetylated scaffold. The ring is flexible, with the stereocentres arranged so the substituents adopt a defined spatial pattern, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. It has no free hydrogen-bond donors, since the only potential donor is the thiol, while the ester carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkene, a hydrocarbon with no rings and no heteroatoms. Its skeleton is one long, unbranched carbon chain, with the only functional group being a single carbon-carbon double bond at one end, between the first and second carbons. The molecule has no substitution pattern to speak of, since every carbon except the alkene terminus is simply bonded to two neighbors in the chain. It has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror-like equivalence of its two ends, and the chain is highly flexible, free to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched chain of fifteen carbon atoms, with a hydroxyl group attached to one terminal carbon, so it is a primary alcohol with no rings, fused systems, or additional substituents. Its skeleton is entirely saturated, with every carbon connected only by single bonds and no double or triple bonds present. The molecule has no stereocenters and possesses a mirror-plane symmetry along the chain axis, meaning it is achiral. The long alkyl chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. The terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic thiol: a saturated, unbranched backbone of fourteen carbon atoms with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. The only functional group is a terminal sulfhydryl group (–SH) attached to one end of the chain, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and there is no substitution pattern beyond that single end group. The molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many carbon–carbon single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry apart from the mirror-like arrangement of the alkyl chain itself. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom can serve as a weak acceptor, and the rest of the structure contributes no polar sites.

The molecule is built on a five-membered cyclic urea, an imidazolidinone ring containing two nitrogen atoms separated by a carbonyl carbon. One ring nitrogen is part of an amide-type linkage to the carbonyl, while the other is a secondary amine within the saturated portion of the ring, with a bulky tert-butyl group attached to the first nitrogen. The ring is not fused to any other ring system and is largely saturated apart from the planar carbonyl unit, giving a compact, moderately rigid scaffold with limited conformational freedom. The tert-butyl group is a branched, non-polar substituent that projects from one side of the ring and contributes steric bulk without any symmetry across the whole framework. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the unsubstituted ring NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a four-membered polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon core, a pyrene-type scaffold, with a four-carbon chain bearing a terminal carboxylic acid attached to one of the peripheral carbons. The fused aromatic system is flat and rigid, built from several six-membered rings sharing edges, while the saturated three-carbon tether linking the ring to the acid group adds conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid is the only polar functional group, offering one hydrogen-bond donor from the hydroxyl and two acceptor oxygens from the carbonyl and hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the chain sits on one edge of the fused system, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry.

Propan-1-amine is an acyclic molecule built on a straight three-carbon chain with no rings, fused systems, or aromatic groups. Its only functional group is a primary amine, in which a nitrogen atom sits at one terminus of the chain and carries two hydrogen atoms, giving it substitution on a single carbon. The structure is achiral and lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial, and the chain is flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. The nitrogen lone pair and its two N-H bonds allow the group to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a simple, acyclic thiol built on a straight three-carbon chain. The carbon skeleton is an unbranched propyl group, with no rings, no fused systems, and no substituents along the chain beyond the terminal sulfur. The only functional group is a sulfhydryl (thiol) group attached to the terminal carbon, giving it a single S–H bond. Because the chain is linear and has no symmetry-breaking features other than the terminal group, the molecule is quite flexible, with free rotation about its C–C single bonds. The thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor compared with oxygen or nitrogen analogues.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that is fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring, giving a 1,3-benzodioxole scaffold with the two oxygen atoms bridged by a single methylene carbon. A piperazine ring is attached through a benzylic CH2 linker at a position adjacent to one of the dioxole oxygens, so the benzene carries a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens; one nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to the benzylic carbon, while the other is a secondary amine with an N–H. The fused aromatic-dioxole system is largely planar and rigid, whereas the piperazine ring and the benzylic linker add conformational flexibility. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitrogen lone pairs together with the dioxole oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a semicarbazide-type compound built on a simple acyclic chain linking two nitrogen-containing groups to a benzene ring. A phenyl ring, a single unsubstituted six-membered aromatic carbocycle, forms the core of the scaffold, with no ring fusion and no additional substituents on the ring, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. A urea-like carbonyl group (a carboxamide attached to a hydrazine nitrogen) and a hydrazine linkage, bearing an N-H group directly attached to the phenyl ring, make up the functional groups. The compound has no molecular symmetry beyond the free rotation of its chain, and the flexible N-N and C-N single bonds give it considerable conformational freedom, although the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. Multiple N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined directly by a single bond: a benzene ring bearing a pyrrole ring attached through its nitrogen atom. The pyrrole is a five-membered, fully unsaturated heterocycle containing one nitrogen, and it is bonded to the phenyl ring at that nitrogen, so there are no additional functional groups or substituents. Both rings are planar and aromatic, and the single linking bond allows some rotation, though the overall framework is fairly rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no obvious symmetry axis through the whole structure. The pyrrole nitrogen carries no hydrogen, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and only the weakly basic pyrrole nitrogen could act as a very weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent at one position, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the benzene ring is planar and rigid. The substituent is a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other, so the two nitrogens sit at the 1 and 4 positions of the ring. The nitrogen attached directly to the benzene ring is a tertiary aryl amine, while the distal nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing a free N–H. The piperazine ring can adopt flexible chair conformations, giving the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility that contrasts with the rigid aromatic ring. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and both nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is N-phenylisatin, built on an indole-2,3-dione (isatin) scaffold. A benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring that carries two adjacent carbonyl groups at positions 2 and 3, forming an α-keto-amide (dicarbonyl lactam) unit. The nitrogen bears a phenyl substituent, so the ring nitrogen has no N–H and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, while the N-phenyl ring is attached through a single bond and can rotate. Both carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a single bond: a benzene ring carrying a phenyl substituent on one ring nitrogen of an imidazole ring. The imidazole is a five-membered ring containing two nitrogens at positions 1 and 3, with the N-1 atom bearing the phenyl group and the N-3 atom left as a pyridine-type nitrogen. Neither ring is fused to the other, so the scaffold is a biaryl-like arrangement with a single rotatable C–N bond between the rings. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, and the imidazole has no additional substituents. The overall framework is planar and largely rigid, with limited flexibility about the connecting bond. The pyridine-type nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a cyclopentane ring in which one carbon bears both a phenyl group and a carboxylic acid group, making that carbon quaternary. The phenyl ring is a simple, unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to the quaternary carbon, so the molecule has one aromatic ring and one saturated five-membered carbocycle joined at a single shared carbon. The carboxylic acid group (-C(=O)OH) provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens. Overall the structure is fairly compact and has no stereocenters, though rotation about the bond to the phenyl ring gives some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring containing one carbon-carbon double bond, so it is a cyclohexene-type scaffold. A phenyl ring is attached directly to one of the two sp2 carbons of that double bond, making the molecule a vinyl-linked aryl-cycloalkene in which the two ring systems are joined by a single bond rather than fused. The remaining four ring carbons are saturated methylene groups, giving the cycloalkene portion a partly flexible, non-planar character while the conjugated styrene-like unit stays largely planar. The molecule contains no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a five-membered pyrazolone-type heterocycle: a ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a ketone carbonyl, and a methylene group, with the ring nitrogen bearing a phenyl substituent. The ring carbon opposite the carbonyl carries a trifluoromethyl group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and adds three fluorine atoms as a compact, sterically defined substituent. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and attached directly to the nitrogen, giving the molecule an extended, mostly planar aromatic-heterocyclic framework with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H positions are absent, but the carbonyl oxygen and the imine-type ring nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent at one position, with no additional ring fusion or heteroatom-containing rings. Attached to that ring is a secondary carbon that carries a hydroxyl group, and this carbon is also bonded to a terminal alkyne (a carbon-carbon triple bond ending in a hydrogen). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the carbinol carbon provides a single point of tetrahedral geometry and some rotational freedom around its bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the alkyne offers a weakly acidic terminal C-H along with a linear, electron-rich triple bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local rotational symmetry of the phenyl ring.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain flanked by a methyl group on one end and a phenyl ring on the other. The central carbon bears an oxime group, with the C=N-OH unit providing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and an acceptor (the nitrogen). Adjacent to this, a ketone carbonyl connects the chain to an unsubstituted benzene ring, giving an aryl ketone. A second carbonyl sits next to the methyl end, so the chain carries two carbonyl oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The benzene ring is monosubstituted and planar, while the rest of the chain is flexible, with no internal symmetry because the two ends differ.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic primary amine built on an unbranched five-carbon backbone, with no rings or ring fusion present. The single functional group is a terminal primary amine (–NH2) attached to one end of the chain, so the molecule has no substitution pattern beyond this end-group placement and no meaningful internal symmetry apart from the mirror-like linear arrangement of the carbon skeleton. The alkyl chain is flexible, with freely rotating carbon–carbon single bonds that allow many conformations. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair of electrons.

This molecule is an acyclic alkenylboronic acid: a straight-chain hex-1-enyl group, with the double bond between the first two carbons, attached to a boron atom that carries two hydroxyl groups. There are no rings, so no ring systems or ring fusion are present, and the skeleton is entirely open-chain. The key functional group is the boronic acid, B(OH)2, which is planar at boron and gives the molecule two hydrogen-bond donors from the O–H groups and two acceptors from the oxygens. The alkene geometry and the four-carbon alkyl tail make the chain flexible, while the trigonal boron center adds a rigid planar region. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the alkyl chain is unbranched and differs from the boronic acid end.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated five-carbon straight chain, a linear pentane skeleton with a hydroxyl group on the terminal carbon, making it a primary alcohol. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so its structure is simply a flexible chain with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the trivial, since the hydroxyl end differs from the methyl end. The hydroxyl oxygen acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the alkyl backbone contributes only nonpolar, non-hydrogen-bonding character.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol, with a five-carbon saturated chain terminated at one end by a sulfhydryl group. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution beyond the terminal thiol, so its scaffold is simply an open aliphatic chain. The chain is fully saturated and conformationally flexible, able to adopt many rotameric arrangements about its single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a notional mirror plane through the chain axis, since the two ends are chemically distinct. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond, while the sulfur atom offers only modest hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkyne, consisting of a single unbranched carbon backbone with no rings, fused systems, or heteroatoms. The terminal end carries a carbon-carbon triple bond, which is the only functional group present and is located at one extremity of the chain. Because the chain is entirely saturated apart from that alkyne, there is no substitution pattern to speak of, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial linear arrangement. Its long, unbranched framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility through rotation about its many single bonds. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since the only heteroatom-free functionality is the terminal alkyne C–H, which is a very weak and generally non-participating donor.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic hydrocarbon chain built from fifteen carbon atoms, with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at one end of the backbone. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups other than that single alkene unit. Because the chain is linear and saturated apart from the terminal vinyl group, there is no substitution pattern or branching to describe, and the molecule possesses no meaningful symmetry beyond its overall linear shape. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow it to adopt numerous conformations. Being composed solely of carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is an unbranched, straight-chain hydrocarbon built on a linear eight-carbon scaffold, with no rings and no fused ring systems. Its defining feature is a terminal alkyne group, a carbon-carbon triple bond at one end of the chain, which makes the molecule a terminal alkyne. The rest of the chain consists of saturated methylene units, so there are no other functional groups and no substitution pattern to speak of. The structure has no symmetry beyond the trivial, is highly flexible because its single bonds allow free rotation, and has the linear alkyne geometry at its terminus. It cannot donate hydrogen bonds, and it has no heteroatoms that could act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched carbon chain of eight carbons, with a terminal alkene at one end and a secondary alcohol on the carbon adjacent to that alkene, making it an allylic alcohol. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is a simple open-chain aliphatic skeleton. The only functional groups are the carbon-carbon double bond and the single hydroxyl group, and the molecule has no symmetry because the hydroxyl sits at an asymmetric position along the chain. The chain is highly flexible, with freely rotating single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkene contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a single unbranched carbon chain of eight carbons. The terminal carbon bears a hydroxyl group, making it a primary alcohol with no other functional groups or substituents along the chain. Its symmetry is low, since the hydroxyl end differs from the methyl end, though the carbon backbone itself is fully saturated and unbranched. The chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many rotational conformations around its single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar.

The molecule is an unbranched, acyclic hydrocarbon chain built from a single terminal alkene. A carbon-carbon double bond sits at one end, with a long, saturated run of methylene units extending from it to form the rest of the skeleton. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond that terminal vinyl unit. The substitution pattern is strictly linear, so the molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry apart from the trivial mirror relationship of the chain. The chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated chain of carbon atoms, with no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing ring systems. A single hydroxyl group (-OH) sits at one terminus of the chain, making it a primary alcohol. Because the skeleton is fully flexible and free to rotate about its many single bonds, it can adopt many conformations, though it has no internal symmetry beyond the mirror-like sameness of its two ends. The hydroxyl group is both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the long hydrocarbon tail is nonpolar and contributes no such interaction sites.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of eighteen carbon atoms, terminated at one end by a thiol group (a sulfur atom bonded to a hydrogen). It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated units, so its scaffold is simply a linear alkyl backbone. The chain has no substituents or branching, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial mirror of the chain's linear arrangement. Its long chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S-H bond and a weak acceptor through the sulfur lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched chain of eighteen carbon atoms, forming a long saturated alkyl backbone with no rings and no double bonds. At one terminus, the chain is bonded to a sulfonyl group, in which a central sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and also bonded to a chlorine atom, creating a sulfonyl chloride functional group. The overall structure is highly flexible, since the long saturated chain can rotate freely about its single bonds, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement at its ends. The sulfonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, as all hydrogens are carried on carbon.

The molecule is built on a five-membered tetrahydrofuran ring, a furanose-type scaffold, bearing four substituents on its carbons. Three of the ring carbons carry ester groups: an acetate on the anomeric carbon, which is attached to the ring oxygen, and benzoate esters on the other ring positions. A fourth, exocyclic CH2 unit links through an ester oxygen to a further benzoate group, so the molecule contains four ester linkages in total. Three phenyl rings are present as unfused, freely rotating aromatic groups that add considerable bulk and flexibility. The stereocentres on the ring define a fixed three-dimensional arrangement, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its multiple carbonyl and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic alkyne, with no rings, no fused systems, and no heteroatoms. Its skeleton is a linear chain of ten carbons in total, with the triple bond located at one terminus, making it a terminal alkyne. The only functional group is the carbon-carbon triple bond, which is linear in geometry and gives the terminal carbon-hydrogen bond some acidity relative to alkanes. The molecule has no substituents or branches, so it lacks any stereocenters and possesses no meaningful symmetry beyond the trivial one. Its chain is highly flexible due to free rotation about the single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since the triple bond and the carbon-hydrogen bonds do not participate in conventional hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a straight-chain primary alcohol: a nine-carbon saturated alkyl backbone terminated at one end by a hydroxyl group. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic and the carbon chain is unbranched. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, and it possesses no internal symmetry beyond the approximate mirror relationship of the extended carbon framework. The terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the lone pairs on oxygen, making it the sole polar site on an otherwise nonpolar hydrocarbon chain.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, making it planar and rigid. A single nitro group (–NO2) is attached to one carbon of the ring system, at a position adjacent to the ring fusion (the alpha position). Apart from this substituent, the molecule consists only of aromatic C–H and C=C bonds, with no other functional groups present. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and offers two oxygen atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any internal symmetry relative to the substituent position, so the two rings are inequivalent.

This molecule is a xanthine-type bicyclic scaffold: a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, sharing a C–C bond. The pyrimidine ring carries two carbonyl groups (lactam-type C=O functions) and is substituted with a methyl group on one nitrogen and a linear n-hexyl chain on the other. The imidazole ring bears a third N-methyl group at a nitrogen on the five-membered side. Thus, three nitrogen atoms are methylated or alkylated, leaving the substitution pattern asymmetric because the hexyl chain differs from the methyl groups. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, while the hexyl chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring nitrogens are substituted, but the two carbonyl oxygens and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a rod-like diarylacetylene built from two benzene rings joined through a linear carbon-carbon triple bond. One ring carries a straight n-butyl chain at the para position, while the other bears a methoxy (ether) group, also para to the alkyne, giving an elongated, roughly centrosymmetric arrangement. The sp-hybridized alkyne linker enforces a rigid, linear geometry, though the butyl chain adds some conformational flexibility at its far end. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the oxygen of the methoxy group.

The molecule is a diaryl alkyne built from two benzene rings joined by a carbon-carbon triple bond. One ring carries a straight n-butyl chain at the para position, while the other carries an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) at the opposite para position, giving a symmetric, linear, rod-like scaffold. The rigid alkyne linker forces the two aromatic rings into a collinear arrangement, and the flexible alkyl tails extend from the ends. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. Attached at the 1-position of the naphthalene is a two-carbon side chain: a methylene group bonded to a nitrile (cyano) group, so the substituent is a flexible cyanomethyl unit. The rest of the ring system is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and asymmetric. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining N–H or O–H positions are absent.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing a single edge, with no heteroatoms in the ring system. A two-carbon chain bearing a primary amide group is attached at the 1-position of the naphthalene, so the substitution pattern is a single side chain on one ring. The amide carries a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and an NH2 group that can donate them, while the aromatic framework itself is planar and rigid. The methylene linker gives the side chain some rotational freedom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry apart from the local symmetry of the unsubstituted ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings sharing one edge, with the isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) attached at the 1-position, the carbon adjacent to the ring fusion. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the linear, cumulated N=C=S unit extends from it in a fixed, nearly straight geometry. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the functional group sits on only one ring at a position next to the fusion, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Its only functional group is the isothiocyanate, which has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur and nitrogen atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic framework is otherwise hydrocarbon in character.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, making it fully aromatic and planar. An acetoxy group, an ester formed from an acetyl unit bonded through an oxygen atom, is attached to one of the carbons on the first ring, adjacent to the ring fusion, at the alpha position. The ester carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since every hydrogen is carbon-bound. The fused aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the acetoxy group has a single rotatable bond connecting it to the ring, giving limited conformational flexibility. Overall, the molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituent sits on one ring only.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Attached at the 1-position of this ring system is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a chlorine atom, which is the only substituent on the molecule. The structure has no stereocenters and no rotatable bonds within the core, so its shape is essentially planar apart from the freely rotating C–C(=O) bond connecting the carbonyl. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with a planar, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to one of the carbons on the ring that is adjacent to the ring-fusion atom, placing it at a peri-like position on the naphthalene framework. The rest of the system is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is a single group on an otherwise bare aromatic skeleton. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond between the ring and the carboxyl group, so it is rigid and essentially flat. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene-type rings fused along a shared edge to form a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A hydroxymethyl group (a methylene carbon bearing an alcohol OH) is attached to one carbon of the ring system, placing it adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2–OH arm can rotate freely about its single bond. The primary alcohol provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site, and the aromatic rings contribute additional weak pi-electron acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, making it a flat, rigid aromatic framework. A boronic acid group, -B(OH)2, is attached at the 1-position, meaning it sits on a carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry aside from the planar aromatic core. The boron atom is trigonal and bears two hydroxyl groups, which together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptor oxygens. The fused aromatic rings contribute extended pi-electron conjugation, and the only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the single bond linking the boron to the ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, with the substituent attached at the 1-position. A CH2 linker connects the ring to a carbonyl carbon, which forms a hydrazide group: the carbonyl is bonded to an NH that carries a terminal NH2. The overall shape is largely planar and rigid across the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom at the CH2 and amide-type bonds. The hydrazide unit offers hydrogen-bond donor capability through its NH and NH2 groups and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms. The lack of additional substituents on the naphthalene rings gives the molecule no internal symmetry beyond what the fused ring framework itself provides.

This molecule is a small, acyclic push-pull alkene built around a central carbon-carbon double bond. One carbon of the double bond carries a methylamino group (an NH bonded to a methyl) and a methylthio group (an S-methyl linked by sulfur), while the other carbon bears a nitro group. Because there are no rings, the scaffold is entirely open-chain and fairly compact. The nitro group contributes two strongly polar oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The sulfur atom and the methyl groups add modest bulk and lipophilic character, and the molecule has no rotational symmetry. Its conjugated system gives it considerable planarity around the double bond, with the methyl groups and sulfur free to rotate.

The molecule is 1-(methylsulfonyl)-1H-benzotriazole, built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered triazole ring, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic scaffold. The three nitrogens of the triazole ring form a contiguous N-N-N unit, and the nitrogen at position 1 carries a methanesulfonyl group, which is a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens and a methyl group. The four benzo hydrogens are unsubstituted, so the benzene portion has no additional substitution. The molecule has no stereocenters and a near-planar arrangement with only limited flexibility around the sulfur-nitrogen bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the sulfonyl oxygens and the uncoordinated triazole nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single saturated five-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a pyrrolidine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The nitrogen atom carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine, and the ring is otherwise made up of sp3-hybridized carbons with no double bonds or aromatic character. Its only functional group is that tertiary amine, which lacks any N-H bond, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the lone pair on nitrogen allows it to act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is flexible and can adopt puckered conformations, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the ring's own geometry.

This molecule is 1-methylpyrrole, built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The ring is fully unsaturated, with the nitrogen bearing a methyl group, so there are no ring fusions and no additional functional groups beyond the N-alkyl substituent. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only flexible element is the small N-methyl group, which contributes no meaningful conformational variability. The nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system and therefore is not available as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and because the nitrogen carries a methyl rather than a hydrogen, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered heterocycle, a piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other (1,4-relationship). One nitrogen carries a methyl group as an N-substituent, while the other is a secondary amine bearing a hydrogen. The ring has no double bonds, no fused rings, and no additional functional groups, so the structure is simple and only the two nitrogens are substituted. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the molecule is achiral with an overall symmetry that is largely lost because of the single methyl substituent. The secondary nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen can act only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings that share one edge and together form a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A single methyl group is attached to one of the carbon atoms adjacent to the ring fusion, placing the substituent at the 1-position of the naphthalene core. Because the ring system is planar and rigid, the methyl group is the only substituent and the only source of conformational variation, and the molecule has an overall mirror plane through the long axis of the rings. The structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it lacks any heteroatoms. It is a purely hydrocarbon aromatic compound.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring.
