The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so it is N-methylated and contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability. A formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached to a carbon) sits at the 3-position of the five-membered ring, which is the carbon adjacent to the fused benzene ring. The fused bicyclic aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde oxygen serving as the only hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks symmetry, since the substituents are placed asymmetrically on the fused system.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. A methyl group sits on one of the ring nitrogens, which makes that nitrogen tertiary and removes its ability to donate a hydrogen bond, while the other ring nitrogen remains a basic acceptor. An aldehyde group (a formyl carbonyl) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the methylated nitrogen, giving a single planar, rigid scaffold with no rotatable bonds apart from the aldehyde. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl and formyl substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen and the unsubstituted ring nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, with two nitrogen atoms separated by a carbon, giving it a planar, rigid scaffold. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so it is N-substituted and contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability. A carboxylic acid group is attached to a carbon adjacent to that methylated nitrogen, forming the only substituent on the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl) and acceptors (its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the remaining unsubstituted ring nitrogen acts as an additional acceptor. Overall the structure is small, largely rigid, and has a single rotatable bond at the carboxyl attachment.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms separated by a carbon, with no fused second ring. One nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it an N-substituted imidazole, while the other nitrogen is an unsubstituted pyridine-like ring atom. Two nitrile groups, each a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, are attached directly to adjacent ring carbons, giving a 1,2-disubstitution pattern on the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with the nitrile groups extending linearly from the ring. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since its only N-H-capable site has been methylated, but the unsubstituted ring nitrogen and the two nitrile nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, which makes it an imidazole scaffold. The ring nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so the ring is N-substituted and has no N-H donor. The remaining nitrogen, at position 3, is a pyridine-type sp2 atom whose lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond. The molecule has no fused rings, no stereocenters, and no rotatable bonds beyond the N-methyl group, so it is small and essentially rigid. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is acceptor-type, arising from the unsubstituted ring nitrogen.

The molecule is a five-membered saturated heterocycle, a hydantoin-type ring core, containing two nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups arranged around the ring. Its skeleton is a single, non-fused ring with no additional rings attached. One ring nitrogen carries a methyl substituent, while the other nitrogen is an unsubstituted amide-type NH, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring contains two carbonyl (C=O) groups, one at each side of the nitrogen atoms, forming a cyclic urea-like and amide-like arrangement, and a methylene (CH2) group that sits between them. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The small, compact ring confers considerable rigidity to the core, with only the N-methyl group providing rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered carbocyclic ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems present. The ring contains one carbon-carbon double bond, placing it in a cyclopentene framework, and a methyl group is attached to one of the two sp2-hybridized carbons of that alkene. Because the ring is small and carries an endocyclic double bond, its conformational freedom is limited, though the saturated carbons can still pucker. The molecule is entirely hydrocarbon in nature, containing no heteroatoms or polar functional groups. As a result, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability and no notable molecular symmetry beyond the local planarity of the alkene unit.

The molecule is built on a five-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopentane scaffold with no fused or bridged rings. A single methyl group and a hydroxyl group are both attached to the same ring carbon, making that carbon a tertiary alcohol center that is the only substituted position on the ring. Because the substitution is confined to one carbon, the molecule has a local mirror plane through the ring and the C–OH and C–CH3 bonds, so it carries no stereocenter and is achiral. The saturated ring is fairly flexible and can pucker between envelope and half-chair conformations. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the rest of the framework is purely hydrocarbon.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane scaffold with no fused or bridged rings and no aromatic or unsaturated bonds. One ring carbon carries both a methyl group and a hydroxyl group, making it a tertiary alcohol, and this quaternary carbon is the only substituted position on the ring. Because the substitution is geminal and the ring can flip between chair conformers, the molecule has no stereocentre and is achiral, with the methyl and hydroxyl groups interchanging axial and equatorial positions. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the framework is nonpolar and conformationally flexible.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl substituent, so it is an N-alkylated nitrogen with no hydrogen-bond donor capacity, while the other ring nitrogen is a pyridine-like site that can accept a hydrogen bond. Attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens (position 2) is a formyl group, an aldehyde that adds a carbonyl oxygen acceptor. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the methyl and aldehyde groups providing limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its overall shape lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents sit on different parts of the scaffold.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a benzene ring sharing an edge with a five-membered imidazole ring, forming a benzimidazole scaffold. The nitrogen at position 1 of the five-membered ring carries a methyl group, so the substitution pattern is N-methylated, with the second nitrogen left unsubstituted and sp2-hybridized. The fused ring system is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with no rotatable bonds beyond the N-methyl group. The only hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since the methylated nitrogen has no N-H, while the unsubstituted imine-type nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, as the methyl group breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent ring system.

The molecule is built on an indazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a pyrazole ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a planar bicyclic aromatic system. A methyl group sits on one of the pyrazole nitrogens, which removes that nitrogen's N-H donor capability and fixes the tautomeric form. The benzene portion carries a single nitro group on a carbon that is meta to the ring-fusion position, so the substituent pattern is asymmetric. The fused aromatic core is rigid and essentially flat, with only the methyl and nitro groups providing any conformational freedom. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the remaining pyrazole nitrogen can also accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic indazole scaffold, in which a five-membered pyrazole-type ring is fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The nitrogen at the ring junction carries a methyl group, so the compound is an N-methylated indazole with no free N-H. A nitro group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing, is attached to the benzene portion of the fused system, placing it on the carbon meta to the fusion point on the far side of the ring. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, and the only rotatable bond is the single bond joining the nitro group to the ring. The molecule has no symmetry beyond its planar framework. Its hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, while the uncharged pyrazole nitrogen and the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a five-membered pyrazolone ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a methyl group on the nitrogen next to the carbonyl. The ring has a carbon-nitrogen double bond conjugated with the adjacent ring system, and a carbonyl group at the position adjacent to the N-methyl nitrogen. A trifluoromethyl group is attached to the carbon of the C=N bond, giving a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent on the ring. The scaffold is a single, unfused ring with no stereocenters, so its shape is essentially planar and rigid. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperazine-type ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 relationship, with one nitrogen bearing a methyl group and the other bearing a hydrogen. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the NH nitrogen, placing the aromatic substituent at a stereogenic carbon center. The ring is fully saturated and non-fused, so the aromatic and aliphatic portions are only connected through a single carbon-carbon bond. The secondary amine N-H can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary N-methyl nitrogen serves only as an acceptor. Because of the single stereocenter and the flexible saturated ring, the scaffold is conformationally mobile, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a five-membered heterocyclic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which places it in the pyrazolone family. The ring contains a carbon-nitrogen double bond, and one of the ring nitrogens carries a methyl substituent, while the adjacent ring carbon bears a carbonyl group, making the ring a lactam-type amide. A linear n-propyl chain is attached to the carbon next to the imine-type nitrogen, which sets up an asymmetric substitution pattern. The scaffold is a single, unfused ring with limited conformational flexibility, apart from rotation of the propyl chain. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all ring nitrogens are fully substituted or part of a double bond.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring is bonded edge-to-edge with a benzene ring, forming a quinolinone-type system. The nitrogen in the heterocycle carries a methyl group, so it is N-substituted and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor. A carbonyl group sits adjacent to that nitrogen, giving a lactam-like amide function that serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group, and it has no internal symmetry axis because the methyl and carbonyl break the symmetry of the fused rings.

The molecule is built on a five-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, a pyrrolidine ring. The nitrogen atom carries a methyl group, so it is a tertiary amide-type nitrogen rather than an amine with a free hydrogen. Adjacent to that nitrogen, one ring carbon is double-bonded to an oxygen, forming a lactam carbonyl, which makes the ring a cyclic amide. The ring is a single fused-free system with no additional substituents, so there are no stereocenters and the substitution pattern is simple. The ring is fairly rigid apart from its puckering, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a loose mirror plane through the nitrogen and carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted.

The molecule is a single six-membered heteroaromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a methyl group on that nitrogen and a carbonyl oxygen on the adjacent carbon, which makes it a pyridone-type scaffold with no fused rings. The nitrogen is N-substituted, so the ring cannot donate a hydrogen bond from that position, while the exocyclic carbon-oxygen double bond provides a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, with the carbonyl contributing to delocalized electron density across the nitrogen and the ring carbons, giving a rigid framework. The methyl group is the only substituent, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the overall molecule has a simple, near-planar shape with no stereocenters.

This molecule is an N-methylated indole bearing a phenyl substituent. The core is a bicyclic fused scaffold in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring is ortho-fused to a benzene ring, giving an aromatic indole framework. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a methyl group, so it has no N–H donor capability and contributes only a lone pair as a weak acceptor within the aromatic system. A phenyl ring is attached at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (position 2), creating an extended, largely planar aromatic system with a single rotatable biaryl bond. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors and offers essentially no conventional acceptor sites beyond the delocalized aromatic framework.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms. One of these ring nitrogens carries a methyl group, so the ring is N-substituted rather than bearing an N-H. Attached to the carbon adjacent to that substituted nitrogen is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl. The scaffold is small, planar, and essentially rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O-H and hydrogen-bond acceptors through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the unsubstituted pyrazole nitrogen can also act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms. One of these nitrogens carries a methyl group, so the ring is N-substituted rather than bearing a free N-H. The remaining carbon of the ring bears a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl attached to a hydroxyl, which makes the molecule's functional character acidic. Because the ring is fully aromatic and the substituents are attached directly, the structure is compact and rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the carboxyl group. The pyrazole nitrogen without the methyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered triazole ring is fused to a benzene ring, forming a benzotriazole scaffold. The triazole portion contains three adjacent nitrogen atoms, and one of them carries a methyl group, so the substitution is on a ring nitrogen rather than on the carbon framework. The fused rings are planar and fully aromatic, making the core rigid, with only the methyl group contributing any conformational freedom. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited symmetry, since the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the only nitrogen bearing a hydrogen is replaced by the methyl group.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings that share a common edge, giving a fully aromatic bicyclic system. A single methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one of the carbon atoms adjacent to a ring-fusion position, so the substitution is on the alpha position of the naphthalene core. The ring system is planar and rigid, and the methyl portion of the ether adds only minor conformational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the two rings onto each other because the substituent breaks the symmetry. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic compound built on a three-carbon backbone with no rings or fused ring systems. Its skeleton is a propane chain in which one terminal carbon bears a methoxy group, and a secondary carbon bears a hydroxyl group, giving an ether linkage and an alcohol function. The molecule has no aromatic character and no stereochemical symmetry, since the central carbon carries a methyl group, a hydroxyl, a methoxymethyl arm, and a hydrogen, making it chiral. Its conformational freedom is high because all bonds are single and rotatable, so it is flexible rather than rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is an acyclic, saturated alkyl halide consisting of a straight three-carbon chain with an iodine atom bonded to one terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds, so its scaffold is simply a linear propyl framework. The only functional group is the carbon-iodine bond at the end of the chain, with the remaining carbons carrying only hydrogen atoms. Because the chain is unbranched and has a single substituent, the molecule has no stereocenters and possesses a mirror plane through the carbon backbone, giving it effectively no chiral character. Its free rotation about the carbon-carbon single bonds makes it flexible, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor capability beyond the weakly polarizable iodine atom.

This molecule is a simple acyclic alkyl halide: a straight, unbranched chain of five carbon atoms with an iodine atom bonded to the terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bond. Because the chain is linear and has no branching or stereocenters, the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the mirror-like equivalence of its two ends, and it is conformationally flexible, able to adopt many rotamers around its single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N–H or O–H groups. Its only potential acceptor is the iodine atom, which is a weak, poorly polarized acceptor compared with oxygen or nitrogen.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl iodide: a linear, fully saturated eight-carbon backbone with no rings, no branching, and no double bonds. A single iodine atom sits at one terminal carbon, giving the molecule a simple, unsubstituted scaffold with no other functional groups. Its only substitution is that terminal halogen, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two ends differ. The carbon chain is highly flexible, with freely rotating single bonds allowing many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor site is the iodine atom, which is a weak one.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A single iodine atom is attached to one of the carbon positions adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, placing it at the alpha position of the naphthalene system. Because the fused aromatic framework is rigid and planar, the molecule has little conformational flexibility. The iodine substituent breaks the symmetry of the parent ring system, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror plane beyond the planar framework itself. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor is the weakly polarizable iodine atom, while the aromatic pi system offers a region of electron density.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl iodide: a linear, fully saturated six-carbon chain with no rings, no double bonds, and no branching. Its scaffold is entirely aliphatic, with the carbon chain running from a terminal methyl group to a terminal carbon bearing a single iodine atom. The only functional group is the carbon-iodine bond at one end, which makes the molecule polarizable at that position. The structure has no symmetry because the iodine sits at one terminus and the other end is an unfunctionalized methyl group. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the only heteroatom, iodine, is a weak halogen acceptor that lacks a lone pair suited to strong hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl iodide, built from a single unbranched saturated carbon backbone of sixteen carbons with an iodine atom attached at one terminal position. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bond at the end of the chain. The substitution pattern is strictly linear, and the molecule possesses no internal symmetry other than the approximate mirror relationship along its length, with the iodine marking one end. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond allowing many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor site is the iodine atom, which is a weak one.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl iodide: a linear, unbranched seven-carbon saturated chain with an iodine atom bonded to the terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bond. The chain is fully saturated and flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds, so it adopts many conformations. Because it is symmetric only in its carbon framework and lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only a weak acceptor character at the iodine atom.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched alkyl iodide: a straight chain of twelve saturated carbon atoms with an iodine atom bonded to one terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic or multiple bonds, so its scaffold is simply a linear saturated hydrocarbon backbone. The only functional group is the carbon-iodine bond at the chain end, which makes the molecule effectively symmetric about the chain axis apart from that terminal substitution. The long, freely rotating carbon chain gives the molecule substantial conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, since the iodine is a weak, poorly polarized acceptor and the alkyl framework carries no heteroatoms.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched alkyl iodide: a straight chain of ten carbon atoms with an iodine atom bonded to the terminal carbon. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system to consider. The only functional group is the carbon-iodine bond at one end, and the substitution pattern is simply monosubstitution at a primary carbon. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation around its many single bonds lets the chain adopt many conformations, and it has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the chain. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and because iodine is a weak acceptor and the chain is entirely hydrocarbon, it offers essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is a simple acyclic haloalkane: a straight, unbranched four-carbon chain (butyl group) bonded to a single iodine atom at one terminus. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bond. The skeleton is fully saturated, so every carbon carries only hydrogens apart from the chain connections. Because the chain is linear and carries no substituents, the molecule has a clear mirror-plane-like symmetry along its long axis and no stereocenters. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is weak: the iodine can act as a very poor acceptor, and there are no donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Two substituents are attached at positions opposite each other, making a para-disubstituted pattern. One substituent is a nitro group, which carries a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with formal charges and acts as a strong electron-withdrawing feature. The other substituent is an iodine atom, a heavy halogen bonded directly to the ring. The arrangement has a two-fold symmetry axis running through both substituents, and the rigid aromatic ring keeps the molecule largely planar with little conformational flexibility. The oxygen atoms of the nitro group can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring: a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one written as N-oxide with a formal positive charge on nitrogen and negative charge on one oxygen) and an iodine atom. These groups are placed meta to each other, with one ring carbon separating them on one side and two carbons on the other. The nitro group is planar and conjugated with the aromatic ring, while the iodine is a heavy halogen attached directly to an sp2 carbon. The scaffold is rigid and flat, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, and the molecule has a mirror plane through the ring that contains both substituents, giving it a degree of symmetry. The oxygens of the nitro group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Two nitro groups (–NO2, each with a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens and carrying a formal positive charge with one oxygen negative) are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, meta to each other. An iodine atom sits at position 5, directly between the two nitro groups, giving a symmetric 1,3-dinitro-5-iodo substitution pattern. The ring is fully rigid and planar, and the nitro groups lie roughly in the ring plane with minimal conformational freedom. The molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry passing through the iodine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. It has no hydrogen-bond donors; the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons: a nitro group (an nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged and one neutral in the usual representation) and an iodine atom. This ortho arrangement makes the molecule asymmetric, with the two groups breaking any mirror or rotational symmetry the ring would otherwise have. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the nitro group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an alkyl halide built on a short, unbranched-at-the-core carbon chain with no ring systems. Its skeleton is a four-carbon chain with a methyl-branched arrangement: a terminal isopropyl-type unit (two methyl groups on one carbon) attached to a carbon that bears an iodine atom. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no additional functional groups beyond the single carbon-iodine bond. The only substituent is the iodine on the terminal methylene carbon, and the two methyl groups on the adjacent carbon are identical, giving the molecule a local mirror-like symmetry about the carbon-carbon axis. The structure is small and highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor is the iodine atom, which is a weak one.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: an iodine atom and two nitro groups, each nitro group consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with formal charges. The two nitro groups sit on carbons adjacent to the iodine-bearing carbon and on the carbon meta to it, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern that makes the ring asymmetric. The nitro groups are strong electron-withdrawing acceptors, and the oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the nitro groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: four methyl groups and one iodine atom, giving a pentasubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Reading around the ring, the iodine sits flanked by two methyl groups, with one additional methyl on each neighboring position, so the substitution pattern is dense and highly crowded on one side. The molecule has no plane of symmetry that reflects it into itself across the full structure, since the methyl placements are uneven around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatom is the iodine, which offers at most weak halogen-bond acceptor character.

The molecule is a bicyclic ketone built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, making it an indanone scaffold. The saturated five-membered ring contains a carbonyl group adjacent to the aromatic ring, while two methylene groups link the carbonyl carbon to the fused benzene ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the only functional group present is the ketone, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at its oxygen and has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The fused system is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring and the bridging five-membered ring, with only modest flexibility in the saturated portion. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring system.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered saturated carbocycle. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, while the saturated ring carries a single hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, making it a secondary alcohol. The molecule has one stereocenter at that carbinol carbon, so it can exist as enantiomers, and it has no internal symmetry plane through the substituted position. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, with limited flexibility beyond small puckering of the five-membered ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the aromatic ring contributes a weak pi-system capable of pi-type interactions.

This molecule is a five-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms, forming an imidazolidine-type scaffold with a carbonyl group at each side of the ring, making it a cyclic bis-amide (a hydantoin-type core). The carbon between the two carbonyls is not present; instead, the carbon adjacent to one nitrogen carries two methyl groups, giving a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern that breaks any symmetry in the ring. The second ring nitrogen bears a hydroxymethyl substituent, a CH2OH group attached through a single bond. The ring is compact and rigid, with only the hydroxymethyl arm providing conformational flexibility. The amide N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an isoquinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine-type ring through a shared edge. The nitrogen sits in the six-membered heteroaromatic ring, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, so the ring carries a hydroxyl substituent at the position flanking the heteroatom. The fully aromatic, planar fused framework makes the molecule rigid, with no rotatable bonds and only a single substituent breaking its otherwise unbranched outline. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon adjacent to nitrogen allows the tautomeric lactam-type arrangement to be considered. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the overall planar shape, since the substitution is confined to one side of the heteroaromatic ring.

The molecule is built around a ketone that links a phenyl ring to a saturated six-membered carbocycle. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so it carries no additional groups and has a flat, aromatic character. The carbonyl carbon is directly bonded to the phenyl ring and to a ring carbon that also bears a hydroxyl group, making that carbon a tertiary alcohol center. The cyclohexane ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible, chair-like conformation, while the phenyl ring is rigid and planar. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a pyrazole ring, with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to one of the ring carbon atoms, which sits at the position two bonds away from the NH nitrogen, giving a 1H-pyrazole with a simple monosubstitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, while the carboxylic acid group adds a single rotatable bond, so the overall framework is largely rigid. The pyrazole N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the free ring nitrogen together with the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen of the acid provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three carbons and two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which is the pyrazole scaffold. It has no fused rings and no substituents beyond hydrogen, so its substitution pattern is unsubstituted and it possesses no stereocenters. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, making it rigid, and its symmetry is limited to a single mirror plane through the ring. One nitrogen carries an N–H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other, pyridine-type nitrogen has a lone pair that can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, giving an indene skeleton. The six-membered aromatic ring is fully conjugated, while the five-membered ring contains a single carbon-carbon double bond that is not part of the aromatic system, so the fused bicyclic framework is essentially planar and rigid. There are no heteroatoms and no classical functional groups, and the molecule carries no substituents beyond the ring fusion. Because it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, its structure offers no such interaction sites. Its symmetry is limited, as the fused ring system is only mirror-symmetric in its overall outline.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrazole-type ring, giving an indazole core. The two rings share a common edge, so the system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The five-membered ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-H group. This N-H unit acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other, sp2-hybridized nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no substituents on the benzene ring, so it shows no substitution pattern beyond the fused framework, and its overall shape is simple and largely symmetric about the plane of the fused system.

The molecule is a straight-chain six-carbon alkyne, with a terminal triple bond between the first two carbons and a saturated four-carbon alkyl tail. It has no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the carbon-carbon triple bond. The terminal alkyne carbon bears a hydrogen, giving the molecule a weakly acidic terminal C–H that can act as a very weak hydrogen-bond donor. The triple bond is linear and rigid, while the four saturated carbons at the far end give the chain conformational flexibility. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since the pi electrons of the triple bond are not a conventional acceptor.

The molecule is a simple acyclic primary amine built on a straight, unbranched six-carbon chain: hexane with an amino group on one terminal carbon. It has no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so its scaffold is entirely linear and flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the nitrogen sits at one end and the alkyl chain extends from the other. The nitrogen carries two hydrogens, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and its lone pair allows it to serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor as well. The overall structure is therefore a long, polar-headed alkyl chain with a single functional group at the terminus.

This molecule is a simple acyclic hydrocarbon built on a straight six-carbon chain, with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at one end, making it an unbranched alkene. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the single C=C unit. The only substitution pattern is the linear chain itself, and the molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the double bond sits at one terminus. Its chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it consists solely of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a straight-chain primary alcohol built on a simple, unbranched six-carbon backbone with no rings or fused systems. The terminal carbon bears a hydroxyl group, which is the sole functional group present. The carbon chain is fully saturated and flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. It lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the hydroxyl end and the terminal methyl end are chemically distinct. The hydroxyl oxygen-bearing hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygen lone pairs can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a simple straight-chain aliphatic thiol, with a six-carbon saturated alkyl backbone terminated at one end by a sulfhydryl group. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom-containing scaffold beyond the single sulfur. The sole functional group is the terminal –SH group, which sits at the end of the chain with no further substitution along the carbon skeleton. The molecule is flexible, since rotation about its many C–C single bonds gives it considerable conformational freedom, and it has no internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the chain. The thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur lone pairs give it only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkyne, consisting of a single unbranched carbon backbone with no rings or fused ring systems. The terminal triple bond sits at one end of the chain, and its terminal carbon-hydrogen bond gives the alkyne a weakly acidic, reactive handle. The remaining carbon atoms form a flexible saturated methylene chain with no substituents, branching, or stereocenters, so the overall skeleton is highly conformationally flexible. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the local linear geometry of the alkyne, no hydrogen-bond donor sites apart from the terminal alkyne C-H, which is a very weak donor, and no hydrogen-bond acceptor atoms because it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated-except-for-one-terminus hydrocarbon chain: a terminal vinyl group (CH2=CH-) attached to a long straight run of methylene units, giving a linear, open-chain scaffold with no rings and no ring fusion. The only functional group is the carbon-carbon double bond at the very end of the chain, so the substitution pattern is simply a single terminal alkene with no branching or heteroatoms. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond a loose, non-identical pattern, since one end is unsaturated and the other is a terminal methyl. It is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow the chain to adopt numerous conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, as it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an unbranched saturated aliphatic chain: a sixteen-carbon backbone with no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no substitution along the chain. The terminal carbon at one end carries a hydroxyl group, making it a primary alcohol, so the scaffold is essentially a linear alkyl chain capped by a single polar functional group. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the approximate mirror arrangement of the nonpolar tail. Its chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen let the molecule act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the structure is purely hydrophobic hydrocarbon.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol: a saturated, unbranched carbon backbone of sixteen carbons terminated at one end by a sulfhydryl group (–SH). There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents along the chain, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and symmetric about its long axis apart from the terminal thiol. The thiol group is the sole functional group; the sulfur atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond and as a weak acceptor through its lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar. The long methylene chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow it to adopt numerous conformations, and it lacks any conjugation or rigid structural elements.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkanesulfonyl chloride, with a sixteen-carbon saturated hydrocarbon tail attached to a sulfonyl group. The skeleton is entirely acyclic, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. The principal functional group is the sulfonyl chloride, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom. The alkyl chain is unbranched and unsubstituted, giving the molecule a single long, flexible axis with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the chain itself. Because the chain is saturated and highly rotatable, the molecule is conformationally flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an open-chain alkyne built on a straight, unbranched six-carbon skeleton, so it contains no rings and no ring fusion. Its single functional group is a terminal carbon-carbon triple bond at one end of the chain, with the remaining carbons carrying only hydrogen atoms and no substituents, which gives a simple, unsubstituted pattern. The molecule has no symmetry beyond a rough linear arrangement, and the chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The terminal alkyne C-H can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the molecule has no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since the pi-electron cloud of the triple bond is not a conventional acceptor.

This molecule is a simple acyclic primary amine built on a straight, unbranched seven-carbon alkyl chain. The scaffold is entirely saturated, with no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Its only functional group is a primary amine (–NH2) attached to the terminal carbon, so there is no substitution pattern beyond that single end-group. The chain has no internal symmetry apart from a mirror-like arrangement of its methylene units, and it is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its carbon–carbon bonds. The nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the alkyl chain contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a straight seven-carbon chain, with no rings and no heteroatoms present. Its only functional group is a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at one end of the chain, which makes that end a site of unsaturation and reactivity while the remainder is fully saturated. The molecule has no substituents branching off the backbone, so its substitution pattern is simply linear and it has no stereocenters. Its structure is highly flexible, since the single bonds along the chain can rotate freely, giving it many accessible conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, because it contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a single unbranched seven-carbon chain. The only functional group is a primary hydroxyl group located on the terminal carbon, which makes the molecule's substitution pattern simple and entirely linear. Because it contains no ring systems or stereocenters, the molecule has a constant, unsymmetrical shape along its length and is highly flexible, with many freely rotating carbon-carbon bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the alkyl chain contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is an open-chain alkyl thiol with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple linear seven-carbon chain. The only functional group is a sulfhydryl group, meaning a sulfur atom bonded to one hydrogen, located at the terminal carbon of the chain. There is no substitution pattern beyond this terminal placement, and the molecule has no symmetry because one end carries the sulfur while the other end is a plain methyl group. The saturated chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond, while the sulfur can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated primary alcohol: a linear, unbranched aliphatic skeleton of seventeen carbon atoms with no rings, no fused systems, and no substituents along the chain. The only functional group is a terminal hydroxyl group attached to one end of the chain, so the substitution pattern is entirely at that terminus. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial chain axis, and its long, freely rotating single bonds make it highly flexible. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the hydrocarbon tail contributes only nonpolar, van der Waals-type contacts.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing three contiguous nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen. This fused pairing of an aromatic six-membered ring with a planar triazole-type ring gives a fully conjugated, flat framework with no rotatable bonds, so it is rigid. The molecule has no substituents on the benzene ring beyond the fusion, and it lacks any stereocenters. Its only hydrogen-bond donor is the N–H on the five-membered ring, while the unprotonated nitrogen atoms of the triazole portion can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic 1,2,4-triazole ring, with no fused ring systems. The ring nitrogen at position 1 carries a methylene linker that connects to a carboxylic acid group, giving an N-substituted triazole with a two-atom side chain terminating in a carboxyl. Because the ring is aromatic and planar and the side chain has only one rotatable bond, the structure is fairly compact and rigid. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the unsubstituted ring nitrogens at positions 2 and 4 serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three nitrogen atoms and two carbon atoms, forming a 1,2,3-triazole ring. It has no fused rings and no substituents beyond the ring atoms, so its scaffold is the bare triazole core. One nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, which makes the ring a 1H-tautomer with a free N-H group. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving it a rigid, flat geometry with little conformational flexibility. The N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, which makes it a simple piperidine-type scaffold with no fused or additional rings. The nitrogen is acylated by a formyl group, so it forms an N-formyl amide in which the carbonyl carbon is bonded to both the ring nitrogen and a terminal hydrogen. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen carries no hydrogen. The five ring carbons are all methylene groups, and the amide linkage gives the ring limited conformational flexibility with some restricted rotation about the N–C(=O) bond. The structure has no stereocenters and only approximate local symmetry around the nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two substituents placed para to each other: a nitro group (an N attached to two oxygens, one drawn as a formal positive charge and the other as a negative charge, together forming a strongly electron-withdrawing group) and a fluorine atom. Because both substituents sit on opposite carbons, the ring has a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern, giving the molecule an approximate axis of symmetry through the two substituents. There are no fused rings, and the aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the nitro group can rotate only slightly out of the ring plane. The nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since the only hydrogens are aromatic C–H bonds.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused together through a shared edge to form a rigid, flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A single fluorine atom is attached to one of the carbons in the ring fusion-adjacent position (the alpha position), so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis beyond the overall planar shape. The fluorine is a weakly polar substituent, but the compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine itself can only act as a very weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. Because the framework is entirely sp2-hybridized and planar, the molecule is essentially conformationally rigid with no rotatable bonds.

This molecule is a simple benzene derivative: a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused rings, so its scaffold is just the benzene core. Two halogen substituents sit on the ring, a fluorine and an iodine, placed para to each other, which gives the molecule a highly symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern with a two-fold axis through the ring centre. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the only freedom of motion involves the small vibrations of the carbon-halogen bonds. Neither halogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the fluorine can act only as a very weak acceptor, so the molecule offers essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions relative to each other: a nitro group, which consists of a nitrogen atom bonded to two oxygen atoms with one formal positive and one formal negative charge, and a fluorine atom. The nitro group sits on one ring carbon and the fluorine on a carbon separated from it by one intervening carbon, placing the two groups in a meta arrangement. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, with the nitro group largely coplanar with the ring. The molecule has a mirror plane passing through the ring, giving it a limited degree of symmetry. The nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring carbons carry hydrogen or the two substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring, carrying two halogen substituents on adjacent positions. One fluorine atom and one iodine atom are attached to neighboring carbons, giving an ortho-disubstituted (1,2) pattern with no other ring or functional groups present. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule is a small, relatively compact scaffold with a low degree of conformational freedom. Because the two halogens differ, the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one of the ring itself. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor character comes from the weakly basic fluorine atom, with the iodine offering little acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Three substituents are attached to this ring: a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, with one formally charged), a fluorine atom, and an iodine atom. Their positions are meta to one another, so the nitro group sits at one carbon, with fluorine two carbons away on one side and iodine two carbons away on the other, creating a 1,3,5 arrangement. The ring is fully planar and rigid, and the substituents have few rotational degrees of freedom beyond the nitro group. The nitro group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine and iodine atoms can contribute weak halogen-based interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, and it contains no fused ring systems. Three ring positions carry substituents: two methyl groups and a nitro group, along with a fluorine atom, giving a fully substituted pattern of four ring substituents in total. The nitro group, with its charge-separated N-O bonds, is a strong electron-withdrawing feature and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine adds a weak acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since none of its substituents carries an N-H or O-H bond. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the methyl groups are the only freely rotating parts, so the overall structure shows little conformational flexibility and no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons: a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged, forming a planar, strongly electron-withdrawing unit) and a fluorine atom. This ortho-disubstituted pattern gives the molecule a lower symmetry than the para or meta isomers, with a single mirror plane passing through the two substituents. The ring is rigid and flat, while the nitro group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The oxygen atoms of the nitro group are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the fluorine can also weakly accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two halogen substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. One position carries a fluorine atom and the neighboring position carries an iodine atom, so the substitution pattern is 1,2 on a single six-membered aromatic core. The ring is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has only a single mirror plane through the two halogens, giving it limited symmetry. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the iodine contributes no meaningful acceptor capability. The compound contains no true flexible chains, so its conformational freedom is essentially nil.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: two nitro groups (each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one written as N+ with O- and drawn as a charge-separated form) and one fluorine atom. The nitro groups sit at positions that make them ortho and meta to one another relative to the fluorine, giving a 1-fluoro-2,5-dinitro pattern, so the ring is unsymmetrical. The ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no rotatable bonds apart from the nitro groups. The nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorine is a weak acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a fully aromatic polycyclic hydrocarbon built on a fused multi-ring scaffold, with no heteroatoms and no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its core is a compact, peri-fused system of several six-membered carbocyclic rings sharing edges and interior carbons, which makes the framework essentially planar and rigid. A single terminal alkyne group, a carbon-carbon triple bond bearing a hydrogen at one end, is attached to one of the outer aromatic carbons, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. Because the ring system is rigid and lacks rotatable bonds beyond the linear alkyne, the molecule has very little conformational flexibility, and its overall shape is flat with one linear protrusion.

The molecule is built on a cyclopentane ring, a saturated five-membered carbocycle with no fused or bridged rings. A single quaternary carbon on that ring bears two substituents: a hydroxyl group and a terminal ethynyl (alkyne) group, so the ring carbon is both a tertiary alcohol and an alkyne-bearing center. The remaining four ring carbons are plain methylene units, giving the molecule no further substitution or stereodefined centers beyond that one carbon. The ethynyl group is linear and rigid, while the cyclopentane ring offers modest conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the alkyne is only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its pi system.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane scaffold, a saturated six-membered carbon ring with no fused or additional rings. A single quaternary carbon on the ring carries two substituents: a hydroxyl group and a terminal ethynyl (acetylenic) group, so the substitution pattern is geminal and the ring carbon is a tertiary alcohol center. The molecule has no stereocenters, and the mirror plane through the substituents gives it effective local symmetry at the substituted carbon. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to interconvert between chair forms, while the linear alkyne unit is rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the terminal alkyne offers only a weak acidic C–H and no meaningful acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no fused or additional rings. The ring nitrogen carries an ethyl group, making it a tertiary amine with no N-H bond. The remaining five carbons are sp3-hybridized CH2 units, so the scaffold is fully saturated and aliphatic with no aromatic character, double bonds, or other functional groups. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the ethyl substituent can rotate freely. The molecule has no N-H or O-H donors, so its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor through the lone pair on the nitrogen.

This molecule is built on a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship, forming a piperazine-type ring. The ring nitrogen bearing the ethyl group is tertiary, while the other nitrogen is part of an amide, so it is a secondary lactam nitrogen with an N–H group. Adjacent to the amide carbonyl is a second carbonyl, giving a vicinal dicarbonyl unit (an α-keto amide) fused into the ring, which makes the scaffold a piperazine-2,3-dione. The N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is largely non-planar and conformationally flexible, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the ethyl substituent sits on only one nitrogen.

This molecule is a diarylalkyne, with two benzene rings joined through a linear carbon-carbon triple bond. Each ring is para-substituted: one carries a straight n-propyl chain and the other an ethyl group, both at the position opposite the alkyne linkage. The rigid, rod-like alkyne spacer enforces a nearly linear, extended geometry, and the overall skeleton is largely planar with only the terminal alkyl chains showing conformational flexibility. The structure contains no heteroatoms or hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its only functional unit is the alkyne. It possesses an approximate two-fold symmetry through the long molecular axis, with the two alkyl chains differing in length.

The molecule is built on a diarylalkyne scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a linear carbon-carbon triple bond. One ring carries an ethyl group and the other a methyl group, both positioned para to the alkyne linkage, giving a symmetric, elongated, rod-like arrangement. The two aromatic rings are unfused and the triple bond enforces rigid linearity along the long axis, leaving only the terminal alkyl groups with rotational freedom. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the molecule's only heteroatom-free features are the pi-electron-rich aromatic and alkyne systems, so it has no conventional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed para to one another, meaning they sit on opposite carbons of the ring: an ethyl group (a two-carbon saturated chain) on one side and an iodine atom on the other. The para arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry along the axis running through both substituents. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the ethyl chain adds a small amount of conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N-H or O-H groups, and it offers essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, because the iodine and the aromatic carbons do not function as meaningful acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, rod-like diarylalkyne in which two benzene rings are joined through a carbon-carbon triple bond. One ring carries a hexyl chain (six-carbon saturated alkyl group) at the para position, and the other carries an ethyl group, also para to the alkyne linkage. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted otherwise, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical at the ends. The alkyne unit enforces a rigid, straight geometry, while the two flexible alkyl tails add conformational freedom at the extremities. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so its only potential interactions are weak hydrogen-bond-free contacts via the aromatic and alkyne π-systems.

The molecule is a diarylalkyne, with two benzene rings joined through a linear carbon-carbon triple bond. One ring carries an ethyl group at the position para to the alkyne, while the other carries a methoxy group, also para to the alkyne, giving a symmetric-looking but electronically differentiated 1,4-disubstitution on each ring. There are no fused ring systems and no stereocenters, and the rigid, linear alkyne spacer keeps the two aromatic rings roughly coplanar and extended. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the oxygen of the methoxy ether and the weakly basic pi-system of the alkyne.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, a heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The nitrogen at position 1 carries an ethyl group, while a methyl group sits on the ring carbon adjacent to the other nitrogen, and a carboxylic acid group is attached to the carbon at the opposite side of the ring. This arrangement gives the ring an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic core is flanked by small, freely rotating alkyl and carboxyl substituents, making the overall framework largely planar with limited conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the unsubstituted ring nitrogen contributes an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

This molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. The indole nitrogen carries an ethyl group, which removes its N-H hydrogen-bond donor capability and leaves the molecule without any hydrogen-bond donors. A phenyl ring is attached at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen on the five-membered ring, extending the aromatic system outward. The overall framework is largely planar and rigid, with only the ethyl chain and the rotation of the phenyl ring providing conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry axis because the ethyl, phenyl, and fused benzo substituents sit in different positions.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated chain of carbon atoms terminated by a single hydroxyl group at one end, giving a primary alcohol. It has no rings, no fused ring systems, and no aromatic or unsaturated bonds, so its scaffold is simply a linear alkyl backbone. The only functional group is the terminal –OH, which sits at one end of the chain and leaves the other end as a plain methyl group. The molecule is linear and has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror-like arrangement along its length. Its flexibility is high because the saturated carbon-carbon single bonds allow free rotation along the chain. The hydroxyl oxygen and hydrogen together allow the molecule to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the chain offers no such capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkyne, consisting of a linear carbon skeleton with no rings, branches, or heteroatoms. The defining feature is a carbon-carbon triple bond at one end of the chain, where the terminal carbon carries a hydrogen, giving it a reactive terminal alkyne functional group. Apart from that end, the remaining carbons form a continuous run of saturated methylene units with no substitution, so the structure has no stereocenters and no meaningful molecular symmetry beyond the chain's linear geometry. The molecule is highly flexible because the single bonds along the chain can rotate freely, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched hydrocarbon chain of twelve carbons with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, so it is an alkene rather than a ring-based scaffold. There are no rings, ring fusions, or heteroatoms, and therefore no functional groups beyond the single terminal alkene. The chain is linear and carries no substituents, giving it no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry apart from the mirror-like linearity of the backbone. Its long, freely rotating single bonds make it highly flexible, with the rigid element limited to the planar sp2 terminus. Because it contains only carbon and hydrogen, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no rings, no branching, and no substitution beyond the terminal group. A single unbranched carbon chain of twelve carbons forms the entire scaffold, with the hydroxyl group bonded to one terminal carbon. Because the chain has no ring systems or double bonds, it is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations, and the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond the local rotational freedom of the chain. The sole polar feature is the hydroxyl group, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar hydrocarbon.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol: a linear, unbranched twelve-carbon saturated backbone terminated at one end by a sulfur atom bearing a single hydrogen, giving a thiol (sulfanyl) functional group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substitution beyond the terminal position, so the skeleton is entirely acyclic. The carbon chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about each single bond and no conformational constraints. The molecule has no internal symmetry apart from the idealized mirror-like arrangement of the alkyl chain itself. The thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond and a weak acceptor through the sulfur lone pairs, while the alkyl chain offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is an aliphatic sulfonyl chloride built on a straight, unbranched twelve-carbon chain with no rings or stereocenters. The alkyl tail is fully saturated and flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon bond, so the molecule adopts many conformations. At one terminus sits a sulfonyl group, where the sulfur is bonded to two double-bonded oxygen atoms and to a chlorine atom. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local tetrahedral geometry around sulfur. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor through the sulfonyl oxygens, since it carries no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic tertiary amine built on a straight three-carbon chain. A methyl group is attached to a central carbon that carries a hydroxyl group, and a CH2 links that carbon to a nitrogen bearing two N-methyl substituents. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The two functional groups are a secondary alcohol and a tertiary amine. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrogen lone pair serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor since it carries no hydrogen. The molecule is asymmetric because the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group is a stereocenter, and it is not specified here.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. One ring carbon bears a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, with one formally charged), and the carbon directly opposite it bears a difluoromethoxy group, an oxygen linked to a carbon that carries two fluorine atoms and one hydrogen. This places the two substituents in a para, 1,4-relationship across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the difluoromethoxy ether linkage offers some rotational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the two substituents. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, and the ether oxygen is a weaker acceptor, while the difluoromethyl C–H is a weak donor and the molecule has no strong donor groups.

The molecule is a short acyclic nitroalkene with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple open chain of three carbons. Two methyl groups sit on one nitrogen, which is bonded to a vinyl carbon, and the carbon-carbon double bond carries a trans (E) geometry that rigidly fixes the arrangement of the chain. The other end of the double bond bears a nitro group, a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group with formally charged nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Because the two methyl groups are identical and the molecule lies in a planar, extended conformation, it has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry. Its rigid, conjugated framework contributes little conformational flexibility, the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a straight-chain terminal alkyne, a linear hydrocarbon scaffold with no rings and no heteroatoms. A carbon-carbon triple bond sits at one end of the chain, where the terminal carbon carries a single hydrogen, giving the alkyne its characteristic reactivity at that position. The remaining nine carbons form an unbranched, saturated alkyl tail, so the structure is highly flexible with many freely rotating single bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, since the two ends differ. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, as the only functionality is the carbon-carbon triple bond itself.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched hydrocarbon chain built from ten carbon atoms, with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at one end (a 1-decene-type scaffold). It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond that single alkene unit. Because the skeleton is a straight chain with no substituents, the substitution pattern is simply linear and the molecule has no internal symmetry apart from the trivial mirror plane of the chain axis. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, and the terminal alkene is the only region with restricted rotation. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since it consists solely of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a single unbranched carbon chain of eleven carbons ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The chain is fully saturated, with no double bonds, aromatic rings, or other heteroatoms, and there is no substitution pattern beyond the one hydroxyl at the end. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry apart from a mirror-like plane along the chain, and it is highly flexible because the many single C–C bonds can rotate freely. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the oxygen lone pairs, while the rest of the chain is nonpolar.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl thiol with ten carbon atoms in an unbranched, fully saturated chain, terminated at one end by a sulfur atom bearing a single hydrogen, making it a primary thiol. There are no rings, ring fusions, or aromatic systems, and the only functional group is the sulfhydryl (–SH) group on the terminal carbon. The chain has no substituents or branching, so the substitution pattern is simply linear, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the idealized mirror-like extended conformation of the carbon backbone. The alkyl chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The sulfhydryl group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond and as a weak acceptor through the sulfur lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a simple saturated skeleton: a cyclopentane ring bearing a single substituent at one carbon. That substituent is a secondary alcohol carbon, which carries a bulky tert-butyl group, so the carbinol center is flanked by a quaternary carbon on one side and the ring on the other. There are no ring fusions, double bonds, or aromatic systems, and the only functional group is the hydroxyl. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond local rotation, and it is fairly flexible at the ring and the single bonds, though the tert-butyl group sterically constrains the carbinol. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

This molecule is an aliphatic sulfonyl chloride built on a straight, unbranched ten-carbon chain with no rings or aromatic systems. The terminal carbon of the chain is bonded to a sulfur atom that carries two double-bonded oxygen atoms and one chlorine atom, giving a tetrahedral sulfonyl group. The sulfonyl chloride is the sole functional group, and it sits at one end of the chain, so there is no meaningful substitution pattern along the alkyl backbone. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror-like arrangement around the sulfur center. The long saturated chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds. The oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a five-membered carbocyclic ring, specifically a cyclopentene, with one ring double bond. Attached directly to one of the ring's sp2 carbons is a carboxylic acid group, so the ring is conjugated with the carbonyl. The ring is unfused and carries no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The ring is partially rigid because of the endocyclic double bond, while the carboxyl group can rotate about its single bond. The carboxylic acid supplies one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl O–H) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is built from two rings joined by a single bond: a five-membered lactam (a pyrrolidin-2-one ring) and a saturated six-membered cyclohexane ring. The lactam contains a carbonyl group adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the amide carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen carries no hydrogen and therefore offers no hydrogen-bond donor site. The cyclohexane ring is fully saturated with no additional functional groups, giving the molecule a largely aliphatic character. The attachment through the nitrogen creates an N-substituted lactam with no symmetry element beyond local ring features, and the rings themselves limit conformational freedom, with the cyclohexane able to adopt chair-like arrangements.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring containing one carbon-carbon double bond, making it a cyclohexene scaffold. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to one of the sp2 carbons of that double bond, so the acid conjugates with the alkene. The ring is non-fused and carries no other substituents, giving a simple unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The ring is partly flexible through its saturated CH2 positions, while the conjugated alkene-acid unit is relatively planar and rigid.
