The carboxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and an acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

The molecule is built around a single six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexene, with one carbon-carbon double bond positioned inside the ring. Attached to one of the sp2 carbons of that double bond is a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group, so the acid sits one methylene unit away from the ring. The ring is unsubstituted apart from this side chain and contains no heteroatoms or fused rings, making the scaffold simple and monocyclic. The carboxylic acid group provides both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its two oxygen atoms. Overall the structure has no symmetry axis of note and retains some conformational flexibility from the saturated ring carbons and the rotatable side chain.

The molecule is built on a piperidine scaffold, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused or additional rings. The ring nitrogen carries a substituent consisting of a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group, so the nitrogen is tertiary and bears no hydrogen. The chain is flexible, and the piperidine ring can adopt a chair conformation, giving the overall structure moderate conformational freedom. The molecule has no stereocenters and no element of symmetry beyond the local ring symmetry, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the nitrile nitrogen and the tertiary amine nitrogen, although the amine nitrogen is sterically shielded by the ring.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring bearing two methyl groups, one at a carbon position and one at the other carbon position adjacent to the substituted nitrogen, giving a 3,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The ring nitrogen that is not substituted retains a lone pair and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Attached to the other ring nitrogen is an acyl group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a CH2 linker that terminates in a nitrile (cyano) group, which adds a carbonyl oxygen and a nitrile nitrogen as additional acceptor sites. The scaffold is fully planar in its aromatic core, while the acyl-cyanomethyl side chain provides modest rotational flexibility around the N–C(=O) and CH2–CN bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local pseudo-mirror relationship between the two methyl-substituted ring carbons.

The molecule is built on a three-membered cyclopropane ring, a highly strained carbocycle with no fused or additional rings. A single quaternary carbon on this ring carries two substituents: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a carboxylic acid group (a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl). The remaining two ring carbons are unsubstituted methylene units, so the substitution pattern is geminal on one carbon. The compact, rigid cyclopropane framework limits conformational flexibility, while the carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The nitrile nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane through the substituted carbon beyond a local mirror relating the two methylene carbons.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridazine ring, forming a phthalazine core. The six-membered diazine ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms and is fused to the benzo ring at a shared carbon-carbon bond, so the entire scaffold is flat and rigid. A single chlorine atom is attached to the carbon of the diazine ring that sits next to the ring-fusion carbon, giving a simple one-substituent pattern with no stereocenters. The molecule has no rotatable bonds and only a modest degree of symmetry, since the chlorine breaks the symmetry of the fused system. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered pyridazinone-type ring, giving a phthalazinone-like scaffold. The heterocyclic ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which bears a hydrogen and sits next to a carbonyl group, forming a cyclic amide-like lactam unit. A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon of the pyridazine ring that lies between the other nitrogen and the fused benzo portion, so the substitution pattern is one chloro group on the heteroring. The fused system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The lactam N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the unprotonated ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl halide: a nine-carbon saturated backbone with no rings, double bonds, or branching. The carbon framework is fully flexible, with free rotation about each single C–C bond, so it can adopt many conformations. A single chlorine atom sits at one terminal position, the sole functional group, which makes the molecule itself unsymmetrical in the sense that its two ends differ. The chlorine carries no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only a weak acceptor character, while the alkyl chain contributes no hydrogen-bonding sites at all.

The molecule is a naphthalene core, a bicyclic aromatic system made of two fused six-membered benzene-type rings sharing one edge. A single chlorine atom is attached to one of the fused-ring carbons adjacent to the ring junction, placing it at an alpha position on the same ring that carries the substituent. Because the parent scaffold is planar and fully aromatic, the structure is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The only functional feature is the carbon-chlorine bond, which is weakly polar and can accept a hydrogen bond only poorly, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. It lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the unsubstituted ring.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic compound built on a naphthalene-like scaffold in which one ring is a pyridine. The two rings share a fused edge, so the framework is flat and fully conjugated with no rotatable bonds, making it rigid. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the position flanking the nitrogen within the pyridine ring. The nitrogen lone pair lies in the plane of the ring, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure is asymmetric, since the chlorine and the nitrogen break any mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is a straight-chain alkyl halide, with a seven-carbon saturated backbone terminated by a single chlorine atom on one end, giving the formula C7 with one chloro substituent. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-chlorine bond. The chain is fully saturated and aliphatic, and the chlorine sits at the terminal (primary) position, so the substitution pattern is entirely linear with no branching and no symmetry elements beyond a simple conformational mirror. The molecule is highly flexible, since the sp3 carbon-carbon bonds allow free rotation along the chain. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small acyclic ester built on a two-carbon chain, with no rings and no aromatic system. One terminal carbon carries a methyl group and a chlorine atom on the same carbon, which is bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl carbon that also bears a second chlorine atom. Its functional groups are an alpha-chloroalkyl ether linkage and an acyl chloride, both centered on the single ester oxygen and carbonyl. The structure has no internal symmetry because the two chlorinated carbons sit in different chemical environments. The chain is flexible around its single bonds, though the planar carbonyl group restricts local geometry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a simple acyclic alkyl halide built on a straight, unbranched five-carbon chain, so it has no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic character. A single chlorine atom is attached to one terminal carbon of the chain, which places the halogen at the end of the skeleton and makes the arrangement inherently asymmetric. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. Its only polar feature is the carbon-chlorine bond, which can accept weak hydrogen bonds but cannot donate any, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on an anthraquinone-type scaffold: a central six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups at opposite positions (9 and 10), flanked by two fused benzene rings. The tricyclic core is fully fused and planar, which makes it rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the framework. A single chlorine atom sits on one of the outer benzene rings, adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, so the substitution pattern breaks the overall symmetry of the parent system. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an adamantane-type cage, a rigid, highly symmetric tricyclic framework of three fused cyclohexane-like rings sharing bridgehead carbons. A single chlorine atom is attached to one of the bridgehead carbons, which is the substitution site. The structure contains no double bonds, no heteroatoms other than that halogen, and no hydrogen-bond donors. Its saturated hydrocarbon cage gives it very little conformational flexibility, and the chlorine is its only polar feature, so it can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small heterocycle built around a five-membered ring containing one carbonyl group and two nitrogen atoms, specifically a pyrazolidinone-type scaffold with the carbonyl carbon adjacent to one ring nitrogen. The second ring nitrogen carries an exocyclic amide, a chloroacetyl group in which a carbonyl is bonded to a CH2 bearing a chlorine atom. The ring is saturated apart from its carbonyl, so it is non-aromatic and fairly rigid, while the chloroacetyl side chain adds a degree of conformational freedom. There is no internal symmetry, since the two carbonyl environments and the nitrogen substitution differ. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, as both nitrogens are fully substituted, and it offers two carbonyl oxygens as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with fully delocalized pi bonding. Two substituents sit on the ring in a para (1,4) relationship: a nitro group, in which a nitrogen bears two oxygens (one double-bonded, one charge-separated), and a chlorine atom. Because the ring is flat and fused to nothing else, the scaffold is rigid, and the only real rotational freedom lies in the nitro group about its bond to the ring. The substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold axis of symmetry through the two substituents, so the ring hydrogens above and below the axis are equivalent. The nitro oxygens are good hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two halogen substituents on opposite positions, making it a para-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a chlorine atom and the other is an iodine atom, attached at carbons separated by three bonds around the ring. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and it is planar and rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has high symmetry, with a C2 axis through the midpoints of the two substituent-bearing bonds and a mirror plane containing the substituent axis. It lacks hydrogen-bond donors entirely, and the halogens can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no ring fusion, bearing two halogen substituents. One fluorine atom and one chlorine atom are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 4, so they sit opposite each other in a para arrangement. The substitution pattern gives the molecule a centre of inversion and a two-fold rotational axis, making it highly symmetric. The scaffold is fully rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. Neither halogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the fluorine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold. Attached to that ring are three substituents: a nitro group (an electron-withdrawing N-oxide-type unit bearing two oxygen atoms), a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The nitro group sits on one ring carbon, the chlorine on a carbon adjacent to it, and the fluorine on a carbon that is meta to the nitro group, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, and the substituents add little conformational flexibility. The nitro group's oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a short, saturated, acyclic alkyl chloride built on a straight chain of carbons. Its backbone contains a branched isopentyl-type skeleton: a terminal isopropyl-like end with two methyl groups on one carbon, linked to a three-carbon chain that ends in a single chlorine atom on the terminal carbon. The structure contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no double or triple bonds, so it is entirely flexible, with free rotation about its single carbon-carbon bonds. The only heteroatom is the chlorine substituent, which is attached at the end of the chain rather than in the middle, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and only a weak, halogen-type acceptor at the chlorine, so its intermolecular interactions are dominated by van der Waals contacts.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent-to-meta positions: a nitro group (an N-bonded group with two oxygens, one formally charged, written as a strongly electron-withdrawing group) and a chlorine atom. Because the two substituents sit at positions separated by one carbon on the ring, the pattern is meta, a 1,3-relationship. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with the substituents lying in the ring plane. The molecule has a mirror plane through the ring, so it shows a degree of symmetry in its overall shape, though the two substituents are different. It has no hydrogen-bond donors. The oxygen atoms of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the chlorine atom contributes only weakly as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms each bearing a methyl group) are attached to the ring, and a chlorine atom sits on the ring as a halogen substituent. The three substituents occupy alternating positions around the ring, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern, so the two methoxy groups are equivalent and the molecule has a mirror plane through the chlorine and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups have some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms in the ring. It carries three halogen substituents: one chlorine and two bromines, placed at positions that make the substitution pattern 1,3,5 around the ring, so the three halogens sit at alternating meta positions. This arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a mirror plane passing through the chlorine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is rigid and planar, and the halogen atoms are attached directly to it without any flexible linkers. Because halogens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and have no hydrogen-bond donor capability, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only very weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two nitro groups, each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, are attached to adjacent carbons on the ring, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon para to one of them, giving a 1,2-dinitro-4-chloro substitution pattern. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the two nitro groups occupy different positions relative to the chlorine. The core is rigid and planar, while the nitro groups can rotate only slightly about their bonds to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups are acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, a nitro group and a chlorine atom, on neighboring carbons, which gives it an ortho substitution pattern. The nitro group is attached as a formally charged N-oxide-type unit, with one oxygen double-bonded and the other carrying a negative charge, making it a strong electron-withdrawing group that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms. The chlorine is a halogen substituent that also withdraws electron density and offers only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its overall symmetry is low because the two different substituents break the mirror symmetry of the ring.

This molecule is a small, acyclic alkyl halide built on a branched four-carbon skeleton. Its carbon framework is a butane chain with a methyl branch on the second carbon, giving an isobutyl-type arrangement in which the chlorine sits on a terminal methylene. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, and the only functional group is a primary carbon–chlorine bond. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local symmetry of the two terminal methyl groups, and its single-bond framework allows considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atom can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two halogen substituents on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. There are no fused rings, and the single six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully rigid, with no rotatable bonds. One chlorine atom and one iodine atom are attached to neighboring positions around the ring, and the remaining four ring positions carry hydrogen atoms. The arrangement has only a mirror-plane symmetry through the two substituents, with no stereocenters. Neither halogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and both can weakly accept hydrogen bonds through their lone pairs, so the molecule has no meaningful hydrogen-bonding capacity beyond that.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two halogen substituents on adjacent carbons, with one fluorine and one chlorine placed ortho to each other. The aromatic six-membered ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Neither halogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, and both carry weak acceptor character through their lone pairs. The substitution pattern lowers the overall symmetry to that of a C2v-type arrangement along the axis through the two substituted carbons. The scaffold is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two carbon-halogen bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two nitro groups and one chlorine atom. Reading around the ring, a chlorine sits between the two nitro groups on adjacent-to-each-other positions, with the second nitro group located para to the chlorine, giving a 1,2,4 substitution pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the nitro groups are rigid, conjugated, electron-withdrawing units that carry formal positive and negative charges. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, so its scaffold is simply a monocyclic arene. It carries three halogen substituents: fluorine atoms on two ring carbons and a chlorine atom on a third, arranged so the halogens occupy positions that are not all adjacent to one another. Because the ring is flat and fully conjugated, the molecule is rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core structure. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry that would make the substituted positions equivalent.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: a nitro group, two fluorine atoms, and one chlorine atom. The nitro group (an N-oxide-type NO2 unit) sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by fluorine-bearing carbons, while the chlorine occupies the position para to the nitro group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond an approximate mirror line through the nitro group and the chlorine. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the fluorines and chlorine can act as weak acceptors; the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents: two nitro groups and one bromine atom. Reading the SMILES, the nitro groups sit on adjacent-to-bromine positions, with one nitro group ortho to the bromine and the other nitro group meta to it on the opposite side, giving an asymmetric 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, though the nitro groups can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring. Each nitro group contributes two oxygen acceptors and no hydrogen-bond donors, and the molecule has no N-H or O-H groups, so its hydrogen-bond donor capacity is zero while its acceptor capacity is four oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Because the core is rigid and planar and no rotatable bonds connect substituents to a flexible chain, the structure is fully rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens provide only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three halogen substituents: two chlorine atoms and one bromine atom, placed at non-adjacent positions around the ring, with the bromine flanked by a chlorine on one side. The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying four halogen substituents. Two fluorine atoms sit on carbons that are meta to each other, one fluorine is ortho to a bromine, and the remaining positions are unsubstituted C–H. Its only functional groups are carbon–halogen bonds, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no classical acceptor sites beyond the weak lone-pair character of the halogens. The aromatic framework is planar and rigid, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, which gives the molecule no mirror plane or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. It carries four halogen substituents: three chlorines and one bromine, distributed around the ring so that the bromine sits adjacent to two chlorines. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds connecting substituents to the core. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O–H or N–H groups. Its only potential acceptors are the halogen atoms, which are weak and generally not considered significant hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, and it carries no fused ring systems. Five of the six ring positions bear methyl groups, and the remaining position carries a bromine atom, giving a densely and asymmetrically substituted arene. The methyl groups occupy adjacent and alternating positions around the ring, and the bromine sits between two methyl-bearing carbons, so the substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is the bromine, which can act as a very weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyrrole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. The nitrogen is acylated by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, which carries a bulky tert-butyl ester that adds steric bulk and removes the N–H hydrogen-bond donor capability of the ring. A formyl (aldehyde) group sits on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, providing a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is essentially planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl group is highly symmetric and rotationally flexible at its single bonds. Overall, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptor oxygen atoms.

This molecule is built on a piperazine scaffold, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One ring nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate group, which bears a tert-butyl ester on the other side of the carbonyl, so that nitrogen is non-basic and planar in character. The other ring nitrogen is a secondary amine with an unsubstituted N-H, making it a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, branched alkyl substituent that adds steric bulk but no additional heteroatoms. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the two nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a piperidine scaffold, a six-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring with no fusion or additional rings. At one ring carbon, positioned at the 3-position relative to the nitrogen, sits an ethyl ester group, while the ring nitrogen itself carries a tert-butoxycarbonyl carbamate protecting group. The two substituents are therefore on different atoms, giving a non-symmetric substitution pattern with the molecule lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the carbamate and ester linkages add some rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H positions are absent, but the two carbonyl oxygens of the ester and carbamate can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, with the ring nitrogen capped by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, which is a carbamate linked to a bulky tert-butyl ether. At the carbon opposite the nitrogen (the 4-position) sits a carboxylic acid group, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the ring. The ring is non-aromatic and chair-capable, giving moderate conformational flexibility, while the bulky tert-butyl group adds steric shielding around the carbamate. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, and the carbamate carbonyl and ether oxygen add further acceptor capability.

This molecule is an N-Boc-protected indoline. Its core is a bicyclic scaffold in which a five-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring (N1, with two CH2 groups) is fused to a benzene ring, giving a fused aromatic-aliphatic system with a planar benzo portion and a puckered five-membered ring. The nitrogen is acylated by a tert-butyl carbamate group, where a carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that carries a bulky tert-butyl substituent. The carbamate carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted. The tert-butyl group adds steric bulk and a three-fold local symmetry, but the overall molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that spans the whole structure. Rotation around the carbamate C–N bond is restricted, so the molecule is only moderately flexible.

The molecule is an N-acylated imidazole: a single five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, with the N1 nitrogen bearing a carbamate-type acyl group. That acyl group is a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that carries a tert-butyl group, which contributes a compact, bulky, nonpolar cap. The imidazole ring is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl ester linkage gives the molecule a small amount of rotational freedom around the C–O and N–C(=O) bonds. The tert-butyl group is highly symmetric, with three equivalent methyl groups around a central quaternary carbon, and the imidazole ring has no internal symmetry once substituted. The unsubstituted ring nitrogen (N3) can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring and alkyl positions lack acidic N–H or O–H hydrogens. The carbonyl oxygen can also serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an azetidine scaffold, a saturated four-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The ring nitrogen carries a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate bearing a bulky tert-butyl ester oxygen, which is an acyl-type substituent rather than a free amine. A carboxylic acid group is attached at the 3-position of the ring, giving a single substitution pattern with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The four-membered ring is strained and rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk and some conformational freedom at the carbamate linkage. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbamate carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indazole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a five-membered pyrazole-type ring is fused to a benzene ring. The nitrogen at position 1 of the fused ring system carries a tert-butyloxycarbonyl group, which is a carbamate attached through a carbonyl bonded to a bulky tert-butyl ether oxygen. A primary aromatic amine sits on the benzene ring, giving the molecule one substituent that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and another that can act as an acceptor. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds bulk but no real conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the amino group and the carbamate sit at different positions on the scaffold.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, with the nitrogen bearing a tert-butoxycarbonyl group: a carbamate linking the ring nitrogen to a bulky tert-butyl ester oxygen. Positioned four atoms around the ring from the nitrogen is a ketone carbonyl, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis through the nitrogen and the carbonyl carbon. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the bulky tert-butyl group adds steric demand near the carbamate. The ketone oxygen and the carbamate carbonyl oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and carbon positions are substituted.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, with the ring nitrogen bearing a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, which is a carbamate linking a bulky tert-butyl ether oxygen to a carbonyl attached to the nitrogen. At the 4-position of the ring, opposite the nitrogen, sits a hydroxymethyl substituent, a primary alcohol CH2OH arm. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a chair-like conformation, giving a fairly rigid core, while the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbamate carbonyl and ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the nitrogen is non-basic because it is acylated.

This molecule is a tert-butyl carbamate, with the nitrogen of a piperidine ring bearing the carbamate group. The core scaffold is a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle (piperidine) with no ring fusion or additional rings. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon directly opposite the nitrogen, at the 4-position, giving the ring a symmetric substitution pattern that places both ring-carbon arms in equivalent positions relative to the functional groups. The bulky tert-butyl group attached through an ester oxygen adds steric bulk but no additional rings or stereocenters. The piperidine ring is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-like forms, while the carbamate linkage adds partial planarity. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbamate carbonyl and oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a piperidine scaffold, a six-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring with no fused or additional ring systems. The ring nitrogen is capped by a tert-butyl carbamate group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to the nitrogen and to an oxygen that carries a tert-butyl unit with three methyl groups on a central quaternary carbon. A nitrile (cyano) group is attached to the carbon at the 4-position of the ring, directly opposite the nitrogen, which gives a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern. The ring adopts a chair-like conformation, so the overall framework is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the bulky tert-butyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbamate oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a five-membered saturated lactam-type ring, a pyrrolidin-3-one core, with its ring nitrogen bearing a tert-butoxycarbonyl group. The carbamate carbonyl sits on the nitrogen, and a tert-butyl ester-type oxygen links to a quaternary carbon carrying three methyl groups, giving a bulky, sterically shielded substituent. The ketone sits at the 3-position of the ring, opposite the nitrogen across the ring. Because the ring is fully saturated and contains no fused or aromatic systems, the scaffold is relatively flexible, with the bulky tert-butyl group limiting rotation around its attachment. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two carbonyl oxygens and the carbamate oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated ring containing one nitrogen atom, which makes it a piperidine-type scaffold. The nitrogen is acylated by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate bearing a bulky tert-butyl ester, and a ketone sits on the ring at the carbon two positions away from the nitrogen on the opposite side, so the ring carries a lactam-free, non-aromatic carbonyl. The ring is not fused to any other ring and has no aromatic character, and its chair-like conformation gives moderate rigidity, while the tert-butyl group contributes a compact, sterically demanding, nearly symmetric appendage. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogen and oxygen atoms are fully substituted, but the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated heterocycle, a piperazin-2-one ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions and a lactam carbonyl adjacent to one of them. The nitrogen across from the lactam is acylated by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate bearing a bulky, symmetric tert-butyl ester unit. The ring is non-aromatic and carries no fused rings, and its chair-like conformations give moderate flexibility, while the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two carbonyl oxygens along with the ring's tertiary carbamate nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall framework lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the two ring nitrogens are differently substituted.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no ring fusion and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. The nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that carries a tert-butyl group, giving a bulky, branched ester-like handle. A secondary hydroxyl group sits on a ring carbon two positions away from the nitrogen, which places it at the 3-position relative to the nitrogen. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the hydroxyl substitution breaks the ring's symmetry, and the piperidine ring can adopt chair-like conformations, so it is moderately flexible. The hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbamate carbonyl and its ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrogen itself offers no donor capability.

The molecule is built around a four-membered azetidine ring, a saturated nitrogen-containing heterocycle with one nitrogen and three carbons. The ring nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that connects to a tert-butyl group, giving the nitrogen a bulky, sterically shielded substituent. A hydroxyl group sits on the ring carbon at the 3-position, opposite the nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is 1,3 across the ring. The scaffold is non-fused, has no aromatic rings, and is fairly rigid because of the strained four-membered ring, though the carbamate and tert-butyl portions add conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbamate carbonyl and ether-type oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on an azetidine scaffold, a saturated four-membered nitrogen-containing ring with no fused rings. The ring nitrogen is capped by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate linked through a carbonyl to a bulky quaternary tert-butyl ether oxygen. A nitrile (cyano) group is attached to the ring carbon at the 3-position, giving a single substitution pattern with no internal symmetry, since the 3-carbon and the nitrogen-bearing positions are distinct. The strained small ring is conformationally restricted, while the bulky tert-butyl group adds steric bulk. The carbamate carbonyl oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a four-membered azetidine ring, a saturated nitrogen heterocycle with one carbonyl group on the ring carbon opposite the nitrogen, making it an azetidin-3-one. The ring nitrogen is acylated by a tert-butyloxycarbonyl group, a carbamate in which the carbonyl is bonded to a tert-butyl ester oxygen, so the bulky tert-butyl group is attached through oxygen. The ring is not fused to any other ring and carries no further substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the scaffold is essentially unbranched. The strained four-membered ring is rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds a compact, highly symmetric, three-fold-symmetric hydrocarbon region. The molecule has two carbonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but no hydrogen-bond donor sites since the nitrogen is fully substituted.

This molecule is an N-acylated lactam built on a six-membered piperidin-2-one ring, where the ring nitrogen carries a tert-butoxycarbonyl group. The carbamate linkage consists of a carbonyl bonded to the ring nitrogen and to a tert-butyl oxygen, giving a bulky, three-methyl-branched quaternary carbon at one end. The ring itself is saturated apart from the amide-type carbonyl adjacent to nitrogen, so the scaffold is a single unfused ring with no aromatic character. Because the nitrogen is fully substituted and the carbonyls are electron-withdrawing, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; its two carbonyl oxygens and the ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring adopts a flexible, non-planar conformation, while the bulky tert-butyl group imposes some local steric restriction.

The molecule is built on a pyrrole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The nitrogen is acylated with a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate in which a bulky tert-butyl ester is attached through an oxygen to the carbonyl carbon bonded to nitrogen. At the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, the ring carries a dimethylsilanol substituent, a silicon atom bearing two methyl groups and a hydroxyl group. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2-disubstituted, with no symmetry across the molecule because the two substituents differ. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl and silyl groups add some conformational freedom about their single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbamate carbonyl and ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring bearing a ketone at the 4-position, so it is a 4-piperidone scaffold. The ring nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate group, which is itself esterified to a benzyl group, so the N-substituent is a benzyloxycarbonyl unit carrying a single unfused phenyl ring. The ring is not aromatic and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the carbamate and ketone carbonyls add planar, rigid segments. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring, with the phenyl ring freely rotating. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two carbonyl oxygens and the carbamate ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a flexible ether linkage: a 4-bromophenyl ring is connected through an oxygen atom to a CH2 group that bridges to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving a benzyl aryl ether scaffold. The bromine sits para to the ether oxygen on the first ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,4-disubstituted and that ring retains a two-fold axis of symmetry through the Br and O positions. Neither ring is fused to another, and there are no additional stereocenters. The CH2 and ether oxygen allow considerable rotational flexibility between the two aromatic systems. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from two aromatic benzene rings joined through an ether linkage. One ring is a para-disubstituted benzene bearing an iodine atom on one carbon and an oxygen atom on the carbon directly opposite, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the ring. The oxygen connects to a methylene group (–CH2–) that is attached to the second benzene ring, which is unsubstituted and carries no additional functional groups. The aryl ether oxygen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central CH2 link gives the scaffold some conformational flexibility, whereas the two aromatic rings themselves are planar and rigid.

The molecule is an aryl benzyl ether built from two separate benzene rings joined through a single oxygen and a methylene linker. One ring carries an iodine atom at a position meta to the ether oxygen, giving a 1,3-disubstituted (meta) pattern on that ring, while the other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached to the CH2 unit. There are no fused ring systems; the two aromatic rings are independent and connected by a flexible C–O–C–C linkage that allows rotation about several single bonds. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of each ring, since the iodine breaks the symmetry of the substituted ring. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing a benzyl-type linker: a methylene group connects the phenyl ring to one nitrogen of an imidazole ring. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle with two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, and it is attached through its N-1 position, so the second nitrogen remains a free, unsubstituted ring nitrogen. There is no ring fusion; the two aromatic rings are joined only by a flexible sp3 CH2 bridge, which gives the structure moderate conformational freedom around that linker. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so there is no substitution pattern to describe. The imidazole's pyridine-like nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a barbiturate-type pyrimidine-2,4,6-trione ring: a six-membered heterocycle containing two NH groups flanked by three carbonyl carbons, with the C5 position bearing a phenyl substituent and one ring nitrogen (N1) carrying a benzyl group. The benzyl and phenyl groups are both unfused, pendant aromatic rings attached through single bonds, so the core ring is fused to nothing. The molecule has no stereocenter beyond C5, which is a tertiary carbon, and it lacks any symmetry because the two ring nitrogens carry different substituents. The imide-like ring confers rigidity, while the two benzyl and phenyl arms add conformational flexibility. The two NH groups serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the three carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion or additional rings. A hydroxyl group sits on one carbon of the ring, positioned four atoms away from the nitrogen, so the ring carries a single secondary alcohol substituent. The ring nitrogen is tertiary, bearing a benzyl group, which is a phenyl ring attached through a methylene linker. The molecule has no stereocenters specified and only limited symmetry, and the saturated ring with its flexible linker gives moderate conformational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen and hydroxyl hydrogen act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary amine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated piperidine ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no ring fusion and no fused or additional ring systems. At the carbon opposite the nitrogen (the 4-position) sits both a hydroxyl group and a nitrile group, giving a geminal substitution pattern on a single quaternary carbon. The ring nitrogen carries a benzyl substituent, meaning a phenyl ring attached through a single CH2 linker. The piperidine core is conformationally flexible, though the bulky benzyl group and the quaternary center add some steric constraint. Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the hydroxyl group can act as both a donor and an acceptor, the tertiary amine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as acceptors, and there is no further donor site.

The molecule is built on a piperazine core, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One nitrogen is acylated by a carbamate group, in which a carbonyl is bonded to an oxygen that carries a tert-butyl group, giving a bulky, branched alkyl ester. The other nitrogen bears a benzyl substituent, a phenyl ring attached through a single methylene linker. The two nitrogen substituents sit on opposite sides of the ring, so the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the piperazine. The piperazine ring is conformationally flexible, while the carbamate linkage is partly rigid because of its planar character. The carbamate carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the tertiary amine nitrogens and the ether-type oxygen add further acceptor sites, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrazole-type ring, giving an indazole core. The five-membered ring contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, and the nitrogen bearing the benzyl group sits at the N1 position, where a phenylmethyl substituent is attached. The carbon at position 3 carries a hydroxyl group, which can exist in tautomeric equilibrium with a ring carbonyl form. The fused framework is planar and rigid, while the benzyl arm adds a degree of rotational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is modest: the hydroxyl group can act as a donor and an acceptor, and the ring nitrogen at position 2 serves as an acceptor.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring attached through a single methylene linker to a nitrogen atom within a fully saturated 12-membered macrocycle containing four nitrogen atoms and eight carbon atoms arranged alternately in a repeating pattern. This macrocyclic polyamine scaffold is flexible, with rotatable bonds throughout the ring, while the aromatic phenyl group remains planar and rigid. The four ring nitrogens are secondary or tertiary amines, one of which carries the benzyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any meaningful rotational symmetry. Each secondary amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary benzylated nitrogen functions only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the structure a strong capacity for intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic 1,2,3-triazole ring, which contains three adjacent nitrogen atoms. The nitrogen at position 1 carries a benzyl group, a CH2 linker attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the benzene ring is pendant rather than fused. Two carboxylic acid groups sit on the triazole carbons flanking the N-substituted nitrogen, giving a 1,2-dicarboxylic acid arrangement on the heteroaromatic core. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid across the triazole and its direct substituents, while the benzyl linker adds some rotational flexibility. Each carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the C=O), and the triazole nitrogens provide additional acceptor sites.

The molecule is an N-benzoyl piperidine: a benzene ring bearing a carbonyl group attached to the nitrogen of a six-membered saturated piperidine ring. The amide linkage joins the planar aromatic ring to the flexible, chair-capable piperidine ring, with no fused ring systems. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the molecule has no substitution pattern on the aryl ring, and the phenyl group rotates relative to the amide plane. The tertiary amide carbonyl is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen carries no hydrogen.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone in which a benzoyl group is attached to the 1-position of a naphthalene ring system. The central carbonyl carbon bridges a phenyl ring and a naphthyl ring, giving a bicyclic-plus-monocyclic aromatic scaffold with three fused or pendant benzene-type rings. The naphthalene unit is a fused bicyclic system, and the carbonyl is attached at an alpha position on the second ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The two aryl rings are conjugated through the ketone and can rotate about the single bonds, giving moderate rigidity overall. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a six-membered piperidin-4-one ring, which contains a nitrogen atom and a ketone carbonyl located para to it. The nitrogen is acylated by a benzoyl group, meaning a benzene ring bearing a carbonyl attached directly to the nitrogen, so the amide-type nitrogen and the aromatic ring are connected through a single carbonyl linker. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, carrying no additional groups beyond that single attachment, and the piperidinone ring is not fused to any other ring system. Because the amide bond has partial double-bond character, the nitrogen is largely planar and the overall shape is moderately rigid, though the saturated ring can still adopt different conformations. The molecule has two carbonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while it has no hydrogen-bond donors since all ring and amide nitrogens are fully substituted.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. One nitrogen is bonded to a benzhydryl-type carbon, which carries two separate, unsubstituted phenyl rings, so the overall scaffold is a diphenylmethyl group attached to the piperazine. The second piperazine nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing an N–H, giving it hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the tertiary nitrogen acts as an acceptor. The two phenyl rings lack further substituents and are arranged around a tetrahedral central carbon, so the molecule has no fused ring systems and only a modest degree of symmetry. The piperazine ring can adopt flexible chair conformations, while the diaryl carbon contributes some conformational freedom about its single bonds.

This molecule is a fully saturated 18-membered macrocycle built from repeating ethylene-oxy units, with alternating ether oxygens and two-carbon bridges, closed by a single tertiary amine nitrogen. The ring contains six ether oxygens and one secondary-to-tertiary amine nitrogen, the nitrogen being the only ring atom bearing a hydrogen-bond donor site, while the six oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. There are no fused rings, aromatic groups, or pendant substituents, so the substitution pattern is uniform around the ring. The macrocycle has approximate pseudo-symmetry, with the heteroatoms distributed evenly, and its flexible ethylene linkages allow considerable conformational freedom. Overall, the structure is a simple, unbranched, polyether-amine crown-type ring.

The molecule is a polycyclic aromatic amine built on a fused four-ring carbon framework, with a primary amino group attached to one of the peripheral carbons. The ring system is fully fused and planar, consisting of interlocking six-membered rings that share edges and central atoms, giving a compact, rigid, and flat scaffold. The amino group sits on a terminal ring position and breaks the otherwise symmetric carbon skeleton, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitrogen of the amine can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the extensive aromatic surface offers no further polar donor or acceptor sites. Overall the structure is highly rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built on a tetralin-like bicyclic scaffold in which a saturated five-membered... let me be precise: the ring system consists of a benzene ring fused to a saturated cyclopentane ring, forming an indane skeleton. The aromatic six-membered ring is fused to a five-membered carbocycle, and an amino group is attached to the sp3 carbon adjacent to the fusion point, so the nitrogen sits at a benzylic position. The only functional group is this primary amine, which has two hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and a lone pair that can act as an acceptor. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the stereocenter bearing the amine breaks it. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the amine provides the only significant conformational freedom.

The molecule is an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold: two outer benzene rings fused to a central six-membered ring that contains two carbonyl groups at the 9 and 10 positions, giving a planar, rigid, conjugated framework. One of the outer rings carries a primary amino group, placed on a carbon adjacent to a ring-fusion position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks the mirror symmetry of the unsubstituted parent. The two ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site through its lone pair. Because the fused ring system is essentially fixed, the molecule is conformationally rigid, with only the amino group capable of limited rotation about its C–N bond.

The molecule is built on an anthraquinone scaffold, a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central para-quinone ring bearing two ketone (C=O) groups. One outer ring carries a primary amino (NH2) group adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, while the other outer ring carries a chlorine atom positioned next to the same peri region, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, and the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an anthraquinone-type tricyclic scaffold, with two outer benzene rings fused to a central six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups at positions across from each other. One of the outer rings bears an amino group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent-to-fusion positions, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern on that ring. The other outer ring is unsubstituted. The fused system is planar and rigid, with the carbonyl oxygens and the hydroxyl and amino groups available to act as hydrogen-bond acceptors and donors. The substitution pattern makes the molecule asymmetric, with no mirror plane relating the two outer rings.

This molecule is an anthraquinone scaffold, consisting of three fused six-membered rings in which the central ring bears two carbonyl groups at opposite positions. One outer ring carries an amino group adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon, along with two bromine substituents at positions meta to each other on that same ring, giving it an asymmetric substitution pattern. The unsubstituted outer benzene ring is flat and contributes to a largely planar, rigid aromatic framework with little conformational flexibility. The two ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the primary amine provides two N–H donor sites and an additional acceptor lone pair.

The molecule is built on an adamantane-type cage, a rigid, three-dimensional arrangement of fused cyclohexane rings that share carbon atoms in a diamond-like framework. A single hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to one of the bridgehead carbons of the cage, so the molecule is a primary alcohol. The cage itself is saturated and contains no double bonds or aromatic rings, which makes the scaffold highly rigid with little conformational flexibility. The substitution is at only one position, so the overall shape carries no mirror-image or rotational symmetry beyond the cage's own high internal symmetry. The hydroxyl group can both donate one hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds through the oxygen lone pairs, while the hydrocarbon cage contributes only nonpolar surface.

The molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, highly symmetric tricyclic framework of fused cyclohexane rings. A two-carbon hydroxyethyl chain (–CH2CH2OH) is attached to one of the bridgehead carbons, so the substitution pattern is a single substituent on the cage. The terminal primary alcohol provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the structure is purely saturated hydrocarbon. The cage itself is conformationally locked, with little flexibility apart from rotation of the side chain.

The molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, diamond-like tricyclic hydrocarbon framework made of three fused cyclohexane rings sharing a central core. Attached to one bridgehead carbon of this cage is a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group, so the cage carries a single -CH2-COOH substituent. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its two oxygen atoms. The cage itself is saturated, highly symmetrical, and conformationally locked, while the flexible acetic acid side chain is the only region with notable rotational freedom.

Parsing the SMILES: an acetyl group (CH3-C(=O)-) is attached to a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon core. The core contains four fused six-membered rings arranged in a compact, pyrene-like pattern. Because the rings are fully aromatic with no sp3 atoms in the scaffold, the framework is planar and rigid, and the single acetyl substituent breaks any mirror symmetry the bare core would have. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The single rotatable bond joins the acetyl group to the ring, giving limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered piperidine ring, with no fused or additional rings. The ring nitrogen carries an acetyl group, making it an amide (N-acylated) rather than a basic amine. At the carbon opposite the nitrogen (the 4-position) sits a carboxylic acid group, giving a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern across the ring. The piperidine ring is non-planar and conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair forms, while the amide bond adds some rigidity around the nitrogen. The carboxylic acid OH acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygens of both the amide and the acid serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a piperidine scaffold, a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen atom, so it is non-aromatic and conformationally flexible. The ring nitrogen is acylated by an acetyl group, forming a tertiary amide whose carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen itself contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability. At the carbon opposite the nitrogen (the 4-position) sits an acyl chloride, a highly reactive carbonyl bearing a chlorine atom, which is also a hydrogen-bond acceptor only. The substitution pattern is 1,4 across the ring, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors at all. Overall, the structure lacks any internal symmetry beyond the ring's approximate mirror arrangement, given the differing N-acyl and C-acyl groups.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite one another across the ring. One of these nitrogens carries an acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group, forming a tertiary amide, while the other nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing a hydrogen atom. There are no fused or additional ring systems, and the ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The substitution pattern is 1,4 across the ring, giving the molecule an approximate mirror plane through the two nitrogens. The amide carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the secondary amine nitrogen can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system made of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, which makes it planar and rigid. An acetyl group, a ketone bearing a methyl substituent, is attached to one of the carbon atoms adjacent to the ring fusion, at the position that is alpha to the bridgehead. The aromatic framework contains no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is a single monosubstitution on the fused ring system. Because the acetyl group sits off-axis on an otherwise symmetric skeleton, the molecule lacks any overall rotational symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring plane. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is N-acetylisatin, built on an isatin (indoline-2,3-dione) scaffold. A benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, and that five-membered ring carries an adjacent pair of ketone carbonyls at the 2- and 3-positions. The ring nitrogen is acylated by an acetyl group, which adds a second amide-type carbonyl to the molecule. The benzo-fused bicyclic core is essentially planar and rigid, with the acetyl group the only substituent off the core. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the plane of the fused rings. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, but its three carbonyl oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, a planar heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at non-adjacent positions. One of these ring nitrogens carries an acetyl group, a carbonyl attached to a methyl group, so the nitrogen is acylated and the ring bears no free N-H. The second ring nitrogen remains unsubstituted and possesses a lone pair that is available to accept a hydrogen bond. The carbonyl oxygen of the acetyl group provides an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the ring is aromatic and the acyl linkage is short, the structure is compact and largely rigid, with only the terminal methyl group offering limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on an indoline scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring, with the nitrogen acylated by an acetyl group, so it is an N-acetylindoline. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar in its aromatic portion, while the saturated two-carbon bridge of the five-membered ring adds limited flexibility. A nitro group sits on the benzene ring, meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen's neighboring CH2 and para to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, which breaks any symmetry in the molecule. The amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an N-acetylated indoline, built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, which gives a bicyclic scaffold with the two rings sharing an aromatic carbon-carbon bond. The nitrogen of the saturated ring carries an acetyl group, forming a tertiary amide, so the nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl. A single bromine atom sits on the benzene ring, in a position that is meta to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen and para to the other side of the fused system, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, while the acetyl group adds limited rotational freedom. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the amide carbonyl oxygen and no hydrogen-bond donors, since the amide nitrogen has no attached hydrogen.

The molecule is built on an indoline (2,3-dihydroindole) scaffold, in which a five-membered saturated nitrogen-containing ring is fused to a benzene ring. The indoline nitrogen is acylated by an acetyl group, giving a tertiary amide whose carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitrogen itself donates no hydrogen bond. The benzene ring carries a bromine atom and a nitro group, which sit meta to each other and are placed so that the nitro group lies adjacent to the ring fusion carbon bearing the nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid, whereas the saturated two-carbon bridge and the acetyl group retain some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and lacks any element of symmetry.

The molecule is built on a piperazine core, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One nitrogen is acylated, bearing an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl), so it forms an amide. The other nitrogen is bonded directly to a para-substituted phenyl ring, which carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon opposite the point of attachment. The piperazine ring is conformationally flexible yet largely rigid overall, and the aromatic ring is planar. The molecule has an approximate mirror-like arrangement through the two nitrogens, with no stereocenters. The hydroxyl group and the amide carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic OH can also act as a hydrogen-bond donor.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, linear chain with no rings, so it has no fused or bridged ring system. Its backbone is a short sequence of atoms that begins with an acetyl group, bonded to a hydrazine-type N–N unit, which in turn connects to a thiourea-like carbon bearing a terminal primary amine and a double-bonded sulfur. The acetyl carbonyl oxygen, the two nitrogen atoms in the hydrazide linkage, and the terminal NH2 group together provide several hydrogen-bond donor sites (the amide NH and the amine NH2) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl oxygen and the thiocarbonyl sulfur). The chain has rotatable single bonds, giving it considerable conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because its two ends carry chemically distinct groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings that share one edge and form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic system. Attached to one of the fused-ring positions adjacent to the ring junction is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, which contributes a hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygen. Directly beside it on the same ring sits a hydroxyl group, whose oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The two substituents are ortho to each other, so they are positioned to engage in intramolecular hydrogen bonding. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the planar framework because the two substituents occupy one ring only, and its rigidity comes from the fused aromatic core, with only the acetyl group offering limited rotational freedom.

This molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, highly symmetric tricyclic hydrocarbon scaffold of three fused cyclohexane rings. A single acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, CH3C(=O)NH-) is attached at one bridgehead carbon of the cage. The amide nitrogen carries one hydrogen bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen bond acceptor. Because the substituent sits at a bridgehead position, the rest of the framework is saturated, strain-free, and carries no further substitution, giving the molecule a high degree of three-dimensional symmetry around the attachment point. The overall structure is rigid, with the cage locking the carbon framework in place and only the acetamide side chain offering limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated ketone with no rings, aromatic systems, or heteroatoms beyond the single carbonyl oxygen. Its scaffold is a long, unbranched hydrocarbon chain of straight-chain alkyl groups, with a carbonyl (C=O) group at the central carbon, which lies roughly midway along the chain and flanks two identical alkyl arms of seventeen carbons each. The overall arrangement is therefore mirror-symmetric about the carbonyl carbon. Because all carbon-carbon bonds are single and freely rotatable, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyether: a single 18-membered ring made of repeating units of two carbons and one oxygen, with six ether oxygens and twelve methylene carbons alternating around the loop. It contains no fused or bridged rings, no aromatic rings, and no other functional groups beyond the ether linkages. The ring is highly flexible, with the methylene segments free to rotate, though the oxygens can organize into a cavity that binds cations. The six oxygens are all hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The symmetric repeating pattern gives the ring a high degree of rotational symmetry.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, so its scaffold is simply a long saturated carbon backbone. At one end sits a carboxylic acid group, C(=O)OH, and at the other end a primary alcohol, CH2OH, which together make it a bifunctional, linear omega-hydroxy acid. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, and it has no symmetry because the two terminal groups differ. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the two ends: the carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the terminal hydroxyl can likewise donate and accept, with the chain itself contributing only nonpolar hydrocarbon character.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, so it has no fused or substituted ring scaffold. At one end sits a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl carbon bearing both a double-bonded oxygen and a hydroxyl, and at the other end a primary alcohol, so the two terminal functional groups are placed on opposite ends of a long methylene backbone. Because the chain is composed almost entirely of freely rotating carbon-carbon single bonds, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Its symmetry is low, since the two end groups differ in type, though the central chain is nearly uniform. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, while the terminal alcohol contributes one donor and one acceptor, giving the molecule two hydrogen-bond donors and three acceptors overall.

The molecule is a long, unbranched aliphatic ketone: two straight saturated alkyl chains of thirteen carbons each flank a single carbonyl carbon, giving a symmetric, C2-like arrangement about the C=O group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms other than the one oxygen of the carbonyl, so the scaffold is purely a linear hydrocarbon backbone with one functional group. The carbonyl sits at the central position of the chain, which is the only substitution point, and the molecule is highly flexible because the all-carbon chains rotate freely about their single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since every hydrogen is on carbon.

The molecule is an acyclic dialkyl ketone: a single carbonyl carbon bonded to two unbranched saturated alkyl chains of eleven carbons each, giving a symmetric, linear scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. The only functional group is the ketone C=O, located at the central position, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about that carbonyl carbon. The long methylene chains make the structure highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds and no rigid elements. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a straight-chain, saturated aliphatic compound with no rings, so its skeleton is fully flexible and lacks any ring fusion or planar scaffold. A carboxylic acid group sits at one terminus of a long carbon chain, while a secondary alcohol is located at the carbon roughly midway along the chain, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. Because the chain carries no aromatic or unsaturated features, its conformational freedom is high. The carboxylic acid acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the hydroxyl group contributes an additional donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched chain of twelve carbon atoms, with no rings or fused ring systems present. At one end sits a primary amine group, and at the other end a carboxylic acid group, so the two functional groups are located at opposite termini of the chain. Because the skeleton is entirely saturated and acyclic, it has no substitution pattern along the chain and no internal symmetry beyond the trivial linear arrangement. The long methylene segment confers considerable conformational flexibility, allowing the chain to adopt many rotameric arrangements. The amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carboxylic acid can donate and accept hydrogen bonds through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is a long, unbranched saturated carbon chain of twenty-two carbons, with no rings and no double bonds, so it has a flexible, linear scaffold. A single secondary hydroxyl group sits at the central carbon of the chain, flanked by ten-carbon alkyl arms on each side, which gives the molecule a near-mirror-symmetric arrangement about that carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore simple: one polar hydroxyl branch point within an otherwise nonpolar hydrocarbon backbone. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the rest of the molecule offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated-except-for-one-site carbon chain built on a straight aliphatic scaffold with no rings at all. At one terminus sits a terminal alkyne, a carbon-carbon triple bond bearing a hydrogen, which is linear in geometry and carries a weakly acidic terminal C-H. The opposite terminus carries a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, which is planar at its functional core. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, so it is effectively one-dimensional in shape. Its long methylene segment gives considerable conformational flexibility, while the alkyne and carboxyl ends are rigid. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens, and the terminal alkyne contributes only weak hydrogen-bonding character.

The molecule is an unbranched, fully saturated aliphatic chain of eleven carbons with no rings, aromatic systems, or fused scaffolds. Its only functional group is a primary alcohol located at one end of the chain, with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond at the opposite end. The chain is linear and carries no substituents, so the molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond its conformational freedom. Its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkene terminus contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built from a straight, saturated chain of ten methylene units ending in a terminal hydroxyl group, attached at its other end to a benzene ring. The benzene ring is a single, unfused six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no additional substituents, so the aromatic portion is unsubstituted and carries no positional pattern to distinguish. The molecule has only one functional group, a primary alcohol, which can both donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept one through its oxygen lone pairs. The long alkyl linker is highly flexible, with many rotatable single bonds, while the phenyl ring remains rigid and planar. Overall, the molecule is asymmetric, with its polar hydroxyl end contrasting with its nonpolar aromatic end.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom at opposite positions. The nitrogen carries a methyl substituent, while the sulfur sits as a thioether bridge linking the two aromatic rings.
