The central ring is non-planar, adopting a folded, butterfly-like conformation along the sulfur-nitrogen axis, which gives the framework moderate rigidity with some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and approximates a mirror-symmetric arrangement through its central axis. The nitrogen is a tertiary amine-type center with no N-H, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the nitrogen lone pair and the sulfur atom can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a tricyclic fused aromatic system built from three six-membered rings sharing edges, with a nitrogen atom in one of the outer rings. A hydroxyl group sits on a carbon of the outer ring adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, placing the oxygen in a peri-like position relative to the nitrogen-containing ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the hydroxyl and nitrogen break the symmetry of the framework. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is a long, unbranched aliphatic chain with a carboxylic acid at one terminus and a conjugated diyne (two carbon-carbon triple bonds separated by a single bond) near the middle. Its scaffold is entirely acyclic, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. The only functional groups are the terminal carboxylic acid, which carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the alkyne units, which are rigid, linear segments. Because of the diyne, the chain is locally rigid and straight, while the saturated alkyl segments on either side remain flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the acid sits at one end and the alkyl chains on either side of the diyne are of unequal length.

This molecule is a long, unbranched aliphatic chain with a terminal carboxylic acid group at one end. The chain contains a conjugated diyne unit, meaning two carbon-carbon triple bonds separated by a single bond, which makes the central portion linear and rigid. Apart from this rigid diyne segment, the remainder of the skeleton consists of saturated methylene units, so the molecule is largely flexible with rotation possible along the alkyl stretches. There are no rings, branches, or stereocenters, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends differ. Its only hydrogen-bond donor is the carboxylic acid hydroxyl, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens together serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a linear, unbranched dicarboxylic acid with a long aliphatic chain of about twenty carbon atoms. Both ends terminate in a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept four. Near the center sits a conjugated diyne unit, two triple bonds separated by a single bond, which makes that region rigid and rod-like. The rest of the chain consists of saturated methylene units that add flexibility. The overall structure is symmetric, with the diyne unit at its midpoint and identical substitution at both ends.

The molecule is built on a tricyclic dibenzo-fused scaffold: two benzene rings are joined through a central seven-membered ring that contains a nitrogen atom, with a two-carbon saturated bridge linking the two aromatic rings. The nitrogen sits at the junction of the central ring and bears a carboxamide group, a urea-type unit in which the nitrogen is attached to a carbonyl that is further bonded to a terminal NH2. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the aromatic portions carry no additional substituents. The overall framework is fairly rigid across the fused aromatic regions, while the ethylene bridge and the seven-membered ring allow some conformational flexibility. The amide-type group offers both hydrogen-bond donor capacity through its NH2 and acceptor capacity through its carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two trifluoromethyl groups in a meta (1,3) relationship, with a pyrrol-1-yl group attached at the position between them, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern on the central aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion. The pyrrole is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle linked to the benzene through its nitrogen atom, so its N-H is replaced and it contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically compact, while the molecule's only heteroatom acceptor is the pyrrole nitrogen, whose lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring. The overall framework is rigid and largely flat, with only the single bond to the pyrrole ring permitting rotation.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents at the meta positions relative to each other: a 1-hydroxyethyl group (a secondary alcohol attached through a saturated carbon) and, on the same ring, two trifluoromethyl groups at positions 3 and 5. The ring is fully aromatic and flat, with no fused ring systems. The two CF3 groups sit symmetrically on either side of the attachment point, giving the aromatic core an approximate mirror plane through the carbinol substituent, although the side chain itself has a stereocenter. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid, and the ethyl alcohol side chain adds limited rotational flexibility.

This molecule is a straight-chain, saturated aliphatic diol: a linear chain of ten carbon atoms with a hydroxyl group attached to each terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers, so its scaffold is simply an unbranched alkane backbone. The molecule has a mirror-like symmetry about the midpoint of the carbon chain, with both ends identical. Because of the many freely rotating single bonds, it is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Each terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the two oxygen-bearing ends are the molecule's only polar regions.

The molecule is a linear, fully conjugated dienone built around a central carbonyl group flanked on both sides by a two-carbon, trans-configured diene arm. Each arm terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold is symmetric about the carbonyl carbon. The carbonyl oxygen is the only heteroatom and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the four C=C double bonds and the aromatic rings are all conjugated and in extended planar geometry, the structure is rigid and largely flat, with the only rotational freedom arising from the single bonds linking the phenyl rings to the polyene chains.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diamine: a linear, unbranched chain of nine methylene units capped at each end by a primary amine group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom ring systems. Its skeleton is fully saturated and highly flexible, since rotation about the many carbon-carbon single bonds gives it a wide range of conformations. The molecule is symmetric about its central methylene carbon, with the two terminal amino groups occupying equivalent positions. Each primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair, making the molecule capable of multiple intermolecular hydrogen-bonding interactions at both ends.

This molecule is 1,9-nonanediol, an acyclic straight-chain scaffold of nine carbon atoms with no rings, branches, or substituents along the chain. Each terminal carbon carries a primary hydroxyl group, so the two functional groups sit at opposite ends of an otherwise saturated aliphatic backbone. The molecule has a symmetrical arrangement, with the two hydroxyl groups related by a mirror plane through the middle carbon. Its long methylene chain is highly flexible, free to adopt many conformations through rotation about its C–C single bonds. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two such sites at either end.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic hydrocarbon with no rings, consisting of a linear eight-carbon backbone. Both terminal carbons carry a carbon-carbon triple bond, making it a symmetric diyne, with each alkyne unit sitting at one end of the chain. The structure is flexible, since the saturated methylene segments in the middle allow free rotation about the single bonds, while the linear geometry of each triple bond keeps the ends rigid. It lacks any heteroatoms or polar groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a naphthalene-based cyclic imide: a naphthalene core whose peri positions (carbons 1 and 8) are bridged by a five-membered ring containing a C(=O)–NH–C(=O) unit, giving a fused tricyclic system. The imide ring is fused across the peri positions, so the naphthalene and the imide ring share a rigid, nearly planar framework with no rotatable bonds. The three benzenoid rings of the naphthalene are unsubstituted apart from this fusion, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the molecular midline running through the imide nitrogen. Two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the imide N–H provides one hydrogen-bond donor site.

This molecule is a naphthalene-based cyclic anhydride, with a six-membered anhydride ring fused across the peri positions (1 and 8) of a naphthalene core. The anhydride ring contains two carbonyl carbons bridged by a single ring oxygen, so the two C=O groups are the principal hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The three-ring-fused polyaromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The unsubstituted aromatic rings lend the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the anhydride oxygen and the naphthalene midline.

This molecule is a simple acyclic alkane chain: a straight, unbranched skeleton of nine carbon atoms, with a chlorine atom bonded to each terminal carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no other functional groups beyond the two carbon-chlorine bonds at the ends. The structure is linear and symmetric, since the two chlorine-bearing termini are mirror images of each other across the middle of the chain. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many carbon-carbon single bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a tricyclic anthraquinone-type scaffold: two benzene rings fused to a central six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups at opposite positions, giving a planar, rigid, fully conjugated framework. Each outer benzene ring bears one chlorine atom, placed on the carbon adjacent to the ring-fusion position, so the two chlorines sit in a symmetric arrangement across the central axis. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because no N-H or O-H groups are present. The overall structure is largely inflexible, with no rotatable bonds within the fused core.

The molecule is a straight, fully saturated eight-carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or branching. A bromine atom sits at each end of the chain, so the two halogen substituents are placed at the terminal positions, which makes the structure symmetric about the midpoint of the carbon backbone. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond, allowing many conformations. Because it contains only carbon, hydrogen, and bromine with no polar heteroatoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 15-membered macrocyclic polyamine, a diazacyclopentadecane-type ring bearing four nitrogen atoms spaced around the ring with three-carbon and two-carbon linkers between them. Two of the nitrogens are tertiary and each carries a benzyl group, which projects outward from the ring, while the other two nitrogens are secondary amines with N-H bonds. The benzyl substituents sit on nitrogens that are separated across the ring, giving the molecule an approximately two-fold arrangement in its substitution pattern. The flexible saturated chains allow considerable conformational freedom, although the macrocyclic ring constrains the overall shape. All four nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs, and the two secondary amines can additionally serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bicyclic amidine built from two fused saturated rings sharing a common nitrogen-carbon bond at the ring junction. One ring is a seven-membered ring and the other is a six-membered ring, giving a fused bicyclic scaffold with no aromatic character. A C=N double bond sits at the ring fusion, creating an amidine-type unit in which one nitrogen is double-bonded to carbon and the other nitrogen is a tertiary amine bonded to three ring carbons. The remaining carbons are all methylene groups, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and unsubstituted, and the molecule has no stereocenters. The fused ring system is fairly rigid at the junction but the saturated rings retain conformational flexibility. The imine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge. Two primary amino groups are attached, one on each ring: one at a position adjacent to the ring fusion (peri to the other) and the other at the position on the opposite side of that same fused system. Both substituents are on the same side, so the two amines sit close together in the peri arrangement, which creates a constrained spatial relationship between them. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the amino groups adding limited flexibility through rotation about the carbon-nitrogen bonds. Each amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through the nitrogen lone pair), while the aromatic rings contribute only weak acceptor character. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the central fusion bond, which is broken only by the identical but mirror-related placement of the amines.

The molecule is a saturated bicyclic ether built on a bicyclo[2.2.2]octane scaffold, in which two of the bridgehead-adjacent carbons are linked through a single oxygen atom to form an oxa-bridge. One bridgehead carbon carries a methyl group, and the carbon bearing the oxygen carries two additional methyl groups, giving a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern next to the ether oxygen. The ring system is fully saturated, with no double bonds or aromatic rings, and the cage-like framework is conformationally rigid. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no hydroxyl or amine groups, but the ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. Its overall shape is roughly symmetric about the axis through the bridgeheads, with the methyl substituents breaking that symmetry only slightly.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge. Both substituents are dimethylamino groups, each consisting of a nitrogen atom bonded to two methyl groups, and they sit on the 1 and 8 positions, which are peri to each other across the ring fusion. This 1,8-disubstitution places the two nitrogens in close proximity on the same side of the scaffold, creating a sterically crowded, rigid, planar framework. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the central C-C bond axis. The nitrogens are tertiary amines with no N-H bonds, so they cannot act as hydrogen-bond donors, but their lone pairs allow them to serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a tricyclic scaffold built from a central ring fused between two benzene rings, giving an anthracene-like three-ring arrangement in which one of the central positions is a ketone (C=O) and the opposite central position is a methylene (CH2) group, so the middle ring is non-aromatic. Each outer benzene ring carries one hydroxyl group positioned adjacent to the ring fusion, close to the carbonyl, so the two OH groups sit in a mirror-related pattern. The fused, nearly planar framework is rigid, with little conformational freedom. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a fully aromatic, planar polycyclic system built from two pyridine-type rings fused to a central benzene-type ring, forming a phenanthroline-like tricyclic framework with three rings sharing edges. Each of the two terminal rings contains one ring nitrogen, and both nitrogens sit on the same side of the molecule in a bay-like arrangement, so they are positioned to coordinate a metal or hydrogen-bond through a convergent pocket. The scaffold has no substituents or functional groups beyond the aromatic C–H positions, and it possesses a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the central ring. Because every atom is part of a rigid fused aromatic system, the molecule is essentially inflexible, and the two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while providing no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic diol: a linear eight-carbon backbone with no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom substitution beyond the two terminal oxygens. Each end of the chain carries a primary hydroxyl group, so the two functional groups sit at opposite termini and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry about its midpoint. The carbon chain is flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds allowing it to adopt numerous conformations. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, giving the molecule substantial capacity for intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge. Each ring is aromatic and planar, so the whole framework is rigid with no rotatable bonds. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the carbons of the fused system, one on each ring, placing them at positions that flank the ring junction on opposite sides, which gives the molecule a pseudo-symmetric, roughly C2-like arrangement of substituents. Both hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H groups and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs. The fused aromatic core is electron-rich and conjugated, contributing to the planarity of the structure.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic diamine built on a straight, unbranched chain of eight carbon atoms, with an amino group attached at each terminal carbon. Because it contains no rings or ring fusions, its scaffold is entirely flexible, with many rotatable single bonds that allow the chain to adopt numerous conformations. The two primary amine groups sit at opposite ends, giving the molecule a symmetrical, linear shape with a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the carbon chain. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor, through its two N–H bonds, and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, through its lone pair of electrons. The molecule carries no other substituents or unsaturation.

The molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain alkane dithiol: a six-carbon saturated backbone with a thiol group (–SH) attached at each terminal carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so the structure is fully symmetric about the midpoint of the chain. The flexible, unbranched carbon chain allows many rotational conformations, and each terminal sulfhydryl group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond. The sulfur atoms can also serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, though they are considerably less electronegative than oxygen or nitrogen.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diol, specifically hexane-1,6-diol, with no rings or fused ring systems. Its skeleton is a linear, unbranched chain of six carbon atoms, each saturated with hydrogens, so there is no aromaticity or unsaturation. Hydroxyl groups sit at both terminal positions, giving the molecule a symmetric, two-ended arrangement with a mirror plane through the middle of the chain. The chain is highly flexible because of free rotation about its many single C–C bonds, so it can adopt numerous conformations. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor and two acceptor sites at its ends.

This molecule is built around a central hexa-2,4-diyne chain, a linear four-carbon-plus-two backbone containing two adjacent carbon-carbon triple bonds, with a methylene group at each end. Each terminal CH2 is bonded through an ether oxygen to a phenyl ring, so the structure is symmetric, with the two aryloxy arms mirror-related across the central diyne axis. The diyne core is rigid and linear, while the two ether linkages add rotational freedom to the aromatic ends. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on carbon. The two ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the aromatic rings offer pi-electron density for stacking interactions.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached as ether substituents, one on each ring, at positions that place them on opposite sides of the fused system, which makes the substitution pattern asymmetric overall. The ring system contains no heteroatoms apart from the ether oxygens, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Each methoxy oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the remaining C–H positions on the aromatic rings are non-polar and inert to hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a linear, fully saturated six-carbon alkyl chain, with an unbranched backbone of methylene units and no rings or fused ring systems. Each terminus carries an isocyanate group, where a carbon is double-bonded to both nitrogen and oxygen in a cumulated N=C=O arrangement. The two functional groups are placed symmetrically at opposite ends of the chain, giving the molecule a centrosymmetric, two-fold symmetric overall shape. The chain is highly flexible because of free rotation about its sp3 carbon-carbon bonds, while the isocyanate units are linear and rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups, but each isocyanate nitrogen and oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the ring carbons, one on each ring, so the compound is a dihydroxynaphthalene with the substituents placed at non-equivalent positions, which breaks the symmetry that the bare ring system would otherwise have. The rigid aromatic framework allows little conformational flexibility, and the planar surface can engage in stacking interactions. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is a straight, fully saturated chain of seven methylene units capped at both ends by nitrile groups, giving a linear, unbranched scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Each terminal carbon of the chain bears a carbon-nitrogen triple bond, so the two functional groups are identical and placed symmetrically at opposite ends. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the center of the chain, and the flexible saturated backbone allows free rotation about its single bonds. The nitrogen atoms of the nitrile groups are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a straight-chain saturated hydrocarbon skeleton of six carbon atoms, with a chlorine atom attached to each terminal carbon. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the two carbon-chlorine bonds at the ends of the chain. The substitution pattern is strictly linear and symmetric, since the two chlorine atoms sit at opposite ends and the molecule has a two-fold mirror-like symmetry through the chain's center. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds allowing many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring, and an adjacent hydroxyl group sits next to it, placing the two functionalities ortho to each other on the same ring. Two bromine atoms are attached at separate positions, one on each ring of the fused system, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Because the core is fully aromatic and the substituents are attached directly, the structure is essentially rigid, with only the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups capable of rotation. The carboxylic acid and the phenolic hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptor sites on their oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched chain of six carbon atoms, with a bromine atom attached to each terminal carbon, so it is a simple acyclic alpha,omega-dibromoalkane. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the two carbon-bromine bonds at the chain ends. The structure is symmetric, with a mirror-related pattern of substitution at both ends of the chain, and the methylene units along the backbone are freely rotatable, making the molecule highly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the bromine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diamine: a six-carbon, fully saturated alkane backbone with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic groups. Each terminal carbon carries a primary amine group (-NH2), so the two functional groups sit at opposite ends of an otherwise unbranched chain and the molecule is symmetric about its center. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single C-C bonds and no conformational constraints. Each primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair on nitrogen, giving the molecule two donor-acceptor sites at its ends.

The molecule is a saturated bicyclic sugar-derived scaffold: a six-membered carbocyclic ring (cyclohexane-type, with four ring carbons bearing hydroxyl groups) fused to a tetrahydrofuran-containing bridged acetal system through two adjacent stereocentres, giving a fused ring arrangement. The ring system contains an ether oxygen in each of the two bridging linkages, and four secondary alcohol groups are arranged around the carbocycle with defined stereochemistry, making the substitution pattern highly oxygenated and asymmetric. The scaffold is conformationally constrained by the fused rings, though the molecule retains some flexibility from the ring puckering. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors, so the molecule has many hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain alkane-dithiol: a linear five-carbon saturated backbone (pentane) with a thiol group (–SH) attached at each terminal carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no branching or additional substituents, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation about each C–C bond. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry, mirrored about the central carbon of the chain. Each thiol sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H group, while the sulfur atoms themselves are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The remaining carbon framework contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diol with no rings, so its scaffold is a linear five-carbon alkane backbone. Each terminal carbon carries a single hydroxyl group, giving the two functional groups at opposite ends of the chain in a symmetric, unbranched substitution pattern. The chain is fully saturated and highly flexible, with free rotation about its many C–C bonds allowing many conformations. Both hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H bonds and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs.

The molecule is a bicyclic system in which a saturated six-membered carbocycle is fused to an aromatic tetrazole ring through a shared carbon–nitrogen bond, giving a fused scaffold. The tetrazole portion is a five-membered aromatic ring containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, and it carries no substituents beyond the fusion. The fused six-membered ring is fully saturated, containing only methylene units, so the molecule has a rigid aromatic half joined to a flexible aliphatic half. There are no stereocenters and no obvious symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the aromatic ring. The nitrogen atoms of the tetrazole can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an open-chain hydrocarbon with no rings, built on a six-carbon linear skeleton. It contains two terminal carbon-carbon double bonds, one at each end of the chain, so it is a diene with the double bonds placed in a 1,5 relationship. It has no heteroatoms or other functional groups, and its only substitution is the unsubstituted terminal vinyl ends. The structure has a symmetric framework, since the two ends are mirror images of each other. Because it has no rings and no polar groups, it is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic, rigid framework. Two nitro groups (–NO2) are attached as substituents, one on carbon 1 and one on carbon 5 of the naphthalene system, so they sit on different rings at positions related by the ring fusion. The two nitro groups are electron-withdrawing and can each accept hydrogen bonds through their oxygen atoms, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the substitution is not mirror-symmetric about the fusion bond, the molecule lacks a full symmetry axis, though it retains a near-planar, rigid shape with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings that share a single bond and are therefore planar and fully aromatic. Two methyl groups are attached as the only substituents, one on each ring, so there are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups. The substitution is positioned at the 1 and 5 locations on the fused core, which breaks the symmetry of the parent skeleton, giving the molecule a C2h-like arrangement with a centre of inversion. Because the ring system is rigid and the methyl groups rotate only freely about single bonds, the structure is essentially flat with minimal conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since its only atoms are carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is 1,6-dichlorohexane, a fully saturated, unbranched six-carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or other heteroatoms. Each terminus of the hexane backbone carries one chlorine atom, so the only functional groups are two primary alkyl chloride groups located at opposite ends of the chain. The structure is symmetric, with a two-fold axis passing through the midpoint of the carbon chain, and it is highly flexible because each C–C bond can rotate freely. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no remaining aromatic hydrogens. Two nitro groups (–NO2) are attached at positions that are meta to each other, and two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, so the ring carries an alternating pattern of strongly electron-withdrawing groups. The core is a single planar six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule has an approximately twofold symmetry axis relating the two halves of the ring. Its rigid planar framework limits conformational flexibility, though the nitro groups can rotate slightly about their bonds to the ring. The oxygen atoms of the nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic system built around a central six-membered ring containing two carbonyl groups located opposite each other, flanked on both sides by benzene rings, which places it in the anthraquinone family of polycyclic aromatic diketones. Each outer benzene ring carries a single chlorine atom at the same relative position, adjacent to the ring fusion, so the two halogen substituents sit in a mirror-related arrangement. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with extended conjugation across all three rings. The two ketone oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorines contribute only weak halogen-type interactions.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two nitro groups, two chlorine atoms, and no other ring. The nitro groups sit in a meta-like relationship to each other and each is positioned to withdraw electron density from the aromatic core, while the chlorines occupy the remaining positions, giving a fully substituted, asymmetric pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is a single rigid aromatic ring, with the nitro and chloro groups lying essentially in the ring plane and contributing little conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups act as acceptors.

This molecule is 1,5-dibromopentane, an acyclic saturated scaffold consisting of a straight chain of five carbon atoms. Each terminal carbon carries a single bromine substituent, giving the molecule a symmetric substitution pattern that mirrors itself end to end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds, so the structure is entirely sp3-hybridized and built from single bonds only. The chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many rotameric conformations around its carbon-carbon bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatoms are the two bromines, which can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated straight-chain aliphatic diamine: a linear five-carbon backbone with no rings, no double bonds, and no aromatic character. Each terminal carbon carries a primary amine group, giving the two nitrogen atoms identical, symmetric positions at opposite ends of the chain. The C–C single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility through rotation along the backbone. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two six-membered aromatic rings sharing one edge, making it fully planar and rigid. Two primary amino groups are attached to the ring carbons, one on each of the two rings, at positions flanking the fusion region in a 1,5 (peri-free, para-like across the fusion) relationship. The substitution pattern is symmetric with respect to a mirror plane passing through the central fused bond, giving the molecule a C2h-like overall symmetry in its idealized planar form. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair. The aromatic core contributes extended pi-electron delocalization across both rings.

The molecule is built around a flexible five-carbon saturated chain that links two phosphorus atoms. Each phosphorus is a tertiary phosphine center carrying three phenyl rings, so the structure is a bis-triarylphosphine joined by a pentamethylene spacer. There are no fused ring systems; the only rings are the two sets of three separate, unsubstituted benzene rings, giving a symmetric arrangement about the midpoint of the chain. The chain is largely flexible, while the phenyl groups are rigid planar units. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the phosphorus lone pairs provide only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a five-membered heterocyclic ring, an imidazolidine-2,4-dione (hydantoin-type) core containing two nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups at positions flanking the ring. One nitrogen carries a methyl group, while the carbon between the two carbonyls bears two methyl substituents, giving a gem-dimethyl quaternary center. The ring is small, saturated at the sp3 carbon, and essentially planar across its amide-containing portion, so it is quite rigid with little conformational freedom beyond the methyl rotations. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, because the N-methyl and gem-dimethyl substitution break symmetry. The unsubstituted NH is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a piperazine core, a six-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other, with no fused or additional ring systems. Each of the two ring nitrogens carries a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), so the substitution pattern is symmetrical, with the two side chains attached at the 1 and 4 positions. The ring is flexible, adopting chair-like conformations, while the nitrile groups are linear and rigid. Both tertiary amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrile nitrogens can also accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. Two identical cyanomethyl groups, each a methylene carbon bearing a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond), are attached at positions 1 and 4 of the ring, giving a para substitution pattern. This arrangement gives the molecule a centrosymmetric, linear-like shape with two-fold symmetry along the ring axis. The nitrile nitrogens are good hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The benzene core is rigid, whereas the two CH2 linkers allow some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two identical side chains at opposite (para) positions, giving it a symmetric, linear arrangement. Each side chain consists of a single methylene linker attached to a carboxylic acid group, so the scaffold is a simple benzene core bearing two acetic acid-type arms. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two methylene-carboxyl arms add some conformational flexibility around their single bonds. Each carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, so the molecule has two donor sites and four acceptor oxygen atoms in total.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic carbon framework, with two isothiocyanate groups (–N=C=S) attached at the 1 and 4 positions, so they sit directly opposite each other (para substitution). Each isothiocyanate group is linear and cumulative, consisting of a central carbon double-bonded to both nitrogen and sulfur. The molecule has a high degree of symmetry, with a two-fold axis and a plane of symmetry running through the ring, and its rigid, planar aromatic core limits conformational flexibility. The nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it lacks N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a single six-membered saturated ring containing one oxygen atom and one nitrogen atom placed across from each other, forming a morpholine-type heterocycle that is fused to nothing else. The nitrogen is part of a lactam, meaning it is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that sits adjacent to it within the ring, so the ring is a seven-membered cyclic amide rather than a simple six-membered one, with the carbonyl oxygen as an exocyclic double bond. The ring carries no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and the molecule has a plane of symmetry only approximately, with the ring adopting a non-planar, partially flexible conformation. The amide N–H provides one hydrogen-bond donor site, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring ether oxygen both serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing one sulfur and one oxygen atom in a 1,4-relationship across the ring. The sulfur is fully oxidized, bearing two double-bonded oxygen atoms, which makes it a sulfone, and it sits adjacent to a CH2 unit that links to the ether oxygen. The ring is non-aromatic, has no fused partners, and carries no substituents beyond the sulfonyl oxygens, so the scaffold is unsubstituted and highly symmetric about an axis through the sulfur and oxygen. Its ring is conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair-like arrangements, yet the sulfonyl group is strongly polar. The two sulfonyl oxygens and the ether oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor atoms.

This molecule is a naphthalene-1,4-dione, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered ring containing two carbonyl groups at positions opposite each other. The non-aromatic ring contains a carbon-carbon double bond between the two carbonyls, making it a conjugated quinone-type system. The fused benzene ring is fully aromatic and unsubstituted, so the molecule is planar and largely rigid. It has no rotatable bonds and no stereocenters. Both oxygen atoms are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain, a butane-1,4-dithiol skeleton with hydroxyl groups on the two central carbons, so it has no rings and no ring fusion. Two terminal primary thiol (sulfanyl) groups sit at the ends of the chain, and two secondary hydroxyl groups flank the centre, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the midpoint. The two stereogenic centres are defined in the SMILES as specified configurations, so the molecule is chiral and its two halves are mirror-related in the sense of a C2-type arrangement. Its flexible single-bond backbone allows many conformations, while the four heteroatom groups each act as hydrogen-bond donors and, through their lone pairs, as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain, with a sulfur-terminated skeleton: two terminal carbons each bear a thiol (–SH) group, and the two internal carbons each carry a secondary hydroxyl (–OH) group. The two stereocenters are both specified, and the arrangement places the hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons with the thiols at the chain ends, giving a symmetric, two-fold-like substitution pattern. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the framework is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Each hydroxyl and thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygen and sulfur atoms can each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two tert-butyl groups attached at the 1 and 4 positions, making it a para-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. Each tert-butyl group is a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, so the molecule contains no heteroatoms and no functional groups such as hydroxyls, carbonyls, or amines. The structure has a high degree of symmetry, with a central axis running through the ring that maps the two halves onto each other. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the bulky alkyl groups are saturated and rotate freely about their bonds to the ring. Because there are no hydrogen-bond donors and no lone-pair-bearing acceptor atoms, the molecule cannot participate in hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring with two substituents placed para to each other, giving a symmetric 1,4-disubstituted scaffold. Each substituent is an oxygen atom bonded to the ring and further linked to an ester carbonyl, so the structure contains two ester groups, each attached through its alkoxy oxygen to the aromatic ring. Each ester terminates in a two-carbon ethyl chain, making the molecule symmetric about the central ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ester side chains add some conformational flexibility. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built from a four-carbon chain in which both terminal carbons are linked to benzene rings, with the two internal carbons joined by a triple bond and each terminal carbon also carrying a triple bond to its adjacent carbon. This gives a linear, rod-like diarylbutadiyne-type skeleton. Each end carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring, with no heteroatoms or additional functional groups present. The two phenyl rings are related by a symmetry element through the center of the molecule, so the structure is highly symmetric. The alkyne units enforce a rigid, extended geometry with little conformational flexibility. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone with a four-carbon linker: a phenyl ring is attached to a carbonyl carbon through a chain of three methylene groups, and the carbonyl is also bonded directly to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. Both aromatic rings are monosubstituted benzene rings with no ring fusion, and the molecule as a whole has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry. The central ketone is the only functional group, providing a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The flexible saturated chain between the two aromatic systems gives the structure considerable conformational freedom, in contrast to the rigid planar phenyl rings at either end.

This molecule is a diaryl ether built from three benzene rings joined in a linear chain: two terminal phenyl groups connected through oxygen bridges to a central para-substituted benzene ring. The central ring carries its two ether linkages at the 1 and 4 positions, giving a symmetric, extended scaffold with no fused ring systems. Each ether oxygen links two aromatic carbons and has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, though its lone pairs allow weak hydrogen-bond acceptance. The molecule has no stereocenters and a near-two-fold symmetry axis running through the central ring, with the aromatic rings relatively rigid but the C–O–C bridges permitting some rotational flexibility around the ether bonds.

The molecule is a small, fully saturated heterocycle built around a six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms, with ring oxygens in a 1,4-relationship. It contains two carbonyl (C=O) groups, both attached directly to ring oxygens, which makes it a cyclic diester (a lactone-type ester arrangement) rather than a simple ketone. The ring carbons are all sp3 except for the two carbonyl carbons, giving a compact, relatively rigid scaffold with little conformational freedom. The structure has no aromatic rings, no fused ring systems, and no substituents beyond the ring atoms, and it possesses a degree of symmetry across the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two carbonyl oxygens and two ring ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered saturated ring containing one oxygen and one additional oxygen in a 1,4-relationship, forming a 1,4-dioxane-type scaffold. Two hemiacetal-type carbons, each bearing a hydroxyl group, sit adjacent to each other across the ring, so the ring carries two secondary alcohol-like substituents on the carbons flanking one ring oxygen. There are no ring fusions and no aromatic rings, and the framework is fully sp3 and conformationally flexible, able to adopt chair and boat-like forms. The two hydroxyl groups and the ring oxygens make it capable of acting as both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single saturated six-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms positioned opposite one another, making it a 1,4-dioxane scaffold. It has no fused rings, no double bonds, and no additional functional groups beyond the two ether oxygens, which sit at the 1 and 4 positions with a methylene unit between each pair of carbons. The ring is unsubstituted, so every carbon carries only hydrogens, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry with a centre of inversion. Because the ring can adopt a flexible chair-like conformation, the scaffold is conformationally mobile rather than rigid. The two oxygen atoms can each accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a central 2,2-dimethyl-1,3-dioxolane ring, a five-membered acetonide that is fused to nothing but is substituted at its two adjacent carbons (the 4 and 5 positions) with CH2 groups, giving a C2-symmetric arrangement with two stereocenters. Each of those CH2 arms is esterified through its oxygen to a para-tolyl sulfonyl group, so the two ends are identical aryl sulfonate esters, each bearing a methyl at the para position of its benzene ring. The molecule therefore has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis passing through the dioxolane. The aromatic rings and the sulfonyl groups are rigid, while the ether-linked CH2 arms and the dioxolane ring allow moderate flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since there are no OH or NH groups, whereas the sulfonyl and ether oxygens provide several acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Two nitro groups, each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, are attached at positions opposite one another on the ring, making it a para-disubstituted pattern. Because the two substituents are identical and sit on opposite sides, the molecule has a high degree of symmetry, with a center of inversion through the middle of the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the nitro groups are largely coplanar with it, so the overall shape is flat and elongated. The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered heterocycle: a piperazine ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite one another (1,4-relationship) and four methylene carbons. Each nitrogen carries one methyl substituent, so the scaffold is a symmetric N,N'-dimethylpiperazine with no fused rings, no aromatic rings, and no additional functional groups beyond these tertiary amine centers. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the molecule has a symmetry element through the two nitrogens and the center of the ring. Both nitrogens are tertiary amines without N–H bonds, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two lone-pair-bearing nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a rigid, flat bicyclic aromatic system. Two methoxy groups (–OCH₃) are attached to the same ring, one at the position adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon and one at the position on the opposite side of that ring, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern. The methoxy oxygens are ether functionalities, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic framework is essentially rigid, with only the methyl groups of the ethers providing limited conformational freedom. The substitution pattern is not symmetric about the full ring system, although it retains a pseudo-mirror relationship through the long axis of the naphthalene core.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds and no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups, each an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 4, which are opposite each other, giving a para substitution pattern. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis running through the two substituted carbons, and the ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy groups can rotate somewhat around their carbon-oxygen bonds. Neither substituent carries a hydrogen bond donor, since there are no hydroxyl or amine groups, but each ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (O-CH3 ethers) are attached to the ring at positions para to each other, and a single fluorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, giving a 1,4-dimethoxy-2-fluorobenzene substitution pattern. The arrangement is asymmetric because the fluorine breaks the mirror symmetry that the two methoxy groups alone would impose. The core is rigid and planar, while the two methyl ethers can rotate about their C-O bonds. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two isopropyl groups, each a central carbon bearing two methyl branches, are attached at the 1 and 4 positions, so they sit para to one another on opposite sides of the ring. This substitution pattern gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a central axis running through the two substituent carbons. The structure contains no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and it is a rigid aromatic core with two flexible but bulky alkyl arms.

This molecule is a simple acyclic alkane chain: a straight, unbranched four-carbon backbone with an iodine atom attached at each terminal carbon, giving a symmetric 1,4-diiodobutane skeleton. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the two carbon-iodine bonds, which serve as the only polar features. The two iodine substituents sit at opposite ends of the chain, so the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the midpoint of the carbon chain. Because the chain is saturated and freely rotatable about its single bonds, the structure is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. Neither iodine nor carbon provides a hydrogen-bond donor, and the iodine atoms are at most weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two iodine atoms, making it a diiodobenzene. The six-membered aromatic ring is a single, unfused scaffold with no additional rings. The two iodine substituents sit at the 1 and 4 positions, directly opposite each other across the ring, which is a para substitution pattern. This arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with the iodine atoms and the ring lying in a common plane. The structure is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors because the only substituents are halogens.

The molecule is a tricyclic anthraquinone-type scaffold: two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring that carries two ketone carbonyls at positions opposite each other. One outer ring is unsubstituted, while the other bears two hydroxyl groups on adjacent-to-fusion positions arranged in a para-like pattern across that ring. The fused tricyclic core is planar and rigid, with the two hydroxyls able to donate hydrogen bonds and the two carbonyl oxygens able to accept them, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl groups are positioned for possible intramolecular interaction. The overall framework has an approximate mirror symmetry through the central ring, though the hydroxyl substitution breaks full symmetry on one side.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered saturated heterocycle, a piperazine ring, with nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 4. Both ring nitrogens are fully substituted by formyl groups (–CHO), so each nitrogen forms an N-formyl amide linkage and the ring carries no free N–H. The ring is unfused and contains only sp3 methylene carbons apart from the two carbonyl carbons, giving a symmetric, centrosymmetric substitution pattern in which the two formyl groups are equivalent. The ring can adopt chair conformations, but the two amide-like carbonyl oxygens are the only polar features, so the scaffold is comparatively rigid at the amide bonds with some flexibility in the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is 1,4-difluorobenzene, built on a single benzene scaffold: a six-membered aromatic ring of sp2 carbons with no fused ring systems. Two fluorine atoms are attached at opposite positions (the para or 1,4 pattern), so the substitution is symmetric, giving the molecule a centre of inversion and a two-fold axis through the ring. The ring is planar and fully rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The C–F bonds are polar, but fluorine is a very weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with six carbons arranged in a flat, fully aromatic six-membered scaffold and no fused rings. Four of the ring positions carry substituents in a 1,2,4,5 pattern: two methoxy groups (oxygen bonded to a methyl) and two fluorine atoms, alternating around the ring so that each methoxy sits next to a fluorine. The arrangement has approximate two-fold symmetry, with the methoxy groups and fluorines related by a central axis through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid, while the two methoxy groups retain some rotational freedom about their C–O bonds. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two ethyl groups in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving a symmetric dialkylbenzene scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and it carries no heteroatoms or polar functional groups. Each ethyl substituent is a saturated two-carbon chain attached directly to the ring, which adds some conformational flexibility at the side chains while the ring itself stays planar and rigid. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the ring's para carbons. Because it contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, its capacity for hydrogen bonding is essentially nil.

This molecule is a symmetric para-disubstituted benzene ring, bearing two ethoxy groups (–O–CH2–CH3) at positions 1 and 4 of the aromatic core. There are no additional ring systems or ring fusion, so the scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with a flat, rigid planarity. The two ether oxygens are the only heteroatoms and act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since all hydrogens are attached to carbon. The terminal ethyl groups add modest conformational flexibility through rotation about the C–O and O–C bonds, and the overall arrangement possesses a center of inversion and a two-fold axis, giving it high molecular symmetry.

The molecule is a biphenyl-like scaffold in which two cyclohexyl rings are attached directly to a central benzene ring at para positions, making it a symmetric 1,4-dicyclohexylbenzene. The central aromatic ring is planar and fully unsubstituted apart from the two saturated carbocycles, which adopt chair conformations and are fused to nothing, so there are no fused ring systems. The substitution pattern is strictly para and the molecule possesses a center of inversion, giving it high symmetry. Its only functional groups are alkyl C–C and aromatic C–H bonds, with no heteroatoms. Consequently it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, and its rotatable single bonds linking the rings give moderate conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a simple acyclic alkane, a straight five-carbon chain with a chlorine atom bonded to each terminal carbon, so it is a 1,5-dichloropentane. The scaffold is entirely saturated, with no rings, no double bonds, and no fused ring systems. Its only functional groups are two primary alkyl chlorides located at opposite ends of the chain, which makes the substitution pattern linear and symmetric about the central carbon. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds allowing many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, since the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors and the carbon backbone offers none.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 4, so they sit directly opposite each other, giving a para substitution pattern. The arrangement has a center of symmetry and a twofold axis through the ring, making it highly symmetric. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Neither chlorine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the halogens are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, so the molecule offers essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two nitro-group-free substituents plus one nitro group, forming a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. A nitro group (–NO2, drawn here with its charge-separated form) is attached to one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms occupy other positions on the ring, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern in which the two chlorines sit adjacent to each other and the nitro group sits meta to one chlorine. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring, though the nitro group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry that would make all its substituent positions equivalent, so it has no mirror plane or rotational axis beyond the ring's own local arrangement. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyridazine-type six-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, with two chlorine substituents attached to the carbons flanking the nitrogens' ring positions. This aromatic diazine core is fused to a bridged bicyclic hydrocarbon framework, a norbornane-like cage, sharing two adjacent carbons. The fusion creates a compact, largely rigid polycyclic scaffold with limited conformational freedom. The chlorine atoms are the only heteroatom substituents on the periphery, with no hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups present. Because the two nitrogens lack attached hydrogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, since the aromatic and aliphatic halves differ in character.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three halogen substituents. Two chlorine atoms sit at positions that are para to each other across the ring, and an iodine atom occupies a position adjacent to one of the chlorines, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the halogens are attached directly to it without flexible linkers, so the overall shape is essentially flat and inflexible. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no OH, NH, or similar groups. Its halogen atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the aromatic pi system offers a modest electron-rich face.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three halogen substituents: two chlorine atoms and one fluorine atom, arranged in a 1,2,4-pattern around the ring, with the fluorine flanked by one chlorine on one side and a hydrogen-bearing carbon on the other. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the substitution pattern breaks the mirror planes a symmetric arrangement would have. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the halogens lying in the same plane and little conformational flexibility. Because the substituents are all halogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, saturated aliphatic chain of six carbon atoms with no rings and no double bonds, so it is fully flexible. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents: one sits on the second carbon, creating a secondary alkyl bromide with a methyl branch, and the other sits on the terminal carbon, giving a primary alkyl bromide at the end of the chain. The two halogen-bearing carbons are at different positions, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups. Its only heteroatoms are the two bromines, which can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, so it is fully aromatic and planar. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents on the same ring: one on the alpha position at C1 and one on the para-related position C4, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 across one ring and the other ring stays unsubstituted. The overall framework has a two-fold axis of symmetry through the fused edge, and the rigid aromatic core gives very little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatoms are the two halogens, which can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is 1,4-dibromobutane, a straight, fully saturated four-carbon chain with no rings and no double bonds. Each end of the chain carries one bromine atom bonded to a terminal methylene carbon, so the scaffold is a linear alkyl backbone with a halogen at each terminus. The molecule possesses a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the central C–C bond, making the two halves identical. Because all the bonds are single bonds and the chain is unbranched, the structure is highly flexible and can adopt many rotameric conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms can act only as weak halogen-type acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a planar six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused or additional rings. Two bromine atoms are attached directly to the ring at positions 1 and 4, so they sit on opposite sides of the ring in a para arrangement. This substitution pattern gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a centre of inversion and a two-fold axis passing through the midpoints of the two carbon-bromine bonds. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, and the molecule has no rotatable bonds. Because it carries only halogen substituents, it has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries two nitro groups and two bromine atoms as substituents. One nitro group is attached to the ring at one carbon, and the other substituents sit at the adjacent carbons and at the position across from them, giving a substitution pattern that is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core and the planar nitro groups make the structure rigid and flat. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H bonds. Its nitro oxygens and the bromine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two bromine substituents and one fluorine substituent, all attached directly to the ring. Reading around the ring, the fluorine sits on one carbon and a bromine on the carbon meta to it, while the second bromine occupies the position ortho to the fluorine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal mirror symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the halogen substituents are fixed in place, so the molecule has essentially no conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The halogens alternate around the ring, so the substitution pattern is a 1,4-dibromo-2,5-difluoro arrangement, which gives the molecule a centre of symmetry through the ring. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, and the fluorine and bromine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the structure is compact and highly rigid, with essentially no conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring with six aromatic carbons, forming a flat, rigid scaffold. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon.

With no rings and only single bonds separating the core atoms, the scaffold is highly flexible, with rotation possible about the central carbon–carbon bond.

The molecule is a symmetric diaryl ether built around a central benzene ring. Two benzyloxy arms are attached at the para positions, so the central ring carries an oxygen bridge on each side, and each oxygen connects through a flexible CH2 linker to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The two methylene linkers add conformational flexibility, while the aromatic cores remain rigid and planar.

This molecule is a symmetric diaryl diketone built around a central benzene ring bearing two benzoyl groups in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each carbonyl carbon links the central ring to a terminal unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold consists of three benzene rings joined linearly through two ketone bridges. The structure possesses approximate two-fold symmetry through the central ring. Its two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bridged bicyclic amine built around a diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane skeleton. Two nitrogen atoms sit at opposite bridgehead positions, and three two-carbon bridges connect them, so the scaffold is fully saturated with no aromatic rings and no double bonds. Each nitrogen is a tertiary amine bonded to three ring carbons, which makes both atoms hydrogen-bond acceptors but gives neither any hydrogen-bond donor capability. The cage is highly symmetric, with three equivalent ethylene bridges radiating from the nitrogen-to-nitrogen axis, and its rigid bridged framework leaves no rotatable bonds within the core.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic chain of four carbon atoms, with a primary amine group attached at each terminal carbon, giving a linear, unbranched skeleton. Because there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers, the structure is entirely flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond. The molecule possesses a two-fold symmetry, mirrored about its central carbon-carbon bond, and its substitution pattern is identical at both ends. Each nitrogen carries two hydrogens, so the molecule contains four hydrogen-bond donor sites, and each nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an anthraquinone scaffold, consisting of three fused six-membered rings in a linear-angular arrangement where the central ring bears two carbonyl groups. Two amino groups sit on the same terminal ring at positions that flank the fused junction, giving a 1,4-diamino substitution pattern on one side of the tricyclic core. The unsubstituted benzo ring on the opposite side is fully aromatic. The fused planar framework is rigid, with little conformational freedom. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two primary amine groups can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

This molecule is built on a piperazine core, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. Each of those nitrogens is acylated by an acryloyl group, a vinyl ketone unit in which a carbon-carbon double bond sits directly beside a carbonyl, so the structure is symmetric about the ring.
