The piperazine ring adopts a chair-like conformation, but the amide bonds introduce partial planarity and restricted rotation, giving the molecule moderate rigidity. The terminal vinyl groups are reactive, flexible appendages extending outward from the central ring.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diester built around a four-carbon butane backbone with no rings. Each end of the chain carries an acetyl group bonded through an ester oxygen, so the two terminal carbons are each attached to a carbonyl carbon that bears a methyl group. The structure is symmetric, with the two ester units mirrored across the center of the chain. The chain is flexible because of its many freely rotatable single bonds. Each ester contributes two oxygen atoms: the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the ether-type oxygen can also act as an acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring with two substituents placed in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a symmetric, flat aromatic core. Each substituent is an acetate ester group, consisting of an oxygen atom attached to the ring and bonded to a carbonyl carbon that carries a methyl group. The two ester groups are identical, so the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the centre of the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the ester linkages allow some rotation around the single bonds. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it contains no N-H or O-H groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, linear compound built on a four-carbon chain containing a central carbon-carbon triple bond, which makes the backbone rigid and rod-like. Each end of the chain carries a methylene group bonded to an acetate ester, so the molecule is a symmetric bis-ester with an identical substitution pattern at both termini. There are no ring systems or ring fusion. Each ester group contributes a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N-H or O-H bonds. Its overall conformation is largely fixed along the alkyne axis, although the ester arms retain some rotational freedom.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring with no heteroatoms in the ring itself, built from a cyclohexane-type skeleton. Two ketone groups sit on the ring at positions 1 and 4, so they are para to each other across the ring, giving a symmetric substitution pattern with a two-fold axis through the midpoints of the two C-C bonds that separate them. The ring is saturated apart from the carbonyl carbons, and it adopts a fairly rigid, puckered conformation with limited flexibility. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring with no heteroatoms, so its scaffold is purely hydrocarbon. The ring contains three carbon-carbon double bonds arranged in a non-conjugated pattern, with one sp3-hybridized methylene carbon separating the double bonds. There are no functional groups and no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The ring is largely planar with limited conformational flexibility, and the structure has a mirror plane of symmetry through the methylene carbon, though the ring puckers slightly out of planar geometry.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diol with four methylene units separating two terminal hydroxyl groups, giving a linear, unbranched carbon backbone with no rings or fused ring systems. Both ends of the chain carry a primary alcohol group, so the molecule is symmetric about its midpoint and has no stereocenters. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single C–C bonds allowing a range of conformations. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with the two substituents sitting on opposite carbons of the aromatic core. Each substituent is an ethynyl linker that carries a trimethylsilyl group at its terminal end, so the overall scaffold is a linear, rod-like arrangement with a benzene ring at the center and a carbon-carbon triple bond on each side. The molecule has no stereocenters and high symmetry, with a two-fold axis and a center of inversion through the ring. The triple bonds and the aromatic ring make the structure rigid and extended, while the methyl groups on the silicon atoms add bulk at the ends. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the pi systems of the alkyne and arene units.

This molecule is a linear, symmetric diyne built around a four-carbon unsaturated chain. Two carbon-carbon triple bonds are joined by a single bond, forming a rigid, rod-like backbone with no rings or fusion. Each terminal end of the chain carries a trimethylsilyl group, a silicon atom bonded to three methyl groups, giving the molecule a two-fold symmetry through its center. The structure contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N-H or O-H bonds, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, because it lacks electronegative heteroatoms such as oxygen or nitrogen. Its functional character comes entirely from the alkyne units and the silicon-carbon bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two trifluoromethyl groups at the 1 and 4 positions, making it a para-disubstituted aromatic compound. The central scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion or additional rings. Each trifluoromethyl substituent carries three fluorine atoms on a single carbon attached to the ring, and these groups are strongly electron-withdrawing. The structure has high symmetry, with a center of inversion and two mirror planes passing through the ring, and it is rigid, since the aromatic core allows no conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the weakly basic fluorine atoms.

The molecule is a symmetric bis(phenylethynyl)benzene: a central para-disubstituted benzene ring bearing two carbon-carbon triple bonds, each of which links to a terminal unsubstituted phenyl ring. The scaffold is fully conjugated and linear, with the alkyne units enforcing a rod-like geometry and the two ends related by a center of symmetry. There are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, and no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, so the molecule is purely hydrocarbon in character. Its rigidity comes from the alkyne linkers, which limit rotation and conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. Each substituent is a glycidyl ether group: an oxygen atom attached to a CH2 linker that connects to a three-membered epoxide (oxirane) ring. The two epoxide-bearing arms are chemically identical, giving the molecule a centrosymmetric, symmetrical outline. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ether linkages and CH2 spacers add some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its two ether oxygens and two epoxide oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a symmetric bisphosphine built from a flexible four-carbon (butane-1,4-diyl) chain whose two ends each carry a phosphorus atom. Each phosphorus is bonded to the chain and to two separate phenyl rings, so the phosphorus centers are trivalent and tertiary, and the structure contains six unfused benzene rings with no fused ring systems. The molecule has no stereocenters and a near-C2 or mirror-like symmetry about the midpoint of the central methylene chain. The aliphatic linker gives it considerable conformational flexibility, while the aromatic rings are rigid and planar. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the phosphorus lone pairs can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, fully aromatic oligoheteroaryl chain built from a central para-phenylene ring flanked on each side by an oxazole ring, with each oxazole further bearing a phenyl substituent at its 5-position. Both oxazole rings are attached at their 2-positions to the central benzene, giving a near-symmetric, rod-like scaffold with a twofold axis through the middle of the central ring. The ring nitrogens of the two oxazoles can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The extensive conjugation and single-bond linkages between rings make the molecule largely planar and rigid.

Let me parse the structure: the central unit is a para-phenylene ring bearing two oxazole rings at its 1 and 4 positions. Each oxazole carries a methyl group at one carbon and a phenyl ring at the adjacent carbon, with the oxazole bonded to the central ring through its C2 position. The fused-looking aromatic framework is a rigid, extended, conjugated system with few rotatable bonds.

The molecule is built around a central piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other. It offers four hydrogen-bond donors from the two terminal primary amines, and its four nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a symmetric, fully aromatic hydrocarbon built from three benzene rings connected in a line. A central para-substituted benzene ring carries an ethylene (two-carbon) linker on each of its two opposite positions, and each linker terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The molecule contains no heteroatoms, functional groups, or stereocenters, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. Its linear, extended shape is mostly rigid due to the aromatic rings, with some rotational flexibility at the two ethylene bridges.

The molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring bearing two identical trans-styryl arms, so it is best described as a central 1,4-phenylene core linked through two vinylene bridges to two ortho-tolyl groups. Each ortho-tolyl unit carries a methyl group adjacent to the point of attachment, and the two aromatic rings are unfused, connected only through rigid, planar C=C double bonds. The overall skeleton is highly conjugated and nearly linear, with a two-fold symmetry axis running through the central ring. Lacking any hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donors and offers only weak, aromatic-based acceptor character, and the rigid stilbene-like linkages restrict conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying two identical substituents at the para positions, giving it a symmetric, linear arrangement. Each substituent is a 1-(hydroxymethyl)ethyl group, consisting of a branched carbon bearing a methyl group and a CH2OH arm. The two primary alcohol groups provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability at both ends of the molecule. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the side chains contain rotatable single bonds that add conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents at the para positions, so the scaffold is a simple 1,4-disubstituted aromatic core with no fused rings. Each ring carbon attached to the core is bonded to an ether oxygen, which links through a methylene group to a terminal trifluoromethyl group, giving two symmetric arms. The molecule has a two-fold axis and a center of inversion through the ring, so it is highly symmetric and fairly rigid in the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom in the flexible CH2–O linkers. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a symmetric diol built around a central diyne unit, with two carbon atoms each bearing a hydroxyl group and a cyclohexane ring. Each cyclohexane ring is saturated and unfused, and the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group also serves as the attachment point linking the ring to the rigid butadiyne bridge. The two halves are identical, giving the whole structure a mirror-symmetric, linear arrangement. The linear alkyne segment imposes substantial rigidity along the central axis, while the cyclohexane rings retain conformational flexibility. Each tertiary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule has two donor sites and two acceptor sites overall.

The molecule is built from two saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing rings joined directly by a single carbon-nitrogen bond, so there is no fused ring system. One ring is a piperidine in which the nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to three carbons, while the other is a piperidine whose nitrogen is secondary, carrying an N-H group, and which is attached through its carbon at the 4-position to the first nitrogen. The overall skeleton is fully saturated, with no aromatic rings, double bonds, or other functional groups beyond the two amine nitrogens. Both rings adopt flexible chair-like conformations, and the molecule has a rotatable connection between them. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while both nitrogen lone pairs can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring, giving a bicyclic 2,3-dihydro-1,4-benzodioxine scaffold. The two oxygen atoms of the dioxane ring are attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the ethylene bridge between them is flexible while the fused benzene portion is planar and rigid. A sulfonyl chloride group, with a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, sits on the benzene ring at a position para to one of the ring oxygens and meta to the other. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring oxygens also act as weak acceptors. The overall arrangement is asymmetric because the sulfonyl chloride breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a 1,4-dioxane ring, giving a bicyclic benzodioxane scaffold in which the two oxygen atoms of the saturated ring are attached to adjacent aromatic carbons. The fused ring system is largely planar on the aromatic side, while the two-carbon ethylene bridge of the dioxane ring adds some conformational flexibility. A single aldehyde group (a formyl, –CHO) is attached to the benzene ring, giving the molecule a carbonyl acceptor site. The substitution pattern is 1,3,4 on the benzene ring relative to the fused oxygens, which leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry axis. The two ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a 1,4-benzodioxane scaffold, in which a saturated six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring is fused to a benzene ring through two adjacent aromatic carbons. The saturated ring contains two ether oxygens, and a carbon bearing a thiocarboxamide group (a primary thioamide, C(=S)NH2) is attached at the position next to one of those oxygens. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid because of the aromatic ring, while the saturated ring can adopt a puckered conformation. The thioamide group offers two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 and a weaker acceptor through its sulfur, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane.

The molecule is built on a 1,4-benzodioxane scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring through two adjacent oxygen-bearing carbons. The saturated dioxane ring contains two ether oxygens and a stereogenic carbon at the 2-position, which carries a carboxylic acid group. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion shows no additional substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is fairly rigid, while the carboxylic acid group and the dioxane ring's puckering allow limited conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the two ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the carboxylic acid on the saturated ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a six-membered 1,4-dioxane ring, giving a bicyclic benzodioxane scaffold. An aromatic primary amine (an –NH2 group) sits on the benzene ring, and it is positioned meta to one ring oxygen and para to the other, placing it on a carbon adjacent to one fused-ring carbon. The two ether oxygens are part of the saturated ring, which contains a flexible two-carbon ethylene bridge, while the fused aromatic ring remains planar and rigid. Overall the molecule lacks any symmetry because the amino group breaks the otherwise symmetric arrangement of the fused system. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the two ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is 1,4-benzenedithiol, built on a single benzene ring with six aromatic carbons. Two thiol groups (-SH) are attached at the 1 and 4 positions, which are para to each other on the ring, giving a symmetric, linear substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the thiol groups can rotate about their C-S bonds, adding only minor flexibility. Each sulfur carries a hydrogen that can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, and the sulfur atoms can also serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, so its scaffold is a simple six-membered aromatic core. Two hydroxymethyl groups (–CH2OH) are attached at the 1 and 4 positions, making the substitution pattern para and giving the molecule a centrosymmetric, highly symmetric shape. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the two CH2–OH arms add some conformational flexibility around their single bonds. Each terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule has two of each capability at opposite ends.

This molecule is a large macrocyclic polyamine-type scaffold containing a 15-membered-type ring built from alternating nitrogen and alkyl chain segments, with three of its four ring nitrogens acylated. Three tert-butyl carbamate (Boc) groups are attached to three of the nitrogens, each contributing a carbonyl oxygen acceptor and a bulky tert-butyl ester moiety that adds significant steric bulk. The fourth ring nitrogen is a free secondary amine, which serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The macrocycle is flexible, with multiple methylene linkers allowing conformational freedom, while the Boc groups break any overall symmetry and create an asymmetric substitution pattern around the ring.

The molecule is a saturated macrocyclic polyamine built from a ring of alternating nitrogen and saturated carbon atoms, with four tertiary nitrogen atoms each carrying an N-methyl group. The ring contains two-, three-, and four-carbon linkers between nitrogens, so it is a fourteen-membered-type cyclic polyamine rather than a fused polycycle, with no aromatic rings or double bonds. The four nitrogens are spaced around the ring, giving a substitution pattern that is symmetric across the ring's midpoint. Because all nitrogens are tertiary and bear methyl groups, the molecule has no N–H or O–H groups and therefore no hydrogen-bond donor capability, but each nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is conformationally flexible, though the saturated framework limits how freely it can fold.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyamine built on a single large ring containing four tertiary nitrogen atoms, with two-carbon and three-carbon linkers alternating between them, giving a cyclic scaffold with mixed ring sizes. Each of the four nitrogens carries an arm of the form CH2-C(=O)-O-CH2CH3, so the molecule bears four ethyl ester groups. The arrangement of the four identical pendant arms around the ring gives a high degree of local symmetry. The ring is fairly flexible, though the ring nitrogens restrict conformational freedom to some extent. The molecule has no N-H or O-H groups, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor, but its nitrogen and ester oxygen atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a cage-like polyamine built from a bicyclic framework of fused and bridged saturated rings, containing four tertiary nitrogen atoms and no carbonyls, aromatic rings, or other functional groups. Every nitrogen is bonded to three carbon atoms within the cage, so none carries a hydrogen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The four nitrogen lone pairs, however, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The structure is rigid and three-dimensionally compact, with the nitrogens sitting at bridgehead-like positions that lock the ring system into a fixed geometry. The overall arrangement shows high symmetry, reflecting the repeating ethylene and propylene linkers between the nitrogen centers.

The molecule is a single macrocyclic ring built from alternating ethylene and propylene linkers joined by secondary amine nitrogens, giving a fourteen-membered saturated polyaza ring containing four ring nitrogens. There are no fused rings, aromatic systems, or exocyclic functional groups beyond the amine N–H bonds, and the four nitrogens are spaced symmetrically around the ring, so the scaffold has a pseudo-symmetric arrangement with a regular repeating pattern. Because every ring atom is sp3-hybridized and the ring is saturated, the framework is fairly rigid in its core but conformationally flexible at the methylene bonds. Each of the four secondary amine nitrogens can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. It carries four methyl substituents, all attached to carbon atoms of the aromatic rings, so there are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups present. The methyl groups sit at the 1, 2, 4 and 6 positions in a non-symmetric arrangement, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its substitution pattern. The rigid planar ring system leaves very little conformational flexibility, since the only rotatable bonds are the single bonds to the methyl groups. Because it contains no oxygen or nitrogen atoms and no N–H or O–H groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a macrocyclic polyether-thioether ring, built from a 21-membered-type cyclic backbone of repeating two-carbon units separated by sulfur and nitrogen atoms. Its skeleton is one large saturated loop containing three thioether sulfur atoms and one secondary amine nitrogen, with no fused or bridged ring systems and no aromatic rings. The only functional groups are the thioether linkages and the secondary amine, and the heteroatoms are distributed around the ring with no repeating symmetry beyond a rough pseudo-threefold arrangement. Because the ring is saturated and built from many single bonds, it is highly flexible, though the sulfur and nitrogen atoms restrict it somewhat. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen and sulfur atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small cyclic sulfonate ester built on a four-membered-or-larger heterocycle: the ring contains one sulfur atom bearing two terminal oxygen atoms (a sulfonyl group, S=O twice) and one ring oxygen bonded to that sulfur, with three ring carbons completing the cycle. Because the sulfur is fully oxidized and joined to the ring oxygen, the scaffold is a saturated, monocyclic sultone-type system with no ring fusion and no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted apart from the sulfonyl oxygens. The sulfonyl group is tetrahedral at sulfur and the saturated carbon chain is flexible, though the small ring constrains its conformations, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond what the ring geometry imposes. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the ring ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic chain of three carbon atoms, with a sulfur atom bonded to each end, giving a linear, straight-chain scaffold. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no double bonds, so it is highly flexible and can adopt many rotameric conformations about its C–C and C–S single bonds. Each terminal sulfur carries a single hydrogen, making these thiol groups, and the molecule has two equivalent ends, so its overall structure is symmetric about the central carbon. The thiol hydrogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a symmetric diester built from two para-toluenesulfonyl (tosyl) groups linked through a three-carbon propane-1,3-diyl chain. Each end carries an aromatic benzene ring bearing a methyl group para to the sulfonyl attachment, so the two halves are identical and the molecule has a mirror or two-fold symmetric arrangement about the central chain. The sulfonate ester linkages (S(=O)(=O)O) are the key functional groups, and the sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The three-carbon chain gives moderate conformational flexibility, whereas the two aromatic rings are rigid planar units.

The molecule is a short, fully saturated acyclic chain of three carbon atoms, with a hydroxyl group attached to each terminal carbon, giving a linear skeleton with no rings or ring fusion. Both functional groups are primary alcohols, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical, and the two ends are chemically equivalent. The chain is flexible, since its carbon-carbon bonds allow free rotation and many conformations. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H group and an acceptor through its lone pairs, so the molecule has two donor and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two identical cyanomethyl groups attached at the 1 and 3 positions, giving a meta substitution pattern. Each substituent is a methylene linker bonded to a terminal nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond), so there are no fused rings and the aromatic core is the only ring system. The structure has a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring's C2 and C5 positions, and the aryl ring and linkers make it fairly rigid, while the CH2-CN arms retain some rotational freedom. The nitrile nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents placed meta to each other, giving a 1,3-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. Each substituent is a carboxymethyl group, meaning a methylene bridge linking the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid. The two carboxylic acid groups each contain both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, so the molecule can engage in multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two flexible methylene-carboxyl arms add conformational freedom. The substitution pattern lacks a true mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two arms identical in every orientation, though the meta arrangement gives it an approximate two-fold relationship between the arms.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two isocyanate groups (–N=C=O) on meta positions, so the two substituents sit separated by one carbon on the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings, and its substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring's C-2 and C-5 positions. Each isocyanate group is a linear, cumulated N=C=O unit that is largely planar with the ring, so the overall scaffold is rigid and flat with little conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H bonds. Its oxygen and nitrogen atoms serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two sulfur atoms, a 1,3-dithiane ring. The ring has no fused rings and no substituents, so its substitution pattern is unsubstituted and its skeleton consists only of carbon and sulfur atoms joined by single bonds. The sulfur atoms sit at the 1 and 3 positions, separated by a methylene carbon, which gives the ring a mirror-plane symmetry through the central carbon and the opposite methylene. The chair-like ring is conformationally flexible but has no rotatable side chains. The molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two thioether sulfur atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, forming an indane-type scaffold. The five-membered ring contains two ketone carbonyl groups, one at each end of a central methylene linkage, so the ring is a 1,3-dione that sits directly against the aromatic ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, bearing only hydrogens, and the fused system is largely planar and rigid, with limited conformational freedom. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The methylene carbon between the two carbonyls is acidic and can tautomerize to an enol form.

The molecule is built on an isobenzofuran-type scaffold, specifically a benzofuran core in which the furan ring is fused to a benzene ring, so the bicyclic system is planar and largely rigid. Two phenyl rings are attached as substituents: one at the 1-position and one at the 3-position of the five-membered furan ring, both flanking the oxygen atom. The molecule contains no polar functional groups beyond the ring ether oxygen, which can only accept hydrogen bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its overall shape is roughly symmetric about the axis through the furan oxygen and the fused benzo ring, though the phenyl rings can twist relative to the core, giving some conformational flexibility at those two bonds.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds. Two tert-butyl groups are attached to the ring, each consisting of a central quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups. The two substituents sit at the 1 and 3 positions, a meta arrangement that gives the ring a mirror plane through the unsubstituted carbons. The bulky tert-butyl groups are bonded to the ring by single bonds and rotate around them, but the aromatic core itself is planar and rigid. The molecule contains no heteroatoms, so it has no functional groups such as hydroxyls, carbonyls, or amines, and it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor.

The molecule is a diphenylguanidine-type structure: a central guanidine carbon bearing an imine nitrogen (=NH) and two amine nitrogens, each of which connects to an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The two benzene rings are not fused to anything; each is a simple six-membered aromatic ring attached through a single nitrogen, so the scaffold is a flat, conjugated core with two separate aryl arms. The arrangement is approximately symmetric about the central C–N framework, though the imine nitrogen breaks strict symmetry. Rotation about the C–N bonds gives moderate flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid. The guanidine unit provides multiple hydrogen-bond donors from its N–H groups and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability at the imine nitrogen and the delocalized nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is a symmetrical ketone built from two benzyl groups joined through a central carbonyl, giving a 1,3-diphenylacetone-type scaffold. Each terminal ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so there are no ring fusions and no substituents on the aromatic carbons, leaving the two phenyl groups mirror-related about the carbonyl carbon. The only functional group is the ketone, whose oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two methylene linkers provide some conformational flexibility, while the phenyl rings remain planar and rigid.

This molecule is built on a four-carbon chain bearing two separate phenyl rings. One phenyl group is attached to a carbonyl carbon, forming an aryl ketone, while the second phenyl ring sits on a branched methine carbon along the chain, giving the scaffold a flexible, non-fused architecture with no bridged or fused ring systems. The two benzene rings are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple, and the overall arrangement lacks any internal symmetry because the two aromatic groups occupy chemically distinct positions. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all its hydrogens are carbon-bound. Rotation about the several sp3 carbon bonds makes the chain fairly flexible.

The molecule is a short, flexible acyclic scaffold built from a three-carbon chain bearing a secondary hydroxyl group on the central carbon, with a phenoxy group attached through an ether oxygen at each terminal carbon. Its two benzene rings are unfused and independent, each unsubstituted, so the aromatic portions carry no additional functional groups. The molecule is roughly symmetric about the central carbinol carbon, with the two phenoxymethyl arms mirror-related. Because the chain contains several rotatable single bonds, the structure is conformationally flexible. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a diaryl ether built from three benzene rings joined in a meta-linked chain: two phenoxy groups attached to the 1 and 3 positions of a central benzene ring. Each ether oxygen bridges two aromatic carbons, so the scaffold is fully aromatic with no sp3 carbons and no fused ring systems. The only functional groups are the two ether linkages, and the substitution pattern on the central ring is meta, which breaks any mirror symmetry through the middle ring and gives a bent, non-linear shape. The two terminal rings are unsubstituted phenyl groups. The C–O–C bonds allow some rotation about the aryl-oxygen bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility around the core. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 1,3-diketone built from a three-carbon chain with carbonyl groups at both ends, each bearing an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The central methylene carbon sits between the two carbonyls, making it an acidic, flexible linker that can enolize. Both aromatic rings are monosubstituted benzene rings with no ring fusion, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the central CH2 group. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors in its diketo form. Its rotatable single bonds give it moderate conformational flexibility around the central chain.

The molecule is a single saturated five-membered ring containing one oxygen atom at the 1-position and a second oxygen atom at the 3-position, giving a 1,3-dioxolane scaffold. Every ring carbon is sp3-hybridized and bears two hydrogens, so there are no double bonds, aromatic rings, or other functional groups beyond the two ether oxygens. The ring is unsubstituted, and the two oxygens sit across from each other, which places the molecule in a relatively symmetric, low-strain arrangement with some conformational flexibility from ring puckering. Each oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pairs, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diarylguanidine built around a central carbon bearing three nitrogen atoms, one of which is doubly bonded to the carbon as an imine. Two identical ortho-tolyl groups, each a benzene ring carrying a methyl group adjacent to the nitrogen attachment, are attached to the two amino nitrogens of the guanidine core. The substitution pattern is ortho on both rings, which places the methyl groups near the guanidine and makes the two aryl halves structurally equivalent, giving the molecule approximate two-fold symmetry. The aryl rings can rotate about their C–N bonds, so the framework is moderately flexible, though the planar guanidine unit imposes some conformational restriction. The imine nitrogen and the two NH groups provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the aromatic rings contribute additional lipophilic surface.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two nitro groups, each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, a meta relationship. This 1,3-substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror plane passing through the two substituted carbons and the carbon between them, so it has a high degree of symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the nitro groups can rotate somewhat around their bonds to the ring. The oxygen atoms of the nitro groups are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a six-membered heterocycle built around a thiobarbiturate-type scaffold: a ring containing two nitrogen atoms, two carbonyl carbons, and a thiocarbonyl carbon, with one methylene carbon between the two carbonyls. Both ring nitrogens each carry an unbranched n-butyl chain, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the ring. The thiocarbonyl sits between the two nitrogens and the two carbonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the nitrogens are fully substituted and cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The ring is non-aromatic and relatively flexible, and the two butyl chains add conformational freedom, although the amide-like planarity of the nitrogen-carbonyl linkages limits rotation within the core.

The molecule is a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, with carbonyl groups on the carbons flanking the nitrogens, which gives it a uracil-like pyrimidinedione scaffold. Both ring nitrogens carry a methyl substituent, so the ring has no N-H hydrogen-bond donors. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ring is largely planar, with a conjugated system of two C=C and two C=O bonds. The two remaining ring carbons are unsubstituted and sp2-hybridized, one bearing a hydrogen and the other part of the C=C bond. Overall, the structure is rigid and fully aromatic-like, with only the N-methyl groups providing limited rotational freedom and no molecular symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the C5 and C2 positions.

This molecule is built on a six-membered heterocyclic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, with three carbonyl groups arranged around it. Both nitrogens carry a methyl substituent, and one of the ring carbons is a methylene (CH2) group flanked by two carbonyls, so the ring is fully saturated at that position with no additional fusion or appended rings. The scaffold has a cyclic imide-type arrangement with two carbonyls bridging each nitrogen, giving the ring a largely planar and rigid character. The methyl groups are placed symmetrically on the two nitrogens, lending the core an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central methylene. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since both nitrogens are fully substituted, while the three carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyrimidine-2,4-dione ring, a uracil-type heterocycle carrying two nitrogen-bound methyl groups, one on each ring nitrogen flanking the carbonyl carbons. The ring is fully substituted: a methylamino group sits on one ring carbon and a formyl (aldehyde) group sits on the adjacent carbon, which creates a compact, ortho-arranged pairing of substituents. The scaffold is a single fused-free ring with no additional ring systems, so the framework is rigid and largely planar, with only the methyl and aldehyde groups providing rotational freedom. Two carbonyl oxygens and the aldehyde oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the secondary amine N–H is the sole hydrogen-bond donor. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two N-methyl groups occupy different environments relative to the amino and formyl substituents.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, which makes it a cyclic urea scaffold. One ring nitrogen bears a methyl group and is directly bonded to a carbonyl carbon, which forms the urea functionality, while the second nitrogen also carries a methyl group and is attached to that same carbonyl carbon. The three methylene groups in the remaining ring positions are sp3 hybridized, giving the ring a flexible, non-aromatic character. The substitution pattern is symmetric about the carbonyl, with both nitrogens N-methylated and no free N-H groups. Consequently, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a five-membered saturated heterocycle, an imidazolidinone-type ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite one another across the ring. One nitrogen carries a methyl group and sits adjacent to a carbonyl carbon, forming a cyclic amide (lactam) with the carbonyl oxygen as an exocyclic double bond. The second nitrogen is a tertiary amine also bearing a methyl substituent, and it is connected to two ring methylene carbons. The ring is not fused to any other ring and is conformationally flexible in its saturated portion, while the amide linkage is planar. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since both nitrogens are fully substituted.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused heteroaromatic system: a five-membered pyrrole-type ring fused to a six-membered pyrimidinedione ring, giving a pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine-2,4-dione scaffold. The five-membered ring carries an N-propyl group on its nitrogen and a carboxylic acid substituent on the adjacent carbon, while the six-membered ring bears two N-methyl groups flanking two carbonyl groups. The two carbonyl oxygens and the carboxylic acid provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, and the carboxylic acid's hydroxyl also acts as a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused ring framework is largely planar and rigid, with the propyl chain and carboxylic acid providing the main points of conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the propyl, carboxyl, and methyl substituents are placed asymmetrically around the core.

The molecule is 1,3-dimethoxybenzene, built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms each bonded to a methyl group) are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, meta to one another, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical about an axis running through the carbon at position 2 and the carbon at position 5. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two ether side chains have some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. Each oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pairs, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds and no heteroatoms. Two isopropyl groups, each a central carbon bearing two methyl branches, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, giving a meta substitution pattern. Because the two substituents are identical and sit symmetrically across the ring, the molecule has a mirror plane and a twofold axis through the ring, so its structure is highly symmetric. Apart from the single aromatic ring, the molecule contains no fused rings, no polar functional groups, and no heteroatoms. Its only motion comes from rotation of the two isopropyl groups, so the skeleton is largely rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is 1,3-diiodopropane, a simple acyclic three-carbon chain with an iodine atom bonded to each terminal carbon. Its scaffold is a linear saturated propane backbone with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. The only functional groups are the two carbon-iodine bonds at the ends of the chain, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical and both halogens sit at equivalent positions. The molecule has a mirror plane through the central carbon, giving it a high degree of symmetry, and it is fairly flexible because rotation about its single bonds allows many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and because iodine is a weak acceptor and the molecule lacks any polar heteroatoms other than the halogens, its hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

The molecule is 1,3-diiodobenzene, built on a single benzene ring with a planar, fully aromatic six-membered carbon scaffold. Two iodine atoms are attached to ring carbons separated by one carbon, giving a meta substitution pattern. The molecule has a mirror plane through the ring, so it belongs to a relatively high-symmetry, C2v-type arrangement. The ring is rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the iodine substituents are monovalent halogen groups that add no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, so it is planar and rigid. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the same ring at positions that are meta to each other across the ring, giving a 1,3-substitution pattern on one side of the fused system. The other ring is unsubstituted, leaving the molecule without any mirror or rotational symmetry. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, so the molecule has two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

This molecule is a fully saturated six-membered ring containing one oxygen atom, a tetrahydropyran-type scaffold. Two carbons of the ring each carry a hydroxymethyl group and a hydroxyl group, and the ring oxygen is flanked by a hemiketal-type carbon, giving a second, anomeric-like hydroxyl adjacent to the ring oxygen. There is no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern places a total of four hydroxyl groups and two hydroxymethyl arms around the ring, making the molecule highly polar and quite flexible in its side chains. It has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry because the stereocentres are defined and asymmetric. Every hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ring oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two ethoxy substituents, each consisting of an oxygen atom linked to an ethyl group. The two ether groups sit at the 1 and 3 positions of the aromatic ring, giving a meta substitution pattern. The benzene core is planar and rigid, while the two ethyl chains add conformational flexibility at their ends. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring, reflecting its near-symmetric layout. Each ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing two fluorine atoms as its only substituents. The two fluorines sit at the 1 and 3 positions relative to each other, meaning they are separated by one unsubstituted carbon, so the substitution pattern is meta. The arrangement has a mirror plane passing through the carbon between the two fluorines and the opposite carbon, giving the molecule a simple symmetric shape. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and cannot act as hydrogen-bond donors, so the molecule has no donor capability.

The molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple linear butene backbone. The double bond between the second and third carbons has E (trans) geometry, with a chlorine atom on each terminal carbon: one on the vinylic carbon at the chain end and one on the terminal sp3 carbon, making it a dichlorinated butene. The molecule has no stereocenters and its two chlorine-bearing ends are not symmetric, so it lacks any meaningful symmetry element beyond the trans geometry. Its flexibility comes from free rotation about the two single C–C bonds, while the central C=C bond is rigid. The compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic ketone built on a three-carbon chain, with a central carbonyl group flanked by two chloromethyl arms. The carbonyl carbon sits at the center, with one chlorine-bearing methylene group on each side, giving a symmetric substitution pattern in which each terminal carbon carries a single chlorine atom. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the molecule is flexible, since its single bonds allow free rotation around the carbon backbone. The oxygen of the carbonyl group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it lacks any O–H or N–H bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms, making it a dichlorobenzene. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings or additional ring systems. The two chlorine substituents are attached at positions 1 and 3 of the ring, meta to each other, which gives the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring. The ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds beyond the C–Cl bonds. Neither chlorine acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and both can only weakly serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, so the molecule has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries three halogen substituents: two chlorine atoms and one iodine atom, all attached directly to the ring. The substitution pattern is meta-like, with the halogens spaced at alternating positions around the ring, giving the molecule a threefold-related arrangement of substituents. Because the halogens are placed asymmetrically relative to one another, the overall structure has only a limited symmetry element, a mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the halogens offer no hydrogen-bond donor capability, while their lone pairs make them only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework. A nitro group, consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, is attached to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions meta to the nitro group and meta to each other, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern across the ring. The molecule has a mirror plane passing through the nitro-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it, so it is highly symmetric and planar in its core. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the nitro group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three halogen substituents are attached: one fluorine and two chlorines, placed at positions that give a 1,2,4-substitution pattern around the ring, with the two chlorines adjacent to each other on one side and the fluorine opposite the lone chlorine on the other. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited symmetry, since the three halogens are not arranged identically. Because the halogens are not hydrogen-bond donors and their lone pairs are weak acceptors, the molecule offers essentially no hydrogen-bond donating capacity and only minimal acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a five-membered hydantoin-type ring, a saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms and two carbonyl groups, with the carbons flanking one nitrogen bearing two methyl groups. Both ring nitrogens are substituted with chlorine atoms, so the scaffold carries two N-chloro functional groups. The two carbonyl groups sit at positions adjacent to the nitrogens, making the ring a cyclic diacylamine. Because the ring is small and fully saturated, its conformation is fairly constrained, and the molecule has no internal symmetry that would make its two halves identical. The ring nitrogens bear no hydrogens, so they cannot act as hydrogen-bond donors, but the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. A nitroso group (N=O) is attached to one ring carbon, and chlorine atoms sit on the two carbons immediately flanking it, giving a 2,6-dichloro substitution pattern around the nitroso group. The remaining three ring positions carry hydrogens, so the substitution is asymmetric about the ring but the two chlorines are symmetrically placed relative to the nitroso group. The nitroso nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is rigid and planar, with few rotatable bonds beyond the single bond joining the nitroso group to the ring.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon chain (a propane skeleton) with no rings and no fused systems. Its central carbon carries a hydroxyl group, making it a secondary alcohol, and the two terminal carbons each bear a chlorine atom, so the substitution is symmetric about that central carbon. Because the chain is unbranched and has only single bonds, the molecule is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the chlorine atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is 1,3-dibromopropane, a simple acyclic three-carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms other than the two terminal bromine substituents. The scaffold is a straight, unbranched propane backbone, with one bromine atom bonded to each of the two terminal carbons, giving it a symmetrical linear arrangement. There are no ring systems or fused rings to describe, and the only functional groups are the two primary alkyl bromide (C–Br) bonds. The molecule is flexible, since rotation about its carbon–carbon single bonds is essentially free. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three halogen substituents. Two chlorine atoms and one fluorine atom are attached at adjacent positions around the ring, giving a 1,2,3-trihalogenated substitution pattern in which the fluorine sits between the two chlorines. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the halogens lie in the ring plane, so the structure has no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no symmetry axis that maps it onto itself beyond a single mirror plane through the fluorine-bearing carbon and the opposite carbon. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O-H or N-H groups. The halogen atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: fluorine, bromine, iodine, and a second bromine, with the remaining two ring positions carrying hydrogen atoms. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The halogens are arranged around the ring with the iodine flanked by the two bromines, and the fluorine sits meta to one bromine. Because the substituents are not symmetrically distributed, the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the ring, so its symmetry is low. The aromatic scaffold is rigid and planar, and the halogen atoms add no hydrogen-bond donor capability; the compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogens can only act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring at the meta positions relative to each other, meaning they are separated by one carbon atom, giving a 1,3-disubstitution pattern. The ring carries no other functional groups, so the only substituents are these two halogen atoms. Because the bromines sit symmetrically across the ring, the molecule has a mirror plane through the ring's C2 and C5 positions. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor sites beyond the weakly polar carbon-bromine bonds.

The molecule is built on a single acyclic carbon skeleton: a central quaternary carbon bearing two ethyl groups and two bromomethyl groups, so it has no rings and no fused ring systems. Each bromomethyl arm carries one bromine atom attached to a primary carbon, which are the only functional groups present. The substitution pattern is fully symmetric around the central carbon, with the two ethyl groups identical and the two bromomethyl groups identical. The chain is flexible because all bonds are single and freely rotatable, so the molecule can adopt many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built around a single tetrahedral carbon that carries two methoxy groups, making it an acetal-type center. Two bromomethyl arms extend from that same carbon, so the framework is a compact, branched aliphatic skeleton with no rings and no aromatic systems. Each bromomethyl group places a carbon-bromine bond at a primary position, which serves as a reactive electrophilic site. The two ether oxygens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the central carbon is fully substituted and the chain is short, the structure is fairly flexible about its single bonds yet compact overall.

This molecule is a symmetric diester built from a central benzene ring bearing two substituents at the 1 and 3 positions (a meta-disubstituted arene). Each oxygen on the central ring is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that is attached to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the structure contains three aromatic rings joined by two ester linkages. The ester groups are the only functional groups present, and each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two outer phenyl rings are unsubstituted, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry about the central ring. The ester linkages add some conformational flexibility, though the aromatic rings keep the overall framework fairly extended and rigid.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, namely a hexahydropyrimidine-type ring, with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached to one ring carbon. Both ring nitrogens are tertiary amines, each bearing a benzyl group (a CH2 linker to a phenyl ring), so the scaffold carries two separate aromatic rings and no ring fusion. The substitution pattern is asymmetric because the nitrile sits on a carbon that is not equidistant from the two nitrogens, although the two benzyl groups are chemically similar. The ring is conformationally flexible yet sterically encumbered by the bulky benzyl substituents. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all nitrogens are fully substituted, while the nitrile nitrogen and the two ring amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible propane backbone. Two primary amine groups sit at the two terminal carbons, while a secondary hydroxyl group is attached to the central carbon, which makes that central carbon a stereocenter. The structure is fully substituted only at those three positions and has no aromatic or fused ring systems, so it is conformationally flexible with free rotation about its single bonds. Each amine nitrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their attached hydrogens and as acceptors through their lone pairs. There is no internal symmetry because the central carbon carries a hydroxyl that differs from the hydrogen on the same carbon, though the two terminal amino groups are structurally equivalent.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic diamine built on a simple three-carbon chain. Its skeleton is linear and unbranched, with a primary amine group attached at each of the two terminal carbons. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups or substituents beyond these two amines. The structure is symmetric, since the same amino group sits at both ends of the chain, and it is highly flexible because rotation about its single bonds is essentially unrestricted. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor, through its N–H bonds, and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, through its nitrogen lone pair.

This molecule is a benzene-based diaryl ketone built on a central 1,3-disubstituted (meta) benzene ring. Two benzoyl groups, each a carbonyl bonded to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, are attached at positions 1 and 3 of the central ring, giving a symmetrical, C2-like arrangement across the central ring. The structure contains no fused ring systems; it is three separate aromatic six-membered rings linked through two carbonyl carbons. The two C=O groups are the only heteroatom-bearing functionalities, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and two carbonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The biaryl-like linkages allow moderate rotational freedom around the carbon-carbon bonds to the carbonyls, while the aromatic rings themselves remain rigid and planar.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two acetyl groups, each a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 3, giving a meta substitution pattern. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, so the two acetyl groups are equivalent. The ring and the planar carbonyl groups make the scaffold largely rigid, with some rotational freedom around the bonds to the methyl groups. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. Two acetyl groups are attached: one carbonyl-bearing acetyl sits on carbon 3 of the pyrrole-type ring, and the other is bonded directly to the ring nitrogen, so the nitrogen is acylated and no longer carries an N–H. Both acetyl carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor, since the only N–H has been replaced. The four benzo-ring carbons are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is limited to the pyrrole ring. Apart from the rotation of the two acetyl methyl groups, the framework is largely rigid, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element that maps it onto itself.

This molecule is a symmetric diaryl compound built from two pyridine rings joined by a flexible three-carbon chain. Each pyridine is a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, and the two rings are connected through a saturated propylene linker, so there is no ring fusion. The nitrogen atoms sit at the 4-positions of their respective rings (para to the attachment point), giving the molecule a pseudo-C2 symmetry axis through the central chain. Both nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors via their lone pairs, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central propyl linker provides conformational flexibility, whereas the two aromatic rings are planar and rigid.

This molecule is a chalcone-like enone in which a carbonyl group bridges two thiophene rings. One thiophene is attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, while the other is linked through a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond, giving a conjugated, planar-leaning backbone of roughly ten heavy atoms across the two aromatic five-membered rings. Each thiophene is an unsubstituted, electron-rich sulfur heterocycle, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no substituents beyond the ring hydrogens. The overall framework is largely rigid because of the conjugated enone, though the single bonds to each ring allow some rotation. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single eight-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclooctadiene skeleton, with no fused rings or substituents attached to it. Its two carbon-carbon double bonds sit at the 1 and 7 positions, so they are separated by a run of four saturated methylene carbons on one side and a single saturated carbon on the other side. The ring is non-planar and fairly flexible, able to adopt several conformations, and it has no polar functional groups. It carries no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its overall structure lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry that would make its faces or halves identical.

The molecule is a five-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopentane skeleton bearing two ketone groups at positions 1 and 3 relative to each other, which makes it a cyclopentane-1,3-dione. The ring is saturated apart from the two carbonyl carbons, and the two carbonyls are separated by a single methylene carbon, so the scaffold has a 1,3-dicarbonyl arrangement. The ring is small and conformationally constrained, with only modest flexibility from puckering. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any obvious rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the ring atoms.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane skeleton bearing two ketone (carbonyl) groups, which places it in the family of cyclic 1,3-diketones. The carbonyls sit at ring positions separated by one methylene carbon, so the two C=O groups are meta to each other across the ring. The ring is non-aromatic and not fused to any other ring system, and it adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a planar-projection approximation, since the two carbonyls are not equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while each carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a central three-carbon chain flanked by two amine nitrogens, with each terminal nitrogen bearing a quaternary carbon that carries three hydroxymethyl groups. Each of the two nitrogens is secondary, linked to one methylene-bridged propyl spacer on the other side. The molecule has no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and flexible, with multiple rotatable bonds along the linear propylene linker. It is roughly mirror-symmetric about the center of the propyl chain, since both halves carry identical tris(hydroxymethyl)methyl-substituted amine groups. Each of the six hydroxyl groups can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two secondary amine nitrogens can serve as additional donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is a single six-membered carbocyclic ring with no heteroatoms, so its scaffold is purely hydrocarbon. The ring contains two carbon-carbon double bonds, placed so that they are separated by two sp3 methylene carbons, which gives a non-conjugated, cyclohexa-1,4-diene-type arrangement. There are no ring fusions, no substituents, and no functional groups beyond the alkene units themselves. The molecule is fairly rigid at the double bonds but the saturated portion of the ring can pucker and flex. Because it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, it cannot participate in hydrogen bonding in either direction.

The molecule is a single saturated six-membered carbocycle, a cyclohexane ring with no fused or bridged rings and no double bonds. It carries two hydroxyl groups, each attached to a ring carbon, and these two carbons are separated by one methylene carbon, so the substituents sit in a 1,3 relationship on the ring. Because the ring is fully saturated, its geometry is flexible, able to adopt several chair and boat-like conformations, while the hydroxyl groups provide two hydrogen-bond donors and two hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks a mirror plane through the ring's substituted carbons in a way that yields two stereoisomeric forms, and the framework contains no aromatic or heteroatom ring components beyond the oxygens of the hydroxyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two trifluoromethyl groups, each attached to the ring carbon through a single bond. The two substituents sit at the 1 and 3 positions, making this a meta-disubstituted arrangement, and the scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion. Each CF3 group consists of a central carbon bonded to three fluorine atoms, giving the molecule a threefold local symmetry at each substituent and an overall mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the C–CF3 bonds allow limited rotation of the substituents. Lacking any N–H or O–H groups, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a meta-disubstituted benzene ring, with two trimethylsilyl-capped ethynyl groups attached at positions 1 and 3. Each alkyne is a rigid, linear unit, so the scaffold is essentially flat and stiff, with the silicon atoms extending outward from the ring through the triple bonds. The two arms are related by a mirror plane through the ring, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only heteroatoms are the silicon centers, which are tetravalent and carry only methyl groups, so there are no classical hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built from a flexible three-carbon propylene chain bridging two phosphorus centers, each of which carries two phenyl rings. Each phosphorus atom is trivalent and bonded to three aromatic-carbon-bearing groups, so there are six unsubstituted benzene rings in total, with no ring fusion and no additional functional groups. The overall arrangement is symmetric about the central CH2-CH2-CH2 linker, with the two diphenylphosphino units mirror-related. The propylene linker gives the scaffold considerable conformational flexibility, while the six phenyl rings add rigid planar bulk at each end. Because the phosphorus atoms carry only lone pairs and no N–H or O–H groups, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the phosphorus lone pairs.

The molecule is a small acyclic urea, with a central carbonyl group bonded to two nitrogen atoms, giving a simple linear scaffold with no rings and no ring fusion. Each nitrogen carries a hydroxymethyl substituent (–CH2–OH), so the two substituents are placed symmetrically on either side of the carbonyl and the molecule has a two-fold mirror-type symmetry in its connectivity. The hydroxymethyl groups are conformationally flexible because the single bonds allow rotation, although the amide-like C–N bonds of the urea core have partial double-bond character that restricts rotation about them. Each N–H and each terminal O–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the molecule substantial hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two identical substituents at the meta positions (1 and 3). Each substituent is a carbinol carbon that carries a hydroxyl group and two trifluoromethyl groups, so the molecule contains two tertiary alcohol centers and six C–F bonds in total. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the bulky hexafluoro-substituted carbinol arms can rotate around their single bonds to the ring. The overall structure has approximate two-fold symmetry through the benzene ring's axis perpendicular to the meta-substituent line. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built from two piperidine rings, each a saturated six-membered ring containing one secondary amine nitrogen, linked through a flexible three-carbon chain. Each piperidine is attached at its 4-position (the carbon opposite the nitrogen), so the two rings are related by a symmetric substitution pattern. The central propylene linker of three methylene groups allows considerable conformational freedom, so the molecule is flexible rather than rigid. Both ring nitrogens carry an N-H group, making each a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the molecule as a whole possesses a near-mirror-symmetric arrangement about the center of the linker.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two sulfonyl chloride groups, each consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, are attached at the 1 and 3 positions, giving a meta substitution pattern. The arrangement has a mirror plane running through the ring's carbon atoms at positions 2 and 5, so the molecule is symmetric about that plane. The ring is rigid and planar, while the sulfonyl groups add only limited rotational freedom around the carbon-sulfur bonds. The oxygen atoms of the sulfonyl groups are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing two oxygen atoms bridged by a single methylene carbon, forming a 1,3-benzodioxole scaffold. The aromatic six-membered ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern consists only of the two shared carbons that connect it to the dioxole ring. The fused ring system is essentially planar and rigid, and the molecule has a mirror plane through the methylene carbon, giving it a high degree of symmetry. The two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, it contains an aromatic ring and a cyclic acetal-type ether functionality with no other functional groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon scaffold. Three tert-butyl groups, each a central carbon bearing three methyl substituents, are attached to the ring at positions 1, 3, and 5, giving a symmetric meta-substitution pattern. There are no heteroatoms and no other functional groups, so the molecule is purely hydrocarbon. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the bulky tert-butyl groups are sterically crowded and largely non-polar. Because it lacks any hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, its only interactions are dispersive, and the structure has an approximately threefold symmetry axis through the ring centre.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxymethyl groups, each a CH2 unit bonded to an OH group. The two substituents sit on carbons separated by one ring carbon, giving a meta (1,3) substitution pattern on an aromatic six-membered ring that has no ring fusion. The structure has a mirror plane through the ring, so it is symmetric about that axis. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two CH2–OH arms add some rotational flexibility. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the oxygen atoms are the only heteroatoms present.

This molecule is a central benzene ring carrying three phenyl substituents at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a 1,3,5-triarylbenzene scaffold built entirely from aromatic six-membered rings with no fused ring systems or heteroatoms. Each attached phenyl ring is linked by a single bond to the central core, and the molecule has no functional groups, so there are no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The substitution pattern is symmetric, with the three outer rings related by a threefold axis through the central ring, which makes the overall framework planar-to-twisted and fairly rigid, with restricted rotation about the biaryl bonds.

The molecule is built on a six-membered heterocyclic core containing three nitrogen atoms and three carbonyl carbons arranged alternately, forming a fully substituted triazinane-trione scaffold. Each of the three ring nitrogens carries a flexible two-carbon chain terminating in a hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is symmetric, with the three side chains placed at identical positions around the ring. The ring is fused to nothing else, and its rigid planar-leaning core contrasts with the three freely rotating hydroxyethyl arms. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and each terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, and it carries no fused rings. One nitrogen bears a methyl group, while the ring also has three carbon-attached substituents: two methyl groups and a formyl (aldehyde) group, which together define a fully substituted, asymmetric substitution pattern. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all N-H or O-H sites are absent. The planar aromatic core is rigid, with only the aldehyde and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered heterocycle built on a 1,3,5-trioxane scaffold, meaning a ring of alternating carbon and oxygen atoms with three oxygens and three methylene carbons. It contains no fused rings, no substituents, and no functional groups beyond the ether linkages themselves, so every ring atom is simply a CH2 or an ether oxygen. The structure has high symmetry, with threefold rotational symmetry about an axis through the ring centre, and the ring adopts a relatively rigid chair-like conformation. The three oxygen atoms can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since it carries no O-H or N-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at alternating positions, at carbons 1, 3, and 5 relative to one another, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern. Because of this arrangement, the molecule has a threefold axis of symmetry through the ring center, and the three ether side chains are chemically equivalent. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while each methoxy group can rotate about its C–O bonds, adding modest conformational flexibility. The oxygen atoms are hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which places it in the pyrazole family.
