The ring carries three methyl substituents: one on each of the two non-adjacent carbon positions and one on the nitrogen atom bearing the N-H-free, fully substituted nitrogen (N1). Because the ring is fully substituted with no free N-H or exposed carbon-hydrogen positions on the ring itself, the scaffold has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The pyridine-like nitrogen (N2) retains a lone pair and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule is small, planar, and rigid, with the methyl groups as its only flexible elements, and it possesses an approximate mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings and no heteroatoms. Three isopropyl groups, each a two-carbon branch attached through a central carbon, are bonded to the ring at alternating positions, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted pattern with the substituents evenly spaced around the ring. Because of this arrangement, the molecule has three-fold rotational symmetry along the ring axis. The ring is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl groups have some rotational freedom about their bonds to the ring. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen atoms with no polar functional groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Three methoxy groups (oxygen atoms each bonded to a methyl group) are attached to the ring at three positions, and a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygen atoms, one double-bonded and one charged) occupies one of the remaining positions, flanked by two of the methoxy groups. The substitution pattern is therefore highly symmetric, with a mirror plane passing through the nitro-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy groups have some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. The ether oxygens and the nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at alternating positions, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern in which the substituents are symmetrically distributed around the ring. The arrangement gives the molecule a high degree of symmetry, with a three-fold rotational axis through the ring centre and the ring itself is rigid and planar. Each fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with fully conjugated, planar bonding and no fused rings. Three chlorine atoms are attached as substituents at alternating positions around the ring, at carbons 1, 3, and 5, giving a symmetric 1,3,5 substitution pattern. Because of this arrangement, the molecule has a threefold rotational axis and a high degree of symmetry, and the ring itself is rigid and flat with no rotatable bonds. The compound has no hydrogen-bond donor groups and no hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative atoms. The chlorine atoms can weakly act as halogen-type acceptors, but the molecule offers essentially no strong hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three terminal alkyne groups, each attached directly to the ring at alternating positions, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings. Each ethynyl substituent is linear and rigid, extending the molecule outward in a flat, star-like geometry with three-fold symmetry about the ring center. The terminal C-H bonds on the alkynes can act as weak hydrogen-bond donors, while the pi-electron-rich triple bonds offer only weak acceptor character, and the molecule contains no strong hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with fully conjugated pi bonds. Three fluorine atoms and one nitro group are attached as substituents. The nitro group, which consists of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with a formal positive charge on nitrogen, sits on one ring carbon, and fluorines occupy the two positions adjacent to it on one side and a third position across the ring, giving a 2,4,6-type arrangement of halogens relative to the nitro group. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only flexibility comes from rotation of the nitro group about its bond to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the ring's local planarity. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent because there are no N-H or O-H groups. The oxygens of the nitro group and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four halogen substituents: three chlorine atoms and one iodine atom, giving a tetrahalogenated aromatic scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-halogen bonds. Reading around the ring, the substituents sit at positions 1, 3, 4 and 5 (relative to a chosen starting carbon), so the iodine lies between two chlorines in a crowded 1,2,3-pattern flanked by hydrogens on the remaining carbons. The arrangement lacks a full mirror or rotational symmetry because the iodine is unique in both identity and position. The rigid aromatic core and halogen atoms create no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold. Three chlorine atoms and one nitro group are attached to that ring. The nitro group, drawn as an N-oxide with a positive nitrogen and negative oxygen, is a strongly electron-withdrawing acceptor-type substituent. The three chlorines sit at positions that leave the ring with no fused partners, so there is no ring fusion and the molecule is entirely planar and rigid, with only the nitro group able to rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the nitro group is flanked by two chlorines on one side and the remaining chlorine is set apart from it, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the chlorines offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three bromine atoms are attached directly to the ring at alternating positions, one at each of the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a symmetric substitution pattern. Because of this arrangement, the molecule has a threefold rotational symmetry axis through the centre of the ring, and the carbon-hydrogen positions between the bromines are equivalent. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the bromine substituents are the only functional groups present. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the halogens do not act as classical hydrogen-bond acceptors in this context.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Every ring carbon carries a halogen substituent, alternating between fluorine and chlorine around the ring, so the pattern is fully substituted with three fluorines and three chlorines. The arrangement has a threefold rotational symmetry axis through the ring center, giving it a highly symmetric, rigid, planar shape with no rotatable bonds. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, and its only acceptors are the weakly electronegative halogen atoms.

This molecule is built on a central benzene ring carrying three benzoyl groups, each attached through a carbonyl carbon, in a 1,3,5-substitution pattern that gives it three-fold symmetry. Each peripheral phenyl ring is unsubstituted and joined to the core by a ketone linkage, so the structure is a flat, extended aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems. The three carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Rotation about the single bonds connecting the carbonyl carbons to the rings gives moderate conformational flexibility, though the aromatic rings remain rigid.

The molecule is built around a saturated six-membered 1,3,5-triazinane ring, in which three nitrogen atoms alternate with three methylene carbons. Each of the three nitrogens carries a benzyl group, a phenyl ring attached through a single CH2 linker, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the central ring. The ring contains no double bonds and is not fused to any other ring system, while the three pendant benzene rings are unsubstituted. The nitrogens are tertiary amines with no N-H groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its three nitrogen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the scaffold is conformationally flexible at the benzyl linkers and at the ring, though its three-fold symmetry is preserved.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three acyl chloride groups (–C(=O)Cl) placed at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a symmetric meta-substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the three carbonyl substituents are conjugated with it, with the molecule possessing threefold symmetry about the ring's central axis. Each acyl chloride carbon is electrophilic and reactive toward nucleophiles, which makes the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygens but gives it no hydrogen-bond donor capability. There are no ring fusions, stereocenters, or flexible linkers, so conformational freedom is limited to rotation of the three acyl groups about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three carboxylic acid groups, each attached directly to the aromatic carbon framework, which makes it a benzenetricarboxylic acid scaffold. The three substituents sit at positions 1, 3, and 5 around the ring, giving a symmetric, evenly spaced arrangement with three-fold symmetry about the ring centre. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carboxyl groups can rotate somewhat about their single bonds to the ring. Each carboxyl group contains a hydroxyl that can donate a hydrogen bond and a carbonyl oxygen that can accept one, so the molecule offers three donor and up to six acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on an indoline (2,3-dihydroindole) scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The fused system is planar in its aromatic portion, while the saturated five-membered ring contributes some conformational constraint. Position 2 of the five-membered ring carries an exocyclic methylene group, and position 3 is a fully substituted quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, which makes that carbon non-chiral with respect to its two identical methyl substituents. The nitrogen is tertiary, bearing an N-methyl group, so it has no N–H donor capability. Its lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, with its overall shape being fairly compact and rigid.

The molecule is built on a single eight-membered carbocyclic ring with alternating double and single bonds, giving it a fully conjugated, unsaturated cyclic skeleton. Its ring carries no substituents, so every ring carbon bears one hydrogen and the overall pattern is perfectly symmetric, with each carbon chemically equivalent in a time-averaged sense. There are no heteroatoms, no ring fusion, and no functional groups of any kind, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The ring is conformationally flexible, able to adopt non-planar arrangements to relieve strain, while the conjugated double-bond system imposes local rigidity along its path.

This molecule is a small acyclic aliphatic diol with a three-carbon backbone, namely propane-1,2-diol. It contains no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated groups. The two hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, one at a secondary position and one at a primary position, so the substitution pattern is unbranched apart from the methyl group on the central carbon. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry because the two hydroxyl-bearing carbons are inequivalent. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic diester built on a three-carbon chain (a propane-1,2-diol skeleton) with no rings present. Both terminal hydroxyl positions of the diol are capped as acetate esters: one ester is attached to the unbranched primary carbon, and the other to the secondary carbon bearing a methyl branch, so the two acetoxy groups sit at different positions on the backbone. The molecule has no stereocenter symmetry, since the branched secondary carbon makes the two ester arms chemically distinct. Being built from a flexible sp3 chain with rotatable single bonds, it is conformationally flexible. Each ester carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two adjacent substituents, so it has an ortho disubstitution pattern. Each substituent is a carboxymethyl group, meaning a methylene bridge attached to a carboxylic acid, so the skeleton is a benzene core flanked by two two-carbon chains that each end in a terminal carboxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two side chains provide some conformational flexibility around their single bonds. Two carboxylic acid groups are present, each offering one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens. The arrangement lacks any internal symmetry that would make the two arms equivalent in every orientation, though the molecule is constitutionally symmetric about the ring axis.

The molecule is built on a benzene core bearing two substituents on adjacent (ortho) carbons. Each substituent is a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group: a cyanomethyl unit attached directly to the ring, so the structure is essentially a 1,2-bis(cyanomethyl)benzene scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two side chains have free rotation about their single bonds, giving the molecule some conformational flexibility at the periphery. The molecule has no stereocenters and retains an approximate mirror plane through the ring, so it is structurally symmetric. Each nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a bicyclic sugar-derived scaffold built from a furanose ring fused to a 1,3-dioxolane ring, with the two rings sharing a C–C bond so the fused system is rigid. The five-membered oxygen-containing ring carries a side chain of two carbons bearing a secondary hydroxyl and a primary hydroxyl, which gives the molecule a chiral, sugar-like appearance. The acetal carbon bearing two methyl groups on the dioxolane ring forms an isopropylidene-type ketal that protects two adjacent hydroxyls. One free secondary hydroxyl remains on the fused bicyclic core, and together with the two side-chain hydroxyls it makes the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The stereocenters are arranged so the molecule is asymmetric, with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a five-membered dioxaphospholane-type ring in which a phosphorus atom bears a single chlorine substituent and is bonded to two oxygen atoms. Each oxygen is attached to an adjacent carbon of a benzene ring, so the phosphorus-containing ring is fused to the aromatic six-membered ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The benzene portion carries four hydrogen-substituted positions and no additional substituents, giving an unsubstituted, planar aromatic framework. The overall scaffold is a rigid, largely flat bicyclic system with little conformational flexibility. Apart from the chlorine, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its oxygen atoms are the only potential hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short, symmetric acyclic chain built around a two-carbon ethene (C=C) linker. Each end of the linker carries a phosphorus atom bearing one double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups, so it is a bis(phosphonic acid) in which the two phosphonate units sit on opposite carbons of the double bond. The structure has no rings and no ring fusion, and its only substitution is at the two terminal alkene carbons. Its overall shape is roughly linear and planar about the double bond, and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the C=C bond. The four hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the four phosphoryl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic chain of nine carbons, with no ring systems and no aromatic or unsaturated portions. Its backbone is a straight run of six carbons ending in a branch point, where a secondary hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the terminal primary alcohol. The two hydroxyl groups are the only functional groups present, and they are positioned at the end of the chain, giving the molecule a vicinal diol arrangement with no symmetry. Because the carbon framework is composed entirely of freely rotating single bonds, the structure is highly flexible. Both hydroxyl oxygens and their hydrogens allow the molecule to act as two hydrogen-bond donors and two hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aliphatic epoxide: a three-membered oxirane ring bearing a long, unbranched alkyl chain. The chain contains sixteen carbon atoms in a straight run and is attached to one carbon of the strained ring, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted at the ring with no additional branching. The ring itself is a fused-free, non-aromatic cyclic ether carrying an oxygen atom bridging two carbons, and its angular strain makes the ring highly reactive toward nucleophilic opening. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one, and the extended alkyl chain gives it considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen in the ring can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is 1,2-ethanedithiol, a small acyclic two-carbon chain with a thiol group on each terminal carbon. Its scaffold is a simple saturated ethane backbone, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. The two sulfur-bearing groups sit at opposite ends of the same two-carbon unit, giving a symmetric, linear arrangement with a two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the C–C bond. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation about the central carbon–carbon single bond interconverts its conformers freely. Each thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond, while the sulfur atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule consists of two benzene rings joined by a flexible two-carbon linker, with an ether oxygen on each end of the chain (an ethylene-bridged bis-aryl ether). Each benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from the single oxygen attached to it, so the scaffold is a monosubstituted phenyl group on either side. The molecule is symmetric, with both halves identical and related by a two-fold axis through the midpoint of the ethylene bridge. The two aromatic rings are fully planar and rigid, while the central CH2-CH2 linker and the two C-O bonds give the overall structure considerable conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O-H or N-H groups, but its two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is 1,2-diphenylethane, built from two benzene rings joined through a flexible two-carbon ethylene bridge. Each ring is a simple unsubstituted six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused ring systems and no heteroatoms. The molecule contains no functional groups beyond the aromatic rings and the saturated CH2–CH2 linker. Its two phenyl groups are related by a symmetry relationship across the central bond, giving a symmetric overall framework. The ethylene linker rotates freely, so the molecule is conformationally flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is an acyclic ether with a two-carbon ethylene bridge connecting two methoxy-type termini: one end is a methyl group bonded through oxygen to a CH2CH2 unit, and the other end is a second oxygen bonded to a methyl group. Its skeleton is entirely saturated and carries no rings, aromatic systems, or fused frameworks. The only functional groups are two ether oxygens, which are the sole sites of polarity. The structure is essentially symmetric about the central C–C bond, with each oxygen flanked by a methyl and an ethylene carbon. Because it has single bonds throughout and no ring constraints, it is highly flexible, adopting multiple conformations. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring containing two nitrogen atoms at non-adjacent positions. The ring nitrogen bearing a methyl group sits on one side, and the other ring nitrogen is unsubstituted, which gives the core its characteristic basic, hydrogen-bond-accepting character. A methyl group is attached to a ring carbon adjacent to the unsubstituted nitrogen, and a nitro group (a strongly electron-withdrawing, polar substituent with two oxygen atoms) is attached to the other ring carbon. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, since the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring. Its rigid, planar aromatic core contrasts with the freely rotating methyl and nitro groups, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, with acceptor sites on the unsubstituted ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring, bearing two small alkyl substituents. The ring contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship: one nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary, pyrrole-type nitrogen, while the other is an unsubstituted, pyridine-type nitrogen. A second methyl group is attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens, so the scaffold has no ring fusion and no additional functional groups. Because the ring is planar and fully aromatic with only small methyl substituents, the structure is rigid and has no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl groups. The pyridine-type nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since all ring nitrogens are substituted or lone-pair bearing and no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is 1,2-diiodoethane, an acyclic two-carbon chain with an iodine atom bonded to each carbon. Its skeleton is simply a saturated ethane backbone, with no rings, no fused systems, and no additional functional groups beyond the two carbon-iodine bonds. Because the chain is free to rotate about the central carbon-carbon bond, the molecule is highly flexible, and its two iodine substituents can adopt different relative arrangements. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only weak acceptor character at the iodine atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents on its six carbons, arranged so that two methoxy groups sit side by side at adjacent positions and two nitro groups sit side by side at the opposite pair of adjacent positions, giving a 1,2-dimethoxy-4,5-dinitro substitution pattern. Each nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing N-oxide-type unit with two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while each methoxy oxygen is an ether acceptor with a methyl group attached. The two methoxy groups and two nitro groups are arranged with a center of symmetry through the ring, so the substitution is symmetric. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it contains no N–H or O–H groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. The scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused rings or extended conjugated appendages. Its substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis passing through the midpoint of the two substituted carbons, and the molecule is essentially planar and rigid. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and carry no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since the molecule has no N-H or O-H groups. Overall, the structure contains only carbon-hydrogen bonds on the ring apart from the two C-F bonds.

The molecule is a bicyclic hydrocarbon built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring that contains a single carbon-carbon double bond, giving a dihydronaphthalene-type scaffold. The aromatic ring is ortho-fused to the partially unsaturated ring, so the two rings share one edge of two adjacent carbons. There are no heteroatoms or functional groups such as hydroxyls, carbonyls, amines, or halogens, so the substitution pattern is simply the unsubstituted fused framework. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, with the fused system being nearly planar apart from the sp3-hybridized methylene carbons in the saturated portion of the second ring. Because it lacks any hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, its only interactions with other molecules are nonpolar, van der Waals-type contacts.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings and no heteroatoms. Two ethyl groups are attached to adjacent carbons of that ring, so the substitution pattern is ortho, placing them on neighboring positions. There are no functional groups beyond these alkyl substituents, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is planar and rigid, while the two ethyl chains are flexible and can rotate, though their proximity limits their conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make both substituents identical in environment, though it retains a local mirror plane through the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents in a 1,2,4,5-pattern: two adjacent methoxy groups (-OCH3) occupy positions opposite each other across the ring from two adjacent fluorine atoms, giving a symmetric arrangement with an apparent two-fold axis through the ring centre. The scaffold is a single aromatic ring with no fused rings, so the core is rigid and planar, while the two methoxy groups add modest rotational flexibility around their C-O bonds. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all its hydrogens sit on carbon. The fluorine atoms are electron-withdrawing and contribute to the polarity of the ring without providing hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is 1,2-diethoxybenzene, built on a single benzene ring with two ethoxy groups attached at adjacent carbons (ortho positions). Each ethoxy group consists of an oxygen atom bonded to the aromatic ring and to an ethyl chain, so the molecule contains two ether linkages and no other functional groups. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the two flexible ethyl tails can rotate freely, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility. The ortho substitution pattern leaves the molecule without a mirror-symmetric arrangement along the two ethoxy arms, though it retains an overall near-C2v-like shape. The two ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors but there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acyclic ether with a linear, flexible carbon-oxygen backbone: two ethyl groups bridged by a two-carbon ethylene-oxy-ethylene linker and a second ether oxygen. It contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters. Its two oxygen atoms are each bonded to two sp3 carbons, making them ether functionalities with no hydroxyl or carbonyl groups. The structure is highly symmetric, possessing a mirror-like arrangement about the central CH2-CH2 bond, and it is conformationally flexible owing to free rotation about its many single bonds. Each oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms in the ring. Two chlorine atoms are attached to adjacent carbons of that ring, so they sit in an ortho arrangement, one next to the other. Apart from these two halogen substituents, the remaining four ring positions carry only hydrogen. The structure has a two-fold symmetry axis that passes through the midpoints of the carbon-carbon bonds bearing the chlorines, and it is essentially rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds to speak of. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since chlorine is a weak, non-directional halogen and the molecule contains no N, O, or other polar functional groups.

This molecule is a short, fully saturated acyclic chain of three carbon atoms, with a chlorine atom bonded to each terminal carbon, giving a 1,3-disubstituted propane scaffold. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds, so its skeleton is entirely sp3 and flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. The molecule has a mirror plane through the central carbon, so its two chlorine-bearing ends are equivalent, giving it a symmetric substitution pattern. Its only functional groups are the two carbon-chlorine bonds, which do not act as hydrogen-bond donors and only weakly accept hydrogen bonds, so the molecule has no meaningful hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is a short, acyclic saturated hydrocarbon chain of four carbons with no rings, so its scaffold is flexible and open rather than rigid. Two chlorine atoms are attached as substituents: one sits on the second carbon, creating a secondary alkyl chloride, and the other is on the terminal carbon, forming a primary alkyl chloride. Because the chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions along the chain, the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, and the second carbon is a stereocenter. The compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, and its only acceptor-type sites are the weakly polar chlorine atoms, which accept hydrogen bonds poorly.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing four substituents. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, and an iodine atom sits on the carbon directly across the ring from the chlorine at the 4-position relative to the first chlorine. The overall substitution pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted, giving the molecule no mirror-symmetric axis through all three halogens, so it is asymmetric in its substitution. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the halogen substituents lying in the ring plane and little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. A nitro group (–NO2) is attached to one carbon of the ring, acting as a strong electron-withdrawing substituent and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, but it has no hydrogen-bond donors. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, forming a 1,2-dichloro arrangement, and they lie in a meta-like relationship to the nitro group, specifically at the 3 and 4 positions relative to it. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the ring itself. Overall, the structure is compact and rigid, with only the nitro group capable of rotation about its bond to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying a nitro group and two chlorine atoms, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The nitro group, drawn as a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one charge-separated, is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group attached to one ring carbon. The two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, with one of them flanked by the nitro group, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no symmetry axis that maps it onto itself, so it is asymmetric. The rigid aromatic ring makes it largely planar and conformationally restricted, with only the nitro group able to rotate. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three halogen substituents. A fluorine atom and two chlorine atoms are attached to adjacent and nearby ring carbons, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern in which the two chlorines sit on neighboring positions and the fluorine occupies a position across from the outer chlorine. The scaffold has no stereocenters and only a single molecular axis of approximate symmetry is lost because of the asymmetric halogen placement. The ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds beyond the carbon-halogen bonds themselves. Because all three substituents are halogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon chain (propane skeleton) with no rings, so it is fully flexible with free rotation about its single C–C bonds. It carries two bromine substituents: one on the central carbon and one on a terminal carbon, giving a 1,2-dibromo pattern on adjacent carbons. The molecule lacks symmetry because the two bromine-bearing carbons are in different environments, leaving a single stereocenter at the central carbon. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O–H or N–H groups. Its only potential acceptors are the halogen atoms, which are weak and not typically considered significant hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three halogen substituents on adjacent and near positions: two chlorine atoms and one iodine atom. Parsing the SMILES, the chlorine sits on one ring carbon, the iodine is positioned meta to it, and a second chlorine occupies the carbon adjacent to the first chlorine, so the two chlorines are ortho to each other. The scaffold is a single fused-free aromatic six-membered ring with no additional rings, making it planar and rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane approximation of symmetry through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak halogen-bond acceptors or contribute polarizability.

The molecule is an acyclic, saturated alkane skeleton built from a straight chain of four carbons, with no rings and no multiple bonds. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents: one sits on an interior carbon of the chain and the other on a terminal carbon, so the two halogens are on adjacent-but-separated positions along the same backbone. The structure lacks any mirror symmetry because the bromine substitution pattern is uneven, and the single-bond framework allows considerable conformational flexibility through free rotation about its C–C bonds. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since no O–H or N–H groups are present, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors in the classical sense, as the only heteroatoms are the halogens, which are weak acceptors at best.

This molecule is 1,2-dibromoethane, a two-carbon acyclic chain with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system. Each carbon carries two hydrogens and one bromine atom, and the two bromines sit on opposite ends of the C–C bond. The molecule is small, unbranched, and highly symmetric, with a center of inversion in its most stable conformations, and the C–C bond rotates freely, so the structure is flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks O–H or N–H groups, and the bromine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing four halogen substituents. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, and two bromine atoms occupy the neighboring positions, giving a 1,2-dibromo-4,5-difluoro substitution pattern. The arrangement has a two-fold symmetry axis that runs through the midpoints of the two C–C bonds bearing the halogens, so the two fluorines are equivalent and the two bromines are equivalent. The ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying two bromine substituents. The two bromines sit on adjacent carbons, so the substitution pattern is ortho, placing them next to each other on the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N–H or O–H groups, and it has no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors either. Its framework is entirely rigid and planar, with the only conformational freedom being the rotation of the C–Br bonds, and it has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoints of the C–C bonds between the substituted and unsubstituted carbon pairs.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated four-carbon chain (a butane-type skeleton) with no rings or ring fusion. Its central quaternary carbon carries a bromine atom and a nitrile group, and it is flanked by a bromomethyl arm on one side and a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal nitrile on the other. Two nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) groups and two carbon-bromine bonds are the only functional groups present. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two ends of the chain differ, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. Its flexible sp3 backbone allows free rotation about the single bonds, while the linear nitrile groups are rigid. The nitrogen atoms of the nitriles can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries five substituents on that ring: three fluorine atoms and two bromine atoms, with the hydrogen-bearing positions occupying the remaining sites. The two bromines sit on adjacent carbons, creating an ortho dihalogen pair, while the fluorines are spread around the ring at meta and para relationships to one another. Because the ring is fully substituted except for one carbon-bound hydrogen, the overall pattern is asymmetric and the framework is rigid and planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks any N-H or O-H groups, and its only potential acceptors are the halogen atoms, which act as weak acceptors at most.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a flexible two-carbon linker, with each ring bearing a secondary amine attached directly to the aromatic carbon. Each N-H nitrogen connects the phenyl ring to a methylene group of an ethylene bridge, so the scaffold is a symmetric N,N'-diphenylethylenediamine framework with no fused or heteroaromatic rings. Both phenyl rings are unsubstituted, so the aromatic substitution pattern is simple and identical on each side, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the center of the ethylene bridge. The central CH2-CH2 unit gives considerable conformational flexibility, while the two aromatic rings remain planar and rigid. Each of the two NH groups can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the nitrogen lone pairs can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diketone built on a central benzene ring bearing two benzoyl groups at adjacent (ortho) positions. Each carbonyl carbon links one aromatic ring to the central ring, so the scaffold consists of three benzene rings joined through two ketone bridges. The central ring is 1,2-disubstituted, while the two terminal phenyl rings are unsubstituted. The two ketone carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aryl-carbonyl linkages allow considerable rotation, so the structure is fairly flexible, though the ortho arrangement introduces steric crowding that restricts how the rings can twist relative to one another.

This molecule is a symmetric diketone built on a four-carbon chain, with a carbonyl group at each end. Each carbonyl carbon is attached to a phenyl ring, so the scaffold consists of two unfused benzene rings joined by a flexible saturated linker of two methylene groups. The two aryl ketone units are chemically equivalent, giving the molecule a near-mirror-symmetric, unsubstituted pattern with no additional functional groups on the rings. The chain bridging the rings allows conformational flexibility, while the aromatic rings remain planar and rigid. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built from two para-tolyl rings joined through a flexible two-carbon ethylene bridge, giving a symmetric scaffold with a central CH2–CH2 linker and no ring fusion. Each aromatic ring is a simple benzene ring carrying one methyl substituent positioned para to the bridge, so the substitution pattern is identical on both sides and the molecule possesses an approximate two-fold symmetry about the midpoint of the linker. Apart from the aromatic rings themselves, the only functional features are the alkyl methyl groups and methylene units, which are non-polar. Because the structure contains no heteroatoms, carbonyls, or N–H or O–H bonds, it cannot donate hydrogen bonds and offers no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The two ethylene carbons provide rotational freedom around the central bond, so the molecule is comparatively flexible, while each aromatic ring remains rigid and planar.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic diamine built on a three-carbon propane backbone. It has a methyl group on the central carbon, with a primary amine attached to that same carbon and a second primary amine on the terminal carbon, so the two amino groups sit on adjacent carbons in a 1,2-relationship. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic or unsaturated bonds, leaving the framework fully saturated and flexible with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two amines are on different carbons and the methyl branch breaks the chain's symmetry. Both amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their nitrogen lone pairs.

The molecule is a six-membered saturated carbocycle, cyclohexane-1,2-dione, in which two adjacent ring carbons each carry a ketone (C=O) group. There are no ring fusions, no heteroatoms other than the two oxygens, and no substituents beyond these carbonyl groups, so the scaffold is a simple, unbranched ring. The two carbonyls are vicinal, giving the ring an adjacent dicarbonyl motif, and the remaining four CH2 groups form a flexible aliphatic chain that closes the ring. The overall shape has no rotational or mirror symmetry in its full sense, though the 1,2-dione pattern gives it a local two-fold arrangement around the carbonyl pair. The carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present.

This molecule is a symmetric dimer built from two dihydronaphthalene units joined through a central two-carbon ethylene bridge. Each half contains a benzene ring fused to a partially saturated six-membered ring that carries one endocyclic carbon-carbon double bond, so the fused bicyclic framework is a 1,2-dihydronaphthalene-type system. The two bicyclic halves are attached at their alkene-bearing carbons through a CH2–CH2 linkage, giving a roughly mirror-symmetric arrangement. The molecule contains no heteroatoms and therefore no functional groups beyond aromatic rings and isolated alkenes. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it is an entirely hydrocarbon framework. The fused rings are rigid, while the central ethylene linker gives the molecule some conformational flexibility.

The molecule consists of two unsubstituted benzene rings, each attached through a sulfur atom to opposite ends of a two-carbon ethylene linker, giving a symmetric 1,2-bis(phenylthio)ethane skeleton with no fused ring systems. Each sulfur is a thioether (sulfide) functional group bridging a phenyl ring and a saturated CH2 unit, and the aromatic rings carry no other substituents. The molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through the central C–C bond, and the two flexible sulfur–carbon bonds allow considerable conformational freedom, while the phenyl rings remain planar and rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, and the sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a 1,2-diarylethane, in which two benzene rings are joined by a two-carbon saturated bridge. Each benzene ring carries a trifluoromethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment to the ethylene linker, so the two substituents are ortho to the bridge and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the middle of the CH2–CH2 bond. The trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no conventional hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors. The two ethylene carbons provide rotational flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and planar.

The molecule is a symmetric sulfone built around a two-carbon ethylene bridge that connects two sulfonyl groups. Each sulfur atom carries two oxygen atoms in a double-bonded sulfonyl arrangement and is bonded to a phenyl ring, so the scaffold consists of two identical benzenesulfonyl units joined end to end. Both benzene rings are unsubstituted, lacking any additional functional groups, which gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry through the central CH2–CH2 axis. The sulfonyl groups are strongly polar and act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic rings and sulfonyl groups provide rigidity, whereas the central ethylene linker permits conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a bis-phosphine built around a flexible two-carbon ethylene bridge (–CH2–CH2–) that links two tertiary phosphorus centers. Each phosphorus atom carries three phenyl rings, so the structure contains six benzene rings in total, each unsubstituted and attached directly to phosphorus. There are no fused ring systems, and the molecule has no rings beyond these simple aromatic units. The central P–C–C–P linkage gives the scaffold conformational flexibility, while the bulky triphenylphosphine ends add steric bulk. The molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry through the central C–C bond and contains no hydrogen-bond donors, though the phosphorus lone pairs can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at the 1 and 2 positions, an ortho-disubstituted pattern. Each substituent is a methanesulfonamide group: a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens, bearing a methyl group, and linked through an NH to the aromatic carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl groups add some conformational flexibility around the C–N and N–S bonds. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry relating its two halves. Each NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated chain of five carbons and two phosphorus atoms, with the skeleton P–C–C–P flanked by methyl groups: each phosphorus carries two methyl substituents and a two-carbon ethylene bridge links the two phosphorus centers. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no multiple bonds, so the scaffold is simply a flexible, open-chain bis(phosphine)-type framework. The molecule is essentially symmetrical, with a mirror-related arrangement at the two phosphorus termini and identical methyl substitution on each. Its conformational freedom about the single bonds makes it flexible rather than rigid. Lacking any N–H or O–H groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donor capacity, and the phosphorus lone pairs are its only notable sites for hydrogen-bond or coordination interactions.

The molecule is built around a two-carbon bridge connecting two phosphorus atoms, with each phosphorus bearing two phenyl rings and the bridge formed by an ortho-phenylene unit (a benzene ring with the two phosphorus substituents on adjacent carbons). Overall it is a bis-phosphine: three aromatic rings sit on each phosphorus in a propeller-like arrangement, giving the molecule a large, bulky, three-dimensional shape. The phenyl groups carry no substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple, and the molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry across the central phenylene. Its many aromatic rings make it fairly rigid around the central unit, though the phosphorus-phenyl bonds allow rotation. Its phosphorus lone pairs can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic, flexible chain built from a two-carbon ethylene unit bridged on each side by a thioether sulfur, giving a symmetric S-CH2-CH2-S core. Each terminal sulfur carries a methylene group that is attached to a carboxylic acid, so the molecule has two identical arms arranged around a central axis. Because there are no rings, the scaffold can rotate freely about its single bonds and adopts many conformations. Each carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the two thioether sulfurs act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic organosilicon compound built around a two-carbon ethylene bridge that links two silicon centers. Each silicon atom is tetrahedral, carrying two methyl groups and one chlorine atom, so the molecule has a symmetric, dumbbell-like shape with a central C–C linkage. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic or polar heteroatom functional groups beyond the Si–Cl bonds. The molecule is flexible, since rotation about the central carbon–carbon bond and the silicon–carbon bonds is essentially unhindered. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors, because the chlorine atoms are bonded to silicon and the molecule lacks N–H or O–H groups.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two phosphorus-containing substituents on adjacent carbons, giving it an ortho substitution pattern. Each phosphorus atom is a phosphonate-type center bearing a double-bonded oxygen and two methoxy groups, so the molecule is a bis(dimethyl phosphonate) of benzene. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the P–O–CH3 linkages provide some rotational flexibility. The two phosphoryl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement is not symmetric in a simple way because both phosphorus groups sit next to each other on one side of the ring, leaving the remaining ring carbons unsubstituted.

The molecule is a short, acyclic, fully saturated chain built from a central ether linkage flanked by two 2-chloroethyl-type arms. Its backbone is a flexible polyether: two oxygen atoms separate three ethylene-like segments, with a chlorine atom sitting at each terminus, so the scaffold is linear and carries no rings or fused systems. The only functional groups are the ether oxygens and the two primary alkyl chlorides, and the substitution pattern is symmetric, with the two chloroalkyl ends mirrored about the central ether unit. Because all bonds are single and rotatable, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no O–H or N–H groups, but its two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a flexible two-carbon ether linker, with an oxygen atom at each end bonded to the respective ring. Each aromatic ring carries a nitro group (-NO2) on the carbon directly adjacent to the ether oxygen, so the two substituents sit in ortho positions relative to the linker. Because both rings are identical and substituted in the same way, the molecule has an approximate mirror or two-fold symmetry through the central ethylene bridge. The two aryl ether units are not fused and the central CH2-CH2 segment allows considerable rotational freedom. Nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing both nitrogen and oxygen atoms, forming a benzo-fused 1,2-oxazole scaffold. The five-membered ring carries a carbonyl group at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a lactam-type amide functionality within the ring. The nitrogen bears a hydrogen, so the ring has one N–H donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The benzo portion is unsubstituted, so there are no additional side chains and the molecule has a flat, planar, rigid framework with an approximate mirror plane through the fused ring system. The ring oxygen and ring nitrogen contribute further lone-pair acceptor character to the heteroaromatic core.

The molecule is built from two naphthalene units joined by a two-carbon ethylene bridge, so it is a 1,2-di(naphthyl)ethane with the link at the 1-position of each naphthalene ring. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge, and the central ethylene linker is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. There are no heteroatoms and no functional groups, so the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The two naphthyl halves are arranged roughly symmetrically about the central CH2–CH2 linker, while the bulky aromatic faces give the overall framework a large, mostly planar, hydrophobic footprint.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two hydroxymethyl groups, each a carbon bearing a hydroxyl, are attached to adjacent (ortho) positions on the ring, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern with a plane of symmetry through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the two CH2OH arms can rotate about their single bonds, adding some conformational flexibility. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule offers two donor and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring, with two thiol groups attached to adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted benzene. Each thiol consists of a sulfur atom bonded to one hydrogen, so the two sulfur-bearing positions sit next to each other on the ring. The scaffold is flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two S–H bonds, and the molecule has a two-fold axis of symmetry passing through the midpoints of the C–C bond between the substituents. Each thiol group can donate a hydrogen bond through its S–H, while the sulfur atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four halogen substituents and no other functional groups. Reading the SMILES, the ring carries three chlorine atoms and one iodine atom. Going around the ring, the substituents sit at positions that leave two adjacent ring carbons bearing hydrogen, so the pattern is asymmetric and has no mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the halogens lie in the ring plane. Because all substituents are halogens, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carbon chain of six carbons, with no rings or ring fusion. It carries three hydroxyl groups: one at each terminal carbon and one on an internal carbon near the end of the chain, so it is a triol. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the hydroxyls sit at different positions along the backbone. The molecule has a stereogenic center at the internal carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, and no internal mirror symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Four methyl groups are attached to the ring, at positions that leave two adjacent hydrogen-bearing carbons, so the substitution pattern is a tetrasubstituted arrangement with two unsubstituted ring positions sitting next to each other. There are no heteroatoms and no functional groups beyond the alkyl substituents, so the structure is purely hydrocarbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the four methyl groups add some local rotational freedom but no significant conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites, since it contains only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a four-carbon chain whose two ends each carry a benzoyl group, making it a 1,4-diketone with two aromatic ketones. The carbon chain bears phenyl substituents on the two central carbons, so the structure has four unfused benzene rings and no heteroatoms beyond the two carbonyl oxygens. The arrangement is flexible through the saturated backbone, though the bulky phenyl groups restrict some rotation. The molecule has no stereocenters in a symmetric pattern, but the overall framework is approximately symmetric about the central bond. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is as an acceptor at the two carbonyl oxygens, with no donor groups present.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three chlorine substituents, making it a trichlorobenzene. The aromatic six-membered carbon ring is the sole scaffold, with no fused rings or additional functional groups present. The chlorine atoms sit at three of the six ring positions, with two adjacent to one another and the third separated from them, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The planar aromatic core is rigid, while the chlorine atoms are simple, non-rotating halogen substituents. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the chlorine atoms, which are weak.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Four of the six ring positions carry halogen substituents: three fluorine atoms and one nitro group, which consists of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, with one oxygen formally charged and the nitrogen carrying a positive charge. The fluorines occupy adjacent positions on the ring, creating a vicinal pair, while the remaining fluorine and the nitro group are arranged so that the substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The benzene core is planar and rigid, and the nitro group is largely coplanar with it, so the molecule has little conformational flexibility. The nitro group's oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it bears no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings and no heteroatoms within the ring. Three bromine atoms are attached as substituents at positions 1, 2 and 4 of the ring, with the two adjacent bromines flanking one side and the third separated from them by one unsubstituted carbon, giving an unsymmetrical 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters, and its rigid planar aromatic core limits conformational flexibility to essentially none. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms can only act as weak halogen-bond or acceptor sites, so hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four halogen substituents, with three chlorine atoms and one iodine atom attached to the aromatic carbons. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and the substituents sit at a pattern where the iodine is flanked by a chlorine on one side and a hydrogen on the other, while the remaining two ring positions carry hydrogens. Because the halogens occupy unequal positions, the molecule lacks a full mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make all substituents equivalent. The scaffold is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the bonds to the halogens. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O–H or N–H groups, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three nitrogen atoms and two carbon atoms, forming a 1,2,4-triazole-type ring. It is fully unsaturated and planar, with no fused rings and no substituents attached to the ring atoms, so its scaffold is simply the bare triazole core. One ring nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, which makes that position an N-H tautomeric site, while the remaining nitrogens are pyridine-like and act as acceptors. The ring is essentially rigid with no rotatable bonds, and the N-H group provides one hydrogen-bond donor site, while the unprotonated nitrogens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The structure has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry because the nitrogen placement breaks the ring's symmetry.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a six-membered pyridine-type ring is joined to a five-membered ring sharing a nitrogen-carbon bond, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. The five-membered ring contains an adjacent pair of nitrogens, one of which carries a hydrogen, and it is conjugated with a carbonyl carbon that forms an exocyclic C=O at the position next to the ring nitrogen. The unsubstituted benzo-like six-membered ring carries no additional substituents, so the substitution pattern is minimal and the molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry. Because of the N-H group, the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the unprotonated ring nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered 1,2,4-triazole ring sharing one edge with a six-membered pyridine ring, forming a triazolopyridine scaffold. The bridgehead nitrogen links the two rings, and the fused system is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the scaffold rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds. A thiol group (–SH) is attached at the carbon of the triazole ring adjacent to the bridgehead nitrogen, and this sulfur-bearing position is the only substituent on the scaffold. Because the ring nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds and the thiol can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, the molecule offers both donor and acceptor capability, though it has no symmetry.

The molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain, a butane-1,2,4-triol, with no rings or ring fusion present. It carries three hydroxyl groups, one on each of the terminal carbon and the two central carbons, so the skeleton is flexible with freely rotatable single bonds. The hydroxyls are distributed along the chain without symmetry, so the molecule is chiral at the carbon bearing the middle hydroxyl. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule three donor sites and three acceptor sites overall.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three acetate ester groups (–O–C(=O)–CH3) at the 1, 2, and 4 positions, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused ring systems. Each ester oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all ring and side-chain hydroxyls are capped as acetates. The three ester arms are flexible single bonds that can rotate, so the molecule is conformationally flexible, while the substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make all substituents equivalent.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with four methyl groups attached at positions that give it a 1,2,4,5-tetramethyl substitution pattern. Its core is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the two remaining ring positions carry hydrogen atoms. The molecule has a twofold axis of symmetry through the midpoints of the two unsubstituted C–H positions, so the two halves of the ring mirror one another. It contains no polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its only flexibility comes from rotation of the four methyl groups around their bonds to the ring, while the aromatic core itself is rigid.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered anhydride ring, giving a rigid bicyclic scaffold often described as a phthalic anhydride core. The anhydride unit consists of two carbonyl groups bridged by an oxygen atom, sharing an edge with the aromatic ring. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the benzene ring at a position that is not symmetric with respect to the anhydride fusion, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The planar, fused framework makes the molecule quite rigid, with little conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is dominated by the carboxylic acid, which can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, while the anhydride carbonyls and ring oxygen serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Four of its six ring positions carry fluorine atoms, leaving two adjacent positions bearing hydrogen. The fluorines occupy the 1, 2, 4, and 5 positions in a pattern that breaks the ring's full symmetry, so the molecule has no mirror plane through all its atoms and only a limited set of symmetry elements. The ring is planar and rigid, and the carbon-fluorine bonds are fixed in direction, so the molecule has essentially no conformational flexibility. Fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold with no ring fusion. Four isopropylthio groups (–S–CH(CH3)2) are attached at four of the six ring positions, giving a 1,2,4,5-tetrasubstituted pattern with the two unsubstituted ring carbons located opposite each other. The sulfur atoms are thioether linkages, and the bulky isopropyl groups are flexible through rotation about the C–S bonds. The molecule has an approximately two-fold symmetry axis through the midpoints of the two unsubstituted ring C–H bonds, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with fully conjugated, delocalized pi bonds and no fused rings. Four of the six ring positions carry bromine atoms, while the remaining two positions bear hydrogen atoms, so the substitution pattern is tetrabromo on the ring. The bromines occupy adjacent and alternating positions, which places the two unsubstituted carbons next to one another in a 1,2 relationship. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donor capability and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, since the only heteroatoms are halogens that do not act as conventional acceptors in this context.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four chlorine substituents, making it a tetrachlorobenzene. The aromatic six-membered carbocycle is the sole ring system, with no ring fusion and no additional functional groups beyond the carbon-chlorine bonds. The chlorines occupy four of the six ring positions, leaving two adjacent hydrogen-bearing carbons, which gives an asymmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The planar, rigid aromatic core has no rotatable bonds, so the structure is essentially fixed in shape. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic alkane skeleton, a three-carbon chain (propane backbone) with no rings and no ring fusion. Chlorine atoms are attached at all three carbons: two terminal carbons each bear one chlorine, and the central carbon bears a second chlorine, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the middle carbon. It contains no other functional groups, and its only heteroatoms are the three chlorines, which are halogen substituents rather than hydrogen-bond donors. Lacking any hydrogen-bond donors and having no lone-pair-bearing acceptor groups beyond the weakly accepting halogens, its intermolecular hydrogen-bonding capacity is negligible. The chain is flexible, since free rotation about its single C–C bonds allows multiple conformations.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. A nitro group (–NO2, drawn as a nitrogen bearing a positive charge with one oxygen double-bonded and one bearing a negative charge) is attached to one ring carbon, and three chlorine atoms occupy three adjacent carbons on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,3-trichloro substitution pattern relative to each other, with the nitro group placed meta to the nearest chlorine. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are not evenly distributed around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the nitro group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings, and it carries three chlorine atoms as its only substituents. Two chlorines sit on adjacent carbons, and the third sits on the carbon next to one of them, so the three halogens cluster together on one side of the ring with the remaining two ring positions bearing hydrogens. This 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern gives the molecule only a mirror plane passing through the middle chlorine and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is planar and rigid, and the carbon-chlorine bonds are fixed in the ring plane. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, and its chlorine atoms can only act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated three-carbon chain (a propane skeleton) with a bromine atom attached to each carbon, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. The two terminal carbons each carry one bromomethyl group, while the central carbon carries a single bromine, giving a symmetric substitution pattern in which the outer two bromines are equivalent and the central one is distinct. The C–Br bonds are the only polar functional groups present, and the chain is flexible because rotation about its single bonds is free. Because the molecule contains no N–H or O–H bonds and no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms other than the halogens, it has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one nitro group and three chlorine atoms, giving a fully substituted aromatic core with no remaining ring hydrogens. The nitro group sits on one carbon, and the three chlorines occupy three adjacent carbons, so the substituents are clustered on one side of the ring. The benzene scaffold is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no rotatable bonds of significance beyond the nitro group's rotation about its attachment bond. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chlorine atoms are weak acceptors at most, and the overall arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom and two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which corresponds to a 1,2,3-thiadiazole ring with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached directly to one carbon of the ring, and the remaining ring carbon is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and asymmetric. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only rotatable bond is the one linking the carboxyl group to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogens can also act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three acetyl ester groups are attached to the ring through oxygen atoms, one on each of three adjacent carbon atoms, and the substitution pattern is 1,2,3, with the two outer esters flanking the central one. The arrangement lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry in its full form, though the flanking groups are chemically equivalent to each other. Each ester contributes a carbonyl oxygen and a bridging ether-type oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ester side chains retain some rotational flexibility around their C–O bonds.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated four-carbon chain, with no rings or double bonds, so its scaffold is a simple linear butane-type backbone. It carries three hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, with two secondary alcohols and one primary alcohol at the chain terminus, which together form a polyol pattern. The lack of any ring system or aromatic character means the skeleton is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through free rotation about its single bonds. Each hydroxyl oxygen can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule substantial hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle with a single fused-free ring containing one sulfur atom and two adjacent nitrogen atoms, forming a 1,2,3-thiadiazole core. An aldehyde group (a formyl substituent, C=O bonded to hydrogen) is attached to one carbon of the ring, so the ring carries a single substituent with no other branching. Because the ring is flat and fully aromatic, the skeleton is rigid, and the only conformational freedom comes from rotation of the aldehyde group. The ring nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds through their lone pairs, while the aldehyde oxygen is an additional acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The structure has no meaningful molecular symmetry beyond its planar geometry.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic amine built from a benzene ring fused to a saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing ring, giving a tetrahydroquinoline-type scaffold. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portion carries only hydrogen atoms, and the fused ring is partly saturated, with three consecutive methylene units linking the aromatic carbon to the ring nitrogen. The secondary amine nitrogen sits directly attached to the benzene ring, which makes it an aniline-like nitrogen whose lone pair conjugates weakly with the aromatic system. The structure is fairly rigid overall because of the fused rings, though the saturated portion can adopt a puckered conformation. The nitrogen bears one hydrogen, so it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a six-membered ring containing three nitrogen atoms, forming a benzotriazinone scaffold. The triazinone ring carries a carbonyl group adjacent to one ring nitrogen, and a second nitrogen in the ring bears a hydrogen, so the ring is partially saturated at that position. The benzene portion is unsubstituted, with four aromatic CH positions and no additional substituents. The fused framework is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogens provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is a bicyclic hydrocarbon built from two six-membered rings sharing a single edge, giving a fused scaffold. One ring is fully aromatic, with six sp2 carbons bearing alternating double bonds, while the other ring is saturated, consisting of four methylene units that link the two shared carbons. The structure contains no functional groups, no heteroatoms, and no substituents beyond hydrogen, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted throughout. The aromatic and saturated rings together give a partially rigid framework, with the saturated ring able to adopt flexible puckered conformations. Because it lacks any hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, it has no capacity to form hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a tetrahydrocarbazole, built from an indole core fused to a saturated six-membered carbocycle. The aromatic portion consists of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring containing an NH group, giving an electron-rich indole scaffold. A cyclohexane-type ring is fused onto the pyrrole's C2–C3 bond, so the four additional carbons are sp3-hybridized and the molecule is essentially a flat aromatic tricyclic system with one puckered ring. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the lone pair on that nitrogen is delocalized into the aromatic system and offers little acceptor capability. The unsubstituted benzo ring and the partially saturated ring leave the scaffold without stereocenters and with no substituents beyond the ring fusion, so its overall shape is largely rigid.

This molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a partially saturated nitrogen-containing ring, giving a tetrahydroisoquinoline framework. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted and fully planar, while the fused ring contains two adjacent CH2 groups and a CH2 flanked by a secondary amine nitrogen. The secondary amine (N–H) can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the lone pair on nitrogen gives basic character to the structure. The saturated portion of the second ring introduces some conformational flexibility, whereas the fused aromatic system remains rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry element beyond the mirror-like arrangement of the planar aromatic ring.
