The molecule is built from two 2-pyridone rings joined through a central thiocarbonyl carbon, which bonds to the ring nitrogen of each pyridone. Each ring is a six-membered aromatic-like heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one ring carbonyl (C=O) adjacent to that nitrogen, so the two halves are mirror-related and the whole structure has approximate C2 symmetry around the central carbon. The thiocarbonyl group (C=S) is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and each ring carbonyl oxygen adds further acceptor sites. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The rings are largely planar and rigid, while the bonds linking them to the central carbon allow some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Four of its six ring carbons carry fluorine atoms, leaving two adjacent positions bearing hydrogen; the fluorines occupy one contiguous run of three adjacent carbons plus one further position, giving a densely fluorinated, asymmetric substitution pattern. The molecule contains no conventional hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no OH, NH, or similar groups, though the electronegative fluorine atoms can act as weak acceptors. Its rigid, planar aromatic core gives it very little conformational flexibility, and there are no rotatable bonds beyond the C–F bonds, which lie in the ring plane.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and two separate phenyl rings, so it is a diarylalkanol with no fused ring systems. Each benzene ring is unsubstituted, bearing only hydrogens, and the two rings are attached to the same central carbon, which gives the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry through that carbon. The tertiary alcohol is the only functional group, and its hydroxyl oxygen can both donate one hydrogen bond and accept one. The two aryl groups and the sp3 central carbon make the scaffold fairly rigid around the core, although the bonds to the rings and the hydroxyl allow some rotation.

The molecule is 1,1-diphenylethylene, built on a two-carbon scaffold in which one terminal carbon bears two phenyl rings and the other is a methylene group joined to it by a carbon-carbon double bond. Both phenyl rings are unsubstituted benzene rings attached directly to the same sp2 carbon, so there are no additional functional groups, heteroatoms, or ring fusions. The molecule has no stereocenters and no E/Z isomerism, and the two phenyl rings can rotate about their single bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility around the aryl attachments. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it consists only of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a terminal alkyne, a hydroxyl group, and two phenyl rings, making it a tertiary propargylic alcohol. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, and the two rings are not fused to each other or to any other ring system. The central carbon is sp3-hybridized and bears four different groups, so the molecule has no mirror plane through its core, though the two phenyl rings are identical and the whole arrangement is locally pseudo-symmetric. The linear C≡C–H unit adds rigidity at one end, while the tetrahedral central carbon allows the two aromatic rings to adopt varying orientations relative to each other. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the alkyne and aromatic π-systems offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain: a methyl group bonded to a ketone carbonyl, which connects to a central sp3 carbon carrying two phenyl rings. Each phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the aromatic portions are simple and unfused, and the two rings sit on the same carbon, giving the molecule an approximately twofold-symmetric arrangement about that central carbon. The only functional group is the ketone, whose oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central carbon is a branch point that allows considerable conformational flexibility, with the two aryl groups able to rotate, so the molecule is not rigid overall despite its aromatic character.

The molecule is built around a single cyclopropane ring, a three-membered all-carbon ring that makes the scaffold compact and rigid. One carbon of this ring is quaternary, carrying both a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is in turn bonded to a methyl group) and a free carboxylic acid group. The two substituents sit on the same ring carbon, giving a geminal disubstitution pattern, while the other two ring carbons are unsubstituted CH2 units. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational freedom, since the ring is fixed and the ester and acid groups can rotate only about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites, while the ester carbonyl and ether-type oxygen act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene-type bicyclic scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered sulfur-containing ring. That sulfur carries two oxygen atoms as a sulfone, making the heterocycle strongly electron-withdrawing and planar in its fused core. A chloroformate ester group is attached through a methylene linker to the carbon adjacent to the sulfone, so the substituent is flexible while the bicyclic core is rigid. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, and its sulfone and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the structure is asymmetric, with the reactive acyl chloride positioned at the end of a short, freely rotating side chain.

The molecule is built around a cyclohexane ring whose single carbon at position 1 is quaternary, bearing two identical carboxymethyl arms (–CH2–COOH). Because both arms are attached to the same ring carbon, the substitution pattern is geminal and the molecule has a mirror plane through that carbon, giving it local symmetry. The six-membered saturated ring is non-aromatic and carries no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aliphatic system with considerable conformational flexibility from the ring and the two side chains. Each side chain ends in a carboxylic acid group, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. In total the structure presents two donor sites and four acceptor sites.

The molecule is built around a single three-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopropane, bearing two carboxylic acid groups on the same ring carbon, making it a geminally disubstituted scaffold. The ring is fully saturated and highly strained, which makes it rigid, while the two carboxyl substituents project in a fixed geometry from the one quaternary carbon. There is no ring fusion and no stereocenter, so the molecule possesses a plane of symmetry through the ring carbon and the two methylene groups. Each carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites overall.

This molecule is built around a single carbonyl carbon that bridges two identical five-membered aromatic rings, making it a symmetric urea-type scaffold. Each ring is an imidazole, a planar five-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, and each imidazole is attached through its ring nitrogen to the central carbonyl. The overall framework is a N,N'-carbonyl bis(imidazole), and the two ring halves are related by a mirror plane through the carbonyl oxygen and carbon. The imidazole rings are unfused and connected by a single carbon center, so the molecule is fairly compact but has limited rigidity around the N–C(=O) bonds. The unsubstituted imidazole nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors since no N–H or O–H groups are present.

The molecule is built around a single central carbonyl carbon, which is bonded to two piperidine rings through their nitrogen atoms, giving a symmetric urea-type scaffold. Each piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and five methylene carbons, so the two rings are chemically identical and related by a mirror plane through the carbonyl. There are no aromatic rings, no ring fusion, and no other substituents; the only functional group is the tertiary amide-like C=O flanked by two nitrogens. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because both nitrogens are fully substituted. The piperidine rings can adopt chair conformations, giving moderate conformational flexibility around the N–C(O) bonds.

The molecule is a binaphthyl scaffold: two naphthalene units joined by a single bond between their carbons adjacent to the fusion region, giving a biaryl core. Each naphthalene bears one hydroxyl group on the ring carbon next to that linking bond, so the two hydroxyls sit on the same side, forming a symmetric 2,2'-disubstituted arrangement. The two naphthalene halves are related by a two-fold axis through the central bond. The biaryl linkage is hindered, which restricts rotation about the central bond and keeps the two ring systems twisted relative to each other. Each hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the aromatic rings contribute additional π-system character.

This molecule is a small acyclic nitroalkene built around a single two-carbon backbone. One carbon carries two methylthio groups, each a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group, while the other carbon is a terminal CH bearing a nitro group. The carbon–carbon double bond links these two halves, making the arrangement conjugated, with the electron-withdrawing nitro group polarizing the alkene. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely flexible apart from the rigidity imposed by the planar alkene unit. The two methylthio substituents are constitutionally identical on the same carbon, giving a local symmetry that is not reflected in any stereocentre. The nitro group provides two oxygen hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic chain with no rings, no double bonds, and no branching. Its skeleton consists of a continuous run of twelve methylene units, with a hydroxyl group attached to each terminal carbon, making it a symmetric α,ω-diol. The two primary alcohol groups sit at opposite ends of the chain and are the only functional groups present. Because the chain has no rings or double bonds, it is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations, with rotation possible about every carbon-carbon bond. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the methylene core contributes no polar interaction sites.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic dicarboxylic acid: a saturated, unbranched carbon chain with a carboxylic acid group capping each end. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The two terminal carboxyl groups are the only functional groups, and they sit at opposite ends of the chain, giving the molecule a symmetrical, linear substitution pattern with a mirror plane through the midpoint of the carbon chain. The long methylene backbone is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Each carboxyl group can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, so the molecule offers two donor and four acceptor sites in total.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated aliphatic diamine: a straight chain of twelve methylene (CH2) units capped at each end by a primary amine group (-NH2). It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers, so its scaffold is simply an unbranched alkyl backbone. The two terminal amino groups are identical and placed symmetrically at opposite ends, giving the molecule a C2-like symmetry about its midpoint. The long, freely rotating carbon chain makes the molecule highly flexible, with many accessible conformations. Each primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its two N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through the nitrogen lone pair), while the central methylene chain contributes no polar hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated hydrocarbon chain of twelve methylene carbons, with a bromine atom attached at each terminus. It contains no rings, no fused ring systems, and no double bonds or other unsaturation. The only functional groups are two primary alkyl bromide groups, located at the two ends of the chain. The molecule is symmetric about its center, with the two bromines related by a mirror or inversion relationship. Its long, all-carbon backbone gives it a high degree of conformational flexibility, since rotation about the many C–C single bonds is essentially free. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain alkane skeleton of ten carbon atoms, with an iodine atom bonded to each of the two terminal carbons. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no other functional groups beyond the two carbon-iodine bonds at the chain ends. The structure is fully symmetric about the midpoint of the chain, so the two halves are mirror-equivalent. The long methylene backbone is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations through rotation about its single bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the iodine atoms are poor acceptors and the chain carries only C-H bonds.

The molecule is built on a fully aromatic, planar tricyclic framework of three fused six-membered rings, with two nitrogen atoms incorporated into the outer rings. The two nitrogens sit adjacent to the ring-fusion carbons on opposite sides of the system, so the molecule has a pair of bidentate nitrogen sites positioned to face one another across the central region. Because every ring atom is sp2 and the skeleton is flat and rigid, there is essentially no conformational flexibility. The structure has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all carbon-hydrogen positions are non-polar, but the two pyridine-type nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors and metal-coordinating sites. The arrangement possesses approximate two-fold symmetry through the central ring.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain alkane dithiol: a linear saturated carbon backbone of eleven methylene units with a thiol group (–SH) at each terminus. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no branching, so its scaffold is entirely flexible and can adopt many extended and folded conformations. The two sulfhydryl groups are the only functional groups and sit symmetrically at opposite ends, giving the molecule a two-fold symmetry along its long axis. Each thiol can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H bond, while the sulfur atoms offer only limited hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

This molecule is a straight, fully saturated chain of ten carbon atoms, with a bromine atom bonded to each terminal carbon, so it is a linear alkane scaffold with no rings and no fused systems. Its only functional groups are two primary alkyl bromide (carbon-bromine) groups located at opposite ends, giving a symmetric, bis-substituted pattern in which the two halogens are identical and mirror one another. The chain is highly flexible, since rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond is essentially free, allowing many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the two bromine atoms, which are weak.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. It consists of a twelve-carbon methylene backbone capped at both ends by a nitrile group, so the scaffold is fully symmetric about its midpoint, with each terminus bearing a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. Each nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all of its hydrogens sit on saturated carbons. The long methylene chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds, and it contains no substitution pattern beyond the two terminal cyano groups.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic diol: a linear, unbranched carbon backbone of ten methylene units with a hydroxyl group attached at each terminus. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom substituents beyond the two terminal alcohol groups. The structure is symmetric, with identical functionality at both ends of the chain. The long saturated chain is highly flexible, able to adopt many conformations, while the two hydroxyl groups each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built on a four-carbon butadiene backbone, with two C=C double bonds connected by a single bond between the central carbons. Each of the four backbone carbons bears a phenyl ring, so the scaffold is a 1,1,4,4-tetraphenylbutadiene skeleton. There are six benzene rings in total, all unfused and attached only by single bonds to sp2 carbons, giving no fused ring systems. The molecule has no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its overall shape is extended and fairly rigid around the conjugated diene core, with the phenyl rings free to rotate about their single bonds, and it possesses approximate two-fold symmetry about the center of the butadiene unit.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, at one position, with two phenyl rings attached at the two meta positions relative to it, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted benzene core. The three rings are linked by single bonds and carry no fused ring system, so the scaffold is a central arene flanked by two biaryl arms. The arrangement is roughly symmetric about an axis running through the boron-bearing carbon, and the two outer phenyl rings are unsubstituted. The C–C links between rings allow rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible. The two B–OH groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and accept one through their oxygen atoms, while the remaining aromatic rings offer only weak π-type interactions.

The molecule is a linear disiloxane, built from a central oxygen atom bridging two silicon centers in an Si–O–Si backbone. Each silicon carries one hydrogen and one methyl group, so the skeleton is a simple acyclic chain with no rings and no ring fusion. The two silicon atoms are equivalent, giving the molecule a mirror-symmetric, flexible structure with rotation possible about the Si–O bonds. There are no classical functional groups beyond the Si–H bonds and the siloxane ether linkage. The oxygen atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability because it lacks O–H or N–H bonds.

The molecule is built around a single sp-hybridized carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and two phenyl rings, giving a tertiary alcohol. That same carbon is attached to a rigid alkyne linker that connects to a third phenyl ring, so the scaffold is a triaryl carbinol joined through a linear carbon-carbon triple bond. There are no fused ring systems; the three benzene rings are separate, unsubstituted aromatic rings. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkyne and aromatic π-systems offer only weak interactions. The alkyne segment is rigid and linear, which limits conformational freedom, although the propeller-like arrangement of the phenyl groups around the central carbon introduces some three-dimensional bulk.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic framework: a benzene ring fused to a naphthalene-like unit, with a five-membered ring containing a carbon-nitrogen double bond (an imine, or 3H-indole-type ring) fused onto it. This is a benz[e]indole-type scaffold. The partially saturated five-membered ring carries a quaternary sp3 carbon bearing two methyl groups (a gem-dimethyl unit) adjacent to the ring fusion, and a third methyl group sits on the carbon of the C=N bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the imine nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic rings make the core largely rigid and planar, while the gem-dimethyl group adds local steric bulk and a three-dimensional feature to an otherwise flat framework. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the methyl substitution is asymmetric.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated, acyclic fluorinated ether with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic units, so its skeleton is a short two-carbon chain. One terminal carbon bears a methoxy group (an oxygen linked to a methyl), and the same carbon carries two fluorine atoms, while the other carbon carries one hydrogen and two fluorines, giving a dense fluorine substitution pattern on the chain. The ether oxygen is the only heteroatom that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors because no N–H or O–H groups are present. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local rotational freedom, and its single C–C and C–O bonds allow rotation, so it is conformationally flexible rather than rigid.

The molecule is a short, acyclic haloalkene built on a two-carbon backbone. One terminal carbon carries three fluorine atoms, forming a trifluoromethyl group, and this carbon is joined by a single bond to one alkene carbon. The double bond between the two central carbons carries chlorine atoms on both ends, with a total of three chlorines distributed across the alkene. The skeleton contains no rings and no fused ring systems, so it is conformationally flexible about its single bond, though the double bond itself is planar and rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry because of the uneven halogen placement. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and offers only weak acceptor character from its halogen atoms.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a methyl group and three hydroxymethyl arms, giving a compact, fully saturated aliphatic scaffold with no rings and no double bonds. Each of the three CH2OH groups contributes a primary alcohol, so the molecule is rich in hydroxyl functionality. The central carbon's branching makes the three arms equivalent, yielding a high degree of local symmetry around that center. Because the structure lacks rings and contains only single bonds, it is conformationally flexible, though the bulky quaternary center restricts rotation somewhat. Each hydroxyl oxygen and hydrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, so the molecule can form extensive hydrogen-bonding networks.

The molecule is an acyclic, saturated two-carbon skeleton, a simple ethane backbone with no rings and no multiple bonds. Each carbon carries two chlorine substituents, so the substitution pattern is symmetric: the two carbons are equivalent and each bears a geminal pair of chlorines. The structure is flexible, since rotation about the central carbon-carbon single bond is essentially free, allowing multiple conformations. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, because there are no hydrogen atoms bonded to electronegative atoms, and the chlorine atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a two-carbon backbone, with one carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and a hydrogen, and the adjacent carbon bearing that same carbon's partner substituents. Each carbon carries two substituents of the trifluoromethyl type: the first carbon bears one CF3 group and the second carbon bears another CF3 group alongside the hydroxyl-bearing center. The structure contains no ring systems, so it is an acyclic, flexible skeleton with free rotation about the central carbon–carbon bond. Its only polar functional group is the single secondary alcohol, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry because the hydroxyl group breaks the symmetry between the two halves.

The molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that carries a methyl group and three chloromethyl arms, giving it a compact, branched, acyclic scaffold with no rings and no ring fusion. Its only functional groups are three primary alkyl chloride (C–Cl) bonds, one at the end of each chloromethyl branch, while the remaining carbon framework consists entirely of saturated C–H and C–C bonds. The three chloromethyl groups are attached symmetrically to the central carbon, so the molecule has three-fold local symmetry around the central carbon, with the methyl group as the unique fourth substituent. Because every bond is a single sigma bond about sp3 carbons, the molecule is conformationally flexible, though the bulky branching around the central carbon restricts rotation somewhat. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule has a central azodicarbonyl unit, in which two carbonyl carbons are joined through an N=N double bond, forming a symmetric linear core. Each carbonyl carbon is bonded to the nitrogen of a saturated piperidine ring, so the two six-membered rings are attached to the core through their nitrogen atoms in a mirror-image arrangement. The piperidine rings are fully saturated and adopt chair conformations, while the central N=N-C(=O) portion is planar and conjugated. The molecule therefore has a high degree of symmetry across its central axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every nitrogen is either part of an amide-like linkage or the azo group. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a short, fully halogenated two-carbon chain built around a single ether oxygen linking two carbon centers. One carbon bears three fluorine atoms, forming a trifluoromethyl group attached directly to the oxygen. The other carbon is quaternary, carrying one fluorine, one iodine, and a second trifluoromethyl group. The structure is acyclic, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor capability comes from the ether oxygen, which is sterically shielded by the surrounding fluorinated groups. Its flexibility is limited by the bulky, heavily halogenated substituents around the central C–O–C linkage.

The molecule is built on an imidazole scaffold, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at non-adjacent positions. One ring nitrogen is substituted by a trimethylsilyl group, a silicon atom bearing three methyl groups, so the substitution pattern is N-silylation with no further ring substitution. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the three methyl groups on silicon add some local rotational freedom. The unsubstituted ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor, since the only N-H position has been replaced by the silyl group.

The molecule is built on a cyclopentane ring, a saturated five-membered carbocycle with no fused or bridged rings. One ring carbon bears two substituents on the same position: a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) and a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3), making that carbon quaternary. The remaining four ring carbons are plain methylene units, so the substitution pattern is geminal and the scaffold has no stereocenter. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors. The cyclopentane ring is fairly flexible, undergoing rapid puckering, but the bulky quaternary carbon constrains the orientation of its two functional groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and a sulfonyl group in a para (1,4) relationship, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens, links the aromatic ring to the nitrogen of a pyrrole ring, which is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle. The result is an N-sulfonylated pyrrole, with no ring fusion, so the two aromatic systems are connected by a single tetrahedral sulfur linker. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Both aromatic rings are rigid and planar, though rotation around the sulfur–nitrogen and sulfur–carbon bonds gives the overall shape some conformational flexibility.

The molecule consists of a cinnamoyl unit, a three-carbon chain bearing a phenyl ring at one end, linked through a carbonyl to the nitrogen of an imidazole ring. The phenyl ring is a monosubstituted benzene, and the imidazole is an unfused five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship. The carbon-carbon double bond between the carbonyl and the phenyl-bearing carbon has a trans (E) configuration, which keeps the scaffold largely planar and extended. The N-acyl linkage makes the imidazole an activated amide-like system, with the carbonyl oxygen and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen serving as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its conjugated framework gives it limited conformational flexibility around the single bonds.

The molecule consists of a pyrrole ring whose nitrogen is bonded to a sulfonyl group, which in turn is attached to a benzene ring, forming an N-arylsulfonyl pyrrole scaffold. The five-membered pyrrole and six-membered phenyl ring are not fused; they are joined through the central sulfur atom, which carries two double-bonded oxygens and so presents a tetrahedral-like sulfonyl unit. The phenyl group is unsubstituted, giving a monosubstituted benzene with no additional functional groups, while the pyrrole ring bears only hydrogens at its carbon positions. The overall framework has a mirror-plane-like shape around the S–N and S–C axes, but no stereocenters. Rotation about the S–N and S–C bonds gives moderate flexibility, and the two aromatic rings are fairly rigid planar units. The sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring, with the nitrogen of the pyrrole bearing a substituent. That nitrogen is bonded to a sulfonyl group (SO2), which links it to a para-tolyl ring, a benzene ring carrying a methyl group opposite the sulfonyl attachment. The sulfonyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing tetrahedral unit with two oxygen atoms acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused indole and the attached tolyl ring give the molecule a largely planar, rigid aromatic framework, with the sulfonyl bridge providing a single point of conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any mirror symmetry through its whole length, since the two aromatic halves are chemically distinct.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring bearing a tertiary alcohol at one carbon, which is the same carbon that carries a phenylethynyl substituent, so the ring is saturated and fully sp3 apart from that alkyne. The alkyne is a rigid linear unit linking the ring to a benzene ring, which is unsubstituted, giving the aryl portion no further substitution pattern and a high degree of local symmetry. The hydroxyl group is the only hydrogen-bond donor and also acts as an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, while the pi system of the alkyne and benzene offers weak additional acceptor character. Overall the molecule combines a flexible saturated ring with a rigid, linear acetylenic linker to an aromatic ring.

This molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring. The indole nitrogen is not bare: it carries a phenylsulfonyl group, so a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens is attached directly to a benzene ring and to the nitrogen. The sulfonyl unit is a strong electron-withdrawing group, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only N–H position has been replaced. The sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, with the phenyl ring attached through a single sulfur–nitrogen bond that allows some rotational freedom.

This molecule is an N-acyl imidazole, built from a pentafluorobenzoyl group bonded to the N1 nitrogen of an imidazole ring. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogens separated by one carbon, and it is attached through its pyrrole-type nitrogen. The acyl carbonyl links this ring to a benzene ring carrying five fluorine atoms, one on each remaining position, so the aryl ring is fully substituted and lacks any hydrogen atoms. The two rings are connected by a single bond through the carbonyl, giving the molecule moderate rigidity with some rotational freedom about the C–N and C–C bonds. The carbonyl oxygen and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five fluorine atoms and one 1-hydroxyethyl group, so the aromatic core is fully substituted at all six positions. The side chain is a two-carbon unit in which a methyl group and a secondary alcohol carbon attach directly to the ring. Each of the five ring fluorines is a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent, and the ring has no internal symmetry because the single side chain breaks the pattern. The benzene ring is rigid and planar, while the ethyl-alcohol side chain has rotational freedom around the bond to the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic fluorines are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an imidazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship. One ring nitrogen carries a methanesulfonyl group, a methyl bonded to a sulfur that is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms, so the sulfonyl sits directly on the nitrogen without any ring fusion. The other ring nitrogen is unsubstituted and bears a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the carbon atoms of the ring are unsubstituted C–H positions. The compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H sites are absent, but its two sulfonyl oxygens and the free ring nitrogen serve as acceptors. The scaffold is small and essentially planar in the ring, with the sulfonyl group providing a single rotatable bond that gives modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated heterocycle with two nitrogen atoms placed at opposite positions. One of these nitrogens is bonded directly to a benzene ring, which itself carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, while the piperazine ring is flexible and adopts non-planar conformations. The second nitrogen of the piperazine is a secondary amine bearing a hydrogen, so it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The first nitrogen, attached to the aryl group, serves mainly as a weaker hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall structure lacks any symmetry because the methyl-substituted aryl group breaks the symmetry of the scaffold.

The molecule is an acyclic cyanoacetyl group attached to a saturated five-membered nitrogen heterocycle. The ring is a pyrrolidine, a fully saturated system with no double bonds, so it adopts a puckered, flexible conformation. The nitrogen of the ring is acylated, forming a tertiary amide in which the carbonyl is bonded directly to the ring nitrogen. The carbonyl carbon is linked to a methylene group that carries a terminal nitrile, giving a linear C≡N unit at one end of the molecule. The structure has no stereocenters and no aromatic rings, and it contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since all N–H and O–H positions are absent. The amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an N-acyl imidazole, with the imidazole nitrogen bonded to a carbonyl carbon that leads into a perfluorinated three-carbon chain ending in a trifluoromethyl group. The five-membered aromatic imidazole ring is planar and contains two nitrogens, one of which is substituted by the acyl group while the other is a basic, hydrogen-bond-accepting sp2 nitrogen. The chain carries six fluorine atoms on its two internal carbons plus three on the terminal carbon, making it bulky and electron-withdrawing with a sterically dense, flexible, rotatable tail. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A chloromethyl group (–CH2Cl) is attached to one of the carbons on the ring adjacent to the fusion point, placing the substituent at the alpha position of the naphthalene system. Apart from this single substituent, the structure contains only aromatic carbon-hydrogen bonds, so there are no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the chlorine. The core is rigid and planar, while the chloromethyl group provides the only rotatable bond, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility overall. The compound lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent breaks the symmetry of the parent naphthalene.

The molecule is built around a piperidine ring, a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. The ring nitrogen is acylated, forming a tertiary amide whose carbonyl carbon is attached to a two-carbon chain that ends in a nitrile group. The nitrile nitrogen and the amide carbonyl oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The piperidine ring is unsubstituted on carbon, so the substitution pattern is limited to this single amide linkage, and the molecule has no stereocenters. Its six-membered ring confers moderate conformational flexibility, and the amide bond adds partial planarity around the nitrogen-carbonyl junction.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A methoxy group (an ether, -O-CH3) sits on one ring at a position remote from the fusion, while a 1-hydroxyethyl side chain, a secondary alcohol bearing a methyl branch, is attached to the other ring. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the two substituents break any mirror symmetry of the parent ring system. The aromatic core is rigid, while the side chain's C-C and C-O bonds allow some rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen serves as an acceptor only.

This molecule is a cyclopentane-based amino acid derivative, where a single saturated five-membered carbocycle forms the central scaffold. One ring carbon bears both a carboxylic acid group and a nitrogen that is part of a carbamate, so the two functionalities are attached to the same quaternary carbon. The nitrogen is capped by a tert-butyl ester of carbonic acid, which places a bulky, branched alkyl group on the carbamate oxygen. The ring is fully saturated and non-fused, and the quaternary center removes any stereochemical symmetry around the ring junction, giving limited rigidity overall. The carbamate N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of both groups serve as acceptors.

The molecule is an azo dye built from a para-nitrophenyl ring joined through a trans N=N double bond to a naphthalene unit. The nitro group sits on one benzene ring at the position opposite the azo linkage, making the arrangement strongly electron-withdrawing at one end. The naphthalene portion is a fused bicyclic aromatic system, bearing a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the azo attachment, which provides a hydrogen-bond donor. The nitro oxygens and the azo nitrogens and hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The planar, conjugated framework with its rigid azo bridge gives the molecule limited conformational flexibility and little internal symmetry.

The molecule is built from a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle, bearing a single substituent at the position para to the ring nitrogen. That substituent is a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions, attached to the pyridine through one of its nitrogens, which makes that nitrogen tertiary. The other piperazine nitrogen is a secondary amine with an N-H group, giving the molecule a hydrogen-bond donor site. The pyridine nitrogen and both piperazine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is flat and rigid, while the piperazine ring is flexible and can adopt chair-like conformations. The overall structure has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local two-fold arrangement of the piperazine ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a nitro group, which is a strongly electron-withdrawing, planar functional group with two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Opposite it sits a saturated six-membered piperidine ring attached through its nitrogen, so the aromatic ring is fused to nothing but is directly linked to a tertiary amine. The piperidine ring adopts a flexible chair conformation, while the benzene core is rigid and flat, giving the molecule a partly rigid, partly flexible character. The overall arrangement has an approximate linear, elongated shape with a two-fold symmetry axis running through the ring centers. The nitrogen of the piperidine has no hydrogen to donate, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors but offers several acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) and an ether linkage at positions para to each other. The ether oxygen connects the ring to a three-carbon chain that carries a secondary hydroxyl group on the middle carbon and a primary hydroxyl group on the terminal carbon, giving a 2,3-dihydroxypropyl ether side chain. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the propyl chain is flexible and can rotate freely around its single bonds. There is no internal symmetry beyond the local para arrangement on the ring. The nitro group and the three hydroxyl groups make the molecule a good hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two hydroxyls can also act as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a pyrazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which is substituted at three positions. One ring nitrogen bears a para-nitrophenyl group, a benzene ring carrying a nitro group opposite the point of attachment. A trifluoromethyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to that substituted nitrogen, and a carboxylic acid group is attached to the carbon at the opposite side of the ring. The overall framework is a biaryl-type linkage with no fused ring systems, so the molecule has a fairly rigid, planar aromatic character with only limited rotational freedom about the single bond joining the two rings. Its hydrogen-bond capability is provided by the carboxylic acid, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the nitro oxygens and pyrazole nitrogen act as additional acceptor sites.

The molecule is a chalcone-type scaffold: an aryl ketone whose carbonyl is joined to a trans-configured vinyl bridge (C=C) that leads to a thiophene ring. The carbonyl's other side is attached directly to a benzene ring bearing a nitro group para to the carbonyl attachment point, so the two aromatic rings sit at opposite ends of a conjugated, largely planar enone linker. The five-membered thiophene ring is unfused and connected at its 2-position, while the benzene ring is 1,4-disubstituted, giving an overall extended, elongated shape with limited conformational flexibility. The ketone oxygen and the two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a rigid, linear diarylalkyne core in which a para-propylphenyl ring and a para-methoxyphenyl ring are joined through a carbon-carbon triple bond. Both aromatic rings are monosubstituted benzene rings with substituents at opposite positions, giving the molecule an elongated, roughly rod-like shape with an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the alkyne. The propyl group is a flexible saturated chain attached to one end, while the methoxy group, an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl, sits at the other end. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H bonds, but the ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the structure combines a rigid central axis with flexible alkyl and ether termini.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group), attached as an ether. The other is an imidazole ring joined through one of its nitrogen atoms, giving an N-aryl five-membered aromatic heterocycle with two nitrogen atoms. The imidazole's remaining nitrogen is a basic, hydrogen-bond-accepting site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The system is largely planar and rigid, with only the methoxy group offering limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group, attached to the ring), which is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The opposite side carries a 1,2,4-triazole ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms, leaving the ring's remaining nitrogens free to act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two aromatic rings are joined by a single bond, and the overall scaffold is planar and largely rigid, with the methoxy group giving only limited rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its substitution pattern is symmetric about the long axis through the two ends of the ring system.

The molecule is built around a linear, rigid core in which two benzene rings are joined by a carbon-carbon triple bond, creating a diarylalkyne scaffold with no ring fusion. One ring carries an n-pentyl chain at the position para to the alkyne, while the other carries a methoxy group, also para to the alkyne, giving a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern on each ring. The alkyne and the aligned aromatic rings make the core very rigid and extended, with only the pentyl chain and methoxy group providing conformational flexibility. The molecule has an overall pseudo-linear shape with approximate inversion-type symmetry. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the ether oxygen of the methoxy group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a diacylhydrazine: two carbonyl groups joined by a central N–N bond, with one carbonyl bearing a para-methoxyphenyl ring and the other bearing a naphthalen-1-yl group, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings. The methoxy group is attached at the para position of the benzene ring, giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The two aromatic systems are rigid, while the hydrazide linkage provides some conformational flexibility around its amide bonds. Each N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two carbonyl oxygens and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single cyclohexane ring whose carbon bears both a nitrile group and a para-methoxyphenyl ring, making that one carbon quaternary. The aromatic ring is a benzene bearing a methoxy group (an ether oxygen attached to a methyl) at the position opposite the cyclohexyl attachment, giving a para-disubstituted pattern. The nitrile is a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ether oxygen is a weaker acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The cyclohexane ring is saturated and can adopt chair conformations, whereas the aromatic ring is planar and rigid. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry plane through the full molecule, though the aryl ring itself is symmetric about its methoxy-to-substituent axis.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing an iodine atom at one position and a pyrrole ring attached at the opposite (para) position through its nitrogen atom. Both rings are simple monocyclic aromatic systems with no ring fusion, and the pyrrole nitrogen is substituted, so it carries no N-H. The structure has no conventional hydrogen-bond donors, and the only lone-pair-bearing site is the pyrrole nitrogen, which is delocalized into the aromatic ring and is a weak acceptor. The two rings are joined by a single C–N bond that allows rotation, giving the molecule modest conformational flexibility, while the aryl rings themselves are planar. The overall arrangement is a linear, rod-like, elongated shape with a plane of approximate symmetry running along the long axis.

The molecule is built from a biphenyl core, with one phenyl ring bearing a methoxy group at the para position and the other carrying a sulfonyl group at its para position. That sulfonyl group is bonded to the nitrogen of a pyrrolidine ring, which is a saturated five-membered ring, and the carbon next to that nitrogen carries a carboxylic acid. The two aromatic rings are linked directly by a single bond and can rotate relative to each other, giving moderate flexibility. The sulfonamide and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the carboxylic acid also provides a hydrogen-bond donor, while the methoxy oxygen serves as an additional acceptor. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents on the two ends differ.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a hydroxyl group on one side and a tetrazole ring on the other. The tetrazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, attached to the benzene through one of its ring nitrogens, and it bears a thiol group on the carbon adjacent to that attachment point. The overall scaffold is a flat, rigid biaryl-type framework with few rotatable bonds, and the aryl-to-heterocycle link allows only limited rotation. The hydroxyl group and the thiol group can each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen atoms of the tetrazole and the oxygen of the hydroxyl can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the para axis of the benzene ring, since the two ends carry different functional groups.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing a fluorine atom and a piperazine ring attached through one nitrogen, with the two substituents placed para to each other on the aromatic ring. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens at opposite positions, so it adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the fluorinated phenyl ring is planar and rigid. The aryl-linked nitrogen is a tertiary amine bonded to the ring carbons, whereas the distal nitrogen is a secondary amine carrying a free N–H, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The fluorine atom acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall arrangement has a rough mirror-plane symmetry through the long axis of the molecule.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a fluorine atom, and the other is a pyrrole ring attached through its nitrogen atom, which makes the ring nitrogen part of the aromatic system rather than a basic amine. Both rings are planar and fully aromatic, with no fused ring system, and the single bond joining them allows some rotational freedom. The overall shape is linear and flat, with a twofold-like symmetry axis running through the fluorine and the pyrrole ring's nitrogen. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on carbon, and its only acceptor site is the electronegative fluorine atom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monosubstituted-pattern aromatic scaffold with two substituents placed para to each other. One substituent is an ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain), which contributes an ether linkage with a flexible two-carbon tail. The other is a 1-hydroxyethyl group, a secondary alcohol attached to the ring through a stereogenic carbon that carries a methyl branch. The para arrangement gives the aromatic core a rigid, planar framework, while the saturated side chains add conformational flexibility. The molecule has a chiral center at the benzylic carbon, and its overall shape is not symmetric about the ring because the two side chains differ. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from two para-substituted benzene rings joined by a rigid carbon-carbon triple bond, giving a linear, rod-like scaffold. One ring carries a straight n-pentyl chain at the para position, while the other carries an ethoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to an ethyl group) at its para position. Both substituents sit on opposite ends of the aromatic core, so the molecule has an approximately centrosymmetric, elongated shape with limited conformational freedom apart from the flexible alkyl and ethoxy tails. The only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the ether oxygen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built around a cyclopropane ring, a three-membered carbocycle that gives the structure a compact and fairly rigid core. One carbon of this ring is quaternary, bearing both a carboxylic acid group and a para-chlorophenyl substituent, so the two groups are attached to the same atom. The benzene ring carries a single chlorine atom at the position opposite its point of attachment, which gives it a symmetric substitution pattern. The carboxylic acid contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen) capability, while the chlorine offers only weak acceptor character. Overall, the molecule is conformationally restricted by the cyclopropane and has limited flexibility apart from rotation around the bond linking the aromatic ring to the cyclopropane.

The molecule is built around a para-chlorophenyl ring attached to a sulfonyl group, which is in turn bonded to a methylene carbon that connects to a ketone flanked by a bulky tert-butyl group. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered ring carrying a chlorine atom at the position opposite the sulfur-bearing carbon, giving a para substitution pattern with a local two-fold symmetry axis through the ring. The sulfone (SO2) linkage is tetrahedral at sulfur and provides two strong hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, while the ketone carbonyl adds a third acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its chain segment between the ring and the tert-butyl group contains rotatable single bonds, giving it moderate conformational flexibility around the aryl-sulfonyl and methylene connections.

The molecule is built around a cyclohexane ring in which one carbon bears two substituents: a carboxylic acid group and a para-chlorophenyl ring. The phenyl ring is a simple benzene with a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving it a symmetric, para-disubstituted pattern. The saturated cyclohexane ring is non-fused and adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the carbon that carries both substituents is quaternary. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, whereas the chlorine and the aromatic ring offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a biphenyl system, two benzene rings joined by a single bond, with one ring bearing a 1-hydroxyethyl group at the para position relative to the biaryl linkage. That secondary alcohol carbon carries both a methyl group and a hydroxyl group, making it a stereogenic center. The unsubstituted phenyl ring is attached through a direct carbon-carbon bond, so the scaffold is largely planar and rigid, though rotation about the central bond remains possible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two rings are substituted differently. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak acceptor character through their pi systems.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a 1-hydroxyethyl group, meaning a two-carbon chain whose terminal carbon carries a secondary alcohol, while the other substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, whereas the side chain has a rotatable bond, giving the molecule modest conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the bromine contributes a weakly polarizable, halogen-type acceptor site. The structure has a stereocenter at the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group, and its overall shape is elongated and approximately mirror-symmetric about the ring axis.

The molecule is built from a three-carbon chain bearing a terminal alkyne, a secondary alcohol, and an ether oxygen linked to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single unfused benzene carrying a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the ether oxygen, which makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The propargylic alcohol portion gives the molecule one stereocenter and a flexible chain that connects the rigid aryl ring to the linear alkyne. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen and the fluorine atoms serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with two substituents placed para to each other, so there is no ring fusion. One substituent is a 1-hydroxyethyl group, a two-carbon chain bearing a secondary alcohol at the benzylic position and a stereocenter there, while the other is a primary amine attached directly to the aromatic ring. The para pattern gives the aromatic core a symmetric, rod-like shape, though the side chain introduces some conformational flexibility through rotation around its single bonds. Both the hydroxyl and the amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, and both can accept them through their lone pairs, making the molecule capable of extensive hydrogen-bonding interactions.

The molecule is a diacylhydrazine, with two carbonyl groups joined through a central N–N bond. One acyl unit is a 3-methoxybenzoyl group, a benzene ring bearing a methoxy substituent at the meta position relative to the carbonyl. The other acyl unit is a 1-naphthoyl group, a naphthalene ring system attached through its alpha carbon, which gives a fused bicyclic aromatic scaffold. The two aromatic systems are linked by the flexible hydrazide core, so the molecule is only moderately rigid overall and lacks any internal symmetry. Each amide-type N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a three-carbon chain bearing a terminal alkyne, a secondary alcohol, and an aryl ether linkage. The terminal carbon-carbon triple bond sits at one end of a short flexible segment, with a hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon and a methylene bridge leading to an oxygen attached to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused benzene system carrying one chlorine atom at the meta position relative to the ether oxygen, so the substitution pattern is 1,3. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically along the chain and ring. The alkyne and the aromatic ring provide some rigidity, while the saturated linker permits rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other, so there is no ring fusion and no aromatic character. One nitrogen carries a three-carbon chain terminating in a hydroxyl group, giving a flexible primary alcohol tail attached to the ring. The other nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing a hydrogen. The ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the propyl chain adds conformational freedom. Both nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the secondary amine N–H and the terminal hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the hydroxyl oxygen is an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on that ring at meta positions relative to each other: a primary amino group (–NH2) on one carbon and a 1-hydroxyethyl group (–CH(OH)CH3) on the carbon three positions away. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the secondary alcohol in the side chain offers one donor and one acceptor site. The side chain contains a stereogenic carbon, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the two substituents onto each other. Apart from rotation about the single bonds linking the side chain and amine to the ring, the structure is fairly rigid.

The molecule is built around an imidazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. The ring is monosubstituted: one ring nitrogen carries a three-carbon linker (propyl chain) that terminates in a primary amine group. The other ring nitrogen is unsubstituted and remains available as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the terminal primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The unbranched, saturated chain gives the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility, in contrast to the rigid planar aromatic core. The structure has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry, since the ring substitution is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methyl groups, giving a 1,2-dimethyl substitution pattern, with a piperazine ring attached at the para position relative to one of the methyls. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 arrangement; one nitrogen is bonded directly to the aromatic ring as a tertiary aryl amine, while the other remains a secondary amine with an N–H. The aryl-piperazine linkage is flexible, as the saturated ring can adopt chair conformations, whereas the benzene core is planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane that would render the aromatic substitution fully symmetric. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and both nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, although the aryl-bound nitrogen's lone pair is partly delocalized into the ring.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring that carries two methyl groups at the carbon positions flanking the nitrogen, which makes it a 2,5-dimethylpyrrole unit. The pyrrole nitrogen is bonded directly to a benzene ring, so the two aromatic systems are joined by a single N-aryl bond rather than being fused. That benzene ring bears two chlorine atoms at its meta positions relative to the attachment point, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstitution pattern. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since the nitrogen is fully substituted, while the lone pair on the nitrogen is delocalized into the aromatic ring and only weakly accepts hydrogen bonds. Overall the structure is largely planar and aromatic with limited conformational flexibility, apart from rotation about the N-aryl bond.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing a trifluoromethyl group on one carbon, with the adjacent (ortho) carbon bonded directly to the nitrogen of an imidazole ring, giving a 1,2-disubstituted, non-fused arrangement. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogens separated by one carbon, and it is attached to the phenyl ring through its N1 position, leaving the second nitrogen free. The CF3 group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky, and conformationally rigid substituent. Because the two rings are joined by a single bond flanked by an ortho group, they are twisted relative to one another, which limits the overall flexibility of the molecule. The unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent chlorine atoms at the 3- and 4-positions, with a piperazine ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms at the 1-position of the benzene. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens opposite each other, so the molecule is an N-aryl piperazine. The aryl nitrogen is tertiary, bonded to the benzene and two ring carbons, while the distal nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing one hydrogen. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, and the piperazine adopts a chair-like conformation attached by a single bond, giving moderate flexibility. The molecule lacks a mirror plane or significant symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the piperazine ring, and the substitution pattern on the phenyl ring is asymmetric. The secondary amine provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor site, while the tertiary aryl nitrogen and the chlorine atoms contribute additional weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a 1,3-diketone in which a thiophene ring is attached to one carbonyl carbon. The thiophene is a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom and is connected directly to a ketone, giving a flat, conjugated aryl ketone. The other side of the diketone chain is a methylene group followed by a second carbonyl bearing a trifluoromethyl group, which places three fluorine atoms on a single carbon. The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the central methylene is relatively acidic and can tautomerize to an enol form that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds in the chain, with the aromatic ring remaining rigid and planar.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings, with a hydroxyl group sitting on one ring adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon. An azo linkage (N=N) connects the naphthalene at the position next to that hydroxyl to a thiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the hydroxyl and azo groups sit on one side of the fused system and the thiazole is attached through a single nitrogen-bonded linkage. The fused aromatic framework and the planar azo bridge make the structure largely rigid and conjugated. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thiazole nitrogen and the azo nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered piperidin-4-one ring, a saturated nitrogen heterocycle bearing a ketone carbonyl at the position opposite the nitrogen. The ring nitrogen is tertiary, carrying a two-carbon ethyl linker that terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the aromatic group is attached through a flexible chain rather than being fused to the core. The scaffold contains no ring fusion, and the phenyl ring is monosubstituted with no additional substituents. Because the chain and the saturated ring can adopt multiple conformations, the molecule is fairly flexible, with the aromatic ring able to orient freely relative to the heterocycle. The ketone oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the tertiary amine nitrogen can also accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, with a hydroxyl group on one ring that sits adjacent to the azo linkage. The azo group (N=N) connects that naphthol carbon to a pyridine ring at its 2-position, so the molecule contains three aromatic ring systems in an extended, nearly planar arrangement. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, with no meaningful internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic framework and the conjugated azo bridge limit rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine nitrogen, the azo nitrogens, and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a diarylalkyne with a rigid linear core: two phenyl rings are joined through a carbon-carbon triple bond, and that alkyne sits on a para-substituted benzene ring. The opposite side of that central ring carries a two-carbon ethylene linker that connects to a third phenyl ring, so the whole framework is an extended chain of three aromatic rings with no fused ring systems. The alkyne and the para substitution make the central portion essentially linear and quite rigid, while the saturated CH2–CH2 linker adds a degree of flexibility at the far end. There are no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its only overall symmetry is the near-linear pseudo-axis running through the chain.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent positions. One position bears a nitro group, a nitrogen atom doubly bonded to two oxygens in a charge-separated arrangement, which is strongly electron-withdrawing. The neighboring position bears a piperidine ring attached through its nitrogen, a saturated six-membered ring of five carbons and one nitrogen. This makes the scaffold an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system with a tertiary amine linked directly to the arene. The piperidine ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond local rotational freedom in the saturated ring. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing a nitro group and a pyrrole ring joined directly through a single bond between the two rings. The nitro group, drawn as a charge-separated N(+)-O(-) unit, sits on one carbon of the benzene ring, and the pyrrole nitrogen is bonded to the adjacent carbon, making this an ortho-disubstituted arrangement. The two aromatic rings are not fused but are connected by a single rotatable bond, so the molecule has some conformational flexibility, though the ortho substituents will hinder free rotation and favor a twisted geometry. The nitro group is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the pyrrole nitrogen is fully substituted by the aryl linkage.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, with the substituent attached at the 2-position of the naphthalene. A ketone carbonyl links this aromatic ring to a three-atom chain containing a second ketone, and that chain terminates in a trifluoromethyl group, so the molecule is a 1,3-diketone bearing a CF3 group at one end. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and because the methylene between them is flanked by two carbonyls, the chain can adopt enolic tautomers that also carry a hydrogen-bond donor. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the aliphatic diketone chain is comparatively flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent sits on only one ring of the naphthalene.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. A 1-hydroxyethyl group is attached at the 2-position of one ring, creating a secondary alcohol with a stereocenter at the carbon bearing the hydroxyl, a methyl group, and the aromatic ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the side chain offers some rotational freedom around the bond to the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic system contributes only weak acceptor character through its π-electron cloud.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. One nitrogen is bonded to a phenyl ring that carries a methoxy group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, placing the two substituents in an ortho arrangement. The other piperazine nitrogen is an unsubstituted secondary amine, while the methoxy oxygen and the aryl-bonded nitrogen act as weak acceptors. The aromatic ring and the chair-capable piperazine give the structure a moderate degree of conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local symmetry of the piperazine ring.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered piperidine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The ring nitrogen carries a 2-hydroxyethyl side chain, a two-carbon chain ending in a primary alcohol, so the only functional groups present are a tertiary amine and a primary hydroxyl. The remaining ring carbons are unsubstituted, giving a simple, unsymmetrical substitution pattern with the chain sitting entirely on nitrogen. The piperidine ring adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, and the side chain can rotate freely about its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the tertiary nitrogen can only act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a saturated seven-membered diazepane ring, a 1,4-diazepane, in which two nitrogen atoms sit at opposite positions separated by three carbons on one side and two on the other. One of the nitrogens carries a 2-methoxyethyl side chain, an ether-linked two-carbon arm terminated by a methyl ether, while the other nitrogen is a secondary amine with a free N–H. The ring contains no double bonds or fused rings, so the scaffold is fully sp3 and conformationally flexible. The molecule has no symmetry because the two nitrogens bear different substituents. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and both nitrogen lone pairs and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered saturated ring containing one carbonyl group and a nitrogen atom adjacent to it, forming a cyclic urea-type lactam with a ring carbonyl flanked by two nitrogens. The ring is not fused to any other ring system, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic core with no bridging or additional rings. A 2-hydroxyethyl chain is attached to the ring nitrogen that is not bonded to the carbonyl, placing a primary alcohol at the terminus of a flexible two-carbon linker. The structure has no internal symmetry, since the substituent sits on only one nitrogen. Hydrogen-bond capability is present on both ends: the ring N-H and the terminal hydroxyl act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other, with no fused or additional rings. One nitrogen atom carries a 2-hydroxyethyl side chain, a two-carbon chain ending in a primary alcohol, while the other nitrogen is an unsubstituted secondary amine with an N-H group. The molecule has no stereocenters and possesses a plane of symmetry running through both nitrogen atoms, though the ring can interconvert between chair conformations and the side chain adds conformational flexibility. Both the hydroxyl group and the secondary amine N-H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two nitrogen atoms and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a two-part structure: a five-membered aromatic furan ring bearing, at its 2-position, a two-carbon vinyl linker that carries a nitro group on the terminal carbon. The furan ring is a single unfused heteroaromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, with the remaining three ring carbons unsubstituted. The carbon-carbon double bond in the linker has a trans (E) geometry, which makes the attached nitro-vinyl unit planar and rigid, extending conjugation from the furan into the nitro group. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the conjugated system. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the furan oxygen and the two oxygens of the nitro group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a piperazine scaffold, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One of these nitrogens carries a 2-fluorophenyl group, meaning a benzene ring bearing a fluorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment. The other piperazine nitrogen is an unsubstituted secondary amine, so it bears a hydrogen. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the piperazine ring is flexible and can adopt chair-like conformations. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two ring substituents differ. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and as an acceptor, while the tertiary aryl-substituted nitrogen and the fluorine can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other. One of these nitrogens is acylated, forming an amide linkage to a furan-2-carbonyl group, which is a planar, aromatic five-membered oxygen-containing ring attached through its carbon adjacent to the oxygen. The other piperazine nitrogen remains a secondary amine with an N–H bond, making it both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor. The amide carbonyl oxygen and the furan oxygen serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the two ring nitrogens carry different substituents, while the piperazine ring retains conformational flexibility through chair-like interconversion.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined directly by a single bond: a benzene ring carrying a primary amino group on one carbon, and a pyrrole ring attached through its nitrogen atom to the benzene carbon adjacent to that amine. The benzene ring is therefore ortho-disubstituted, with the amino group and the pyrrole nitrogen on neighboring positions.
