Both rings are planar and aromatic, while the single bond between them permits rotation, giving the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited internal symmetry. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair acceptor, whereas the pyrrole nitrogen is substituted and contributes its lone pair to the aromatic system, so it is not a hydrogen-bond donor and acts only weakly as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A nitro group (–NO2, drawn here as a charge-separated N+ and O− pair) is attached to one carbon of the ring, and a two-carbon chain ending in a bromine atom is attached to the carbon directly opposite it, giving a para-disubstituted pattern. The ethyl linker bearing the terminal bromide adds conformational flexibility, while the aromatic core and nitro group remain planar and rigid. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, broken only by the difference between the two substituents. The nitro group contains two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two methyl groups in a 1,4 (para) relationship to each other, with the remaining positions bearing a piperazine ring attached through one of its nitrogens. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, and the methyl groups sit on positions that give the benzene ring a pattern of substitution that is asymmetric overall, since the piperazine is attached at a different position than the two methyls. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens opposite each other; one nitrogen is bonded directly to the aryl ring as a tertiary amine, while the other is a secondary amine with an N-H. Because the piperazine ring is saturated, it adopts a chair-like conformation and provides some conformational flexibility, whereas the aromatic portion is rigid and planar. The secondary amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and both nitrogen atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered saturated piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite each other (1,4-relationship). One ring nitrogen carries a 2-aminoethyl side chain, a two-carbon linker ending in a primary amine, while the other ring nitrogen is a secondary amine with an N-H bond. The ring adopts a flexible, non-planar chair-like conformation, and the side chain can rotate freely about its single bonds, so the overall structure is conformationally mobile. There are no aromatic rings or ring fusions, and no stereocenters, so the molecule is achiral. Because it contains two N-H donors on the primary and secondary amines and three nitrogen lone-pair acceptors overall, it can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built around a piperazine ring, a six-membered saturated heterocycle with nitrogen atoms at opposite positions. One nitrogen is bonded to a benzene ring, which carries two fluorine atoms on the aromatic carbons at the 2- and 5-positions relative to that attachment point, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The other piperazine nitrogen is a secondary amine with an N-H bond, so it can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the aryl-bonded nitrogen acts mainly as a weak acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the piperazine ring is flexible and can adopt chair-like conformations. Overall, the molecule has no internal symmetry, combining a flat fluorinated aromatic portion with a more three-dimensional saturated heterocycle.

The molecule is built on a cyclohexane ring, with a single saturated quaternary carbon bearing both a hydroxyl group and a but-2-ynyl chain (a methyl group attached to an alkyne, which is linked to the ring carbon). The ring is fully saturated and contains no fusion or additional substituents, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic six-membered carbocycle. The carbon-carbon triple bond makes the side chain linear and rigid at that point, while the cyclohexane ring adopts flexible chair conformations. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane because the substituted carbon is unique. The tertiary hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, whereas the alkyne and saturated carbons contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three isopropyl groups and one sulfonyl group, giving a crowded, highly alkylated aromatic core. The three isopropyl substituents sit at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the sulfonyl attachment, producing a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The sulfonyl group bridges the arene to a 1,2,4-triazole ring through a nitrogen atom, forming an N-sulfonyl azole linkage. The triazole is an aromatic five-membered ring containing three nitrogen atoms, which can accept hydrogen bonds at its ring nitrogens, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bulky isopropyl groups flanking the sulfonyl linkage restrict rotation and make the overall structure fairly rigid.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para arrangement. One position bears a thioether linkage to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, so the core scaffold is an aryl thioacetic acid. The other para position carries a trifluoromethyl group, which is a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky substituent. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2–S–CH2 linker and the carboxylic acid group add conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the sulfur and fluorine atoms offer weak acceptor character.

The molecule consists of two saturated six-membered nitrogen-containing rings joined by a single carbon-to-nitrogen bond, so there is no ring fusion and no aromatic system. One ring is an N-methylated piperidine, in which the ring nitrogen carries a methyl group, and the other is an unsubstituted piperazine ring linked through one of its nitrogens to the carbon at the 4-position of the first ring. Both nitrogens of the piperazine ring are basic amines, with one bearing the bond to the piperidine and the other being a secondary amine that is free to donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule is fully saturated and conformationally flexible, with the two rings able to adopt chair conformations and rotate about the connecting bond. It has no stereocenters and an overall bis-amine framework.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One side carries a sulfonyl group (SO2) that is bonded to a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile (C≡N), so the sulfur links the aromatic ring to a cyanomethyl unit. The opposite side of the ring carries a trifluoromethyl group (CF3), which is strongly electron-withdrawing. There are no fused or additional ring systems; the aromatic ring is the only cyclic element. The molecule has an approximately linear, rod-like shape with a rigid aromatic core and a more flexible sulfonyl-methylene linkage. Its sulfonyl oxygens and nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short acyclic carboxylic acid built on a two-carbon chain, with a trimethylsilyl group attached to the carbon next to the carboxyl. The silicon atom is tetrahedral and bears three methyl substituents plus the CH2 linker, giving a bulky, nonpolar silyl end. The terminal carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) contains one carbonyl oxygen that can accept a hydrogen bond and one hydroxyl group that can both donate and accept one. There are no rings or fused systems, and the molecule is highly flexible because of the many rotatable single bonds. The three methyl groups on silicon are arranged around a single center, giving the silyl end local threefold symmetry, while the overall molecule lacks a mirror or inversion center.

The molecule is built on a symmetric, fully aromatic scaffold made of two benzene rings joined by two ethylene bridges, forming a rigid macrocyclic loop. Each benzene ring is connected through its ortho-related and para-related positions to the bridges, so the two rings sit across from one another in a para-linked arrangement. The overall framework has high symmetry, with a central axis that the two aromatic units and their bridges mirror. The structure contains no heteroatoms and no functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its only features are the aromatic rings and the saturated CH2 bridges, which together make the core largely rigid and nonpolar.

This molecule is built from two linked ring systems: a pyridine ring bearing a single substituent at the 3-position, joined to a saturated five-membered pyrrolidine ring. The pyrrolidine nitrogen carries a methyl group, making it a tertiary amine, and the carbon bonded to the pyridine is a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral. The two rings are not fused but connected by a single carbon–carbon bond, which allows some rotation and gives moderate flexibility around that linkage. The pyridine nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogens are substituted or aromatic. Overall, the structure is asymmetric, with the aromatic and saturated halves contrasting sharply.

The molecule is a 1,2-diphenylethane-1,2-diol, with two phenyl rings each attached to one of two adjacent stereogenic carbons that each carry a hydroxyl group. The central two-carbon chain links the two benzene rings through a flexible sp3 backbone, giving the molecule a C2-type symmetry when its stereocenters are considered. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the aromatic portions carry no additional functional groups. The two secondary hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic rings contribute pi-electron density but no hydrogen-bonding capability of their own.

This molecule is a five-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen in the ring, with a carbonyl at the 2-position of a carbamate-like unit and a second carbonyl adjacent to the ring oxygen, forming an oxazolidine-2,5-dione scaffold. A sec-butyl group is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, creating a single stereocenter at that position. The ring is essentially planar and fully unsaturated at its two carbonyls, giving it limited conformational flexibility, while the sec-butyl chain adds some rotational freedom. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two carbonyl oxygens along with the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution at the stereocenter.

The molecule is a quaternary stereogenic carbon bearing four different substituents: a methoxy group, a carboxylic acid, a phenyl ring, and a trifluoromethyl group, making it a mandelic-acid-type scaffold with the alpha-hydroxyl converted to a methyl ether. The phenyl ring is a single unfused benzene ring attached directly to the central carbon, and the trifluoromethyl group adds three strongly electron-withdrawing fluorine atoms at the same position. The carboxylic acid is the main functional group, offering both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the ether oxygen provides an additional acceptor site. The molecule is compact and fairly rigid around the stereocenter, with the phenyl ring and carboxyl group as the principal structural anchors and no internal symmetry, since the four substituents on the central carbon are all distinct.

The molecule is a Boc-protected 3-aminopiperidine: a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle (piperidine) bearing a carbamate substituent at the 3-position. The ring is fully saturated with no double bonds or fused rings, so it adopts a chair-like conformation that is comparatively rigid. The exocyclic nitrogen forms a carbamate linkage to a tert-butyl ester group, which carries three equivalent methyl groups giving a bulky, symmetric tert-butyl end. The stereocenter at the ring carbon bearing the carbamate is defined, making the molecule chiral. The carbamate N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the ester oxygen, and the ring secondary amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with the ring NH also able to donate.

The molecule is built on a five-membered thiazolidine ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, with the nitrogen acylated by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group (a carbamate bearing a bulky tert-butyl ester). Adjacent to the ring carbon next to nitrogen sits a free carboxylic acid, creating a single stereogenic center with a defined (chiral) configuration. The scaffold is saturated and non-fused, so the ring is relatively rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk and the carbamate and acid groups confer hydrogen-bond donor capability (the acid OH) and multiple acceptor sites (carbonyl and ether oxygens). The molecule lacks any symmetry because of the single chiral center and its differently substituted ring positions.

The molecule is an acyclic, aliphatic compound built from a branched carbon chain with no rings and no aromatic groups, so its scaffold is flexible and open rather than rigid. A terminal carboxylic acid (–COOH) sits at one end of the chain, separated from a stereogenic carbon bearing an isobutyl-type branch, and that same carbon carries a carbamate nitrogen. The nitrogen is acylated by a tert-butoxycarbonyl-type group, an O-linked tert-butyl ester of carbonic acid, which adds a bulky, quaternary carbon cluster to one end of the molecule. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the carboxylic acid (one donor and two acceptor oxygens) and the carbamate N–H and carbonyl oxygen, while the many methyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk.

This molecule is a Boc-protected beta-amino acid built on a linear chain with a single stereogenic center. The nitrogen is capped by a tert-butyl carbamate, a bulky tert-butyl group bonded through an oxygen to a carbonyl that is in turn bonded to the nitrogen. The chiral carbon carries a free carboxylic acid arm (CH2-COOH) and a CH2 linker to a pyridine ring. That pyridine is a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle attached at its 4-position, giving a symmetric, unfused ring. The molecule has rotatable single bonds, so it is fairly flexible apart from the planar carbamate and aromatic ring. Hydrogen-bond donors are the carbamate N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H, while acceptors include the carbonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen.

This molecule is a Boc-protected, phenyl-substituted beta-amino acid derivative. A tert-butyl carbamate group, with its bulky quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, is attached through an NH to a stereogenic carbon that carries a carboxymethyl arm (CH2-COOH) and a benzyl group. The benzyl unit is a monosubstituted phenyl ring, unfused and with no further substitution, giving the molecule a flexible acyclic backbone with a single aromatic ring. The carbamate NH and the carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of the carbamate and acid serve as acceptors. Only one stereocenter is present, so the molecule is chiral and lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a Boc-protected phenylalanine-type amino acid homolog, built on a flexible acyclic chain bearing one monosubstituted benzene ring at its terminus. The tert-butyl group sits on a carbamate, which links through an NH to a single stereogenic carbon carrying a terminal carboxylic acid. Two methylene units separate that carbon from the phenyl ring, so the aromatic ring is not directly attached to the backbone. The benzene ring is unsubstituted and gives the molecule an unbranched, extended shape with limited rigidity overall. The carbamate NH and the carboxylic acid OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of both groups serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered lactam ring, a pyrrolidin-2-one (gamma-lactam) scaffold, with a single carbonyl group adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring is saturated apart from that amide carbonyl, and it carries no fused or additional ring systems. At the carbon next to the nitrogen, opposite the lactam carbonyl, sits a carboxylic acid group, giving the molecule a single stereogenic center with a defined configuration. Its overall shape is compact and fairly rigid because of the cyclic amide, though the carboxylic acid can rotate freely. The molecule has no internal symmetry. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the lactam carbonyl oxygen and both oxygens of the carboxylic acid act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the acid's hydroxyl also functions as a donor.

This molecule is a tert-butyl carbamate built on a six-membered saturated nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring. The nitrogen of the ring is acylated by a carbonyl group that is bonded to a tert-butoxy group, giving the carbamate its characteristic N-C(=O)-O linkage. A hydroxyl group sits on a ring carbon adjacent to the carbon bearing the nitrogen-linked CH2, creating a 3-hydroxy substitution pattern with a single stereocenter. The bulky tert-butyl group is attached through an oxygen and projects away from the ring. The ring is fully saturated and adopts a chair-like conformation, so the structure is relatively rigid, though the carbamate bond has restricted rotation. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with a methoxy group on one ring at the position two atoms from the fusion on the far side. The second ring carries a single substituent: a propanoic acid unit attached through a stereogenic carbon bearing a methyl group, so the chain is branched and chiral. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group acts as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the side chain attached to it has rotational freedom around its single bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered carbocyclic ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. The ring carries two substituents: a methyl group on one ring carbon sitting across a ring double bond, and an isopropenyl group (a carbon bearing a methyl and a terminal methylene) attached at a stereogenic ring carbon. The ring contains one endocyclic carbon-carbon double bond, which imposes local rigidity, while the remaining sp3 ring atoms allow some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no heteroatoms and no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its only substitution is hydrocarbon in nature. Because the isopropenyl-bearing carbon is a single stereocenter with no internal mirror plane, the molecule is chiral and lacks overall symmetry.

The molecule is a beta-amino acid derivative built on a single acyclic carbon chain bearing a stereocenter. One end carries a tert-butyl carbamate (Boc-type) group, in which a tert-butyl ester oxygen links to a carbonyl that is bonded to the nitrogen. The other end is a terminal carboxylic acid, separated from the stereocenter by one methylene unit. The stereocenter also bears a para-bromophenyl ring, a benzene ring with a bromine atom opposite the point of attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern with no fused ring systems. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the chiral center and the differing ends. Its aromatic and carbamate portions are relatively rigid, while the aliphatic chain and tert-butyl group add conformational flexibility. The carbamate N–H and carboxylic acid O–H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl and ether oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built around a saturated five-membered thiazolidine ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, with a stereocenter at the carbon between them. The nitrogen is protected by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group, a carbamate linked to a bulky tert-butyl ether, which makes the nitrogen non-basic and adds considerable steric bulk. A free carboxylic acid is attached directly to the stereocenter, making it an alpha-amino-acid-like scaffold. The ring is non-aromatic and has modest conformational flexibility, while the carbamate and acid carbonyls provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, and the carboxylic acid OH supplies one hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated piperidine ring, with the nitrogen atom at position 1 bearing a tert-butoxycarbonyl group. This carbamate consists of a carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring nitrogen and to an oxygen that carries a tert-butyl group, with the three methyls of the tert-butyl unit giving a bulky, symmetric end. A single hydroxyl group sits on a ring carbon at position 3, relative to the nitrogen, which creates a stereogenic center and breaks the ring's symmetry. The ring adopts a chair-like conformation with limited flexibility, and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The carbamate carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl group at one position, with a flexible two-carbon chain extending from the sulfur. The sulfur is in a sulfone arrangement, bonded to two oxygen atoms through double bonds and to the aromatic ring and a methylene group. The methylene carbon connects to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the molecule has a single carboxyl group at one end. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and the overall structure has no stereocenters and little internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring. The carboxylic acid OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a simple two-part scaffold: a benzene ring bonded through a sulfur atom to a two-carbon acetic acid chain. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered ring of alternating double bonds, with the sulfur attached at one position and the remaining four positions unsubstituted. A thioether linkage (C–S–C) joins the ring to a methylene group, which is in turn bonded to a terminal carboxylic acid. The carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the sulfur atom can act as a weak acceptor. The chain is flexible due to rotation about the single bonds, whereas the phenyl ring is rigid and planar.

The molecule is built around a central phosphorus atom bonded to three aryl rings: two unsubstituted phenyl groups and one pentafluorophenyl ring, giving a triarylphosphine scaffold. Each aromatic ring is a single benzene ring with no ring fusion. The pentafluorophenyl ring carries five fluorine substituents at all positions except the one attached to phosphorus, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the P–C bond axis. The two phenyl rings are unsubstituted and equivalent to one another, so the overall molecule has only a partial mirror-type symmetry around the pentafluorophenyl axis. Rotation about the three P–C bonds gives moderate conformational flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid. The phosphorus lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors; the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing one substituent at its carbon-1 position, with no fused rings and no stereocenters. That substituent is a sulfonyl group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms), which links the aromatic ring to a methylene carbon. This methylene is in turn bonded to a primary amide, a carbonyl carbon attached to an NH2 group. The aryl sulfone and the amide together make the molecule polar and flexible, since the CH2 linker and the sulfur-carbon bonds allow rotation. The amide NH2 supplies two hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The phenyl ring has no internal symmetry axis relevant to the full structure beyond its local mirror plane, so the overall molecule lacks higher symmetry.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated aliphatic compound with no rings or aromatic systems. Its backbone is a short chain of three sp3 carbons: a terminal methyl group bonded to a secondary amine nitrogen, which connects to a central methine carbon. That central carbon carries two methoxy groups (an acetal-type arrangement), so the molecule combines a secondary amine with a dimethyl acetal. The structure is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds and no stereocenters or internal symmetry, since the central carbon bears two identical methoxy substituents. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and its nitrogen lone pair as an acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a three-carbon backbone. A terminal carboxyl group (-C(=O)OH) sits at one end, and a methylthio group (-S-CH3) is attached to the carbon adjacent to it, so the thioether sulfur is alpha to the carboxyl carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters, and the chain is highly flexible because all of its bonds are single bonds that can rotate freely. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the sulfur atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall structure has no internal symmetry, since the two ends carry chemically distinct groups.

The molecule has a central three-carbon chain in which a carbon-carbon double bond joins a terminal methyl-bearing carbon to a carbon that carries a phenyl ring, while the second carbon of the alkene also carries a second phenyl ring, so the scaffold is a 1,2-diphenylpropene framework. Both benzene rings are unsubstituted, simple six-membered aromatic rings attached to the alkene, and the molecule has no heteroatoms, so it contains no functional groups beyond the alkene and aromatic systems. The stilbene-like arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold relationship between its phenyl groups, though the methyl group breaks perfect symmetry. The rigid, planar alkene and the aromatic rings restrict conformational freedom, while the single bonds to the phenyl groups permit some rotation. With no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, the molecule has no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a tertiary phosphine oxide built around a central pentavalent phosphorus atom bearing a double-bonded oxygen. Two phenyl rings are attached directly to the phosphorus, giving a diarylphosphinyl core, and the remaining substituent is a methoxymethyl group (–CH2–O–CH3) that is flexible and acyclic. The two benzene rings are unfused and freely rotating about the P–C bonds, so the scaffold is fairly flexible and lacks a fixed symmetry plane. The phosphoryl oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ether oxygen provides a weaker acceptor site, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen, with a carbonyl group attached at the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen. From the carbonyl extends a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond that terminates in a dimethylamino group, giving an enaminone-type conjugated chain. The ring system is a single unfused aromatic ring, while the side chain is largely planar and rigid due to the double bond and conjugation with the ketone. The pyridine nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any significant symmetry because the two ends of the chain differ substantially.

The molecule is a substituted stilbene-type scaffold: a central alkene carbon bearing a nitrile group (C≡N) and a para-chlorophenyl ring, double-bonded to a CH that carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring. The two aromatic rings are separate benzene rings joined through the alkene, with no ring fusion. The chlorine sits at the para position of one ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern overall. The conjugated C=C linkage between the rings keeps the framework largely planar and fairly rigid, with limited rotation about the double bond. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a flexible two-atom-linked scaffold, with a benzene ring attached through a benzylic CH2 group to a sulfur atom, which connects to a CH2 bearing a terminal carboxylic acid. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, a simple monosubstituted benzene with no fused rings and no heteroatoms within the aromatic system. The carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the thioether sulfur provides a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The chain of sp3 carbons and the thioether linkage gives the molecule considerable conformational flexibility, and the lack of any symmetry element beyond a local mirror-like arrangement of the phenyl ring leaves the overall shape asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a cyclopropane scaffold, a three-membered all-carbon ring with no fused or additional rings. One ring carbon bears a substituent consisting of a methylene group linked to a chlorine atom, so the molecule is a chloromethyl-substituted cyclopropane with a single substitution site and no stereocenters beyond the ring carbon that carries the group. The ring is strained and rigid, while the chloromethyl arm adds some conformational freedom around its single bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains only C–H bonds. Its only polar feature is the carbon–chlorine bond, which gives the chlorine atom weak acceptor character, and the overall structure lacks any symmetry beyond local ring symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with alternating double bonds. One ring carbon carries a tert-butyl group, a central quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, which provides bulk. The carbon directly opposite on the ring, para to it, bears an ether oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 across the ring. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the ring axis, and the aromatic ring is rigid while the ether and cyanomethyl portion retains some rotational freedom. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a five-membered 1,3,4-thiadiazole aromatic ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom. At one ring carbon sits a thioether linkage that connects to a flexible CH2 group bearing a terminal carboxylic acid, giving the molecule a carboxymethyl sulfanyl arm. The opposite ring carbon carries a free thiol (sulfanyl) group, so the two carbon positions of the ring are substituted at 2 and 5. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the thioether-linked acetic acid chain adds conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group and the thiol serve as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carboxyl oxygens and ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two ring substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a fluorine atom, and the other is a thioether linked to a two-carbon unit that terminates in a nitrile group, so the ring carries a sulfur-bridged cyanomethyl chain. There is no ring fusion, and the aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the S-CH2-C≡N chain has some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring axis and sulfur atom, giving it a fairly symmetric shape. Its hydrogen-bond donor capacity is zero because it has no N-H or O-H groups, whereas the nitrile nitrogen, the fluorine, and the sulfur can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring containing two nitrogen atoms separated by one carbon. The ring is unfused, so it stands alone with no additional rings attached. One nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, making it a pyrrole-type nitrogen that can donate a hydrogen bond, while the other nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept one. At a carbon position adjacent to the NH-bearing nitrogen sits a cyanomethyl side chain, a methylene group bonded to a nitrile. The nitrile nitrogen provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The molecule is small, largely planar, and has few rotatable bonds, so it is conformationally rigid apart from the side chain.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement, with no ring fusion present. One substituent is a fluorine atom, which sits opposite the other side chain, giving the ring a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern. The side chain attached through a sulfur atom is a thioether linked to a two-carbon unit ending in a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule carries a terminal acid functionality. The only rotatable bonds lie in the flexible thioether-acetic acid tail, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, and the fluorine and sulfur atoms can each act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a phenyl ring bearing a chlorine atom and a thioether-linked acetic acid side chain. A benzene ring carries a chlorine substituent at the position para to the sulfur atom, giving a 1,4-disubstituted, electron-poor aromatic core. The sulfur bridges the ring to a methylene group, which connects to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the chain is linear and fairly flexible around the sulfur and CH2 bonds. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine and thioether sulfur act only as weak acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and no ring fusion, and its overall shape is roughly planar in the aromatic region with a mobile tail.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a chlorine atom, attached directly to the ring, and the other is a thioether linkage (a sulfur atom bonded to the ring) that connects to a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen). The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, while the CH2 unit linking sulfur to the nitrile gives the side chain some rotational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis, though the chain itself is unsymmetrical. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, while the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a chlorine atom, and the other is a sulfonyl group, which links to a two-carbon unit ending in a nitrile. The sulfonyl group carries two S=O bonds and is directly attached to the aromatic ring, making it strongly electron-withdrawing. The nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, sits at the far end of a flexible CH2 linker. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2 unit provides some conformational freedom. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and substituents, giving it a largely symmetric shape. The sulfonyl oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single ether substituent, making it an aryl alkyl ether. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and unfused, giving a flat, rigid core, while the four-carbon chain attached through the oxygen is flexible and can adopt multiple conformations. The terminal carbon of that chain carries a bromine atom, which functions as a reactive alkyl halide site. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure is asymmetric, with a rigid aromatic head and a flexible linear alkyl tail ending in a halogen.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement: a chlorine atom and an oxygen-linked side chain. The side chain is an aryloxy group attached to a two-carbon unit ending in an acyl chloride, which is a reactive carbonyl bearing a chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ether-linked CH2 and carbonyl portion adds some conformational flexibility. The structure has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis, with no stereocenters. The ether oxygen and carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with an N-methyl group on the ring nitrogen. Attached to the carbon adjacent to that ring is a para-fluorophenyl group, a benzene ring carrying one fluorine atom opposite the point of attachment. The neighboring ring carbon bears a hydroxymethyl substituent, so there is a primary alcohol with one hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen acceptor. The two adjacent ring substituents are cis-disposed on stereogenic centers, and the molecule is chiral with no internal mirror symmetry. The piperidine ring is conformationally flexible, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused system in which a five-membered lactone ring shares an edge with a saturated pyrrolidine ring through a nitrogen atom and an adjacent carbon, giving a rigid, angularly fused scaffold. The lactone carbonyl is an ester-type C=O bearing an oxygen within the ring, and the ring oxygen is bonded to a carbon that also carries a trichloromethyl group, so the substitution pattern places a bulky CCl3 group adjacent to the ring junction. The bridgehead nitrogen is tertiary, with no N–H present, so the molecule can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at its carbonyl and ring oxygen and nitrogen but has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. Its two stereocenters give it defined three-dimensional chirality, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis or mirror plane.

The molecule is a tetrahedral silicon center bearing three methoxy groups and one 3-chloropropyl chain, making it an alkoxysilane with a single silicon atom at its core. Its skeleton is acyclic, so it contains no ring systems or ring fusion. The chloropropyl arm is a three-carbon saturated chain terminated by a chlorine atom, which serves as the only halogen-bearing functional group, while the three Si–O–CH3 units provide ether-type oxygen atoms. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond the local threefold arrangement of the methoxy groups around silicon, and its bonds are largely single and rotatable, so it is flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no O–H or N–H bonds are present, but the oxygen atoms and the chlorine can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: two adjacent methoxy groups (one at position 3 and one at position 4 relative to the thioether), and a thioether linkage. The sulfur atom connects the aromatic ring to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, so the acid is separated from the ring by a flexible CH2 and sulfur spacer. Because the ring is a single unfused aromatic system and the chain is attached through a single sulfur bond, the scaffold is largely planar at the core but has rotational freedom in the side chain. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the two ether oxygens and the sulfur serve as additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a bromine atom, and three methyl groups distributed around it, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with one remaining aromatic C–H. A secondary amide links the ring through its nitrogen to a carbonyl-bearing CH2 group, which is attached to a tertiary amine nitrogen. That nitrogen carries two carboxymethyl arms, each ending in a carboxylic acid group, so the chain is flexible and branched rather than rigid. The amide N–H and the two carboxylic acid OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide and acid carbonyl oxygens, together with the tertiary nitrogen, serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic, saturated diol with a straight-chain skeleton of seven carbons, bearing a hydroxyl group on the second and sixth carbons. Both stereocenters are defined, giving the molecule a chiral, non-superimposable arrangement, and the two terminal methyl-bearing carbinol units are chemically equivalent in connectivity, so the carbon framework has a symmetric pattern. There are no rings, no unsaturation, and no other functional groups, so the structure is flexible and can adopt many conformations about its single bonds. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act both as a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is a small acyclic chain built from two carbons, with a hydrazine group at one end and a hydroxyl group at the other, giving the skeleton H2N-NH-CH2-CH2-OH. It contains no ring systems and no ring fusion, and it has no substitution pattern beyond these two terminal heteroatom groups. The two nitrogen atoms form a N-N single bond, and the terminal oxygen carries a hydroxyl. Because the chain is saturated and unbranched, the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry and is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Both the hydrazine nitrogens and the hydroxyl oxygen and hydrogen can participate in hydrogen bonding, acting as donors and acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three carboxylic acid-containing groups. Directly attached to the aromatic ring is a tertiary amine nitrogen, which carries two carboxymethyl arms, each consisting of a CH2 linked to a terminal carboxylic acid. The third carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring at the position adjacent to the nitrogen, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The benzene ring is the only ring system, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three acid-bearing substituents differ in their attachment. The flexible methylene linkers allow considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic core remains planar. The three carboxylic acid groups provide multiple hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the amine nitrogen adds a further acceptor site.

The molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered sulfur- and nitrogen-containing ring, forming a 1,4-benzothiazine-type scaffold. The fused ring contains a thioether sulfur bonded to the aromatic ring and a methylene carbon, and a lactam-type amide carbonyl adjacent to an aryl-substituted nitrogen. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the molecule has no additional substituents beyond the fused ring system. Its partially saturated heterocycle gives it limited conformational flexibility, with the fused framework largely planar and rigid. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short, acyclic chain with no rings, so it has a flexible backbone built from a two-carbon ethylene unit linked through an ether oxygen to a methylene and then a terminal carboxyl carbon. At one end sits a primary amine (-NH2) attached to the ethylene chain, and at the other end a carboxylic acid (-COOH) group forms the terminus. The ether oxygen sits between the two carbon segments and serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The amine and carboxylic acid groups each carry hydrogen-bond donor capability, with the carboxyl group providing both donor and acceptor sites. Because the chain has no branching or ring constraints, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry and adopts many conformations.

This molecule is a simple aryl alkyl halide built on a benzene scaffold. A six-membered aromatic ring carries a single substituent: a two-carbon ethyl chain that terminates in a bromine atom, so the bromine sits at the end of the chain rather than directly on the ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted otherwise, giving it a monosubstituted pattern with a high degree of local symmetry around the ring axis. The molecule is largely flat in its aromatic portion, while the saturated two-carbon linker and the terminal carbon-bromine bond provide some conformational flexibility. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the halogen, which is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a bicyclic saturated amine built on a diazabicyclo[2.2.1]heptane-type core, with the bridged framework making the ring system rigid and three-dimensional. One nitrogen in the bicycle is a secondary amine that is free and available to donate or accept a hydrogen bond, while the other nitrogen is acylated as a carbamate. That carbamate carries a tert-butyl ester group whose bulky quaternary carbon sits at one end of the molecule, offering a sterically demanding, non-polar terminus. The carbonyl oxygen of the carbamate serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the overall scaffold is chiral with two defined stereocenters at the bridgehead positions, giving it an asymmetric shape.

The molecule has a two-carbon chain whose first carbon bears a methyl group and whose second carbon carries a hydroxyl group and a phenyl ring, giving an acyclic backbone with two adjacent stereocentres. The phenyl ring is a simple unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to the carbinol carbon. The first carbon is bonded to a pyrrolidine ring, a saturated five-membered ring containing one tertiary nitrogen. Because the nitrogen is a tertiary amine with no hydrogen on it, it can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one, while the secondary alcohol provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site. Overall the structure is moderately flexible along the acyclic chain and has no internal symmetry.

This molecule is a bicyclic camphor-derived sultam built on a bornane-type framework, with a fused carbocyclic and bridged ring system. A gem-dimethyl group sits on one bridge carbon, and the cage is rigid and compact with a defined three-dimensional shape. The sultam ring is a six-membered cyclic sulfonamide, in which a sulfur atom bearing two oxo groups is bonded to a nitrogen that is itself part of the bicyclic cage. The nitrogen carries one hydrogen, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal mirror symmetry because of its chiral centers.

This molecule is a bicyclic camphor-derived sultam, built on a rigid bornane-type carbon framework. A five-membered ring is fused to a six-membered ring, bridged so the two rings share a quaternary carbon that carries a gem-dimethyl group, which gives the skeleton a compact, cage-like shape. The five-membered ring contains a cyclic sulfonyl group (SO2) bonded to a nitrogen that is doubly bonded to a carbon, forming a cyclic N-sulfonyl imine. The sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no N-H or O-H groups and therefore no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid, largely saturated framework contrasts with the planar, polarized sulfonyl imine unit, which is the most chemically distinctive feature of the structure.

This molecule is camphorquinone, a bicyclic terpenoid built on a bornane (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) skeleton. Its rigid norbornane framework contains two bridgehead carbons, each bearing a methyl group, and a gem-dimethyl arrangement on one bridge carbon. The defining feature is an adjacent pair of ketone carbonyls (a 1,2-dione) located on the bicyclic core, which makes the two carbonyl oxygens strong hydrogen-bond acceptors while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The compact, cage-like scaffold is conformationally rigid and lacks any internal rotational freedom, and it is chiral, lacking a plane of symmetry.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-like scaffold built from a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane) core bearing two gem-dimethyl groups on one bridge carbon. A cyclohexane-like ring is not present; instead the two fused five-membered rings share a bridgehead framework that makes the structure rigid and cage-like. A ketone (carbonyl) sits on one carbon of the bicyclic ring system, and a methylene-linked sulfonyl chloride group (–CH2–SO2Cl) is attached at the other bridgehead-adjacent quaternary carbon. The molecule is chiral with defined stereocenters, and its overall shape is asymmetric because the two substituent positions differ. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid ketone built on a bornane-type skeleton, consisting of a six-membered ring and a five-membered ring sharing two carbons to form a rigid bridged framework. Three methyl groups are attached to the bridge and ring positions, including a gem-dimethyl pair on one bridgehead-adjacent carbon, giving the scaffold a compact, sterically crowded shape. A single carbonyl group sits within a ring as a ketone, and this is the only functional group present. The bridged cage structure is highly rigid with little conformational flexibility, and the molecule has a chiral framework with defined stereocenters. Its sole hydrogen-bond acceptor is the carbonyl oxygen, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a bicyclic lactone built on a norbornane-like framework, with two rings sharing a bridging carbon arrangement that makes it rigid and compact. One ring is a five-membered lactone (a cyclic ester) fused across the bicycle, and it carries a carbonyl group. Three methyl groups sit on the skeleton, two on one bridgehead-adjacent carbon and one on the other bridgehead, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. An acyl chloride group is attached directly to a ring carbon, serving as a reactive carbonyl functional group. The structure has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens of the lactone and acyl chloride can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a saturated cyclopentane ring that carries a gem-dimethyl pair on one carbon and a single methyl on the adjacent carbon, so it is an alicyclic scaffold with no aromatic rings and no ring fusion. Two carboxylic acid groups are attached to neighbouring ring carbons, one on a stereocentre bearing a hydrogen and one on the quaternary carbon that also holds the methyl group. The substitution pattern is dense and asymmetric, with the two acid groups sitting on differently substituted carbons. The ring is rigid, with the bulky methyl groups restricting conformational freedom, while the carboxyl groups can rotate. Each carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type lactone built on a bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane-type) skeleton. A five-membered gamma-lactone ring is fused across the bicycle through a shared quaternary bridgehead carbon, forming a rigid, cage-like three-dimensional framework. Substituents include a carboxylic acid group on one bridgehead-adjacent quaternary carbon, a methyl group on the other, and a gem-dimethyl unit on the bridge carbon. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane, and its rigid ring system limits conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the lactone carbonyl and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is camphorquinone, a bicyclic terpenoid built on a norbornane (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) skeleton. Two adjacent ketone carbonyls sit on the bridge-adjacent carbons of the bicyclic framework, forming a 1,2-dione, and the cyclohexane-type ring carries gem-dimethyl and angular methyl substituents on the bridgehead and neighboring carbons. The rigid cage limits conformational flexibility, and the molecule is chiral with a single defined stereocenter arrangement at the bridgehead positions. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid alcohol built on a bornane-type scaffold, consisting of a norbornane (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane) core with gem-dimethyl groups on one bridge and an angular methyl at a bridgehead. The fused bicyclic framework is rigid and cage-like, with the two rings sharing a common bridge. The single hydroxyl group sits on a carbon adjacent to the gem-dimethyl carbon, so it is the only functional group present. That hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is purely hydrocarbon and contributes no polar interactions. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because of the single substituted position, and its stereocenters fix a defined three-dimensional shape.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type skeleton built from a cyclohexanone fused to a cyclopentane, forming a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane framework with a ketone at the bridge-adjacent position. Two methyl groups sit on the same bridgehead-adjacent carbon, and a methylene linker carries a sulfonic acid group (-SO3H) on the quaternary bridgehead carbon. The rigid, cage-like ring system gives little conformational freedom, and the molecule is chiral with defined stereocenters. The sulfonic acid group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites (the O-H) and multiple acceptor oxygens, while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a bicyclic terpenoid-type scaffold built from a bridged bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane (norbornane-type) core bearing gem-dimethyl groups on one bridge carbon. A ketone sits on the ring system, adjacent to a quaternary bridgehead carbon that also carries a sulfonyl chloride-bearing methyl substituent (a –CH2–SO2Cl group). The rigid, cage-like framework is conformationally constrained, with the sulfonyl chloride and carbonyl providing the principal polar features. The ketone oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring and substituent hydrogens are attached to carbon.

This molecule is camphor, but I'll describe only its structure as requested. It has a bicyclic skeleton built from two fused five-membered rings sharing a common bridge, giving a rigid, cage-like bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane framework. A ketone (carbonyl) group sits on one of the carbons of the bridge-adjacent ring, which serves as the sole functional group. Three methyl groups are attached to the skeleton, two on the same bridgehead-adjacent carbon and one on the other bridgehead, giving the framework a sterically crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with defined stereocenters. The rigid cage limits conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; its carbonyl oxygen can act as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, a 1-bromoethyl group, so it has a simple one-ring aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The side chain consists of a saturated two-carbon unit in which the carbon attached to the ring also carries a bromine atom, making it a secondary alkyl halide at a benzylic position. Because the benzene ring is monosubstituted, the molecule has no positional isomers to distinguish on the ring, and it contains one stereocenter at the carbon bearing the bromine, so it is chiral. The side chain can rotate about its single bonds, giving moderate flexibility around the ring-to-chain linkage. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor is the bromine atom, which is a weak one.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two benzene rings fused together along a shared edge to form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic system. A bromomethyl group (–CH2Br) is attached to one carbon of the fused system, at a position on the outer ring that is not directly adjacent to the ring fusion. This substituent adds a flexible single bond that can rotate, while the aromatic core remains planar and fixed. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a low degree of symmetry, since the single substituent breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent naphthalene. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, because no O–H or N–H groups are present, and the aromatic π-system offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain, specifically a 1,2-dibromoethyl group attached to the ring at one carbon. The benzene ring is a single, unfused aromatic six-membered system with no additional rings, and its substitution pattern is monosubstitution, so the ring retains a plane of symmetry through the attachment point and the para position. The side chain contains two bromine atoms on adjacent carbons, one terminal and one benzylic, which are the only functional groups present. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no conventional hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the halogens are weak acceptors at best. The single-bond side chain gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, while the aromatic ring is rigid.

The molecule is built around a 2-oxazoline ring, a five-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen joined through a carbon-nitrogen double bond. The ring's C=N carbon is bonded to a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups at the positions flanking the attachment point, giving a 2,6-dimethoxyphenyl substitution pattern. The oxazoline's saturated carbon adjacent to nitrogen carries two methyl groups, making that position a gem-dimethyl center. The aromatic and heterocyclic rings are linked by a single bond, and the flanking methoxy groups impose some steric crowding that restricts rotation. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the ring nitrogen and oxygen and the two methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a flexible, acyclic chain built from a two-carbon ethylene unit, an ether oxygen, and a second two-carbon unit, with a terminal primary amine on one end and a terminal primary alcohol on the other. It contains no rings, so the scaffold is a simple linear diether-type backbone rather than a fused or aromatic system. The two functional groups sit at opposite ends, giving the molecule an overall symmetric arrangement of heteroatoms along a single axis, though the nitrogen and oxygen termini differ in chemistry. Because all bonds are single and rotatable, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. The amine group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the hydroxyl group as both a donor and acceptor, and the central ether oxygen as an acceptor only.

The molecule is built from a benzimidazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. At the 2-position of the imidazole ring sits a 2-aminophenyl group, a benzene ring bearing a primary amino substituent on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment. The imidazole nitrogen bearing a hydrogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other imidazole nitrogen and the amino group's nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is largely planar and rigid because of its fused aromatic framework, with the biaryl bond permitting only limited rotation. It lacks any meaningful symmetry, since the amino group is placed asymmetrically on the pendant ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent (ortho) positions. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to the ring. The other is an acrylic acid chain, a three-carbon unit with a carbon-carbon double bond joined to a terminal carboxylic acid, with the double bond locked in the E (trans) geometry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the trans double bond adds further rigidity, while the single bonds to the boronic acid and carboxylic acid groups allow some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid and both boronic acid hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens can accept them. The molecule has no internal symmetry element that maps one half onto the other.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methoxy group (O-CH3) sits at one position, a chlorine atom is on the adjacent carbon, and the remaining substituent is a two-carbon chain attached through a tertiary carbon that carries both a nitrile (C≡N) and an acetyl (C(=O)CH3) group. The ring is aromatic and planar with no ring fusion, while the side chain has a stereogenic center and rotatable single bonds, giving it moderate flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. Its hydrogen-bond acceptors include the ether oxygen, the carbonyl oxygen, and the nitrile nitrogen. Overall the structure has no internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, a chlorine atom and an ethoxy-linked side chain, giving it an ortho substitution pattern. The side chain is a two-carbon linker that connects the aromatic ring through an ether oxygen to a terminal primary amine, so the aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the flexible CH2-CH2 chain allows rotation about several single bonds, making the overall shape moderately flexible. There is no molecular symmetry of note, since the two ring substituents differ in kind and the side chain is not mirrored. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor and the chlorine contributes little hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) oxygen-linked substituents, making it a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One oxygen carries an ethyl group, forming an aryl ethyl ether, while the other oxygen links to a two-carbon chain ending in a bromine atom, giving a 2-bromoethoxy ether side chain. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, and the molecule contains no fused ring systems. Its ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate them, since there are no N–H or O–H groups. The flexible ethyl and bromoethyl chains provide rotational freedom, whereas the benzene core remains rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built around a saturated five-membered imidazolidine ring, with nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, and each of those nitrogens is attached to a phenyl ring. The carbon between the two nitrogens, the aminal carbon, carries a furan ring, an aromatic five-membered oxygen heterocycle. The structure has two benzene rings and one furan ring, which together make the molecule fairly bulky and rigid, though the saturated ring offers some conformational flexibility. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the two tertiary amine nitrogens and the furan oxygen, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from two linked rings: a furan (a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom) attached through a carbon to the C2 position of a piperazine ring. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms positioned 1,4 across the ring, so it is non-aromatic and can adopt flexible chair-like conformations. The furan and piperazine are joined by a single C–C bond, so there is no ring fusion, and the furan is monosubstituted at the carbon adjacent to its oxygen. Both nitrogens in the piperazine are secondary amines bearing hydrogen atoms, so they can act as hydrogen-bond donors as well as acceptors. The furan oxygen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substitution is asymmetric.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a single 2-hydroxyethyl substituent on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho to nitrogen. The aromatic six-membered ring is a single, unfused, planar scaffold with no additional rings. The side chain is a flexible two-carbon linker ending in a primary alcohol, which gives the molecule rotational freedom about its single bonds. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, and the terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the substituent is attached at a single, asymmetric position on the ring.

The molecule is built from a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. At the 2-position of this thiazole ring, a second benzene ring is attached directly by a single bond, creating a biaryl linkage. That phenyl ring bears a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is ortho. The fused and linked aromatic system is essentially planar and rigid, with the two ring systems able to be nearly coplanar. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the thiazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any obvious rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built around a central five-membered 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Two phenyl rings are attached to this core at the 2 and 5 positions. One is an unsubstituted phenyl group, while the other carries a methoxy group at the ortho position relative to the bond to the oxadiazole, which introduces a twist between the two aromatic rings. The ether oxygen of the methoxy group and the ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the methoxy group and the biaryl linkages.

The molecule is built around a saturated six-membered piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned at opposite corners (1,4-relationship) and is non-planar, adopting a chair-like conformation. Attached to one carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen is a phenyl ring bearing a methoxy group at the ortho position, so the aromatic ring and the saturated heterocycle are joined by a single C–C bond with no ring fusion. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituted aryl group sits on only one side of the piperazine. Both ring nitrogens are secondary amines, so each can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The ether oxygen of the methoxy group provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site, while the aromatic ring contributes a relatively rigid, planar region to an otherwise flexible saturated core.

The molecule is built around a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at ortho positions. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is a saturated five-membered 1,3-dioxolane ring, formed by two oxygen atoms bridging a quaternary carbon that also carries a methyl group and the aryl ring. The dioxolane is fused to nothing else, so the scaffold is a bicyclic-free arrangement of one aromatic ring linked to one saturated acetal-type ring. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the dioxolane oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The stereocenter at the quaternary carbon leaves the molecule without internal symmetry, and the ring system is moderately rigid around the aromatic core with some flexibility from the rotatable aryl-to-dioxolane and aryl-to-boron bonds.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a planar, rigid aromatic core. A 2-hydroxyethoxy side chain is attached at the 2-position of the naphthalene ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ether oxygen linked to the ring and the terminal primary alcohol provide two oxygen acceptor sites, while the hydroxyl group supplies one hydrogen-bond donor. The two-carbon linker gives the side chain conformational flexibility relative to the otherwise rigid aromatic system.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. At one position on that bicyclic system, a piperazine ring is attached through a carbon atom adjacent to one of its nitrogens, so the piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring with nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 4 positions. The piperazine ring is flexible relative to the aromatic core and can adopt chair-like conformations. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the attachment point on the piperazine breaks its symmetry. Both secondary amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic system contributes only weak interactions.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated chain built from a butyl group joined through a series of ether oxygens to an ethyl acetate terminus. The backbone contains two ethylene-glycol-type repeat units separated by ether linkages, giving a flexible, unbranched skeleton with no ring systems or fused rings. The terminal functional group is an ester, formed by an acetyl carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that links into the chain, while the internal oxygens are simple ether linkages. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any meaningful symmetry beyond its linear connectivity. Because of its many rotatable single bonds, it is highly flexible. It carries no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O–H or N–H groups, but its three ether oxygens and two carbonyl-associated oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic heterocycles joined by a single carbon-carbon bond. One part is a benzimidazole unit, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring containing two nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen. The other part is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring with one nitrogen, attached at the position next to that nitrogen. The two ring systems are essentially planar and fully conjugated, giving the structure a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bulk beyond the single linking bond. The pyridine nitrogen and the unprotonated imidazole nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the N-H group on the imidazole can donate one.

The molecule consists of a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic sulfur heterocycle, joined by a single bond at its 2-position to a piperazine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 4 positions. The thiophene is unfused and carries no further substituents, while the piperazine is attached through a carbon adjacent to one nitrogen, giving a 2-substituted piperazine pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the saturated piperazine ring is conformationally flexible and can adopt chair-like shapes. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent is positioned asymmetrically on the piperazine ring. The two secondary amine nitrogens of the piperazine can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the thiophene sulfur acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built from two aromatic heterocycles joined by a single carbon-carbon bond. One ring is a six-membered pyridine, which contains a nitrogen atom that sits adjacent to the linking carbon, while the other is a five-membered thiophene containing a sulfur atom. Neither ring is fused to the other, so the scaffold is a biaryl-type arrangement with a free, rotatable single bond between the two rings. The molecule carries no separate functional groups beyond the aromatic rings themselves, and its substitution pattern is simple: each ring is linked at only one position. Both rings are fully planar and aromatic, which lends overall rigidity, although rotation about the inter-ring bond gives some conformational flexibility. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: two adjacent methoxy groups (OCH3) occupy the ring positions ortho to each other, and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain (CH2CH2OH) sits at the position para to one of the methoxy groups. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the two-carbon ethanol side chain provides the only meaningful flexibility. Its terminal primary alcohol can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, whereas the two ether oxygens can only accept them. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the three substituents make the ring asymmetric.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on adjacent ring carbons, creating a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern, and a two-carbon ethylamine chain (–CH2CH2NH2) is attached at the position para to one of those methoxy groups. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ethylamine tail adds conformational flexibility. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair for acceptance, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the substituents are not arranged identically around the ring.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group. At the 2-position of this indole core, a phenyl ring is attached directly through a single bond, giving a biaryl-type linkage. The phenyl ring bears a fluorine atom and a chlorine atom on adjacent carbons, with the substitution pattern placing the halogens at the para and meta positions relative to the link to the indole. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, while rotation about the single bond joining the two ring systems gives limited conformational flexibility. The indole N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the aromatic nitrogen and the halogen atoms offer weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character.

The molecule is built from two linked aromatic ring systems. One end is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, attached at its meta position to the second system. That second system is a benzimidazole, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring bearing two nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-H group. The two ring systems are joined by a direct carbon-carbon single bond, which allows relatively free rotation but favors a mostly planar overall arrangement. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, approximately mirror-symmetric shape. The imidazole N-H acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine nitrogen and the unprotonated imidazole nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two linked ring systems: a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring and a six-membered saturated piperazine ring. The thiophene carries a single substituent at the 3-position, so the link to the piperazine is not at the carbon next to sulfur. The piperazine ring is fully saturated and contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship, with one nitrogen being a secondary amine (N–H) and the other also bearing hydrogen. The attachment point is a carbon adjacent to one of the ring nitrogens, which gives the molecule a stereogenic center and an asymmetric overall shape. The aromatic and saturated rings are joined by a single bond, so the molecule has moderate conformational flexibility around that link. The two amine nitrogens can both act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the thiophene sulfur is a weak acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a primary amino group attached directly to the aromatic ring, which can donate a hydrogen bond and lone-pair electron density into the ring. The other is a tertiary carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and two trifluoromethyl groups, giving a bulky, electron-poor, branched side chain. The aromatic ring has no fusion, and the overall structure is fairly rigid at the ring but flexible around the single bond linking the side chain to the ring. The hydroxyl and amino groups each serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain (-CH2CH2OH) sits on the carbon directly opposite it, giving a para substitution pattern. The two substituents are arranged symmetrically across the ring, so the aromatic core has a mirror-like arrangement along its long axis. The ethyl linker between the ring and the terminal alcohol adds some conformational flexibility, while the ring itself remains rigid and planar. The primary amine and the primary alcohol each can donate hydrogen bonds and accept them, making the molecule capable of multiple hydrogen-bonding interactions.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The ring is para-disubstituted: one carbon bears an aminoethyl side chain (a two-carbon saturated linker ending in a primary amine), and the carbon directly opposite carries a primary aromatic amine attached directly to the ring. Both nitrogens are primary amines, each with two N–H bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and each nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond. The para arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring, and the flexible ethyl linker allows some conformational freedom compared with the rigid aromatic core.
