This molecule is a biphenyl-based tertiary alcohol: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with one ring bearing a para-substituent of a 2-hydroxypropan-2-yl group, which is a quaternary carbon carrying two methyl groups and one hydroxyl. The biphenyl unit is largely planar and conjugated, though rotation about the central bond gives it some flexibility. The rings are not fused, so the scaffold is simply two separate aromatic systems linked end to end. The substitution pattern is para on one ring and unsubstituted on the other, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis through the whole structure. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak, non-directional interactions.

The molecule has a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2 and 5 positions of this ring are two aryl groups: one is a para-substituted phenyl bearing a tert-butyl group at the position opposite the oxadiazole, and the other is a para-biphenyl unit whose terminal phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The result is a linear, rod-like, largely planar framework of several conjugated aromatic rings, with the oxadiazole sitting in the middle and both ends extended. The bulky tert-butyl group adds a small three-dimensional protrusion on one end, breaking the symmetry somewhat. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two oxadiazole nitrogens and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a biphenyl system bearing a 2-aminoethyl chain on one terminal ring, giving a phenethylamine-type scaffold. Two benzene rings are joined by a single C–C bond with no ring fusion, and the second ring is unsubstituted. The aminoethyl group sits para to the biaryl linkage on the first ring, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 on that ring. The primary amine is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak, hydrophobic interactions. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, but the aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, and the flexible ethyl linker adds conformational freedom.

The molecule is built around a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen and two nitrogen atoms. This core is flanked on one side by a para-bromophenyl group, where the bromine sits opposite the point of attachment on a benzene ring. On the other side it carries a 1-naphthyl group, a fused bicyclic aromatic system attached through an alpha carbon. The overall scaffold is a flat, largely conjugated array of three aromatic units linked directly by single bonds, giving it a rigid, rod-like shape with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxadiazole nitrogen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2-position is a para-bromophenyl ring, and at the 5-position is an unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the two aryl groups sit on opposite sides of the heterocycle. The framework is fully aromatic and largely planar, with the three rings conjugated through single bonds, which makes the overall shape rigid and elongated. The bromine atom sits at the para position of one terminal ring, giving that ring a single substitution point, and the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the oxadiazole. The ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and an aryloxy-acetyl side chain, with the substituents arranged on adjacent and meta-related positions. The aromatic ring is fully planar and conjugated, while the attached ether oxygen, methylene linker, and amide-type carbonyl introduce a modestly flexible chain. The terminal portion contains a hydrazide group, a C(=O)NH-NH2 unit, which bears two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl oxygen plus the ether oxygen as acceptors. Overall the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl, chlorine, and side chain sit at distinct positions on the ring. The chlorine contributes a halogen substituent that is electron-withdrawing, and the sequence of polar groups gives the molecule a strong capacity to engage in intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a carboxylic acid group ortho to the ketone, which makes the scaffold a 2-benzoylbenzoic acid core. The second ring is substituted para to the ketone with a chlorine atom and meta to the ketone with a nitro group, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the two aromatic rings are not equivalent. The two aryl rings are attached to the carbonyl carbon through single bonds, giving moderate rotational flexibility around those links, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and planar. Hydrogen-bond capability is clear: the carboxylic acid offers both a donor (O–H) and acceptor sites, the ketone and nitro oxygens serve as acceptors, and no other donor groups are present.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone in which one phenyl ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the position ortho to the carbonyl bridge, giving a 2-benzoylbenzoic acid framework. The second phenyl ring bears a chlorine atom at the para position relative to the ketone linkage. Both aromatic rings are unfused benzene rings connected through a single sp2 carbonyl carbon, so the scaffold is fairly flexible about the aryl–carbonyl bonds but lacks any fused ring system. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two rings differ in their substitution. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a single methylene bridge. One ring is a benzene bearing a chlorine atom at the para position relative to the bridge, giving a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern. The other ring is a pyridine, with the bridging carbon attached at the 2-position adjacent to the ring nitrogen. Neither ring is fused to another, and the two rings are connected through a flexible sp3 CH2 linker that allows rotation about two bonds. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its N–H and O–H sites are absent.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit para to each other on that ring: a chlorine atom on one side and a 2-hydroxyethoxy chain on the other, which is an ether oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The para arrangement gives the aromatic core a symmetric, linear pattern, though the flexible hydroxyethyl tail breaks overall symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the ether-linked side chain adds conformational flexibility. The terminal alcohol can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor, and the chlorine contributes weak halogen-bonding character without donating hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is built on a two-carbon acyl backbone: a carboxylic acid group sits on a quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups and an ether oxygen linking to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered benzene with a chlorine atom placed para to the ether oxygen, giving a symmetric 1,4-disubstitution pattern. The aryl ether and the gem-dimethyl carbon add some bulk, while the aromatic ring and the tetrahedral center keep the framework relatively rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the ether linkage. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the ether oxygen contributes an additional weak acceptor site.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at one position and an aryl ether linkage at the adjacent position, giving an ortho-substitution pattern on the heteroaromatic core. The ether oxygen connects the pyridine to a second benzene ring, which carries a single chlorine atom at the position para to the ether linkage. The carboxylic acid functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the ring nitrogen and ether oxygen provide additional acceptor sites. The two aromatic rings are joined by a flexible single ether bond, allowing some rotational freedom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two rings differ in substitution.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group. A 4-chlorophenyl group is attached at the 2-position of the indole, the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen on the five-membered ring. The para-chloro substituent sits on the pendant phenyl ring, giving a single halogen on an otherwise unsubstituted benzene ring. The fused aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, with the biaryl bond permitting only limited rotation. The indole N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the chlorine offers only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a diaryl thioether, with two benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom. One ring carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a fluorine atom on adjacent positions, with the sulfur attached ortho to the nitrile. The other ring bears a chlorine atom positioned para to the sulfur linkage. Both aromatic rings are planar and unfused, while the C–S–C bridge gives the molecule some rotational flexibility around the two aryl bonds. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a diaryl thioether built from two benzene rings joined through a single sulfur atom. One ring carries an aldehyde group (a formyl substituent) at the position ortho to the sulfur linkage, while the other ring bears a chlorine atom para to the sulfur, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern. Both aromatic rings are planar, fully unsaturated six-membered systems with no ring fusion, and the C–S–C bridge provides only modest rotational flexibility around its two bonds. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups. The carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the sulfur and chlorine atoms offer weak acceptor character. The overall arrangement is asymmetric because the two rings carry different substituents.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at the 3-position, with a sulfur atom linking the 2-position to a separate benzene ring. That benzene ring carries a chlorine atom at the position para to the sulfur, giving a diaryl thioether scaffold with two aromatic rings joined by a single flexible C–S–C bridge. The two rings are not fused, so the structure has no shared ring atoms and offers rotational freedom about the sulfur linkage. The carboxylic acid is a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor. The chlorine substituent and the thioether sulfur add further lipophilic and polarizable character to the framework.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxane ring, which contains two oxygen atoms separated by a single carbon and a saturated CH2-CH-CH2 segment. A linear pentyl chain is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to one of the ring CH2 groups, giving the core a flexible, aliphatic character. The acetal carbon at position 2 of the dioxane bears a para-substituted phenyl ring, which carries a nitrile group on the opposite side of the ring. The aromatic ring and the nitrile are planar and rigid, contrasting with the more flexible saturated portion. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring oxygens and the nitrogen of the nitrile act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a six-membered 1,3-dioxane ring, which is a saturated ring containing two oxygen atoms separated by a single carbon. A propyl chain is attached to one carbon of this ring, placed adjacent to a CH2 group that links toward the second oxygen, giving the ring a defined substitution pattern. The carbon between the two oxygens, the acetal position, bears a para-substituted phenyl ring that carries a nitrile group (a carbon-nitrogen triple bond) on the opposite side from the ring attachment. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated dioxane ring is flexible and can adopt chair-like conformations. The oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrile nitrogen is also an acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two substituents sit para to each other across the ring: an ethoxy group (an oxygen bearing an ethyl chain) on one side and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain on the other. The ether oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the terminal primary alcohol can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The para substitution gives the ring a symmetric arrangement about its long axis, though the flexible ethyl and hydroxyethyl side chains break overall symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid, whereas the two side chains rotate freely about their single bonds.

This molecule is a 2-arylpyrimidine: a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring with two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, bearing a phenyl ring at the carbon between the two nitrogens. The pyrimidine carries an n-propyl chain on the carbon meta to that linkage, and the phenyl ring carries an ethyl group at the position para to the bond connecting it to the pyrimidine, giving a linear, elongated shape. The two aromatic rings are not fused but joined by a single bond, so they can rotate relative to one another, and the alkyl chains add some conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall it has no symmetry element beyond an approximate planar arrangement of the aromatic core.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at the 3-position and an aryloxy group at the 2-position, so it is a 2-aryloxynicotinic acid scaffold. The ether oxygen links the pyridine to a benzene ring that carries a single fluorine atom para to the ether linkage, giving a simple diaryl ether arrangement with no additional ring fusion. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen and ether oxygen serve as further hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two aromatic rings are connected through a single flexible C–O–C linkage, so the molecule has moderate conformational flexibility and no overall symmetry. The fluorine substituent is the only halogen and sits on the terminal phenyl ring.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring sharing one edge. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a free N-H, giving the scaffold one hydrogen-bond donor site, while the aromatic framework offers pi-electron density but no additional strong acceptor groups. At the 2-position of the indole, a para-fluorophenyl ring is attached through a single bond, creating a biaryl linkage. The fluorine atom sits at the para position of this pendant phenyl ring, a substitution pattern that gives the side ring a single polar C-F bond. Overall, the molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with few rotatable bonds beyond the biaryl link, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond the local mirror plane of the aromatic rings.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monosubstituted-then-disubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The ring carries two groups in a para (1,4) relationship: a phenolic hydroxyl directly attached to one ring carbon, and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain (–CH2CH2OH) on the opposite carbon. Both substituents are polar, giving the molecule two hydroxyl groups that can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The para arrangement gives the molecule a degree of local symmetry about the long axis of the ring, while the two-carbon chain adds a modest degree of conformational flexibility. Overall, the structure is compact and mostly planar at the aromatic core, with its flexibility confined to the side chain.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, making it a phenol. The other is a three-carbon-skeleton chain: a secondary carbon carrying a methyl group and a terminal carboxylic acid, so the acid sits one carbon removed from the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the side chain contains rotatable single bonds and a stereogenic center at the carbon bearing the methyl group. The molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry because of this asymmetric side chain. It offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the phenolic and carboxylic OH groups) and three acceptor oxygens across the hydroxyl and carbonyl functionalities.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built from two aromatic rings joined through a single carbonyl carbon. One ring is a benzene ring carrying a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the position para to the carbonyl attachment, so the substitution pattern is 1,4 on that ring. The other ring is a five-membered thiophene, attached to the carbonyl through its carbon adjacent to the sulfur atom. Both aromatic rings are planar and unfused, giving the molecule a largely rigid, conjugated framework that is rotatable only about the two single bonds linking the rings to the carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one ring carbon, and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain (two saturated carbons ending in an alcohol) sits on the carbon directly across the ring, giving a para substitution pattern. The arrangement has approximate two-fold symmetry through the ring axis, and the flexible ethyl linker gives the side chain conformational freedom while the ring stays rigid. The terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a primary amine, a trifluoromethyl group, and a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen. The amine and the morpholine nitrogen sit on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho relationship, while the trifluoromethyl group is positioned meta to the amine and para to the morpholine. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen, which is non-planar and gives the scaffold modest conformational flexibility at that point. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and adds three fluorine atoms that are not hydrogen-bond acceptors in the usual sense. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and the ring oxygen serves as an acceptor, while the morpholine nitrogen is tertiary and aryl-substituted.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents: a primary amino group (NH2) and a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by two carbons on each side, giving it a chair-like, fairly flexible conformation. The aromatic ring is planar and unfused, so the scaffold consists of two separate ring systems linked by a direct nitrogen-to-carbon bond, which allows rotation about that bond. The ortho arrangement of the amine and morpholine groups creates an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability is mixed: the NH2 group can act as both a donor and an acceptor, the morpholine oxygen and tertiary nitrogen serve as acceptors, and no other donors are present.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 arrangement. At one ring carbon sits an octyl chain, a straight eight-carbon saturated alkyl group, and at the carbon flanked by both nitrogens sits a para-substituted phenyl ring. That phenyl ring carries a hexyloxy group, a six-carbon chain attached through an ether oxygen, positioned opposite the point of attachment to the pyrimidine. The overall scaffold is a linear, elongated arrangement of three rings joined directly to one another with no fused rings. The two aromatic rings are rigid and planar, while the long alkyl chains are flexible. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining polar atoms are the ether oxygen, which can also accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that contains two nitrogen atoms. The imidazole nitrogen bearing a hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other imidazole nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Attached at the 2-position of the imidazole ring is a pyridin-4-yl group, a six-membered aromatic ring with a single nitrogen para to the point of attachment, which adds a further acceptor site. The fused bicyclic core and the directly bonded pyridine ring are essentially planar and fully aromatic, giving the molecule a rigid, flat geometry. Its only rotatable bond is the single bond linking the two ring systems, so conformational flexibility is limited.

The molecule is a para-disubstituted benzene ring, with a tert-butyl group on one side and a 2-hydroxyethyl chain on the other. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, symmetric quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, which gives that end of the molecule a compact, rigid shape. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion. The two-carbon linker to the terminal primary alcohol gives the molecule some rotational flexibility at that end. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic ring and alkyl groups are nonpolar. Overall, the structure has a rod-like, elongated shape with a polar tip.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone in which one phenyl ring carries a para-methyl group and the other carries a carboxylic acid at the ortho position relative to the central carbonyl. The two aromatic rings are joined through a single ketone carbon, giving a non-fused, twisted, moderately flexible scaffold with no stereocenters. The ring bearing the methyl group is para-disubstituted, while the ring bearing the acid is ortho-disubstituted, so the molecule lacks overall symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from the carboxylic acid, which can donate one hydrogen and accept two, and the ketone oxygen, which acts as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is a small five-membered lactone, a 2(5H)-furanone scaffold. Its ring contains one ring oxygen, a carbonyl carbon directly bonded to that oxygen, and a single carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the carbonyl, making the ring nearly planar and rigid. There is no ring fusion and no additional substituents, so the structure is unsubstituted apart from the ring itself and has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. The ester-type carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the ring oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a 1,2-oxazole (isoxazole) ring, which is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The hydroxyl and the isoxazole are on adjacent carbons of the benzene ring, while the methyl sits on the carbon meta to the isoxazole, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The two aromatic rings are joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, so they can rotate relative to one another, adding some conformational flexibility, although the phenol and isoxazole are each planar and rigid. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two five-membered and six-membered aromatic rings joined by a single bond. One ring is a phenol: a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the two rings are ortho-related. The other ring is an isoxazole, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, connected to the benzene ring through a carbon next to the ring oxygen. The two aromatic systems are not fused, but the single bond between them permits rotation, giving the scaffold some conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps one half onto the other.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A nitro group (–NO2) is attached to the ring, positioned meta to the nitrogen on the carbon that sits two atoms away from the ring nitrogen on one side. On the other side, at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, an ether oxygen links to a flexible two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The scaffold is planar and aromatic, while the hydroxyethoxy side chain adds conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are at different positions. It can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through the terminal hydroxyl, and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the ring nitrogen, the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the nitro oxygens.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge. A thioether sulfur links the ring at one position to a CH2 group, which in turn bears a terminal carboxylic acid, giving an S-linked acetic acid chain. A chlorine atom sits on the peri position of the other ring, adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon near the sulfur substituent. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfur and methylene linkage provides rotational flexibility to the carboxylic acid end. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, and the sulfur and chlorine atoms act only as weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. At one ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen sits an allyl thioether, a sulfur atom bonded to a three-carbon chain that ends in a terminal vinyl group. On the neighboring carbon, a carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the ring, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The substitution pattern is therefore 2,3-disubstituted, with no symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the allylthio side chain adds some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a single aminomethyl group, so its scaffold is one six-membered aromatic heterocycle with no ring fusion. The ring contains one nitrogen atom, and the aminomethyl substituent (a CH2 linked to a primary amine) is attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to that ring nitrogen, a 2-substitution pattern. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the substituent sits on one side of the ring nitrogen. Its rigid aromatic core contrasts with the single rotatable bond joining the ring to the flexible CH2NH2 arm. The primary amine can both donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H groups and accept them through its lone pair, while the pyridine nitrogen acts as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen. At the 2-position of that ring sits a carbamate linkage: an NH bonded to a carbonyl that is in turn bonded to an oxygen carrying a tert-butyl group, which is a bulky, three-methyl quaternary carbon. A nitrile (C≡N) group sits on the ring at the 5-position, para-like to the carbamate-bearing carbon across the ring, making the substitution pattern 2,5-disubstituted. The molecule is largely planar through the aromatic core and conjugated carbamate, while the tert-butyl group adds a rigid, three-dimensionally bulky terminus with no symmetry across the whole structure. The carbamate N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring nitrogen, and nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring bearing two adjacent groups at the ortho positions: a tert-butyl carbamate (Boc-protected amine) attached through its nitrogen, and a boronic acid, B(OH)2, directly bonded to the ring carbon. The carbamate unit consists of a carbonyl flanked by an NH linker and a tert-butyl ester oxygen, which carries three methyl groups radiating from a quaternary carbon, giving the tert-butyl portion a bulky, rigid shape. The aromatic core is planar and fully unsaturated, while the carbamate and boronic acid substituents provide conformational flexibility around their single bonds. Hydrogen-bond capability is pronounced: the carbamate N-H and the two boronic acid hydroxyl groups serve as donors, and the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygen, and boronic acid oxygens act as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two ortho substituents differ in nature.

This molecule is a carbamate built from a tert-butyl group bonded through an ester oxygen to a carbonyl, which in turn links to a secondary amide-type nitrogen. That nitrogen is attached to the 2-position of a pyridine ring, a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, so there is no ring fusion. The tert-butyl group is a bulky, symmetric three-methyl cluster that contributes steric hindrance but no polar features. The overall scaffold is fairly compact and conformationally modest, with rotation possible about the C–N and C–O single bonds. The NH group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, ester oxygen, and pyridine ring nitrogen can all serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a 2-naphthyl ketone: a naphthalene scaffold made of two fused benzene rings, with a ketone carbonyl attached at the 2-position of one ring. The carbonyl carbon is bonded to a CH2 group that carries a bromine atom, so the side chain is a bromomethyl ketone. The fused bicyclic aromatic core is largely planar and rigid, while the bromomethyl group adds a small degree of rotational freedom at the single bond to the ring. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible planar mirror plane, and its shape is asymmetric because of the substituent. The carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small aromatic ketone built around a five-membered thiophene ring, which is a sulfur-containing heteroaromatic ring with no fused rings. A carbonyl group is attached directly to the thiophene carbon adjacent to the sulfur, and the carbonyl carbon bears a bromomethyl group, so the chain reads as a thiophene–C(=O)–CH2–Br unit. The bromine sits on a primary carbon alpha to the ketone, making that position a reactive, electrophilic site. The molecule is largely planar and fairly rigid across the aromatic ring and carbonyl, with only modest flexibility in the bromomethyl side chain. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of that ring, making it a 1,2-disubstituted (ortho) pattern. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing; it can accept hydrogen bonds at the nitrogen but cannot donate them. The other substituent is a bromomethyl group, a flexible CH2 linker bearing a bromine atom, which gives a reactive alkyl halide site. The overall structure is largely planar and rigid in its aromatic core, with some rotational freedom around the CH2 linkage, and it has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement of the two substituents.

The molecule is a benzothiazole, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The fusion creates a flat, rigid planar framework. Attached to the carbon at the 2-position of the thiazole ring is a bromomethyl group, a CH2 unit bearing a bromine atom, which provides the only substituent and makes the molecule asymmetric. The thiazole nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bromomethyl side chain adds a small degree of rotational flexibility around its single bond to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the ring, and the other is an ether oxygen linking the ring to a two-carbon chain that ends in a second carboxylic acid group. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, while the oxyacetic acid side chain adds conformational flexibility through its rotatable single bonds. Both carboxylic acid groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents are chemically distinct.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent (ortho) carbons. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the ring, and the other is a thioether linkage (a sulfur atom) bonded to a two-carbon chain ending in a second carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfur-containing side chain provides a flexible region with rotatable bonds. The 1,2-disubstitution pattern gives the molecule no internal symmetry. Both carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their hydroxyl hydrogens and as acceptors through their carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the thioether sulfur is a weak acceptor only.

This molecule is an acyclic amino alcohol built on a short two-carbon chain. A tertiary amine nitrogen carries two ethyl groups and is bonded to a 2-hydroxyethyl arm, so the scaffold is a simple open-chain ethanolamine with no rings or ring fusion. The only functional groups are the tertiary amine and a primary alcohol, separated by a flexible two-carbon linker. The molecule has no stereocenters and approximate local symmetry about the nitrogen, since its two ethyl groups are identical. Its rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrogen lone pair serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which is both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The neighboring substituent is a difluoromethoxy group, an ether oxygen attached to a carbon bearing two fluorine atoms and one hydrogen, which adds a weak acceptor site and a polarized C–H. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the difluoromethoxy and carboxyl groups retain some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ring pattern, because the two substituents differ in character.

The molecule is built on a short two-carbon ethyl chain with a nitrogen at one end and a hydroxyl group at the other, so it has an acyclic, open-chain scaffold with no ring systems or ring fusion. The nitrogen carries two methyl groups, making it a tertiary amine, and the terminal carbon bears a primary alcohol group. Because the chain is unsubstituted and has no stereocenters, the molecule is highly symmetric about the nitrogen with respect to its two methyl groups and is quite flexible, able to rotate freely around its single bonds. The nitrogen lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, and the hydroxyl group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, giving the molecule a dual hydrogen-bonding character.

This molecule is an acyclic ester with no ring systems, built on a short linear skeleton. A terminal vinyl group (C=C) is conjugated to a carbonyl, forming an acrylate ester whose oxygen links to a two-carbon ethylene chain. That chain ends in a tertiary amine, where the nitrogen carries two methyl groups. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond the local equivalence of the two N-methyl groups, and its many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ether-type ester oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the tertiary amine nitrogen is an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a short, flexible chain. Its core is a methacrylate unit: a terminal vinyl group (C=C) bearing a methyl substituent on the carbon attached to the carbonyl, which in turn is bonded to an oxygen that links through a two-carbon ethylene spacer to a tertiary amine. The nitrogen carries two methyl groups and no ring is present, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the equivalence of the two N-methyl groups, and its many rotatable single bonds make it conformationally flexible. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the tertiary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzoic acid bearing a triarylphosphine group at the ortho position: a benzene ring carrying a carboxylic acid (-COOH) and, adjacent to it, a phosphorus atom bonded to two additional unsubstituted phenyl rings. The scaffold is therefore a central trivalent phosphorus atom surrounded by three aromatic rings, with a 1,2-disubstituted benzene linking the phosphorus to the carboxyl group. There are no fused ring systems; all four rings are separate benzene units connected through single bonds. The phosphorus center is pyramidal and gives the molecule a propeller-like, non-planar shape around the P atom, while the aryl-P bonds allow considerable rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the phosphorus lone pair provides an additional, weaker acceptor site.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, so the two rings sit on adjacent positions and are not fused. The first ring carries a dimethylamino group, a tertiary amine with two methyl substituents on nitrogen, at the position ortho to the biaryl bond. The second ring carries a phosphorus atom, also ortho to the biaryl bond, which is bonded to two tert-butyl groups and a lone pair, making it a trialkyl-type tertiary phosphine. The two bulky substituents flank the biaryl axis, which restricts rotation about the central bond and gives a fairly rigid, non-planar arrangement. The nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a methyl group ortho to the biaryl linkage, while the other carries a phosphorus atom, also ortho to the linkage, which is bonded to two tert-butyl groups. Because the two rings are twisted out of plane by the bulky ortho substituents, the structure is conformationally restricted and asymmetric overall. The phosphine center is a trivalent, electron-rich site, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially only weak acceptor capability at the phosphorus lone pair.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an ethyl ester, where a carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring is linked through an oxygen to an ethyl group. The other is an isocyanate group, in which a nitrogen is double-bonded to a central carbon that is itself double-bonded to an oxygen, giving a linear N=C=O arrangement. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ester's ethyl tail adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks a plane of symmetry because the two substituents differ. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the ester and isocyanate oxygens and the nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule has a simple acyclic skeleton with no rings, built from a two-carbon ethyl group attached to a nitrogen atom, which is in turn linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group. The central feature is a secondary amine, where the nitrogen carries one hydrogen and two carbon substituents, and the molecule is unsubstituted otherwise, so there is no aromatic system or ring fusion. The terminal alcohol provides a primary hydroxyl group at the far end of the chain. Because it lacks any branching or ring constraint, the molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single carbon-carbon and carbon-nitrogen bonds. The amine nitrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the N-H and O-H hydrogens can each serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic chain with no rings, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. Its backbone is a two-carbon ethyl group bonded to a sulfonyl group, which is a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms, and that sulfur connects to a two-carbon chain ending in a primary hydroxyl group. The sulfone and the terminal alcohol are the only functional groups, and the sulfonyl group sits between the two ends of the chain. The structure is flexible because all of its bonds are single bonds that can rotate freely. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because its two ends differ.

This molecule is a small, acyclic thioether-alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple open-chain backbone. It contains a single sulfur atom bonded to two carbon chains: an ethyl group on one side and a two-carbon chain ending in a terminal hydroxyl group on the other. The primary alcohol at the chain end acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thioether sulfur offers only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor capability. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry, and its many single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Attached to the carbon next to the ring nitrogen is an ethylthio group, a sulfur atom bonded to a two-carbon ethyl chain, which adds a flexible, non-aromatic substituent. On the adjacent carbon sits a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The pyridine nitrogen also acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, with the two substituents on adjacent ring positions. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ethyl chain and the carboxylic acid group retain some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. An ethylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to an ethyl chain) sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while an acyl chloride group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a chlorine atom) is attached to the neighboring carbon, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, with only the ethyl and acyl chloride substituents providing conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents differ. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen can also serve as an acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzoate diester built around a central benzene ring bearing two amino groups at the meta positions (1,3-relationship) relative to each other, with the ester carbonyl attached at position 5, giving a symmetric 3,5-diaminobenzoyl core. The ester linkage connects this aromatic unit through a flexible two-carbon ethylene glycol bridge (–O–CH2–CH2–O–) to a methacrylate fragment, whose terminal alkene (C=C bearing a methyl group) sits on the α-carbon of the second carbonyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethylene bridge and ester linkages add rotational flexibility. The two primary aromatic amines and the two ester carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the amino groups additionally serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries an ester at one position and two nitro groups at the meta positions relative to it, giving a 3,5-dinitro substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the two nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and symmetrically placed across the ring. A flexible two-carbon ethylene linker joins the benzoate ester oxygen to a second ester whose acyl portion is a methacrylate group, containing a terminal carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with the carbonyl. The nitro oxygens and both ester carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two adjacent substituents: a methyl ester group (a carbonyl bearing an oxygen that is bonded to a methyl group) and a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom is bonded to two hydroxyl groups. Because the two substituents sit on neighboring carbons of the aromatic ring, the substitution pattern is ortho. The aromatic core is a single, flat, unfused six-membered ring, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited mirror-plane symmetry through the substituents. Its rotatable bonds connecting the substituents to the ring give it modest flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups on boron and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two boronic hydroxyl groups can also serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at the ortho positions, making it a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methyl ester, with a carbonyl group bonded directly to the ring and an oxygen-linked methyl group extending from it. The other is a primary sulfonamide, in which a sulfur atom carrying two double-bonded oxygens is attached to the ring and also bears an NH2 group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ester and sulfonamide bonds offer limited rotational freedom. The sulfonamide NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, a methyl ester group (–C(=O)OCH3) and an isocyanate group (–N=C=O), giving it an ortho substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ester and isocyanate groups add some conformational flexibility around their single bonds. The ester carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygen of the ester, along with the isocyanate oxygen, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The isocyanate's linear N=C=O unit is a highly electrophilic, cumulated double-bond system, which is a notable reactive feature of the structure. Overall, the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents differ in nature.

This molecule is a small, acyclic amino alcohol built on a two-carbon ethane backbone. One end carries a methylamino group, a secondary amine bearing a single methyl substituent, while the other end carries a primary hydroxyl group. Because there are no rings or fused ring systems, the scaffold is entirely open-chain and highly flexible, with free rotation about its single carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any meaningful symmetry, since the two functional termini differ. Both the secondary amine nitrogen and the hydroxyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the N-H and O-H groups can each serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional rings. A methylamino group (an NH bearing a methyl substituent) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, placing it at the 2-position. The ring carbons are sp2 hybridized and the system is planar and rigid, with the exocyclic N–CH3 bond the only notable point of flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond its local arrangement, since the amino group breaks the symmetry of the ring. The secondary amine N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the amine nitrogen can both serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at ortho positions. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded to a nitrogen that is in turn attached to the aromatic ring, forming a secondary amide. The other substituent is a methylsulfonyl group, a sulfur atom in its highest oxidation state carrying two oxygen atoms and a methyl group. The aromatic core is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is strictly 1,2 (ortho). Both functional groups are polar and can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their carbonyl and sulfonyl oxygens, while the amide N–H provides a single hydrogen-bond donor site. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, and its rotatable bonds allow moderate conformational flexibility around the amide and sulfonyl linkages.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methylsulfonyl group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a methyl group, attached directly to the ring. The other substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which carries a carbonyl and a hydroxyl. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ. Both the sulfonyl oxygens and the carboxylic acid oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carboxylic hydroxyl serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic compound built on a two-carbon chain. One terminus carries a methyl group bonded to a sulfur atom that is fully oxidized, bearing two double-bonded oxygen atoms, which makes it a sulfone group. The other terminus of the chain ends in a primary alcohol, a hydroxyl group attached to a terminal carbon. Because there are no rings, the scaffold is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds along the chain. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond trivial conformational averaging, since the sulfone and hydroxyl ends are chemically distinct. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two sulfone oxygens serve as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion. Attached at the 2-position of the ring is a methylsulfonyl group, in which a sulfur atom bears two double-bonded oxygens and one methyl group, making it a sulfone. The substitution pattern is therefore monosubstituted, and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the sulfonyl group, though the methyl group rotates freely. The thiophene core is rigid and planar, while the sulfone linkage gives limited rotational flexibility. The two sulfonyl oxygens are good hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group), attached directly to the ring as a thioether. The neighboring carbon carries a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom is bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups add limited rotational freedom. The two hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, whereas the thioether sulfur serves mainly as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring sharing one edge, giving a planar bicyclic aromatic system. The imidazole ring carries an NH group at one nitrogen, which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen is a pyridine-like acceptor. At the carbon between the two nitrogens sits a methylthio substituent (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group), a thioether that adds a flexible, weakly polarizable side chain. The benzene portion is unsubstituted, so the overall framework is rigid and largely flat, with only the methyl group of the thioether providing conformational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group), which is a thioether with no hydrogen-bond donor capacity but a weak acceptor at sulfur. The other is a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the ring, which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and strong acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and thioether side chains retain some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methylthio group, a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group, which is attached to the ring through the sulfur. The other is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, directly attached to the ring. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core and the linear nitrile give the structure considerable rigidity, with only the methyl rotation providing flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local planar mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a bicyclic system of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat and rigid aromatic core. A single methylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one of the carbons on the fused ring system, at a position away from the ring fusion. The fused aromatic framework has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom is only a weak acceptor. Because the substituent sits on one side of the naphthalene core, the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond its planar aromatic framework and is largely rigid, with only a small degree of flexibility from rotation about the carbon–sulfur and sulfur–methyl bonds.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. At one position sits a methylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group), and at the neighboring carbon sits a carboxylic acid group, which is a carbonyl attached to a hydroxyl. Because the substituents are ortho to each other and the ring is not fused to any other ring, the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid core with a relatively flexible methylthio tail. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen), while the sulfur atom contributes only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A methylthio group (a sulfur atom bearing a methyl substituent) is attached at the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, while an acyl chloride group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to chlorine) sits on the adjacent ring carbon, giving a 1,2-substitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully aromatic with no fusion, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the ring plane. Its rigidity comes from the aromatic core, though the carbonyl and thioether bonds allow limited rotation. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered 1,3-oxazole ring is fused to a six-membered pyridine ring, forming an oxazolo-pyridine scaffold. The oxazole portion carries a methylthio (S-CH3) group on the carbon between the ring nitrogen and oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen sits in the fused six-membered ring at a position remote from the substituent. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with the only notable flexibility coming from rotation of the thioether methyl group. Both ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the ring oxygen can contribute weak acceptor character, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the heteroatoms and the thioether substituent are placed asymmetrically across the fused rings.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms placed para to each other (1,4-positions) within the ring. A methylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a methyl group, forming a thioether) is attached to one of the ring carbons adjacent to a ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a rough planar outline. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the sulfur-methyl bond provides only minor rotational flexibility. The two ring nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because all its hydrogen atoms are attached to carbon.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group adjacent to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, an iodine atom on a carbon meta to the ring nitrogen, and an amino group on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen. That amino nitrogen connects through a methylene to a carbonyl, forming an ester whose alkoxy part is a bulky tert-butyl group. The amine N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the ester oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the glycine-type ester side chain is flexible, and the molecule lacks any notable symmetry.

The molecule is a simple acyclic ether-alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a flexible, unbranched chain. A six-carbon linear alkyl segment is joined through a single ether oxygen to a two-carbon segment that terminates in a primary hydroxyl group. There are no aromatic or fused ring systems, and the substitution pattern is strictly linear, giving the molecule no internal symmetry. The ether oxygen can act only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the terminal hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Its many rotatable single bonds make the structure highly flexible.

This molecule is a small, non-aromatic heterocycle built on a five-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one sulfur atom, forming a thiazolidine core. The ring carries an exocyclic double bond from the carbon adjacent to both heteroatoms, which is conjugated to a nitro group (-NO2) attached through that carbon, making it a nitroalkene. The ring is saturated apart from that exocyclic alkene, so its shape is relatively flexible, and the molecule lacks any symmetry. The secondary amine N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group and the ring nitrogen and sulfur can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. Attached to the carbon immediately next to the ring nitrogen is a flexible n-propyl thioether group, meaning a sulfur atom bonded to a three-carbon chain. On the adjacent ring carbon sits a primary carboxamide, a carbonyl bearing an NH2 group. The substitution pattern is therefore ortho, with the two substituents on neighboring carbons. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the propylthio chain adds conformational flexibility. The amide NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and it has no fused ring systems. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to one ring carbon, next to the carbon bearing a propylthio group (a sulfur atom bonded to a straight three-carbon chain), so the two substituents sit on adjacent positions, with the acid group flanked by the ring nitrogen's neighbouring carbon. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the pyridine nitrogen adds a further acceptor site. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, whereas the propylthio chain is flexible and can rotate freely. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built around a central sulfonyl group, with the sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to two aromatic rings. One ring is a plain benzene ring, while the other is a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring containing a sulfur atom in its ring. The two rings are not fused to each other; they are joined only through the tetrahedral sulfonyl linker, which gives the molecule a twisted, non-planar shape. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted apart from the sulfonyl attachment, so there is no additional substitution pattern and no internal symmetry beyond local ring symmetry. The sulfone oxygens are good hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered cyclic imide, with two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen carries a two-carbon ethyl linker terminating in a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a chlorine. The fused aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is limited to the imide nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, while the ethyl linker adds some conformational flexibility. The two imide carbonyl oxygens and the two sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an azo compound built on a benzoic acid scaffold, with two benzene rings joined by a central nitrogen-nitrogen double bond (an azo linkage). The first ring carries a carboxylic acid group, which is an acidic group that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The acid sits ortho to the azo bridge, so the two groups are adjacent on the same ring. The second ring is para-substituted, with a hydroxyl group opposite the azo linkage, adding a phenolic donor and acceptor site. Both aromatic rings are planar and rigid, while the azo bond is largely planar as well, giving an extended, conjugated framework with limited flexibility. The molecule lacks an overall symmetry axis because the two rings bear different substituents.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a sulfonyl-containing side chain placed in a para arrangement across the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and planar. The sulfur atom is fully oxidized as a sulfone, bearing two oxygen atoms, and it links the ring to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a primary alcohol. The methyl and sulfonyl groups sit opposite each other, giving the aromatic portion an approximately two-fold symmetric outline, while the flexible ethyl chain breaks overall symmetry. The sulfone oxygens and the terminal hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the hydroxyl also serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The aryl ring is rigid, whereas the sulfonylethyl side chain retains rotational freedom around its single bonds.

The molecule is a diaryl ether, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom. One ring carries a methyl group para to the ether linkage, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern on that side. The other ring bears an aldehyde group (a formyl substituent) at the position directly adjacent to the ether oxygen, making it a 1,2-disubstituted, ortho arrangement. The two aromatic rings are not fused and can rotate fairly freely about the C–O–C bonds, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than rigid. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry overall because the two rings bear different substituents. The ether oxygen and the aldehyde oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group (a carbonyl bonded to an NH2), which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds through its N-H and C=O. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethoxy group, an oxygen attached to a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms, which is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor and sterically bulky. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the C-O bonds allow some rotational freedom at the substituents. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring, reflecting its unsymmetrical substitution pattern.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, which contributes two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that can act as acceptors. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethoxy group, an ether oxygen bonded to a carbon carrying three fluorine atoms, which is electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the trifluoromethoxy and boronic acid groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane relating the two substituents, so the ring positions are distinct.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a primary sulfonamide group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to an NH2 group and to the aromatic ring. The neighboring position carries a trifluoromethoxy group, an ether oxygen bonded to a carbon that carries three fluorine atoms. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the trifluoromethoxy group adds bulk and limited rotational freedom around the aryl-oxygen bond. The sulfonamide NH2 offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ortho arrangement.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, where a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and single bonded to a chlorine atom and to the ring. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to the ring and to a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. The ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl and ether linkages allow some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the substituents. Its oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placing them in an ortho relationship. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which is attached directly to the aromatic ring and gives the molecule both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethoxy group, an oxygen atom linking the ring to a carbon that carries three fluorine atoms, which makes this portion bulky and strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and the ether linkage offer limited rotational freedom. Overall, the structure has no symmetry axis because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a phenylacetic acid scaffold, with a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon chain that ends in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is substituted at the adjacent (ortho) position by a trifluoromethoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to a carbon carrying three fluorine atoms. The benzene ring is a single fused-free aromatic system, and the methylene linker and the ether oxygen give the molecule modest rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen and fluorine atoms act as weaker acceptors. The overall arrangement is asymmetric because the two substituents are placed on adjacent ring positions with different chemistry.

This molecule is an acetanilide derivative built on a single benzene ring, with an acetamide group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl and an NH) attached to one carbon of the ring. The adjacent carbon bears a trifluoromethyl group, so the two substituents sit ortho to each other on the aromatic core. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the amide linkage gives the molecule a degree of conformational freedom around the C–N and C–C bonds. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group are weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because of the asymmetric ortho substitution pattern.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon attached to a methyl group, which is an electron-withdrawing ketone. The other is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and bulky. The aromatic ring and the two substituents are essentially planar and fairly rigid, with limited rotational freedom about the ring bonds. The molecule has no symmetry axis that exchanges the two substituents, so it is asymmetric. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic compound built on a three-carbon backbone. A terminal vinyl group (C=C) is attached to a central carbon that also carries a carboxylic acid group and a trifluoromethyl group, so the scaffold is an α-substituted acrylic acid. There are no rings, so the structure is fairly compact and flexible about its single bonds, though the C=C double bond fixes the local geometry at the alkene. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The three fluorine atoms on the trifluoromethyl group make that end of the molecule strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the vinyl, carboxyl, and CF₃ groups are all distinct.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused partners. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons, giving an ortho substitution pattern: a primary amino group (-NH2) and a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3) attached to the carbon that bears three fluorine atoms. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its nitrogen lone pair, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the CF3 group rotates freely about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local three-fold symmetry of the CF3 group.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a formyl group, an aldehyde with a carbon-oxygen double bond attached directly to the ring, and the other is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the aldehyde and trifluoromethyl groups add little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the ring's local arrangement, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the fluorine atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds as well.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group, which carries a carbonyl oxygen acceptor and an NH2 group that can act as two hydrogen-bond donors. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group attached directly to the ring, a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky, and lipophilic feature with three fluorine atoms that are weak acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond to the amide, so it is fairly rigid overall, with limited symmetry because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, which carries two hydroxyl groups on a trigonal boron atom. The other is a trifluoromethyl group, CF3, attached to the neighboring ring carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two substituents give the molecule limited conformational freedom around their bonds to the ring. The two B–OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms of the CF3 group are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ in character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a primary sulfonamide group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and bonded to an NH2 group, making it a hydrogen-bond donor through the nitrogen and an acceptor through the oxygens. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms that is strongly electron-withdrawing and bulky. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the only notable flexibility arising from rotation around the bonds connecting the sulfonamide and trifluoromethyl groups to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two adjacent substituents differ in identity and polarity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. One substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to a chlorine atom and to the ring. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms attached directly to the ring. The sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic core and the tetrahedral trifluoromethyl group give the molecule limited conformational flexibility, and the lack of any internal symmetry axis means it has no symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH), which can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3) attached to the same ring carbon framework next to the acid, contributing a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing, non-hydrogen-bonding feature. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and trifluoromethyl groups have limited rotational freedom about their single bonds to the ring. The structure lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, since the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a nitrile group, a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at the nitrogen but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a tetrahedral carbon bearing three fluorine atoms that is bulky, electron-withdrawing, and only weakly polar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only limited conformational freedom from rotation of the trifluoromethyl group.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings.
