One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a trifluoromethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment to the carbonyl, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aromatic rings are not fused, but they are connected through a single sp2 carbon, which allows some rotational flexibility about the bonds to the carbonyl. The overall framework is not symmetric because of the asymmetric placement of the trifluoromethyl group.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine, which is a reactive electrophilic center. The neighboring substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms, which is bulky and strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the rest of the structure has little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor sites are the carbonyl oxygen and, weakly, the fluorine atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no ring fusion. One substituent is a hydroxymethyl group (a carbon bearing a hydroxyl), which contributes a primary alcohol functional group. The other is a trifluoromethyl group attached directly to the ring, with three fluorine atoms on a single carbon that gives the scaffold a strongly electron-withdrawing character. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm retains some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms) is attached to one ring carbon, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 unit bearing a bromine atom) is attached to the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky, while the bromomethyl group provides a reactive, polarizable C–Br bond at a benzylic position. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor-type sites are the lone pairs on the fluorine and bromine atoms, which are weak. Its skeleton is compact and largely rigid, with only the bromomethyl group offering rotational freedom.

The molecule is a cinnamic-acid-type structure: a benzene ring bearing an acrylic acid side chain, with the carboxylic acid attached through a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond to the aromatic ring. A trifluoromethyl group sits on the ring at the position ortho to the alkenyl substituent, giving a 1,2-disubstitution pattern. The molecule is largely planar and rigid because of the conjugated aromatic ring and the double bond, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond to the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The three fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors and add steric bulk near the side chain.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons flanking the nitrogen: a carboxylic acid group directly on one side and a trifluoromethyl group on the other, giving a 2,3-disubstitution pattern. The molecule is planar and largely rigid, with limited rotational freedom apart from the orientation of the acid and trifluoromethyl groups. Its hydrogen-bond capability includes a donor from the carboxylic acid hydroxyl and acceptors from the carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the pyridine nitrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. A hydroxyl group is attached to one ring carbon, and directly adjacent to it on the next carbon is a trifluoromethyl group, so the two substituents sit in an ortho arrangement. The three fluorine atoms on the trifluoromethyl carbon give that group a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky character. The hydroxyl oxygen can donate one hydrogen bond and accept hydrogen bonds, while the fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has only a limited, mostly local degree of conformational freedom from rotation about the bonds to its substituents.

This molecule is a phenothiazine: a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused to a central six-membered ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom placed para to each other. The nitrogen bears a hydrogen and acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a weak acceptor, while the sulfur is a thioether-type acceptor. A trifluoromethyl group (CF3) sits on one of the outer benzene rings, at a position meta to the nitrogen-bearing carbon, adding strong electron-withdrawing character and a bulky, lipophilic substituent. The fused tricyclic core is essentially planar but folded along the sulfur-nitrogen axis, giving it a modest butterfly-like bend, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane because of the single off-center CF3 group.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group attached through a single methylene linker, so the acid carbon is one atom removed from the ring. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group directly bonded to the ring, which places a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky, fluorine-rich motif beside the side chain. The molecule has no ring fusion and only one ring, with a flexible CH2 linker allowing rotation of the acid group relative to the rigid aromatic core. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon atom carrying three fluorine atoms, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky. The other is a cyanomethyl group, a flexible two-atom chain ending in a nitrile, where the linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methylene linker gives the nitrile arm some rotational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no additional ring fusion. One substituent is a hydrazine group, a nitrogen-nitrogen single bond in which the terminal nitrogen carries two hydrogens and the attached nitrogen carries one. The other substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms that is rigidly attached to the ring. The hydrazine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds and as acceptors through their lone pairs, whereas the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors only. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydrazine linkage provides some rotational freedom. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local symmetry of the substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and it is monosubstituted at the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen (the 2-position). That carbon bears an alkyne unit, a carbon-carbon triple bond, whose far end is bonded to a silicon atom carrying three methyl groups, so the silicon is tetrahedral and the substituent is a trimethylsilyl-ethynyl group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the linear alkyne adds a stiff, rod-like extension and the methyl groups give the silicon end a bulky, freely rotating profile. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond an approximate local mirror plane through the ring and the alkyne axis. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered heteroaromatic ring. The five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom arranged as N–S–N, which makes it a 2,1,3-benzothiadiazole scaffold. The benzene ring carries four hydrogens and no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted. The fused framework is planar and fully conjugated, giving it a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds and a symmetrical arrangement across the fusion axis. The two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small acyclic alcohol built on a two-carbon skeleton: a primary hydroxymethyl group (CH2OH) is bonded to a single carbon that carries three bromine atoms. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the framework is entirely open-chain and flexible, with free rotation about the central C–C bond. The functional groups are one primary hydroxyl and three C–Br bonds clustered on the same carbon, giving a strongly localized, symmetric substitution pattern at that terminus. The hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen allow the molecule to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a two-carbon chain. One terminal carbon bears an ethyl group, and the other end carries a single carbon bearing three chlorine atoms, which is attached to a carbon that bears both a hydroxyl group and an ethoxy oxygen. The arrangement places a hemiacetal-type carbon, bonded to two oxygen atoms and a hydrogen, next to a trichloromethyl group. The trichloromethyl group gives the central region strong electron-withdrawing character and a bulky, roughly tetrahedral profile. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no stereocenters beyond the substitution pattern, so the chain is flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a short two-carbon backbone: a terminal carboxamide group (a carbonyl carbon bearing both a carbonyl oxygen and an NH2 group) attached to a second carbon that carries three chlorine atoms. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters, so the structure is compact and acyclic. The trichloromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, sterically bulky substituent on the alpha carbon, giving the molecule a roughly tetrahedral local geometry around that carbon. The amide NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Because the bonds are all single or the amide C=O, the molecule has limited conformational flexibility, with rotation mainly around the C–C bond and the C–N bond restricted by amide resonance.

This molecule is an acyclic two-carbon skeleton, with no rings or ring fusion. One carbon bears a hydroxyl group, giving it a primary alcohol function, while the adjacent carbon carries three chlorine substituents, forming a trichloromethyl group at one end of the chain. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the hydroxyl-bearing terminus differs fundamentally from the fully halogenated terminus. Its chain is flexible, with free rotation about the carbon-carbon single bond. The hydroxyl oxygen and hydrogen allow it to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a short acyclic carbonate-type ester built on a two-carbon chain. A carbonyl carbon bears a chlorine atom and a single-bonded oxygen, making it a chloroformate, and that oxygen links to a methylene group. The adjacent carbon carries three chlorine atoms, so the terminal end is a trichloromethyl group. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic character. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor of note, since the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local three-fold arrangement of chlorines on the terminal carbon.

The molecule is a small, acyclic amide built on a single carbon centre. A carbonyl group is bonded to an amino group (–NH2) on one side and to a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3) on the other, so the scaffold is a simple two-carbon-equivalent backbone with no rings and no fused systems. The three fluorine atoms are all attached to the same carbon, giving a compact, highly symmetric trifluoromethyl unit with three-fold local symmetry around the C–CF3 axis. The structure is small and rigid around the amide linkage, with only limited rotational freedom about the C–N and C–C bonds. The amide nitrogen carries two N–H bonds that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built around a single carbonyl carbon that links a phenyl ring to a trifluoromethyl group, making it an aryl trifluoromethyl ketone. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so it has no positional isomers to consider and is planar and rigid, with the two ring atoms bearing a carbonyl and a trifluoromethyl group. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The three fluorine atoms on the terminal carbon form a compact, strongly electron-withdrawing group that makes the carbonyl carbon unusually electrophilic. The overall structure is small and relatively compact, with only one rotatable bond connecting the ring and the carbonyl.

This molecule is a two-carbon chain, with a terminal primary alcohol group attached to a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic and flexible, with free rotation about the central carbon-carbon bond. The fluorines sit on one carbon in a trifluoromethyl arrangement, making that end strongly electron-withdrawing and giving the molecule an approximate threefold local symmetry around the C–C axis. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The fluorine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a methyl group and a sulfonate ester group in a para (1,4) arrangement, giving it a symmetric, elongated shape with no fused ring systems. The sulfonyl group is a sulfonate ester, with two sulfonyl oxygens and an ester oxygen linking to a 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl chain, where the three fluorines sit on the terminal carbon. The aromatic ring and the sulfonyl unit are rigid, while the O–CH2–CF3 tail retains some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The sulfonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon.

This molecule is a sulfonate ester built around a central sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens, forming a sulfonyl group. The sulfur is attached on one side to a trichloromethyl carbon and on the other to an oxygen that links to a two-carbon chain ending in a trifluoromethyl group. There are no rings, so the scaffold is a small, acyclic, flexible chain with a highly substituted carbon at each end. The three chlorines and three fluorines are arranged as symmetric triads, each set rotating freely around its single bond. The sulfonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small ester built around a single carbonyl carbon bonded to an oxygen that links to a 2,2,2-trifluoroethyl group. The acyl side carries a trifluoromethyl group, so the structure is essentially a trifluoroacetate ester with no rings and no fused systems. Both ends are heavily fluorinated: six fluorine atoms sit on two carbons, giving a strongly electron-withdrawing, highly substituted framework. The molecule is acyclic and fairly flexible about its single bonds, though the rotation around the ester linkage is somewhat constrained. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen is on carbon and none is attached to heteroatoms, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ester oxygen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a trifluoroacetamide built around a single pyridine ring. A secondary amide group links a trifluoromethyl-substituted carbonyl carbon to a methylene bridge, which connects to the carbon at the 2-position of an aromatic six-membered nitrogen heterocycle. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes three fluorine atoms to the carbonyl side of the amide. The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its only rotatable bonds are around the methylene linker and the amide, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single central carbon that carries a primary amide group, with a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups attached to it. This gives a compact, acyclic scaffold with no ring systems and no ring fusion. The only functional group is the carboxamide, in which the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds and the two amide N–H hydrogens can donate them. The tert-butyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon is bulky and highly symmetric, with three equivalent methyl arms arranged around the central quaternary carbon, giving the fragment local threefold symmetry. Rotation about the carbon–carbon bond to the amide is relatively unhindered, so the molecule is small and fairly flexible in its acyclic portion.

This molecule is a small acyclic thioamide built on a quaternary carbon framework. A tert-butyl group, with a central carbon bearing three methyl groups, is bonded directly to a thiocarbonyl carbon that carries a primary amino group, so the scaffold has no rings and no ring fusion. The thioamide unit (C(=S)NH2) is the sole functional group, and its substitution pattern is simple: the sulfur sits on the carbonyl-type carbon and the nitrogen is unsubstituted. The tert-butyl portion has threefold rotational symmetry about the bond to the thioamide carbon, while the molecule overall is fairly rigid around the C=S and C–N bonds. The two NH hydrogens act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a short, fully saturated perfluorinated carboxamide built on a two-carbon chain. The first carbon is a carbonyl bearing a terminal primary amide group (NH2 and C=O), and it is directly bonded to a carbon carrying two fluorine atoms. That carbon connects to a terminal trifluoromethyl group, so the skeleton is a simple linear chain with no rings and no ring fusion. All hydrogens on the carbon backbone have been replaced by fluorine, giving a highly substituted, nearly symmetric pattern about the central C–C bond. The chain is flexible about its single bonds, though the bulky fluorines limit rotation somewhat. The amide NH2 provides two hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and amide nitrogen provide acceptor sites, while the fluorines are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, fully saturated four-carbon chain with a hydroxymethyl group at each terminus, so it has no rings and no double bonds. Each of the two interior carbons is fully fluorinated, bearing two fluorine atoms, while the two terminal carbons each carry a primary alcohol group. The structure is therefore a perfluorinated central segment capped by two CH2OH units, giving a symmetric molecule that is C2-symmetric through its central axis. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its C–C single bonds. Each terminal hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, fully saturated acyclic chain of four carbons with no rings or double bonds, so it is entirely flexible. Its backbone is a linear sequence of carbon atoms, with a primary alcohol group (–CH2OH) at each end. The two central carbons each carry two fluorine atoms, giving a symmetric, geminal difluorination pattern on the interior of the chain. The molecule has a mirror-symmetric structure about its central C–C bond. Both terminal hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. Each ring carries two hydroxyl groups on the same side, positioned at the 2- and 4-positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, so the two rings are substituted identically. The arrangement is symmetric about the central carbonyl carbon, and the rings can rotate around the single bonds to the carbonyl, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The four phenolic hydroxyls act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a bromine atom at the para position relative to a carbonyl group, making it a para-disubstituted aromatic system. The carbonyl carbon links the ring to a dibrominated carbon, so the overall scaffold is a simple aryl ketone with a CHBr2-type terminus, a dibromomethyl group bonded directly to the ketone. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the ketone and the attached bromoalkyl group provide some conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The molecule has an approximate two-fold relationship across the ring axis but no true high symmetry because the two bromine environments differ. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an aryl ketone built on a benzene ring, with the carbonyl group bonded directly to the ring and bearing a chloromethyl substituent on its other side. The benzene ring carries two chlorine atoms, one at the position adjacent to the carbonyl attachment and one at the position para to it, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two-atom linker from the ring to the chlorine-bearing carbon offers modest rotational freedom around the ring-carbonyl bond. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic alcohol built on a branched carbon chain with no rings or aromatic systems. Its backbone contains a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, flanked by an isopropyl-substituted carbinol carbon and a primary hydroxymethyl group, giving a compact, highly branched arrangement. Two hydroxyl groups are present, one secondary and one primary, so the molecule can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor at each oxygen. The structure has no internal symmetry element that makes both halves identical, since the two hydroxyl-bearing ends differ in substitution. Being fully saturated and acyclic with several rotatable single bonds, it is conformationally flexible, though the gem-dimethyl branching restricts rotation somewhat.

The molecule is an acyclic ester built on a branched aliphatic skeleton, with no rings or aromatic systems. A single ester linkage connects an isobutyryl-type acyl group (a carbonyl flanked by an isopropyl branch) to a neopentyl-like alkyl fragment that carries two geminal methyl groups on one carbon. The adjacent carbon bears a secondary hydroxyl group and is attached to an isopropyl substituent, so the chain contains multiple quaternary and methine branch points. The structure is highly branched and largely saturated, with the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen providing the only polar sites. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall it is flexible along its carbon-carbon bonds yet sterically compact around its branched core.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon, so it contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups. Its skeleton is a branched chain of eight carbons built around a central quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, which is attached to an isobutyl-type segment. Because every carbon is sp3-hybridized and joined only by single bonds, the chain is highly flexible and can adopt many rotational conformations. There are no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and the molecule has no symmetry element beyond local methyl-group equivalence.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated-plus-one-alkene nitrogen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyridine-type ring containing a single secondary amine nitrogen. The ring carries four methyl groups, two on each of the two carbons flanking the nitrogen, which creates a gem-dimethyl pattern on both sides and gives the scaffold a bulky, sterically crowded character. A carbon-carbon double bond sits within the ring, conjugated with a primary carboxamide group attached to one alkene carbon. The ring is non-fused and monocyclic, with limited conformational flexibility due to the double bond and the bulky substituents. The amide provides both hydrogen-bond donor capacity through its NH2 and acceptor capacity through its carbonyl oxygen, while the ring nitrogen contributes one additional donor and acceptor site.

This molecule is a biaryl compound made of two benzene rings joined by a single bond between their carbon atoms, so it has no fused rings. Each ring is a simple benzene carrying two methyl groups, placing the methyl substituents at the 2 and 5 positions relative to the connecting bond on each ring. The two rings are twisted relative to one another because the ortho methyl groups crowd the central bond, which limits rotation about it. The molecule is hydrocarbon only, with no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its overall arrangement is approximately C2-symmetric, with the two halves mirroring each other.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, with no fused rings and no aromatic character. The nitrogen atom sits at one position of the ring and carries a hydrogen, making it a secondary amine. Two gem-dimethyl groups occupy both carbons adjacent to the nitrogen, and a third gem-dimethyl pair sits on the opposite carbon of the ring, giving a symmetric 2,2,6,6-tetramethyl substitution pattern. The bulky methyl groups lock the ring into a rigid chair-like conformation with limited flexibility. The nitrogen lone pair and its N–H make it a hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor.

This molecule is a small six-membered heterocycle containing one ring oxygen and one ring ester-type carbonyl, forming a 1,3-dioxin-type skeleton with a single ring. The ring carries a methyl group on an sp2 carbon that sits in a C=C double bond conjugated to the lactone-like C=O, so the ring is largely planar and rigid. An acetal carbon bears two geminal methyl groups, which introduces a sp3 center that breaks the planarity at one end. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any element of symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the acetal carbon. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a terthiophene, built from three thiophene five-membered aromatic rings joined in a linear chain. The central thiophene is connected at its 2- and 5-positions to the outer rings, so the three rings sit in a fully conjugated, planar-leaning backbone with no bulky substituents. Each ring contains a sulfur atom that contributes to the aromatic system, and there are no conventional polar functional groups such as hydroxyls, amines, or carbonyls. The molecule is highly symmetric, with a two-fold axis passing through the central ring, and its extended aromatic framework is essentially rigid. Because it lacks N–H or O–H groups, it has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptors are the sulfur atoms, which are weak.

This molecule is 2,2':6',2''-terpyridine, a linear arrangement of three pyridine rings joined by single C–C bonds at their 2-positions. The central pyridine is substituted at both of its 2 and 6 positions, so the two outer pyridine rings are attached on opposite sides of it, giving a symmetric, roughly planar scaffold. Each ring contains one aromatic ring nitrogen, and these nitrogens are positioned to face inward toward the central core. Because the bonds between rings are single bonds with limited rotation, the framework is largely rigid and conjugated. The ring nitrogen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from two pyridine rings joined directly by a single bond between carbon atoms adjacent to their ring nitrogens, giving a 2,2'-bipyridyl scaffold. Each ring is a fully aromatic six-membered heterocycle with one sp2 nitrogen, and there are no fused rings, substituents, or additional functional groups beyond these nitrogen atoms. The molecule is highly symmetric, with a two-fold axis passing through the central inter-ring bond, and the inter-ring bond gives limited, mostly planar conformational freedom. Each nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The two nitrogens are positioned so they can converge on a single site, making the arrangement a classic bidentate chelating motif.

The molecule is built from two pyrimidine rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond between their C2 positions, giving a biaryl-type scaffold with no bridging atoms. Each six-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms at the 1,3 positions, and neither ring is fused to any other ring system. Because there are no substituents beyond the linking bond, the substitution pattern is symmetric: the two rings are identical and mirror each other across the central bond. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, since aromatic rings connected by a single bond can rotate only slightly, and the nitrogen lone pairs make it a hydrogen-bond acceptor at four ring positions with no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built from two quinoline units joined directly at a single carbon-carbon bond. Each unit is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, so the nitrogen atom sits in a six-membered aromatic ring adjacent to the fusion point. The two quinoline units are attached through their carbons next to the ring nitrogens, placing the nitrogen atoms on the same side and oriented toward each other across the central bond. The framework is fully planar and rigid, with extensive conjugation across all four fused rings. Each ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single sp3 carbon bearing two para-methoxyphenyl rings, so it has a diaryl-methane-type scaffold with the central carbon also linked to a CH2 group that ends in a primary amine. Each benzene ring carries one methoxy ether group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the para position relative to the attachment point, giving the two aryl halves a matching substitution pattern. The two aryl rings are not fused to each other and are connected only through the central carbon, so the framework is flexible and can adopt many rotational conformations around its single bonds. Overall the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the central carbon, broken only by the aminomethyl branch. The primary amine provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the two ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built from a 1,1'-binaphthyl scaffold, two naphthalene units joined by a single bond between their C1 and C1' positions, which gives a twisted, axially chiral framework. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge. At the C2 and C2' positions of the two naphthalene units sit diphenylphosphino groups, each bearing two unsubstituted phenyl rings attached through phosphorus. The phosphorus atoms are trivalent, with lone pairs that can coordinate to metals, making them electron-donating acceptors rather than hydrogen-bond participants. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its phosphorus centers are the only acceptor sites, while the large hindered biaryl core limits conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, with two phenyl rings joined by a single C–C bond. Each of the two ortho positions on that biphenyl core carries a diphenylphosphino group, so the structure is symmetric about the central biaryl axis. The two phosphorus atoms are trivalent and each bears two phenyl rings, giving six additional aromatic rings in total and an all-carbon aromatic framework dominated by sp2 atoms. The bulky, twisted biaryl linkage and the propeller-like arrangement of the phenyl groups around each phosphorus make the molecule fairly rigid. Its only heteroatoms are the two phosphorus centers, which can act as weak electron-pair donors but carry no N–H or O–H groups, so it has essentially no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only very weak acceptor character.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated amine built around a single tetrahedral quaternary carbon bearing three hydroxymethyl groups. The central nitrogen is a tertiary amine carrying two 2-hydroxyethyl arms, and it is directly attached to that quaternary carbon, so the skeleton is a flexible, branched chain with no ring systems or ring fusion. Four primary hydroxyl groups are present, and the tertiary nitrogen provides an additional lone pair, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites. The structure lacks symmetry overall because the nitrogen-bearing branch differs from the three hydroxymethyl branches, and its numerous single bonds make it conformationally flexible.

The molecule is built on a short, branched aliphatic skeleton centered on a single quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group, two hydroxymethyl arms, and a carboxylic acid group. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system, and the structure is fully saturated apart from the carbonyl carbon. The carboxylic acid (-COOH) is the principal functional group, accompanied by two primary alcohol (-CH2OH) groups on the same carbon, giving the molecule a compact, highly substituted pattern. Its geometry is flexible at the single bonds but gains some conformational restriction from the quaternary center, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the carboxyl group differs from the two equivalent hydroxymethyl arms. Overall, it presents three hydrogen-bond donors (the acid and two hydroxyl groups) and several hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, making it strongly capable of hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is 2,2'-bithiophene, built from two five-membered aromatic thiophene rings joined by a single bond between their alpha carbons (positions adjacent to sulfur). Each ring contains one sulfur atom, which lies within the aromatic system, and no other heteroatoms or substituents are present. The two rings are unsubstituted apart from the inter-ring bond, giving a fully conjugated, planar-capable biaryl scaffold. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoint of the central C–C bond, and rotation about that bond gives limited conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single fluorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a para-disubstituted aromatic core. Attached to the ring is a carbonyl group, which connects to a carbon atom carrying two bromine substituents, so the overall skeleton is an aryl ketone with a gem-dibromomethyl unit. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the C–C bond linking the carbonyl to the ring and the bond to the dibromo carbon allow some rotational freedom. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis, though the dibromomethyl carbon is not a stereocenter. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond, with each ring carrying one bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to that linkage, so both bromines sit in ortho positions relative to the inter-ring bond. The two rings are not fused and have no shared atoms beyond that single bond, and each is a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle. The scaffold is therefore a 2,2'-disubstituted biphenyl with a symmetric pattern, since the two halves are chemically identical and mirror one another across the central bond. The only functional groups are the two aryl carbon-bromine bonds, which are weakly polarizable but carry no hydrogen-bond donor capacity and only very weak acceptor character. Steric crowding from the ortho bromines restricts rotation about the central bond, giving the framework a relatively rigid, twisted conformation.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, saturated haloalkane built on a two-carbon backbone with no rings or double bonds. One carbon bears a methoxy group (a methyl ether oxygen) together with two fluorine atoms, while the adjacent carbon carries two chlorine atoms and a hydrogen. The fluorines and chlorines are attached geminally on each carbon, giving a compact, highly halogenated substitution pattern. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens sit on carbon. Rotation about the central carbon–carbon bond gives it considerable conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry because the two carbons carry different halogen sets.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between their ring carbons. Each pyridine ring carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so both halogens sit ortho to nitrogen and flank the biaryl linkage. The two rings are unfused and connected through a single bond, which allows some rotation about the axis, though the chlorine atoms create steric hindrance that restricts free rotation. The structure has no formal symmetry axis that maps the two halves perfectly, but the two pyridyl units are closely related in substitution pattern. Each ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a biaryl compound built from two pyridine rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between their 4-positions. One ring carries a chlorine atom at the 2-position, and the other carries a chlorine at the 2-position relative to its nitrogen, so the two halogens sit on the carbons adjacent to each ring nitrogen. The two rings are unfused and connected by a freely rotating single bond, giving the molecule a relatively flexible linkage that can adopt a range of twist angles between the aromatic planes. Each pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The arrangement is approximately symmetric about the central bond, since both rings carry the same chloro-pyridyl substitution pattern.

This molecule is a short acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone. The terminal carbon is a primary carboxamide group, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to an NH2 nitrogen and to the adjacent carbon. That adjacent carbon, the alpha position, carries two chlorine atoms, making it a geminal dichloride. There are no rings, so the scaffold is fully flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds and no stereocenters because the alpha carbon bears two identical substituents. The amide NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single carbonyl group, making it an aryl ketone. The carbonyl carbon is bonded directly to the phenyl ring on one side and to a dichloromethyl carbon on the other, so the scaffold is a simple two-part arrangement with no fused ring systems. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and unsubstituted apart from its attachment point, giving it no meaningful symmetry breaking beyond the local rotational freedom around the aryl–carbonyl bond. The two chlorine atoms sit on the same terminal carbon, creating a geminal dihalide that adds electron-withdrawing character adjacent to the ketone. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a 1,2-diketone, specifically a benzil-type scaffold in which two aromatic rings are joined through a central carbon-carbon bond flanked by two carbonyl groups. Each phenyl ring carries a single chlorine atom at the ortho position relative to the carbonyl attachment, so the two substituents sit on the same side of the diketone bridge. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoint of the central C–C bond, making the two halves structurally equivalent. The 1,2-dicarbonyl linkage is conformationally flexible about its central bond, while the aromatic rings are rigid planar units. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its two carbonyl oxygens and two chlorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries a carboxylic acid group, a tertiary hydroxyl group, and two identical 2-chlorophenyl rings, so it is a substituted mandelic-acid-type scaffold. Each aromatic ring is a benzene ring with one chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to the attachment point, giving an ortho substitution pattern on both rings. The two aryl groups are attached to the same central carbon, so the molecule has no fused ring systems and is composed of three separate functional units joined at one stereogenic center. The two aryl rings give the structure considerable steric bulk, while the central carbon's single bonds allow moderate conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and three hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two separate benzene rings. Each ring carries a chlorine atom on the carbon immediately adjacent to the point of attachment to the carbonyl, placing both halogens in the ortho position on their respective rings. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other; they are connected only through the single carbonyl carbon, so the scaffold is non-cyclic at the central link and fairly rigid overall. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry relating the two halves, though the rings can rotate around their bonds to the carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on aromatic carbons.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered 1,3-benzodioxole ring, in which the two oxygen atoms bridge the aromatic carbons and are linked by a single difluoromethylene carbon. That CF2 carbon is saturated and sits between the two ether oxygens, so the dioxole ring is non-planar and locally rigid. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the benzene ring, positioned adjacent to one of the ring-fusion carbons, which makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The fused system as a whole is largely flat and rigid, apart from some puckering of the difluorinated ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the two ring oxygens and the fluorine atoms can act as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with the ring fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring that contains a single carbon bearing two fluorine atoms. The carboxylic acid is attached to the aromatic ring at a position meta to one of the ring oxygens and para to the other, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern across the benzene core. The fused dioxole ring is largely planar and rigid, while the carboxyl group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the carboxylic acid breaks the symmetry of the fused system. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the two ring ether oxygens and the fluorines act as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing a carbonyl group directly attached to it, so it is an aryl ketone with no ring fusion. The carbonyl carbon is also bonded to a carbon that carries two fluorine atoms, making the terminal carbon a difluoromethyl group adjacent to the ketone. The benzene ring is unsubstituted apart from this acyl group, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the ring has high local symmetry about the axis through the carbonyl. The overall framework is compact and fairly rigid in the aromatic portion, with some rotational freedom around the bond linking the ring to the carbonyl. The oxygen of the carbonyl can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain: an ethyl group attached to a quaternary carbon that bears two fluorine atoms, which is in turn bonded to a carboxylic acid group. The two fluorines sit geminally on the same carbon, so the substitution pattern is localized at the alpha position relative to the carbonyl. The molecule contains no rings and no fused ring systems, and it is essentially flexible, with rotation possible about the single bonds of the ethyl and carboxyl linkages. Its hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated in the carboxylic acid, where the hydroxyl oxygen acts as a donor and the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond local rotational freedom at the ethyl terminus.

The molecule is built on a cyclopropane scaffold, a three-membered all-carbon ring. One ring carbon bears a carboxylic acid group (a carbonyl attached to a hydroxyl), while the adjacent ring carbon carries two fluorine atoms on the same carbon, making it a gem-difluoro substitution pattern. The ring is highly strained and rigid, and the molecule has no internal mirror plane of symmetry that would make the two sides identical. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is a two-carbon chain with a terminal primary alcohol group on one end and a difluoromethyl group on the other, so it has no ring systems or fused scaffold. The hydroxyl oxygen bears a hydrogen atom, making it both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two fluorine atoms on the adjacent carbon are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The carbon bearing the two fluorines is a stereocenter-free CHF2 unit, and the overall structure is achiral and lacks any rotational symmetry axis beyond the freely rotating C–C bond. The molecule is highly flexible, since rotation about the central carbon–carbon single bond interconverts its conformers readily.

The molecule is a short, fully saturated carboxylic acid built on a two-carbon backbone with no rings. The alpha carbon carries a methyl group and two fluorine atoms on the same carbon, creating a geminal difluoro substitution pattern that makes that carbon tetrahedral and sterically compact. The carboxyl group at the far end, a C=O paired with an O-H, is the single functional group and provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and two acceptor sites through its oxygens. Because there are no ring systems and only single C-C bonds in the backbone, the structure is highly flexible about its central bond, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis of note given the asymmetric placement of the carboxyl group.

The molecule is a short, acyclic dicarboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain: one terminal carboxylic acid group and a second carboxylic acid group attached at the other end through a carbonyl carbon. The central methylene carbon sits between the two ends, and the carbon adjacent to the second carboxyl group bears two fluorine atoms, which form a geminal difluoro substitution pattern. There are no ring systems or fusion features, and the chain is flexible, with rotation possible about its single bonds. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the fluorinated and non-fluorinated ends differ. Both carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their hydroxyl hydrogens and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, giving the molecule several sites for hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a benzophenone: two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group. Each ring carries a hydroxyl group ortho to the ketone and a methoxy group, so the substitution pattern is 2,4-dihydroxy on one ring with the other hydroxyl converted to a methyl ether, with a methoxy group para to the carbonyl on each ring. The two rings are not fused and connect through a single sp2 carbon, giving a flexible but largely planar-capable arrangement around the ketone. The overall skeleton has no rotational symmetry, since the two rings bear different substituent patterns. Both ortho hydroxyls can form intramolecular hydrogen bonds to the carbonyl oxygen, and the methoxy oxygens act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined directly by a single bond between one carbon on each ring, forming a biphenyl scaffold with no fused or bridged ring system. Each ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon immediately adjacent to the linking bond, so both substituents sit in the ortho positions relative to the biaryl bond, and the two rings are mirror-related. The molecule has two hydroxyl groups that each act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak pi-electron interactions. The biaryl bond allows rotation between the two rings, giving the structure moderate flexibility, though the ortho-hydroxyl groups can influence the preferred twist angle through steric and intramolecular hydrogen-bonding effects.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined directly by a single carbon–carbon bond. Each ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group, an ether) at the position adjacent to that inter-ring bond, so the substitution pattern is ortho on both rings. The two aromatic rings are unfused, meaning each is an independent six-membered ring with no shared atoms beyond the linking bond. The molecule has a twofold symmetry axis passing through the central biaryl bond, since the two halves are identical. The ortho methoxy groups hinder free rotation about the central bond, giving the scaffold a degree of conformational restriction. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic ether with a single central quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. Two methoxy groups are attached to that same carbon, each contributing a methyl ether oxygen bonded to a terminal methyl. The structure is fully saturated and highly symmetric, with the two oxygen-bearing arms related by a mirror plane through the central carbon. Because it contains only single bonds and no rigid units, it is flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-oxygen bonds. Its oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, but it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups, forming a compact, acyclic, branched scaffold with no rings and no ring fusion. Each of the two remaining substituents on that central carbon is a hydroxymethyl group, so the two primary alcohol functions sit at the ends of short CH2 linkers attached to the same carbon, giving a symmetrical substitution pattern. The molecule has a mirror plane through the central carbon, and its flexibility comes from freely rotating single bonds, with no rigid elements. Both terminal hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, so the structure offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is an acyclic, saturated alcohol built on a branched carbon skeleton with no rings and no double bonds. The main chain runs through a secondary carbinol carbon bearing a single hydroxyl group, which sits next to a quaternary carbon carrying two methyl substituents and a further ethyl group. The molecule has no elements of symmetry, since the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is flanked by an ethyl arm on one side and a bulky tert-alkyl arm on the other. Its single-bond framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility, with the bulky tert-alkyl group restricting some rotations. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the carbon framework is nonpolar.

The molecule is built on a single saturated acyclic carbon skeleton with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms. A central quaternary carbon bears two methyl groups and an ethyl chain, and the terminal end of that chain is a methyl group, giving a branched alkane framework. Because every carbon is sp3-hybridized and bonded only to carbon and hydrogen, the structure has no functional groups, no substitution pattern beyond simple alkyl branching, and no polar sites. Its only symmetry is a local mirror-like arrangement of the two methyl groups on the quaternary center, and the molecule is highly flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a small, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a branched saturated carbon skeleton. A single carboxyl group, bearing a carbonyl oxygen and a hydroxyl group, sits at one end of the chain, attached to a fully substituted quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups and an ethyl group. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no stereocenters, and the molecule is highly flexible through rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can both donate one hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a saturated, acyclic dicarboxylic acid built on a short aliphatic chain, with no rings and no double bonds other than those within the two carboxyl groups. Its backbone is a five-carbon chain whose central carbon carries two methyl groups, creating a quaternary carbon that gives the skeleton a branched, gem-dimethyl character. One terminus is a carboxylic acid attached directly to that quaternary carbon, and the other is a carboxylic acid at the end of a two-carbon methylene segment. Because the chain has few rotational constraints, the molecule is fairly flexible, though the gem-dimethyl group restricts some conformations. Both carboxyl groups can each donate one hydrogen bond and accept two, so the molecule has two donor sites and four acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a symmetric acyclic anhydride, formed by two identical halves joined through a central carbonyl-oxygen-carbonyl linkage. Each half is a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, linked to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a free carboxylic acid. Because the two arms are equivalent, the molecule has a mirror-like symmetry about the central anhydride oxygen. It contains no rings, so the backbone is flexible, with rotation possible about the single bonds in each chain. Each terminal carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the anhydride carbonyls serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short aliphatic dicarboxylic acid built on a saturated, acyclic carbon chain with no rings and no aromatic groups. A single quaternary carbon carries two methyl groups, so the skeleton has a gem-dimethyl branch point. One terminus is a carboxylic acid attached through a methylene unit, and the other is a carboxylic acid attached directly to the quaternary carbon, so the two acid groups are not symmetric. The chain is flexible with free rotation about its single bonds, and the gem-dimethyl branch adds some steric bulk near one acid group. Each carboxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and four acceptor oxygens in total.

The molecule is built around a single quaternary carbon that carries two hydroxymethyl groups and two n-alkyl chains, giving an acyclic, fully saturated scaffold with no rings. Both hydroxymethyl arms each end in a primary alcohol, so the structure has two hydroxyl functional groups located on the same central carbon. The two butyl-type chains attached to that same carbon are flexible, unbranched hydrocarbon segments that give the molecule considerable conformational freedom. The central carbon sits on a plane of local symmetry, so the two hydroxymethyl groups are equivalent and the two alkyl chains are essentially identical. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the carbon-rich alkyl portions contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single bond between their carbon atoms. Each ring carries one nitro group, and the two nitro groups sit on the carbons immediately adjacent to the biaryl bond, so the substitution pattern is ortho on both rings and the two substituents are placed symmetrically about the central axis. Because the ortho nitro groups are bulky, rotation around the inter-ring bond is restricted, which makes the framework fairly rigid and non-planar. Each nitro group contributes oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a short acyclic carboxamide built on a branched alkyl backbone. A central carbon bears two n-propyl chains and a primary carboxamide group, so the scaffold consists of a seven-carbon chain with the amide carbon at one end and the branch point at its alpha position. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic groups. The only functional group is the primary amide, which contributes one carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and two N-H hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors. The two propyl arms are symmetric about the branch carbon, and the overall structure is flexible because all bonds are single and freely rotatable.

The molecule is a symmetric disulfide built from two pyridine rings joined through a central S–S bond. Each ring is an aromatic six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, and each bears its sulfur-containing linkage on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the two halves mirror one another across the disulfide bridge. The bridge itself is the only flexible element, with a degree of rotation about its two sulfur–carbon and sulfur–sulfur bonds, while the pyridine rings remain planar and rigid. The ring nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors and carry no donor sites, since the molecule has no N–H or O–H groups. The compound is free of stereocenters and contains no additional functional groups beyond the disulfide and the two pyridyl nitrogens.

The molecule is built from two saturated six-membered sulfur-containing rings joined through a short two-carbon linker. One ring is a 1,3-dithiane-type ring containing two sulfur atoms separated by a carbon, and the other is a 1,3-dithiane-type ring as well, so both rings are thioacetal-like with the carbon between the two sulfurs bearing the attachment point. The two rings are not fused; they are connected by an ethylene bridge, so the scaffold is a bis(dithiane) with no aromatic or unsaturated centers. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two ring systems are conformationally flexible, able to adopt different chair-like arrangements and rotate about the linking bonds, which gives the molecule an overall lack of rigid symmetry.

The molecule is a 1,2-diketone in which two furan rings are each attached directly to one carbonyl carbon, so the central two-carbon unit is a vicinal dicarbonyl bridging the two heteroaromatic rings. Each furan is a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, and both are unsubstituted at the remaining positions, giving a simple, symmetric scaffold with a two-fold axis passing through the midpoint of the C–C bond between the carbonyls. The structure is fairly rigid around the aromatic rings, while rotation about the bonds linking the carbonyls to the furans allows some conformational flexibility. The ring oxygens and the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a furil dioxime: a central two-carbon backbone in which each carbon is double-bonded to a nitrogen bearing a hydroxyl group, so each carbon carries an oxime (C=N–OH) unit. Each of these carbons is also bonded to a furan ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom and attached through its C2 position, so the two furan rings are substituted at equivalent positions. The overall framework is essentially planar and conjugated, with rigidity contributed by the C=N double bonds and the aromatic rings, though rotation about the central C–C single bond remains possible. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the central bond, and the two hydroxyl groups and the ring oxygens provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

This molecule is a two-carbon ketone-alcohol skeleton bearing two furan rings. A carbonyl carbon is bonded directly to one furan ring at the 2-position, and the adjacent carbon carries a hydroxyl group and is also attached to a second furan ring at its 2-position, so the two furans sit on opposite sides of the central C(=O)–CH(OH) unit. Each furan is an aromatic five-membered oxygen heterocycle with no ring fusion and no further substitution beyond these linkages. The molecule is not symmetric, because the ketone and the secondary alcohol occupy different positions, yet the two furan rings are chemically similar. The aryl ketone carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl group can both accept hydrogen bonds, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can donate one, and the furan oxygens can accept weaker hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a bis-phenol built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold. Each ring carries a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a chlorine atom on the carbon para to that hydroxyl, so the two halves are near-identical substitution patterns, with the bridge attached ortho to each phenolic OH. The molecule is therefore approximately symmetric about the central CH2 carbon, though the two halves are arranged in a mirror-related rather than identical orientation. The two aromatic rings are not fused, and the CH2 linker gives moderate conformational flexibility around its two bonds. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is a 1,2-diketone bridging two thiophene rings: a central two-carbon unit with adjacent carbonyl groups, each carbonyl bonded directly to the 2-position of an aromatic five-membered sulfur heterocycle. Each thiophene ring is unsubstituted apart from that single attachment point, giving a simple, symmetric, roughly planar arrangement that is conjugated through the diketone linker. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The sulfur atoms in the rings contribute only weak acceptor character. The bond between the two carbonyl carbons and the bonds to the rings allow some rotation, so the scaffold is moderately flexible.

The molecule is a small, achiral, acyclic structure built around a central thioether sulfur atom flanked by two methylene groups. Each arm terminates in a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2), so the scaffold is essentially a two-carbon-unit chain bridged by sulfur, with no ring systems or ring fusion. The molecule is symmetric about the central sulfur, with both halves identical. Its single-bond framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility. Each amide group can both donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H groups and accept them at its carbonyl oxygen, while the thioether sulfur is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, flexible compound built from a linear chain of two carbon-carbon units joined by a central thioether sulfur atom. Each end of the chain carries a terminal primary hydroxyl group, so the skeleton is symmetric, with the sulfur sitting at the midpoint. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers. Because the carbon-sulfur and carbon-carbon bonds rotate freely, the molecule is highly conformationally flexible. Both hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the sulfur can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between their ring carbons. The first ring carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the bond to the second ring, so the link sits ortho to that halogen. The second ring bears chlorine atoms on the carbons flanking the nitrogen and at the position next to the linkage, giving three chloro substituents in total and a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. Each pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic rings are planar and rigid, and the steric bulk of the adjacent chlorines restricts free rotation about the central bond.

The molecule is a 3H-benz[e]indole-type scaffold, built from a benzene ring fused to a naphthalene-like bicyclic system that is in turn fused to a five-membered ring containing a carbon-nitrogen double bond. The five-membered ring carries a methyl group on the imine carbon and a gem-dimethyl group on the sp3 carbon adjacent to the fused aromatic system, which gives the structure a bulky, non-planar substitution pattern at one edge. The fused aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, while the gem-dimethyl groups add steric bulk without introducing significant conformational flexibility. The imine nitrogen is the only heteroatom and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of its substituents on the fused rings.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring, forming an indole-type framework. The five-membered ring contains a carbon-nitrogen double bond (an imine, C=N), with the nitrogen bonded directly to the fused aromatic ring. The carbon at position 3 carries two methyl groups, making it a quaternary sp3 center, while a third methyl group sits on the imine carbon at position 2. The benzo portion is unsubstituted, so the aromatic ring has no additional substituents. Because the fused system is rigid and the gem-dimethyl group creates a non-planar bulk on one side, the molecule has limited conformational flexibility and no overall symmetry. The imine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Five of the six ring carbons carry fluorine atoms, leaving one position occupied by a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group), so the substitution pattern is pentafluoro with one alkoxy substituent on adjacent positions. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group adds a small degree of rotational flexibility around its C–O bonds. The molecule has no symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the methoxy group and the opposite ring carbon, since the fluorines are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five fluorine atoms and one carboxamide group, so it is a pentafluorobenzamide: a single aromatic six-membered ring with every ring carbon except the one carrying the amide substituted. The carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) is attached directly to the ring and supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the NH2 protons) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The five fluorines occupy all remaining positions around the ring, giving a fully substituted, highly electron-poor aromatic system. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only rotatable bond is the one linking the amide to the ring, so flexibility is limited. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry about the amide carbon, though the fluorines around the ring are arranged in a pattern that makes the ring itself quite uniform.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with every ring position except the one bearing the boronic acid group occupied by a fluorine atom, making it a pentafluorophenyl scaffold. The boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, so the substituent is a B(OH)2 unit attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The five fluorines sit on adjacent ring carbons, which gives the ring a strongly electron-poor character and a substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond a single mirror line running through the boron-bearing carbon and the opposite carbon. The ring is planar and rigid, while the B(OH)2 group can rotate about the carbon-boron bond. The two hydroxyl oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond donors through their hydrogens and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs, and the fluorine atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type ketone: a central carbonyl carbon bridges an unsubstituted phenyl ring and a pentafluorophenyl ring. Both aromatic rings are planar six-membered carbon rings with no ring fusion, and the single ketone group is the only polar functional group present. The pentafluorinated ring carries five fluorine substituents at every position except the one attached to the carbonyl, so the substitution pattern is highly uniform and electron-poor. The two rings are joined through a rotatable C–C single bond to the carbonyl, giving the framework moderate flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that makes both halves identical. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five fluorine atoms and one hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH), giving a fully fluorinated aromatic core with a single substituent. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, and all ring positions except the one carrying the CH2OH group are occupied by fluorine atoms. Because the hydroxymethyl group is the only non-fluorine substituent, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and side chain. The primary alcohol contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and one acceptor (the oxygen), while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The CH2 linker gives the hydroxyl group a degree of rotational freedom relative to the ring.

The molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, consisting of two six-membered aromatic rings joined by a single C–C bond. One ring is a fully substituted benzene bearing four fluorine atoms, arranged at the 2, 3, 4, and 5 positions relative to the linkage, while the other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. Each ring is planar and aromatic, and the two rings are not fused, so they can rotate about the central bond, giving the overall framework moderate rigidity. The four fluorines are electron-withdrawing but are not hydrogen-bond donors, and fluorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its only symmetry is the local two-fold axis through the biaryl bond in the unsubstituted ring, with the fluorinated ring having no internal symmetry.

This molecule is an acrylic acid derivative: a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group, with the terminal alkene carbon attached directly to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is fully fluorinated, carrying five fluorine atoms on the five remaining positions, so the substitution pattern is uniform and the ring is a single unfused six-membered system. The carbon-carbon double bond linking the acid and the ring is conjugated with the aromatic system, which makes the framework fairly planar and rigid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local pseudo-symmetry of the pentafluorophenyl ring.

This molecule is an aryloxyacetic acid built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. The ring is fully substituted: five of its six positions carry fluorine atoms, and the sixth bears an ether oxygen linking to a two-carbon chain. That chain ends in a carboxylic acid group, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the ether oxygen and the fluorines act as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the oxymethylene-carboxyl side chain provides rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the single ether substituent breaks the symmetry of the pentafluorinated ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries five fluorine atoms, one on each of five consecutive ring carbons, with the sixth ring carbon bearing a two-atom side chain. That side chain is a methylene group linked to a carboxylic acid, so the molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative with a fully fluorinated aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with no additional rings attached. The substitution pattern is pentasubstituted at the ring positions adjacent to the side chain and the fluorines, leaving no ring hydrogens. The molecule is largely planar and rigid in its aromatic portion, while the CH2 linker provides some rotational flexibility to the carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the fluorine atoms can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Five of the six ring positions carry fluorine atoms, and the sixth carries a methyl group, so the substitution pattern is fully substituted on every carbon of the ring. Because the methyl group sits at one position and the fluorines occupy all the others, the molecule has only approximate mirror symmetry through the methyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl group is the only freely rotating part. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O-H or N-H groups. Its fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ring's pi electron system offers limited additional acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Five of its six ring positions carry methyl groups, leaving one ring carbon bearing an acetyl group, so the substitution pattern is fully crowded around that single position. The acetyl unit is a ketone, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group and to the ring. Because the ring is nearly fully substituted, the molecule has little internal symmetry beyond the ring itself, and the bulky neighbouring methyl groups restrict rotation about the bond joining the acetyl group to the ring. The structure has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries five methyl groups and one benzoyl group, leaving a single unsubstituted-by-alkyl position occupied by the carbonyl link. The aromatic core is a fully substituted benzene ring, with methyl groups filling every adjacent position except the one bearing the ketone. The ketone carbon bridges this ring to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving a diaryl ketone scaffold with no additional ring fusion. The two rings are connected through a single sp2 carbonyl carbon, so the molecule has moderate rotational flexibility around the two C–C bonds flanking the ketone. The only polar functional group is the carbonyl oxygen, which can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Five of the six ring positions carry methyl groups, and the remaining position bears a hydroxymethyl group, giving a pentamethyl-substituted benzene scaffold. The substitution pattern is highly crowded and non-symmetrical, since the hydroxymethyl group occupies a single position while the methyl groups surround it on both sides. The ring itself is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl arm adds a small degree of rotational freedom around its single bonds. The primary alcohol group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen, whereas the aromatic hydrocarbon core contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, fully substituted with six groups: five methyl groups and one chloromethyl group, so it has no remaining aromatic hydrogens on the ring. The ring is planar and rigid, and there are no fused ring systems. The chloromethyl substituent (–CH2Cl) is the only functional group and is a primary alkyl halide, while the methyl groups are simple alkyl substituents.
