The substitution pattern is sterically crowded, with the methyl groups flanking the chloromethyl carbon, and the overall framework has only limited symmetry because the chloromethyl group breaks the symmetry of the otherwise methylated ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor sites are the weakly polar carbon–chlorine bond, so its hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single carboxamide group, with four fluorine atoms attached to the remaining four ring positions. The carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) is a primary amide, contributing both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its two N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional ring systems. The fluorine atoms occupy adjacent positions on one side of the ring, creating a dense, electron-withdrawing substitution pattern with no internal symmetry, since the carboxamide sits at only one position. The overall scaffold is rigid and planar, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the amide to the ring.

This molecule is a boronic acid built on a single benzene ring, with the boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic ring is fully substituted: one position carries the B(OH)2 group, and the other five positions are occupied by fluorine atoms arranged in a contiguous block of four fluorines plus one unsubstituted-by-F ring carbon, giving a tetrafluorophenyl scaffold. The ring is rigid and planar, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its carbon-boron bond. Substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement of the fluorines. The two boron-bound hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single carboxylic acid group, with four fluorine atoms attached to the remaining four ring positions. The aromatic core is a flat, fully unsaturated six-membered ring, which makes the scaffold rigid, and the only rotatable bond is the one joining the carboxyl group to the ring. The fluorines occupy the adjacent positions around the ring, leaving one unsubstituted carbon-hydrogen position, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and no meaningful molecular symmetry is present. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the carbon-fluorine bonds contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle built from a benzene ring fused to a seven-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms. The benzene ring is ortho-fused to the diazepine ring, so the two rings share a single edge of two adjacent carbons. The seven-membered ring is partially saturated: one nitrogen sits in a secondary amine that is benzylic, and the other is an aniline-type nitrogen attached directly to the aromatic ring. Both nitrogens bear a hydrogen, so each can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and each lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond. The unsubstituted aromatic ring and the absence of any other substituents give the structure no stereocenters and a relatively flexible, puckered seven-membered ring.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrrole ring containing one nitrogen atom that carries a hydrogen. The ring is fully substituted, with methyl groups attached at all four carbon positions, so there are no unsubstituted ring hydrogens apart from the N–H. The substitution pattern is therefore symmetric about the axis running through the nitrogen and the opposite carbon, though the methyl groups themselves are not all identical in position. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with the only rotational freedom coming from the four methyl groups. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pair, being part of the aromatic system, is a poor hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four fluorine atoms and a boronic acid group, giving it a single aromatic six-membered carbocyclic scaffold with no additional fused rings. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and the four fluorines occupy the remaining positions, with the substitution pattern placing three adjacent fluorines flanking one side of the boron-bearing carbon and a single fluorine on the opposite side. Because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond the trivial identity. The planar aromatic core is rigid, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its carbon-boron bond. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a pyranose sugar ring, a six-membered oxygen-containing saturated ring, bearing four substituents. The anomeric carbon, adjacent to the ring oxygen, carries a free hydroxyl group, making it a hemiacetal. The remaining three ring hydroxyls are each converted to benzyl ethers, and the exocyclic primary carbon is likewise linked to a benzyl ether through an oxygen-CH2 bridge. Three phenyl rings are present as flexible, freely rotating appendages on the otherwise rigid, chair-like core. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor (the free anomeric hydroxyl) and several oxygen acceptors from the ring and ether linkages.

The molecule is built on a six-membered saturated oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyran ring, which serves as the central scaffold. A hemiacetal carbon at one position of the ring carries a free hydroxyl group, making it the anomeric center, and the remaining ring carbons each bear a benzyloxy substituent, with a fourth benzyloxy-methyl arm attached at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. Four phenyl rings are present as pendant, unfused aromatic groups linked through ether oxygens and methylene spacers. The stereocenters make the scaffold rigid, while the benzyl arms add conformational flexibility. The free anomeric hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring and ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle built on a thiophene scaffold, which is a single sulfur atom within a planar ring of four carbons. It carries three bromine substituents, one on each of the carbons flanking the sulfur (positions 2 and 5) and one on the adjacent carbon at position 3, so the substitution is asymmetric and leaves only a single ring hydrogen at position 4. The ring is fully unsaturated and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the bromine atoms are electron-withdrawing halogens that do not provide hydrogen-bond donors. The sulfur and the aromatic pi system offer only weak acceptor character, so the molecule has essentially no hydrogen-bond donor capability and only minimal acceptor capability.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a ketone group, with a chloromethyl unit attached to the carbonyl carbon, forming an aryl chloromethyl ketone. The aromatic ring is substituted at the position para to the ketone by one chlorine atom and at the adjacent meta position by a second chlorine, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom around the bond joining the carbonyl to the ring, so it is fairly rigid overall. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying an acetyl group, which is a ketone in which a methyl group is bonded to a carbonyl carbon attached directly to the aromatic ring. Three chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at adjacent positions, so they cluster together on one side of the aromatic core while the remaining two ring positions are bare hydrogens. The molecule is a single fused-free aromatic ring with no additional rings, making its scaffold rigid and planar, with only the acetyl methyl group capable of meaningful rotation. Its symmetry is low, since the trichloro substitution pattern is asymmetric about the acetyl group. The carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with three chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The sulfonyl chloride, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine, sits at one position on the aromatic ring and serves as the principal functional group. The three chlorines occupy adjacent positions on the ring, creating a contiguous halogenated region that makes the substitution pattern asymmetric. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the sulfonyl group able to rotate about its bond to the ring. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an aryl isothiocyanate built on a single benzene ring. The isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and three chlorine atoms occupy the adjacent ring positions, giving a contiguous trichloro substitution pattern on one side of the ring. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused ring systems, and the chlorine and isothiocyanate substituents lie in the same plane. The only rotatable bond of note is the one joining the nitrogen to the ring, so the molecule is quite rigid overall. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur, nitrogen, and chlorine atoms offer weak acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) at one position and three fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 2,3,4-trifluorobenzamide scaffold. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the fluorines occupy one contiguous edge of the ring while the amide sits on the opposite side, creating a strongly asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful internal symmetry. Apart from rotation of the amide group about its bond to the ring, the structure is rigid. The amide provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites on its nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site on its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms contribute weak acceptor character.

This molecule is an arylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring, with a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to one ring carbon. The ring carries three fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, positioned at the carbons next to and across from the boron-bearing carbon, giving a contiguous trifluoro substitution pattern on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its carbon-boron bond. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group on one carbon and three fluorine atoms on three adjacent carbons, creating a 2,3,4-trifluorobenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no fused ring systems, and the fluorines occupy a contiguous substitution pattern that makes the molecule asymmetric. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only rotation about the bond joining the carboxyl group to the ring.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing one hydroxyl group and three fluorine atoms as substituents. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, and the three fluorines occupy three adjacent positions on the ring, with two of them flanking the hydroxyl-bearing carbon's neighbor and the remaining position left as an unsubstituted aromatic C-H. Because the substituents are clustered on one side of the ring, the overall structure lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry and is therefore asymmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxyl group can rotate about its C-O bond. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O-H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Three adjacent hydroxyl groups sit on consecutive ring carbons, forming a contiguous catechol-like triol arrangement, while a ketone-bearing acetyl group (a methyl ketone) occupies the position opposite that cluster. The hydroxyl groups can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group has limited rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one aldehyde group and three hydroxyl groups, making it a trihydroxybenzaldehyde with a fully substituted aromatic core. The aldehyde carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the three phenolic hydroxyls occupy adjacent positions (two contiguous hydroxyls flanked by a third), which creates a crowded, contiguous substitution pattern with no hydrogen atoms on two of the three ring-bearing hydroxyl-adjacent carbons. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, since the aromatic ring and the directly attached carbonyl carbon lie in one plane, with the hydroxyls able to rotate only slightly. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the planar framework, because the three hydroxyls are not equivalent to one another. Its three phenolic hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aldehyde oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges an unsubstituted phenyl ring and a second benzene ring bearing three adjacent hydroxyl groups on positions 2, 3, and 4 relative to the carbonyl attachment, forming a 2,3,4-trihydroxy substitution pattern. The two aromatic rings are connected through a single sp2 carbonyl carbon, giving the molecule a non-planar but largely conjugated framework with limited conformational flexibility around the ring-carbonyl bonds. The phenyl ring carries no substituents and has local symmetry, while the trihydroxylated ring is asymmetric. The three adjacent phenolic groups make the molecule a strong hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen together with the hydroxyl oxygens serves as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring, and a formyl group (–CHO) is also present, so the aldehyde carbonyl is the main polar functional group. The substitution pattern is contiguous on one side: two methoxy groups sit adjacent to each other, and the aldehyde occupies the position next to one of them, leaving the remaining ring carbons bearing hydrogens. The overall arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, and the aromatic core is rigid while the three methoxy groups add some conformational freedom. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy and carbonyl groups can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups and one boronic acid group, giving a 2,3,4-trimethoxyphenylboronic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the framework is planar and fairly rigid, though the methoxy and boronic acid groups can rotate about their bonds. The three adjacent methoxy substituents sit on consecutive ring carbons, and the boronic acid occupies a position flanked by one of them, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The boronic acid group contributes two hydroxyl hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the boronic acid can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and three methoxy (ether) substituents, arranged on adjacent and nearby carbons of the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and it sits ortho to one methoxy group, with the remaining two methoxy groups placed at the 2,3 and 4 positions relative to the acid, giving a crowded, contiguous substitution pattern on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with no additional rings. The structure is largely planar and conformationally restricted by the ring, though the methoxy and carboxyl groups can rotate about their bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the three ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: three methoxy groups and one nitrile group. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene with no additional rings. The nitrile (C≡N) is attached directly to the ring, and the three methoxy (–OCH3) groups occupy adjacent and nearby positions, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern without any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy groups can rotate about their ring-oxygen bonds, giving limited conformational flexibility. The oxygen atoms and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated hydrocarbon built on a single continuous carbon chain with branching methyl groups along its length. It contains no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no heteroatoms, so there are no functional groups present. The substitution pattern places methyl branches at several internal carbons, giving the skeleton an irregular, asymmetric arrangement with no meaningful internal symmetry. Because every bond is a single sigma bond about which rotation is essentially free, the framework is highly flexible rather than rigid. Having only carbon and hydrogen, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyran (pyranose-type) ring containing one ring oxygen and five sp3 carbons with defined stereochemistry. Three of the ring carbons carry benzyloxy substituents, each consisting of an ether oxygen bonded to a CH2 linker that is attached to a phenyl ring, while the anomeric carbon bears a free hydroxyl group. The substitution pattern places the hydroxyl at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, with the three benzyl ethers distributed on the remaining carbons, creating a non-symmetric arrangement. The ring adopts a chair-like conformation that is fairly rigid, though the three benzyl arms add considerable conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group is the only hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring oxygen and the four ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a tribenzylated pyranose: a six-membered saturated oxane (tetrahydropyran) ring carrying one free hemiacetal hydroxyl at the anomeric carbon next to the ring oxygen, and three benzyl ether groups on the remaining carbons. Each benzyl ether consists of an oxygen bridging to a CH2 linked to a monosubstituted phenyl ring, so the aromatic rings are unfused and attached only through flexible ether linkages. The ring carbons are all stereodefined, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the hydroxyl and the three benzyl ethers occupy different positions around the ring. The ring is conformationally flexible, while the bulky benzyl groups add considerable rotational freedom. The free hydroxyl is the only hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring oxygen plus the four ether and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing four chlorine substituents at the 2, 3, 5, and 6 positions. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings or additional functional groups beyond the carbon-chlorine bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the single unsubstituted carbon sits at the 4 position, flanked by two chlorines, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the nitrogen-carbon axis. Its rigid planar framework allows essentially no conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one amino group and four fluorine atoms, giving a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The amino group sits on one carbon, and the four fluorines occupy the remaining positions, with two adjacent fluorines flanking the amine on one side and two more on the other, leaving a single unsubstituted aromatic C–H position. The fluorine atoms are strongly electron-withdrawing, which makes the ring electron-poor, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, and the only rotatable bond is the C–N bond to the amine. The primary amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to one carbon. Four fluorine atoms occupy the remaining ring positions, with two adjacent fluorines flanking the boron-bearing carbon, and the substitution pattern places fluorines on the ring carbons adjacent to one another in pairs. The ring is aromatic and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry, while the B(OH)2 group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that passes through every atom, because the fluorine placement is asymmetric relative to the boron substituent. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four fluorine atoms and one nitrile group, so it is a tetrafluorobenzonitrile-type scaffold with no fused rings. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the aromatic ring and carries a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond, which makes it a strong electron-withdrawing group. The four fluorine substituents occupy four of the six ring positions, leaving one ring carbon bearing a hydrogen, and the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. The aromatic ring and the nitrile are rigid and planar, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH substituent) and four fluorine atoms on the remaining ring carbons. The fluorines are arranged so that two adjacent pairs flank the ring, leaving a single unsubstituted aromatic C–H position, which gives the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is a single fused-free aromatic ring, so it is planar and rigid, while the CH2–OH arm adds a small degree of rotational flexibility around the bond to the ring. The primary alcohol provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and one acceptor (the oxygen), whereas the aromatic fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no additional fused rings. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the ring at positions 1 and 4, making it a para-substituted diol, and the remaining four ring positions each carry a fluorine atom. The fluorines occupy the 2, 3, 5, and 6 positions, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the two hydroxyl-bearing carbons. Because the ring is flat and fully conjugated, the scaffold is rigid, with only the hydroxyl hydrogens free to rotate. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group and four fluorine atoms, giving a tetrafluorinated phenol scaffold. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion or saturated rings present. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by fluorine-bearing carbons, while the remaining fluorines occupy the other positions around the ring, leaving a single unsubstituted ring carbon between two fluorinated positions. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic fluorines are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying four fluorine atoms and one hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) attached to a single carbon of the ring. Its scaffold is a simple, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is contiguous: the hydrazinyl group sits next to two adjacent fluorines, with the remaining two fluorines on the opposite side of the ring, leaving one aromatic C–H. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the substituent pattern is unequal around the ring. Apart from the aromatic ring, which is rigid and planar, the hydrazine tail is flexible, rotating about its single bonds. The two nitrogen-bound hydrogens of the hydrazine act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen atoms and the electronegative fluorines can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aromatic ketone built on a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to the ring. The benzene ring is fully substituted with five groups in total: the acetyl group plus four methyl groups, arranged so that the acetyl carbonyl is flanked by two ortho methyl groups, creating a crowded, sterically hindered environment around the ketone. The remaining two ring positions carry hydrogen, one of which sits between two methyl-bearing carbons and one of which is adjacent to a single methyl. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis of note, so its substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group has some rotational freedom about the ring-carbonyl bond, though steric crowding from the flanking methyls restricts it. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four methyl groups and one sulfonyl chloride group, which together form a fully substituted aromatic core. The methyl groups occupy positions that cluster on one side of the ring, leaving only one aromatic hydrogen, so the substitution pattern is highly congested and asymmetric. The sulfonyl chloride, SO2Cl, is the key functional group: its sulfur is tetrahedral with two oxygen atoms double-bonded to it, and the attached chlorine makes this group strongly electrophilic. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the sulfonyl group offering a small degree of rotational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring with no ring fusion, carrying five substituents in total: four methyl groups and one hydroxymethyl group. The benzene core is fully substituted apart from one aromatic C-H position, giving a densely crowded pattern in which the hydroxymethyl group sits between two methyl groups and is flanked on the other side by a methyl. The ring itself is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl group contributes a single rotatable C-C bond and some conformational freedom. The primary alcohol supplies one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor through its oxygen atom, and no other heteroatoms are present. The substitution pattern is not symmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry element beyond the trivial one.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents, so it is a pentasubstituted aromatic compound with a single unsubstituted-position-free arrangement: methyl groups occupy four of the ring carbons and one ring carbon carries a chloromethyl group. The aromatic ring is fully conjugated and planar, with no fused rings. Going around the ring, the methyl groups sit at adjacent and alternating positions, and the chloromethyl group is flanked by two methyl groups, giving the molecule a partial, but not full, mirror plane through the ring. The only ring hydrogen sits at the position between two methyl-bearing carbons. The molecule is rigid at the ring core, with some rotational freedom in the chloromethyl arm. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is the chlorine in the side chain, which is a weak acceptor.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyrazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms placed para to each other across the ring. Four methyl groups are attached to the carbon atoms of this ring, occupying every carbon position, so the scaffold is fully substituted with no free ring hydrogens. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and it is rigid, with the methyl groups adding little conformational flexibility. The molecule has a high degree of symmetry, with the two nitrogens and the four methyl groups arranged so that a two-fold axis and mirror planes pass through the ring. The two ring nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. Three bromine atoms are attached directly to the ring carbons, occupying the 2, 3, and 5 positions, which leaves only one ring carbon bearing a hydrogen at position 4. The ring is planar and rigid, and the bromine substituents are the only groups present, so there is no conformational flexibility. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the three bromines sit at non-equivalent positions around the ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds apart from the ring sulfur, which is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, written as B(OH)2, attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic core. Three chlorine atoms are placed on the ring, with two of them flanking the boron-bearing carbon in the ortho positions and the third sitting meta to it on the far side, giving a 2,3,5-trichloro substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the chlorines are not arranged in a mirror-related pattern around the ring. The boronic acid group contributes two hydroxyl oxygens that can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the chlorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom in the ring, which is a thiophene scaffold. Three chlorine atoms are attached directly to ring carbons, occupying three of the four available positions, with the single remaining ring carbon bearing a hydrogen. Because the ring is fully aromatic and fused to nothing, the structure is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The only substituents are halogens, so there are no functional groups capable of donating hydrogen bonds, and the sulfur and chlorine atoms offer only weak acceptor character. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the planar framework.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a carboxylic acid group on one ring carbon and fluorine atoms on three of the remaining carbons. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and it carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The ring itself has no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the carboxyl C–O bond available for rotation. Fluorine substitution occurs at positions adjacent to the nitrogen and at two carbons next to the carboxylic acid, producing an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The pyridine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule two acceptor sites in total beyond the carboxyl oxygens.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and three iodine atoms, making it a triiodobenzoic acid. The six-membered aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no ring fusion. The carboxyl group (-COOH) sits on one ring carbon, and the three iodines occupy the positions at the ring carbon adjacent to the acid and at two positions meta to it on the opposite side, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern. Because the ring is rigid and the substituents are directly attached, the scaffold is conformationally restricted apart from rotation of the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the iodine atoms are weak halogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a tetrasubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. Three of the ring positions carry methyl groups, and the remaining one carries a hydroxyl group, so the phenol unit is flanked by a methyl on one side and a methyl-substituted carbon on the other. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror plane or rotational symmetry that would make the ring positions equivalent. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add minor local steric bulk and the hydroxyl oxygen can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The molecule therefore has one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor, both located at the phenolic oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH₂) on one carbon, with three fluorine atoms attached to the remaining ring positions. The fluorines sit at the positions ortho to the amide (adjacent carbon), and at two other ring positions, giving a 2,3,6-trisubstituted pattern relative to the carboxamide. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the three fluorines are not arranged equivalently around the ring. The amide group offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH₂) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to the aromatic carbon, with three fluorine atoms on the remaining ring positions. The fluorines occupy the two positions adjacent to the carboxylic acid-bearing carbon and one position para to it, creating a 2,3,6-trifluoro substitution pattern on the benzoic acid scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the carboxylic acid group is conjugated with it, which makes the overall framework rigid with only limited rotational freedom about the C–C bond linking the acid to the ring. The carboxyl group contains a hydroxyl that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and a carbonyl oxygen that can act as an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion, bearing one hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH substituent attached to the ring) and three fluorine atoms. The fluorines occupy three adjacent-to-each-other positions on one side of the ring, with two of them flanking the hydroxymethyl-bearing carbon, while the remaining two ring positions carry hydrogen atoms, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful molecular symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2OH group provides a single rotatable bond that adds limited conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic fluorines serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused or additional rings. It carries one hydroxyl group on one ring carbon, and the remaining positions are substituted with three fluorine atoms, two of which sit directly beside the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern on one side and a single fluorine opposite on the para position. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only conformational freedom lies in the rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, since the substituent arrangement is not symmetric about the hydroxyl carbon. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and carries a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the ring. Three fluorine atoms sit on the ring, two flanking the nitrogen at positions adjacent to it and one on the carbon beside the carboxylic acid, leaving a single ring carbon bearing hydrogen. The ring is flat and fully aromatic, so the scaffold is rigid, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the two oxygens), and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor, though its basicity is reduced by the electron-withdrawing fluorines. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituents are placed unevenly around the ring.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a benzene ring ortho-fused to a pyrazine ring, forming a quinoxaline scaffold. The pyrazine ring contains two nitrogen atoms positioned para to each other across the fused bond region, making the core fully aromatic and planar. Three methyl groups are attached as substituents, one on the benzenoid ring and two on the pyrazine ring at adjacent carbons. Because the scaffold is flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core, its overall shape is essentially two-dimensional apart from the methyl group rotations. The two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two trifluoromethyl groups. One CF3 group sits on the carbon at the 3-position and the other on the carbon at the 2-position, directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substituents are ortho to each other and flank the nitrogen on one side. The ring itself is planar and rigid, with no fused rings or additional functional groups. The two bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing CF3 groups create steric crowding around the nitrogen and make the aromatic system electron-poor. The molecule has no rotational flexibility in its core and lacks any hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the pyridine nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a four-carbon, straight-chain skeleton with no rings and no ring fusion. Two carbonyl groups sit at the terminal and second positions of the chain: one carbonyl carbon is bonded to a methyl group, and the central pair of carbons each bears a methyl group and a carbonyl, so the two ketone functions are directly adjacent to one another. Because there are no stereocentres, the molecule is achiral and possesses a mirror-symmetric, nearly planar arrangement around the central carbon-carbon bond. It is conformationally flexible about its single bonds, though the adjacent carbonyls favour a planar, extended geometry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no O-H or N-H groups, but its two oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, open-chain compound built on a four-carbon backbone with no rings and no aromatic system. One end carries a methyl ketone (a carbonyl group flanked by a methyl group), and the adjacent carbon is double-bonded to a nitrogen that bears a hydroxyl group, forming an oxime. The two functional groups are conjugated through the central carbon, which gives a relatively planar, rigid arrangement around that unit, while the terminal methyl groups remain free to rotate. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the ketone and oxime ends differ. As hydrogen-bond partners, the oxime hydroxyl acts as both a donor and an acceptor, while the ketone oxygen and the oxime nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge and forming a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. Two primary amino groups are attached to the same ring at adjacent positions, making this a vicinal 2,3-diamino substitution pattern on one side of the fused system. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the long axis of the naphthalene core, and its rigid planar framework allows little conformational flexibility. Each amino group can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept one through its nitrogen lone pair, so the compound offers multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. Two primary amino groups are attached to adjacent carbons, one directly beside the ring nitrogen and the other on the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-substitution pattern. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, so the structure is rigid, with only the two amino groups able to rotate about their carbon-nitrogen bonds. Each amino group contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and both amino nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the two amino substituents occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the ring nitrogen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two amino groups on adjacent carbons, with a methyl group on a third ring carbon. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the core is planar and rigid. The two primary amine groups sit next to each other (ortho), and the methyl group occupies a position adjacent to one of them, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. Each amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the methyl group contributes only nonpolar bulk. The only conformational freedom comes from rotation of the amino and methyl substituents about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain, a butane-1,4-diol skeleton with a bromine atom on each of the two central carbons (C2 and C3). Its two terminal carbons each carry a primary hydroxyl group, so the molecule is a symmetric diol with two identical bromo-substituted stereocenters arranged across the middle of the chain. Because there are no rings or double bonds, the backbone is highly flexible and can adopt many rotational conformations. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the bromine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents on one aromatic core, with no fused rings. Going around the ring, it carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl), a free hydroxyl group adjacent to that methoxy, and an aldehyde (a carbonyl bonded to hydrogen) on the opposite side, with two bromine atoms on the carbons between the aldehyde and the hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is therefore dense and asymmetric, with no mirror or rotational symmetry in the arrangement. The aromatic ring and the aldehyde are planar and conformationally rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the carbonyl and methoxy oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the bromines contribute only weakly to polarity.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Two bromine atoms and one chlorine atom are attached as halogen substituents: the chlorine sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while the two bromines occupy the neighboring carbon adjacent to that nitrogen and the carbon one position further around the ring. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The compact aromatic core is rigid and flat, with the halogens adding no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an aromatic ketone built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) arrangement. A bromoacetyl group, consisting of a carbonyl carbon bonded to a CH2 that carries a bromine atom, is attached to one ring carbon, while a second bromine atom sits directly on the ring at the position two carbons away. There are no fused or additional ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic core. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The benzene ring and carbonyl make the framework largely planar, while the CH2 linker between the carbonyl and the bromine allows some rotational freedom, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two bromines occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a four-carbon chain, with the carboxyl carbon at one end and a methyl group at the other. Two bromine atoms sit on adjacent carbons near the carboxyl end, one on the second carbon and one on the third, so the substitution pattern is vicinal. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), which gives it strong hydrogen-bonding capacity. The molecule has no ring systems and no internal symmetry, since the two bromine-bearing carbons carry different substituents. Its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility around the central carbon-carbon bonds.

The molecule is a three-carbon acyclic chain built on a propanamide backbone. The terminal carbon of the chain is a primary amide group, bearing a carbonyl oxygen and an NH2 group. The central carbon, alpha to the carbonyl, carries one bromine atom, and the terminal carbon opposite the amide carries a second bromine, so the two halogens sit on adjacent and terminal positions. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no stereocenter-induced symmetry, making the structure flexible with free rotation about its single bonds. The amide group provides both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its two N-H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional rings. The nitrogen atom sits within the ring, making the scaffold a heteroaromatic system that contributes a weakly basic lone pair as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Two bromine atoms are attached to the carbons directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2- and 3-positions, so the substitution is on the same side of the nitrogen. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining positions carry aromatic C–H bonds. Its planar, rigid aromatic framework has no rotatable bonds, and it has no internal symmetry because the two bromines occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the nitrogen.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon chain (an allyl-type skeleton) with no rings and no fused ring systems. A terminal carbon-carbon double bond is located at one end, and the second carbon of that alkene carries a chlorine atom, so the sp2 carbon bears a vinyl chloride feature. The third carbon of the chain is a saturated methylene group that also bears a chlorine atom, placing halogens on both ends of the chain. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, since it has no O-H or N-H bonds, and it has no lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms beyond the chlorines, which act only as weak acceptors. The chain is flexible about its single bonds, and the overall structure has no symmetry because the two chlorine atoms sit in non-equivalent positions.

This molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring that is fully unsaturated, with two ketone carbonyl groups sitting opposite one another, making it a para-quinone-type scaffold. Two nitrile groups are attached to adjacent ring carbons, and two chlorine atoms occupy the remaining two positions on the ring, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, and the nitrile and carbonyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing. Because the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two carbonyl oxygens and the two nitrogen atoms of the nitrile groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with three halogen substituents arranged around the ring. Reading the SMILES, the carboxylic acid (-COOH) sits on one ring carbon, a fluorine atom occupies the adjacent position, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon next to the acid on the other side, with a further chlorine at the para position relative to the fluorine. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid framework with no ring fusion or additional rings. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the substituents are distributed unevenly around the ring. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with one amino group and two chlorine atoms attached to adjacent and neighboring carbons around the ring. Specifically, the amino group sits on one ring carbon, a chlorine occupies the carbon meta to it, and a second chlorine sits on the carbon directly beside the amino-bearing carbon, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. There is no ring fusion, and the aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the substituents lying in the ring plane and offering little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the planar framework, because the three substituents are distinct in position. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acceptor site, while the chlorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) on one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons next to it, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it contains no N–H or O–H groups. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy methyl group providing conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the ring's local pattern.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen) on one ring carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, with the chlorines placed ortho to each other and the aldehyde sitting next to one of them. This 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern leaves three hydrogens on the remaining ring carbons, so the ring has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a local plane through the molecule. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the only hydrogen attached to a heteroatom is absent.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, one of which sits directly beside the amide-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is 2,3-dichloro relative to the amide. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with no additional rings, giving a compact, essentially planar scaffold. Because the two chlorines occupy adjacent positions on one side, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a local planar arrangement. The aryl–carboxamide bond allows some rotation, so the molecule is only moderately flexible. The amide group offers two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, written as B(OH)2, on one carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the adjacent carbons next to it, one at the ortho position and one at the meta position relative to the boron-bearing carbon, which places both halogens on the same side of the ring. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the two chlorines are in different positions. The boronic acid's two hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and their oxygens as acceptors, while the chlorines contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a sulfonamide group, with the sulfur atom bonded directly to the ring and carrying two double-bonded oxygens and an NH2 group. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring on adjacent carbons, with one chlorine sitting ortho to the sulfonamide and the other at the meta position relative to it, giving a 2,3-dichloro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and fully unsaturated, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two chlorines are not equivalent. The sulfonamide's tetrahedral sulfur adds some conformational flexibility around the carbon-sulfur and sulfur-nitrogen bonds, while the ring itself stays rigid. The NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 2,3-dichlorobenzenesulfonyl chloride scaffold. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused partners, so the framework is planar and rigid. The sulfonyl group, with its two S=O bonds and one S–Cl bond, is the dominant functional feature, and the chlorines are ring substituents positioned ortho and meta to the sulfonyl attachment. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring. The two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, forming a 2,3-dichlorobenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, so the core is rigid, while the carboxyl group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The two chlorine substituents sit on adjacent positions, with one flanking the carboxylic acid group, which creates steric crowding around that side of the molecule. Overall the structure has no internal symmetry, since the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The carboxylic acid is both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the chlorines contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on one ring carbon, with two chlorine atoms on the two adjacent carbons flanking it, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic system with no additional rings, so the overall framework is rigid and planar. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the chlorines sit at ortho positions relative to each other and the nitrile occupies the central position between them, so the molecule has only a mirror plane through the nitrile carbon and the ring atoms opposite it. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The two chlorine atoms contribute electron-withdrawing character to the ring but offer only weak acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an acyl chloride group, which is a carbonyl carbon bonded to both a double-bonded oxygen and a chlorine atom. Two additional chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at the positions adjacent to one another, next to the acyl chloride carbon, so the substitution pattern is 2,3-dichloro relative to the carbonyl group. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or stereocenters, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The acyl chloride carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it lacks N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group and two chlorine atoms, forming a phenol scaffold with no fused or additional ring systems. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and the two chlorine substituents occupy the adjacent position and the position directly next to it, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern in which the chlorines flank the hydroxyl on one side. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the substituents adding little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a phenoxyacetic acid: a benzene ring bearing an ether-linked CH2–COOH side chain, where the oxygen-bearing carbon is flanked on the ring by two chlorine atoms at adjacent positions, giving a 2,3-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the ether oxygen. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, while the oxyacetic acid tail is flexible, with rotatable bonds between the ring oxygen, methylene, and carboxyl group. The terminal carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the ether oxygen contributes an additional acceptor site. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative: a benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl (–CH2–COOH) group on one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, with one chlorine ortho to the side chain and the other at the neighboring meta position, giving a 2,3-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the acetic acid arm. The benzene ring is aromatic and fully planar, while the single methylene linker allows the carboxylic acid group some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the two chlorines are inequivalent. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two chlorine substituents on adjacent carbons next to the nitrogen. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The chlorine atoms sit at the 2- and 3-positions relative to the ring nitrogen, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond the ring plane. The scaffold is small and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups, is attached at one ring carbon, which is positioned meta to the nitrogen. Two chlorine atoms occupy the two ring positions adjacent to the nitrogen and the carbon bearing the boronic acid, giving a crowded, fully substituted and unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The scaffold is flat and rigid, with only the two B–OH bonds permitting rotation. The boronic acid's two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazine ring across a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving two nitrogen atoms in the six-membered heteroaromatic ring at the 1 and 4 positions. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the carbons of that pyrazine ring, one on each of the two carbons not involved in ring fusion, so the substitution is symmetric about the molecular axis. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, with a sulfonyl chloride group (SO2Cl) attached at one alpha carbon adjacent to the sulfur atom. The remaining two ring carbons carry chlorine substituents on adjacent positions, one at the beta position and one at the other alpha-adjacent carbon, giving a fully substituted pattern of two chlorines and one sulfonyl chloride on the heteroaromatic core. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, while the sulfonyl chloride group offers a small degree of rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the two sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with one methyl group and two chlorine atoms attached in a contiguous cluster of substituents. The two chlorines sit on adjacent carbons, and the methyl group is placed next to one of them, so the three substituents occupy three consecutive positions on the ring and leave the remaining three ring carbons as plain C–H. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion or stereocenters. The arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the substitution pattern look identical from every side, so the molecule is asymmetric overall. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and its only heteroatoms are the two halogens, which act at most as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a nucleoside analog built from a six-membered pyrimidinone ring bearing an amino group, joined through a nitrogen to a saturated five-membered oxolane (tetrahydrofuran) sugar-like ring. The pyrimidine ring carries a ring carbonyl and an exocyclic amine, with the amine located on the carbon opposite the nitrogen that links to the sugar-like ring. The oxolane ring is fully saturated and carries a hydroxymethyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which adds a flexible side chain. The two stereocenters on the oxolane ring fix a defined three-dimensional arrangement, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donors include the amino group and the terminal hydroxyl, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring nitrogens, ring oxygen, and hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms, giving a single aromatic six-membered scaffold with no additional fused rings. The formyl (CHO) group sits at one position, a phenolic OH is para to it, and the two fluorines occupy adjacent positions ortho to each other, with one fluorine also ortho to the hydroxyl. This substitution pattern leaves the ring with no internal symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. Its framework is rigid and planar, with only the aldehyde and hydroxyl bonds allowing limited rotation. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen, the fluorines, and the hydroxyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at one position, with a hydroxyl group and two fluorine atoms as additional substituents on the same ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents occupy adjacent and meta-related positions, giving the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid and the phenolic hydroxyl each contribute a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site, while the two fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The rigid aromatic ring constrains the molecule to a flat framework, with the carboxylic acid group being the most conformationally flexible part.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, carrying a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on one carbon, a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons. The nitrile and hydroxyl groups sit para to each other, with the hydroxyl flanked by one fluorine, and the remaining fluorine sits ortho to the nitrile. This arrangement gives the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the substituents are small and attached directly, so the overall shape is compact and flat. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrile nitrogen and the fluorine atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold, with no fused ring systems. The ring carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bearing a methyl) and a primary amino group, along with two adjacent fluorine substituents, arranged so that the substituents occupy several consecutive positions around the ring. Because the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar framework. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the methoxy group has a modest degree of rotational freedom about its C–O bonds. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, and the ether oxygen and fluorine atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methoxy group, a carboxylic acid, and two adjacent fluorine atoms. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and one fluorine sits ortho to it, with the second fluorine adjacent to that one, forming a vicinal difluoro pattern. The methoxy group is located para to the carboxylic acid, creating an asymmetric substitution arrangement with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxyl and methoxy groups can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the methoxy oxygen and the fluorine atoms serve as additional weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no ring fusion present. Bearing five substituents around the ring, it carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen linked to a methyl), a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), and three fluorine atoms. The fluorines occupy two adjacent positions and the third sits next to the nitrile, giving a densely and asymmetrically substituted pattern with no meaningful molecular symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group contributes only minor conformational flexibility. The nitrile nitrogen and methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on one ring carbon, an aminomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a primary amine) on another, and two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons next to the aminomethyl-bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore crowded and asymmetric, with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aminomethyl groups add some conformational freedom through their single bonds. The primary amine provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, the ether oxygen and the two fluorines act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the rest of the scaffold is largely nonpolar.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings, so its scaffold is a single planar monocyclic arene. Around the ring sit a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and two adjacent fluorine atoms, arranged in a contiguous pattern that leaves two ring positions bearing hydrogen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the methoxy oxygen and the two fluorines serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituents are not distributed evenly, and its rigidity arises from the aromatic ring, with only the methoxy and hydroxyl groups providing limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused or additional ring systems. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on one side by a fluorine atom, while a second fluorine occupies the adjacent position and a methyl group sits on the carbon across the ring from the acid. The pattern of substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The carboxyl group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents, with a single hydrogen remaining on the ring, so it is a fully substituted aromatic core. A methyl group sits on one carbon, a nitrile (cyano, C≡N) group sits on the carbon directly opposite it in a para arrangement, and two fluorine atoms occupy the two adjacent carbons next to the nitrile. The fluorines are ortho and meta to the methyl, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the linear nitrile group extending the framework along its axis. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since its only N–H or O–H sites are absent.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion, carrying a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms as substituents. The hydroxyl group sits on one carbon, with a fluorine on the adjacent carbon and a second fluorine next to it, so the two fluorines are vicinal and flank the phenolic oxygen's neighbor position. The methyl group occupies a position para-related to the hydroxyl on the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl rotors add only limited conformational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzoic acid core, meaning a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to the ring. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fusion to other rings, and it is flat and rigid. Three substituents sit on the ring: the carboxylic acid, a hydroxyl group on the carbon meta to it, and two adjacent fluorine atoms positioned ortho and meta to the acid, creating a 2,3-difluoro arrangement relative to the carboxyl group. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the fluorine atoms can accept them, giving the structure several hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents in a contiguous pattern: a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl), two adjacent fluorine atoms, and an aldehyde (formyl) group. Reading around the ring, the methoxy and aldehyde groups sit on neighboring carbons, with the two fluorines occupying the next two positions, so the substitution is 1,2,3,4-type on a single aromatic core with no fused rings. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the methoxy and fluorine atoms can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy methyl and the aldehyde C–H bond providing limited rotational freedom. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a benzoic acid derivative, with a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) at one position. Adjacent to the carboxylic acid, on the ring, is a methoxy group (OCH3), and the ring also carries two fluorine atoms on the carbons next to one another, positioned meta and para relative to the acid-bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore fully contiguous around the ring, with the methoxy and carboxyl groups flanking one another in an ortho arrangement. The ring is aromatic and planar, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituents are distinct and unevenly placed. The carboxylic acid can donate one hydrogen bond through its OH and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the methoxy oxygen and the two fluorine atoms can serve as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Going around the ring, it carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two adjacent fluorine atoms, and a nitrile group, with the nitrile placed next to the methoxy-bearing carbon, giving a crowded, unsymmetrical 1,2,3,4-substitution pattern. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group adds only modest conformational flexibility. The fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, the ether oxygen is a moderate acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen is a linear acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents on six carbons, leaving one unsubstituted position. Starting from a methoxy group, the ring carries two adjacent fluorine atoms positioned meta and para relative to the methoxy-bearing carbon, and a bromomethyl group on the carbon next to the methoxy group, so the substitution pattern is fully contiguous and lacks any symmetry axis. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ether oxygen and the CH2–Br linkage add limited rotational freedom. The oxygen of the methoxy group can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the fluorines are weak acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and alternating positions: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms, with the two fluorines sitting next to each other on the ring. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is compact and planar. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group and the fluorine atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Rotation is limited to the methoxy and hydroxyl groups, so overall the structure is largely rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) sits on one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group occupies the neighboring carbon, and two fluorine atoms are attached to the next two adjacent carbons. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no additional ring fusion, so the scaffold is a single six-membered carbocycle. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The nitro and hydroxyl groups are directly adjacent, and the hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group and the hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The fluorine atoms contribute only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character. Rotation about the single bonds to the nitro and hydroxyl groups is restricted, so the molecule is fairly rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group on one carbon and two adjacent fluorine atoms on the neighboring carbons, forming a 2,3-difluorobenzamide pattern. The aromatic six-membered ring is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional rings present. The primary amide group (–C(=O)NH2) is the principal functional group, and its carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds while its two N–H groups can donate them. The two fluorine substituents are electron-withdrawing and sit on the ring, adding no hydrogen-bond donor capability but contributing acceptor character.
