The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituents occupy positions that are not mirror-related across the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two fluorine atoms, making it a substituted benzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring carbon, and two adjacent fluorine atoms occupy the neighboring positions, giving a 2,3-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the acid group. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two fluorines are inequivalent to the carboxyl group's placement. The rigid aromatic ring contributes little conformational flexibility, though the carboxyl group can rotate. The acid group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic-type acid built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent fluorine atoms at the meta and ortho positions relative to the side chain. A single carboxylic acid group is attached through a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond, giving an extended, planar conjugated system from the ring to the acid. The benzene ring is aromatic and fused to nothing, and the two fluorine substituents are non-symmetric, so the overall framework has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the conjugated arm. The rigid alkene and aromatic ring restrict conformational freedom, while the carboxylic acid can donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen. The fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aryl-substituted hydroxy acid built on a benzene ring. A two-carbon chain attached to that ring carries a terminal carboxylic acid group and a secondary alcohol on the carbon next to it, giving a 2-hydroxy-2-arylacetic acid skeleton. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered benzene ring with two adjacent fluorine atoms at the positions ortho and meta to the side chain, a 2,3-difluoro substitution pattern that breaks any symmetry through the ring. The molecule has one stereogenic center at the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group, and the side chain is fairly flexible. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and accept hydrogen bonds, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl-type and fluorine substituents, specifically a phenol with fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons. The six-membered aromatic carbocycle is fully planar and unfused, forming a rigid scaffold with no rotatable bonds other than the O-H. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a fluorine occupies the ortho position beside it, with a second fluorine on the adjacent carbon, giving a 2,3-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the oxygen. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are not evenly distributed around the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

This molecule is a small aromatic carboxylic acid built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain. A methylene group links the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the carbonyl and hydroxyl groups sit on a flexible CH2 spacer that lets the acid group rotate relative to the planar aromatic core. The ring carries two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, one of which is ortho to the side chain and the other directly beside it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the side chain provides the molecule's main conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen), while the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused tricyclic aromatic framework: a naphthalene core with an additional saturated five-membered ring fused across its peri positions, so that a CH2 group and a CH2-NH unit bridge two carbons of the naphthalene system. This creates a rigid, nearly planar polycyclic scaffold with two fused aromatic rings and one partly saturated ring. The ring system carries no substituents beyond the ring atoms themselves, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted. It has a secondary amine nitrogen within the saturated ring, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (N–H) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The molecule has no stereocenters and approximates mirror symmetry through its central plane.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a seven-membered heterocycle containing two oxygen atoms. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so it carries no additional functional groups beyond the fused ring system. The heterocyclic portion includes a lactone-type ester: a carbonyl carbon bonded to one ring oxygen and directly attached to the benzene ring, with a second ether oxygen linking through a two-carbon ethylene bridge back to the aromatic ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two ring oxygens can also accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fused architecture is fairly rigid, though the saturated ethylene bridge and the ester linkage introduce some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a benzoxazinone scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing both an oxygen and a nitrogen atom, with the nitrogen acylated by a carbonyl group. The aromatic ring carries a single methyl substituent positioned meta to the ring-fusion point, which breaks any symmetry in the benzene portion. A 2-cyanoethyl chain is attached to the nitrogen, adding a flexible, linear, nitrile-terminated arm. The lactam-like amide and the ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since the nitrogen is fully substituted. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, with the side chain providing the main conformational flexibility.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system built around a five-membered imidazole-type ring that is joined to a saturated thiazoline-type ring through a shared nitrogen and carbon, giving a rigid, nearly planar aromatic core with a short, flexible two-carbon linker. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, providing a monosubstituted benzene group that extends conjugation across the scaffold. An aldehyde group (formyl) sits on the carbon next to the bridgehead nitrogen, making it the principal polar functional group. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the phenyl and aldehyde substituents occupy different positions on the fused core. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the aldehyde oxygen and the pyridine-like ring nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic ether built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered oxygen-containing ring. The benzene ring is ortho-fused to a dihydrofuran, so the two rings share one edge, and the saturated portion contains a two-carbon ethylene bridge that links the benzylic position to the ring oxygen. The oxygen atom is attached directly to the aromatic ring, making this an aryl alkyl ether, and the ring as a whole is largely planar with limited conformational flexibility. The scaffold has no substituents on the benzene ring beyond the fusion, so it shows no meaningful symmetry breaking, and it contains a single oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds while offering no hydrogen-bond donor capability.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons: an aldehyde (formyl) group and two hydroxyl groups. The two hydroxyls sit on neighboring carbons, with the aldehyde on the carbon next to one of them, giving a contiguous three-substituent pattern on the aromatic core. The scaffold is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic ring with no additional ring systems, so the framework is planar and fairly rigid, with only the aldehyde and hydroxyl bonds free to rotate. Symmetry is low because the three substituents are not arranged in an equivalent pattern. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the two phenolic hydroxyls can act as both donors and acceptors, while the carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde serves as an acceptor only.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, and two hydroxyl groups (–OH) sit on adjacent ring carbons, one of which lies directly beside the carboxylic acid, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The substituents are not symmetric about the ring, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups can rotate only slightly. The molecule carries three hydrogen-bond donors (the acid OH and two phenolic OH groups) and four hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), with the ortho-hydroxyl able to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the carboxyl group.

This molecule is built on a flavonol scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. At the 3-position of the pyranone sits a hydroxyl group, and at the 2-position is a phenyl ring that carries a single hydroxyl group at its ortho position. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the 2-aryl bond allows only limited rotation, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility. The three hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing a common edge, with the fusion giving a rigid, planar, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the same ring at adjacent positions, forming a 1,2-diol (catechol-type) arrangement on one half of the fused system, while the other ring carries only hydrogens. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the hydroxyls, because the substitution is confined to one ring. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two adjacent groups can also cooperate in intramolecular or intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The overall structure is largely inflexible, with only the rotation of the O–H bonds available.

The molecule is a substituted benzoquinone built on a six-membered ring containing two carbonyl groups positioned para to each other across the ring, forming a conjugated cyclohexadienedione scaffold. Two methoxy groups sit on adjacent carbons, and a single methyl group occupies a third position on the ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and no mirror or rotational symmetry is present. The ring is planar and conjugated, giving it a rigid framework, while the methoxy and methyl substituents add only limited conformational freedom through rotation about their single bonds. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can also accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all of its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) and two adjacent methoxy groups (OCH3) placed at positions that flank the aldehyde on one side, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid benzene framework. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond an approximate mirror plane through the ring axis that contains the aldehyde and the nearby methoxy group. Its two ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all of its hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two adjacent methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one oxime group (–CH=N–OH) attached through the carbon of an aldehyde-derived C=N bond. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the methoxy groups occupy the positions next to each other, leaving the oxime group on the carbon beside one of them, which gives a crowded 1,2,3-trisubstituted substitution pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three substituents differ in position and character, so the two methoxy groups are not equivalent. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups and the oxime side chain can rotate about their single bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The oxime hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the oxime and the two methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group and two adjacent methoxy substituents. Its scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused or additional ring systems, so it is rigid and planar apart from the rotatable C–O and C–B bonds of its side groups. The substitution pattern places a boronic acid, –B(OH)2, on one ring carbon and two methoxy groups, –OCH3, on the two neighboring carbons, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted arrangement with the boronic acid at one end of the contiguous set. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, since the substituents are not equivalent. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid can donate hydrogen bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the two methoxy ethers can accept them.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no additional fused rings. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, and two methoxy groups (–OCH3) occupy the two adjacent ring positions next to it, one of them flanking the acid on one side. This 2,3-dimethoxy substitution pattern on the aromatic ring makes the arrangement asymmetric, since the acid sits at a different position relative to the two ethers. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and carboxyl groups add some rotational freedom at their single bonds. The carboxylic acid can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl group and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen, and the two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile group (C≡N) and two methoxy groups (O–CH3). The two methoxy groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, and the nitrile occupies the position next to one of them, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with the nitrile at one end of the substitution sequence. The ring itself is a single planar aromatic system with no ring fusion, and the nitrile is linear, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation of the two methoxy groups. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups. It can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the nitrogen of the nitrile and the two ether oxygens.

This molecule is a nitrostyrene derivative built on a benzene ring carrying two adjacent methoxy groups. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with three substituents: two methoxy ether groups on adjacent carbons, and a nitrovinyl side chain at the position next to one of them. The vinyl linker is an E-configured carbon-carbon double bond connecting the ring to a nitro group, which is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group. The molecule has no fused ring systems, so the overall scaffold is planar and conjugated across the ring and side chain, giving limited conformational flexibility. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the oxygen atoms of the two methoxy groups and the nitro group, while it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small, acyclic hydrocarbon built on a branched carbon skeleton with no rings, heteroatoms, or aromatic systems. It contains two carbon-carbon double bonds, each terminal and each bearing a methyl substituent, so the two alkene units are joined directly through a single central bond. The structure is essentially symmetrical about the midpoint of that central bond, and its flexibility comes mainly from rotation around that single bond. Because it has no oxygen, nitrogen, or other electronegative atoms and no N–H or O–H groups, it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor.

The molecule is built on a short, fully acyclic carbon skeleton with no rings, aromatic systems, or heteroatoms. It contains a terminal alkene, where one carbon bears a methyl branch and is double-bonded to a CH2 group, and a neighboring sp3 carbon carries a methyl and a further methyl branch, giving a branched hydrocarbon framework. There are no functional groups beyond the carbon-carbon double bond, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its branched, unsymmetrical substitution pattern gives it no internal symmetry, and it is conformationally flexible because all of its bonds are freely rotatable single bonds except the one double bond.

The molecule is a pyridine N-oxide scaffold: a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom that carries an oxygen substituent, giving a formally charged N-oxide. The ring bears two adjacent methyl groups on the carbons flanking the nitrogen, and a nitro group on the carbon two positions away from the nitrogen on the other side of the ring. The fully aromatic, planar ring is rigid, with the methyl and nitro groups lying in the ring plane. The N-oxide oxygen and the two oxygens of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. It has no internal symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains an N-H group. The pyrrole ring carries two methyl groups on adjacent carbons, at the 2- and 3-positions. On the benzene portion, a nitro group is attached at the 5-position, para to the ring nitrogen's fusion side. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the methyl and nitro substituents lying in the same plane. The indole N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the local arrangement of its substituents.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Going around the ring, it carries a nitro group, an amino group on the carbon directly beside the nitro group, and two methyl groups on adjacent carbons that sit next to the amino group. The substituents are therefore clustered on one side of the ring, leaving the remaining ring positions as unsubstituted carbon-hydrogen sites. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically, the molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits flexibility, although the nitro and methyl groups can rotate slightly. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group can accept them.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, one of them flanked by the amino group on the other side, so the substitution pattern is a 1,2,3-trisubstituted arrangement with the amine at one end of the crowded cluster. The only functional groups are a primary aromatic amine, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and two non-polar alkyl methyl groups. Because the ring is rigid and the methyls and amine are attached directly to it, the molecule has little conformational flexibility and no element of symmetry, since the three substituents are not arranged to be equivalent. It is essentially a small, planar, rigid aromatic scaffold with a single polar site.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents on adjacent positions. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one ring carbon, and two methyl groups occupy the two neighboring carbons, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern in which the methoxy is flanked by the two methyls. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy and methyl groups providing minor rotational freedom. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry along the ring, so the molecule is asymmetric overall.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group and a second methyl group on adjacent carbons, plus a carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) on a carbon next to one of the methyl-bearing positions. This gives a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems, so the core is a single six-membered aromatic ring. The carboxamide contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its two N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen. The two methyl groups are nonpolar and sterically crowd the amide, which constrains rotation about the bond joining the amide to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions around the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, with two methyl substituents on adjacent carbons. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid phenyl core. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached to one ring carbon, and it contains two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that can act as acceptors. The two methyl groups sit on ring carbons next to each other, with the boron-bearing carbon flanked by one methyl, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, and its only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the bond joining boron to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two methyl groups on adjacent carbons, giving a 2,3-dimethylbenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its substitution pattern places the carboxyl group flanked by one ortho methyl group, with the second methyl group adjacent to that one on the opposite side. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the three substituents occupy unequal positions around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and methyl groups can rotate about their single bonds, giving modest conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion. Two adjacent positions carry methyl groups, and the third substituent is a nitrile (cyano) group attached on the ring carbon next to one of those methyls, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar aromatic framework. The ring is rigid and planar, while the two methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a second methyl group, and an acyl chloride group (–C(=O)Cl). The two methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, and the acyl chloride is on the carbon next to one of them, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted. Because the acyl chloride sits between the ring and the lone chlorine, the carbonyl is flanked by an aromatic system and a halogen, making the group highly electrophilic. The structure has no stereocenters and only partial symmetry, since the ring substitution is asymmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the carbonyl-chloride bond can rotate relative to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; the carbonyl oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that contains one nitrogen atom. The nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. Two methyl groups sit on the five-membered ring, one on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen and one on the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-dimethyl substitution pattern. The benzene portion is unsubstituted. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through its long axis.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. Two methyl groups are attached to the same ring at adjacent positions, one on each of the two carbons next to each other on the substituted ring, creating an ortho-dimethyl pattern. The unsubstituted ring remains a plain benzo ring with no heteroatoms or polar functional groups. Because the core is rigid and planar, the molecule has little conformational flexibility, and it has a mirror plane through the long axis of the ring system (approximately, given the asymmetric substitution). It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it has only carbon and hydrogen atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple substituted aromatic compound with no fused or additional rings. Two adjacent positions carry methyl groups, and a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon next to one of them, so the three substituents occupy three contiguous ring positions. This arrangement breaks the ring's symmetry, leaving no mirror plane through the substituted pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add minor conformational freedom through their rotation. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the remaining framework contributes no additional polar sites.

The molecule is an aryloxyacetic acid built on a single benzene ring with no fused or additional ring systems. The ring carries two adjacent methyl groups at positions 2 and 3 relative to the ether oxygen, which sits at position 1, giving a 2,3-disubstituted (ortho-dimethyl) aromatic core. The oxygen connects through a methylene to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the chain contributes both an ether linkage and a carbonyl-bearing acid group. The aromatic portion is planar and rigid, while the -OCH2COOH side chain is comparatively flexible and can rotate about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor site. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local mirror plane of the ring, since the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned para to each other across the ring. Two methyl groups are attached to adjacent carbon atoms, so the substitution pattern is ortho-dimethyl on the ring, creating a 2,3-disubstituted scaffold. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl groups, and it displays a degree of symmetry along the axis through the substituted carbons. The two ring nitrogens each carry a lone pair that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring and methyl hydrogens are bonded to carbon.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazine ring that contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. Both the benzene and pyrazine rings are aromatic and fully planar, making the overall framework rigid. Two methyl groups are attached to adjacent carbons of the pyrazine ring, giving a symmetric 2,3-disubstitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a four-membered cyclobutenone ring, a strained carbocycle containing one carbonyl group conjugated with a carbon-carbon double bond. Two phenyl rings are attached to adjacent sp2 carbons of this core, one on each side of the double bond, so the arrangement is a 1,2-diaryl cyclobutenone. Each benzene ring is unsubstituted and planar, and the overall framework is largely rigid, with limited rotation about the bonds linking the phenyl groups to the four-membered ring. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry axis passing through the carbonyl and the midpoint of the ring double bond. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a 2,3-diphenylpyrazine, built from a central six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at para positions (1,4-diazine). Two phenyl rings are attached to adjacent carbon atoms of the pyrazine core, creating an ortho substitution pattern on the heteroaromatic ring. The pyrazine nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fully aromatic, planar core is rigid, though the two phenyl substituents can rotate about their single bonds to the ring, and steric crowding between neighboring groups tends to twist them out of plane.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazine ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. Two phenyl rings are attached at the two carbon atoms of the pyrazine ring that sit between the nitrogens, giving a 2,3-diphenyl substitution pattern. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, while the two phenyl groups can rotate around their single bonds to the core, introducing some conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry axis through the midpoint of the pyrazine ring. Its two pyrazine nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic 1,2-diketone with no rings, so its skeleton is a flexible, open-chain carbon framework. It contains a propanoyl-type group (a three-carbon chain ending in a ketone) bonded directly to an acetyl group, giving two adjacent carbonyl carbons joined by a single C–C bond. The structure has no aromatic rings and no substitution pattern beyond a linear alkyl tail on one end and a methyl group on the other. There is no meaningful molecular symmetry, and the single bonds allow considerable rotational freedom. Both oxygen atoms are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is a bicyclic furanose-type sugar scaffold: a five-membered oxolane ring fused to a cyclobutane-like ring formed by a gem-dimethyl-bearing carbon, creating a compact, fairly rigid fused framework. The ring system carries two tertiary hydroxyl groups at the ring fusion, one primary hydroxymethyl group on the oxolane ring, and an ether oxygen within the ring. Attached at the anomeric-like carbon is a uracil ring, a pyrimidine-2,4-dione bearing an N-H and two carbonyl groups, linked through a ring nitrogen. Overall, the molecule is chiral with no internal symmetry, and its bulky fused core limits conformational flexibility. It presents multiple hydrogen-bond donors (hydroxyl and N-H groups) and numerous acceptors (oxygens and the uracil carbonyls).

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a fully conjugated heterocycle in which one ring carbon has been replaced by a nitrogen atom. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring carbons that sit directly beside each other, one adjacent to the nitrogen and the other on the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-disubstituted substitution pattern. The scaffold has no fused rings, no stereocenters, and no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl groups, so the framework is rigid and planar. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, but the pyridine nitrogen, with its lone pair lying in the plane of the ring, can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The arrangement has no symmetry beyond the planar mirror plane of the ring, because the two methyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions.

This molecule is a five-membered 1,3-dioxolane ring, saturated and containing two oxygen atoms, with a geminal dimethyl group on one carbon adjacent to an oxygen (an acetonide-type ketal carbon). The remaining two ring carbons each carry a hydroxymethyl substituent, placing them in adjacent positions on the ring, and the molecule has two stereocenters with defined configurations. Its skeleton is therefore a rigid, non-aromatic cyclic acetal framework bearing two primary alcohol groups. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no aromatic rings and only limited conformational flexibility, mainly from rotation of the hydroxymethyl arms.

This molecule is a saturated five-membered cyclic acetal, a 1,3-dioxolane ring bearing two methyl groups on the same carbon, which makes it a 2,2-dimethyl-1,3-dioxolane. The ring carries two hydroxymethyl substituents on adjacent carbons, one on the carbon next to the ring oxygen and one on the neighboring carbon, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern that is stereogenic and chiral. The ring is not fused to any other ring, and its sp3 framework gives it modest conformational flexibility. The two primary hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two ring oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic 1,2-dicarbonyl compound, with a straight carbon chain of five carbons and no rings or fused ring systems. Its backbone consists of an ethyl group attached to one carbonyl carbon, with the adjacent carbonyl bearing a methyl group, so the two ketone groups sit directly next to each other. Both carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it contains no N-H or O-H bonds. The adjacent ketones give the structure a modest, flexible framework with rotatable single bonds, and the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry because the two ends carry different alkyl groups.

This molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a three-carbon, conjugated enone bridge, with a ketone carbonyl adjacent to one ring and a trans carbon-carbon double bond linking to the other. The ring attached to the carbonyl carries a hydroxyl group at the position para to the ketone and another hydroxyl ortho to it, while the second ring bears a single hydroxyl group para to the alkenyl attachment. The bridge is rigid and planar in its conjugated portion, while the rings are free to rotate about single bonds, so the molecule is fairly flat overall with limited flexibility. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two aryl rings carry different substitution patterns. Three phenolic hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a single methoxy group in the para position relative to the carbonyl, giving a simple para-disubstituted pattern. The other ring carries two methoxy groups, one para and one ortho to the carbonyl, so it is trisubstituted and asymmetric. The two aryl rings are not fused, but they are connected through the sp2 carbonyl carbon, which allows some rotational flexibility around the single bonds. The methoxy oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated-apart-from-one-site hydrocarbon built on a branched chain of carbon atoms. It contains a single terminal alkene, where a methylene group is double-bonded to a carbon bearing a methyl substituent, so the double bond sits at one end of the chain. Adjacent to this alkene is a methylene linker, which connects to a quaternary carbon carrying two methyl groups, giving the skeleton a pronounced gem-dimethyl branch. There are no rings, heteroatoms, or other functional groups, so the molecule is flexible and lacks any hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its structure is also asymmetric overall, because the two ends of the chain differ in substitution.

The molecule is an acyclic branched alkene built on a six-carbon chain. Its backbone carries two methyl groups on one carbon and a single methyl group on the other end of a carbon-carbon double bond, with a tert-butyl-like quaternary carbon at the terminus. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the carbon-carbon double bond. The structure is highly branched and sterically crowded around the quaternary center, and its only non-hydrocarbon feature is the alkene itself. Because it contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors and no polar groups, it has no capacity to form hydrogen bonds, and it is conformationally flexible through rotation about its single bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methyl group and three bromine atoms, giving a tribromotoluene framework. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no ring fusion or additional ring systems. The three bromine atoms sit on adjacent and meta-related carbons, leaving two aromatic hydrogens on the ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis or mirror plane. The rigid planar core has only the small rotational freedom of the methyl group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, since it bears no O–H or N–H groups, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one amino group and three chlorine atoms, giving it a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The amino group sits on one carbon, and the three chlorines occupy the remaining positions in a pattern that breaks the ring's symmetry, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar framework. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the substituents attach directly to it without any flexible linkers, so the overall shape is essentially fixed. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds and one acceptor site through its lone pair, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type polar character and are poor hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) on one carbon, with three chlorine atoms attached at the remaining positions. The chlorines occupy the positions that leave the ring asymmetrically substituted, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the plane of the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonamide group contributes some rotational freedom around the carbon–sulfur bond. The sulfonamide nitrogen carries two hydrogens, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with three chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The sulfonyl group, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine, is attached at one ring carbon, and the chlorines occupy the other positions around the aromatic ring, giving a 2,4,5-trichloro substitution pattern relative to the sulfonyl group. The aromatic core is a single rigid, planar six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the molecule has little symmetry because the chlorine positions are unequal. The sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the scaffold is compact and conformationally restricted, with only limited rotational flexibility around the bond linking the sulfur to the ring.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic scaffold. Attached to one carbon is an isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit that is a reactive, electrophilic functional group. Three chlorine atoms occupy the remaining ring positions, giving a trisubstituted pattern with the chlorines clustered on one side of the ring and an open position between the isothiocyanate and a chlorine. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, and its rigid aromatic core combined with the linear isothiocyanate group makes it structurally stiff. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur and nitrogen of the isothiocyanate act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a phenylboronic acid, with a single benzene ring as its central scaffold. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one carbon of the ring, and three fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions that make the substitution pattern asymmetric, with two adjacent fluorines flanking the far side of the ring. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid core, while the boronic acid group can rotate around its single bond to the ring. Each of the two hydroxyl groups on boron can donate a hydrogen bond, and the oxygen atoms and fluorine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, which is the principal functional group, attached to one carbon of the aromatic ring. Three fluorine atoms are placed on the ring at the positions that make up its substitution pattern, so the ring carries four substituents in total, with the carboxyl group flanked by fluorines on one side. The ring itself is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic system with no additional rings, giving a compact, largely planar and rigid scaffold. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The lack of any mirror or rotational symmetry in the substitution pattern means the molecule has no symmetry axis through the ring.

This molecule is a cinnamic acid analogue built on a benzene ring bearing three fluorine atoms, which sit at positions that make the ring substitution pattern asymmetric. The aromatic ring is attached through a carbon-carbon double bond with defined E (trans) geometry to an acrylic acid unit, whose terminal carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The three fluorine substituents are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and contribute strong electron-withdrawing character across the ring. The conjugated, planar arrangement of the ring, alkene, and carboxyl group makes the scaffold fairly rigid, with rotation limited mainly around the single bonds linking these units.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing four substituents. One ring carbon carries a hydroxyl group, making it a phenol, and the remaining positions carry fluorine atoms. The fluorines occupy the positions adjacent to one another on one side of the ring and the third fluorine sits ortho to the hydroxyl group, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydroxyl group can rotate about its carbon-oxygen bond. The hydroxyl oxygen can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds through its lone pairs, whereas the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

This molecule is a phenylacetic acid, built on a single benzene ring with no fused or additional rings. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached through a single methylene (–CH2–) linker to the aromatic ring, so the acid is not directly conjugated to the ring. Three fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions that are not symmetric about the molecule's long axis, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2–COOH arm offers some rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the fluorines can act as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group and three methoxy substituents, making it a substituted benzaldehyde. The six-membered aromatic ring is a single, unfused, planar core with no additional ring systems. The three methoxy (–OCH3) groups sit at positions that give an asymmetric pattern around the ring, while the aldehyde (–CHO) carbonyl is conjugated directly with the aromatic system. Because the ring is aromatic and the substituents are attached by single bonds with only modest flexibility, the overall scaffold is fairly rigid, with some rotational freedom around the methoxy and aldehyde bonds. The carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and three methoxy substituents. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid (–COOH) sits on one ring carbon, and three ether-linked methoxy groups (–OCH3) occupy the remaining positions, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern across the ring. The substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid, while the methoxy and carboxyl groups add modest rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid can donate one hydrogen bond and accept two, and each methoxy oxygen can accept one hydrogen bond.

The molecule is an aromatic ketone built on a single benzene ring, bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to the ring. Three methyl substituents sit on the ring: two adjacent to each other and one positioned ortho to the acetyl group, giving a crowded, contiguous substitution pattern with no fused rings. The ring is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group has limited rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring in its planar conformation, and it lacks any stereocenters. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three methyl groups are attached around the ring at the 1, 3 and 5-type positions relative to the hydroxyl group, giving a crowded, uneven substitution pattern on one side of the ring. The hydroxyl group is the only polar functional group, so it acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only small steric bulk and no real conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the three methyl groups and the hydroxyl are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a central imidazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms. Three phenyl rings are attached to it: one on the carbon between the two nitrogens (position 2), and two on adjacent carbons (positions 4 and 5), so the three benzene rings are not fused to each other or to the core. The imidazole nitrogen bearing a hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other, unsubstituted nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The three phenyl groups are unsubstituted and their rotation about the single bonds to the core gives the molecule some conformational flexibility. The overall arrangement has no element of mirror or rotational symmetry because the phenyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a cyclic siloxane built from a six-membered ring alternating silicon and oxygen atoms, which is a tetrasiloxane ring with four silicon centers and four bridging oxygens. Each silicon in the ring carries two substituents: one methyl group and one vinyl group (a terminal C=C double bond), so the ring has no fused or appended ring systems. The pattern of substitution is uniform, with every silicon bearing the same methyl/vinyl pair, which gives the scaffold a high degree of symmetry. The Si–O bonds are relatively flexible, though the ring itself is fairly compact. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its oxygen atoms can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered cyclic siloxane, a ring of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms with three Si–O–Si linkages and no carbon atoms in the ring. Each silicon atom carries one methyl group and one hydrogen atom, so the substitution pattern is fully regular and the ring is fused to nothing. The core is therefore a saturated, monocyclic Si–O scaffold with pendant methyl groups arranged in an alternating, approximately threefold-symmetric pattern. The ring is fairly rigid, though the Si–O bonds allow some puckering. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are bonded to silicon, and its oxygen atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or additional ring systems. The nitrogen atom sits in the ring and is flanked by methyl groups at both adjacent positions, which makes it a 2,6-disubstituted pyridine. A third methyl group is attached at the 4-position, opposite the nitrogen, so the molecule carries three methyl substituents and no other functional groups. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups present. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor conformational freedom, and the arrangement has a degree of symmetry about the axis through the nitrogen and the 4-position carbon.

The molecule is built around a central 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms at alternating positions. Each of the three carbon atoms of this triazine core carries a pyridin-2-yl substituent, so the structure is a symmetric, threefold-substituted scaffold with the pyridine rings attached through their carbon atoms adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The fully aromatic, fused-free arrangement of four-plus-two rings is largely planar and conformationally rigid, with only modest rotation possible about the single bonds linking the rings. The nitrogen atoms of the triazine and each pyridine ring act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while no hydrogen-bond donors are present.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrimidine ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other within the ring. Three primary amino groups (–NH2) are attached to the ring carbons, giving a substitution pattern that places them at three of the four carbon positions not occupied by ring nitrogens. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amino substituents, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make all three amines equivalent. Each amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its N–H bonds, while the two ring nitrogens and the amine nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the molecule a dense, multi-point hydrogen-bonding character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methyl group, three bromine atoms, and one hydroxyl group, making it a tribrominated methylphenol. The six-membered aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no ring fusion present. The hydroxyl group is attached to one ring carbon, flanked by a bromine on one side and a bromine-bearing carbon path on the other, while the methyl group sits adjacent to a bromine-substituted carbon, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The scaffold is rigid, with only the methyl and hydroxyl rotors offering limited conformational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine atoms serve only as weak halogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and three bromine atoms occupy the remaining positions at three of the other ring carbons, giving a substitution pattern that is unsymmetrical because the bromines are not evenly spaced around the ring. The amino nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the bromine atoms contribute only weak halogen-bonding and van der Waals character. Overall, the structure has a compact, rigid framework with little conformational flexibility, since the only rotatable bond is the C-N bond to the amino group.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no fused or additional rings. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and three bromine atoms occupy the remaining positions: two flank the hydroxyl at the ortho positions, and the third sits para to it, giving a 2,4,6-substitution pattern around the ring. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis running through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the molecule has little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the bromine atoms serve only as weak halogen-type acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with two hydroxyl groups and three bromine atoms distributed around the ring, leaving no unsubstituted aromatic carbon. The two hydroxyl groups sit para-related across the ring, and the three bromines are placed between them, giving a fully substituted, aromatic scaffold with a mirror-symmetric substitution pattern. The phenolic oxygens each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the bromine atoms contribute bulky, electron-withdrawing character without hydrogen-bonding capability. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the O–H bonds free to rotate.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries one methyl group and three bromine atoms as substituents, arranged so that the methyl sits between two bromines on adjacent positions, while the remaining bromine sits meta to that cluster on the opposite side of the ring. Because the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the flat ring framework. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the methyl and bromine groups add no significant conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the halogens are weak acceptors and the methyl group is inert in this regard.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. It carries one primary amine group (–NH2) on one ring carbon and three chlorine atoms attached to the remaining ring carbons, positioned so that the chlorines sit at alternating positions around the ring relative to the amine. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis that would make all positions equivalent. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds within the core, though the amine hydrogens can orient freely. The amine group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its lone pair, while the chlorine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors.

This molecule is a benzenesulfonamide: a single benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group, –SO2NH2, attached directly to one ring carbon. Three chlorine atoms sit on the remaining ring positions, two of them flanking the sulfonamide-bearing carbon in ortho positions and one in a meta position relative to the sulfonamide, giving a 2,4,6-trichloro substitution pattern on the aryl ring. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, while the sulfonamide group rotates somewhat about the carbon–sulfur bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring axis, since the three chlorines are not equivalent in position relative to the sulfonamide. The sulfonamide nitrogen bears two hydrogens, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group (–SO2Cl) on one carbon, with three chlorine atoms attached to the remaining ring positions. Going around the ring from the sulfonyl-bearing carbon, chlorines sit at the two ortho positions and one meta position relative to it, giving a 2,4,6-trichloro substitution pattern with no fused rings. The sulfonyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, tetrahedral center with two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the sulfonyl bond providing rotational flexibility, and the overall structure lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, which serves as the principal functional group and is attached directly to the aromatic core. Three chlorine atoms are distributed around the ring, with one ortho to the acid and the other two positioned on the opposite side of the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry in the substituent arrangement. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, while the carboxyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), whereas the chlorine atoms act only as weak, lipophilic-leaning substituents without donor capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached directly to one ring carbon. Three chlorine atoms are bonded to the ring at positions flanking the nitrile and at a more distant position, giving a 2,4,6-trichloro substitution pattern relative to the nitrile carbon. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion or saturated portions. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane passing through the nitrile carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the opposite ring carbon, so its substitution pattern is symmetric about that axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor is the nitrogen of the nitrile group.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group and three chlorine atoms, making it a trichlorinated phenol. The hydroxyl sits at one ring carbon, with chlorines at both ortho positions and at the meta position on the far side, giving an asymmetric 2,4,6-substitution pattern around the aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen allowed rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, with a mirror plane passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing an isothiocyanate group, a reactive heterocumulene consisting of a carbon double-bonded to both nitrogen and sulfur, attached directly to one ring carbon. Three chlorine atoms are substituted around the ring, two of them flanking the isothiocyanate on either side and the third positioned meta to it, giving an asymmetric 2,4,6-trisubstituted pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the linear N=C=S unit extending the flat geometry outward. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate, together with the halogen atoms, provide weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three chlorine atoms and one hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The hydrazine nitrogen bonded to the ring acts as a substituent on the benzene scaffold, with a free terminal NH2 extending from it. The three chlorines sit at positions adjacent to and across from the hydrazine, creating a substitution pattern that leaves the ring with only two aromatic hydrogens and no internal symmetry axis through the hydrazine. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the hydrazine linkage adds some conformational flexibility. The hydrazine nitrogens provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through their N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through their lone pairs, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-based polarity.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1,3-positions, which is a pyrimidine scaffold. Three chlorine atoms are attached as substituents to the ring carbons: one at the 2-position, flanked by both nitrogens, and one each at the 4- and 6-positions, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about an axis running through C2 and C5. The ring is flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no fused rings. The molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring hydrogens have been replaced by chlorine. The two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the chlorine atoms contribute to the electron-poor character of the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold, with no fused ring systems. Three substituents sit on the ring: one amino group (-NH2) and three fluorine atoms, arranged so the amino group is flanked by two fluorines at adjacent positions, giving a 1,2,4-type pattern of substitution around the ring. The fluorines are highly electronegative, which withdraws electron density from the ring and makes the carbon framework strongly polarized. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorines act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane that includes all substituents, so it is asymmetric overall.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen) on one carbon and three fluorine atoms on the remaining ring positions. The fluorines sit at the two positions flanking the aldehyde and at one position meta to it, giving a 2,4,6-trifluoro substitution pattern that is symmetric about an axis running through the aldehyde carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the formyl group able to rotate only slightly out of the ring plane. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are on the ring and the aldehyde carbon.

The molecule is a boronic acid built on a benzene ring, with a B(OH)2 group attached directly to one ring carbon. The aromatic core is a six-membered carbocycle bearing three fluorine substituents at the positions flanking and meta to the boron-bearing carbon, giving a 2,4,6-trifluoro substitution pattern that lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a single local plane. The ring is fully aromatic and planar and is not fused to any other ring, so the scaffold is rigid, while the C–B bond and the two B–OH bonds allow some rotational freedom. The boronic acid group contributes two hydroxyl hydrogen-bond donors and two oxygen hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the fluorine atoms add several weak hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and three fluorine atoms, giving it a fully aromatic, planar, and rigid scaffold with no fused or additional ring systems. The carboxylic acid (–COOH) sits on one ring carbon, and the three fluorine atoms occupy the remaining positions on the ring, two of them flanking the acid group in an ortho-fluorinated arrangement and the third on the far side, in a 2,4,6-substitution pattern relative to the carboxyl. Because the substitution is asymmetric about the carboxyl axis, the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the acid group, though the fluorines are arranged in a rough threefold-like pattern around the ring. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is otherwise conformationally restricted, with only the carboxyl group capable of limited rotation about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold, bearing three fluorine atoms and one nitrile group. The nitrile (C≡N) is attached directly to the ring and functions as a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing group. The three fluorine substituents occupy the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the nitrile, giving a 2,4,6-trisubstituted pattern that is symmetric about the axis running through the nitrile carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic ring and the linear nitrile make the framework fully rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups, but the nitrogen of the nitrile and the ring fluorines can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three hydrogen atoms on that ring are replaced: one by a hydroxyl group (–OH) and two by fluorine atoms, while the remaining two positions bear hydrogens. The hydroxyl group sits between two fluorine substituents, so the fluorines flank the phenolic carbon on one side and occupy the meta-related positions across the ring. The molecule is essentially flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the O–H. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three fluorine atoms at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to a acetic acid side chain, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the ring carbon attached to the side chain and the carbon opposite it. The side chain is a methylene group linking the ring to a carboxylic acid, which provides a flexible single-bond connection that can rotate relative to the planar aromatic ring. The aromatic core itself is rigid and planar, with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid group offers both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The three fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three fluorine atoms sit on the ring at alternating-adjacent positions, one of them flanking the carbon that carries a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2). That hydrazine substituent is the principal functional group, and its two nitrogen atoms provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity through their N–H bonds and acceptor capacity through their lone pairs. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and add electron-withdrawing character to the ring. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydrazine side chain has rotational freedom around its single bonds.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three hydroxyl groups are attached to the ring, making it a phenol, and three iodine atoms occupy the remaining positions, so every ring carbon carries a substituent. The substitution pattern is alternating along the ring, with the hydroxyl groups and iodines interleaved, which gives the molecule an approximate threefold symmetry about the ring centre. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, leaving only rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the iodine atoms are weak halogen-bond donors and poor hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four substituents: one acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) and three isopropyl groups. The three isopropyl groups sit at the carbons adjacent to and across from the acetyl group, leaving two unsubstituted ring positions that are meta to each other. There is no ring fusion, and the aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl groups add bulk and rotational freedom. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is the sole hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational axis of symmetry that would make it fully symmetric.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three isopropyl groups and one primary sulfonamide group. The aromatic core is fully substituted at a 1,2,3,5-pattern on the six-membered ring, so the isopropyl groups sit flanking the sulfonamide and one additional isopropyl group lies meta to it on the opposite side. The sulfonamide, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bearing an NH2 group, is the only polar functional group and provides both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its amine hydrogens and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its oxygens. The bulky isopropyl groups create steric crowding around the sulfonamide and restrict rotation about the aryl-sulfur bond, giving the molecule a moderately rigid core with flexible alkyl branches. The structure lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three isopropyl groups and one sulfonyl azide group. The isopropyl groups sit at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the sulfonyl azide, creating a symmetric substitution pattern across the aromatic ring. The sulfonyl group, bonded to a terminal azide, is the only polar functional group, offering oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the bulky isopropyl substituents add steric crowding around the ring, and the sulfonyl azide chain provides some conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused rings. Three isopropyl groups (CH(CH3)2) are attached to the ring at positions that leave two ring hydrogens, so the substitution pattern is bulky and asymmetric at the ring positions. The fourth substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, -SO2Cl, which is strongly electrophilic at sulfur and features two sulfonyl oxygens. The sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic core contrasts with the rotatable isopropyl and sulfonyl bonds, and the crowded arrangement around the sulfonyl group restricts its conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a carboxylic acid group attached at one position and three isopropyl groups distributed around the remaining carbons. The three isopropyl substituents are arranged in a 2,4,6 pattern relative to the carboxyl group, so the ring carries a clear, roughly threefold-symmetric substitution pattern in its placement, though the two ring hydrogens sit in meta-like positions relative to each other. Because the ring is aromatic and fully substituted apart from those two hydrogens, the core is rigid, while the isopropyl groups add bulky, rotatable branching around it. The carboxylic acid is a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. Its position between two bulky isopropyl groups means it is sterically crowded, which can restrict its orientation.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three isopropyl groups are attached at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the acyl chloride, so the ring is substituted in a symmetric 1,3,5-pattern across its alternating positions. The one reactive functional group is an acyl chloride, a carbonyl carbon bonded to chlorine, attached directly to the ring. The aromatic core and bulky isopropyl groups make the scaffold rigid, while the isopropyl groups add steric crowding around the acyl chloride. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only the carbonyl oxygen as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no ring fusion. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at alternating-looking positions, and a single acetyl group (a methyl ketone, –C(=O)CH3) sits between two of them, giving a crowded, symmetric substitution pattern along a mirror axis through the acetyl carbon and the ring carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and acetyl side chains retain some rotational freedom. The ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no hydroxyl or amine groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, so it is a single aromatic ring with no fused rings. Three of the ring positions carry methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to a methyl), and one carries a formyl group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen, attached directly to the ring). The methoxy groups sit at alternating positions around the ring, giving a symmetric arrangement with a mirror plane passing through the formyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring and carbonyl are planar and rigid, while the three methoxy methyl groups can rotate. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks O-H or N-H bonds, but the three ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: three methoxy groups and one nitrile group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, giving a flat, rigid scaffold. The nitrile (C#N) is attached to one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by methoxy (OCH3) groups, while a third methoxy sits on the carbon across the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking the two-fold symmetry that a fully symmetric arrangement would show. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every oxygen and the nitrogen carry no hydrogens. The three ether oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: three methoxy groups and one methyl group, arranged in a 1,3,5-pattern with the methyl sitting between two methoxy groups on one side. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and its planar, rigid framework is decorated by the flexible ether side chains. The methoxy oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors but carry no donor groups, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors at all. Overall the arrangement is approximately symmetric about an axis passing through the methyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, since the two outer methoxy groups are equivalent.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three methyl groups are attached to the ring, and a primary amino group sits between two of them, so the substitution pattern is symmetrical about an axis running through the amino-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it. Because the ring is aromatic and the substituents are small, the framework is essentially rigid and planar, with only the methyl and amino rotors providing minor flexibility. The amino group is the only hydrogen-bond donor, offering two N–H hydrogens, and its nitrogen lone pair can also serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring carbons and methyl groups contribute no additional polar functionality.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three methyl groups and one boronic acid group, giving a substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The boronic acid, B(OH)2, is attached to one ring carbon and flanked on both sides by methyl groups, so the ring carries three methyls in a 2,4,6 arrangement relative to the boron-bearing carbon. This crowded pattern gives the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the boron and the para carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its carbon–boron bond. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the boron center is a Lewis acid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no ring fusion present. Three methyl groups are attached to the ring at positions that leave the two remaining aromatic carbons bearing hydrogen, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. A carboxylic acid group sits between two of the methyl groups, which forces it to twist out of the plane of the ring. The molecule is largely rigid because of the aromatic core, though the carboxylic acid can rotate about its bond to the ring. The acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the methyl groups contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents, with no fused ring systems.
