Three of the ring positions carry methyl groups and one carries a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH), giving a substitution pattern in which the methyls sit at positions that leave the ring with mirror symmetry through the hydroxymethyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl group adds a small degree of rotational flexibility about its ring-to-carbon bond. The primary alcohol group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the oxygen lone pairs, while the rest of the scaffold is entirely hydrocarbon and offers no additional polar interaction sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, so its scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic core. The ring carries four substituents: three methyl groups and one chloromethyl group, arranged in a 1,3,5 and 2 pattern that gives it a substitution layout with some local symmetry across the ring. The chloromethyl group (a CH2Cl unit) is the only reactive functional handle, while the methyl groups are unreactive alkyl substituents. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the aromatic ring and alkyl groups lack heteroatoms able to accept hydrogen bonds, and the chlorine is a weak acceptor at best. Overall, the structure is rigid in its ring but has limited flexibility from the rotation of the chloromethyl and methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: three methyl groups and one thiomethyl-type group, which is a CH2 linked to a thiol (SH). Reading around the ring, the methyl groups sit at positions that give the molecule a symmetric 2,4,6-trimethyl pattern, with the CH2SH group located on the carbon flanked by two methyl-bearing carbons. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the ring itself is rigid and planar, while the CH2SH arm adds a small degree of rotational flexibility. The thiol sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H group and as a weak acceptor through its lone pairs, whereas the hydrocarbon ring and methyl groups offer no hydrogen-bonding capacity.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing three methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, giving a phenol scaffold. Reading around the ring, the hydroxyl sits at one position flanked on both sides by methyl substituents, while the remaining methyl groups occupy the other meta-related positions, producing a symmetric 2,4,6-trisubstituted arrangement with a mirror plane passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, with no fused rings or stereocenters, and the methyl groups add modest steric bulk around the hydroxyl. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the molecule has no other heteroatoms to contribute additional polar interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three methyl groups are attached to the ring at alternating positions, giving a symmetric 2,4,6-trimethyl substitution pattern around the core. The remaining ring position carries an isocyanate group, an N=C=O unit attached directly to the aromatic carbon, which is the sole functional group present. The ring and its substituents are essentially planar and rigid, while the methyl groups add minimal flexibility. The compound has a single mirror-symmetric axis through the isocyanate carbon and the opposite ring carbon. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, since no N-H or O-H groups are present, while the oxygen and nitrogen of the isocyanate can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents in a fixed pattern: three methyl groups and one isothiocyanate group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid and planar. The isothiocyanate group, written as N=C=S, is attached to one ring carbon and is nearly linear, extending outward from the ring. The three methyl groups sit at the positions flanking and meta to that group, which gives the molecule an approximate mirror plane passing through the isothiocyanate carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H bonds. It has only weak acceptor character, mainly at the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate group.

The molecule is built around a central 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with three nitrogen atoms placed alternately in the ring. Each of the three carbon atoms of this core carries a phenyl group, so the structure is a symmetric, trisubstituted scaffold with three benzene rings radiating outward from the central ring. The rings are joined by single bonds to the triazine core rather than fused, which gives the molecule a flat, rigid, largely conjugated framework with few rotatable bonds. The three ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene core bearing a primary amine group, with three phenyl rings attached at the ring positions adjacent to and across from it, giving a fully substituted aromatic ring with terphenyl-like connectivity. The amine sits on one carbon, flanked by two of the phenyl substituents, which creates a crowded substitution pattern around that position. Overall the structure is a triaryl aniline with a single unsubstituted carbon remaining on the central ring, so the arrangement is asymmetric in its placement of the substituents. Because the phenyl groups connect through single bonds to the central ring, they can rotate, though steric crowding near the amine restricts that motion somewhat. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acting as an acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak hydrogen-bonding character.

The molecule is built on a single aromatic six-membered heterocycle, a 1,3,5-triazine ring containing three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms. Each of the three ring carbons carries an allyloxy group, meaning an oxygen atom bonded to the ring and to a CH2-CH=CH2 chain, so the substitution pattern is fully symmetric about the ring. The ring itself is flat and rigid, while the three allyl tails are flexible and can rotate freely. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. Its ring nitrogens and ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two aromatic six-membered rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a biaryl scaffold. One ring is a pyridine bearing its nitrogen at a position adjacent to the linking carbon, while the other is also a pyridine, with its nitrogen located para to the linkage. Both rings are fully aromatic and planar, and the connecting bond allows only limited rotation, so the overall framework is fairly rigid. The molecule has no substituents beyond the two ring nitrogens, and it lacks hydrogen-bond donors entirely, while the two ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The arrangement is not symmetric, because the two nitrogens sit in different positions relative to the bond between the rings.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four methyl-type substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two adjacent positions carry chloromethyl groups (–CH2Cl), while the remaining ring positions carry methyl groups, giving a 1,2,4,5-type pattern of alternating substituents: methyl, chloromethyl, methyl, and chloromethyl around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two chloromethyl arms add some conformational freedom through rotation about the ring-to-carbon bonds. The molecule lacks hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, and it has no hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the weak contribution of the chlorine atoms. Its symmetry is limited, as the two chloromethyl groups are not related by any symmetry element that would make the molecule fully symmetric.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with two trifluoromethyl groups attached to the ring. The carboxylic acid sits at one position, and a trifluoromethyl group occupies the position para to it, while a second trifluoromethyl group is ortho to the carboxylic acid, giving an unsymmetrical 2,4-substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the carboxyl group and the two CF3 groups as its only substituents. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine atoms of the CF3 groups act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. One substituent is a phenoxyacetic acid group, an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The other two are tertiary alkyl groups, each a quaternary carbon carrying two methyls and an ethyl chain, placed on the carbon adjacent to the ether oxygen and para to it. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, while the bulky tertiary alkyl groups add steric hindrance around one side of the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen acts as an additional acceptor. Apart from the ethyl and methyl groups, the molecule lacks any symmetry element and has modest conformational flexibility from the side chains.

The molecule is built on a quinazoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrimidine ring. The pyrimidine portion carries two primary amino groups, one at each of the two carbon positions flanking the ring nitrogens, which makes the pyrimidine ring electron-rich. A single fluorine atom sits on the benzo ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, giving the carbocyclic portion an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with only the two amino groups able to rotate. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a 1,3,5-triazine core, a six-membered aromatic ring with three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbon atoms. One of the ring carbons carries a para-tolyl group, meaning a benzene ring bearing a methyl substituent opposite the point of attachment. Two of the remaining triazine carbons each bear a primary amino group, so the triazine has two NH2 substituents and one aryl substituent. The biaryl linkage between the two rings is a single bond, which allows some rotation, while the fused-free aromatic framework keeps the overall structure largely planar and rigid. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbons. Two of the three ring carbons carry primary amino groups, so the ring bears two NH2 substituents at positions that flank the third carbon. The remaining ring carbon is bonded to a phenyl ring, which carries a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the point of attachment. The aromatic system is fully planar and largely rigid, with the phenyl ring able to rotate about its single bond to the triazine. The amino groups supply hydrogen-bond donor capacity, while the ring nitrogens and fluorine atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single aromatic 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered heterocycle with three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbon atoms. Two of the ring carbons each carry a primary amino group, giving the scaffold a symmetric-looking but not fully symmetric substitution pattern, since the third ring carbon bears a long unbranched alkyl chain of eleven carbons. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, contrasting with the planar and rigid triazine core. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The overall shape is an amphiphilic arrangement of a polar, hydrogen-bonding head attached to a nonpolar, extended tail.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a pyrimidine ring is fused to a benzene ring, forming a quinazoline-type scaffold. The pyrimidine ring contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, and two primary amino groups are attached to the ring carbons flanking those nitrogens, one at the carbon between the two ring nitrogens and one at the carbon adjacent to the fused benzene ring. The fused bicyclic core is fully planar and rigid, with an extended aromatic surface and no rotatable bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two amino groups occupy non-equivalent positions. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional rings present. Two amino groups sit on the ring, one at a position para to the methyl group and one ortho to it, so the substitution pattern is a 1,2,4-arrangement of a methyl and two amines. Each amino group carries two hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen lone pairs can accept hydrogen bonds. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methyl group and the amines contributing modest flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a central 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms alternating with carbon. Two of the triazine carbons each carry an anilino group, meaning an NH linker bonded to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, and these two phenyl rings are unfused and attached through single bonds. The third triazine carbon bears a morpholine ring, a saturated six-membered ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, attached through its nitrogen. The arrangement gives the molecule a roughly threefold pseudo-symmetry around the triazine core, though the morpholine breaks the symmetry of the substituent set. Its aromatic rings and triazine core make the framework fairly rigid, while the NH linkers and the morpholine ring add some conformational freedom. The two NH groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the triazine nitrogens and morpholine oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyrimidine core, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. A boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one ring carbon, which sits between the two ring nitrogens' neighboring positions on the side away from the other substituents. Two benzyloxy groups, each an oxygen linked to a CH2 bridge that terminates in an unsubstituted phenyl ring, are attached to adjacent ring carbons, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. The two phenyl rings are flexible through their CH2-O linkages, while the central pyrimidine core is rigid and planar. The boronic acid hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogens and ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings or heteroatoms within the ring itself. An amino group (-NH2) sits at one position, flanked on one side by a bromine atom, which together with a second bromine placed meta to the amine on the opposite side defines a 2,4-dibromo pattern relative to the amine. A trifluoromethyl group (-CF3) occupies the position adjacent to the amine on the other side, making the substitution pattern asymmetric with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic scaffold is rigid and planar, while the trifluoromethyl group rotates freely about its single bond to the ring. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, which makes it an aniline-type scaffold. Going around the ring from that amine, there is a fluorine atom on the adjacent carbon, and two bromine atoms are placed on carbons further along, giving a 2,4-dihalogenated substitution pattern relative to the amine. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotatable bonds beyond the amine hydrogens, so its overall shape is essentially flat with little conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair, while the halogen atoms contribute only weak halogen-bonding or acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon, with two bromine atoms and one fluorine atom attached at other ring positions. The hydroxyl sits adjacent to a fluorine and to a bromine, creating a crowded 2,4-dibromo-6-fluorophenol-type substitution pattern on a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion. The scaffold is fully aromatic and planar, so the core is rigid, with the halogen and hydroxyl substituents lying in the ring plane and contributing little conformational flexibility. The substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local arrangement. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine and bromine atoms can serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and alternating positions: a primary amino group, a nitro group, and two bromine atoms. The amino group sits ortho to the nitro group, and one bromine sits ortho to the amino group, while the second bromine is meta to the amino group on the opposite side of the ring. The nitro group is planar and strongly electron-withdrawing, and the amino group contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites. The nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitrogen of the amino group and the bromines add further polarizability. The aromatic scaffold is rigid and planar, with only limited rotational freedom about the nitro and amino bonds, and the substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is an aryl ketone built on a benzene ring that carries a bromine atom at the para position relative to the carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon links the ring to a bromomethyl group, so the scaffold is a simple phenyl ketone with a terminal primary alkyl bromide. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the molecule has no stereocenters. Its only other flexibility comes from rotation about the single bonds joining the carbonyl to the ring and to the CH2Br group. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. It carries one primary amine group (-NH2) attached to one carbon of the ring, with two bromine atoms attached at the adjacent position and at a position across the ring, creating a 2,4-dibromo substitution pattern relative to the amine. The substituents are not symmetrically placed, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the amine hydrogens able to orient freely. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the bromine atoms are poor hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, so it has no fused or additional ring systems beyond the aromatic core. A methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one position, with two bromine atoms at the positions ortho and para to it, arranged so that the two bromines are meta to each other on the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the methyl of the methoxy group adding conformational freedom. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its substitution pattern is asymmetric, so it lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

This molecule is a benzenesulfonyl chloride, with the sulfonyl group (SO2Cl) attached to one carbon of a single, unfused benzene ring. Two bromine atoms sit on the ring: one para to the sulfonyl group and one ortho to it, giving a 2,4-disubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two halogen substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The sulfonyl chloride is the most reactive functional group, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while its two sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms in the core. Its substituents are two bromine atoms and three methyl groups, arranged so that the aromatic ring carries five substituents and one remaining hydrogen. The two bromines sit at adjacent positions, flanked on one side by a methyl group, which crowds the ring around them. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor local motion. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, because the bromine and methyl substituents cannot participate in such interactions.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms are attached at the positions ortho and para to it, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern around the ring, with one bromine adjacent to the hydroxyl and the other on the opposite side. Because the substituents are unequal in position, the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework. The aromatic ring is rigid and flat, and the substituents add little conformational flexibility, since the C–O bond of the hydroxyl can rotate only slightly. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, while the bromine atoms serve mainly as weak halogen-bond donors and very weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a phenoxyacetic acid scaffold: a benzene ring bearing an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 group that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered ring carrying two bromine substituents, one at the position adjacent to the ether linkage and one further around the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor. The aryl ring is rigid and planar, whereas the OCH2COOH side chain is flexible, able to rotate about its single bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents on its six carbons, so it is a fully substituted aromatic core with no remaining aromatic C–H positions. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitro group, two chlorine atoms, and a hydroxyl group, giving it a substituted phenol scaffold. The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group, a substituent that consists of a carbonyl carbon attached to a methyl group and to the ring. The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a primary carboxamide group, with the amide carbon directly attached to one ring carbon. The molecule is a benzoic acid core, meaning a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to one ring carbon. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings. The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached directly to one ring carbon. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six positions, with substituents at four of them. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ether oxygen serves as an acceptor only, and the chlorines contribute weak halogen-bonding character without donating hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: two nitro-type groups in the sense of a nitro group (N with two oxygens, one charged) at one position, a trifluoromethyl group, and two chlorine atoms. The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries a nitro group, a hydroxyl group, and two chlorine atoms, giving a substituted phenol scaffold. The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other within a planar, fully conjugated framework. The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system built on a quinazoline scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrimidine ring through a shared edge. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a single benzene ring, so it has a simple aromatic benzene scaffold with no ring fusion. The ring carries four substituents: a primary amino group (NH2), an iodine atom, and two chlorine atoms, arranged on adjacent and alternating positions around the ring. The molecule is a single benzene ring, so it has a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the chlorine atoms offer weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, with a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle and no fused rings. This molecule is a substituted benzylamine built on a single benzene ring. The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, a diazine with nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on other ring positions. The molecule is a diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges two benzene rings. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a trifluoromethyl group and two chlorine atoms. The trifluoromethyl group sits at one position on the aromatic ring, and the two chlorines occupy adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern in which the chlorines are ortho to each other and the trifluoromethyl group is para to one of them. Its scaffold is planar and rigid, with the trifluoromethyl group rotating freely around its single bond to the ring. The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl bonded directly to the ring with a chlorine atom on the carbonyl carbon. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH unit) attached at one position. This molecule is an N-methyl acetanilide, built on a single benzene ring as its scaffold. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the substituents lying in the ring plane, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an oxyacetic acid side chain: an aryl ether oxygen connects the ring to a CH2 group that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid group is both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, and the ether oxygen adds a further acceptor site. The molecule is built on a phenoxyacetic hydrazide scaffold: a benzene ring bearing an ether oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain that ends in a carbonyl group bonded to a hydrazine (–C(=O)NHNH2) unit. The hydrazide group offers hydrogen-bond donor capability through its N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs, while the ether oxygen and chlorine atoms add further weak acceptor character.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents: a cyanomethoxy group (–O–CH2–C≡N) attached to one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms on adjacent-to-each-other positions that sit ortho and para relative to the ether oxygen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the isocyanate unit is linear and essentially restricts rotation near the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the isocyanate group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) on one carbon, with two chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. Its acceptor character comes from the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate group and the two halogen substituents, which are weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain: a carboxylic acid group attached through a methylene (CH2) linker to one ring carbon, which makes it a phenylacetic acid scaffold. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring, one at the position para to the side chain and one at an adjacent ortho position, giving a 2,4-disubstituted pattern relative to the CH2 attachment. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a cyanomethyl group (a nitrile carbon attached through a CH2 linker) and two chlorine atoms. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, giving a flat, rigid scaffold. The two chlorine substituents sit at adjacent positions on the ring, with the cyanomethyl group occupying the position next to one of them, producing an unsymmetrical 2,4-type substitution pattern. The nitrile group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor at its nitrogen, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The CH2 linker adds a small degree of rotational flexibility to the otherwise rigid aromatic framework.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two chlorine substituents. One chlorine sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen (the 2-position), and the other sits on the carbon two positions away from the nitrogen on the opposite side (the 4-position), giving a 2,4-disubstituted pattern. The ring is fully planar and aromatic, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the structure is entirely rigid. The molecule has no symmetry that would make the two chlorines equivalent, since their positions relative to the nitrogen differ. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, which makes it a pyrimidine scaffold. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring, one at the carbon between the two nitrogens and one at a carbon adjacent to a single ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no additional fused rings. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and two chlorine atoms, giving it a substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems. Starting from the methyl-bearing carbon, one chlorine sits ortho to the methyl group and the second chlorine sits para to the methyl group on the opposite side of the ring from one another, creating a 1,2,4-trisubstitution pattern. The molecule is planar and rigid, with the aromatic core constraining the attached groups, and it lacks any internal symmetry that would make all its substituent positions equivalent. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, and its only potential acceptor character comes from the lone pairs on the chlorine atoms, which are weak.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group and two fluorine atoms. The nitro group, drawn as a nitrogen with a formal positive charge and an oxygen with a formal negative charge, is attached to one ring carbon, with fluorine atoms at the adjacent ortho position and at the meta position relative to it (the other fluorine sitting para to the nitro group). The ring is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a single unsubstituted-by-fusion benzene core. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a potential planar arrangement. Its rigid aromatic framework gives little conformational flexibility, apart from rotation of the nitro group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitro oxygens and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methoxy group, two fluorine atoms, and a primary carboxamide, with no fused rings. The carboxamide sits on the ring at one position, flanked by a fluorine on the adjacent carbon, while a methoxy group and a second fluorine occupy the neighboring positions, giving a densely substituted, unsymmetrical pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, though the methoxy group and the amide carbonyl can rotate about their single bonds to the ring. The amide's NH2 group provides two hydrogen-bond donors, and its carbonyl oxygen, along with the methoxy oxygen and the fluorines, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a methoxy group, and two fluorine atoms, arranged on a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the methoxy oxygen sits between two fluorine-bearing carbons, so the two fluorines flank the methoxy group on one side and the ring carries a 2,3,6-type substitution pattern relative to the acid. Because the substituents are not symmetrically placed, the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and methoxy groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the two carboxyl oxygens), and the methoxy and fluorine atoms serve as additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Around that ring sit a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) on one carbon, two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons flanking it, and a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) on the carbon opposite the methoxy side. The substitution pattern is therefore highly crowded, with the methoxy group sandwiched between two fluorines. The aromatic core and nitrile are rigid and planar, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom. The nitrogen of the nitrile and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing six positions, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Starting from the methyl-bearing carbon, the ring carries a methyl group, two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons flanking that methyl position, and a nitrile (cyano) group para to one of the fluorines. The substitution pattern is therefore unsymmetrical: the methyl and two fluorines cluster on one side of the ring while the cyano group sits on the opposite side. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the nitrile contributing a linear, rod-like extension. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile and the two fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no ring fusion. The ring carries a methyl group, and two fluorine atoms are attached at positions that flank the methyl-bearing carbon, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. A carbonyl group bearing a chlorine atom, an acyl chloride, sits on the ring at the position opposite the methyl group, making it the most reactive functional group present. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the acyl chloride and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atoms.

The molecule is an anilide built on a single benzene ring, with an acetamide group (CH3C(=O)NH-) attached to one ring carbon. The ring carries two fluorine atoms on adjacent positions relative to the amide nitrogen (one ortho and one meta, with the other meta-related fluorine placed para to the amide attachment point), giving a trisubstituted aromatic core. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the amide linkage adds limited conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two fluorines occupy inequivalent positions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries one primary amine group (–NH2) on one ring carbon, which serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and two fluorine atoms attached to adjacent and nearby ring positions, giving a 2,4-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the amine. The substituents are not symmetrically placed, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the substituted carbons and has only the planar symmetry of the aromatic core. The ring is rigid and flat, while the amine group can rotate only slightly about its carbon–nitrogen bond. Overall, the structure is compact, with the amine as the main site for hydrogen bonding and the fluorines contributing electronegative polar character to the ring.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, which serves as the principal functional group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered benzene ring with no additional fused rings, giving a flat, rigid scaffold. Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring: one ortho to the aldehyde carbon and one in the para position relative to it, with the remaining positions carrying hydrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the plane of the ring. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and the aldehyde and fluorine substituents are the only sites of polar character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no fused ring systems. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, providing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the NH2) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). Two fluorine atoms occupy the ring positions adjacent to one another and para-related to the amide substituent, one meta and one ortho to the carboxamide, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amide bond gives limited rotational freedom to the otherwise flat structure. Fluorine atoms contribute electron-withdrawing character but are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and cannot act as donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, with two fluorine atoms on the ring. The boronic acid, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic ring, and the two fluorines sit on adjacent carbons at a 2,4-substitution relative to the boron-bearing carbon, giving an asymmetric pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is a single, planar, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, which makes the scaffold rigid, while the C–B bond allows limited rotation of the boronic acid group. The two hydroxyl groups on boron can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group on one carbon, with two fluorine atoms on the ring at positions that are meta and para relative to each other, giving a 2,4-difluorobenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the local ring. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydroxyl hydrogen that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds. The two fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and add electron-withdrawing character to the ring. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid group has limited rotational freedom about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and two fluorine atoms occupy adjacent positions on the ring, one ortho to the nitrile and one meta to it, giving a 2,4-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the nitrile carbon. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial. Because the ring and the linear nitrile are both rigid, the structure has essentially no conformational flexibility. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a fluorine atom at the para position relative to the carbonyl attachment, while the other carries a fluorine at the ortho position. Each aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered benzene system, and the molecule has no stereocenters. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aryl rings can rotate about their bonds to the carbonyl carbon, giving moderate flexibility, and the ortho fluorine introduces asymmetry, so the two halves are not equivalent.

This molecule is a mandelic acid derivative built on a simple two-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring. The chain bears a carboxylic acid group and a secondary alcohol on the carbon adjacent to the ring, making that central carbon a stereocenter. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered benzene ring with two fluorine atoms at the 2 and 4 positions relative to the side chain, which breaks the ring's symmetry. The core is fairly flexible because the single bonds of the side chain can rotate, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups together can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the fluorine atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acetamide in which the nitrogen carries both an N-methyl group and a difluorophenyl ring, making it a tertiary amide. The aromatic core is a single benzene ring with no ring fusion, bearing two fluorine atoms at positions that give a 2,4-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the amide nitrogen. The overall shape is largely planar around the aromatic ring, with the amide group providing modest conformational flexibility through rotation about the nitrogen-aryl and nitrogen-carbonyl bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two fluorines sit at unequal positions on the ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since the nitrogen is fully substituted and no N-H or O-H groups are present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group and two fluorine atoms, making it a difluorophenol. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbon ring with no ring fusion, and it is fully planar and rigid. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, with one fluorine atom on the adjacent carbon (ortho position) and another fluorine atom on the carbon two positions away from it, separated by one carbon, in a meta arrangement relative to the hydroxyl. Because the substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no rotational symmetry and lacks a mirror plane through the substituent positions. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a phenylacetic acid, built from a single benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH) on one ring carbon. Two fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions that are meta and para to each other relative to the side chain, with one fluorine adjacent to the attachment point and the other at the opposite side of the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methylene linker and carboxylic acid provide limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and contribute to the electron-poor character of the ring.

This molecule is a chalcone, built from two aromatic rings joined by a three-carbon α,β-unsaturated ketone bridge with a trans (E) double bond. One aryl ring carries a single methoxy group at the ortho position, while the other ring bears a ketone-adjacent 2,4-dihydroxy substitution pattern, giving it two phenolic hydroxyl groups. The conjugated enone linker keeps the scaffold largely planar and fairly rigid, with rotation possible only about the single bonds to the aryl rings. The hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the carbonyl oxygen and methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two rings carry different substituents.

This molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a three-carbon bridge containing a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond and a ketone, giving a chalcone-type skeleton. One ring carries a phenolic hydroxyl group at the position next to the carbonyl attachment, while the other bears a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group in a 1,2,4-pattern relative to the vinyl linkage. The alkene and carbonyl conjugate with both aromatic rings, which makes the scaffold largely planar and rigid, though the single bonds allow some rotation. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the two rings are substituted differently. Its hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, the methoxy oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. Its skeleton carries three substituents: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) and two hydroxyl groups, along with one methyl group on the ring. The acetyl group and the two phenolic OH groups sit at adjacent or near positions, so the ring is densely functionalized and asymmetric. The ketone carbonyl oxygen and both phenolic oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two phenolic OH groups can each act as hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the acetyl group offering a small degree of rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which serves as the central aromatic scaffold, bearing three substituents. An acetyl group (a ketone carbonyl attached to a methyl) is attached at one ring carbon, and two hydroxyl groups sit at ring positions that are meta and para relative to the acetyl group, one of them ortho to it. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The benzene core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group and hydroxyls have limited rotational freedom. The phenolic oxygens and the ketone oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the two hydroxyl groups can donate them, with the ortho hydroxyl able to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, bearing four substituents: an aldehyde group (a formyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen) and three hydroxyl groups. The aldehyde is attached at one ring carbon, with the two hydroxyl groups positioned on adjacent ring carbons that sit ortho and para relative to it, giving a 2,4-dihydroxy substitution pattern around the carbonyl-bearing carbon. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups are small and conformationally limited, so the overall structure is rigid. The molecule has no symmetry because the hydroxyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ortho-hydroxyl can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent aldehyde.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a hydrazide group, a carbonyl bearing two nitrogen atoms in a chain (-C(=O)-NH-NH2), attached directly to one ring carbon. Two hydroxyl groups sit on the ring, one ortho to the hydrazide and one para to it, giving a 2,4-dihydroxy substitution pattern on a monosubstituted-carbonyl aromatic core. The aromatic ring is flat and fully unsaturated, and the hydrazide chain is largely planar, so the scaffold is fairly rigid with only the terminal NH2 able to rotate freely. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two hydroxyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the two phenolic OH groups and the hydrazide NH and NH2 act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygens serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries two hydroxyl groups, positioned at the 2- and 4-positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, giving a 2,4-dihydroxy substitution pattern. Both aromatic rings are simple six-membered benzene rings with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no stereocenters. The two phenyl rings can rotate about the single bonds linking them to the carbonyl, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid. Each phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ortho hydroxyl can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a propanoyl group, which is an ethyl ketone attached directly to the aromatic carbon, forming an aryl ketone. Two hydroxyl groups sit on the same ring, one ortho to the ketone and one para to it, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the six-membered aromatic core. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, while the ethyl chain on the carbonyl gives the molecule a small amount of conformational flexibility. Because the substitution lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, the structure is asymmetric. Both phenolic hydroxyls can donate hydrogen bonds, and the carbonyl oxygen and both hydroxyl oxygens can accept them, with the ortho hydroxyl able to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the nearby ketone.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused heteroaromatic system: a pyrimidine-2,4-dione ring is fused along one edge to a pyrazine ring, giving a flat, rigid, fully conjugated scaffold. The six-membered ring that carries two carbonyl groups contains two adjacent NH positions, each flanked by a C=O, so the ring has two N–H donors and two carbonyl oxygen acceptors. The pyrazine portion contributes two additional aromatic ring nitrogens that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because the core is planar with no rotatable bonds and no substituents off the ring system, the structure has no stereocenters and possesses a high degree of symmetry in its heavy-atom framework.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused or additional ring systems. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached at positions that are meta and ortho to each other, and a single iodine atom sits on the ring between them in a 1,2,4-substitution arrangement. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two methoxy groups add some rotational flexibility around their C–O bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. Each ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring, and a nitro group (–NO2) occupies a third position. The substitution pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted: the two methoxy groups sit on adjacent carbons, and the nitro group is placed on the carbon next to one methoxy group and para to the other. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane, so the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. Its skeleton is rigid and planar, though the methoxy methyl groups can rotate. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Attached to the ring is an acetyl group (a ketone carbon bearing a methyl), and two methoxy ethers sit on the ring at positions that place them on either side of the acetyl group, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 (trisubstituted). The ketone carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The methoxy and acetyl groups can rotate about their single bonds, adding some conformational flexibility, but the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries an amino group and two methoxy groups, both ether oxygens bonded to methyl groups, placed at positions around the ring that make the substitution pattern asymmetric. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor and both ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the aromatic core and methyl ethers give it a largely rigid planar framework with limited flexibility beyond rotation of the two methoxy groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Attached to the ring is an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, bearing one hydrogen), along with two methoxy groups, each an oxygen bonded to a methyl group. One methoxy sits ortho to the aldehyde and the other sits meta to it on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups have limited rotational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its three oxygen atoms can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups (O-CH3) and one aldoxime group (CH=N-OH). The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two methoxy groups sit on carbons that are meta to each other, and the oxime-bearing carbon lies ortho to one of them, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no molecular symmetry. The oxime and methoxy ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the oxime hydroxyl provides a hydrogen-bond donor. The aromatic core and C=N double bond are rigid, though the methoxy and oxime hydroxyl groups retain some rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group and two methoxy groups, making it a 2,4-dimethoxyphenylboronic acid type scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, so it is planar and rigid, though the methoxy and boronic acid substituents can rotate about their bonds. The boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, giving the molecule two hydrogen-bond donors from the O–H groups. The two ether oxygens of the methoxy substituents and the hydroxyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, with the methoxy groups at positions ortho and para relative to the boronic acid, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) sits on one carbon, flanked on one side by a methoxy group, while a second methoxy group is located on the ring carbon meta to the sulfonamide, giving a 2,4-dimethoxy-type substitution pattern relative to the sulfonyl attachment. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and sulfonamide groups able to rotate about their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis that maps the whole structure onto itself, since the two methoxy groups occupy inequivalent positions. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated in the sulfonamide: the two NH hydrogens act as donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a sulfonyl chloride group (–SO2Cl) and two methoxy groups (–OCH3). The sulfonyl chloride sits at one ring position, with a methoxy group on the adjacent carbon ortho to it and a second methoxy group para to the sulfonyl chloride, giving a 2,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, while the methoxy methyl groups and the tetrahedral sulfur add some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry because the substituents are unequally placed. The methoxy oxygens and the sulfonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two methoxy (–OCH3) groups, giving it the skeleton of a substituted benzoic acid. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the carboxylic acid sits at one position while the two methoxy ethers occupy the position ortho to it and a position meta to the acid across the ring. Because the ring carries substituents at three positions, the overall pattern is asymmetric and lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, though the methoxy and carboxyl groups can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen, while the two ether oxygens act only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring, one at the position para to the nitrile and one at the position ortho to it, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern across the ring. A nitrile group (–C≡N) forms the third substituent, a strongly electron-withdrawing, linear, rod-like unit. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. Its rigid aromatic core is flanked by fairly flexible methoxy arms, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a single aromatic core with no ring fusion. An acyl chloride group (a carbonyl bonded to chlorine) sits on one ring carbon and serves as the reactive electrophilic functional group. Two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) are attached at the positions adjacent to and para to the acyl chloride, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic ring keeps the core planar, while the methoxy and acyl chloride groups add modest rotational freedom. The two methoxy oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three substituents decorate the ring: two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) and one hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 carrying an OH). The methoxy groups sit at positions that place them meta to each other across the ring, while the hydroxymethyl group sits adjacent to one of them, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and hydroxymethyl arms rotate freely about their single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups (O-CH3) on adjacent-to-each-other positions relative to the nitrovinyl side chain, giving a 1,3-dimethoxy pattern around the aromatic core. Attached to the ring is a trans-configured vinyl linker terminating in a nitro group (–CH=CH–NO2), which is a strongly electron-withdrawing, conjugated unit. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated with the alkene and nitro group, so the scaffold is rigid and flat, with limited rotational freedom apart from the methoxy methyl groups. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon, while the two ether oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. It has no internal symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the conjugated chain.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries two methoxy groups (–OCH3) and one isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S). The methoxy groups sit ortho and para to each other, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the ring, leaving the molecule without any internal symmetry axis. The isothiocyanate is a linear, electrophilic cumulene-type unit, while the ring itself is planar and rigid, with the methoxy groups able to rotate about their C–O bonds. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the sulfur atom can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) at one position, and two methoxy groups (oxygen-linked methyl ethers) on adjacent ring carbons, placed so that the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid group offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The methylene linker and the methoxy groups add some conformational flexibility, whereas the aromatic ring itself remains rigid.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrimidine ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions. It carries two methoxy groups, each an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group, attached to carbon atoms flanking the ring nitrogens, so the substitution pattern is 2,4-dimethoxy on the pyrimidine core. The ring has no fusion to any other ring system, and the bonds to the methoxy oxygens and methyl groups give a compact, planar, fairly rigid framework with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, but the two ring nitrogens and two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated alcohol built on a branched six-carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. Its skeleton consists of a central carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, flanked on each side by a carbon that carries two methyl branches, giving a symmetric arrangement about that central carbon. The single hydroxyl group is the only functional group, acting as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and lone pairs. The molecule is conformationally flexible because all of its bonds are single bonds that can rotate freely, while the bulky isopropyl-type branches introduce some steric hindrance around the hydroxyl-bearing carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, bearing four substituents at positions around the ring. Two methyl groups sit on carbons that are meta to one another, giving a symmetric arrangement along one axis of the ring. An amino group (–NH2) and a nitro group (–NO2) occupy the two adjacent positions between the methyls, so the ring is fully substituted with no unsubstituted hydrogens except one. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing acceptor, while the amino group offers two hydrogen-bond donors and a lone pair acceptor, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the nitro and amino groups capable of limited rotation about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing five substituents: a methyl group at two positions, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group, with one ring position left as a hydrogen. The hydroxyl and nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, so they are ortho to each other, which allows an intramolecular interaction between them. The two methyl groups are placed meta to one another across the ring, giving the overall substitution pattern a somewhat asymmetric arrangement with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is aromatic and planar and rigid, while the methyl and nitro groups add limited conformational freedom at their attachment points. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitro group contributes strong hydrogen-bond acceptor character through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups and one primary amino group are attached to the ring, giving a trisubstituted pattern in which the amine sits between a methyl group and a ring hydrogen, while the second methyl is positioned meta to the amine along the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the methyl groups add only modest flexibility through rotation. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds and one acceptor site at the nitrogen lone pair. The structure has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, because the two methyl groups occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the amine.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a methyl group, a second methyl group on the adjacent position, and a formyl (aldehyde) group, so it is a trisubstituted benzene. The two methyl groups sit ortho and meta to each other, and the aldehyde is located ortho to one methyl group and para to the other, giving the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic core with a single rotatable aldehyde bond makes the structure largely planar and conformationally restricted.

The molecule is an arylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring, so its core scaffold is one aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit on the ring, one at the position para to the boronic acid and one at the ortho position, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, which together form the boronic acid functional group, and these OH groups can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its carbon-boron bond, adding a small degree of flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two methyl groups, placed on adjacent positions and one meta position relative to the acid, so it is a 2,4-dimethylbenzoic acid pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while its hydroxyl hydrogen can donate one, giving the acid group both donor and acceptor capability. The two methyl groups are nonpolar, electron-donating substituents that add steric bulk around the acid. The structure is planar and rigid across the ring, with only modest flexibility from rotation of the carboxyl and methyl groups, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis because the substituents are not evenly distributed.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, specifically a substituted imidazole ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3 of the ring. One nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen has a lone pair that makes it a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on a carbon adjacent to the NH nitrogen and one on a carbon next to the other nitrogen, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar ring system is rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl groups, which rotate freely but add little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a branched saturated hydrocarbon built on a linear chain of carbon atoms, with no rings and no heteroatoms. Its skeleton consists of a six-carbon main chain carrying two methyl branches, one at each of two internal positions, giving a 2,4-dimethylpentane-type scaffold. Because the chain is entirely sp3-hybridized and single-bonded, there are no ring systems, double bonds, or aromatic units to fuse or conjugate. The molecule contains no functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. Its branching creates a somewhat compact, irregular shape with only modest symmetry, and its freely rotating single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on that ring: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a second methyl group. The hydroxyl is a phenolic OH, which makes it a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two methyl groups are simple nonpolar alkyl substituents. The two methyls are adjacent to each other and the hydroxyl sits next to one of them, so the three groups occupy a contiguous cluster on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the substituents add little conformational flexibility, with only rotation of the OH and methyl groups available. The arrangement has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry because the three substituents differ in position and identity.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent ring positions, and the third substituent is an oxyacetic acid chain, an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the core a rigid, flat character, while the ether and acetic acid side chain adds a degree of rotational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the methyl groups and the side chain occupy non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a second methyl group, and an isothiocyanate group (-N=C=S). The two methyl groups sit ortho and meta to the isothiocyanate on the aromatic ring, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror symmetry beyond the local ring plane. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the overall framework is rigid, with the linear isothiocyanate group extending from the ring in a fixed geometry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are carbon-bound. Its only heteroatom functionality is the isothiocyanate group, whose nitrogen and sulfur can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a vinyl group (C=C) and two methyl groups, so it is a trisubstituted aromatic hydrocarbon built on a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The vinyl group sits on one ring carbon, with two adjacent methyl groups placed ortho and meta to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern without any mirror or rotational symmetry. The structure contains no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The ring is rigid and planar, while the vinyl group offers a small degree of conformational freedom around its single bond to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two nitro groups and one trifluoromethoxy group. The nitro groups sit at positions adjacent to one another, with one nitro group ortho to the trifluoromethoxy ether oxygen, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted substitution pattern on a single aromatic ring with no ring fusion. The trifluoromethoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a carbon carrying three fluorine atoms) adds a bulky, electron-withdrawing, fluorinated motif. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a possible local planarity, and the rigid aromatic core with nitro groups largely coplanar makes it fairly conformationally restricted, though the ether linkage allows some rotation. The oxygen atoms of the nitro and ether groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene skeleton, a fused pair of benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a rigid, planar aromatic framework. Two nitro groups (–NO2) are attached to the ring system, one on each of the two rings, and a hydroxyl group (–OH) sits on the carbon adjacent to one nitro group, so the substituents are unevenly distributed and the molecule lacks any symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Because the ring system is fully aromatic and the substituents are attached directly to it, the structure is essentially rigid with little conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries three substituents: one primary amino group and two nitro groups. The amino group sits at one ring position, and the two nitro groups are attached at the positions para and ortho to it, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no symmetry axis. The nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing, while the amino group is electron-donating, so the arrangement sets up a push-pull electronic character across the ring. Because the scaffold is a flat aromatic ring with largely planar substituents, the molecule is rigid. The amino group contributes two N–H hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the two nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group), and two nitro groups, each consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with formal charges. The nitro groups are attached at positions that are ortho and para relative to the methoxy group, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom about its C–O bond. The nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) sits at one position, and two nitro groups (NO2) occupy the positions adjacent to and para to it, giving a 1-carbonyl-2,4-dinitro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no fused or additional ring systems. The molecule has no symmetry, since the two nitro groups sit in inequivalent positions relative to the aldehyde. Its hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, as there are no OH or NH groups, while the oxygen atoms of the aldehyde and the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a sulfonyl chloride group and two nitro groups. The sulfonyl chloride, with its sulfur doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine, sits at one position on the ring, while the two nitro groups occupy the position adjacent to it and a position meta to it, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and planar, though the sulfonyl and nitro groups add some rotational freedom at their attachment points. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents differ in position and identity. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent since there are no N–H or O–H bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro and sulfonyl groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group (-COOH) at one position, and two nitro groups (-NO2) on the ring. The nitro groups sit at positions that are ortho and para to the carboxylic acid, respectively, giving an asymmetric 2,4-dinitro substitution pattern relative to the acid. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional ring systems, and the nitro and carboxyl groups are attached directly to the ring with limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the two nitro groups act as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps all three substituents onto one another.
