This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on one aromatic core: two nitro groups and a bromomethyl group. The nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons and at a meta-related position relative to each other on the ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The bromomethyl group is a CH2 linker bonded to a bromine atom, giving a flexible sp3 handle attached directly to the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the bromomethyl arm retains some rotational freedom. The nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. Two nitro groups (each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one drawn as a charged form) are attached to the ring, and a hydroxyl group bears the third substituent. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, with one nitro group on the adjacent carbon and the other nitro group on the carbon at the opposite meta-like position across the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the nitro and hydroxyl groups add some rotational freedom at their single bonds to the ring. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A thiocyanate group (–S–C≡N) is attached to one ring carbon, and two nitro groups (–NO2) occupy the adjacent position and the position para to the thiocyanate, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the linear, rod-like thiocyanate unit extends outward from it, so the overall framework is rigid with little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different and not arranged symmetrically around the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present, but the oxygen atoms of the two nitro groups and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing an acetic acid side chain, meaning a carboxylic acid group attached through a flexible methylene linker. Two nitro groups sit on the ring: one ortho to the linker and one para to it, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the aromatic core, with the ring itself being fully aromatic and planar. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while each nitro group contributes two oxygen acceptors. The CH2 linker gives the side chain rotational freedom, whereas the ring and nitro groups are comparatively rigid. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond its local planar geometry because the two nitro groups occupy inequivalent positions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with a methyl group attached to one ring carbon. Two nitro groups (–NO2) are attached to the ring, one para to the methyl group and one ortho to it, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the six-membered ring. There are no fused rings, and the aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and nitro groups add only minor conformational freedom. The molecule lacks a clear symmetry axis because the two nitro groups sit at different positions relative to the methyl. The nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two bulky tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls, are attached to the ring, and a hydroxyl group sits on the ring carbon between them. The hydroxyl is a phenolic OH that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygen's lone pairs and the ring's pi system make it a modest acceptor. The two tert-butyl groups are arranged on adjacent positions relative to the OH and on a third position across the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The tert-butyl groups are sterically crowded around the hydroxyl, and the ring itself is rigid, while the tert-butyl groups are conformationally fixed relative to it, so the molecule as a whole is rigid with little conformational flexibility and lacks any element of symmetry.

This molecule is a short, linear acyclic chain of six carbons, specifically a hexa-2,4-diyne skeleton with a hydroxyl group on each terminal carbon. Its two carbon-carbon triple bonds are conjugated through a single bond at the center, which makes the backbone rigid and rod-like, with essentially no ring systems or ring fusion. The molecule is symmetric about its central axis, since the two ends are identical mirror images of one another. Each terminal primary alcohol can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O-H group and an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, giving the molecule two donor and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is a straight, fully unsaturated six-carbon chain, hex-2,4-diyne, with two carbon-carbon triple bonds separated by a single sigma bond. It contains no rings, no heteroatoms, and no functional groups beyond the alkyne units, so its only substituents are two terminal methyl groups. The skeleton is linear and rigid around each alkyne, which forces the four sp-hybridized carbons into a collinear arrangement along the long axis. The molecule possesses a center of inversion and a two-fold symmetry axis, giving it a highly symmetric, rod-like shape. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no lone-pair acceptor sites, since the pi electron clouds of the triple bonds are the only electron-rich features.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one ring nitrogen, a pyridine scaffold. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring: one on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (position 2) and one on the carbon at position 4, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl groups. The lone pair on the nitrogen makes it a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic, unbranched five-carbon chain (pentane-derived skeleton) with two ketone carbonyl groups, one at each of the second and fourth carbon positions. Each carbonyl carbon is bonded to a terminal methyl group, so the structure is symmetric about the central methylene carbon that links the two carbonyls. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no stereocenters. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Each ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups (no O–H or N–H bonds).

The molecule is an acyclic, unbranched six-carbon chain with two methyl groups at the chain ends and a central CH2 linker. Each of the two internal carbons is double-bonded to an oxygen-bearing nitrogen, so the structure carries two oxime functional groups, one on each end of the chain. The two oxime units are located at the 2 and 5 positions of the hexane backbone, which gives the molecule an overall mirror-symmetric arrangement. Its flexible, open-chain skeleton contains no rings, and each oxime offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and an acceptor (the nitrogen lone pair and the oxygen).

The molecule is a small, fully saturated five-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one sulfur atom in the ring, with two carbonyl groups. The ring contains a lactam-type amide, where the nitrogen is bonded to a carbonyl carbon within the ring, and a thiocarbamate-type unit, where the sulfur is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that is also bonded to the ring nitrogen. There are no substituents on the ring, so the substitution pattern is unbranched and the structure is compact and nearly planar. The ring offers an N-H group that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the ring plane, and its rigid ring limits conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzothiazole, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. A methyl group sits on the carbon between the nitrogen and sulfur of the thiazole ring, and two additional methyl groups occupy adjacent positions on the benzene ring, giving a 5,6-dimethyl substitution pattern. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with the methyl substituents adding modest steric bulk but no major conformational freedom. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single approximate mirror plane through the fused system, so its symmetry is limited. The thiazole nitrogen is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is built around a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen and two nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2- and 5-positions of this ring are two naphthalene units, each connected through a single carbon-carbon bond at its alpha position. Each naphthalene is a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two benzene rings sharing an edge, so the scaffold is fully aromatic and largely planar. The two naphthyl groups are linked directly to the heterocycle without any flexible spacer, giving the molecule a rigid, extended shape with a near-twofold relationship between the two halves. The structure contains no conventional hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. The ring nitrogens and the oxadiazole oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, fully aromatic scaffold built from a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring bearing two para-linked phenyl-based arms on opposite sides. Each side consists of a para-substituted benzene ring attached directly to the oxadiazole, and the far end of each arm carries a further unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving four benzene rings in total connected by direct carbon-carbon single bonds. The oxadiazole is a five-membered heteroaromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, which is the only heteroatom-containing ring in the structure. The molecule is highly symmetric, approximately C2-symmetric about an axis through the oxadiazole, and it is rigid and planar with extended conjugation along its length. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens and the ring oxygen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a linear, fully aromatic oligoaryl system built around a central 1,3-oxazole ring that is substituted at its 2- and 5-positions. The oxazole's 5-position carries a para-linked phenyl ring, which is in turn bonded to a second para-substituted phenyl ring, giving an extended rod-like chain of aryl units. The 2-position carries a para-biphenyl group, so the two ends of the molecule are both terminated by unsubstituted phenyl rings. The structure has an approximately centrosymmetric, rod-shaped geometry and is conformationally rigid, with the aromatic units largely coplanar. The only heteroatoms are the oxazole oxygen and nitrogen, which can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a central 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2 and 5 positions of this ring are two para-nitrophenyl groups, each a benzene ring carrying a nitro group opposite the point of attachment. The overall skeleton is linear and highly conjugated, with the three aromatic rings coplanar and rigid, and the molecule possesses a two-fold axis of symmetry running through the oxadiazole ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the heterocycle and the oxygens of the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from a central thiophene ring flanked on both sides by aryl groups, with each terminus capped by a benzoxazole unit, giving a long, rigid, nearly linear π-conjugated scaffold. Each benzoxazole is a benzene ring fused to an oxazole, containing one oxygen and one nitrogen in a five-membered ring. Two tert-butyl groups sit on the benzene rings at the same relative position on each end, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the molecular center. The fused and linked aromatic system is largely flat and rigid, with few rotatable bonds. Ring nitrogens are the only hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two methyl groups and two chloromethyl groups, arranged in a 1,4-dimethyl-2,5-bis(chloromethyl) pattern (a para-disubstituted pattern on each side with alternating substituents). The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and planar. Each chloromethyl group (–CH2Cl) provides a reactive alkyl halide center, while the methyl groups are unreactive hydrocarbon substituents. The arrangement has an approximate center of inversion, giving it a fairly symmetric shape. The molecule is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, with only modest flexibility from rotation around the two CH2 linkers. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no conventional hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2) on one carbon and two trifluoromethyl groups (-CF3) on the others, giving a 2,5-bis(trifluoromethyl) substitution pattern relative to the sulfonamide. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused ring systems, so the scaffold is planar and rigid apart from rotation about the sulfur-carbon and carbon-carbon bonds to the substituents. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The sulfonamide contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the NH2 group and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl groups act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with two trifluoromethyl groups attached to the ring. The sulfonyl chloride, SO2Cl, sits on one ring carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group sits meta to it on the same ring, while a second trifluoromethyl group is ortho to the sulfonyl chloride, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single rigid, planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three substituents differ in position. The sulfonyl oxygens and the chlorine are polar, and the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two trifluoromethyl groups. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to one ring carbon, and the two CF3 groups are placed at the meta and para positions relative to it, so the substitution pattern is 1,3,4 (on the benzene ring, a trifluoromethyl sits meta to the carboxyl and the second sits para to the first). The scaffold is a single fully aromatic, planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion and no stereocenters, so its overall shape is rigid apart from rotation about the single bonds to the substituents. The molecule lacks symmetry because the two CF3 groups occupy inequivalent positions. The carboxylic acid group offers both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl and acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms of the CF3 groups are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered thiazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. Two trimethylsilyl groups, each bearing three methyl substituents on a silicon atom, are attached to the ring at two different carbon positions, one adjacent to the sulfur and the other adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The ring itself is planar and aromatic and carries one remaining aromatic C–H position, while the bulky silyl groups project outward and add considerable steric volume. The nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the silicon-carbon bonds contribute a flexible, nonpolar periphery.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two acetoxy groups, each consisting of an ester linkage (an oxygen bonded to the ring and to an acetyl carbonyl). The two ester groups sit para to one another across the ring, and a methyl group is attached to the carbon ortho to one of them, giving a trisubstituted aromatic core. The structure has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its overall shape is largely planar apart from rotation about the ester bonds, so it is fairly flexible at the side chains. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since all oxygen-bearing sites are carbonyl or ether-type oxygens, but the four oxygen atoms in the two ester groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis that fully maps the two ester groups onto each other because the methyl group breaks the symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying four substituents. Two amino groups sit on the ring, positioned para to each other, and a sulfonic acid group occupies a position adjacent to one of the amines, creating an ortho relationship between them. The aromatic core is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the sulfonic acid and amino hydrogens free to rotate slightly. Because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The sulfonic acid group contributes an acidic hydroxyl donor and multiple oxygen acceptors, while the two amino groups each supply hydrogen-bond donor capacity and nitrogen lone pairs that can act as acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The ring nitrogen sits at one position, and two primary amino groups are attached to the ring, one adjacent to the nitrogen and one further around the ring, giving a 2,5-diaminopyridine substitution pattern. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amino groups. The molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two amino groups equivalent. Both amino groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, which contains one sulfur atom in the ring. Two bromine atoms sit on the carbons flanking the sulfur, at the 2- and 5-positions, while two nitro groups occupy the remaining 3- and 4-positions, so every ring carbon is substituted. The compound is fully substituted and essentially planar, with a rigid framework and limited conformational flexibility apart from rotation of the nitro groups. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the two nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine) as its principal functional group. Around the ring, two bromine atoms and two fluorine atoms occupy the remaining positions in an unsymmetrical pattern, with the sulfonyl group flanked by one fluorine and one bromine on adjacent carbons. The aromatic core is a single, fully planar, rigid six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial one. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. The halogen substituents contribute additional weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional ring fusion. It carries a methyl group and two bromine atoms as substituents, placed at positions that give the ring an asymmetric arrangement, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The two bromines sit on carbons flanking the nitrogen and on the opposite side of the ring, while the methyl group sits adjacent to one bromine-bearing carbon, creating a crowded substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the only rotational freedom comes from the methyl group. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a methyl group and two bromine atoms as substituents. The ring is fully aromatic and planar with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a single rigid unit. Bromine atoms sit at two positions flanking the ring nitrogen's neighboring carbons, and the methyl group occupies an adjacent carbon, giving a trisubstituted, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The only freely rotating bond is the one connecting the methyl group to the ring, so the molecule is essentially rigid. The pyridine nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms are attached to the ring at the positions that flank it, giving a 2,5-dibromoaniline-type substitution pattern in which the amine is meta to one bromine and ortho to the other. The substituents are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the rotation of the C-N and C-Br bonds is essentially free. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the bromines contribute only weak halogen-bonding acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group (a formyl group, CHO) on one carbon, with two bromine atoms attached at the positions meta and para relative to each other across the ring, specifically at the 2 and 5 positions relative to the aldehyde. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the substituents are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis beyond the aromatic ring itself. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all ring and formyl hydrogens are bonded to carbon. The planar aromatic core is rigid, though the aldehyde group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring.

This molecule is a benzenesulfonyl chloride, built on a single benzene ring with no fused ring systems. The sulfonyl chloride group, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a chlorine, is attached directly to one ring carbon and serves as the principal functional group. Two bromine atoms sit on the ring at positions ortho and meta relative to the sulfonyl group, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonyl chloride tetrahedral geometry allows limited rotation about the carbon-sulfur bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two bromine atoms, giving a dibromobenzoic acid scaffold. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to one ring carbon, and the two bromine substituents sit on the ring at positions adjacent to that acid group and meta-related to each other, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the carboxyl group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, whereas the bromine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors and contribute no donor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a trifluoromethyl group and two bromine atoms. The two bromines occupy adjacent positions on the ring (ortho to each other), while the trifluoromethyl group sits on a neighboring carbon, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry plane through the ring. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the CF3 group is the only substituent with rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. The three fluorine atoms of the CF3 group and the bromine atoms can act only as weak acceptors, so overall hydrogen-bonding capability is very limited.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms other than the two bromine substituents. Its substitution pattern is 1,4-dibromo-2,5-dimethylbenzene: the two bromine atoms sit para to each other, and each is flanked by one methyl group, placing the methyls ortho to the bromines on opposite sides of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two methyl groups are small freely rotating appendages. The structure has a centre of inversion, giving it a high degree of symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the bromine atoms and the hydrocarbon framework provide no lone pairs or polar N–H or O–H groups able to participate in hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring: one at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (the 2-position) and one at the carbon meta to it on the opposite side (the 5-position), giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal rotational flexibility. Its overall shape is asymmetric because the two bromines sit at non-equivalent positions relative to the nitrogen. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle built on a thiazole scaffold, containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom in the ring. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents, one on the carbon between the nitrogen and sulfur and one on the carbon adjacent to the sulfur on the opposite side. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, so the framework is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no functional groups beyond the halogens and the ring heteroatoms, and it lacks any hydrogen-bond donors. The ring nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the bromine atoms contribute to polarizability.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, namely a thiophene ring, bearing two bromine substituents. The bromines sit at the two positions flanking the sulfur (the 2 and 5 positions), so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the sulfur atom and the midpoint of the opposite C3–C4 bond. The ring is planar and rigid, with its pi electrons delocalized around the entire aromatic system. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since it has no N–H or O–H bonds. Its only potential hydrogen-bond acceptor character comes from the weakly basic sulfur atom and the halogen atoms, which are poor acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two bromine atoms and two methyl groups, making it a dibromotoluene-type compound with a single six-membered aromatic ring and no fused rings. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape. The substituents sit at positions 1, 2, 4, and 5 relative to one another: one methyl group and one bromine are adjacent on the ring, while the other bromine is positioned para to the first bromine's neighboring carbon, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatoms are the two halogens, which can act as weak acceptors. Overall, the structure is compact, lipophilic in character, and contains no polar functional groups such as hydroxyls, amines, or carbonyls.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with two carbonyl groups positioned para to each other, making it a cyclohexadienedione. The ring contains two carbon-carbon double bonds conjugated with the two ketone groups, giving a fully planar, rigid framework with no ring fusion. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring carbons adjacent to the carbonyls, arranged symmetrically across the ring's central axis. The structure has a high degree of symmetry, with a two-fold axis passing through the midpoints of the two double bonds. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom. Two chlorine atoms are attached at the two carbons flanking the sulfur, leaving the other two ring carbons each bearing a nitro group. The two nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons next to each other, and both are strongly electron-withdrawing. The structure is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring and only limited torsional freedom for the nitro groups. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the sulfur atom and the midpoint of the opposite bond. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom among its ring positions. It carries three halogen substituents: two chlorine atoms and one iodine atom, distributed around the ring so that the substitution pattern is asymmetric, with no mirror or rotational symmetry. There are no fused ring systems and no additional functional groups beyond these halogens. The rigid, planar aromatic framework leaves little conformational flexibility, since the halogens lie in the plane of the ring. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group, and two chlorine atoms, so it is a fully aromatic, rigid, flat scaffold with no saturated rings and no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the two chlorines sit on adjacent carbons, one of which is next to the acid-bearing carbon, while the nitro group lies meta to the acid on the opposite side of the ring. Because the four substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro group contributes two oxygen hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the structure is compact, planar, and only the carboxylic acid group has meaningful rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings or extra ring systems. Going around the ring, it carries an amino group (–NH2) that acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, a nitro group (–NO2) that acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, and two chlorine atoms as ring substituents. The two chlorines sit at positions that leave the ring asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the nitro and amino groups can rotate only slightly about their bonds to the ring. Overall, the structure offers both donor and acceptor sites on a compact, flat framework.

The molecule is an acetoacetanilide-type structure: an acetyl group (CH3-C=O) connected through a methylene to an amide carbonyl, which is bonded to a nitrogen attached to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring carries two chlorine atoms at the meta and para positions relative to the amide nitrogen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The amide linkage gives one hydrogen-bond donor (the N-H) and two acceptors (the two carbonyl oxygens). The aryl ring is planar and rigid, while the acetoacetyl side chain is comparatively flexible.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) on one ring carbon and two chlorine atoms on the remaining positions. The chlorines sit at positions that place one halogen meta to the acetyl group and the other ortho to it, giving an unsymmetrical 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused ring systems. The acetyl carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Apart from rotation about the bond linking the carbonyl to the ring, the scaffold is largely rigid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two chlorine atoms and one primary amino group are attached to the ring. The amino group sits at one carbon, with a chlorine on the adjacent carbon and another chlorine positioned meta to the amine on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational flexibility beyond the amine hydrogens. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its nitrogen lone pair, while the chlorine substituents are weak halogen acceptors. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are unevenly placed.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, with two chlorine atoms as substituents on the same ring, giving a disubstituted benzaldehyde scaffold. The aldehyde carbon sits directly on the aromatic ring and is flanked by a chlorine atom at one ortho position, while the second chlorine occupies the meta position relative to the aldehyde, so the two halogens lie on the same side of the ring and are not symmetrically placed. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, rigid and planar, with the carbonyl group conjugated to the ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the substitution pattern breaks any mirror plane through the ring. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent, as there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzamide, with a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group (a carbonyl attached to an NH2 group) on one carbon. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions meta and para relative to each other across the aromatic core, with one chlorine ortho to the amide group and the other para to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the amide carbonyl and NH2 group can rotate only modestly about the ring-carbonyl bond. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 hydrogens and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The chlorine atoms are weak halogen contacts and do not act as meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors in this context.

The molecule is a phenyl ring bearing a boronic acid group, with two chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The boronic acid, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and the two chlorines sit on the ring at positions that give a 2,5-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the boron-bearing carbon. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered system with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring. The boronic acid's two hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and their oxygen atoms as acceptors, while the chlorines contribute only weak halogen-type interactions. Overall the scaffold is rigid and largely planar, with the B(OH)2 group offering the main rotational flexibility around its single bond to the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries a sulfonyl chloride group, with two chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The sulfonyl group, SO2Cl, is attached to one ring carbon, and the two chlorines sit on the ring at positions ortho and meta relative to it, giving a 2,5-dichloro substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is flat and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the molecule has only a limited, mostly rotational flexibility around the sulfur–carbon bond. It lacks any symmetry beyond a possible planar arrangement, since the substituents are unevenly placed. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms and a carbohydrazide group, which is a carbonyl carbon attached to a hydrazine unit (NH-NH2). The aromatic ring is substituted at three positions: the hydrazide carbonyl sits at one carbon, a chlorine at the meta position relative to it, and a second chlorine at the ortho position, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The amide-like C=O can accept hydrogen bonds, while the terminal NH and NH2 groups can donate them. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the hydrazide linkage contributes some rotational flexibility around its single bonds.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two chlorine atoms, with the acid carbon attached directly to the ring. Because the ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, the scaffold is compact and essentially planar, and the molecule is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the carboxyl group. The two chlorines sit ortho and para relative to the acid carbon's neighboring positions, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry plane through the whole molecule. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH substituent, i.e., a primary alcohol bearing a benzylic carbon) is attached at one ring position, and two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions that place them adjacent to one another and to the hydroxymethyl-bearing carbon, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2OH group retains some rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the chlorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions that are para to each other across the ring, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 carbon bearing a bromine) sits on the carbon adjacent to one of the chlorines, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the bromomethyl side chain provides a single rotatable bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, and the halogens can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and two chlorine atoms, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two hydroxyl groups sit para to each other on the ring, and each chlorine is placed ortho to one of the hydroxyls, giving a symmetric 2,5-dichloro-substitution pattern across a hydroquinone-type core. The structure has a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoints of the C–C bonds that carry the hydroxyls and chlorines. Because the ring is aromatic and rigid, with only the hydroxyl oxygen–hydrogen bonds free to rotate, the molecule is largely planar and inflexible. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on that ring: a hydroxyl group (–OH) and two chlorine atoms. The hydroxyl is attached at one carbon, one chlorine sits meta to it, and the second chlorine sits para to the hydroxyl on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern about the ring. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically, the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the O–H bond providing rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework. Attached to one ring carbon is an isocyanate group, a nitrogen double-bonded to a carbon that is itself double-bonded to oxygen, which makes this a highly electrophilic, linear, cumulene-type functional group. Two chlorine atoms are bonded to the ring at positions ortho and meta to the isocyanate, creating a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern. The molecule is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system and only limited flexibility from the linear isocyanate unit. It has no internal symmetry plane due to the asymmetric placement of the substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen and nitrogen atoms of the isocyanate and the chlorine atoms can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent positions, so it is a dichlorinated phenylhydrazine with the substituents at ortho and meta relative to the hydrazine attachment. The aromatic core is a single fully conjugated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The hydrazine group is flexible and can rotate about its C–N and N–N bonds, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar. The two terminal NH and NH2 hydrogens act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the nitrogen atoms, along with the chlorine atoms, can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two methyl groups and two chlorine atoms, arranged so that the two chlorines sit on carbons separated by the methyls in a 2,5-dichloro-p-xylene-type pattern. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Its only functional groups are the aryl chlorides and the alkyl methyl groups, with no hydroxyl, amine, carbonyl, or other polar groups present. The substitution pattern is para-related on the methyls and the chlorines are placed to give a centrosymmetric arrangement, so the molecule has a high degree of symmetry. Because the ring is planar and rigid with only methyl rotors, it is conformationally restricted, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability beyond weak halogen contributions.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, a pyridine scaffold with two chlorine atoms attached as substituents. One chlorine sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position, and the other is on the carbon three positions away at the 5-position, giving a 2,5-disubstituted substitution pattern with no additional ring fusion. The structure is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the C–Cl bonds, and it lacks any molecular symmetry because the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the chlorines serve only as weak halogen-type contacts.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing three substituents. A boronic acid group, -B(OH)2, is attached at one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions flanking the nitrogen and at a position meta to the boron-bearing carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the pyridine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, namely a thiophene ring. It carries two chlorine substituents, one on each carbon flanking the sulfur, which places them at the 2 and 5 positions. This symmetric substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold axis of symmetry through the sulfur atom and the midpoint of the opposite carbon-carbon bond. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the chlorines contribute no hydrogen-bond donors and only very weak acceptor character, so the molecule has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a thiophene scaffold, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to one ring carbon, which is adjacent to the sulfur, while the remaining ring carbons carry chlorine substituents at the positions flanking the sulfur on one side and at the 4-position on the other side. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type interactions. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no additional fused rings. Two chlorine atoms and one methyl group are attached to the ring as substituents, with the methyl group positioned adjacent to one chlorine, creating a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Because the ring is planar and aromatic and the substituents are small and rigid, the molecule is essentially inflexible, with only the methyl group's C–H bonds able to rotate freely. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, so its substitution pattern is asymmetric. It has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and the chlorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two ethoxy groups (–OCH2CH3) and one primary amino group (–NH2). The ring is a single, unfused aromatic six-membered system, so the scaffold is simple and fully planar. The two ethoxy groups sit para to each other, with the amino group ortho to one of them, giving a 1,4-diethoxy-2-aminobenzene substitution pattern. The ethyl tails are flexible, while the aromatic core is rigid. Hydrogen-bond capability is modest: the amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds, and the nitrogen and the two ether oxygens can each accept them.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two ethoxy groups (–OCH2CH3) and a benzamide-type amide substituent, with the amide nitrogen bonded to the central ring and its carbonyl bonded to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are linked through the amide bridge, so the molecule consists of two separate six-membered aromatic rings joined by –NH–C(=O)–. The two ethoxy groups sit on the same ring at positions that are meta and para to one another relative to the amide attachment, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern on that ring, while the other phenyl ring is monosubstituted. Overall the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry, and its rotatable ethoxy chains and amide linkage give it moderate flexibility around the aromatic cores. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, two fluorine atoms, and one hydroxyl group, giving a single aromatic six-membered scaffold with no fused rings. The aldehyde carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the substituents are arranged around the ring so that the two fluorines sit at positions meta and para to the aldehyde, with the hydroxyl located between them on one side. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups add limited rotational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The arrangement lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: a methoxy group, two fluorine atoms, and an aldehyde (formyl) group, arranged so the ring carries a single aromatic core with no ring fusion. The methoxy group is an ether oxygen linked to a methyl, and the aldehyde carbonyl is attached directly to the ring, making it an aryl aldehyde. The two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent-to-carbonyl and meta-related positions, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is essentially rigid and planar, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups able to rotate about their single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups are not present in that sense; instead the ring carries one methoxy substituent (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group, attached to the ring), two fluorine atoms, and one nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen). The fluorines sit ortho to each other, and the nitrile is positioned adjacent to one of them, while the methoxy group occupies a separate position on the ring, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core and the nitrile are rigid and planar, though the methoxy group has some rotational freedom about its ring bond. The nitrile nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two amino-related substituents: one primary amine (-NH2) and two fluorine atoms, arranged on adjacent positions around the aromatic core. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no additional ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid benzene framework. The amine is ortho to one fluorine and meta to the other, giving an unsymmetrical 1,2,4-type substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its two N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through the nitrogen lone pair), while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall the molecule is small, compact, and conformationally rigid apart from rotation of the amine group.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group (a primary amide, with one nitrogen bearing two hydrogens and a carbonyl oxygen) on one ring carbon. Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions ortho and meta relative to that carboxamide, specifically one ortho to it and one on the opposite side of the ring at a meta-like arrangement, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the amide C–N bond gives a degree of conformational restriction without adding significant flexibility. The amide group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, and the fluorine atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group, with two fluorine atoms on the ring. The sulfonamide carbon-sulfur bond is attached to one ring carbon, and the sulfur carries two oxygen atoms and an NH2 group. The two fluorines sit on adjacent ring positions, with one fluorine ortho to the sulfonamide and the other meta to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the sulfonamide adding only modest rotational freedom. The NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the sulfonyl oxygens and the fluorines can accept them.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with two fluorine atoms attached at positions that flank the acid-bearing carbon in a 2,5-relationship on the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic benzenoid system with no ring fusion. The carboxyl group is a strong hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar framework. Its rigidity is high because the aromatic ring is planar and only the carboxyl group has a single rotatable bond connecting it to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group on one carbon and fluorine atoms on two other ring positions, giving a compact aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The nitrile (cyano) group is a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing substituent that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, while the aromatic fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and carry no donor capability. The substituents sit in an asymmetric pattern around the ring, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar frame. The fully aromatic ring is rigid and flat, and the substituents lie in the plane of the ring with little conformational freedom, so the molecule as a whole is essentially inflexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a substituted cinnamic-type acid built on a benzene ring, with a three-carbon acrylic chain attached to one side. The chain consists of a carboxylic acid group joined to an alkene that has a trans (E) geometry across its carbon-carbon double bond, which keeps the acid and aryl portions extended in a roughly linear arrangement. The benzene ring carries two fluorine atoms on adjacent positions relative to the alkenyl attachment point, placed at the ortho and meta positions, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal mirror symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the conjugated alkene and carboxyl group add some conformational limits, and rotation about the single bond linking the alkene to the ring allows modest flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the fluorine atoms can serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms, one on the 2-position and one on the 5-position relative to the side chain. Attached to the ring is a two-carbon unit: a secondary alcohol carbon that also carries a carboxylic acid group, giving an alpha-hydroxy acid motif. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the side chain offers some rotational freedom around the bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two fluorines sit at unequal positions relative to the side chain. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups together provide three hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms and one hydroxyl group, so it is a difluorophenol. The aromatic six-membered carbocycle is a single planar scaffold with no ring fusion. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, with a fluorine on the adjacent carbon and another fluorine positioned on the ring at a meta relationship to the hydroxyl, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is fully rigid, while the hydroxyl's O–H bond can rotate freely. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the fluorine atoms serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, and carries a two-carbon side chain ending in a carboxylic acid group (a CH2 linker attached to a C(=O)OH unit). Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions meta to each other relative to the side chain, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2-COOH arm allows rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) and a fluorine atom, with a second fluorine on the ring at a position meta to the hydrazine. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the fluorines make the substitution pattern asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, while the hydrazine side chain has rotatable single bonds that give it conformational flexibility. The terminal and internal nitrogens of the hydrazine group can both act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms and one methyl group, with no fused or additional ring systems. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbocycle, and the substituents sit at three positions around it: a methyl group on one carbon, with fluorine atoms on the carbon adjacent to the methyl group and on a carbon across the ring from it (a 1,2,4-type pattern relative to the methyl). The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The planar aromatic framework is rigid, while the methyl group can rotate freely. Fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a five-membered sulfur-containing ring, specifically a sulfolene scaffold, with one carbon-carbon double bond located within the ring and a methyl group attached to one of the sp2 carbons. The sulfur atom is fully oxidized, bearing two terminal oxygen atoms in a sulfone arrangement, which makes it the dominant polar feature of the structure. The ring is not fully flat or fully rigid, since the saturated carbon next to the sulfone adds some conformational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl substituent breaks any mirror relationship. The sulfone oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries an acetyl group, a ketone with a methyl attached to the carbonyl carbon, on one ring carbon, and two hydroxyl groups, which are phenolic OH substituents, on other ring carbons. The two hydroxyls sit in a 1,4 relationship to each other, while the acetyl group sits ortho to one of them, giving a trisubstituted aromatic ring with an asymmetric substitution pattern. The core is rigid and planar, with only the acetyl methyl and carbonyl offering limited rotational freedom. The hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and their oxygens as acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Attached directly to the ring is an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen), along with two hydroxyl groups placed at positions that give a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern, so the substituents are not symmetrically arranged. The aromatic core and the planar carbonyl make the scaffold rigid and flat, with the hydroxyl groups able to rotate only slightly about their ring bonds. Both hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a propiophenone-type structure: a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon ketone chain (an ethyl group attached to a carbonyl) directly on one ring carbon. Two hydroxyl groups sit on the ring at positions that create a 1,3-relationship to the ketone and a para-like pairing with each other, giving a 2,5-dihydroxy-substituted aryl ketone pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the ethyl and carbonyl portion providing conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the ketone and the two hydroxyls occupy inequivalent positions. Both phenolic hydroxyls can donate hydrogen bonds, and the ketone oxygen plus the hydroxyl oxygens can accept them, with one hydroxyl able to form an intramolecular interaction with the adjacent carbonyl.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle, bearing two iodine atoms as its only substituents. One iodine sits on a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen (the 2-position), and the other sits on a carbon two positions away from the nitrogen on the opposite side of the ring (the 5-position), giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern. The scaffold is planar and fully rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no fused rings. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since there are no N–H or O–H groups, but the ring nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. It has no molecular symmetry axis because the two iodines occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the nitrogen.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with a single sulfur atom and four carbon atoms. Two iodine atoms are attached directly to the ring carbons flanking the sulfur, at the 2 and 5 positions, giving a symmetric 2,5-disubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the bulky, polarizable iodine substituents extend outward from it without introducing any flexible chain. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Its only potential acceptor sites are the sulfur atom, which is a weak acceptor, and the iodine atoms, which can act as weak halogen-bond donors rather than conventional acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring in a 1,4 (para) relationship, and an acetyl group (–C(=O)CH3) sits at a position ortho to one of the methoxy groups, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, while the acetyl and methoxy groups add some conformational freedom through rotation about their single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen of the ketone and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. It lacks any internal symmetry axis because the acetyl group breaks the symmetry of the substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring: two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) and one primary amino group. The methoxy groups sit para to each other, while the amino group lies ortho to one of them, giving a 1,4-dialkoxy, 2-amino substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy groups add modest conformational flexibility around their C–O bonds. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry that would make all positions equivalent, because the amino group breaks the symmetry of the substitution pattern. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the oxygen atoms of the two methoxy groups together with the nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring, located para to one another, and a formyl group (–CHO) sits on a carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, giving a 1,4-dimethoxy-2-formyl substitution pattern. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two ether oxygens provide additional acceptor sites and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and formyl groups can rotate about their single bonds, adding modest conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric because the aldehyde breaks the mirror relationship that the two methoxy groups would otherwise create.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups and one boronic acid group, giving a simple aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The two methoxy substituents (–OCH3) sit in a para relationship to each other on the ring, while the boronic acid group, –B(OH)2, is attached on the carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, making it a 1,2,4-trisubstituted arrangement. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, though the methoxy and boronic acid groups can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the boronic acid. The two hydroxyl groups on boron can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one primary sulfonamide. The two methoxy groups are attached at positions that are para to each other, while the sulfonamide sits ortho to one of them, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and its planar geometry is largely rigid, with only the methoxy and sulfonamide groups able to rotate about their bonds. The sulfonamide (SO2NH2) contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the nitrogen and two acceptor oxygens on the sulfur, while the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and a sulfonyl chloride group. The two methoxy (–OCH3) groups sit para to each other on the ring, one at the 1-position and the other at the 4-position, while the sulfonyl chloride (–SO2Cl) is attached at the 2-position, ortho to one of the methoxy groups. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring, so the scaffold is compact and rigid, with only the methyl rotations of the ether groups and the sulfur–carbon bond adding conformational freedom. The molecule lacks an overall mirror or rotational symmetry because the sulfonyl chloride breaks the otherwise symmetric para-dimethoxy pattern. The ether oxygens and the sulfonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two methoxy groups, forming a 2,5-dimethoxybenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the carboxyl group sits at one position with the two methoxy ether oxygens at the positions meta and para to the one adjacent to it, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern without any mirror or rotational symmetry. The molecule is largely planar and rigid across the ring, while the two methoxy and one carboxyl group contribute some rotational flexibility around their single bonds. Hydrogen-bond capability is asymmetric: the carboxylic acid offers one donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while each methoxy oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached through oxygen atoms, one at a position para to the other and one ortho to a nitrile group (–C≡N), which is a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing carbon-nitrogen triple bond. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,4-trisubstituted, which leaves the ring without any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the two methoxy groups retain some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the two ether oxygens and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: two methoxy groups (–OCH3) at the positions para to each other and an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) on a carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, giving a 1,4-dimethoxy-2-isocyanato substitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane-like approximate symmetry about the axis through the isocyanate and the opposite ring carbon, with the methoxy groups being the flexible parts. The isocyanate's linear N=C=O unit is rigid, while the methoxy groups can rotate. The ether oxygens and the isocyanate oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups and one isothiocyanate group, making it a substituted aromatic compound with a single six-membered carbocyclic ring and no ring fusion. The two methoxy substituents (–OCH3) sit at positions para to each other, while the isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) is attached to the carbon adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, giving a 1,4,2-substitution pattern on the ring. The molecule has no strict rotational symmetry because the isothiocyanate group breaks the symmetry of the two methoxy groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups add some conformational freedom around their C–O bonds. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups can accept hydrogen bonds, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a phenylacetic acid scaffold: a single benzene ring bearing a –CH2–COOH side chain. The aromatic ring is fully substituted with two methoxy groups (–OCH3) placed on positions that are meta to each other across the ring, with the acetic acid arm attached between them, giving a 2,5-dimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the side chain. There are no ring fusions, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no true symmetry axis because the side chain breaks the symmetry of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methylene linker and the methoxy groups provide some rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, and each ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a trisubstituted aromatic compound with a single six-membered carbocyclic scaffold and no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached at positions para to each other, while a methyl group sits adjacent to one of the methoxy-bearing carbons, creating an ortho-relationship between the methyl and one methoxy group. The ether oxygens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it contains no N–H or O–H groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and methyl groups provide limited rotational freedom. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane that passes through all three substituents.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle built on a 1,3,4-thiadiazole core, which contains one sulfur atom and two adjacent nitrogen atoms in the ring. It carries two methyl substituents, one on each of the two carbon atoms that flank the nitrogen pair, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis running through the sulfur atom. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, making the overall scaffold rigid with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks N–H or O–H groups, but the two ring nitrogen atoms can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an acyclic, unbranched-backbone hydrocarbon of eight carbons, built around a central chain that carries two terminal alkene groups. Each terminal carbon is a methylene (=CH2) bonded to a quaternary sp2 carbon that also bears a methyl substituent, so the two double bonds sit at the ends of the molecule and are symmetrically placed. The overall skeleton is C2-symmetric, with the molecule having no rings and no stereocenters. Because there are no rings and only single-bond linkages between the chain segments, the structure is fairly flexible. It contains no heteroatoms or polar groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a 2,5-dimethylpyrrole ring with its nitrogen bonded to a phenyl group, giving an N-aryl pyrrole scaffold. The five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring carries two methyl substituents on the carbons flanking the nitrogen, placed symmetrically at the 2 and 5 positions. The phenyl ring is attached directly to the pyrrole nitrogen and is unsubstituted, so the two aromatic rings are linked by a single N–C bond, with no ring fusion between them. The biaryl-like connection permits some rotation about the N–C bond, though steric crowding from the adjacent methyl groups restricts it somewhat. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the pyrrole nitrogen is fully substituted, and its aromatic nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the ring, so it offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built around a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries two methyl groups and an aldehyde (formyl) group, with an N-linked phenyl ring attached to the nitrogen. The pyrrole core is aromatic and planar, and the phenyl ring is joined to its nitrogen by a single bond, which allows some rotation about that bond. The formyl group sits on a carbon adjacent to the methyl-bearing ring carbon, giving a substitution pattern that is asymmetric overall. The carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because all N–H and O–H positions are absent.

The molecule is an acyclic hydrocarbon built on a branched, six-carbon chain with two carbon-carbon double bonds. Its backbone contains a conjugated diene unit, with one double bond on each end of a central single bond, and methyl groups sit at both internal positions, creating a symmetric, roughly linear scaffold. There are no rings, no heteroatoms, and no functional groups beyond the alkene units. Because the molecule has no polar atoms, it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor. Its conjugated, unbranched core gives it limited flexibility, with rotation possible mainly around the single bonds bearing the methyl substituents.

This molecule is a linear, fully conjugated dicarboxylic acid built around a six-carbon chain with a central carbon-carbon double bond and an additional terminal-like alkene pattern, giving a symmetric backbone with two methyl branches. Each end of the chain carries a carboxylic acid group attached to an alpha carbon bearing a methyl substituent, so the substitution pattern mirrors itself across the center. The conjugated diene system is rigid and planar, restricting rotation about its double bonds and fixing the overall shape. There are no ring systems or ring fusions present. Each carboxyl group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, making the molecule capable of extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carbon chain built from a six-carbon backbone with no rings and no double bonds, so it is entirely flexible and can adopt many conformations. Each terminal carbon is quaternary, bearing two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, so the two ends are structurally equivalent and the molecule has a two-fold symmetry through its central portion. The two functional groups are tertiary alcohols, meaning each hydroxyl oxygen is attached to a carbon that carries no hydrogen. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving two donor and two acceptor sites in total. The methyl groups on the ends are sterically bulky, which shields the hydroxyl groups somewhat.

The molecule is a substituted furan, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, bearing two methyl groups on the ring at positions that flank the oxygen and the adjacent carbon. The third ring position carries an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both a double-bonded oxygen and a chlorine atom, which makes it a highly reactive acylating functional group. The ring itself is planar and rigid, while the acyl chloride group can rotate slightly about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no OH or NH groups, but the ring oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiazole ring, containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, bearing three substituents. A methyl group sits at the 2-position of the ring, adjacent to the nitrogen, and a second methyl group occupies the 5-position next to the sulfur. The 4-position carries an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached through a single bond, which can rotate relative to the heterocycle and so adds some conformational flexibility. The structure has no stereocenters and only a limited degree of symmetry, since the substituents are not arranged symmetrically around the ring. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.
