The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no fused ring systems. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, and a primary amino group is attached to a third carbon, so the substitution pattern is a trisubstituted benzene in which the amine sits adjacent to one of the methyls. The compound is aromatic and essentially planar, with limited conformational flexibility beyond the rotation of the methyl and amino groups. Its only hydrogen-bond donors are the two hydrogens on the amino nitrogen, and the nitrogen lone pair can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The arrangement lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and one boronic acid group, giving a 2,5-dimethylphenylboronic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and it is flat and rigid. The two methyl groups sit para to each other on the ring, one of them positioned ortho to the boronic acid carbon, which breaks any mirror symmetry across the ring. The B(OH)2 group is a trigonal planar boron bearing two hydroxyl groups, so the molecule offers two hydrogen-bond donors through the O-H bonds and two acceptor sites through the oxygen atoms. The methyl groups are nonpolar and contribute only steric bulk and mild electron donation to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and one carboxylic acid group, giving it a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the two methyl substituents sit at positions that flank it on one side and lie across the ring on the other, producing an asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful internal symmetry axis. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carboxyl and methyl groups provide limited rotational freedom around their single bonds to the ring. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, making it the dominant site for intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The methyl groups are nonpolar and contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic aromatic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring, forming a benzothiazole core. The thiazole portion contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom separated by a carbon that bears a methyl substituent, while the fused benzene ring carries a second methyl group on the carbon meta to the ring fusion. The fused system is fully planar and aromatic, giving it a rigid, flat geometry with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a loose resemblance between the two ring faces, because the two methyl groups sit at asymmetric positions. The thiazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit on the ring, and a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH substituent) is attached adjacent to one of them, giving a 1,4-dimethyl substitution pattern with the hydroxymethyl group on the position next to a methyl. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions around the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The alcohol oxygen carries a hydrogen that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and its lone pairs can act as an acceptor.

The molecule is a substituted cinnamic acid built on a benzene ring that carries two methyl groups at positions that place them on opposite sides of the attachment point, giving a 2,5-dimethyl-substituted pattern relative to the vinyl side chain. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to it is a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond leading to a carboxylic acid group, so the side chain is an α,β-unsaturated acid conjugated with the aromatic ring. This conjugation and the planar arrangement of the double bond make the acid portion fairly rigid, while the molecule as a whole has no symmetry axis because the methyl groups are not equivalent. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the methyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen atom, which is a furan ring. It carries two methyl groups, one on each carbon adjacent to the oxygen, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the ring oxygen (2,5-dimethyl). The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the two methyl C–C single bonds, which rotate freely. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, since it lacks any O–H or N–H groups. The ring oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substitution pattern carries two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group on the ring, with the hydroxyl flanked by one methyl on an adjacent carbon, giving a 1,2,5-type arrangement of the three substituents around the ring. Because the substituents are not symmetrically placed, the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond what the planar ring itself provides. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups are free to rotate, so overall flexibility is low. The phenolic hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and no other polar functional groups are present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and a carboxymethyl side chain, making it a substituted phenylacetic acid. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings. The ring carries methyl substituents at two positions and a CH2-COOH group at a third, which sits adjacent to one of the methyl groups, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The carboxylic acid is the main functional group, offering one hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the CH2 linker gives the acid group some rotational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two methyl groups and a cyanomethyl (acetonitrile-type) side chain. The aromatic six-membered ring is the central scaffold, with no ring fusion, and it carries three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern: one methyl at position 1 and one methyl at position 4 (para to each other), and the CH2–C≡N group at position 2, adjacent to one of the methyls. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2–C≡N side chain provides a degree of rotational freedom about the single bond joining it to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring itself.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 (para) relationship, forming a pyrazine scaffold. Two methyl groups are attached to ring carbons, one at position 2 and one at position 5, giving a symmetric 2,5-disubstituted pattern across the ring. The fully conjugated, planar aromatic core is rigid, with the two methyl substituents as the only flexible-free additions and no rotatable bonds of significance. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall, the structure is compact, flat, and possesses a centre of inversion symmetry.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered pyrazole-type ring is fused to a six-membered pyrimidinone-type ring through a shared nitrogen-carbon bond, forming a planar, rigid scaffold. The five-membered ring carries a single methyl substituent on one carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, while the six-membered ring bears a second methyl group on the carbon next to an N-H nitrogen, together with a carbonyl (C=O) group that sits opposite the fusion. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and the unprotonated ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Its only notable flexibility comes from the rotation of the two methyl groups, since the fused core itself is essentially flat.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a vinyl group (CH=CH2) and two methyl groups. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the core is planar and rigid. The vinyl group sits on one ring carbon, flanked by a methyl group on the adjacent carbon, while a second methyl group occupies a position para to the vinyl-bearing carbon's neighbour, giving an asymmetric 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocentres and only limited symmetry, and it lacks any hydroxyl, amine, or carbonyl groups, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds and has no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor sites beyond the delocalised pi system.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, namely a thiophene ring, bearing two methyl substituents. The two methyl groups sit on the carbons flanking the sulfur (positions 2 and 5), which makes the substitution pattern symmetric about an axis running through the sulfur atom. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl C–C bonds. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom is only a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor because its lone pairs are partly delocalized into the aromatic system.

This molecule is built from a central five-membered 1,3,4-oxadiazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen and two adjacent nitrogen atoms. Attached at the 2- and 5-positions of this ring are two phenyl groups, giving a symmetric 2,5-diaryl substitution pattern. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted and bonded directly to the heterocycle, so the scaffold is a linear, fully conjugated system of three connected aromatic rings. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with few rotatable bonds. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens and the ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a five-membered, partially unsaturated sulfur heterocycle: a sulfolene-type ring containing one sulfone group (SO2) and one ketone carbonyl, which together make the ring electron-poor. Two phenyl rings are attached, one to the carbon-carbon double bond and one to the saturated carbon adjacent to the sulfone, giving an aryl-substituted, non-planar scaffold with some conformational freedom around the single bonds to the phenyl groups. The enol-type hydroxyl group on the alkene carbon adds an additional hydrogen-bond donor site, while the sulfone oxygens and the ketone oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the two phenyl groups sit on different carbons of the ring.

The molecule is built on a central five-membered furan ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen atom. Attached at the 2 and 5 positions of this furan are two phenyl rings, one on each side, so the overall scaffold is a linear, symmetric diaryl furan. All three rings are aromatic and fully conjugated, giving the structure a flat, rigid, and extended shape with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation about the single bonds joining the rings. The molecule contains no conventional functional groups such as hydroxyls, amines, or carbonyls. Its only heteroatom is the furan oxygen, which can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on an oxazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom. Two phenyl rings are attached to this core: one at the carbon between the oxygen and nitrogen (position 2) and one at the carbon at position 5, which sits next to the ring oxygen. The overall scaffold is a fully conjugated, planar arrangement of three aromatic rings, which makes the molecule rigid with very little conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups, but the ring nitrogen and oxygen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric about the central ring, with the two phenyl groups attached at different positions.

This molecule is a para-benzoquinone core, a six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups at opposite positions with two C=C double bonds between them. Two phenyl rings are attached to the quinone ring at the two remaining carbon positions, which are related by a center of symmetry through the middle of the ring, giving the molecule a centrosymmetric arrangement. The quinone carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. The conjugated, fully planar framework, together with the directly bonded aryl groups, makes the structure rigid with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which serves as the central aromatic scaffold, bearing six positions of substitution. Two tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, are attached to the ring, and two hydroxyl groups are attached as phenolic substituents. The substitution pattern places the two hydroxyls para to one another, with each tert-butyl group ortho to one hydroxyl, giving the ring a symmetric arrangement with a centre of inversion. The bulky tert-butyl groups restrict rotation around the ring-substituent bonds and contribute a rigid, sterically crowded shape. Each phenolic hydroxyl can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, so the molecule has two donor and two acceptor sites.

This molecule is a substituted para-benzoquinone, built on a six-membered cyclohexadiene-dione ring that is fully conjugated and essentially planar. Two carbonyl groups sit opposite each other on the ring, and two tert-butyl groups occupy the remaining positions, one on each side of the quinone core, giving a 2,5-di-tert-butyl substitution pattern. The molecule has a centre of inversion, so it is symmetric about its middle. The bulky tert-butyl groups are rigid and sterically demanding, limiting flexibility to little more than rotation of their methyl groups. The carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a straight, unbranched five-carbon chain, with no rings and no fused ring systems, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic. Two ketone carbonyl groups sit at the chain termini positions, each bearing a methyl group on one side, making it a symmetric 2,5-dione with the two carbonyls related by a mirror plane through the central methylene pair. The molecule is fairly flexible because all of its bonds are single bonds apart from the two C=O groups, allowing free rotation along the carbon backbone. Each carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since it carries no O–H or N–H bonds.

The molecule is a bridged bicyclic hydrocarbon built from a seven-carbon framework in which two carbon-carbon double bonds sit on opposite sides of the bridged system. Its scaffold is a norbornadiene-type core: a central five-membered ring linked by a one-carbon bridge, giving a compact, cage-like geometry. The structure contains no heteroatoms and no functional groups beyond the two alkene units, and it carries no substituents, so the substitution pattern is unadorned. The framework is rigid, with the bridged rings locked in place, and the molecule has a degree of local symmetry about its central axis. It has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since its only atoms are carbon and hydrogen.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexene-dione scaffold, containing one carbon-carbon double bond conjugated with a ketone. Two ketone groups sit on the ring: one is conjugated with the alkene, and the other is an adjacent carbonyl flanking a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, which gives a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern. A third methyl group is attached to an alkene carbon, so the ring carries three methyl substituents in total. The ring is fully carbocyclic with no fusion or heteroatoms, and its sp2 centers keep it fairly rigid, while the gem-dimethyl carbon adds a bulky, non-planar feature. Lacking any N–H or O–H bonds, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but its two carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-disubstituted scaffold. One substituent is a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), which is a strong electron-withdrawing group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen. Flanking it on the other side is a 2,2,2-trifluoroethoxy group, and the same ether unit appears on the opposite ortho position, so the two trifluoroethoxy arms sit at positions 1 and 2 relative to the nitrile on a single aromatic ring. The three trifluoromethyl-bearing carbons are saturated and flexible, so the ether linkages add some conformational freedom, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, with acceptor capability located at the nitrile nitrogen, the two ether oxygens, and the fluorine atoms.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing six positions of substitution, with no fused rings. Going around the ring, a methyl group sits on one carbon, a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) on a second, and a hydroxyl group (–OH) on the carbon between the two hydroxymethyl-bearing positions. A second hydroxymethyl group occupies the next position, and the remaining carbon carries a hydrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, because the methyl and the hydroxyl-bearing ring carbon are not equivalent, so the molecule has no mirror plane through the ring. The ring itself is rigid and planar, while the two hydroxymethyl arms add rotational flexibility around their single bonds. The phenolic oxygen and both primary alcohol groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, giving three hydrogen-bond donors and three acceptors in total.

This molecule is built on a central pyridine ring bearing two aryl substituents at the 2 and 6 positions, making it a 2,6-diarylpyridine scaffold. Each of the two flanking benzene rings carries a methyl group at the para position relative to the bond to the pyridine. The molecule has an approximate twofold symmetry axis running through the pyridine nitrogen and the C4 carbon, since the two p-tolyl arms are identical. The biaryl linkages allow some rotation about the single bonds, but the aromatic core is planar and rigid. The pyridine nitrogen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on one carbon and two trifluoromethyl groups, CF3, on the two carbons adjacent to it, so the substitution pattern is a 1,2,3-arrangement with the boronic acid flanked on both sides. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no fused rings and no additional stereocenters. The two bulky CF3 groups create steric crowding around the boron, which restricts rotation of the C–B bond. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that can act as acceptors. The three fluorine-rich CF3 groups are strongly electron-withdrawing, and the molecule has only partial symmetry, lying on a mirror plane through the boron-bearing carbon and the ring's para position.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two trifluoromethyl groups. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring carbon, and the two CF3 groups occupy the adjacent ortho positions on either side of it, giving a 2,6-bis(trifluoromethyl) substitution pattern. The structure has a mirror plane passing through the carboxyl carbon, the ipso carbon, and the para carbon, so it is symmetric with respect to the two sides of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl group and CF3 groups can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), whereas the fluorine atoms of the CF3 groups are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, bearing two trifluoromethyl groups. One trifluoromethyl group (–CF₃) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, and the second is attached to the other carbon flanking the nitrogen, so the two substituents sit symmetrically on either side of the ring nitrogen. The ring is planar and fully aromatic with no ring fusion, and the bonds to the bulky, rotationally symmetric CF₃ groups give the scaffold a rigid, highly symmetric outline. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the carbon-bound fluorines are poor acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a pyridine ring bearing two acetyl groups, one at each position flanking the ring nitrogen (positions 2 and 6), so it has a symmetric substitution pattern across the nitrogen. The aromatic core is a single six-membered heteroaromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the two C(=O)CH3 ketone substituents extend outward from the ring carbons adjacent to nitrogen. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and each carbonyl oxygen provides an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all hydrogens sit on carbon. The scaffold is largely rigid and planar, with the acetyl groups able to rotate about their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or extra ring systems. Two amino groups sit on the carbons flanking the ring nitrogen, and two fluorine atoms occupy the remaining positions on the other side of the ring, giving a fully substituted, asymmetric pattern. The ring is rigid and planar, with the amino groups able to rotate only slightly about their bonds. The two amino groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the ring nitrogen and the fluorine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional ring fusion. Two primary amino groups are attached to the ring, one adjacent to the ring nitrogen and the other at a carbon positioned across the ring from it, giving a 2,6-diamino-type arrangement relative to the nitrogen. The ring also carries a trifluoromethyl group and a fluorine atom on adjacent carbons, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the trifluoromethyl group rotates freely about its single bond. The two amino groups can each donate hydrogen bonds through their N–H bonds, and the ring nitrogen along with the fluorine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic fused heteroaromatic system made of a six-membered pyrimidine ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring, giving a purine-type scaffold with nitrogen atoms at several ring positions. Two primary amino groups are attached to the six-membered ring, one on each carbon flanking a ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the two adjacent amino-bearing carbons. The five-membered ring carries one protonated ring nitrogen (an N-H), which together with the amino groups provides several hydrogen-bond donors. Ring nitrogens without hydrogens, along with the amine nitrogens, serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fully aromatic, planar fused framework is rigid, with only the amino and N-H groups free to rotate or tautomerize.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring bearing two primary amino groups, one on each carbon flanking the ring nitrogen, which places them at the 2 and 6 positions. Its scaffold is therefore a simple monocyclic heteroaromatic system with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The two amino substituents are electron-donating groups attached directly to the ring, giving the molecule a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring nitrogen. The ring is planar and rigid, with only the N–H bonds of the amines free to rotate. Each amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogens can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. Two amino groups sit on the ring: one at the position adjacent to a methyl group and the other at the position meta to it, giving a 1,3-diamino-2-methylbenzene arrangement where the methyl group is flanked by the two substituents on one side. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl group and the two amino groups are small, freely rotating substituents with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry because the methyl and amino substituents occupy non-equivalent positions around the ring. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites overall.

This molecule is a cyclohexanone core bearing two benzylidene groups, one on each side of the carbonyl, making it a bis(arylidene)-substituted six-membered ring. The ring is a saturated cyclohexane-type framework except for the two exocyclic carbon-carbon double bonds that conjugate each phenyl ring to the ketone. Each phenyl substituent is unsubstituted, giving a symmetric arrangement that is roughly mirror-symmetric across the ketone plane. The extended conjugation through the enone systems and the aromatic rings makes the scaffold fairly rigid and planar in its conjugated regions, while the central methylene units retain some flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its carbonyl oxygen serves as the only hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group and two benzyloxy substituents. The central aromatic ring is substituted at three adjacent positions: a cyano group sits flanked on both sides by an ether oxygen linked to a benzyl group, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. Each benzyloxy arm consists of an oxygen atom bridging the core to a phenyl ring through a flexible CH2 linker, so the two terminal phenyl rings are unfused and can rotate relative to the core. The molecule has no stereocenters and only approximate mirror symmetry across the axis passing through the nitrile carbon and the middle ring carbon. The nitrile nitrogen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a biaryl built from two pyridine rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between the 3-position of one ring and the 5-position of the other, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pyridine linked to a 2,4-disubstituted pyridine. Each ring carries one bromine atom adjacent to a ring nitrogen, so both halogens sit at alpha positions relative to the heteroatoms. The two aromatic rings are fully planar and conjugated, and the single inter-ring bond allows only limited rotation, so the scaffold is fairly rigid. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps one half onto the other because the bromine substitution patterns differ. Each pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with six aromatic carbons forming the scaffold and no fused or additional ring systems. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by bromine atoms, so the two bromines occupy the positions adjacent to the amine. A third ring position, roughly opposite the amine, carries a trifluoromethyl group, which is a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent. The remaining two ring positions bear hydrogen atoms. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the amine-bromine-bromine cluster differs from the single trifluoromethyl substituent. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the trifluoromethyl group is the only substituent with rotational freedom. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine and bromine atoms serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms and one fluorine atom occupy the remaining ring positions, giving a heavily halogenated aniline scaffold. The two bromines flank the amine on opposite sides, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond a possible mirror plane through the amine and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the amino group can rotate slightly about its carbon-nitrogen bond. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on the nitrogen lone pair, while the halogen atoms contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, making it a phenol, and two bromine atoms are attached on the carbons immediately flanking that hydroxyl, one on each side. A fluorine atom occupies the position across the ring from the hydroxyl, which gives the molecule an overall pattern of 2,6-dibromo substitution relative to the OH with a para fluorine. The substitution is asymmetric in the sense that the fluorine differs from the bromines, but the arrangement retains an approximate mirror plane running through the hydroxyl carbon and the fluorine-bearing carbon. The ring is fully rigid and planar, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen providing rotational freedom. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with six aromatic carbons forming the scaffold and no additional fused rings. Attached to one ring carbon is an isocyanate group, a nitrogen double-bonded to a carbon that is itself double-bonded to oxygen, giving a linear N=C=O unit. The two flanking positions next to the isocyanate carry bromine atoms, and a fluorine atom sits on the ring meta to the isocyanate on the opposite side. This substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isocyanate group is linear and can rotate only about its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its oxygen, nitrogen, and fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to that ring are an isopropyl group (a CH bearing two methyl groups) and an amino group (NH2), along with two bromine atoms. The substituents sit at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, so the pattern is symmetric: the two bromines flank the amine on either side, and the isopropyl group occupies the position opposite the amine. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl group has some rotational freedom. The primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through the nitrogen lone pair, while the aromatic ring and bromine atoms contribute little to hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Around that ring sit one methyl group, two bromine atoms, and one primary amine (an aniline-type NH2 group), arranged so that the two bromines flank the amine at the 2 and 6 positions relative to it, with the methyl group located para to the amine. This substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror-plane symmetry through the amine and methyl carbons. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and amine groups are free to rotate only slightly. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the bromine atoms are weak halogen-bond acceptors and contribute no hydrogen-bond donor capacity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methyl group, two bromine atoms, and a hydroxyl group, giving a phenol scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, so its geometry is rigid, while the methyl and hydroxyl substituents are attached at single bonds that allow limited rotation. The hydroxyl group is positioned between the two bromine atoms, which flank it symmetrically on either side, and the methyl group sits meta to that central hydroxyl carbon, giving the molecule an approximate mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs. The two bromine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the methyl group contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no fused or additional ring systems. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by bromine atoms, giving a 2,6-dibromo substitution pattern relative to the amine. A nitro group is attached at the position para to the amine, making the arrangement strongly asymmetric in its electronic character. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, with the substituents lying in the ring plane, and the overall framework has a mirror-symmetric shape about the axis through the amine and nitro carbons. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donors and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents, with no fused rings. Its core is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle carrying a methyl group, two bromine atoms, and one nitro group, arranged around the ring with the methyl flanked by a bromine on one side. The nitro group, written as an N-oxide-type [N+](=O)[O-], is a strongly electron-withdrawing group that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The ring has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the molecule is fully rigid because the aromatic core and directly attached substituents do not have freely rotating ring bonds. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two halves identical.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Substituents sit around the ring: a straight-chain propyl group, two bromine atoms, and one primary amino group. The bromines occupy the two positions flanking the amino group, so the amine is sandwiched between them, while the propyl group sits on the opposite side of the ring, meeting the aromatic core at a single carbon. The substitution pattern lacks mirror symmetry because the propyl group is unlike the other three substituents. The aromatic ring is rigid, though the propyl chain can rotate freely. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the bromines are weak halogen-bond participants.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two amino groups on adjacent ring carbons, so the ring bears an aniline-type primary amine, and two bromine atoms on the carbons flanking that amine, giving a 2,6-dibromo substitution pattern relative to the amino group. The bromine atoms are heavy halogen substituents that add steric bulk around the amine and lower its accessibility. The arrangement is largely planar and rigid, with the amine as the only rotatable substituent. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromines contribute only weak halogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene-type rings fused along a shared edge to form a bicyclic aromatic system. Each of the two rings carries one bromine atom, attached as a halogen substituent on a carbon of the aromatic framework. The substitution pattern is positioned on opposite halves of the fused system, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry through the center of the fused bond. Because the core is fully aromatic and planar, the structure is quite rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the exocyclic carbon-bromine bonds. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, and its only potential acceptors are the weakly electronegative bromine atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms occupy adjacent positions on the carbons flanking it, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dibromophenol type with the hydroxyl between the two halogens. This arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the hydroxyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon, making it symmetric about that axis. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the molecule has little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the oxygen and bromine atoms can also serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or additional ring systems. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents: one at the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen (position 2) and one at the carbon on the other side of the nitrogen (position 6), giving a symmetric 2,6-disubstitution pattern. The molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the nitrogen and the carbon opposite it (position 4). It is a small, rigid, planar structure with no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with a cyclohexadienone-type scaffold, containing a carbonyl carbon and a conjugated ring of double bonds. Two bromine atoms sit on the ring at positions adjacent to the carbonyl and on the opposite side of the ring, giving a symmetric halogen substitution pattern. A third exocyclic substituent is an N-chloroimine group, in which a nitrogen is double-bonded to a ring carbon and single-bonded to a chlorine atom. The ring is planar and rigid because of its conjugated double bonds, with no rotatable bonds within the core. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the imine nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying two methyl groups and two bromine atoms as substituents. The two methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, and one bromine is attached directly next to that methyl pair, while the second bromine is on the carbon adjacent to the methyl at the other end of the pair, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with a bromine on each side of the methyl-bearing carbons. Because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no rotational symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups rotate freely. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N–H or O–H bonds, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it has no electronegative lone-pair-bearing heteroatoms such as oxygen or nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with two carbonyl groups located para to each other, making it a cyclohexadienedione. The ring contains two carbon-carbon double bonds in conjugation with the carbonyl groups, giving it a planar, rigid, and fully unsaturated framework with no sp3 centers. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring carbons that sit adjacent to the carbonyls, arranged symmetrically across the ring so the molecule has a high degree of mirror symmetry. The carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it carries no N-H or O-H groups.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. The ring carries a methyl group on one carbon, a chlorine atom on each of the two carbons flanking the nitrogen, and a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon adjacent to the methyl-bearing position. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic scaffold is rigid and flat, while the methyl and nitrile groups add little conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and the ring carries a chlorine atom on each of the two carbons flanking the ring nitrogen. A fluorine atom sits on a carbon adjacent to the chlorinated carbon, so the halogens cluster around one side of the ring. The core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the nitrile. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents: a nitrile (C≡N) group, two chlorine atoms, and a nitro group. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the ring, with one chlorine on the adjacent carbon and a second chlorine on the other side of that same carbon. The nitro group sits on the carbon para to the nitrile-bearing position relative to the ring's other substituent, creating a 2,6-dichloro-substituted, 3-nitro pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional rings present. The molecule lacks any internal rotational symmetry beyond a single mirror-type axis through the substituents, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The nitrogen of the nitrile and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no ring fusion or additional rings. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the carbons flanking the ring nitrogen at the 2- and 6-positions, which are both adjacent to the nitrogen (in pyridine numbering, the chlorines sit at positions 2 and 6 relative to nitrogen). A nitro group, bearing a formally charged nitrogen with two oxygens, is attached to a ring carbon meta to the nitrogen, at the 3-position. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Being a flat, fully aromatic system with few rotatable bonds, it is rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents: a methyl group, two chlorine atoms, and one nitro group, with the remaining positions occupied by hydrogen. The ring is aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, and there are no additional fused rings or flexible linkers. The chlorine and methyl groups sit adjacent to one another on one side of the ring, while the nitro group is positioned para to one chlorine atom, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful internal symmetry. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it carries no N-H or O-H bonds. The chlorine atoms and methyl group are non-polar substituents that add bulk and lipophilic character to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no additional fused rings. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by chlorine atoms, giving it a 2,6-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the nitrogen. A trifluoromethoxy group (an oxygen bearing a CF3 group) is attached at the position para to the amine, with the remaining ring positions bearing hydrogens. The arrangement has approximate mirror symmetry running through the amine and the trifluoromethoxy carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the trifluoromethoxy group offers only limited rotational freedom. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the ether oxygen and fluorine atoms provide weaker acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with two chlorine atoms placed on either side of that acid, flanking it on the ring. This pattern makes it a 2,6-dichlorobenzoic acid scaffold. A trifluoromethoxy group (-OCF3) sits para to the carboxylic acid, giving the ring a 1,2,3,5-type substitution arrangement overall. The core is a single aromatic ring with no fused rings, and the substituents are fairly rigid, though the carboxylic acid and the ether oxygen allow limited rotation. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two chlorines are equivalent but the trifluoromethoxy group is not. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygen and the fluorine atoms can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its aromatic scaffold. Two chlorine atoms and one trifluoromethyl group are attached to the ring, and a primary amino group sits on the carbon adjacent to one chlorine, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and not mirror-symmetric. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, with no fused rings and no rotatable bonds beyond the amine and trifluoromethyl substituents. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine and chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, bearing a sulfonyl chloride group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a chlorine) at one position. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions flanking and adjacent to the sulfonyl group, and a trifluoromethyl group sits on the ring at the position roughly opposite the sulfonyl group, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl chloride and trifluoromethyl groups have limited rotational freedom about their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a loose mirror relationship in the ring substitution, and it contains no hydrogen-bond donors. Its oxygen atoms of the sulfonyl group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorine and chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2) attached directly to the ring. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring positions, one flanking the hydrazine carbon and the other beside it, while a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3) occupies the position para to the hydrazine. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the bond linking the hydrazine to the ring. The hydrazine supplies two N–H donors and two lone-pair acceptor sites, whereas the chlorines and fluorines act only as weak acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Six substituents sit on the ring: an amino group (-NH2) and five halogens, with two chlorines flanking the amine on either side and a third chlorine together with a fluorine sitting on the opposite side of the ring, giving a highly substituted, asymmetric pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. Because the aromatic ring is planar and rigid, the scaffold itself adds little conformational flexibility, and the only rotatable bond is the C-N bond of the amine. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the halogens act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with fully conjugated, planar geometry. One ring carbon carries a hydroxyl group, making it a phenol, and two of the remaining positions carry chlorine atoms, with a fluorine atom on a third. The substituents sit at the 2, 4, and 6 positions relative to the hydroxyl, so the pattern is asymmetric and lacks any mirror plane through the ring. The rigid aromatic core gives the molecule little conformational flexibility, though the hydroxyl hydrogen can rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the halogen atoms serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group (a formyl group, C=O attached to the ring carbon) and three other substituents: a hydroxyl group and two chlorine atoms. The aldehyde carbon sits next to one chlorine, and the two chlorines occupy positions flanking the aldehyde on either side, while the hydroxyl group sits on the far side of the ring, giving a 2,6-dichloro-substituted, 4-hydroxy-benzaldehyde-type pattern. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups, so it is nearly symmetric. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the aldehyde oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only, and the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a simple substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the carbons flanking the nitrogen, at the 2 and 6 positions, and a single iodine atom sits on the carbon opposite the nitrogen, at the 4 position. This arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane passing through the nitrogen and the iodine-bearing carbon, so the two chlorines are equivalent. The rigid aromatic core has no rotatable bonds, making the structure essentially planar and inflexible. The ring nitrogen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with an amino group attached to one carbon and two chlorine atoms on the carbons flanking it, one on each side. A nitro group sits on the carbon opposite the amino group, giving a 1,3,5-type arrangement of the amine and nitro functions around the ring. The scaffold is a fully aromatic, planar six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, so the core is rigid and flat, while the substituents show only limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric pattern because the two chlorines are equivalent but the amine and nitro groups are not, giving it a symmetry that is essentially bilateral across the amine-nitro axis. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the nitro group and the nitrogen lone pair offer hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom within the ring. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the carbons on either side of that nitrogen, at positions adjacent to it, which makes the ring electron-poor. A nitro group, consisting of a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, sits on the ring carbon that lies between the two chlorine-bearing carbons' remote positions, opposite the ring nitrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. Being fully aromatic and planar, the scaffold is rigid, with the nitro group the only substituent capable of rotating. The ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring, which has been converted to a pyridine N-oxide, so the ring nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and an oxygen bearing a formal negative charge. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring carbons directly adjacent to the nitrogen, one on each side of the N-oxide, and a nitro group, with its nitrogen also bearing formal charges, is attached to the ring carbon meta to the N-oxide nitrogen. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the substituents add no additional rings, so the scaffold is rigid with little conformational flexibility. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The N-oxide oxygen and the two nitro oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A carboxylic acid group is attached to one ring carbon, which is adjacent to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position, while the ring also carries a fluorine atom and two chlorine atoms, one on the carbon directly beside the nitrogen and one on the carbon that bears the fluorine. The substitution pattern is highly decorated, leaving only a single aromatic C-H position on the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an acetanilide-type compound built on a single benzene ring, with an acetamide group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group and an NH) attached directly to one ring carbon. The aromatic ring carries two chlorine atoms on the carbons immediately flanking the amide-bearing carbon, giving a 2,6-disubstitution pattern that places both halogens ortho to the nitrogen. Because of this symmetric placement, the ring's substituents are arranged mirror-fashion about the axis through the amide carbon and the para carbon. The amide NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, while the amide linkage retains some rotational freedom around its C–N bond.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group, which is a two-carbon ketone (C(=O)CH3) attached directly to the aromatic ring. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions adjacent to the acetyl-bearing carbon, one on each side, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dichloro around the ketone. Because the acetyl group is flanked on both sides, the ring and ketone are forced to twist relative to one another, giving the molecule limited conformational flexibility and a non-planar arrangement. The structure has a mirror-plane-like symmetry through the acetyl group and the ring carbons. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents. One ring carbon carries a primary amino group (-NH2), which can donate hydrogen bonds and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The two adjacent carbons flanking the amine each carry a chlorine atom, placing the halogens at the ortho positions relative to the amine, giving a 1,2,6-substitution pattern. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetry axis through the substituted carbons, so its substituents are not evenly distributed. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the C-N and C-Cl bonds able to rotate.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no additional ring fusion. It carries three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms on the two carbons flanking it, placing the substituents at the 2, 3, and 6 positions relative to one another in a contiguous, asymmetric pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom about its C–O bond. The ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens sit on aromatic or methyl carbons.

The molecule is a benzaldehyde derivative: a single benzene ring carrying a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O bonded to an aromatic carbon and a hydrogen) on one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring on the carbons flanking the aldehyde-bearing carbon, giving a 2,6-disubstitution pattern. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two chlorines create a symmetric arrangement about the axis running through the aldehyde group, and the molecule is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the formyl group.

This molecule is a substituted benzaldehyde oxime, built on a single benzene ring with no ring fusion. The aromatic ring carries an aldoxime group (a CH=N–OH unit) at one position and chlorine atoms at both positions flanking it, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern with symmetry about the axis through the oxime carbon and the para carbon. The C=N double bond of the oxime is conjugated with the ring and can adopt E or Z geometry, while the rest of the scaffold is rigid and planar. The hydroxyl group on the oxime nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxime nitrogen and oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons flanking the amide, giving a 2,6-disubstituted benzamide pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the amide carbonyl is conjugated with the ring, which keeps the scaffold largely planar and fairly rigid. The two chlorine substituents sit symmetrically on either side of the carboxamide, so the molecule has a mirror plane through the amide and the ring carbon bearing it. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on its NH2 group and one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type interactions rather than hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on one carbon, with chlorine atoms on the two positions flanking it, so it is a 2,6-disubstituted phenylboronic acid. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion and no additional rings, and the two chlorines are placed symmetrically on either side of the boron-bearing carbon, giving the molecule an approximate mirror plane through the B–C bond and the para carbon. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that act as acceptors, while the chlorines are weak acceptors and contribute steric bulk around the boron. The aryl–boron bond allows some rotation, but the ortho chlorines restrict it, so the overall framework is fairly rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group (-SO2Cl) on one carbon, with chlorine atoms on the two positions flanking it, so it is a 2,6-dichlorobenzenesulfonyl chloride scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric about the sulfonyl axis only through the placement of the chlorines, which sit symmetrically on either side of the sulfonyl group. The sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The compound has few rotatable bonds, with flexibility limited mainly to rotation of the sulfonyl group about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two chlorine atoms, arranged as a disubstituted benzoic acid scaffold. The carboxyl group, attached directly to one ring carbon, provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The two chlorine atoms sit on the carbons flanking the carboxyl-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dichloro around that position, leaving the ring's other three carbons unsubstituted. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the carboxyl group able to rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. Because the two chlorines are equivalent and symmetrically placed, the molecule has a mirror plane through the carboxyl carbon and the carbon para to it.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group on one carbon and a chlorine atom on each of the two carbons immediately flanking it, so the nitrile sits between two chlorines at the 2 and 6 positions relative to each other. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted in a contiguous arrangement, which leaves the molecule with a mirror plane running through the nitrile carbon and the ring carbon opposite it. The nitrile group is linear and rigid, acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its overall framework is rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a thiazole ring, giving a planar benzothiazole scaffold. The five-membered ring contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom joined through a carbon that sits between them, and the fused system is fully aromatic and rigid. Two chlorine atoms are attached as substituents: one on the benzene ring and one on the carbon of the thiazole ring positioned between the nitrogen and sulfur. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N-H or O-H groups, but the thiazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall structure has no internal symmetry because the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold. The ring bears an acyl chloride group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen and a chlorine) directly attached to one ring carbon, and three chlorine atoms on the remaining ring positions, with two of them flanking the acyl chloride group on either side. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric with respect to the ring, and the molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis that would make all positions equivalent. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the acyl chloride carbonyl group can rotate only slightly relative to it. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the carbonyl oxygen and, more weakly, the chlorine atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH unit bearing a primary alcohol) attached to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the carbons immediately flanking that hydroxymethyl-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dichloro around the benzyl alcohol core, which leaves the three remaining ring positions as unsubstituted C–H groups. There are no fused rings, and the aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the CH2–OH arm retains rotational freedom about the bond to the ring. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the hydroxymethyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon, giving it a roughly symmetric outline. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors only, and the aromatic ring can participate in weak π-type interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions flanking one carbon, which bears a bromomethyl group (a CH2 linked to bromine), so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted with the bromomethyl group in the middle position. The molecule has a mirror plane passing through the bromomethyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, giving it approximate two-fold symmetry about that axis. Its only functional groups are the aryl halides and the primary alkyl bromide, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor sites beyond the halogens. The ring is rigid, while the CH2Br group can rotate about its bond to the ring, giving it limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three chlorine atoms are attached to the ring, two directly on ring carbons flanking one side, and a third sits on a chloromethyl group (a CH2 carbon bearing a chlorine) attached to the ring carbon between them, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3 on the ring with the chloromethyl at one end. The ring is planar and rigid, while the chloromethyl arm adds some rotational freedom around its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the weakly accepting chlorine atoms. It lacks any overall symmetry because the three chlorines occupy distinct positions.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a nitrovinyl side chain: a two-carbon alkene whose trans (E) double bond links the ring to a nitro group, so the functional groups are an aromatic ring, a conjugated C=C double bond, and an aliphatic nitro group. The benzene ring is substituted at two adjacent positions, with chlorine atoms flanking the carbon that carries the vinyl chain, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the conjugated alkene adds further rigidity, so the molecule has limited conformational flexibility. Its nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all of its hydrogens sit on carbon.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused ring systems. A carboxylic acid group is attached at the 3-position relative to the nitrogen, and chlorine atoms occupy the 2- and 6-positions flanking the nitrogen, giving a substitution pattern that is asymmetric about the ring. The carboxyl group carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the two oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the only notable conformational freedom comes from rotation about the single bond joining the carboxyl carbon to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group and two chlorine atoms, making it a substituted phenol. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, with a chlorine on each of the two carbons immediately flanking it, so the two halogens are ortho to the oxygen-bearing carbon and both lie on the same side of it. The remaining three ring positions carry hydrogen atoms. The core is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the carbon opposite it. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the chlorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with an isocyanate group (N=C=O) attached to one carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the carbons immediately flanking that isocyanate, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3, with the isocyanate in the middle position and the chlorines on either side. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and it has no fused ring systems. The isocyanate carbon is strongly electrophilic and the group is linear, which adds some rigidity to that region. Because the two chlorines are not identical in environment relative to the rest of the ring, the molecule has a mirror plane through the isocyanate. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen and nitrogen of the isocyanate and the two chlorines can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion, bearing two chlorine atoms and one isothiocyanate group (-N=C=S). The isothiocyanate sits on one ring carbon, and a chlorine sits on each of the two carbons directly flanking it, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-disubstituted around that central attachment point, leaving the remaining three ring carbons as unsubstituted CH positions. Because the two chlorines are equivalent, the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the isothiocyanate carbon, ring carbon, and the para position. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the linear isothiocyanate group adds limited conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the sulfur, nitrogen, and chlorine atoms can act as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two chlorine atoms and an acetamide side chain. The aromatic six-membered ring is a single unfused benzene core with no additional ring systems. The side chain is a CH2 linker attached to a primary amide group (-C(=O)NH2), which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through the NH2 and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the carbonyl oxygen. The two chlorine atoms sit on the carbons flanking the point of attachment of the side chain, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern. This arrangement lends the molecule a mirror plane through the side chain, and the ring is rigid while the CH2-amide linker retains some rotational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain: a carboxylic acid group attached through a single methylene carbon (an acetic acid unit) to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring, one on each carbon immediately flanking the carbon that carries the side chain, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dichloro. Because of this arrangement the molecule has a local mirror plane running through the side chain and the ring's para position, giving it a fairly symmetric shape. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker and the carboxyl group add some conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the chlorine atoms can act as weak halogen-bond or acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, and a cyanomethyl group, a CH2 linker bearing a terminal nitrile (C≡N), is attached to a third ring carbon next to one of the chlorines. This gives a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with the substituents clustered on one side of the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the three substituents are different. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker gives the nitrile group some rotational freedom. The nitrogen of the nitrile is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small aromatic heterocycle built on a six-membered pyrimidine-type ring, a planar system containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3 relationship across the ring. It carries two chlorine substituents, one on a carbon adjacent to a nitrogen and one on a carbon at the meta-like position, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold has no fused rings, no sp3 centers, and no rotatable bonds, so it is rigid and flat. The two ring nitrogens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since every ring carbon bears either a hydrogen or a halogen and no N-H or O-H groups are present.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with the nitrogen atom occupying one position of the ring. Two chlorine atoms are attached as substituents at the two carbon positions flanking the ring nitrogen, the 2 and 6 positions, which makes the substitution pattern symmetric about an axis running through the nitrogen and the opposite carbon. The ring is planar and fully rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it contains no fused rings or additional functional groups. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it carries no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, which carries a formal positive charge and an attached oxygen bearing a negative charge, forming an N-oxide. Two chlorine atoms are bonded to the carbon atoms flanking the nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the nitrogen and the carbon opposite it. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no sp3-hybridized carbons, which makes the scaffold rigid. The only polar functional group is the N-oxide, whose oxygen can act as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups since it carries no N-H or O-H bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a thioamide group, with the thioamide carbon (a C=S double bond flanked by an NH2 group) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at the two positions flanking that thioamide attachment, giving a 2,6-disubstituted, symmetric pattern about the axis through the thioamide substituent. The aromatic ring is fully planar and the thioamide carbon is conjugated with it, so the core is fairly rigid, with limited rotational freedom about the ring-to-carbon bond. The NH2 group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom of the C=S group serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two chlorine substituents add steric bulk around the thioamide and contribute to the overall lipophilic, halogenated character of the scaffold.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms are attached to the carbons on either side of it, so the substitution pattern is adjacent, placing the methyl between the two halogens at positions 2 and 6 relative to it. The three substituents create a compact, planar, rigid framework with little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make all positions equivalent, since the methyl group is unlike the chlorines. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only lone-pair-bearing atoms are the two chlorine substituents, which can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, two fluorine atoms, and one hydroxyl group, so it is a substituted benzaldehyde with a phenol. The aldehyde carbon is attached to one ring carbon, and fluorines occupy both positions flanking it, creating a crowded, ortho-disubstituted arrangement around the carbonyl. The hydroxyl group sits para to the aldehyde-bearing carbon, and the ring carries no fused rings or stereocenters, giving a rigid, planar, aromatic scaffold with no internal symmetry. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the two fluorines serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Around that ring sit a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two fluorine atoms, and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), which together give a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with the nitrile and one fluorine adjacent to each other. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group can rotate about its single bond, adding limited conformational flexibility. The nitrile nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fluorines contribute weak acceptor character as well.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries five substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 bearing a bromine) on the carbon between one fluorine and the methoxy-bearing position. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry in its overall arrangement. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and bromomethyl groups add some conformational freedom through rotation about their single bonds. The methoxy oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Around that ring sit five substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two fluorine atoms on adjacent positions, and a hydroxyl group on the ring carbon between one fluorine and the methoxy-bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry across the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group adds a small degree of rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ether oxygen and the fluorines can accept hydrogen bonds, and the fluorines are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group (-C(=O)OH) is attached to one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by fluorine atoms at adjacent positions, while a methyl group sits on a carbon two positions away from the acid. The fluorine and carboxyl groups cluster together on one side of the ring, giving the molecule an asymmetric, unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, though the carboxylic acid can rotate about its single bond to the ring.
