The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group, two fluorine atoms, and a nitro group. Parsing the SMILES, the nitrile carbon is attached to one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by ring fluorines at adjacent positions, and the nitro group sits para to the nitrile-bearing carbon's opposite position, giving a 2,6-difluoro-substituted benzonitrile pattern with a nitro group at the far side of the ring. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, with no ring fusion and no saturated or heterocyclic rings. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks a mirror axis through the ring, though the two fluorines sit in roughly comparable positions. The rigid aromatic core and linear nitrile limit conformational flexibility, while the nitro group's oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group (a formyl group attached directly to the ring) and three other substituents: two fluorine atoms and one hydroxyl group. The two fluorines sit on carbons flanking the aldehyde, so the aldehyde is ortho to both, while the hydroxyl is positioned meta to the aldehyde on the opposite side of the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with limited conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen of the aldehyde and the fluorine atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents on a single aromatic scaffold, with no fused or additional rings. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, flanked by fluorine atoms on both adjacent positions, which makes the phenol unit a 2,6-difluorophenol core. A third fluorine and an iodine atom are attached at the meta and para positions relative to the hydroxyl, respectively, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen able to rotate. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms offer weak acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Around the ring there are five substituents on six positions: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), an amino group, and two fluorine atoms. The methoxy and amino groups sit meta to one another across the ring, and the two fluorines flank the amino group on either side, giving a substitution pattern with a single hydrogen remaining on the ring. The arrangement is roughly symmetric about an axis passing through the methoxy-bearing carbon and the open C–H position opposite it, so the two fluorines are mirror-equivalent. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group adds limited rotational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N–H bonds, and the methoxy oxygen and the ring fluorines can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents on its six carbon atoms, with an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and attached to a hydrogen) occupying the position between the two fluorine atoms. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) sits on the carbon opposite the aldehyde, and the two fluorine atoms are placed symmetrically on either side of the aldehyde, giving the ring a mirror-symmetric substitution pattern across the aldehyde-methoxy axis. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups can rotate only modestly about their single bonds to the ring. The aldehyde oxygen and the methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methoxy group, two fluorine atoms, and a carboxylic acid. Reading around the ring, the carboxylic acid sits between the two fluorines, which flank it on both sides, while the methoxy group occupies the position meta to the acid across the ring, giving a 2,6-difluoro-benzoic acid core with a methoxy at the 4-position. The molecule has a mirror plane running through the carboxyl carbon, the methoxy carbon, and the ring axis, so its substitution pattern is symmetric. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the single bonds to the methoxy oxygen and the carboxyl group allow only limited rotation. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the two oxygens), while the methoxy oxygen and the fluorine atoms serve as additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents on its six carbon atoms, with one position left as an unsubstituted C–H. Going around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one position, and a fluorine atom appears at the position two carbons away, with a nitrile (C≡N) group flanked by two fluorines at the carbon between them. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the substituent pattern is not symmetric, since the methoxy group and the nitrile sit on opposite sides of the ring. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying five substituents on its six carbons, with the remaining position bearing a hydrogen. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) is attached at one position, and two fluorine atoms sit on carbons flanking a bromomethyl group (a CH2 bearing a bromine). The fluorines and the bromomethyl group occupy positions that make the pattern asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational axis of higher order. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, while the methoxy and bromomethyl substituents retain some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents spread around the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms. The fluorines flank the hydroxyl group on either side, while the methoxy group sits meta to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,3,5-type substitution pattern with the hydroxyl centrally placed. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom about its C–O bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen and fluorine atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzaldehyde scaffold: a single benzene ring bearing a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen) on one ring carbon. Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at the positions flanking the aldehyde-bearing carbon, so the aldehyde is ortho to both fluorines and the substitution pattern is 2,6-difluoro. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the aldehyde group able to rotate only modestly about its bond to the ring. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the aldehyde carbon and the ring carbon para to it, giving it a fairly symmetric shape. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxamide group on one carbon, with fluorine atoms on the two positions flanking that carboxamide carbon, giving a 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the fluorines and amide group are arranged symmetrically across the molecular axis through the amide carbon. The primary amide contributes two hydrogen-bond donors on its nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor on its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors. The scaffold is compact and largely rigid, with only the amide C–C bond permitting rotation out of the ring plane.

The molecule is a benzenesulfonamide: a single benzene ring carrying a primary sulfonamide group (–SO2NH2) on one carbon. Two fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions ortho to the sulfonamide and ortho to each other, on the same side of the attachment point, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-difluoro relative to the sulfonyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no fused rings, and the sulfonamide adds only limited rotational flexibility around the C–S bond. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the sulfonyl group and the ring carbons, giving it a symmetric overall shape. The NH2 group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two sulfonyl oxygens and the ring fluorines act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group directly attached to one ring carbon, with two fluorine atoms on the adjacent ring carbons flanking it, giving a 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the carboxyl group. The aromatic benzene core is a planar, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no additional ring fusion, so the scaffold is a single monocyclic aromatic system. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors. The substituents are arranged so the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the carboxyl carbon and the para carbon of the ring. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxyl group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat, rigid six-membered aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A nitrile group (a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and two fluorine atoms occupy the two positions immediately flanking it, giving a 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern around the nitrile. The remaining three ring carbons carry hydrogens, so the molecule has a mirror plane running through the nitrile carbon and the carbon opposite it, giving it a symmetric shape. The only rotatable bonds are essentially none, so the structure is highly rigid. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries two fluorine atoms on adjacent ring positions flanking a bromomethyl (–CH2Br) group, so the three substituents sit on consecutive carbons in a 1,2,3-pattern, with the bromomethyl group in the middle. The fluorines are the only ring halogens, and the bromine is attached to a benzylic carbon, making that position a reactive alkyl halide. The arrangement has a mirror plane passing through the bromomethyl carbon and the ring carbon bearing it, so the molecule is planar and fairly rigid apart from rotation of the CH2Br group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents on adjacent positions: two fluorine atoms flanking one carbon and a chloromethyl group (a CH2 linked to chlorine) on the carbon between them. This 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern on a benzyl chloride scaffold gives the molecule a mirror plane through the chloromethyl-bearing carbon and the para carbon, so it is symmetric about that axis. Its only rotatable bond is the one connecting the CH2 to the ring, so it is fairly rigid. The fluorines and chlorine are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is an aromatic carboxylic acid built around a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms at adjacent positions, ortho to the attachment point of the side chain. The side chain is an acrylic acid unit, with a carbon-carbon double bond joining the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The double bond has trans (E) geometry, which keeps the chain extended and largely planar with the ring. The aromatic core and conjugated alkene make the scaffold fairly rigid, while the carboxyl group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The fluorine atoms add electronegative acceptor sites and lack molecular symmetry across the ring, since the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical.

This molecule is an alpha-hydroxy carboxylic acid, consisting of a two-carbon chain in which a carboxylic acid group and a secondary alcohol share a single alpha carbon. That alpha carbon is also bonded to a benzene ring, making the scaffold a mandelic-type arrangement of an aryl group flanked by a hydroxyl and a carboxyl. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered benzene ring carrying two fluorine substituents on adjacent positions flanking the point of attachment, giving an ortho,ortho'-difluoro substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the chiral alpha carbon breaks the symmetry of the substituent arrangement. The aryl-carbon bond and the side chain allow moderate rotational flexibility, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptor sites, while the fluorine atoms act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries one hydroxyl group on one ring carbon, and two fluorine atoms sit on the two carbons directly flanking that hydroxyl-bearing carbon, giving a 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern relative to the OH. The arrangement is a phenol scaffold with its ortho positions occupied by halogens, which leaves the other three ring positions as unsubstituted C-H. The substitution pattern gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the OH carbon and the opposite ring carbon, so it has approximately two-fold symmetry in its two-dimensional structure. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the O-H bond free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) on one carbon, with fluorine atoms on the two positions flanking it, making it a 2,6-difluoro-substituted phenyl isocyanate. The aromatic six-membered ring is a single, unfused scaffold, and its substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the isocyanate carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The linear, cumulated N=C=O unit is rigid and nearly coplanar with the ring, while the rest of the framework has little conformational freedom. The isocyanate carbon is strongly electrophilic and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen and nitrogen, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative: a single benzene ring bears a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH) on one carbon, with two fluorine atoms attached to the ring at the two positions flanking that carbon, giving a 2,6-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the ring axis that passes through the substituted carbon and the para position. The carboxylic acid group is the principal functional group, offering one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The benzylic CH2 linker gives the molecule modest conformational flexibility relative to the rigid ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional rings fused to it. Two hydroxyl groups are attached to the ring, one on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen and one on the carbon at the opposite side of the nitrogen's neighbor, while a methyl group sits on a carbon between them, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. Because the ring is aromatic and planar, the scaffold is rigid, and the only freely rotating parts are the hydrogens on the methyl and hydroxyl groups. The hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and also accept one at their oxygen, while the ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond. Overall the molecule presents several polar contact points on an otherwise compact, flat framework.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing six positions, with two hydroxyl groups and one acetyl group attached. The acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, is attached directly to the aromatic ring, making it an aryl ketone. The two hydroxyl groups sit on carbons adjacent to one another, one of them flanking the acetyl group, which creates a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The phenolic oxygens can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygens can accept them, with the carbonyl and the neighboring hydroxyl positioned to form an intramolecular interaction. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group provides a small degree of rotational flexibility.

This molecule is a naphthalene-based scaffold: two fused benzene rings forming a bicyclic aromatic system. Each ring carries one hydroxyl group attached directly to an aromatic carbon, placed on opposite rings at positions that are symmetric about the molecule's central axis, giving it a C2-like symmetry. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule offers two donor and two acceptor sites.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Attached to that ring are a nitro group, which is a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one carrying a formal negative charge and the nitrogen carrying a formal positive charge, along with a hydroxyl group and two iodine atoms. The nitro group sits at one position, the hydroxyl group sits between the two iodine atoms, and the arrangement is symmetric about an axis passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the carbon opposite it. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the bonds to the substituents able to rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no additional fused rings, so its scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic core. Two isopropyl groups (each a CH bearing two methyls) sit on the ring, one at each position flanking a primary amine, so the amine is crowded between them and the two bulky substituents are placed symmetrically about that amino-bearing carbon. The amino group is the only polar functional group; its nitrogen can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the aromatic ring and alkyl groups are nonpolar. The bulky isopropyl groups restrict rotation around their bonds to the ring, making the framework fairly rigid, and the overall arrangement has a mirror plane through the amine-bearing carbon.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one C–C bond, giving a fully aromatic, planar, and rigid core. Two isopropyl groups, each a branched three-carbon alkyl substituent, are attached to carbons on different rings, one on each ring at positions remote from the fusion atoms. The molecule is highly symmetric in its substitution pattern, with the two isopropyl groups related by a near-mirror relationship across the long axis of the naphthalene. Aside from the rotation of the two isopropyl groups, the structure is conformationally rigid. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since it has no heteroatoms or polar functional groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two isopropyl groups (each a central carbon bearing two methyl groups) are attached to the ring at the two positions flanking the hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-disubstituted around one phenolic OH. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the bulky isopropyl groups shield it sterically. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the two isopropyl groups have rotational freedom about their bonds to the ring. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the carbon opposite it, giving it local symmetry across the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, two methoxy groups, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the nitro group sits para to one methoxy group and ortho to the other, which places both methoxy groups next to each other and the nitro group flanking one of them. This arrangement is fully substituted on the ring except for two aromatic hydrogens, leaving no internal symmetry axis. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and carboxylic acid groups can rotate somewhat. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the nitro group and methoxy oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and no additional donors are present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two methoxy groups, one methyl group, and one aldehyde (formyl) group. The aldehyde sits on a carbon flanked by a methoxy group on one side, so the two methoxy groups are meta to each other and the methyl is positioned between them on the opposite side of the ring. The core is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents are arranged asymmetrically, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The aromatic ring is rigid, though the aldehyde and methoxy groups can rotate about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Attached to this ring are three substituents: two methoxy groups (each an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and one methyl group, along with one free hydroxyl group. Reading around the ring, the hydroxyl sits between the two methoxy groups, and the methyl group sits meta to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,4-type pattern, with the substituents clustered on one side of the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters, and its aromatic core is rigid while the methoxy and methyl groups retain some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one acetyl group. The two methoxy (–OCH3) groups sit at positions 2 and 6 relative to the acetyl group, flanking it on both sides, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the acetyl carbon and the ring carbon it is attached to. The acetyl group (–C(=O)CH3) is a ketone, with its carbonyl oxygen serving as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups add two further acceptor sites. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl and methoxy groups have some rotational freedom around their single bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an amino group and two methoxy groups. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The amine sits on one carbon, flanked on both sides by methoxy ether groups at the adjacent positions, which gives a 2,6-disubstituted aniline pattern. Because the two methoxy groups are identical and mirror each other across the amine-bearing carbon, the molecule has a plane of symmetry through the amine and the opposite ring carbon. The ring and its small substituents are rigid, while the methoxy methyl groups can rotate. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the nitrogen and two ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one formyl group, making it an aromatic aldehyde derivative. The two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit at positions flanking the aldehyde carbon, so the aldehyde is ortho to both, giving a 2,6-disubstituted pattern with a mirror plane passing through the aldehyde and the ring carbon opposite it. The ring is a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. The formyl group (–CHO) and the ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aldehyde and methoxy groups have modest rotational freedom, though the flanking substituents constrain the aldehyde's orientation relative to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, forming a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on carbons flanking the boronic acid group, which occupies the position between them, giving the ring a symmetric 2,6-disubstitution pattern around the central carbon. The boronic acid, –B(OH)2, is a trigonal boron center bearing two hydroxyl groups, and the methoxy oxygens are ether linkages. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and boronic acid groups can rotate about their single bonds. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an acyl chloride group on one carbon, with two methoxy ether groups flanking it on the adjacent positions, so the substitution pattern is 2,6-dimethoxy around the carbonyl-bearing carbon. The aromatic ring is a single unfused six-membered system, planar and rigid, and the carbonyl carbon is directly attached to it, giving a conjugated aryl ketone-type scaffold. The acyl chloride functional group is a reactive carbonyl carbon bonded to chlorine, and the two methoxy oxygens are ether linkages that each carry a methyl group. The two methoxy groups are arranged symmetrically on either side of the acyl chloride, giving the molecule an approximate mirror plane through the carbonyl and ring carbons. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the two methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused rings and a single aromatic core. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at positions flanking the aminomethyl group, which occupies the carbon between them, giving a 2,6-dimethoxy substitution pattern around a primary aminomethyl (–CH2NH2) side chain. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the aminomethyl carbon, and the aromatic ring is rigid while the methoxy and aminomethyl groups retain some rotational freedom. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on nitrogen, while the two ether oxygens and the nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, making it fully aromatic and planar. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached as ether substituents, one on each ring, at positions that place them on opposite sides of the fused system. The arrangement gives the molecule a centrosymmetric, roughly C2h-like overall shape with a rigid, flat framework and little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the two methoxy groups. The ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring with a cyclohexadienedione core, bearing two carbonyl groups and two methoxy substituents. Its ring contains two ring carbonyls at non-adjacent positions relative to one another (a 1,4-quinone-type arrangement) along with two C=C double bonds, making the ring fully conjugated and planar. The two methoxy groups are attached to ring carbons in a substitution pattern that leaves the ring with a single unsubstituted vinylic position, so the arrangement is asymmetric. The carbonyl oxygens and methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The rigid, conjugated ring system with small substituents gives the structure limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a hydroxyl group flanked on one side by a methoxy group and, on the other side, by a second methoxy group, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its planar, rigid core is decorated with two ether oxygens and one phenolic oxygen. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical overall, although a mirror plane runs through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it, so the two methoxy groups are equivalent. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two ether oxygens can only accept hydrogen bonds. The methoxy groups add modest conformational flexibility around their C–O bonds, but the overall framework remains compact and relatively rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three oxygen-containing substituents: two methoxy groups and an oxyacetic acid side chain (–O–CH2–COOH). The two methoxy groups sit at positions flanking the carboxymethoxy group on the ring, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted, contiguous pattern with the central substituent in the middle. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the ether linkages and the terminal carboxylic acid provide flexibility in the side chain. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane through the ring that makes both methoxy groups identical in their environment, and the side chain is not rigid. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and carries three substituents. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on the ring, one at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen and one at the carbon in the para-like position relative to the boronic acid. The third substituent is a boronic acid group, –B(OH)2, attached to a ring carbon next to the other methoxy group. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the two boronic acid hydroxyl groups are hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the methoxy oxygens are weak acceptors. The fused-free, planar aromatic core gives the scaffold considerable rigidity, while the methoxy and boronic acid groups add limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents on adjacent positions: two methoxy groups (each an oxygen bonded to a methyl) and one methyl group. The two methoxy groups sit at positions flanking the methyl, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with the methyl in the middle. Ether oxygens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid, but the methoxy and methyl groups can rotate, so the molecule is only moderately flexible overall.

This molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated tertiary alcohol built on a branched alkane chain of ten carbons in total. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is a flexible open chain with many freely rotatable single bonds. The sole functional group is a hydroxyl group attached to a quaternary-type carbon bearing two methyl substituents, and a separate isopropyl-type terminus, forming a branched, asymmetric arrangement with no internal symmetry element. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs, while the remaining carbon framework is nonpolar and contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is an acyclic ketone built on a linear seven-carbon chain, with no rings present. Its backbone carries two isobutyl-type branches: one methyl-branched segment sits at each end of the chain, flanking a central carbonyl group. The carbonyl carbon is the sole functional group, bonded to two sp3 methylene carbons, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about that carbon. Because the molecule has no ring systems, its skeleton is highly flexible, with many freely rotatable single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents. Two methyl groups sit ortho to the hydroxyl group (at positions 2 and 6), flanking it on both sides, while an iodine atom occupies the position para to the hydroxyl group. The phenolic hydroxyl is the only functional group, so the molecule carries one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor on that oxygen. The substitution pattern is symmetric: the two methyl groups are mirror-equivalent across the axis through the hydroxyl and iodine. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups add only limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, arranged in a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Going around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits next to a methyl group, which is followed by a hydrogen-bearing carbon, then a nitro group, then another hydrogen-bearing carbon, and finally a second methyl group adjacent to the methoxy-bearing carbon. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and the methoxy oxygen is electron-donating, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and nitro groups can rotate about their single bonds to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no OH or NH groups. It can accept hydrogen bonds at the ether oxygen and at the oxygen atoms of the nitro group.

This molecule is a small, fully aromatic-looking oxygen heterocycle built on a single six-membered ring containing one ring oxygen. The ring carries a ketone-type carbonyl group, placing it in the pyranone family, and it bears two methyl substituents, one on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen and one on the carbon next to the other ring carbon, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The ring is essentially planar and conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid with no rotatable bonds. The carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ring oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an anilide built on a benzene ring that carries an acetamido group (–NH–C(=O)–CH3) on one carbon and two methyl groups on the two carbons flanking that attachment point, giving a 2,6-dimethyl substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered benzene ring with no ring fusion, and its three substituents are arranged in a crowded, roughly symmetric pattern about the amide nitrogen. The amide carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amide N–H serves as a single hydrogen-bond donor. The two ortho methyl groups sterically hinder rotation around the aryl–nitrogen bond, so the molecule is moderately rigid around that linkage, while the acetyl portion remains comparatively flexible.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methyl groups and a carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid (–C(=O)OH) is attached to one ring carbon, and a methyl group sits on each of the two carbons flanking it, so the acid is sterically crowded between the two methyl groups. The remaining ring positions are unsubstituted C–H units, giving a 2,6-disubstituted benzoic acid pattern with a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the axis through the acid carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the carboxyl group and the methyl groups provide limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the methyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a second methyl group sits on the carbon two positions away, and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) occupies the carbon between the two methyl-bearing positions. This gives a 2,6-dimethyl substitution pattern flanking the nitrile, with the molecule showing a mirror plane through the nitrile carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the nitrile is linear, so the framework has little conformational flexibility, with only the methyl groups able to rotate. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a substituted cyclohexadienedione, built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring with two ring carbonyl groups and two methyl substituents. The ring contains two conjugated C=C double bonds alongside the two ketone carbons, which sit in a 1,4-relationship across the ring, giving a fully conjugated, planar quinonoid framework. The two methyl groups are attached to the ring at positions adjacent to the carbonyls, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric, with one methyl beside a carbonyl and the other on an alkene carbon. The ring is rigid and flat, with little conformational flexibility. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, with a methyl group on each of the two carbons immediately flanking it, so the hydroxyl is hindered on both sides. The three substituents occupy adjacent positions, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern that lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a local plane through the hydroxyl and the ring. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups can rotate about their single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, whereas the methyl groups contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is an aromatic isocyanide, with a benzene ring bearing an isocyano group (–N≡C) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two methyl groups sit on the ring carbons immediately flanking the isocyanide-bearing carbon, creating a 2,6-dimethyl substitution pattern that is symmetric about the axis running through the isocyanide carbon and the para carbon. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the linear isocyanide group extends the molecule along one direction. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. The isocyanide carbon can act as a weak donor or coordinating site through its lone pair, but the aromatic ring and methyl groups offer no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity.

The molecule is a substituted pyrazine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4 relationship. It bears two methyl groups on the ring carbons, one adjacent to a nitrogen and the other on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 2,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, and the methyl groups add only minor conformational freedom through rotation. Its two ring nitrogens are weakly basic lone-pair acceptors and cannot donate hydrogen bonds, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The overall structure has a degree of symmetry about the ring's central axis, though the two methyl groups break perfect symmetry.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic compound built on a fused two-ring scaffold, with a nitrogen atom in the second ring. Two six-membered aromatic rings share an edge, giving a flat, rigid naphthalene-like framework in which one ring carbon has been replaced by nitrogen. Two methyl groups are attached, one on the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen and one on the benzenoid ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining hydrogens sit on carbon. Overall, the structure is planar and conformationally inflexible, apart from the freely rotating methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxyl group and two nitro groups, with a fluorine atom also attached to the ring. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, flanked on both sides by nitro groups, while the fluorine occupies the position across from it, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is rigid and planar. The nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms, and the phenolic hydroxyl provides one hydrogen-bond donor and an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A nitrile group (carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and two nitro groups occupy the two ring positions flanking that nitrile carbon, giving a 2,6-dinitro substitution pattern on the benzonitrile core. The nitro groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and roughly planar with the ring, while the nitrile is linear, so the molecule is rigid and flat with no rotatable bonds in the scaffold. The arrangement of substituents gives it a mirror plane through the nitrile carbon and the opposite ring carbon, so it is symmetric about that axis. The nitro oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a biphenyl-type scaffold in which a central benzene ring carries two phenyl substituents. The central ring bears a hydroxyl group on one carbon, and a phenyl ring is attached on each side of that hydroxyl-bearing carbon, so the two aryl groups flank the OH at adjacent positions, giving a 2,6-diphenyl substitution pattern about the phenol. The molecule contains three separate benzene rings, none of them fused to one another, and the aryl-aryl single bonds allow rotation, though steric crowding around the hydroxyl restricts the conformations available. The phenolic oxygen can donate one hydrogen bond and accept another, while the remaining aromatic rings contribute only weak, non-classical interactions. Overall the structure is largely planar within each ring and has no internal symmetry axis that maps the two outer phenyl groups onto each other.

This molecule is built from a central pyridine ring bearing two phenyl substituents, making it a 2,6-diphenylpyridine scaffold. The central six-membered nitrogen heterocycle is aromatic and planar, and each phenyl ring is attached at the carbon positions flanking the nitrogen, giving a symmetric arrangement with a two-fold axis through the nitrogen and the para carbon. There are no aliphatic chains or additional polar functional groups, so the structure is entirely aromatic and largely rigid, with the biaryl linkages permitting only modest rotation about the single bonds. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair oriented in the ring plane, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a rigid aromatic scaffold. A dimethylaminomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a tertiary amine bearing two methyl groups) is attached at one ring position, making the nitrogen a hydrogen-bond acceptor with no donor capability. Flanking a phenolic hydroxyl group on the ring are two tert-butyl groups, one on each side, which are bulky, sterically crowding the OH and giving it both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor role. The substitution pattern is 1,3,5 (meta-related) with the hydroxyl and two tert-butyls occupying adjacent positions, producing a partially symmetric arrangement across the ring's central axis. Overall the aromatic core is rigid, while the alkyl substituents add some conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Around that ring there are four substituents: an ethyl group, two tert-butyl groups, and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl sits between the two bulky tert-butyl groups, which flank it on both sides, while the ethyl group occupies a position meta to one of them on the opposite side of the ring. This arrangement gives the molecule an asymmetric, crowded substitution pattern. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, but the flanking tert-butyl groups sterically hinder its interactions. The ring and its substituents are rigid, with the tert-butyl and ethyl groups contributing some conformational freedom.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Its substitution pattern is 1,3,5-type relative to the methyl group, with a phenolic hydroxyl flanked by two bulky tert-butyl groups at the ortho positions, while a fourth tert-butyl sits meta to the hydroxyl and para to the methyl. The hydroxyl group is the only hydrogen-bond donor and also acts as a weak acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, but the surrounding tert-butyl groups sterically shield it considerably. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the tert-butyl groups are rotationally fixed and contribute bulk rather than conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of its substituents.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carries three alkyl substituents: a methyl group on one carbon and two tert-butyl groups, each consisting of a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, placed on the carbons flanking the nitrogen and at the position opposite it. The arrangement of substituents is asymmetric, since the methyl group sits on a different carbon than the bulky tert-butyl groups, and the two tert-butyl groups are not equivalent to each other. The bulky tert-butyl groups impose significant steric hindrance around the nitrogen, which shields its lone pair. The ring itself is rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl groups rotate freely about their attachment bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor capability resides in the sterically encumbered pyridine nitrogen.

This molecule is a substituted p-benzoquinone, with a six-membered cyclohexadienedione ring bearing two carbonyl groups in a 1,4 (para) relationship. Two tert-butyl groups are attached to the ring at positions flanking the carbonyls, each carbon carrying three methyl groups in a bulky, branched arrangement. The ring is essentially planar and conjugated, with alternating carbon-carbon double bonds, which makes the core rigid, while the tert-butyl groups add steric bulk. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the two carbonyl carbons, and it contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. Its two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a single benzene ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and two tert-butyl groups. The hydroxyl sits between the two bulky tert-butyl substituents, which flank it at the 2 and 6 positions, so the ring has a 2,6-disubstitution pattern around the phenol oxygen. The ring itself is aromatic and planar, with no fused ring systems, while the quaternary tert-butyl carbons are sterically demanding and largely rigid. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the hydroxyl carbon, giving it local symmetry. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor at the oxygen, while the alkyl groups contribute only nonpolar bulk.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring, with no fused rings. The nitrogen atom sits at one position in the ring, and two methyl groups are attached to the carbons directly flanking that nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstituted substitution pattern. Because the two methyl groups are placed symmetrically on either side of the nitrogen, the molecule has a mirror plane running through the nitrogen and the carbon opposite it. The ring is rigid and planar, and the methyl groups add only minimal conformational flexibility. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a simple substituted pyridine: a six-membered aromatic nitrogen-containing ring bearing two hydroxymethyl groups. Each hydroxymethyl substituent consists of a CH2 unit attached to the ring and terminated by an OH group, so the two side chains are attached at the carbon atoms flanking the ring nitrogen, giving a 2,6-substitution pattern. The ring itself is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the molecule has a two-fold mirror symmetry through the nitrogen and the para carbon. The two CH2OH arms are conformationally flexible, since rotation about the single bonds to the ring and to the oxygen is possible. The two hydroxyl groups each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused pair of benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. Two acetyl ester groups are attached as acetoxy substituents, one on each ring, each consisting of an oxygen bonded to the ring and a carbonyl-bearing acetyl unit. The substitution pattern is symmetric: the two ester groups sit at the 2 and 6 positions of the naphthalene system, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold axis through the center of the fused rings. The ester oxygens and carbonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Apart from the rotatable ester linkages, the framework is largely rigid.

This molecule is a tricyclic aromatic ketone built on a fluorenone-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a five-membered ring that contains a carbonyl carbon at position 9. The two outer rings are fused to this central five-membered ring, giving a rigid, essentially planar framework. Each benzene ring carries one bromine substituent located para to the biaryl bond on its own ring, so the two bromines sit in mirror-related positions. The molecule therefore has a twofold symmetry axis passing through the carbonyl group. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a fluorene-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single bond and bridged by a methylene carbon, forming a fused tricyclic system with a five-membered central ring. Each outer benzene ring carries one bromine atom, and the two bromines sit at symmetrically related positions, giving the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry through the central CH2 group. The fused aromatic framework is essentially flat and rigid, with only the sp3 methylene carbon breaking the planarity. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no O–H or N–H groups, and it offers no meaningful acceptor sites beyond weak halogen contributions from the bromines.

This molecule is a naphthalene-based scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings sharing one carbon-carbon bond, giving a planar, rigid aromatic core. Two hydroxyl groups are attached directly to the ring carbons, making it a diphenol-type structure. One hydroxyl sits on the same ring position relative to the fusion carbons as the other, which places the two substituents in a symmetric, distal arrangement across the bicyclic system. The molecule has a two-fold axis of symmetry through the midpoint of the fused bond. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is a naphthalene core, meaning two benzene rings fused together through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic bicyclic scaffold. Two methoxy groups are attached to the ring system, one on each of the fused rings, and they sit at positions that make the molecule roughly symmetric across the long axis of the naphthalene. Each methoxy group consists of an oxygen bonded to an aromatic carbon and to a terminal methyl group, so the ether oxygens can each accept a hydrogen bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no hydroxyl, amine, or N-H groups. Apart from the small rotation of the two methyl groups, the framework is essentially inflexible.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings fused together by sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Two methyl groups are attached as the only substituents, one on each ring, positioned so the molecule has a two-fold symmetry axis running through the centre of the fused system. The ring system is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl C–C bonds. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and no heteroatoms are present to serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, so its polarity is limited to the weak π-electron character of the aromatic rings.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated hydrocarbon with no rings, double bonds, or heteroatoms, so it contains no functional groups. Its skeleton is a branched chain of twelve... let me count carefully: the SMILES CC(C)CCCCC(C)C contains ten carbon atoms arranged as a linear backbone of eight carbons with a methyl branch on each end, giving a 2,8-dimethyl-substituted nonane-like framework. Both branches sit at the chain termini, so the molecule is roughly symmetric about its center. Because all bonds are single and the chain is flexible, rotation about its many C–C bonds gives it considerable conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since every atom is carbon or hydrogen with only nonpolar C–H bonds.

The molecule is a quinoline, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a flat and rigid scaffold. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbocyclic-adjacent carbon of the pyridine-side ring, which places it as a 4-quinolinol-type substituent. Two trifluoromethyl groups are attached: one on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen in the pyridine ring, and one on the benzene ring at the position adjacent to the ring fusion, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The strongly electron-withdrawing trifluoromethyl groups are bulky but rotationally fixed relative to the aromatic plane, so the overall framework remains largely planar and conformationally rigid.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a central ethene (C=C) backbone. One carbon of the double bond carries two methylthio groups (–S–CH3), while the other carries two nitrile groups (–C≡N), making it a push-pull alkene in which electron-donating sulfur substituents face strongly electron-withdrawing cyano groups. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is fully open-chain and planar about the double bond. The two nitrile groups are linear and symmetric with respect to each other, giving the nitrile end a degree of local symmetry, while the two methylthio groups add small, flexible side chains. Overall the framework is rigid at the alkene core with limited conformational freedom from the terminal methyl groups. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the nitrogen atoms of the nitriles and the sulfur atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a tetrahedral silicon center bearing two methyl groups, a p-tolyl ring (a benzene ring carrying a methyl group para to the silicon attachment), and a second phenyl ring. The second aromatic ring is ortho-substituted, carrying a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) adjacent to the silicon linkage. Both benzene rings are unfused and connected only through the silicon atom, so the scaffold is a diarylsilane with flexible Si–C bonds allowing rotation about the linkages. The methyl group on the tolyl ring provides a simple para substitution pattern, while the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two aryl rings differ. The primary alcohol offers one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor site, while the remaining framework is largely hydrophobic and cannot form hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built around a central nitrogen atom bearing two sulfonyl groups, each capped with a trifluoromethyl substituent, so the core is a bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)amide unit. The third substituent on that nitrogen is a pyridine ring, attached through its second carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, with a chlorine atom at the fifth position, making the substitution pattern asymmetric. The pyridine is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused partners, and the attachment to the sulfonylated nitrogen leaves the rest of the scaffold fairly flexible about its single bonds. The sulfonyl oxygens and the pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all nitrogen valences are satisfied by the sulfonyl and aryl groups.

The molecule is built around a central nitrogen atom that bears a pyridine ring, specifically a 2-pyridyl group attached through a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. That same nitrogen is bonded to two sulfonyl groups, each of which carries a trifluoromethyl group, giving a symmetric arrangement of two identical CF3-SO2 arms around the amine. The pyridine ring is an aromatic six-membered heterocycle with no fusion to other rings, and the molecule has no stereocenters. Each sulfonyl unit contributes two strongly electron-withdrawing oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The pyridine nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site, and the rotatable sulfur-nitrogen and sulfur-carbon bonds give the structure moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings. A nitrogen atom sits in the ring, and two amino-type groups are attached at different positions around it. One is an acetamide group, where an acetyl unit is bonded through an amide nitrogen to the ring, and the other is a free primary amine on the opposite side of the ring from the ring nitrogen's neighbor. This gives a 2,5-disubstituted pattern with no symmetry, and the molecule is largely planar and rigid apart from rotation around the amide and acetyl bonds. The amide N–H and the free amine provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the carbonyl oxygen, the pyridine nitrogen, and the amide nitrogen offer acceptor sites.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. Positions 1 and 2 carry an acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, CH3C(=O)NH-) and a carboxylic acid (-COOH) on adjacent carbons, while a bromine atom sits on the carbon para to the acetamido group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the substituents adding limited conformational freedom through rotation about their single bonds. The ring is asymmetric because the three groups differ in identity and position, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of both the amide and acid groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a pyridine ring bearing two substituents: an acetamido group (an acetyl group attached through nitrogen to the ring) at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a bromine atom at the position para-like to it on the far side of the ring. The core is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is compact and planar. The amide linkage gives the molecule an N–H that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry. Apart from rotation around the single bond joining the amide nitrogen to the ring, the structure is rigid.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic thiazole ring, containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom in a 1,3-relationship. An acetamide group (a methyl ketone linked through an amide nitrogen) is attached at the carbon between the sulfur and the ring nitrogen, forming a secondary amide. A chlorine atom sits on the remaining ring carbon adjacent to the sulfur, giving a 2,5-substitution pattern on the heteroaromatic core. The scaffold is essentially planar and rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation about the amide linkage. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the thiazole ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a pyridine-based scaffold, specifically a 2-acetamido-5-nitropyridine. The core is a single six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle with no ring fusion. An acetamide group (a carbonyl bonded to a secondary amine NH and a methyl group) is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the pyridine nitrogen. A nitro group sits at the position para-like to the amide-bearing carbon, on the opposite side of the ring from the acetamide. The molecule is essentially planar and largely rigid, with only the methyl rotation and the amide bond offering limited flexibility. The NH of the amide acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the nitro oxygens, and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a contiguous pattern: an acetamido group (an N-acetylated amine), a chlorine atom, and a carboxylic acid. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the carboxylic acid sits between the chlorine and the acetamido group, so the three substituents are positioned adjacently around one side of the ring. The overall skeleton is planar and largely rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation about the amide and carboxyl bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. Its hydrogen-bond capability is significant: the amide N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H serve as donors, while the amide and carboxyl carbonyl oxygens, along with the carboxyl hydroxyl oxygen, act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents, making it a simple disubstituted aromatic scaffold with no additional ring fusion. One substituent is an acetamido group, an amide in which a carbonyl is attached to a methyl group and to the ring through nitrogen. The neighboring substituent is a carboxylic acid group directly bonded to the ring. The ortho arrangement of these two groups allows an intramolecular interaction between them, and the overall framework has limited symmetry because the two groups differ. Both the amide N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens of each group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid, but the single bonds connecting the substituents allow moderate conformational flexibility.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, which makes this an ortho-disubstituted pattern. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group is attached through an amide nitrogen to the ring, and the other is a free hydroxyl group on the neighboring carbon. The amide N-H and the phenolic O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen act as acceptors. The two substituents can orient toward each other and are capable of intramolecular hydrogen bonding, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a partial mirror relationship that is broken by the amide's conformation.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiazole ring, containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom, with a 2-position acetamide group attached to the carbon between those heteroatoms. That substituent is an N-acyl amide in which a methyl ketone carbonyl is bonded directly to the ring-bearing nitrogen, so the core is a simple, unfused bicyclic-free heteroaromatic system with no additional rings. Because the ring is planar and the amide linkage is conjugated with it, the overall framework is fairly rigid, with only the terminal methyl group free to rotate. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any clear rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the aromatic core. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the thiazole ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acetoacetanilide-type structure: a four-carbon acetoacetyl chain bearing a ketone and an amide carbonyl, with its amide nitrogen attached to a benzene ring. The benzene is a single aromatic ring with no fusion, and the amide nitrogen sits at one position while a methyl group occupies the adjacent (ortho) position, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ and the chain is unsymmetrical. The acetoacetyl segment contains several rotatable single bonds, so the chain is flexible, while the aromatic ring and the amide linkage are comparatively rigid. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the two carbonyl oxygens of the ketone and amide act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent (ortho) carbons of that ring: one is an acetyl ester group (an acetate oxygen linked to the ring and bearing a carbonyl), and the other is a ketone (an acetyl group attached directly to the ring carbon). The ester and ketone each contribute a carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its overall shape is largely planar around the aromatic core, with the two side chains offering moderate rotational flexibility, and the ortho arrangement gives it no internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) is attached to one ring, and a hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon of that same ring, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. This 1,2-relationship allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the phenolic OH and the ketone oxygen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom, mainly around the acetyl bond, so it is largely planar.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: an acetyl group, a fluorine atom, a second fluorine atom, and a carboxylic acid group, arranged on adjacent and nearby carbons. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The acetyl ketone and the carboxylic acid sit ortho to each other, flanking one ring carbon, while the two fluorines occupy the remaining positions on the opposite side of the ring. Because the substituents are asymmetrically placed, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The planar aromatic ring is rigid, while the acetyl and carboxyl groups retain some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, and the ketone oxygen and fluorine atoms serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring that carries three substituents. A phenyl group is attached at the position across the ring from the sulfur atom, and an acetyl group (a ketone bearing a methyl) sits on the carbon adjacent to sulfur, while a primary amino group occupies the remaining ring carbon beside the acetyl-bearing position. The result is a biaryl-type arrangement, with the thiophene and benzene rings linked by a single bond that permits some rotational freedom, though the fused-free aromatic framework remains largely planar. The ketone oxygen and the amino nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptor and donor sites respectively, with the amine's two hydrogens providing donor capability. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a heterocycle containing one sulfur atom. Attached to the ring are two substituents on adjacent carbons: an amino group (-NH2) on one carbon and an acetyl group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl, C(=O)CH3) on the neighboring carbon, creating an ortho substitution pattern. The molecule is essentially planar and largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, with only the methyl rotation of the acetyl group adding flexibility. It has no internal symmetry that would make the two substituents equivalent. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its N-H bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring sulfur serve as hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a thiophene scaffold, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. An acetyl group, a ketone bearing a methyl substituent, is attached to one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, while a bromine atom sits on the neighboring carbon of the ring, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern. The ring system is planar and rigid, with only the acetyl group offering a small amount of rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents are different. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiophene ring that contains a sulfur atom, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C=O attached to a methyl) sits on the thiophene carbon adjacent to the sulfur, while a methyl group occupies the neighboring carbon of the five-membered ring. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is largely rigid because of the fused aromatic system, with only the acetyl group offering a small degree of rotational freedom. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically on the thiophene ring.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion. An acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl, is attached at one alpha position adjacent to the sulfur, while a bromine atom sits at the opposite alpha position, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry beyond the ring's approximate planarity. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The compound is largely rigid and planar, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the acetyl group to the ring.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle, carrying two substituents. An acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl, is attached at one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon at the other position adjacent to the sulfur, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is planar and rigid, with only the acetyl methyl group contributing rotational flexibility. The overall arrangement lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local pseudo-mirror relationship defined by the ring and its substituents.

The molecule is a 5-iodothiophene bearing an acetyl group. Its core is a single aromatic five-membered thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom, which is planar and rigid. The ring carries two substituents on positions flanking the sulfur: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) on one alpha carbon and an iodine atom on the other, giving a 2,5-disubstitution pattern with no internal symmetry beyond a local pseudo-mirror relationship. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The sulfur and the large iodine atom contribute to a polarizable, electron-rich aromatic system.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. Substituents sit at two positions: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) on one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, and a methyl group on the carbon at the opposite alpha position, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern. The ring and its attached carbonyl make the scaffold largely planar and rigid, with only the terminal methyl rotations contributing flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the sulfur atom offers weak acceptor character. Overall the structure has no internal symmetry beyond the approximate pseudo-mirror relationship of the two substituents across the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzofuran scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered furan ring that contains one oxygen atom. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) is attached to the furan ring at the carbon adjacent to the oxygen, giving the ring system a carbonyl functional group. A nitro group (-NO2) sits on the benzene portion of the fused system, positioned para to the ring junction region, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused aromatic bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the acetyl methyl rotating freely. The carbonyl oxygen and nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on the ring: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) at one alpha position and a nitro group (-NO2) at the opposite alpha position, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern. The arrangement is essentially planar, with the conjugated ring and both substituents lying roughly in one plane, and the only notable flexibility comes from rotation of the acetyl methyl group. The ketone oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid aromatic core. One ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) at a position on the outer edge of the fused system, while the other ring bears an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl). The methoxy oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the substituents sit on different rings at non-equivalent positions, the molecule has no symmetry beyond a rough pseudo-planar arrangement, and its only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the single bonds connecting the substituents to the ring.

The molecule is a benzofuran scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered furan ring that shares one edge with it, forming a flat bicyclic aromatic core. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) is attached to the benzene portion at the position adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the furan oxygen, creating an ortho-type substitution pattern. On the furan ring, an acetyl group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl) is attached at the carbon next to the furan oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and is largely planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and acetyl groups providing limited rotational freedom. The ketone oxygen and the ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a linearly fused tricyclic aromatic scaffold, an anthracene-type core with an additional benzo ring fused across one side, so it is a fully conjugated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon. An acetyl group, a ketone bearing a methyl substituent, is attached to one of the outer benzene rings, giving a single carbonyl oxygen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rings are planar and rigid, with the carbonyl group the only significant point of flexibility, and the substitution is asymmetric because the acetyl group sits on one terminal ring rather than at a symmetric position.

This molecule is a 2-acetylbenzofuran, built on a benzofuran scaffold in which a five-membered furan ring is fused to a benzene ring along a shared edge.
