An amino group is attached at the carbon between the ring nitrogen and sulfur, adding a primary amine that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The ring nitrogen also serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule offers a compact, polar edge alongside its otherwise flat, hydrophobic aromatic surface.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. A methyl group sits on one carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a primary amino group sits on the other carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, so the two substituents flank the nitrogen in a 2,6-pattern. The molecule is small, essentially planar, and rigid, with only the rotation of the methyl and amino groups as flexibility. The ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and can also accept hydrogen bonds through its lone pair. The arrangement is not symmetric because the methyl and amino groups differ in character.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The thiazole portion carries a primary amino group on the carbon between the sulfur and the ring nitrogen, giving it a 2-aminobenzothiazole character. On the benzene ring, a nitro group sits at the position para to the ring-fusion nitrogen-bearing carbon, making it a 6-nitro substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the only notable flexibility coming from rotation of the amino and nitro groups. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a primary amino group, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The other is an acetamido group, in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded to an amide nitrogen attached to the ring, providing an additional carbonyl hydrogen-bond acceptor and an N–H donor. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the amide linkage and the acetyl group add a degree of conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ in character. Overall it presents three hydrogen-bond donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a linearly fused tricyclic aromatic scaffold, with three six-membered rings fused edge-to-edge in a straight line, and it carries no non-aromatic rings or flexible chains. Its only substituent is a single primary amino group (–NH2) attached to one of the outer rings, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the molecule has no symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the fused core. The framework is planar and rigid. The amino group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, while the remaining aromatic carbons offer only weak π-stacking character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group (a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to an NH2 group), and the other is a primary amino group attached directly to the ring. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and there are no additional fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The molecule has a relatively rigid core with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the amide to the ring. Both the amide NH2 and the aryl NH2 can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the ring nitrogen-bearing positions provide hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity imposed by the ring.

This molecule is a benzanilide-type scaffold built from two benzene rings joined by a secondary amide linkage. One ring bears an amino group at the position ortho to the carbonyl carbon, so the amide is flanked by an aniline-derived ring on one side and a plain phenyl ring on the other. No fused or bridged ring systems are present; both aromatic rings are simple, unsubstituted benzene cores apart from the single amino group. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the free amino nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The amide bond gives the molecule moderate conformational restriction, though the two aryl rings can still rotate about their attachments, and the overall shape lacks any symmetry because the amino group breaks the otherwise matched arrangement.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, an amino group and a boronic acid group, in an ortho arrangement. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aryl system. The boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, making it a boronic acid functional group, while the aromatic amine contributes a primary nitrogen with two N–H bonds. The two substituents sit next to each other, which places them in close proximity and allows possible intramolecular interaction between the nitrogen and the boron. Both the amine and the hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, giving the molecule moderate flexibility from rotation about the aryl–boron bond.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents. One substituent is a primary amino group attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The other is a sulfonamide group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and bonded to an unsubstituted primary amino group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl linkage gives the side chain some rotational freedom. The arrangement contains several hydrogen-bond donors, from the two amino groups, and several acceptors, from the sulfonyl oxygens and the aromatic amine nitrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, which makes it an ortho-disubstituted benzene. One substituent is a primary amino group attached directly to the ring, and the other is a carbohydrazide group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydrazine unit (–C(=O)–NH–NH2). The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carbohydrazide side chain has some rotational freedom around its single bonds. There is no symmetry element beyond the local planarity of the ring. The molecule offers several hydrogen-bond donors from the two amine-type nitrogens and the hydrazide NH groups, and several acceptors from the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pairs.

This molecule is a 2-aminobenzimidazole, built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a five-membered imidazole ring. The imidazole contains two nitrogen atoms: one pyridine-like nitrogen that accepts a hydrogen bond and one pyrrole-like NH that donates one. An exocyclic primary amino group sits on the carbon between the two imidazole nitrogens, giving the molecule an additional donor site and an acceptor site. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the unsubstituted benzo ring gives the molecule no symmetry beyond its planar outline.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an amino group (–NH2) attached directly to the ring, and the other is a nitrile group (–C≡N) attached to the neighboring carbon. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds in the core. The nitrile is linear and contributes a nitrogen lone pair that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the amino group can both donate hydrogen bonds through its N–H bonds and accept them through its lone pair. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring, since the two substituents are distinct.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone built from two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group. One ring carries a primary amino group on the carbon directly adjacent to the carbonyl attachment point, giving an ortho-substitution pattern, while the other ring is unsubstituted. Both aromatic rings are planar and fused to nothing, so the scaffold consists of two isolated six-membered carbocycles linked by a single sp2 carbon, with no stereocenters and limited conformational freedom around the two aryl-carbonyl bonds. The amino group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the carbonyl oxygen is a good hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the amino substituent breaks the mirror relationship between the two rings.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The thiazole portion contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom positioned so that the sulfur sits on the fused bicyclic framework and the nitrogen is part of the C=N double bond. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to the carbon at position 2 of the thiazole ring, which is the carbon flanked by both heteroatoms. The benzene ring carries no additional substituents, so the fused system is unsubstituted apart from the amine. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the amino group adding limited conformational freedom. The amino group provides hydrogen-bond donor capability through its two N-H bonds, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of that ring, making the substitution pattern ortho: one is a primary amine group attached directly to the ring, and the other is a hydroxymethyl group, a methylene carbon bearing a hydroxyl. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the hydroxyl oxygen can both donate and accept. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the CH2–OH arm gives the molecule some rotational flexibility. The structure has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic amine built on a four-carbon chain, specifically a butan-2-amine skeleton in which a primary amino group is attached to the second carbon of a straight butane backbone. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated groups, so the structure is simple and entirely saturated. The only functional group is the primary amine, which is attached to a secondary carbon, giving the molecule a single stereogenic center and therefore the possibility of two mirror-image forms, though the SMILES as written does not specify one. The carbon framework is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the molecule has no internal symmetry. The nitrogen carries two hydrogens, so it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

The molecule is built on a fluorene scaffold, a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered ring that contains a CH2 bridge. The ring system is fully aromatic on the two outer rings and largely planar and rigid, with the central CH2 providing a small point of sp3 character. A primary amine group (-NH2) is attached to one of the outer aromatic rings, placing it at a position on the fused system rather than on the bridge. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of this single asymmetric substitution. The amine nitrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One ring carbon carries a primary amino group (-NH2), and the neighboring carbon carries a hydroxyl group (-OH), so the two functional groups sit next to each other on the six-membered ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion or stereocenters present. The molecule has only a mirror plane through the substitution axis, so its symmetry is limited. The amino and hydroxyl groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor capability through their N-H and O-H bonds, and both also serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs.

The molecule is 2-aminopyrazine, built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 4 positions, which makes it a diazine with a planar, fully conjugated scaffold. An amino group is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, giving a monosubstituted pattern with no stereocenters and no rotatable bonds within the core. The ring is rigid and flat, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the mirror plane that passes through the substituted carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The exocyclic amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H hydrogens, while the two ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring, bearing one primary amino group attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which places it at the 2-position. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, and the lone-pair-bearing ring nitrogen and the exocyclic amine together form a 2-aminopyridine motif. There are no additional ring fusions, stereocenters, or bulky substituents, so the scaffold is compact, rigid, and essentially unbranched. The molecule has only a rough two-dimensional mirror plane through the ring and lacks any higher symmetry beyond that. The amino group contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. Substituents sit on adjacent carbons: an amino group (-NH2) on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and a formyl group (an aldehyde, -CHO) on the neighboring carbon. Because the ring is aromatic and the two substituents are ortho to each other, the structure is planar and rigid, with only the aldehyde and amino groups able to rotate slightly. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and the aldehyde oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents occupy different positions relative to the ring nitrogen.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, while a primary amino group (–NH2) sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 2-aminopyridine-type arrangement with the two substituents in a 1,4 relationship across the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only limited rotational freedom around the bond linking the amide to the ring. The amide and amino groups together provide several hydrogen-bond donors and the carbonyl oxygen and ring nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to the ring at the position para to the ring nitrogen, while a primary amino group (–NH2) sits on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a 2-amino-substituted, 4-carboxylated pattern. The substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the carboxylic acid bond providing rotational freedom. The amino group and carboxyl OH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, carrying two substituents. An amino group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position, and a hydroxymethyl group is attached to the ring carbon at the 5-position, which is meta-related to the amine across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the hydroxymethyl's C–O bond and the amine's N–H bonds providing modest rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any element of symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically. The amino nitrogen and hydroxyl oxygen can both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen and the oxygen atom serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. At one carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen sits a primary amino group, and at the meta-related carbon (three positions away along the ring) sits a thioamide group, in which a carbon is double-bonded to sulfur and single-bonded to an NH2 group. The ring carries no fused rings and no stereocenters, and the scaffold is essentially planar and rigid, with only the thioamide's C–C bond to the ring permitting rotation. The amino and thioamide NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the pyridine nitrogen and the thiocarbonyl sulfur serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern lacks any symmetry axis, so the two substituents are chemically distinct.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrimidine ring containing two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to the carbon between the two ring nitrogens, which is the only substituent and gives the molecule a simple monosubstituted pattern. The planar, fully conjugated aromatic ring makes the structure rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond, the C-N bond to the amino group. The exocyclic amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is 2-aminothiazole, a small heteroaromatic compound built on a single five-membered ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom separated by a carbon, which makes it a thiazole scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the whole molecule is rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds. An exocyclic primary amino group is attached to the carbon sitting between the sulfur and the ring nitrogen, which is the only substituent and gives the molecule no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic compound built on a single five-membered thiazole ring, which contains one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A primary amino group sits on the carbon between the sulfur and the nitrogen, while a nitrile group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the sulfur on the opposite side. The two substituents are placed on non-adjacent positions, giving the molecule little symmetry. Its rigid, flat framework has essentially no rotatable bonds, and the amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor while the ring nitrogen and nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a central 1,3,5-triazine ring, a six-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms. Two of the three carbon positions on this triazine core each carry a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen, and the remaining carbon carries an anilino group, meaning an NH linker bonded to a phenyl ring. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and planar, so the molecule has a largely flat aromatic region together with two saturated, chair-capable morpholine rings. The two morpholine groups are identical, which gives the molecule a partial mirror-type symmetry about the anilino substituent. The morpholine oxygens and the triazine and NH nitrogens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the single NH group serves as the only hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that shares two adjacent carbon atoms with it. The imidazole ring contains two nitrogen atoms: one is a pyridine-like nitrogen that accepts hydrogen bonds, and the other is an N-H group that can donate one. Attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens is a cyanomethyl side chain, a CH2 group bearing a nitrile (C≡N), which adds a linear, strongly polar hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the side chain offers some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the approximate mirror plane of the fused ring system.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the aromatic system spanning both rings. Attached at the 2-position of the thiazole ring is a cyanomethyl group, a short methylene linker terminated by a nitrile (C≡N) functional group. The nitrile nitrogen and the thiazole ring nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The benzene portion carries four unsubstituted hydrogens, so the substitution pattern is limited to the single side chain.

The molecule is a benzothiazole, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The thiazole portion is aromatic and planar, so the whole fused system is rigid and flat. A hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH substituent) is attached to the carbon at the 2-position of the thiazole ring, between the sulfur and the nitrogen, and this is the only substituent, so the molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring system. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indane-1,3-dione core: a five-membered carbocycle fused to a benzene ring, bearing two carbonyl groups at the 1 and 3 positions. The carbon between the two carbonyls (position 2) is sp3-hybridized and carries a benzoyl substituent, a phenyl ring joined through a ketone. Together the fused bicyclic system is largely planar and rigid, while the benzoyl group adds a single rotatable bond that gives modest conformational freedom. The molecule is not symmetric because the benzoyl group sits on only one side of the central carbon. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the three carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzophenone core in which one phenyl ring carries a carboxylic acid group at the ortho position relative to the central carbonyl. Its scaffold consists of two benzene rings joined through a single ketone carbon, giving a diaryl ketone framework. The ortho-disubstituted ring bears both a carboxylic acid and the carbonyl bridge, while the other phenyl ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are not fused, but the ortho arrangement forces them to twist out of a common plane, making the overall shape moderately rigid with limited conformational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the two oxygens), while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone in which a central carbonyl group links two aromatic systems: one is a simple unsubstituted phenyl ring, and the other is a naphthalene unit attached at its 2-position. The naphthalene is a fused bicyclic system of two benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, extended aromatic framework. The carbonyl carbon is sp2-hybridized and holds the two rings roughly coplanar, so the overall scaffold is largely rigid, with limited rotation apart from the single bonds joining the carbonyl to each ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and no true rotational symmetry, though the phenyl side is locally symmetric. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are attached to carbon. The oxygen of the carbonyl is a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging a phenyl ring and a pyridine ring. The pyridine ring is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, attached to the carbonyl carbon at the position adjacent to that nitrogen (the 2-position). The phenyl ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, so the overall scaffold has no additional substituents. The molecule lacks a plane of symmetry relative to the two rings, since one ring is carbocyclic and the other contains nitrogen, though both aromatic rings are planar. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the pyridine nitrogen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone in which a central carbonyl group links two aromatic rings: one is a benzene ring and the other is a five-membered thiophene ring containing a sulfur atom. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, while the thiophene is attached at its 2-position, the carbon adjacent to the sulfur. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated with the carbonyl, which gives the framework considerable rigidity, though the bonds connecting the carbonyl to each ring allow some rotation. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks overall symmetry, since the two rings differ in size and heteroatom content. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a diarylmethane built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene bridge. One ring is a phenol bearing a hydroxyl group, and the other is a simple unsubstituted phenyl ring. The phenol ring carries a chlorine atom positioned para to the hydroxyl group and meta to the bridging methylene, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4-trisubstituted. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated, while the sp3 methylene linker gives the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility, with no internal symmetry across the molecule as a whole. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the chlorine contributes weak polar character, and the aromatic rings offer π-electron density for stacking interactions.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring bearing an amino group at the 2-position, with a benzyl group attached to that nitrogen, so the skeleton consists of two aromatic six-membered rings joined by a flexible CH2–NH linker. The pyridine nitrogen and the secondary amine nitrogen are both present, and the molecule has no fused ring systems, since the two rings are separated by the methylene and amine bridge. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, and the pyridine ring carries only the single amino substituent, so the substitution pattern is simple. The molecule lacks a mirror plane or rotational axis of symmetry in its overall shape, though each aromatic ring is individually flat and symmetric. The methylene linker gives the structure rotational flexibility, while the two aromatic rings are rigid. The NH group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the pyridine nitrogen together with the amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a cyclohexanone bearing an exocyclic benzylidene group: a six-membered saturated ring whose carbonyl carbon is double-bonded to a carbon that is in turn attached to a phenyl ring through a single bond. The scaffold therefore consists of a cyclohexanone ring conjugated with a benzene ring through an alkene linker, with no fused ring system. The ketone carbonyl and the conjugated C=C bond form an α,β-unsaturated ketone, and the unsubstituted phenyl ring carries no additional substituents, giving the molecule no symmetry beyond a local planar conjugated segment. The alkene and the aryl-carbonyl linkage restrict rotation, making the core fairly rigid, while the cyclohexane ring retains some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as its only hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring bearing a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a benzyloxy group on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit ortho to each other next to the ring nitrogen. The pyridine core is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle, and the benzyl portion consists of a separate, unfused phenyl ring linked through a flexible CH2–O ether bridge. Because there is no ring fusion, the two aromatic systems are connected only by a single methylene and an oxygen atom, which gives the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility around that linker. The ring nitrogen and the phenolic hydroxyl can both act as hydrogen-bond participants, with the hydroxyl functioning as a donor and acceptor and the nitrogen and ether oxygen as acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the substituents are placed asymmetrically on the pyridine ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, a benzyloxy substituent, and two adjacent methoxy groups. Parsing the SMILES, the six-membered aromatic core carries a formyl (CHO) group, which is a carbonyl with an attached hydrogen, and an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 that is bonded to a second, unfused phenyl ring, giving a benzyl ether. The two methoxy groups sit next to each other on the central ring, while the aldehyde and benzyloxy groups are positioned ortho to one another, creating a trisubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry. The two phenyl rings are connected through a flexible CH2–O linkage, so the molecule has moderate conformational freedom around that bridge. The carbonyl oxygen and the three ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A bromine atom sits on one carbon of the ring, and a benzyloxy group is attached at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, meaning the two substituents are positioned in a meta-like relationship across the ring. The benzyloxy side chain consists of an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 group that bears a separate unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the molecule contains two aromatic systems joined by a flexible linker. The ring nitrogen and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is largely planar within each aromatic ring but has rotational freedom around the ether and benzylic bonds.

The molecule is a pyrimidine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. A bromine atom sits on one ring carbon, and a benzyloxy group (an oxygen linking the ring to a CH2 that is attached to a phenyl ring) occupies the position between the two ring nitrogens. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is simple and the scaffold is not fused. The ether linkage and the benzylic CH2 give the molecule some rotational flexibility, while the aromatic rings stay rigid and planar. The ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the ether oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has no symmetry axis because the bromine and benzyloxy groups sit at different positions on the pyrimidine.

The molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid built on a benzene ring that carries a boronic acid group, -B(OH)2, at one position. A fluorine atom sits on the same ring, meta to the boronic acid, and an ortho benzyloxy group (a benzyl ether, -O-CH2-phenyl) is attached adjacent to the boron-bearing carbon. The molecule contains two separate benzene rings linked by a flexible ether-methylene chain, giving it moderate conformational freedom around the C-O and O-CH2 bonds. The boronic acid's two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and their oxygens as acceptors, while the ether oxygen and fluorine serve as additional weak acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps it onto itself.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and at the position across from it on the ring a benzyloxy group is attached through an ether oxygen, which is in turn bonded to a CH2 linking to a phenyl ring. The substitution pattern is therefore a 2,5-disubstituted pyridine: the ether-bearing carbon sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and the hydroxyl is meta to the nitrogen. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks overall symmetry, though the benzyl phenyl ring rotates freely about its single bonds, giving it moderate flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ring nitrogen and ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the aromatic rings contribute planar surfaces.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through an ether linkage: one ring carries a primary amino group, and the other is an unsubstituted phenyl ring connected via a single methylene bridge. The aminophenyl ring is ortho-disubstituted, with the amine and the oxygen on adjacent carbons, while the benzyl portion contributes a flexible CH2 spacer that allows the two aromatic rings to adopt varied relative orientations. There is no ring fusion, and the structure lacks any symmetry element that would make both halves identical. The primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with a hydrogen) and an ether oxygen linking to a benzyl group. The benzyl unit consists of a CH2 spacer attached to a second, unfused phenyl ring, so the scaffold is two separate aromatic rings joined through a flexible ether linkage rather than a fused ring system. The substitution pattern on the first ring is ortho, placing the carbonyl and ether oxygen next to each other. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry, and its single ether bond and benzylic CH2 give it moderate conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present, but the carbonyl oxygen and ether oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on one carbon and an ether linkage on the adjacent carbon. That ether oxygen connects to a benzyl group, a CH2 bridge attached to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring, so the scaffold is two separate benzene rings joined by a flexible –O–CH2– linker. The substitution pattern on the first ring is ortho, placing the two substituents next to each other. The molecule has no fused ring system and no overall symmetry, since the two ends differ. Rotation about the ether and benzylic bonds gives it considerable flexibility. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl hydrogen-bond donors and two oxygen acceptors, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

This molecule is a benzoic acid bearing an ortho substituent: a benzene ring carries a carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) on one carbon and, on the adjacent carbon, an ether oxygen linked to a CH2 group that connects to a second, unsubstituted benzene ring. The scaffold is therefore two phenyl rings joined through a flexible benzyloxy linker, with the substitution pattern being ortho (1,2-disubstituted) on the first ring and monosubstituted on the second. The molecule lacks any ring fusion and has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local phenyl rotation. The rotatable C–O and CH2 bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the OH) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a phenylacetic acid scaffold, with a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH) attached to a benzene ring. Ortho to that carboxymethyl group sits a benzyloxy substituent (–O–CH2–C6H5), so the two substituents occupy adjacent positions on one ring and the other ring hangs off a flexible ether linkage. The molecule contains two separate, unfused benzene rings, each aromatic and planar, joined through a sp3 methylene-ether bridge that gives it considerable conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor. The structure has no symmetry axis or mirror plane because the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two adjacent substituents at the ortho positions: a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 bearing a nitrile, C≡N) and a benzyloxy group (an ether oxygen linking the ring to a CH2 attached to a second, unsubstituted phenyl ring). It contains no fused ring systems; the two benzene rings are connected through a flexible aryl–O–CH2–aryl linkage, giving the molecule considerable conformational freedom. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen is a weak acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry, since the two aromatic rings and their substituents differ in substitution pattern.

This molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a boronic acid group, with a benzyloxy substituent on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The boronic acid, B(OH)2, is attached at the 3-position of the pyridine, while the ether oxygen sits at the 2-position, so the two groups are adjacent to each other. The benzyl unit is a phenyl ring joined to the ether oxygen through a flexible CH2 linker, giving the molecule a rotatable chain that connects two aromatic systems. Overall there are no fused rings and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local planarity of each ring. The boronic acid hydroxyls serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the pyridine nitrogen and ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single methylene carbon, giving a diarylmethane scaffold. Each ring is a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, and the unsubstituted ring carries only hydrogens. The first ring bears a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the methylene linker, placing the two substituents in an ortho relationship. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the rest of the framework is nonpolar and aromatic. The two rings can rotate about the single bonds to the central carbon, so the molecule is moderately flexible and lacks any internal symmetry axis.

The molecule is a benzyl-substituted pyridine: a benzene ring and a pyridine ring are joined through a single methylene (CH2) bridge, with the substituent attached at the 2-position of the pyridine. Both aromatic rings are six-membered, fully conjugated, and planar, and they are not fused to each other, so the scaffold is a diarylmethane-type framework. The only ring nitrogen sits adjacent to the attachment point, giving the pyridine ring an asymmetric substitution pattern. The methylene linker provides some rotational flexibility, allowing the two rings to adopt different relative orientations. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a biphenyl scaffold, two benzene rings joined by a single bond between adjacent (ortho) positions, with a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) attached to one of the rings at the position next to that biaryl bond. Both rings are simple aromatic six-membered carbocycles with no fused ring systems. The ortho-linkage forces the two rings to twist out of coplanarity, giving the molecule a non-planar, somewhat restricted conformation, while the benzylic CH2 and hydroxyl group add a degree of rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry that would make the two rings equivalent. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic rings contribute only weak π-interaction capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries five substituents and one open position: three fluorine atoms and one bromine atom are attached directly to the ring, while the remaining ring carbon bears a hydrogen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, with the bromine flanked by two fluorines on one side and the fluorines spread around the remaining positions, so the molecule has no rotational symmetry axis beyond a single mirror plane through the bromine and the unsubstituted carbon. The ring is rigid and planar, and the halogen substituents add no rotatable bonds, so the structure is essentially inflexible. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor character comes from the weakly basic fluorine atoms.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three halogen substituents on adjacent ring positions: a chlorine and a bromine flank a central position, with a second chlorine on the opposite side of the bromine. The arrangement is a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern, which lowers the overall symmetry to a single mirror plane passing through the bromine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens can only act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused rings and no heteroatoms in the ring. Three halogen substituents are attached to the ring: two chlorine atoms and one bromine atom, occupying positions that give the ring an uneven, asymmetric substitution pattern. The bromine sits between the two chlorines on one side, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the ring's own planarity. The scaffold is rigid and flat, with the halogens attached directly to the aromatic framework and no rotatable bonds. Because the substituents are halogens with no N-H or O-H groups, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogens offer only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three halogen substituents. Two fluorine atoms sit at positions 1 and 4 across the ring (para to each other), and a bromine atom sits at position 2, adjacent to one of the fluorines, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 (a trisubstituted benzene). The molecule has no stereocenters and only a reduced, approximate mirror symmetry through the axis that runs through the bromine-bearing carbon and the opposite carbon, because the three different halogens break full symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar with no rotatable bonds. The compound has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups, and the fluorine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that contains a CH2 group. The fused five-membered ring is saturated, so the arrangement is largely rigid with limited conformational freedom beyond ring puckering. The non-aromatic ring carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydroxyl group on the carbon bonded directly to the benzene ring and a bromine atom on the neighboring carbon. Because these two substituents sit on different carbons of the same ring, the molecule is chiral and has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine is a weak halogen-type acceptor only.

This molecule is a bicyclic compound built on an indanone scaffold, where a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring. The five-membered ring contains a ketone carbonyl at one position and a sp3 CH2 group, and the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl carries a bromine substituent, making it an alpha-halogenated ketone. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is limited to the fused five-membered ring. The fused ring system is rigid and planar in its aromatic portion, with little conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the bromine. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around an imidazole ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms. One ring nitrogen is substituted by a tetrahedral sp3 carbon that carries three separate phenyl rings, giving a bulky trityl-like arrangement. The second ring carbon adjacent to the substituted nitrogen bears a bromine atom, so the heteroaromatic core is halogenated at one position. The three phenyl groups are unfused benzene rings attached to the same quaternary carbon, which gives the overall structure a propeller-like shape with no internal symmetry axis beyond the local threefold arrangement of the phenyls. The imidazole's remaining nitrogen is a basic, sp2-hybridized acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The bulky, rigid aromatic groups restrict rotation around the central carbon-nitrogen bond.

The molecule is a bromomethyl ketone in which the carbonyl carbon links a pentafluorophenyl ring to a CH2Br group. The aromatic core is a single benzene ring with no fused partners, and all five non-carbonyl ring positions carry fluorine atoms, leaving the ring with no hydrogen substituents. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aryl ketone portion is planar and rigid, whereas the single bond to the CH2Br group allows some rotational freedom. Overall the structure lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the carbonyl and ring axis.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two methoxy groups and one bromoacetyl group, giving a 1,3-dimethoxybenzene scaffold with the ketone-bearing substituent placed ortho to one methoxy group and para to the other. The aromatic ring is a single planar six-membered system with no fused rings. The ketone carbonyl is attached directly to the ring and carries a CH2 group bearing a bromine atom, making it an alpha-halo ketone. Both methoxy oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carbonyl oxygen is also an acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid, while the methoxy and bromoacetyl side chains retain some rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that bears two substituents at adjacent positions, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a hydroxyl group directly on the ring, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The other is a ketone carbonyl that links the ring to a bromomethyl group, so the side chain contains a reactive carbon-bromine bond alongside the carbonyl oxygen, which is a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two-atom side chain adds a modest degree of conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ in character and position.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), which is an ether that can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate them. The other is a ketone-linked side chain: a carbonyl attached directly to the ring, followed by a CH2 group carrying a bromine atom on the terminal carbon, giving an alpha-haloketone functionality. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen and carbonyl oxygen serve as acceptors. The benzene ring is rigid and planar, whereas the side chain has rotational freedom around its single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a nitro group (an electron-withdrawing N-oxide-type group with two oxygen atoms), placed ortho to the second substituent, which is a ketone carbonyl attached to a bromomethyl group, giving an alpha-bromoketone. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, while the carbonyl and nitro groups are rigid and largely coplanar with it. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different. The oxygen atoms of the carbonyl and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small acyclic compound built on a single quaternary carbon that carries a nitro group, a bromine atom, and two hydroxymethyl arms. Because the central carbon is fully substituted, the framework has no rings and no ring fusion, and it is quite flexible, with free rotation about each C–C and C–O bond. The nitro group, bearing a formal positive charge on nitrogen and negative charge on one oxygen, is a strong polar functional group, and the two primary alcohols add further polarity. The molecule has no internal symmetry element that makes its two hydroxymethyl arms identical, since the nitro group and bromine occupy the remaining two positions. The two hydroxyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aryl bromomethyl ketone, built on a benzene ring that carries a single trifluoromethyl group at the meta position relative to the ketone. The ketone carbonyl links the aromatic ring to a CH2 group that bears a bromine atom, making the side chain a flexible two-carbon unit attached to a rigid, planar aromatic core. The benzene ring is the only ring system, with no ring fusion, and the meta substitution pattern gives the molecule no symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the ring. The trifluoromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, non-hydrogen-bonding substituent, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. A bromine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms) is attached to the ring carbon meta to the nitrogen on the opposite side of the bromine-bearing carbon. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions on the ring. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fluorine atoms are weak acceptors and the bromine is largely non-polar in this context.

This molecule is an aryl ketone built on a single benzene ring. The ketone carbonyl is bonded directly to the ring, and its other side carries a bromomethyl group, so the carbonyl sits between an aromatic ring and a CH2 bearing a bromine atom. The benzene ring is substituted at the position para to the acyl group with a chlorine and at the adjacent meta position with a second chlorine, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern. The ring is fused to nothing else and is planar and rigid, while the bromomethyl ketone side chain offers some rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused or additional rings. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, and a bromine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, forming an ortho-bromoaniline arrangement. Two trifluoromethyl groups occupy the meta positions relative to the amine, on opposite sides of the ring, giving the scaffold a roughly symmetrical substitution pattern about the axis through the amine and bromine carbons. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the trifluoromethyl groups are attached by single bonds and can rotate. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on its nitrogen, whereas the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing four substituents. Two bulky tert-butyl groups sit ortho to a central hydroxyl group, flanking it on both sides, while a bromoacetyl group (a ketone bearing a CH2Br unit) is attached at the position para to that hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is therefore 3,5-di-tert-butyl-4-hydroxyphenyl, giving the ring a plane of mirror symmetry through the hydroxyl and ketone carbon axis. Because the aromatic core is rigid and the tert-butyl groups are sterically crowded, the overall shape is fairly fixed, with flexibility limited mainly to the rotation of the bromoacetyl side chain. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional functional groups beyond the two halogen substituents. Ring atoms are numbered from the nitrogen, so the chlorine sits on the carbon adjacent to the one bearing the bromine, which places the two halogens on neighboring carbons of the ring, positions 2 and 3 relative to the nitrogen. The molecule is planar, rigid, and essentially symmetry-free, since the two substituents are different halogens in different positions. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while the ring has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the scaffold is small, flat, and compact, with the halogens providing the only substitution pattern to distinguish one side of the ring from the other.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a bromine atom, and a fluorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring carbon, with the bromine on the adjacent (ortho) position and the fluorine on the carbon one position further around the ring, meaning it sits meta to the acid and meta to the bromine. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the carboxylic acid group having rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the halogen atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain with no rings, so its scaffold is entirely flexible and open. The terminal carbon is a fully substituted quaternary center bearing two methyl groups and one fluorine atom, which creates a tertiary alkyl fluoride. The adjacent carbon carries a bromine atom and is bonded to the carboxyl group, placing an alpha-bromo substituent next to the acid functionality. The carboxylic acid group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The two methyl groups are equivalent, but the chiral center at the bromine-bearing carbon removes any overall mirror symmetry.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional fused rings. Two substituents are attached to the ring: a hydroxyl group on one carbon and a bromine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to it, placing them at neighboring positions beside the nitrogen. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fully planar aromatic framework is rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents differ from each other.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so it contains one ring nitrogen and no fused ring systems. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, and an iodine atom on the next carbon around the ring, with the methyl group sitting meta to the nitrogen-bearing carbon. The two halogens are adjacent to each other on the same side of the nitrogen, which gives the substitution pattern a crowded, asymmetric arrangement with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, leaving only the small rotation of the methyl group. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta relationship: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a bromoacetyl group, which is a ketone carbonyl attached to a CH2 that carries a bromine atom. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ketone-CH2Br side chain adds some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The ketone oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, the structure is asymmetric, lacking any internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry because the two substituents differ and sit at unequal positions on the ring.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle with no fused rings. Its ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group, placed so that the bromine sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen and the methyl group sits next to it on the other side. The nitro group is attached at the position meta to the nitrogen, on the carbon opposite the methyl-bearing carbon. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, and the substitution pattern leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry. The pyridine nitrogen and the oxygen atoms of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a bromoacetyl group, a ketone carbonyl attached directly to the ring whose alpha carbon carries a bromine atom. The other substituent is a nitro group, with its nitrogen bonded to the ring and two oxygen atoms. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, rigid and planar, while the bromomethyl ketone side chain adds a small degree of conformational flexibility around the carbonyl-to-ring bond. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane in its planar framework. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups. Hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are present at the ketone oxygen and the two nitro oxygens.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with the nitrogen atom at position one. A nitro group (–NO2) is attached to one ring carbon and a bromine atom is attached to the carbon immediately next to the ring nitrogen, so the two substituents sit on adjacent-to-nitrogen and neighboring carbons. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds within the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents are at different positions on the ring. The nitro group contributes strong hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, and the ring nitrogen is an additional acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring. One side carries a ketone group bonded directly to the ring, and that carbonyl carbon is attached to a CH2 group bearing a bromine atom, making it a bromomethyl ketone. The opposite side of the ring bears a pyrrolidine ring connected through its nitrogen, so the ring nitrogen is a tertiary aromatic amine conjugated with the benzene. The pyrrolidine is a saturated five-membered ring that adds conformational flexibility, while the benzene core and carbonyl group are rigid and planar. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local two-fold pattern of the para-substituted ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the amine nitrogen can also act as a weak acceptor, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side carries a diethylamino group, in which a nitrogen atom is bonded to two ethyl chains and to the ring. The opposite side carries a ketone whose carbonyl carbon is also attached to a bromomethyl group, giving an alpha-halo ketone. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no fused rings, while the two ethyl groups and the bromomethyl unit add conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, although the substituents themselves are not identical. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, whereas the tertiary amine nitrogen is a weak acceptor and has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and separated positions: an amino group, a bromine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. Reading the SMILES, the amino group sits at one carbon, a bromine atom occupies the ortho position beside it, and the trifluoromethyl group sits para to the amino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is fully aromatic and planar with no fused rings, while the trifluoromethyl group is a rotatable but compact, roughly tetrahedral unit. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acting as an acceptor, and the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group can weakly accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local arrangement of the ring, so it is asymmetric overall.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no additional fused rings. A primary sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and that group carries two oxygen atoms and an NH2 that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors and donors. Across the ring from the sulfonamide sits a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3), while a bromine atom occupies the position adjacent to the sulfonamide, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. Only the sulfonamide contributes hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capacity, while the halogens and trifluoromethyl group add steric bulk and electron-withdrawing character.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents: two methoxy groups (O-CH3) and one bromine atom. The aromatic ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no fused ring systems. The acrylic acid side chain, a trans-configured C=C double bond bearing a terminal carboxylic acid, extends from the ring and contributes conjugation with the aromatic system, limiting rotational freedom. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the bromine and the two methoxy groups occupy positions that break any mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the methoxy oxygens serve as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing four substituents. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, a bromine on the adjacent carbon, and chlorine atoms on the two positions flanking the amino-bearing region, giving a 2-bromo-4,6-dichloroaniline substitution pattern. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the halogens occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the amine. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the amino group capable of limited rotation about its C-N bond. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on the nitrogen, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Going around the ring, an amino group sits on one carbon, with a bromine on the adjacent carbon, and a fluorine on the carbon next to that, followed by a second fluorine on a carbon meta to the amine's position. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only conformational freedom is the rotation of the amino group. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (two N–H bonds) and an acceptor through its lone pair, while the two fluorines are weak acceptors. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the bromine and the two fluorines are not placed in a mirror-symmetric pattern about the amine.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Five of its ring positions carry substituents: two methyl groups, an amino group, and a bromine atom, while one position remains a hydrogen-bearing carbon. The methyl groups sit meta to each other, and the amino and bromo groups occupy adjacent positions flanking one methyl group, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern without any mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The ring and its attached groups are essentially rigid, with only the methyl rotations adding minor flexibility. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine is a weak halogen-type acceptor and the ring itself is largely hydrophobic.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing six substituents: an amino group, a bromine atom, two nitro groups, and hydrogen atoms at the remaining two positions. The amino group sits on a carbon adjacent to both a bromine-bearing carbon and a nitro-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is contiguous on one side of the ring. The two nitro groups are positioned meta to one another, giving the ring an asymmetric arrangement with no meaningful internal symmetry. Because the ring is fully aromatic and the substituents are attached directly to it, the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the nitro groups able to rotate slightly about their bonds. The amino group provides hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents in a 1,3,5-pattern-like arrangement: two bulky tert-butyl groups flank a phenolic hydroxyl, and a bromine sits on the ring at the position opposite the hydroxyl's neighbor. The single aromatic six-membered ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the tert-butyl groups are rigid, sterically demanding branches that restrict rotation around the ring. The molecule carries one hydroxyl group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine is a weak halogen acceptor and the rest of the scaffold is nonpolar hydrocarbon. Its substitution is asymmetric overall, with the two tert-butyl groups in different environments relative to the bromine, giving the molecule no full mirror-plane symmetry beyond the local arrangement around the hydroxyl.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built on a single benzene ring bearing a chloro substituent para to the carbonyl attachment point. The carbonyl carbon links the ring to a CH2 group that carries a bromine atom, making it a halomethyl ketone. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and flat, with no ring fusion, and the overall framework is largely rigid apart from rotation about the bond joining the carbonyl to the ring and the bond to the CH2Br group. The molecule lacks symmetry beyond the local two-fold axis of the para-disubstituted ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. An amino group (-NH2) sits on one ring carbon, making it a primary aromatic amine. Moving around the ring, a bromine atom occupies the carbon adjacent to the amine, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon para to the amine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational flexibility beyond the amine hydrogens, with no meaningful symmetry because the three substituents differ. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, making it a phenol, and a bromine atom occupies the adjacent position, so the two are ortho to each other. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon para to the hydroxyl group, giving a 2-bromo-4-chloro substitution pattern relative to the OH. The substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The rigid aromatic core with small, fixed halogen substituents gives little conformational flexibility, while the hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the halogens serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no additional ring fusion. A bromine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the carbon at the opposite side of the ring relative to that bromine, giving a 1,3-type substitution pattern across the heterocycle. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the linear nitrile group extends the molecule's shape along one axis. The overall framework has no meaningful internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, with no additional ring systems or ring fusion. Its six ring positions carry four substituents: an amino group, a bromine atom, a trifluoromethyl group, and a fluorine atom, arranged so that the amino and bromo groups sit on adjacent carbons. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine and trifluoromethyl groups contribute polar C-F bonds that can act as weak acceptors. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the four substituents occupy positions that are not mirrored across the ring. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a tetrasubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused or additional rings. Going around the ring, an amino group sits next to a bromine atom, which is in turn adjacent to a chlorine atom, while a trifluoromethyl group sits on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,3,5-type substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair acceptor, while the halogens and fluorines contribute weak acceptor character. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the trifluoromethyl group is the only freely rotating element, so the molecule is largely inflexible.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional rings. It carries an amino group (–NH2), which serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and four halogen substituents: a bromine on the carbon adjacent to the amine, a chlorine next to that bromine on the other side, and a fluorine positioned meta to the amine. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amino group has limited rotational freedom about its C–N bond. Overall, the structure offers one hydrogen-bond donor pair and a weak acceptor site at nitrogen, with the halogens contributing to polarity without adding hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Its substituents occupy five of the six ring positions: a primary amino group, a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the amine, a bromine atom on the other carbon adjacent to the amine, and a nitro group located para to the amine on the opposite side of the ring. The overall substitution pattern is therefore highly asymmetric, with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the substituents add little conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and, through its lone pair, an acceptor, and the nitro group contributes strong hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with a chlorine and a bromine atom attached to adjacent positions around the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid carbon is bonded directly to the ring and carries a hydroxyl group and a carbonyl oxygen, which together make it both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused or additional ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic benzenoid core. The three substituents occupy three adjacent positions, producing a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern that lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. Apart from rotation about the bond connecting the carboxyl group to the ring, the structure is largely rigid, with the halogen atoms contributing as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a simple monosubstituted pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A fluorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position, while a bromine atom occupies the carbon on the opposite side of that nitrogen, at the 6-position, so the two halogens flank the nitrogen symmetrically. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings or additional rotatable bonds, and its only substituents are the two halogens. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a naphthalene derivative, consisting of two fused six-membered aromatic rings sharing a common edge. One ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on the carbon that sits meta-like to the ring fusion, while the other ring carries a bromine atom on a position across the fused system, giving an unsymmetrical 2,6-type substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar scaffold is rigid, with no rotatable bonds other than the methoxy group. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a trisubstituted aromatic compound with no fused ring systems. Going around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) sits on one carbon, a free hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, and a bromine atom sits on the carbon next to that hydroxyl on the opposite side, so the three substituents occupy neighboring positions in a contiguous 1,2,3-pattern. The ring has no internal symmetry because the three groups differ from one another. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the methoxy oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and it sits between the methyl group on one side and the bromine on the other, which gives a crowded, ortho-disubstituted arrangement around that carbon. Because the ring is fully aromatic and planar, the scaffold is rigid, with the carboxyl group able to rotate only modestly out of the ring plane. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the three substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the bromine and methyl groups contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and alternating positions: an amino group, a bromine atom, a trifluoromethyl group, and a nitro group. The amino and nitro groups sit on neighboring carbons, so the ring carries an ortho amino-nitro pair, while the bromine and trifluoromethyl groups occupy the meta-related positions on the other side. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and rotationally symmetric about its C–C bond, and the nitro group adds further electron withdrawal. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the nitro and trifluoromethyl groups able to rotate. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on the ring: a nitro group (one nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, with one oxygen charge-separated), a bromine atom, and a hydroxyl group. Reading around the ring, the hydroxyl carbon is flanked by the nitro-bearing carbon and the bromine-bearing carbon, so the three groups occupy adjacent positions in a contiguous 1,2,3-pattern. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the three substituents differ. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the bromine offers only weak halogen-bond character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings.
