Three substituents sit on adjacent and nearby positions around that ring: a methyl group, a bromine atom, and a nitro group, which together give a contiguous trisubstituted pattern. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and carries formal charges on its nitrogen and oxygens, and the bromine is a halogen substituent that can take part in weak halogen interactions. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond to the nitro group, so the scaffold is largely rigid and planar. It lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, but the oxygens of the nitro group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone, with no rings present. Its scaffold consists of a carbonyl carbon bearing a primary amide group (-C(=O)NH2) attached to a methylene carbon that carries a bromine atom at the terminal position, making it a halogenated acetamide. The bromine serves as a good leaving group on the sp3 carbon adjacent to the carbonyl, which makes the structure chemically reactive at that site. The chain has free rotation about its single bonds, so the molecule is flexible and lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement at the carbonyl. The amide group provides two hydrogen-bond donors from the NH2 hydrogens and one hydrogen-bond acceptor at the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is an acetanilide-type compound built on a benzene ring. A two-carbon acetyl group is attached through an amide linkage, with the nitrogen bonded directly to the aromatic ring, so the amide sits at one position of the phenyl scaffold. A bromine atom is attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to the amide-bearing carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern on the six-membered aromatic ring. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond its local planarity because the two substituents are different. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall the structure is compact and fairly rigid, with limited conformational freedom around the aromatic core.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, which makes it a simple monosubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Attached to that ring is a carbonyl group, so the aromatic ring is directly bonded to a ketone carbon. The ketone's other side carries a methylene group that bears a bromine atom, placing a halogen alpha to the carbonyl. The aromatic ring itself is planar and rigid, while the two-carbon linker between the ring and the bromine offers some rotational freedom around single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small, acyclic three-carbon compound built on a simple linear skeleton with no rings. The first carbon bears a terminal methylene (C=CH2) double bond, and the second carbon carries a bromine atom alongside that double bond, making it a vinyl bromide. The third carbon is a carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) attached directly to the brominated carbon. Its hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The lack of rings and the presence of a single rotatable C–C bond give the molecule a relatively compact and flexible character with no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a saturated polycyclic hydrocarbon built on an adamantane-type cage, a rigid three-dimensional framework of fused cyclohexane rings sharing bridgehead carbons. A single bromine atom is attached to one of the methylene positions of the cage, so the substitution pattern is monobromo with no other heteroatoms present. The skeleton is highly symmetric, with the parent cage belonging to a high-symmetry point group, though the bromine lowers that symmetry slightly. Because every ring carbon is sp3-hybridized and the cage is locked in place, the structure is very rigid with almost no conformational flexibility. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the only potential acceptor is the bromine atom, which is a weak one.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons: an amino group (–NH2) and a bromine atom, placing them in an ortho relationship to each other. The amino group is a primary amine that can both donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the bromine contributes a polarizable halogen but no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has only limited flexibility arising from rotation of the amino group. Its overall shape lacks any rotational symmetry beyond the ring's own planar framework, since the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no additional ring fusion. One substituent is a methoxy group, consisting of an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group and attached to the ring, while the other is a bromine atom directly bonded to the neighboring carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the methoxy group adds a small degree of conformational flexibility through rotation about the ring-oxygen bond. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The overall structure lacks any symmetry that would make the two ring positions equivalent, since the two different substituents occupy distinct environments.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound built on a single six-membered carbocyclic core with no fused rings. One substituent is a formyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydrogen, which makes it an aldehyde and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through the oxygen. The other substituent is a bromine atom attached to the neighboring ring carbon, which adds steric bulk and a polarizable halogen. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the aldehyde group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its overall shape lacks any rotational symmetry because the two substituents are different.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring, and the other is a CH=N–OH unit, which is an oxime group in which the carbon is linked to the ring through a single bond and the nitrogen carries a hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the oxime side chain has limited rotational freedom around the ring–carbon bond. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxime nitrogen and oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any elements of symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to both an amino group and the ring. The other substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring next to the amide. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different. The primary amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH2 group and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the bromine contributes little hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, which contributes two hydroxyl groups, and a bromine atom. The ortho arrangement of these two groups breaks the ring's symmetry, and the boronic acid group is planar and can rotate about its bond to the ring, so the molecule is mostly rigid apart from that rotation. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid can each donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, giving the molecule two donor and several acceptor sites, while the bromine atom acts only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a benzenesulfonamide: a single benzene ring carries a sulfonamide group, with the sulfur bearing two double-bonded oxygens and a free amino group (NH2). A bromine atom sits on the ring directly adjacent to the sulfonamide, making it an ortho-substituted, 1,2-disubstituted aromatic system. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, and there is no ring fusion or additional stereocenters, so the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the ring's local mirror plane. The sulfonamide group contributes hydrogen-bond donor capacity through its two N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity through its two sulfonyl oxygens, while the bromine is a weak halogen acceptor and adds lipophilic bulk.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a sulfonyl chloride group and a bromine atom. The sulfur is in the hexavalent oxidation state, bonded to two double-bonded oxygen atoms, one chlorine atom, and the aromatic ring, giving a tetrahedral geometry around sulfur. The bromine sits at the ortho position relative to the sulfonyl group, so the substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted. The scaffold is planar and rigid across the aromatic core, with the sulfonyl group offering some rotational freedom about the sulfur-carbon bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring. Its oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a carbohydrazide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrazine unit (an N–N bond with a terminal NH2), while the other is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, and the amide-like C(=O)–NH linkage adds limited rotational freedom to the otherwise compact structure. The hydrazide portion offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites from its NH and NH2 groups and two acceptor sites from the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogens, while the bromine contributes a polarizable halogen but no hydrogen-bonding ability. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis or mirror plane beyond the local planarity of the ring, because the two ring substituents differ in kind.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring through two adjacent carbon atoms, giving a flat bicyclic aromatic system. The imidazole portion contains two nitrogen atoms: one is a pyridine-like nitrogen that accepts hydrogen bonds, and the other is an N-H group that donates one. A bromine atom is attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens, at the C2 position of the five-membered ring. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the only substituent is this single halogen. Because the fused framework is rigid and planar, with little conformational freedom, the molecule has a simple overall shape and only a limited degree of symmetry, which is broken by the bromine.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a bromine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, while the carboxyl group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, and the bromine adds a halogen that can act as a weak acceptor. The overall structure has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing. The other is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring next to the nitrile, so the pattern is ortho-disubstituted. The structure is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the substituent attachments, and it has a local mirror plane through the ring and both substituents. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine, which is highly electrophilic and reactive toward nucleophiles. The other substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring next to the acyl chloride. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carbonyl group can rotate relative to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no ring fusion. One substituent is a hydroxymethyl group, a methylene carbon bonded to a primary alcohol, which provides a flexible rotatable linkage and both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through the hydroxyl oxygen. The other substituent is a bromine atom directly attached to the ring, a halogen that acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl arm adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. Each substituent is a bromomethyl group, in which a single carbon atom is bonded to one bromine atom and to the benzene ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic core with no fused rings. The two CH2Br groups are the only functional groups, both bearing reactive carbon-bromine bonds, while the remaining four ring carbons carry hydrogen atoms. The ortho arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane through the midpoints of the two substituted carbons, and the bromomethyl groups can rotate about their bonds, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors in the conventional sense, since the bromine atoms are weak acceptors only.

This molecule is 2-bromobiphenyl, built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a biaryl scaffold. Both rings are fully aromatic six-membered carbocycles with no ring fusion, and each contains only hydrogen besides the connecting bond, except that one ring carries a bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to the biaryl linkage, placing the halogen in the ortho position. The molecule has no polar functional groups beyond the carbon-bromine bond, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity. The unsubstituted ring possesses a mirror-like local symmetry, while the overall structure lacks a symmetry plane because of the asymmetric bromine placement. The central biaryl bond allows rotation between the two rings, so the scaffold is partially flexible, though ortho substitution restricts this motion.

This molecule is a four-carbon saturated acyclic chain, a butane skeleton with a bromine atom attached to the second carbon, which carries an ethyl group on one side and a methyl group on the other. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no double bonds, so the scaffold is fully flexible, with free rotation about its carbon-carbon single bonds. The only functional group is a secondary alkyl bromide, where the bromine sits on a carbon bonded to two other carbons, and the molecule has a stereocenter at that carbon, so it is chiral and lacks any internal mirror symmetry. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no O-H or N-H bonds. Its bromine atom can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a four-carbon chain: an ethyl group attached to a carbon bearing a bromine atom, which is in turn bonded to the carboxyl carbon. This places the bromine on the alpha carbon, adjacent to the carbonyl, giving an alpha-halogenated acid scaffold. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the framework is entirely open-chain. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the carbon-bromine bond adds a polarizable, weakly accepting halogen site. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the alpha carbon carries four different substituents, and its rotatable single bonds make it fairly flexible.

This molecule is a very small acyclic compound built on a two-carbon ethane backbone, with no ring systems and no fused or aromatic features. One terminal carbon carries a hydroxyl group, making it a primary alcohol, while the other terminal carbon carries a bromine atom, giving a primary alkyl halide at the opposite end of the chain. The two functional groups sit at opposite ends of a flexible, freely rotating carbon-carbon single bond, so the molecule has no fixed three-dimensional shape and lacks any internal symmetry. The hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen can both participate in hydrogen bonding, acting as a donor and an acceptor, while the bromine acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a fluorene scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a five-membered ring containing a CH2 group, giving a fused, largely planar tricyclic framework. A single bromine atom sits on one of the outer aromatic rings, at a position para-like to the biaryl bond, so the substitution pattern breaks the molecule's symmetry. The rigid, fused aromatic system offers little conformational flexibility. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor-type feature is the weakly polarizable carbon-bromine bond, so it has essentially no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a linear chain of five carbons, with the carboxyl carbon at one end. A bromine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group, creating an alpha-halo acid arrangement. The structure contains no rings, so it is fully flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group offers both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and acceptor capability through its oxygen atoms, while the bromine contributes only weak polar character. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the bromine is positioned asymmetrically along the chain.

The molecule is built on an indene scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle. Its six-membered aromatic ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, while the five-membered ring contains a single carbon-carbon double bond that carries a bromine atom on one of its sp2 carbons. The remaining saturated carbon in the five-membered ring is a CH2 group, so the ring is partially unsaturated and the molecule has no stereocenters. The bromine acts as the only substituent and is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fused bicyclic framework is largely planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility, and the lack of any internal symmetry axis aligned with the bromine position means the molecule is not symmetric.

This molecule is a small acyclic carboxylic acid built on a short aliphatic chain. The carbon bearing the carboxyl group is quaternary, attached to two methyl groups and a bromine atom, so the substitution pattern is fully branched at the alpha position. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no stereocenters, so the molecule is conformationally flexible about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the bromine is a weak halogen-type acceptor. The two methyl groups are equivalent, giving the carbon skeleton local threefold symmetry around the central carbon.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a branched four-carbon backbone. Its scaffold is a 2-bromo-3-methylbutanoic acid framework, with a terminal carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) at one end, a bromine atom on the alpha carbon adjacent to that group, and an isopropyl branch attached to the same alpha carbon. There are no ring systems or ring fusions. The bromine sits at a stereogenic center, so the molecule is chiral, and the structure lacks any internal symmetry. The chain is flexible, with rotation possible about its single bonds, though the bulky isopropyl group restricts some conformations. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: three methyl groups and one bromine atom. Its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so it is fully planar and rigid. The bromine sits at one position with methyl groups flanking it on both sides, creating a crowded local environment, while the remaining methyl groups are placed at positions that give the ring a 1,3,5-type pattern of substitution, lending it a degree of mirror symmetry along one axis. Because the molecule contains only carbon, hydrogen, and bromine with no polar heteroatoms, it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying three substituents. Two methyl groups sit at positions flanking one side of the ring, and a bromine atom sits between them on the carbon adjacent to both, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3 with the bromine in the middle. The structure has a mirror plane passing through the bromine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, giving it local symmetry about that axis. Because the ring is rigid and the methyl groups rotate freely, the molecule is largely planar and inflexible in its core. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the only heteroatom is a bromine that does not function as an acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which consists of two benzene rings sharing a single fused edge to form a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic system. A bromine atom is attached to one of the carbons on the outer ring, at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and removes the mirror symmetry the bare naphthalene core would otherwise have. The framework is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor character is weak and arises from the halogen, while the aromatic pi system offers a region of electron density across the ring surface.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached at the 3-position relative to the nitrogen, and a bromine atom sits at the 2-position, adjacent to the nitrogen. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, so the overall scaffold is rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate about its single bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a straight-chain alkane skeleton with five carbon atoms, specifically a pentane backbone, with no ring systems or ring fusion present. A single bromine atom is attached to the second carbon from one end, so the substitution pattern is a secondary alkyl halide, with the bromine bearing a methyl branch on one side and a propyl chain on the other. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a trivial one, since the two sides of the bromine-bearing carbon are different, and the saturated carbon framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the bromine atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a hydroxyl group, which makes the ring a phenol, and the other is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring. The six-membered aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no additional ring systems or ring fusion. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine can participate only weakly as a halogen-bond or acceptor site. The molecule has a mirror plane through the substituted carbons, giving it an overall planar, low-flexibility shape.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a bromine atom, and the other is a 2-cyanoethoxy-type side chain: an ether oxygen attached to the ring, followed by a methylene group bonded to a terminal nitrile (C≡N). The nitrile carbon is sp-hybridized and linear, giving the side chain an extended, somewhat flexible shape, while the phenyl core remains planar and rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local pseudo-mirror relationship of the ring and its substituents. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a bromine atom attached directly to the ring, and the other is a carboxymethyl group, meaning a methylene bridge leading to a terminal carboxylic acid. Because the ring is a simple unfused benzene with no additional ring systems, the scaffold is a flexible, aromatic core with a single rotatable bond between the ring and the side chain. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The molecule lacks any internal symmetry that would make its two substituent positions equivalent, so the ortho substitution pattern is clearly asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A bromine atom sits on one ring carbon, and a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linker bearing a terminal nitrile, C#N) sits on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The nitrile is a linear, strongly polar group that can accept hydrogen bonds at its nitrogen but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the bromine contributes only weak polarizability. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and the aromatic core is rigid while the CH2–CN arm retains some rotational freedom around the ring–CH2 bond.

The molecule is a small acyclic alkyl halide built on a three-carbon skeleton, specifically a propane chain with a bromine atom attached to the central carbon. Its two terminal methyl groups are equivalent, so the molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry through the C–Br bond and the central carbon. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the single carbon-bromine bond is the only functional group present. The structure is highly flexible, since rotation about its single bonds is essentially unhindered. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the bromine atom can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short three-carbon chain built on a propene skeleton, with a carbon-carbon double bond at one end and a methyl branch on the same carbon that carries the double bond. A bromine atom is attached to that same sp2 carbon, making it a vinyl halide. The alkene carbon bearing the bromine and methyl groups is trigonal planar, and the terminal CH2 is attached only by the double bond, so the molecule is essentially flat and rigid with no rotatable bonds. It contains no ring systems and no hydrogen-bond donors, and only weak hydrogen-bond acceptor character from the halogen.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain: a terminal carboxyl carbon, an alpha carbon, and a methyl group. The alpha carbon carries a bromine atom, placing a halogen directly adjacent to the carboxylic acid, which makes the substitution pattern at that position the defining structural feature. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely flexible and open-chained, with rotation possible about its single bonds. The molecule has a stereocenter at the alpha carbon, and it lacks any internal symmetry that would make it superimposable on its mirror image. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the bromine adds a weak halogen acceptor character.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: two methyl groups and one bromine atom. The methyl groups sit at positions that are para to each other across the ring, while the bromine is adjacent to one of them, giving a crowded 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry axis of note. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, and the substituents add little flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor-like site is the weakly polarizable bromine atom.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A bromine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position, while an aldehyde group (a formyl carbonyl) is attached at the 4-position, placing the two substituents in a para-like arrangement relative to each other across the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry because the two substituents differ. The ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it lacks any N-H or O-H groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom among its ring carbons, with no fused ring systems. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached at one ring carbon, positioned meta to the ring nitrogen on the opposite side from the bromine. A bromine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position relative to nitrogen, making the substitution pattern 2-bromo with a 4-carboxamide. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the amide group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The amide nitrogen provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the planar ring framework.

This molecule is a simple six-membered aromatic heterocycle built on a pyrimidine scaffold, containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship within a planar ring. A bromine atom is attached to the carbon sitting between the two nitrogens, at the 2-position, which makes that position the only substituted site. The ring is fully aromatic and rigid, with no fused rings, rotatable bonds, or stereocenters, and the molecule has a flat, low-symmetry shape with the bromine breaking any mirror symmetry in the plane. The two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since every ring atom is either a nitrogen lacking an attached hydrogen or a carbon bearing only hydrogen or the bromine.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge, giving a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. A boronic acid group, -B(OH)2, is attached to the carbon of the pyridine-type ring adjacent to the ring carbon bearing the bromine atom, so the two substituents sit on neighboring positions of the same ring. The nitrogen atom in the heteroaromatic ring acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the two hydroxyl groups on the boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. Because the fused system is planar and the substituents are attached directly to aromatic carbons, the overall framework is largely rigid, and the molecule lacks any significant internal symmetry due to the asymmetric placement of the substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons: a vinyl group (a two-carbon chain with a carbon-carbon double bond) and a bromine atom. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered, fully conjugated carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its substitution pattern is ortho, since the vinyl and bromo groups sit next to each other. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror plane through the ring, so it is essentially planar and rigid apart from rotation about the bond joining the vinyl group to the ring. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is bromine, which provides a weak halogen-bond capability rather than classical hydrogen-bond acceptance.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two carboxylic acid groups and one bromine atom. The two carboxyl groups sit on the ring at positions that are para to each other, giving a linear, centrosymmetric-like arrangement across the aromatic core, while the bromine sits ortho to one of them, breaking that symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the carboxyl groups are conjugated with it, so the scaffold is largely flat and inflexible. Each carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen) capability, so the molecule offers two donor and four acceptor sites in total. The bromine adds a bulky, electron-withdrawing substituent that influences the local electronic environment of the adjacent acid group.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with a thirteen-carbon backbone, meaning there are no rings or ring fusions anywhere in the structure. The carboxylic acid group sits at one terminus, and a bromine atom is attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to it, making this an alpha-bromo substitution pattern. The long saturated hydrocarbon tail is flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, while the head group remains comparatively compact. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the bromine breaks the chain's otherwise uniform shape. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the bromine and the saturated chain contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom, a thiazole scaffold with no fused rings. An aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bearing one hydrogen) is attached at one ring carbon, while a bromine atom sits on the carbon between the sulfur and the nitrogen. The substituents are placed at non-adjacent positions, so the ring is asymmetric and the molecule is essentially planar and rigid. The ring nitrogen and the aldehyde oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiazole ring, containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom separated by a carbon. A carboxylic acid group is attached to the carbon at the 5-position, adjacent to the sulfur, while a bromine atom sits on the carbon at the 2-position, between the nitrogen and sulfur. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, though the carboxylic acid can rotate slightly relative to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the thiazole nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one ring carbon, and directly beside it, on the adjacent carbon, sits a sulfenyl bromide group in which a sulfur atom bridges the ring to a bromine atom. This gives an ortho-disubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the substituents. The ring is rigid and planar, while the C–O–CH3 and C–S–Br linkages allow some rotational flexibility. The oxygen of the methoxy group can accept a hydrogen bond, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. A methyl group and a bromine atom are attached to neighboring positions of a single six-membered aromatic ring, with no additional ring fusion. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, and the aromatic system carries no stereocenters. Its symmetry is limited to a single mirror plane passing through the two substituents. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups, and only weak acceptor character from the halogen.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic alcohol built on a four-carbon, straight-chain-like skeleton: a two-carbon ethyl group and a methyl branch meet at a secondary carbon that carries the hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl oxygen sits at a carbon with two alkyl neighbors, making the alcohol secondary rather than primary or tertiary. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional functional groups beyond the single hydroxyl. The molecule is conformationally flexible because all bonds are single and rotatable, and it lacks any symmetry element that would make its two alkyl arms identical. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs.

The molecule is a small acyclic aliphatic ketone with a four-carbon skeleton. A carbonyl group (C=O) sits at an internal position, flanked by an ethyl group on one side and a methyl group on the other, so the carbonyl carbon bears no hydrogen. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no additional substituents, so the scaffold is simple and essentially unsubstituted. The molecule is small and highly flexible, since its single bonds can rotate freely around the carbon chain. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it lacks any O–H or N–H bonds.

This molecule is a small, acyclic oxime derived from butanone, with a four-carbon chain and no rings. The carbon bearing the C=N double bond carries an ethyl group and a methyl group, and the imine nitrogen is bonded to a hydroxyl group, giving the characteristic C=N–OH functional unit. Because there are no ring systems, the scaffold is flexible, with free rotation about the single bonds of the alkyl chain. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local planarity of the C=N–O unit, since the two substituents on the imine carbon are different. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the imine nitrogen and oxygen can each accept one.

This molecule is a small, acyclic four-carbon chain, so it has no ring systems or ring fusion. Its carbon skeleton contains a carbon-carbon triple bond between the second and third carbons, which makes that portion of the chain linear and rigid, while the terminal methyl and the methylene groups on either end allow some local rotation. The molecule carries a single primary alcohol group at the terminal end, which is its only functional group. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the triple bond offers a site of unsaturation but no additional hydrogen-bonding capability. The structure is asymmetric, with the methyl end and the hydroxymethyl end differing in their chemical environment.

This molecule is 2-butyne, a four-carbon linear alkane-derived skeleton in which a carbon-carbon triple bond sits between the second and third carbons, flanked by a methyl group at each end. It contains no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the alkyne itself. The triple bond forces the four carbon atoms into a single straight line, giving the molecule a rod-like geometry with high symmetry: it possesses a two-fold rotational axis and mirror planes through its long axis, and it is achiral. The molecule is fully rigid along its axis, with no rotatable single bonds that alter its shape in a meaningful way. Because it has only carbon and hydrogen atoms and no lone-pair-bearing electronegative atoms, it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor.

This molecule is a four-carbon linear chain, specifically but-2-yne-1,4-diol, with a carbon-carbon triple bond at the center flanked by two methylene groups. Each terminus carries a primary hydroxyl group, giving two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic. The triple bond imposes rigid linearity on the central C2 to C3 segment, while the terminal CH2–OH arms retain rotational freedom. The molecule possesses a two-fold symmetry axis passing through the midpoint of the triple bond, making the two hydroxymethyl ends chemically equivalent.

The molecule is a short, unbranched four-carbon chain built around a carbon-carbon triple bond. One end carries a terminal methyl group, followed by an internal alkyne, and the other end bears a carboxylic acid group, so the alkyne sits directly adjacent to the carbonyl carbon and the system is conjugated. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no substituents beyond the methyl and carboxyl termini, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has no internal symmetry. The rigid, linear alkyne segment limits conformational freedom, while the terminal acid group can rotate slightly. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a p-toluenesulfonate ester built on a para-substituted benzene ring carrying a methyl group opposite the sulfonyl attachment. The sulfonyl group, S(=O)2, is bonded to the aromatic ring on one side and to an oxygen that links to a four-carbon chain containing an internal alkyne, specifically a but-2-ynyl unit. The aromatic ring is planar and has a two-fold symmetry axis through the methyl and sulfonyl positions. The alkyne imposes a linear, rigid segment, while the CH2 groups and the sulfonate ester oxygen give the chain some flexibility. The two sulfonyl oxygens and the ester oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: an aldehyde (formyl) group, a carboxylic acid, and two adjacent methoxy ethers. The aldehyde and carboxylic acid sit on neighboring carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted pattern, while the two methoxy groups occupy the remaining adjacent positions on the other side of the ring, giving a contiguous trisubstituted-plus-one arrangement with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and carboxyl groups offering modest rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the aldehyde carbonyl and the ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no additional ring fusion. One substituent is a formyl group, an aldehyde with a carbon-oxygen double bond attached directly to the ring, and the other is a carboxylic acid group. The two groups sit next to each other, so they can interact through their oxygen atoms, which lowers the overall symmetry to a C2-like arrangement with a mirror-like plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two carbonyl-bearing groups have only limited rotational freedom about their ring bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites on its oxygens, and the aldehyde oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, a carboxylic acid group and a boronic acid group, in an ortho (1,2) substitution pattern, with no additional ring systems or fused rings. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, giving it a trigonal planar arrangement. Both substituents can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H groups and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two polar groups have some rotational freedom around their bonds to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring and its substituents.

The molecule is built around a single six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned meta to each other, and it carries a methyl group on one carbon of that ring. At the carbon between the two nitrogens, a sulfur atom links the ring to a short two-carbon chain that ends in a carboxylic acid group, so the thioether bridge joins the aromatic core to the acid. The structure has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and it is essentially planar across the aromatic ring, with only the flexible thioether and methylene linker allowing rotation. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the two ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, with two substituents placed on adjacent carbons (ortho substitution). One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, a carbon bearing a double-bonded oxygen and a hydroxyl. The other is a phosphate ester, where an oxygen links the ring to a phosphorus atom carrying a double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and phosphate groups have some rotational freedom around their single bonds. Both acidic groups are strong hydrogen-bond donors through their O-H bonds and good acceptors through their oxygen atoms. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying four halogen substituents and two hydrogen atoms. Going around the ring, it bears fluorine, bromine, chlorine, and bromine at consecutive or near positions, with the two bromines flanking the chlorine so that the substitution pattern is asymmetric overall. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N-H or O-H groups are present. The halogen atoms can act only as weak halogen-bond or acceptor-type contacts, and the molecule is rigid and planar because the aromatic core has no rotatable bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a chlorine atom and two nitro groups. The two nitro groups sit at positions meta to each other, and the chlorine is located between them, on the carbon adjacent to one nitro group and ortho to it. This gives a 1,2,4-type pattern around the aromatic core, leaving three hydrogen-bearing carbons on the ring. The ring itself is planar and fully aromatic, so the scaffold is rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the nitro groups. Each nitro group contributes oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the chlorine breaks the symmetry that the two nitro groups alone might otherwise create.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing two halogen substituents. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring, and one chlorine atom is attached as well, making a trihalogenated benzene. The halogens sit at the 1, 2, and 4 positions relative to one another, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry in the substituent arrangement. The scaffold is fully rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The nitro group (-NO2) is attached at one ring carbon, with the fluorine and chlorine on adjacent carbons located para and meta to it, respectively, which defines the substitution pattern as a trisubstituted aromatic system. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ from one another in both identity and position. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and its oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the halogens contribute weak acceptor character. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since no N-H or O-H bonds are present.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on that ring: a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged and one double-bonded), an iodine atom, and a chlorine atom. The nitro group sits at one position, while iodine and chlorine occupy adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern in which the halogens are neighbors and the nitro group is para to the iodine. The overall framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring and little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygens of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, containing two nitrogen atoms positioned at non-adjacent sites within the ring. One nitrogen carries a methyl group, which makes it a tertiary aromatic nitrogen with no hydrogen-bond donor capacity. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly between the two nitrogens, creating a substitution pattern at the most electron-poor ring position. The pyridine-type nitrogen remains a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the scaffold is small, planar, and essentially rigid with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring bearing a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to one nitrogen, so the ring is 2-chloroimidazole-type with a free ring nitrogen available for coordination. The other ring nitrogen is substituted by a single tetrahedral sp3 carbon that carries three separate phenyl rings, creating a bulky, propeller-like trityl-type arrangement. Each phenyl ring is unsubstituted and monosubstituted only at its attachment point to the central carbon, giving the molecule substantial three-fold-like steric symmetry around that quaternary center. The structure is rigid within each aromatic unit but has some rotational freedom around the bonds linking the phenyl rings to the central carbon. The unsubstituted ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small aromatic ketone built on a single benzene ring. A chloromethyl group is attached to a carbonyl carbon, which in turn is bonded directly to the ring, making it an aryl alkyl ketone with a halogenated alpha carbon. The benzene ring carries two fluorine substituents at positions that flank the ketone attachment point, one ortho and one para to it, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, though the single bond linking the carbonyl to the ring allows some rotational freedom.

This molecule is a substituted anilide built from a benzene ring bearing two ethyl groups flanking the amide-linked nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The nitrogen is part of a secondary amide whose carbonyl carbon carries a chloromethyl group, so the chlorine sits on a carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its ethyl substituents create a symmetric pattern around the N-attached carbon. The amide N-H can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor. The ethyl and chloromethyl groups add some conformational freedom, though the aromatic ring and amide plane remain comparatively rigid.

The molecule is an anilide built on a benzene ring that carries two methyl groups flanking the nitrogen-bearing carbon, giving a 2,6-disubstituted substitution pattern. A secondary amide links the aromatic ring to a two-carbon acyl unit ending in a chloromethyl group, so the chlorine sits on the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the amide and the chloromethyl portion provide some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry axis because the two ortho methyl groups are equivalent but the chloroacetyl chain breaks any mirror relationship. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a simple acyclic saturated carbon skeleton with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems. A central quaternary carbon carries two methyl groups, and it is bonded to an ethyl group and to a chlorine atom, so the chlorine sits on a tertiary carbon. The only functional group is the carbon–chlorine bond, which is a polar but non-hydrogen-bonding feature. Because the chlorine is the sole heteroatom, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and only a weak acceptor capacity at the halogen. The molecule is highly flexible, since all bonds are single and free to rotate, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond local methyl-group equivalence.

The molecule is an anilide built on a benzene ring, with a 2-chloroacetamide group attached to one carbon and a nitro group on the adjacent carbon, making the substitution pattern ortho. The amide nitrogen is bonded to the aromatic ring and to a carbonyl that carries a chloromethyl group, so the chlorine sits on a carbon alpha to the carbonyl. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, planar substituent with two oxygen atoms available as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, but the chloroacetyl chain and the amide linkage provide some rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions: an amino group, a chlorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. Reading around the ring, the amino group sits at one carbon, the trifluoromethyl group at a carbon two positions away, and the chlorine atom between them on the carbon adjacent to both, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. There is no ring fusion, and the single aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the trifluoromethyl group offering rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the three substituents differ. The primary amino group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atoms and the chlorine atom act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons: an aldehyde (formyl) group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a chlorine atom. The aldehyde carbon is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the chlorine sits on the carbon immediately next to it, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The trifluoromethyl group is placed meta to the aldehyde on the opposite side of the chlorine, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the aldehyde and trifluoromethyl groups have limited rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid sits at position 1, the chlorine occupies the adjacent position 2, and the trifluoromethyl group is located at position 3 on the far side of the chlorine, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the scaffold has no stereocenters and only a limited plane of approximate symmetry, since the three different substituents break any higher symmetry. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group and the chlorine atom act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, a chlorine atom sits on the neighboring carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group is on the carbon beyond the chlorine. This pattern places the nitrile and chlorine ortho to each other, with the bulky trifluoromethyl group flanking the chlorine. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the substituents themselves have limited conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, but the nitrogen of the nitrile and the fluorine atoms can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. It has no internal symmetry, because the three substituents are distinct and arranged asymmetrically on the ring.

This molecule is a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, so it has no fused or additional ring systems. One substituent is a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 attached to an OH), which contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor. Adjacent to it on the ring is a chlorine atom, and on the other side of the chlorine sits a trifluoromethyl group, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted with the bulky groups clustered together. The trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor through its fluorines, while the chlorine is a weak acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with flexibility limited mainly to rotation of the hydroxymethyl group; the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane in the aromatic framework.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent carbons: an aminomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a primary amine), a chlorine atom, and a trifluoromethyl group. The chlorine sits directly between the aminomethyl carbon and the trifluoromethyl-bearing carbon, creating a crowded 1,2,3-substitution pattern on one side of the ring, with the remaining positions occupied by hydrogens. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the molecule as a whole is fairly rigid except for rotation about the benzylic CH2 bond. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site through its nitrogen lone pair, while the chlorine and fluorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) at one position, a trifluoromethyl group, and a chlorine atom on adjacent carbons next to the acid-bearing side chain. The benzene core is aromatic and fully planar, with no additional ring fusion. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the chlorine and the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group act only as weak acceptors. The side chain adds some rotational flexibility around its CH2 linker, whereas the ring itself is rigid. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile, C≡N) is attached to one ring carbon, which makes the nitrile a hydrogen-bond acceptor with no donor sites. A trifluoromethyl group sits on a carbon two positions away from the cyanomethyl attachment, and a chlorine atom occupies the carbon between the cyanomethyl and trifluoromethyl groups, creating a crowded 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the cyanomethyl linker adds a single rotatable bond. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms) is attached to the ring carbon next to that chlorine-bearing carbon, creating an ortho substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the trifluoromethyl group adds a bulky, strongly electron-withdrawing feature while contributing no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring nitrogen serves as the only hydrogen-bond acceptor site, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different and placed asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent hydroxyl groups on the aromatic core, giving a catechol unit. A ketone carbonyl is attached directly to the ring at the position para to one of the hydroxyls, and this carbonyl is bonded to a chloromethyl group, so the side chain is a halogenated alpha-carbon adjacent to the carbonyl. The substitution pattern is 1,3,4 on the ring, which leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the chloromethyl ketone side chain offers some rotational freedom. The two phenolic oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two phenolic hydrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: two adjacent methoxy groups, a nitrile (cyano) group, and a chlorine atom. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple substituted benzene. The methoxy groups sit next to each other on one side of the ring, while the nitrile and chlorine occupy the adjacent positions on the other side, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, with only the two methoxy groups offering modest rotational flexibility. The ether oxygens and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents on six positions, making it a single aromatic ring with no fused rings. Going around the ring, there is a methoxy group, then a hydroxymethyl group, then a chlorine atom, and a second methoxy group, with the remaining positions occupied by hydrogen atoms. The two methoxy groups are adjacent to each other, and the chlorine sits next to the hydroxymethyl carbon, giving a crowded substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The scaffold is rigid because of the aromatic core, while the methoxy and hydroxymethyl groups add some rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is fully substituted in a pattern where the chlorine sits ortho to the propenoic acid side chain, and the two methoxy groups occupy adjacent positions on the far side of the ring. The side chain is an acrylic acid unit joined to the ring through a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which makes the chain rigid and largely planar with the ring. The carboxylic acid group provides one hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, while the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups and the chlorine add further weak acceptor character. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with one ring nitrogen and no fused rings or additional substituents beyond the two halogens. Two iodine atoms sit on the ring, one at the 3-position and one at the 5-position relative to the nitrogen, and a chlorine atom occupies the 2-position directly next to the nitrogen. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the three halogens are placed differently around the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The halogens add considerable bulk and polarizability to an otherwise compact aromatic framework.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, two nitro groups, and a chlorine atom, with no additional fused rings. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring position, the chlorine sits on the adjacent carbon, and the two nitro groups occupy the meta positions relative to the acid, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the nitro and carboxyl groups are attached without any flexible linker. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric. The carboxylic acid group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents spread around the ring: two nitro groups (each a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) and a chlorine atom, plus a trifluoromethyl group attached to a carbon. The two nitro groups sit at meta positions relative to each other, and the chlorine lies between one nitro group and the trifluoromethyl group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every remaining position on the ring bears a hydrogen. The overall framework is compact and rigid, with only the nitro and trifluoromethyl groups able to rotate about their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no additional fused rings. Two nitro groups (–NO2) are attached to the ring, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the ring is fully planar and rigid. The nitro groups are strong electron-withdrawing acceptors that make the ring electron-poor, and their oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring nitrogen is also an acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries one primary amino group (-NH2) on one ring carbon, with a fluorine atom on an adjacent carbon, a second fluorine on the carbon two positions further around the ring, and a chlorine atom on the carbon flanked by the amino group and the other fluorine. The arrangement is an asymmetric, crowded 1,2,3,6-type pattern with substituents on four of the six ring positions, leaving two adjacent hydrogen-bearing carbons. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amino group can rotate slightly about its carbon-nitrogen bond. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site on the nitrogen lone pair, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde (formyl) group, so it is a substituted benzaldehyde with a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle and no fused rings. Going around the ring, the formyl carbon sits at one position, flanked on one side by a chlorine atom and on the other by a fluorine atom, with a second fluorine atom located para to the formyl-bearing carbon, giving a 2,3,6-substitution pattern relative to the aldehyde. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three halogen substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the aldehyde group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. As a hydrogen-bond acceptor, the carbonyl oxygen is the main site; the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring and formyl hydrogens are bonded to carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with the carboxyl carbon attached directly to one aromatic carbon. The ring is trisubstituted: the carboxylic acid sits at one position, a chlorine atom occupies the carbon immediately adjacent to it, and two fluorine atoms are placed at the remaining positions on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 2,3,6-substitution pattern relative to the acid group. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single planar aromatic core, so its overall shape is essentially flat with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation of the carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the halogen substituents act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Its substitution pattern is fully defined: a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 attached to an OH) sits on one ring carbon, flanked on one side by a chlorine atom and on the other by a fluorine atom, while two additional fluorine atoms occupy the remaining positions on the far side of the ring. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the halogen substituents are only weak acceptors. Because the substituents are asymmetrically placed around the ring, the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. Apart from the rotatable C–C and C–O bonds of the hydroxymethyl group, the scaffold is rigid and planar.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and alternating positions: a hydroxyl group, a fluorine atom, two more fluorine atoms on the opposite side of the ring, and a chlorine atom, giving a densely halogenated phenol scaffold. The aromatic ring is fully fused-free, a single six-membered carbocycle with no additional ring systems. The hydroxyl group is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the halogen atoms are weak acceptors and contribute to a strongly electron-withdrawing pattern across the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the chlorine and hydroxyl sit side by side on one end while the fluorines are distributed along the other half, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. Its rigid aromatic core, with only the single hydroxyl bond able to rotate, makes the overall shape largely planar and conformationally restricted.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. Its ring carries three substituents: two methyl groups and a chloro group, along with a nitrile (cyano) group attached directly to the ring. The methyl groups sit at two ring positions flanking the nitrogen side and the opposite carbon, while the nitrile and chlorine occupy adjacent positions, giving a fully substituted, asymmetric pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is rigid and planar, and the only flexibility comes from rotation of the methyl groups. The pyridine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. A nitrile group (carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a chlorine atom sits on the neighboring carbon on the other side of that nitrogen. A phenyl ring is bonded directly to the pyridine at the position meta to the nitrile, giving a biaryl arrangement. The whole framework is planar and fully aromatic, so it is rigid, with only limited rotational freedom about the single bond joining the two rings. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring system. A methyl group sits on one carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, a nitrile (cyano) group is attached at the position para to the methyl, and a chlorine atom occupies the carbon between the nitrile-bearing carbon and the nitrogen-adjacent carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore unsymmetrical, leaving the molecule without any mirror or rotational symmetry. Its rigid aromatic core and linear nitrile group make it structurally stiff, with only the methyl group free to rotate. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen offers a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single aromatic pyridine ring, a six-membered heteroaromatic system containing one nitrogen atom in the ring. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons next to that nitrogen: a chlorine atom on the carbon directly beside the ring nitrogen, and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on the neighboring carbon. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen adds a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a six-membered pyridine N-oxide ring, in which the ring nitrogen carries an oxygen atom bearing a formal positive charge and the ring is aromatic. A nitro group, attached through nitrogen and carrying its own formal charges, sits on one carbon of the ring. The remaining ring carbons carry a chlorine atom adjacent to the N-oxide nitrogen and a fluorine atom on the carbon next to it. The substitution pattern is fully asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the nitro and N-oxide oxygens provide strong hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with a nitrogen atom in the ring and no ring fusion. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons next to the nitrogen: a hydroxyl group and a chlorine atom, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern that places the halogen directly beside the ring nitrogen. Because the ring is planar and fully conjugated, the scaffold is rigid, and the only rotational freedom comes from the hydroxyl hydrogen. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the two substituents differ. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a planar, rigid scaffold containing one nitrogen atom in the ring. Two halogen substituents sit on adjacent carbons next to the nitrogen: a chlorine atom on the carbon directly bonded to the ring nitrogen, and an iodine atom on the neighboring carbon. The remaining three ring carbons carry hydrogen atoms, so the substitution pattern is 2,3-disubstituted. The molecule has no rotatable bonds and no internal symmetry, since the two halogens differ. The pyridine nitrogen's lone pair can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. Two substituents are attached to adjacent ring carbons: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a chlorine atom, placed on the carbon next to the nitrogen. The remaining three ring positions carry hydrogen atoms, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the methoxy group can rotate about its single bonds, adding modest conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, and the methoxy oxygen can act as a weaker acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. A methyl group sits on the carbocyclic-adjacent carbon of the pyridine ring, and a chlorine atom occupies the position next to the ring nitrogen, so the substituents are arranged asymmetrically on one side of the bicycle. The pyridine-type nitrogen is the only heteroatom, serving as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. The overall structure is largely hydrophobic apart from the nitrogen lone pair.

The molecule is built on a quinoxaline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazine ring that carries two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship. The fused ring system is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework. The pyrazine ring bears a methyl group on one carbon and a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit side by side on the same side of the heterocycle. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the methyl and chloro groups are different. Both ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.
