The molecule is an anilide built on a single benzene ring, with an amide nitrogen attached to one ring carbon and a nitro group on the carbon two positions away, giving a meta substitution pattern. The amide carbonyl bears a chloromethyl group, so a flexible CH2Cl unit extends from the carbonyl carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the amide linkage and the chloromethyl arm provide some rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local planarity of the ring. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen together with the nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached at one ring carbon, with the nitro group on the carbon two positions away, and the chlorine on the carbon between the carboxylic acid and nitro groups, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted. The ring is a fused-free aromatic system with no additional rings or fusion. Because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no rotational symmetry axis beyond the planar aromatic framework. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and nitro groups can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the nitro group provides additional acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, while a nitro group (–NO2) is attached to the neighboring carbon on the other side of that position. The ring is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational flexibility beyond the nitro group's orientation. The pyridine nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, the structure lacks any symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions around the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents. A methylsulfonyl group (a methyl attached to a sulfur bearing two oxygen atoms, forming a sulfone) sits at one position, a carboxylic acid group sits at another, and a chlorine atom occupies the position adjacent to the carboxylic acid, so the carboxyl and chloro groups are ortho to each other. The aromatic core is a single, flat, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid, though the sulfone and carboxyl groups can rotate about their bonds to the ring. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps it onto itself, since the three substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (its carbonyl oxygen), and the two sulfone oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying three substituents. One ring position bears an acetamide group, with the nitrogen attached directly to the aromatic carbon and the carbonyl forming a secondary amide. A second position, adjacent to the amide-bearing carbon, carries a chlorine atom, while the position para to the amide carries a trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the amide linkage adds limited conformational flexibility. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid, built on a single benzene ring. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached to one ring carbon and serves as the main functional group, with two hydroxyl groups that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. A chlorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, ortho to the boron group, while a trifluoromethyl group, CF3, sits on the carbon para to boron, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is flat and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The CF3 group is strongly electron-withdrawing and bulky, and its three fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying three substituents arranged around it. A primary sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2) sits at one position, a chlorine atom is on the adjacent carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3) occupies the position para to the sulfonamide. There are no fused ring systems, and the aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfonamide and trifluoromethyl groups have limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different and their positions are not mirror-related. The sulfonamide NH2 provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and its two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents on adjacent and near positions: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) directly on the ring, a chlorine atom ortho to that nitrile, and a trifluoromethyl group para to the nitrile. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the nitrile is linear and the trifluoromethyl group rotates freely about its bond to the ring. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local geometry of the substituents. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. Attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (the 2-position) is a chlorine atom, while the 3-position carries a carboxylic acid group. The 4-position bears a trifluoromethyl group, and the 5- and 6-positions are unsubstituted aromatic CH carbons. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the core a rigid, flat geometry, with the substituents adding limited conformational freedom. The carboxylic acid acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with the substituents arranged around the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho relationship between them. Two fluorine atoms occupy the meta and para-like positions on the far side of the ring, leaving one aromatic C–H position unsubstituted. The scaffold is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic ring, so it is planar and rigid, with the carboxylic acid group able to rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a nitrile (cyano) group, two fluorine atoms, and a chlorine atom. Reading around the ring, the nitrile sits at one position, with the chlorine on the adjacent carbon, and the two fluorines occupy the two positions on the opposite side, adjacent to each other, so the substitution pattern is contiguous and asymmetric. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially rigid, with only the nitrile group being linear. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the halogens contribute weak acceptor character and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents: two methyl groups, a hydroxyl group, and a chlorine atom, arranged around a single aromatic core with no additional rings fused to it. The methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, and the hydroxyl and chlorine occupy the two neighboring positions on the opposite side, giving a fully substituted, asymmetric pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add minor rotational freedom but no meaningful flexibility to the overall framework.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-triazine scaffold. Two of the ring carbons each carry an ethylamino group (an NH bonded to an ethyl chain), while the third ring carbon bears a chlorine atom, so the substitution pattern is two identical amino arms flanking one halogen. The ring is fully aromatic and flat, and the ethyl side chains add modest conformational freedom without making the core flexible. Each secondary amine NH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chlorine is a weak acceptor and contributes to the overall electron-poor character of the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and that carbon is flanked on both sides by halogen substituents: a chlorine on one adjacent position and a bromine on the other. A second bromine sits on the ring at a position meta to the amino group, giving a 2,4,6-type halogen pattern relative to the amine. The ring is planar and rigid, with the amino group the only substituent capable of hydrogen-bond donation (two N-H bonds) and the nitrogen lone pair serving as an acceptor. The three halogens contribute polarizability and weak halogen-bonding capacity but no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor strength. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry because the chlorine and the two bromines occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents on consecutive positions: a primary amino group, a fluorine, a second fluorine, and a chlorine, arranged so that the amino group sits between a fluorine and a chlorine. The fluorines are placed meta to each other across the ring, giving the molecule no symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the amino carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the halogens and amine lying in the ring plane. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair. The halogens contribute electron-withdrawing character and can act only as weak acceptors, while the ring itself offers no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic 1,3,5-triazine ring, with three nitrogen atoms alternating with three carbon atoms and no fused rings. Two of the ring carbons carry methoxy groups (–OCH3), each attached through an oxygen, while the third ring carbon bears a chlorine atom, giving a trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has approximate threefold symmetry in its ring arrangement, although the chlorine substituent breaks the symmetry between the three positions. The core is rigid and planar, with the methoxy groups able to rotate about their C–O bonds. The ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with six aromatic carbons and no fused or additional rings. Its substituents are an amino group, a chlorine atom, and two nitro groups, all attached directly to the ring. Reading around the ring, the amino group sits next to a chlorine atom, and the two nitro groups occupy positions that make the substitution pattern asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring and its planar nitro groups give the framework considerable rigidity, while the attached groups add little conformational flexibility. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, and the oxygen atoms of the two nitro groups can accept them.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile (cyano) group, a sulfonyl chloride group, and a chlorine atom. The nitrile is attached directly to the ring at one position, the sulfonyl chloride sits para to it on the opposite side, and a chlorine occupies the position ortho to the sulfonyl chloride, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with no symmetry. The core is a single rigid, planar six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents add little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the sulfonyl group. The nitrile nitrogen and the sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so there is no ring fusion and the scaffold is a simple monocyclic heteroarene. A nitrogen atom sits in the ring, and two substituents are attached to it: a chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon that is one position further around the ring. The two substituents are therefore not adjacent to each other, and the pattern is asymmetric. The ring is planar and rigid, and the nitrile group is linear, so the molecule has very little conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A nitro group (–NO2) sits on one ring carbon, a fluorine atom is located para to it across the ring, and a chlorine atom occupies the position ortho to the nitro group, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 with the nitro group as the reference point. The ring itself is planar and rigid, while the nitro group is conjugated with the aromatic system and remains largely coplanar. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the three different substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the oxygen atoms of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methyl group, a fluorine, a carboxylic acid, and a chlorine, with a single aromatic ring and no fused ring systems. The carboxylic acid group (–COOH) sits para to the fluorine and ortho to the chlorine, while the methyl group occupies the position between the chlorine and the fluorine-bearing carbon, creating a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxylic acid can rotate about its bond to the ring. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen), while the halogens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors at most.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetamido group (an N-acetyl amide, CH3C(=O)NH-), a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the amide nitrogen carries one hydrogen that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor. The chlorine sits ortho to the amide and the fluorine sits para to it, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The acetamido linkage provides some conformational freedom around the C–N and N–aryl bonds, but the core remains rigid and largely flat.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement, with no ring fusion. One substituent is a fluorine atom, attached to the ring carbon opposite the other group. The other is a two-carbon acyl unit: a carbonyl carbon bonded directly to the ring, which carries a chloromethyl group (-CH2Cl) on its other side, making it a ketone with an alpha-halogen. The aromatic ring and the carbonyl plane are largely planar, giving the scaffold a rigid, elongated shape with only a single rotatable bond between the ring and the carbonyl. The molecule has a mirror plane through its long axis, so it is achiral. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen), a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The aldehyde carbon sits at one ring position, the chlorine occupies an ortho position adjacent to it, and the fluorine sits para to the aldehyde on the opposite side of the ring. This 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern leaves the ring asymmetric, with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the aldehyde group can rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with its ring carbons numbered so the acid sits at position 1. A chlorine atom occupies the ortho position relative to the carboxyl group, and a fluorine atom sits para to it, on the opposite side of the ring. This arrangement gives a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic core with no molecular symmetry, since the three substituents are all different. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached at one position. Going around the ring, a fluorine atom sits para to the nitrile, and a chlorine atom sits ortho to it, so the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings or flexible side chains, which makes the overall framework rigid. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) on one ring carbon, a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, and a fluorine atom positioned para to the hydroxymethyl group. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the hydroxymethyl group providing rotational flexibility. The substitution pattern is trisubstituted and lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, making the molecule asymmetric. The primary alcohol can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. Overall, the structure combines an aromatic core with one polar, hydrogen-bonding handle and two electronegative halogen substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings. A fluorine atom sits on one ring carbon, a bromomethyl group (a CH2 linked to bromine) on the carbon two positions around from it, and a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the bromomethyl-bearing carbon, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern on the ring. Because the three substituents are different and placed asymmetrically, the molecule has no rotational or mirror symmetry beyond a local planar arrangement. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker to bromine adds a small degree of conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms and the fluorine can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic-acid-type structure built on a benzene ring bearing a conjugated, trans-configured acrylic acid side chain. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, and it carries two halogen substituents: a chlorine on the carbon adjacent to the side chain and a fluorine positioned para to that side chain, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The carboxylic acid group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the halogens contribute only weak polar character. The C=C double bond between the ring-linked carbon and the carboxyl-bearing carbon fixes the planar, extended geometry, so the molecule is fairly rigid with limited conformational freedom apart from rotation about the single bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxyl group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, with the chlorine on the adjacent carbon ortho to it, and the fluorine on the carbon para to the hydroxyl group. This gives a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused ring systems, and the ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the O–H. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The phenolic hydroxyl acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine and chlorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing an acetic acid side chain, with a fluorine and a chlorine substituent on the aromatic core. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The scaffold is largely planar and rigid because of the aromatic ring and the conjugated carbonyl. There is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the hydroxyl hydrogen. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two substituents are placed at non-equivalent positions. The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two halogen substituents. The ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pair, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining positions carry hydrogen atoms bonded to carbon.

The molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. Going around the ring, a methoxy group sits para to the boronic acid group, and a chlorine atom sits ortho to it, so the three substituents occupy positions 1, 2, and 4 in a 1,2,4 pattern and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to the ring and carries two hydroxyl groups that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The methoxy oxygen and the chlorine are weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and boronic acid groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving it a simple, fully aromatic six-membered carbocyclic scaffold with no fused rings. Moving around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) sits at one position, a bromomethyl group (a CH2 carrying a bromine) occupies the position across from it in a para-like relationship, and a chlorine atom sits adjacent to the bromomethyl carbon, producing a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a hydroxyl group, and a chlorine atom. Its only meaningful flexibility comes from rotation about the C-O bond of the methoxy group. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a cyanomethyl group, and a chlorine atom. The methoxy group (an ether linked to a methyl) sits on one ring carbon, the cyanomethyl chain (a CH2 attached to a nitrile, C≡N) sits on a second, and the chlorine occupies the carbon directly adjacent to the cyanomethyl-bearing carbon, giving an ortho relationship between those two groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the cyanomethyl and methoxy side chains retain some rotational freedom. The nitrile nitrogen and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. Going around the ring from the nitrogen, a chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to nitrogen, a nitro group occupies the next carbon, and a methyl group is attached at the position beyond that. The nitro group contributes strong hydrogen-bond acceptor character through its oxygen atoms, and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, carrying three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donors and one acceptor site on its nitrogen, while the chlorine contributes only weak halogen-type polarity and no meaningful hydrogen-bond capability.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The molecule is a small six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms positioned at the 1,3-relationship, making it a pyrimidine scaffold. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the methyl and chloro groups occupy non-equivalent positions. The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic compound built on a quinoline scaffold, with a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The pyridine-type nitrogen sits in the heteroaromatic ring, adjacent to a ring-fusion carbon. A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon directly next to that nitrogen, while a methyl group is on the carbon at the opposite side of the pyridine ring, giving a 2,4-disubstitution pattern. The fused system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, with no fused or additional rings. The benzene core carries three substituents: a primary amino group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The amino group and the chlorine sit on adjacent carbons, while the nitro group occupies the position para to the amino group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. It has no symmetry element beyond the planar aromatic framework, so the substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a primary carboxamide group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxamide carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the nitro group sits on the carbon para to it (across the ring from the amide). The chlorine occupies the position ortho to the carboxamide, adjacent to the carbon bearing it, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents are largely planar and rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the amide and nitro groups. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are different and arranged asymmetrically. The amide provides two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH₂ group and one acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitro group contributes two oxygen acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the nitro group sits on the carbon para to it, which together form a clear substitution pattern on a single aromatic scaffold with no additional ring fusion. The chlorine occupies the position ortho to the carboxylic acid, creating a crowded arrangement around that side of the ring. The ring is planar and rigid, while only the carboxylic acid and nitro groups rotate slightly about their bonds to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the nitro oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, a nitro group is attached to the carbon para to it, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon ortho to the nitrile. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry in the overall arrangement. The nitro group contributes two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the nitrile nitrogen is also an acceptor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring carbons carry substituents or hydrogens bonded only to carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold. Three substituents sit around that ring: a nitro group (an N-bonded oxygen pair with one oxygen charged), a hydroxyl group, and a chlorine atom. The hydroxyl and chlorine are on adjacent carbons, while the nitro group sits para to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, though the nitro and hydroxyl groups can rotate about their single bonds to the ring. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, the nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the chlorine is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two substituents: a nitro group (an N-oxide-like nitrogen bearing two oxygens) on one ring carbon and a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The rigid aromatic core and the planar nitro group leave little conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens can act as acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a pyridine N-oxide scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom that carries an oxygen as an N-oxide, giving the ring a zwitterionic character. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the N-oxide nitrogen, while a nitro group is attached to a carbon further around the ring, creating a 2,4-disubstituted pattern relative to the N-oxide. The N-oxide oxygen and the two nitro oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group. The nitro group (an N-oxide-type nitrogen with two oxygens, one drawn as a formal positive charge) is attached para to the methyl group, while the chlorine sits ortho to the methyl group and meta to the nitro group. This gives a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with no internal symmetry, since each substituent occupies a distinct position. The core is a single rigid, planar six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the only flexible element is the rotation of the methyl group. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. It carries two chlorine atoms: one attached directly to the ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (the 2-position), and one on a chloromethyl group (-CH2Cl) attached to the ring carbon at the 5-position, meta to the nitrogen across the ring. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three substituents decorate the ring: a primary amine (–NH2), a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3), and a chlorine atom, placed at positions that give a 1,2,4-type arrangement around the ring. The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fusion. A nitrile group (C≡N) sits on one ring carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) is attached meta to it on the opposite side of the ring. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (CH2OH), a trifluoromethyl group (CF3), and a chlorine atom. The molecule is a substituted phenylacetic acid, consisting of a single benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl (–CH2–COOH) side chain. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it contains no N-H or O-H groups.

A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the ring carbon adjacent to the one bearing the hydrogen-free position next to the ring nitrogen, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly next to the ring nitrogen on the opposite side. The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile (cyano) group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so there is no fused ring system and the scaffold is flat and rigid. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with the carboxylic acid group defining the parent scaffold. A carboxyl group (-COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group (-OH) sits on a carbon meta to it, and a chlorine atom occupies the position ortho to the carboxyl group on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a single nitrogen atom within a fully conjugated heterocycle. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a chlorine atom on the carbon immediately adjacent to the acid (ortho position), and an iodine atom on the carbon two positions away from the acid on the opposite side of the ring (meta position relative to the acid). The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The chlorine and iodine are halogen substituents that act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two halogen substituents. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position, while an iodine atom is attached to the carbon at the 5-position, para-like to the chlorine across the ring. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. Its only hydrogen-bond capability is the lone pair on the ring nitrogen, which acts as a weak acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit around that ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group), a chlorine atom, and a primary amino group. The methoxy and amino groups are adjacent to one another, and the chlorine lies on the carbon next to the amine, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom about its C–O bonds. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept them at the nitrogen lone pair, and the ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the chlorine contributes only weak polarity.

This molecule is a benzimidazole, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring sharing a carbon–carbon bond. The imidazole portion contains an NH group, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and a pyridine-type nitrogen that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon between the two imidazole nitrogens, placing a halogen substituent on the heteroaromatic ring. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) sits on the benzene ring, adding an ether oxygen acceptor. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with only the methyl of the methoxy group providing conformational freedom, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the substituents break the symmetry of the core.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a chlorine atom, and a carboxylic acid, arranged in a 1,2,4-type pattern around the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid sits directly beside the chlorine, creating a crowded ortho relationship that can twist the acid group slightly out of the ring plane. The methoxy group sits meta to the acid, on the opposite side of the ring from the chlorine. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the methoxy and carboxyl groups retain some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens, and the methoxy oxygen adds a further acceptor site. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond the trivial one because the three substituents differ.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a primary amine, giving a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The amine (–NH2) acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine and the aromatic pi system contribute weaker polar and polarizable character. The substituents are arranged in a contiguous pattern around the ring: the amino group sits directly beside the chlorine, and the methyl group is located meta to the amine on the opposite side. Because the ring is planar and the substituents are attached directly to it, the core is rigid, and only the rotation of the methyl group and the amine hydrogens adds conformational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis, since the three substituents are all different.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a chlorine atom on the carbon two positions away, and a hydroxyl group on the carbon between the chlorine and the methyl-bearing carbon, which places the substituents in a contiguous, asymmetric pattern. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character. Apart from the ring itself, which is rigid and planar, the molecule has no significant conformational flexibility, and its lack of symmetry means no mirror or rotational symmetry relates its substituent positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a substituted aniline derivative. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, with a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon and a nitro group on the carbon two positions away from the amine, placing the nitro group meta to the amino group and para to the chlorine. The aromatic core is a single, fully planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing functional group, and the primary amine carries two N–H hydrogen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ, and its rigidity comes from the aromatic ring, with only the nitro and amino groups capable of limited rotation.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a formyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen), a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. Reading around the ring, the chlorine sits ortho to the aldehyde, while the nitro group is meta to the aldehyde and para to the chlorine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and only the aldehyde and nitro groups can rotate slightly out of the ring plane. The aldehyde oxygen and the two nitro oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a primary carboxamide group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The carboxamide sits at one ring position, the chlorine on the adjacent carbon, and the nitro group on the meta position relative to the amide, giving a 2-chloro-5-nitrobenzamide substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the amide and nitro groups able to rotate slightly. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom, arranged so that the carboxylic acid and chlorine sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other) and the nitro group is positioned meta to the carboxylic acid and para to the chlorine. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile group, a nitro group, and a chlorine atom. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: an acyl chloride group, a chlorine atom ortho to it, and a nitro group located meta to the acyl chloride and para to the chlorine. The overall arrangement is asymmetric because the three substituents are different and sit at non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents. A nitro group (–NO2) sits on one ring carbon, a chlorine atom occupies the position para to it, and a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to the carbon between the chlorine and the nitro-bearing carbon, placing the chlorine and hydroxymethyl groups ortho to each other. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a planar heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom within the ring. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the methyl group as the only freely rotating substituent, and the substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetic acid side chain (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid group, C(=O)OH) at one position, a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) on the carbon next to the other side of the acetic acid attachment, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. Its only symmetry is the lack of any symmetry plane, since the three substituents are all different. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its OH and accept one through its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine and chlorine atoms offer only weak acceptor character.

This molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two substituents: a trifluoromethyl group on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a chlorine atom on the other carbon next to that nitrogen, so the two substituents flank the nitrogen on opposite sides. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the ring, since the two substituents differ. The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a chlorine atom sits on the other carbon adjacent to that same nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstitution pattern. This molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents, with no fused or additional ring systems. Going around the ring from the methoxy-bearing carbon, it carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen linked to a methyl), then two adjacent hydrogen-bearing positions, a fluorine atom, a nitrile (cyano) group, and a chlorine atom, giving a densely substituted, sterically crowded aromatic core. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Going around the ring from the methoxy carbon, it carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl), a fluorine, a bromomethyl group (CH2Br), and a chlorine on adjacent positions, with the remaining position bearing a hydrogen. The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents, with no fused ring system. Reading around the ring, there is a methyl group, then a fluorine atom, then a formyl (aldehyde) group, and a chlorine atom, with the remaining positions occupied by hydrogens, giving a trisubstituted plus methyl pattern that is contiguous on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the aldehyde and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom. The arrangement lacks any element of symmetry because the substituents are all different.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The fluorine and chlorine atoms contribute weak acceptor character, while the methyl group is purely hydrophobic. Because the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, the molecule has no internal symmetry plane. The aromatic core is rigid, though the carboxamide group can rotate about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a substituted benzoic acid. The aromatic core is a single rigid six-membered ring with no fused rings, while the carboxylic acid and methyl groups provide limited rotational freedom. Because the substituents are all different, the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents, with no fused rings and no additional heteroatom-containing rings. Going around the ring, a methyl group sits on one carbon, followed by a fluorine, a nitrile group (a carbon-nitrogen triple bond), and a chlorine on three consecutive carbons, with the remaining ring positions carrying hydrogens. The molecule is a single benzene ring, a fully aromatic six-membered carbon scaffold with no fused rings, bearing four substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions. Going around the ring from one substituent, there is a methyl group, a hydrogen, a hydrogen, a fluorine atom, a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH unit), and a chlorine atom, which are arranged so that the methyl and chlorine sit on neighboring carbons. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group contributes a single rotatable bond. The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents: a methyl group, a fluorine atom, a bromomethyl group, and a chlorine atom, with the remaining two ring positions carrying hydrogens. Because the ring is aromatic and fully substituted in a contiguous cluster, it is rigid and essentially planar, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters. The bromomethyl group is the most reactive-looking feature in terms of its carbon-bromine bond, while the methyl, halogens, and aromatic ring contribute only lipophilic bulk. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only potential acceptor is the fluorine atom, since the halogens and the aromatic pi system offer weak acceptor character at best. Overall, the structure is compact and asymmetric, with the substituents crowded on one side of the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on six carbons, with no fused ring systems. Reading around the ring from the methyl-bearing carbon, it carries a methyl group, then a fluorine, then a hydroxyl group, and a chlorine that sits between the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the methyl-bearing carbon, giving a contiguous 1,2,3,4-substitution pattern with two adjacent halogens. The phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine and chlorine can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the four substituents are all different. Only the methyl group has meaningful rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzaldehyde derivative built on a single six-membered aromatic benzene ring with no fused rings. An aldehyde group (–CHO) is attached to one ring carbon, and a fluorine atom and a chlorine atom occupy the two positions immediately flanking that aldehyde, giving a 2,6-disubstituted, 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern around the ring. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the aldehyde is sandwiched between two bulky halogens, its rotation is somewhat restricted, and the scaffold is largely planar and rigid apart from that rotation. The arrangement lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry, since the fluorine and chlorine are different substituents at non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: an aldoxime group (a carbon double-bonded to an N-OH nitrogen, i.e., -CH=N-OH) on one carbon, a fluorine atom on the carbon next to it, and a chlorine atom on the carbon on its other side. This 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no fused or additional ring systems. The oxime hydroxyl group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the oxygen and the imine nitrogen), while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically around the ring, the molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry, though the oxime group itself can adopt different orientations about its C=N bond.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a primary carboxamide group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom, with the carboxamide flanked by the halogens on one side. The substitution pattern is contiguous and asymmetric: the amide carbon sits between the ring carbons bearing fluorine and chlorine, which makes the two ortho positions chemically distinct. The amide group contributes two hydrogen-bond donors through its NH₂ and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The halogens are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors at most, and the molecule has no stereocenters.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with a chlorine atom and a fluorine atom attached to adjacent or nearby carbons on the same ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic system with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and it contains both a hydroxyl donor and a carbonyl acceptor, giving the molecule hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability. The halogen substituents are positioned ortho to the acid group, making the substitution pattern asymmetric, and the molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the flat ring plane. The ring is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate around its single bond to the ring, giving limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a nitrile (cyano) group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the fluorine and chlorine flank it on either side, creating a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the nitrile group extends linearly from it, so the overall shape is flat with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the three substituents onto one another, so it lacks meaningful symmetry. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the nitrile nitrogen and the fluorine can act as weak acceptors, the chlorine is a poor acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzothiazole, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring sharing one C–C bond, with the sulfur and nitrogen atoms of the thiazole ring positioned at the fusion-adjacent sites. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon of the thiazole ring lying between the sulfur and the nitrogen, while a fluorine atom is attached to the benzenoid ring at a position meta to the ring-fusion nitrogen-bearing carbon. The fused system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the single fluorine breaks any mirror relationship. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) on one ring carbon, and a fluorine atom and a chlorine atom on the two adjacent carbons flanking it, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused ring systems, and the substituents are arranged so that the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the ring positions equivalent. The benzene scaffold is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl group contributes a single rotatable bond and some conformational flexibility. The primary alcohol offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and one acceptor (the oxygen lone pairs), and the halogens can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain: a nitrovinyl group, in which a carbon-carbon double bond with trans geometry links the ring to a nitro group. The benzene ring is substituted at two adjacent positions flanking that side chain, with a fluorine atom on one neighboring carbon and a chlorine atom on the other, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry axis in the overall framing. The molecule is largely planar and conjugated across the ring, alkene, and nitro group, which limits rotation about the ring-alkene bond, so it is relatively rigid. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydroxyl group, a fluorine atom, and a chlorine atom, forming a 2-chloro-6-fluorophenol-type scaffold. The aromatic ring is fully planar and fused to nothing, so the core is a single six-membered carbon ring with delocalized pi bonding. The substitution pattern is contiguous and asymmetric, with the hydroxyl flanked by the chlorine on one side and the fluorine on the other, which gives the molecule only a single mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core is rigid, while the hydroxyl hydrogen is the only group with rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the halogens and oxygen provide additional acceptor sites.

This molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative, built from a single benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group (–CH2–COOH) on one carbon. The aromatic ring carries two halogen substituents on adjacent positions flanking the side chain: a chlorine atom on one ortho carbon and a fluorine atom on the other ortho-adjacent position relative to the CH2 attachment, giving a 2,6-type ortho-disubstitution pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused ring systems, while the CH2–COOH arm provides rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring systems. Directly attached to the ring is a cyanomethyl group, a CH2 linked to a nitrile (C≡N) that acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor at the nitrogen. The aromatic ring carries a fluorine atom and a chlorine atom on the carbons adjacent to the cyanomethyl-bearing carbon, creating a 2,6-disubstituted pattern that flanks the side chain on both sides. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, and its overall shape is largely planar and rigid around the ring, with only the CH2–C≡N arm offering rotational flexibility. Because the two halogen substituents differ, the molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local orientation of the side chain.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons flanking the nitrogen. One substituent is a hydroxyl group on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and the other is a chlorine atom on the carbon on the opposite side of that nitrogen. Because the hydroxyl-bearing carbon sits beside the ring nitrogen, the hydroxyl can tautomerize into a pyridone-type form, which is a notable feature of this scaffold. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen as an acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a simple benzene derivative, with a single six-membered aromatic ring and no fused rings. Because the three substituents are all different, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond what the flat aromatic framework provides. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic framework. A methoxy group sits on the benzenoid ring, while the pyridine-side carbon adjacent to the nitrogen carries a chlorine atom and a neighboring carbon bears an aldehyde (formyl) group. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry elements beyond the planar ring system itself. The ring nitrogen and the aldehyde oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the methoxy oxygen provides an additional acceptor site, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its conformational flexibility is limited to rotation of the methoxy and formyl groups about their single bonds.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, with no fused rings. Reading the SMILES, the ring carries a methyl group, a nitro group, a chlorine atom, and a primary amino group, arranged so that the amino group sits between the methyl and chlorine on adjacent positions. The nitro group is positioned meta to the chlorine and meta to the methyl group, sitting across the ring from the amino group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl and nitro groups rotate freely about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element, since the four substituents occupy positions that are all distinct. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and its nitrogen acts as an acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a primary amino group, with the amine flanked by the methyl on one side and the chlorine on the other. The amino group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the chlorine contributes only weak halogen-bond character. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the trivial. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the methyl group and the amine's hydrogens offering minor rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents, which makes it a substituted benzaldehyde. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom occupies a position on the ring, with the aldehyde (formyl, –CHO) group attached directly to the carbon between the methyl and chlorine substituents. This 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern leaves the ring with no internal symmetry, since the three groups are all different. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with the aldehyde carbonyl oxygen able to act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The methyl group adds a small amount of steric bulk next to the aldehyde, and the chlorine adds an electron-withdrawing halogen substituent.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2). The carboxamide sits between the methyl and chlorine substituents, creating a crowded, 1,2,3-trisubstituted substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The benzene ring is planar and fully aromatic, with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no symmetry that would make its two ortho positions equivalent. The amide group is the main polar feature, with two hydrogen-bond donors on the nitrogen and one hydrogen-bond acceptor on the carbonyl oxygen. The C–C bond to the amide allows some rotation, though steric crowding from the flanking substituents restricts it.

This molecule is a benzoic acid derivative built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The carboxylic acid group (-C(=O)OH) is attached to one ring carbon, with a chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to it on one side, and a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to it on the other side, so the acid is flanked by two ortho substituents. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the chlorine and methyl groups differ in size and electronic character. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the chlorine acts only as a weak acceptor and the methyl group contributes neither.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. One ring carbon carries a methyl group, its neighbor carries a nitrile (cyano) group, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon on the other side of the nitrile-bearing carbon. The fully aromatic six-membered ring is planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion. The nitrile group is linear and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its substitution pattern lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric apart from the freely rotating methyl group.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to that nitrogen, and a carboxylic acid group is attached on the opposite side of the ring, creating a 1,4-relationship relative to the methyl substituent. A chlorine atom occupies the carbon next to the nitrogen on the other flank, so the ring carries three substituents in an unsymmetrical pattern. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (its oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion. Going around the ring, an amino group and a nitro group sit on adjacent carbons, a chlorine atom sits on the carbon next to the amine, and a trifluoromethyl group sits on the carbon across from the nitro-bearing position, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern with no internal symmetry.
