The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the halogens and fluorines contribute only weakly to hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a primary carboxamide, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group. The carboxamide carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the chlorine sits between the amide and the nitro group, so the nitro and amide groups are ortho to each other across the ring with the chlorine flanking one of them. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the amide and nitro groups can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring. The amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors and one acceptor, and the nitro group serves as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a carboxylic acid group, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group, arranged so that the carboxylic acid sits between the chlorine and the nitro group on one side and the remaining ring carbons on the other. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the substituents attached to it are flat to modest degree, while the nitro and carboxylic acid groups can rotate slightly out of the ring plane. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the nitro group serves as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms. Overall the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three different substituents occupy non-equivalent positions around the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a nitrile group (C≡N), a chlorine atom, and a nitro group (–NO2). The nitro group sits ortho to the nitrile, and the chlorine sits between the nitrile and the next ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is a contiguous 1,2,3-arrangement. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, while the nitro group can twist slightly out of the ring plane due to steric crowding from its neighbours. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the three substituents differ from one another. The nitrile nitrogen and the two nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring: a nitro group (an N bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged), a chlorine atom, and a hydroxyl group, arranged on adjacent and nearby carbons so the hydroxyl sits between the nitro and chloro groups. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,3-trisubstituted and unsymmetrical, with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring and its substituents are essentially planar and rigid, with the nitro group only modestly twisted relative to the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens serve as acceptors and the chlorine is a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group, a chlorine atom, and a nitro group, with the nitro group attached to the carbon next to the methyl-bearing carbon. The benzene core is a fully aromatic, planar, six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is contiguous, leaving the three remaining ring carbons as adjacent C–H positions. The nitro group, drawn as a charge-separated N⁺(=O)O⁻, is strongly electron-withdrawing and can accept hydrogen bonds through its oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The ring framework is rigid, with only the methyl group and the nitro group offering limited rotational freedom, and the overall arrangement lacks any element of molecular symmetry.

This molecule is a diaryl ether, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom. One ring carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a chlorine atom on adjacent positions, which places the ether linkage ortho to the nitrile and the chlorine sits on the other side of the nitrile-bearing carbon. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. The C–O–C linkage gives the molecule some conformational flexibility around the ether bonds, though the two aromatic rings remain planar individually. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The overall structure is asymmetric because the two rings carry different substituents.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, forming a quinoline scaffold. The pyridine nitrogen sits adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon, and the fused system is fully planar and rigid. A chlorine atom is attached to the carbon next to that nitrogen on the heteroaromatic ring, while a methyl group occupies the adjacent position on the same ring. On the carbocyclic ring, a methoxy group is placed meta to the ring-fusion carbon, giving the molecule an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The pyridine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all its substituents are carbon-, oxygen-, or halogen-based.

This molecule is a small, acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone. The skeleton consists of a primary carboxamide group, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to an amino group (NH2) and to a methylene carbon that carries a chlorine atom, so it is a chloro-substituted acetamide. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the single C–C bond and the C–N and C–Cl bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility, with no element of symmetry beyond local mirror planes in the amide unit. The amide nitrogen bears two hydrogens, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chlorine atom is a weak acceptor and adds polarity at the terminal carbon.

The molecule is an anilide built on a benzene ring, with an acetamide group (–NH–C(=O)–CH3) attached to one ring carbon and a chlorine atom on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit ortho to each other. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the overall scaffold is planar and fairly rigid, though the amide C–N bond and the C–C bond to the methyl group allow some rotation. The secondary amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chlorine is a halogen substituent that contributes lipophilic character but no hydrogen-bonding ability, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the unsymmetrical ortho substitution pattern.

The molecule is an acetoacetanilide-type structure: a four-carbon chain bearing a methyl ketone at one end and an amide linkage at the other, connecting to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused benzene ring carrying a chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to the carbon bearing the amide nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho. The amide N-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the ketone oxygen both serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry and is fairly flexible, since the open-chain linker rotates freely about several single bonds. The aromatic ring itself is planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, so it has no fused ring systems and no stereocenters. That substituent is a ketone carbonyl group, with the ring attached directly to the carbonyl carbon, and this carbonyl is bonded on its other side to a chloromethyl group (a CH2 carrying a chlorine atom). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two-carbon linker from the ring to the chlorine is comparatively flexible, since rotation can occur about the single bonds. Overall the structure is achiral and has a mirror plane through the ketone and the ring, giving it a simple, roughly symmetric outline. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small three-carbon chain built on an acrylic acid scaffold, with no rings present. A terminal vinyl (C=C) group is attached at its second carbon to a chlorine atom, making the alkene carbon halogenated and placing the chlorine on a double-bonded position. The opposite end of the chain bears a carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH), which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and hydrogen-bond acceptors through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The molecule is asymmetric, since the chlorine and carboxyl groups sit on the same central carbon but differ fundamentally in character, and the small size gives it limited conformational flexibility around its single bonds. Overall, it is a compact, unsaturated, halogenated carboxylic acid with a planar alkene region and a polar acid terminus.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents are attached to adjacent carbons of that ring: an amino group (-NH2) and a chlorine atom, placing them in an ortho relationship. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the chlorine contributes only a weak halogen-type acceptor character. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and both substituents, so its overall shape is largely flat and fairly compact.

The molecule is built on an anthraquinone-type scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in a linear arrangement, with the central ring bearing two carbonyl groups at opposite positions. One outer benzene ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a single chlorine atom on its aromatic carbon, placed meta to one of the carbonyl-bearing ring-fusion positions. The fused tricyclic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The molecule lacks symmetry because the chlorine breaks the mirror relationship between the two outer rings. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon attached to hydrogen) and a chlorine atom, giving it an ortho substitution pattern. The aromatic six-membered carbocycle is planar and fully unsaturated, and there is no ring fusion or additional ring system. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, with a mirror plane lying through the aldehyde and chlorine substituents. Its rigid aromatic core, with only a single rotatable bond joining the aldehyde to the ring, makes it structurally constrained. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to an amino group, and the other is a chlorine atom attached directly to the ring at the neighboring position. The aromatic core is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with limited conformational flexibility, although the amide group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks an internal axis of symmetry, since the two ring substituents differ. The amide group provides two hydrogen-bond donors through its N–H bonds and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine atom contributes only weak halogen-bonding character.

The molecule is an arylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring. The boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The boron center carries two hydroxyl groups, which can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the B(OH)2 unit can rotate about the carbon-boron bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the ring's local mirror plane, because the two substituents are different.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom and to the ring carbon. The other substituent is a chlorine atom attached directly to the neighboring ring carbon. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a chlorine atom, and the other is a carbohydrazide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrazine unit (an N–N linkage with a terminal NH2). The ring is a simple, unfused aromatic six-membered system with an ortho substitution pattern, so the molecule lacks any symmetry that would make its two sides equivalent. The amide-like carbonyl and the hydrazine nitrogens are fairly rigid around the amide bond, while rotation about the bond linking the carbonyl to the ring provides some conformational flexibility. The terminal NH2 and the adjacent NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a 2-chlorobenzimidazole, built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is joined along one edge to a five-membered imidazole ring. The imidazole ring contains two nitrogen atoms, one of which carries an N-H group and the other a pyridine-like sp2 nitrogen, and a chlorine atom is attached to the carbon between them. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the planar framework. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated imine-type nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents on neighboring carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which carries a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and a hydroxyl group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The other substituent is a chlorine atom attached directly to the ring, which is an electron-withdrawing halogen capable of weak halogen-bonding interactions. The aromatic core is a single fused-free planar six-membered ring with no additional ring systems. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and the rigid aromatic framework limits conformational flexibility, with only rotation of the carboxyl group around its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, which places them in an ortho relationship. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The other substituent is a chlorine atom attached directly to the ring, contributing an electron-withdrawing halogen that is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has an overall flat shape with a mirror plane through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two aromatic benzene rings, making it a benzophenone-type scaffold. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries a chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent (ortho) to the carbonyl attachment point, which breaks the symmetry between the two halves. The two phenyl rings are not fused to each other but are connected through the sp2 carbonyl carbon, giving a fairly rigid, planar-leaning core with some rotational freedom about the single bonds to the carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring, so the scaffold is a benzothiazole core. The fused system is fully aromatic and planar, which makes the framework rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds. The five-membered ring contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom, with the nitrogen sitting adjacent to the carbon at the fusion point. A single chlorine atom is attached to the carbon at position 2 of the thiazole ring, situated between the sulfur and the nitrogen. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, while the ring nitrogen serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall it has no internal symmetry beyond the planar arrangement of its rings.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent at one position. Attached to that ring is a carbon atom that carries three chlorine atoms, giving a trichloromethyl group, so the overall scaffold is a benzylic carbon linked directly to the aromatic core. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, and the substitution pattern is ortho, since a chlorine sits directly adjacent to the trichloromethyl-bearing carbon. The molecule contains only carbon, hydrogen, and chlorine, with no heteroatom functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its overall shape is largely rigid around the ring, with limited rotational freedom at the single bond to the chlorinated carbon, and it lacks any internal symmetry axis because the ortho arrangement breaks the symmetry of the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a trifluoromethyl group, a carbon atom bonded to three fluorine atoms, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and sterically bulky. The other substituent is a chlorine atom attached directly to the ring at the position next to the trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with the two substituents providing no internal rotational freedom beyond the trifluoromethyl group's own rotation about its bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor-like sites are the electronegative fluorine and chlorine atoms, which are weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to both an oxygen (double bond) and a chlorine atom, while the other is a single chlorine atom attached directly to the ring. The scaffold is a single unfused six-membered aromatic ring, which is planar and rigid. The acyl chloride carbonyl is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and it is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the acyl chloride group.

This molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a chlorine atom directly on the ring, and the other is a three-carbon chain that begins with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), followed by a methylene carbon and then a ketone carbonyl attached to the ring. The benzene core is planar and fully aromatic, while the side chain is flexible around its single bonds. The ketone oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 carbon bonded to a hydroxyl), and the other is a chlorine atom attached directly to the ring. The single benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, giving the scaffold a rigid core, while the hydroxymethyl arm retains some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the chlorine is a weak acceptor only. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a mirror plane through the ring and its substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a chloromethyl group, a benzylic CH2 carrying a chlorine atom, and the other is a directly attached chlorine atom on the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and its planar, rigid geometry is combined with the rotatable bond of the chloromethyl arm. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N-H or O-H groups, and its only acceptor-like character comes from the chlorine atoms, which are weak. The overall shape is asymmetric because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a chlorine atom, and the other is a two-carbon chain that ends in a nitro group, with the carbon-carbon double bond fixed in the trans (E) geometry. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, forming the rigid core of the structure, while the vinyl linker adds a flat, conjugated extension. The ortho arrangement of the chlorine and the vinyl chain creates a 1,2-disubstitution pattern that lowers the overall symmetry, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity. The nitro group, with its two formally charged oxygens, acts as a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The chlorine atom contributes a weak halogen-type acceptor site, and the compound overall is largely rigid with limited conformational flexibility around the double bond.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, saturated alkyl halide built on a four-carbon chain. Its skeleton is a branched butane framework: a terminal ethyl group is joined to a secondary carbon that carries both a methyl branch and a chlorine atom. Because there are no rings or double bonds, the scaffold is fully flexible, with free rotation about each carbon-carbon single bond. The only functional group is the carbon-chlorine bond at the secondary position, which makes the molecule a stereogenic center, though no stereochemistry is specified here. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ethyl and methyl arrangement around that carbon. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a short, acyclic aliphatic chain built from a two-carbon ethyl unit attached to a single chiral carbon bearing a chlorine atom, which is in turn bonded to a carboxamide group. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open and flexible, with rotation possible about each single bond. The principal functional group is a primary amide (–C(=O)NH2), which contributes both a carbonyl oxygen that can accept hydrogen bonds and two N–H groups that can donate them. The alpha-chloro substituent adds a polarizable halogen next to the amide carbonyl. The molecule has no internal symmetry and contains one stereocenter, so it is chiral.

The molecule is a cinnamoyl-type acyl chloride, built on a three-carbon chain that carries a benzene ring at one end and an acid chloride at the other. The acid chloride group, a carbonyl bonded to chlorine, is the most reactive functional group present. The two carbons joining the carbonyl to the ring are connected by a double bond with trans (E) geometry, which keeps the chain extended and fairly rigid. The benzene ring is ortho-disubstituted, with a chlorine atom adjacent to the point where the vinyl chain attaches, so the ring carries no symmetry-related substitution. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors; the carbonyl oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a phenylalanine-type skeleton, with the amino group and carboxylic acid both attached to a single chiral alpha carbon. A methylene linker connects that carbon to a benzene ring, which carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, placing the halogen at the ortho position. The benzene ring is the only ring system, with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the chlorine breaks the symmetry of the aromatic ring. The side chain gives the molecule some conformational flexibility around its single bonds, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The primary amine can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carboxylic acid group contributes both donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygen atoms.

This molecule is a small acyclic chain of three carbon atoms with no rings, so its scaffold is simply a linear propyl backbone. A primary alcohol group sits at one terminus, and a chlorine atom is attached to the carbon at the opposite end, giving a 1,3-substitution pattern across the chain. There is no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two functional groups differ. Its chain is highly flexible, with freely rotating single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine can only serve as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para arrangement. One side carries a sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms, which is bonded to a two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom. The opposite side of the ring carries a single fluorine atom. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the saturated ethyl-type chain attached to the sulfone adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane running through the sulfur and fluorine positions of the ring, giving it a largely symmetric overall shape along its long axis. The two sulfonyl oxygens are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring and chain hydrogens are attached to carbon.

The molecule is a small, acyclic ether built on a straight carbon chain. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion, aromaticity, or stereocenters to consider. Its backbone is a four-carbon unit broken by a single oxygen atom, with an ethyl group on one side of that oxygen and a two-carbon chain on the other, and a chlorine atom sits at the terminal carbon of the chain. The only functional groups are the ether linkage and the alkyl chloride, and the molecule has no aromatic or polar heteroatoms beyond these. Because it is flexible and has rotatable single bonds, it adopts many conformations, and it lacks any symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a sulfone in which a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens connects a benzene ring to a two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom. The benzene ring is a simple, unsubstituted six-membered aromatic ring, so there is no ring fusion and the aromatic core is planar and rigid. The sulfonyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and tetrahedral at sulfur, introducing a bent geometry at that point, while the ethyl-type chain beyond it, carrying a terminal chlorine, is flexible. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond local phenyl symmetry, since the two ends differ. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents placed para to each other. One side bears a methyl group, and the other is a sulfonyl group, with the sulfur bonded to two oxygen atoms and to a short saturated two-carbon chain ending in a chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl-ethyl-chloride tail is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The sulfone group is tetrahedral at sulfur and contributes two strongly polar oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The overall structure is elongated and lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local para arrangement on the ring.

This molecule is a short, acyclic organophosphorus compound built from a two-carbon chain linking a phosphorus center to a terminal chlorine atom. The phosphorus atom carries a double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups, giving it a phosphonic acid functional group in which the phosphorus is bonded directly to carbon. The chain is fully saturated and contains no rings, so the scaffold is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the phosphonic acid head and the chlorinated tail are chemically distinct. Its hydroxyl groups can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the phosphoryl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and one chlorine atom, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two hydroxyl groups sit para to each other across the ring, and the chlorine sits adjacent to one of them, giving a 1,4-diol with a halogen substituent at the position between one hydroxyl and the ring carbon beside it. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, since the chlorine breaks the mirror symmetry the bare para-diol would otherwise have. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the hydroxyl groups can rotate about their carbon–oxygen bonds. Each hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the chlorine can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring carrying one chlorine atom on the carbon sitting between the two nitrogen atoms. The ring contains two nitrogens separated by one carbon: one is a pyrrole-type nitrogen bearing a hydrogen, and the other is a pyridine-type nitrogen with a lone pair held in the plane of the ring. There are no additional fused rings or side chains, so the scaffold is compact and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The chlorine atom is a halogen substituent that makes the carbon it is attached to electron-poor. The N–H group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a phenylalanine-type scaffold, with a stereocenter at the alpha carbon bearing a primary amine and a carboxylic acid. A CH2 linker connects that stereocenter to a benzene ring, which carries a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-chloro substitution pattern. The molecule has no ring fusion and only one aromatic ring, so its overall symmetry is low, and it has a fair degree of conformational flexibility around the single bonds of the side chain. The amino group and the carboxylic acid together provide several hydrogen-bond donor sites (N-H and O-H) and acceptor sites (the nitrogen lone pair and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is a mandelic acid derivative: a two-carbon chain bearing a carboxylic acid group and a secondary hydroxyl group, attached to a benzene ring. The benzene ring carries a single chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the point of attachment, so the substitution pattern is ortho. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the side chain attached to it is flexible and can rotate about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor sites, and the alpha-hydroxyl group adds another donor and acceptor. The molecule has a stereocenter at the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group, and it lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons: two methyl groups and one chlorine atom. The methyl groups sit at positions flanking the chlorine, creating a 2,6-dimethyl pattern relative to the chloro substituent, so the arrangement is symmetric about an axis passing through the chlorine-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional rings or heteroatoms. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no OH, NH, or similar groups, and the chlorine is a weak acceptor only. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with the methyl groups providing limited steric bulk around the chlorine.

The molecule is a small, acyclic, linear chain with no ring systems, so its scaffold is simply a two-carbon backbone bearing heteroatoms. A carbonyl carbon is bonded to one oxygen, a chloromethyl group (a methylene carrying a chlorine atom), and an amide nitrogen. That nitrogen is further substituted with a hydroxymethyl group, giving an N-methylol amide motif. The molecule lacks any symmetry and is fairly flexible, since all of its bonds are single rotatable bonds apart from the planar amide C=O. Hydrogen-bond capability is dual: the hydroxyl and amide N–H groups act as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon acetamide backbone. A chloromethyl group sits on the carbonyl carbon, so the chlorine is attached to the carbon alpha to the amide, and the nitrogen of the amide bears a cyclopropyl ring. The cyclopropane is a three-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and it contributes rigidity to an otherwise flexible chain. The secondary amide provides one hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane in the cyclopropyl ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the two substituents are positioned next to each other on the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with the amide group able to rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry because the two substituents are different and placed asymmetrically. The amide group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its NH2 and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional rings. Two electron-withdrawing substituents are attached to the ring: a carbonyl group bearing a chlorine atom, which forms an acyl chloride functional group, and a chlorine atom directly on the ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen. These groups sit on neighboring carbons, giving a 2,3-type substitution pattern relative to the ring nitrogen, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis. The ring is rigid and planar, while the acyl chloride group has limited rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon backbone with no rings or ring fusion. The nitrogen carries two substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) and a methyl group, making it a tertiary, N-methoxy-N-methyl amide, often called a Weinreb-type amide. A carbonyl group sits on the nitrogen, and the carbon beside it bears a chlorine atom, so the substitution pattern is a single halogen on the alpha position. The structure has no internal symmetry and is quite flexible, since all bonds are single except the carbonyl. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: it has no donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen can each act as acceptors.

This molecule is a small acyclic amide built on a two-carbon chain. A methyl group is attached to the nitrogen of a secondary amide, and the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a methylene group that carries a chlorine atom on its terminal carbon, so the chloro substituent sits alpha to the carbonyl. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with rotation possible about the single bonds, although the amide C–N bond has partial double-bond character that restricts rotation. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry elements of note because the methyl and chloromethyl ends differ in substitution.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons of that ring: a hydroxyl group (–OH) and a chlorine atom, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern. The hydroxyl oxygen can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the chlorine contributes only weak acceptor character. Apart from the rotation of the hydroxyl group, the scaffold is essentially rigid and planar, and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because the two substituents differ.

This molecule is a phenothiazine derivative: a tricyclic scaffold in which a central six-membered ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom is fused on either side to a benzene ring. The left-hand benzene ring carries a single chlorine substituent, placed meta to the sulfur-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern breaks the overall symmetry of the framework. The central ring is non-aromatic and adopts a folded, butterfly-like geometry, giving the tricycle moderate rigidity with limited flexibility. The bridging nitrogen is a secondary amine bearing one hydrogen, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen and sulfur atoms can also serve as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a chlorine atom directly attached to the ring, and the other is an oxyacetic acid chain: an ether oxygen linking the ring to a methylene group that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid group, with its hydroxyl hydrogen and carbonyl oxygen, can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the CH2-O-C(=O)OH linker provides rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ in nature and the chain is asymmetric.

The molecule is an acyclic-chain derivative built around a single benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. The benzene core is ortho-disubstituted: one position carries a chlorine atom and the neighboring position carries an oxygen that links through a methylene group to a carbonyl. That carbonyl is part of a hydrazide unit, in which the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a nitrogen that is in turn bonded to a second terminal nitrogen bearing two hydrogens. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ether-methylene-hydrazide side chain is flexible and rotatable. The hydrazide provides multiple hydrogen-bond donors through its N–H groups and hydrogen-bond acceptors at the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms, and the ether oxygen adds a further acceptor site. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two ring substituents and the side chain are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a chlorine atom, attached directly to the ring, while the other is a two-carbon chain: a methylene group linked to a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, whereas the chlorine contributes only weak halogen-bonding character. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, but the CH2 linker gives the carboxyl group rotational flexibility relative to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond a mirror plane through the ring's substitution axis.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. A two-carbon-attached nitrile group (a cyanomethyl substituent, CH2 bonded to a carbon-nitrogen triple bond) is attached to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-disubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local planarity of the aromatic ring, and the rotatable CH2 linker gives it modest conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile group serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the chlorine can contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon skeleton: a central carbon bonded to two terminal methyl groups and to a chlorine-bearing carbon, giving a branched propane framework. It contains no rings and no ring fusion, so the structure is entirely acyclic. The only functional group is a single carbon–chlorine bond, which is a halogen substituent on a secondary carbon bearing one hydrogen. The molecule has a mirror plane through the chlorine and central carbon, so its two methyl groups are equivalent, and its overall shape is compact and conformationally flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the chlorine can act only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small acyclic alkene built on a three-carbon propene skeleton. Its single carbon-carbon double bond sits at the terminal position, where one carbon carries two hydrogens and the other carries a methyl group and a chlorine atom. The chlorine is a vinylic halogen bonded directly to an sp2 carbon, so the framework is planar and rigid around the double bond with no ring systems or ring fusion. Because the substituents on the internal carbon differ, the molecule lacks any mirror plane or symmetry element beyond its local geometry. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the chlorine offers only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring, bearing one chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which is the 2-position. There are no fused rings, no additional side chains, and no other functional groups, so the substitution pattern is a simple monosubstitution. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has only a mirror plane through the nitrogen and the chlorine-bearing carbon, giving it a high degree of symmetry relative to its size. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that can accept a hydrogen bond, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since every ring carbon and the chlorine lack acidic hydrogens.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring in which the ring nitrogen carries a formal positive charge and an attached oxygen bearing a formal negative charge, making it an N-oxide. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the N-oxide nitrogen, giving a monosubstituted pattern with no symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic ring is fully rigid and flat, with no rotatable bonds. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and it carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, and a chlorine atom. The boronic acid is attached at the carbon next to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position, and the chlorine sits directly beside it on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid hydroxyl groups can rotate, adding some conformational flexibility. The two B–OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms along with the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a planar, fully conjugated heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, so no ring fusion is present. An aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bearing a hydrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, the two substituents sitting on neighboring positions. The pyridine nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The rigid aromatic core and the small, nearly planar substituents give the molecule little conformational flexibility, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups, is attached to one ring carbon, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 1,3-relationship between the substituents on the two sides of the nitrogen. There are no fused rings, and the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid offering rotational freedom. The two O–H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms and the pyridine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom is attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 2-chloro-4-formyl substitution pattern on the ring. The ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is fully planar and rigid, with only the aldehyde C–C bond allowing rotation, and it lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry because the two substituents sit at different positions.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) is attached at the carbon three positions around the ring from the nitrogen, while a chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring itself is flat and fully conjugated, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation of the amide group. The amide offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its NH2 and one acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, and the pyridine nitrogen provides an additional acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a chlorine atom sits on a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 1,3-relationship between the substituents across the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with the carboxyl group able to rotate slightly about its single bond to the ring. The molecule is asymmetric because the two substituents are in different positions and different in kind. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, so it is a single ring with no fused systems. A chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached at the carbon three positions away around the ring, giving a 2,4-substitution pattern relative to the nitrogen. The molecule is largely planar and rigid because of the aromatic core, with only the hydroxymethyl group providing rotational flexibility. It has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, since the two substituents occupy inequivalent positions. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrimidine ring, carrying one chlorine atom attached to a carbon that sits between the two ring nitrogens (the 2-position). The ring is fully planar and conjugated, with no fused rings and no sp3 centers, which makes the scaffold rigid and flat. The molecule has no stereocenters, and the ring lacks any internal symmetry axis because the chlorine breaks the symmetry of the two nitrogen positions. Its only substituent is the chlorine, so there are no hydrogen-bond donors, while the two ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic compound built on a naphthalene-like scaffold in which one ring contains a nitrogen atom, making it a quinoline framework. The two rings are fused through a shared carbon-carbon bond, giving a fully aromatic, flat, and rigid system with no rotatable bonds. A single chlorine atom is attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position of the pyridine-type ring. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the only N-H or O-H sites are absent, but the pyridine-type nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Its overall shape is largely planar and lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry.

The molecule is a quinoline-based scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring, forming a bicyclic aromatic system with the nitrogen at a ring-fusion-adjacent position. On the pyridine-type ring sit two substituents, a chlorine atom adjacent to the nitrogen and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, at the neighboring carbon. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen acceptors, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a quinoline bicyclic scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring sharing one C–C edge with the nitrogen in the six-membered heteroaromatic ring. On the pyridine ring, a chlorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) is attached at the neighboring carbon. The fused aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with the aldehyde and chlorine substituents lying in the same plane. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the aldehyde oxygen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placed on neighboring carbons (ortho). One substituent is a vinyl group, a two-carbon unit with a carbon-carbon double bond attached directly to the ring, and the other is a chlorine atom. The aromatic benzene core is a flat, fully conjugated six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and rigid, though the vinyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens sit on carbon, and the only lone-pair-bearing atom is the chlorine, which can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is 2-chlorothiophene, built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom in the ring. A chlorine atom is attached to a carbon directly adjacent to the sulfur, which is the alpha position of the ring. The ring is fully planar and aromatic, with no fused rings, no stereocenters, and no rotatable bonds, so the scaffold is rigid. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the sulfur and the chlorine-bearing carbon, since the substituent breaks the ring's symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur and chlorine atoms offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methyl group and the other is a chlorine atom, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion. There are no heteroatom-containing functional groups beyond the carbon-chlorine bond, and the ring carries no hydroxyl, amino, or carbonyl groups. The compound is rigid and planar in its aromatic core, with only the methyl group contributing rotational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and essentially no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptor capability, since the chlorine is a weak acceptor and the ring is nonpolar.

The molecule is a substituted benzaldehyde built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen) sits on the ring and serves as the main reactive functional group. Adjacent to it is a chlorine atom, and two methoxy groups (oxygen bonded to a methyl) occupy the neighboring positions on the far side of the ring, giving a crowded, trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups can rotate about their single bonds. The oxygen atoms of the carbonyl and the two ether linkages act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered lactone ring, giving a bicyclic benzofuranone-type scaffold. The fused system is essentially planar and rigid, with the benzene ring bearing no substituents beyond the ring fusion. The five-membered ring contains an ester oxygen bonded to the aromatic carbon, a carbonyl carbon, and a methylene carbon linking back to the benzene ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is compact and asymmetric in its ring arrangement, with little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or extra ring systems. It carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached directly to the ring carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring, one at the position meta to the nitrile-bearing carbon on the opposite side of the nitrogen, and one ortho to the nitrile carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The rigid, planar aromatic scaffold and linear nitrile group leave essentially no conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom, so it has no fused ring system. It carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on the carbon directly beside the ring nitrogen, and two iodine atoms on the ring, one adjacent to the nitrogen and one farther around the ring, giving a 2,6-pattern relative to the nitrile on one side. Because the substituents sit on a flat aromatic core, the structure is rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the two iodines occupy different positions. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen both can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, bearing a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen and a fluorine atom on the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern. Because the ring is fully aromatic and planar, the scaffold is rigid, and the two substituents lie in the ring plane with no rotatable bonds. The nitrogen atom of the ring and the nitrogen of the nitrile group both carry lone pairs that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fluorine atom is a weak acceptor, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so it has no fused rings and no saturated portions. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and an iodine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pattern. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds and no internal symmetry because the two substituents are at different positions.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, so it is a single fused-free ring system with no additional rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons flanking the ring nitrogen: a methyl group and a nitrile group, which places the substituents in a 2,3-relationship relative to each other. The nitrile is a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond that is strongly electron-withdrawing and rigid in shape. The structure is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group, and it lacks any symmetry because the two substituents differ. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, so there is no ring fusion. One ring carries a methyl group at the position para to the link, giving a 4-methylphenyl unit. The other ring carries a nitrile (cyano, C≡N) group on the carbon directly adjacent to the linkage, which places it at the ortho position. The two rings can rotate about the central bond, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the methyl and nitrile sit on different rings. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a monocyclic heteroaromatic scaffold containing one ring nitrogen. It carries two substituents: a methyl group on one ring carbon and a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a 2,4-disubstitution pattern relative to the ring nitrogen. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, while the methyl and nitrile groups are small and rigid, so the molecule has little conformational flexibility and no internal symmetry beyond the local plane. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, and the nitrile nitrogen provides a second, weaker acceptor site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position. A fluorine atom sits on the ring carbon at the 5-position, meta to the nitrile-bearing carbon and para-like across the ring from the nitrogen's neighboring carbon. The structure is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, so it has no fused ring system and no stereocenters. A nitrile group (a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen) is attached to one ring carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a fluorine atom sits on the other carbon next to that same nitrogen, giving a 2,6-disubstitution pattern. The two substituents are roughly mirror-related across the ring, but the nitrile and fluorine differ, so the molecule has no rotational symmetry. The rigid planar aromatic core and linear nitrile limit conformational flexibility to essentially none. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen are both hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at the ortho positions: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a formyl group (an aldehyde, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydrogen). This 1,2-disubstituted, planar aromatic scaffold is fully rigid, with the carbon-nitrogen triple bond extending linearly from the ring and the aldehyde carbonyl lying roughly in the ring plane. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane-level symmetry about the axis through the two substituents, so the two ortho groups are chemically distinct. The nitrile nitrogen and the aldehyde oxygen each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) and a primary carboxamide group (a carbonyl bonded to an NH2). The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and planar. The substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted, which gives the molecule a lack of symmetry across the ring and a rigid, largely flat shape with limited conformational flexibility. The amide provides both hydrogen-bond donor capacity through its two N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptor capacity through its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitrile nitrogen acts as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic. One substituent is a nitrile group, a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor at its nitrogen. The other is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to a chlorine atom; the sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors and the group is strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonyl group offers a modest degree of rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that would render all positions equivalent, and it contains no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair. The other substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with no fused rings, while the carboxylic acid carbon is attached by a single bond that allows limited rotation. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane coinciding with both substituents, since the two groups differ in identity.

The molecule is a simple monocyclic aromatic compound built on a six-membered pyridine ring, a planar, fully conjugated scaffold containing one nitrogen atom. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached directly to the ring carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho on the pyridine ring. There are no ring fusions, stereocenters, or other substituents, and the linear nitrile unit extends the rigid, flat framework. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, and the nitrile nitrogen offers a second, weaker acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The structure is rigid with little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexenone scaffold, with no fused or bridged ring systems. A ketone carbonyl sits at one ring position, and a single carbon-carbon double bond is conjugated directly with that carbonyl, forming an α,β-unsaturated enone unit. The remaining ring atoms are sp3-hybridized methylene groups, and there are no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the molecule has no stereocenters. The ring is fairly rigid because of the planar enone portion, while the saturated segment retains some conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents at ortho positions: a carboxylic acid group and a cyclohexyl ring. The carboxylic acid is a planar, conjugated unit attached directly to the aromatic ring, and it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The cyclohexane ring is saturated and adopts a flexible chair-type conformation, linked to the aromatic ring by a single bond that allows rotation. The overall substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the two groups differ in shape and electronic character. The aromatic core provides rigidity, while the saturated ring adds three-dimensional bulk.

The molecule is 2-cyclohexylethanol, built from a saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring (cyclohexane) bearing a single two-carbon side chain at one carbon. The ring is fully sp3-hybridized with no fusion or unsaturation, and the only functional group is a primary alcohol at the terminus of the ethyl linker, giving a single substitution point on the ring. The structure lacks any internal symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, and its chain and ring offer considerable conformational flexibility, with the cyclohexane ring able to interconvert between chair forms. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the remainder of the molecule is nonpolar hydrocarbon.

This molecule is an acyclic, saturated secondary alcohol with a straight-chain scaffold: a ten-carbon backbone in which the hydroxyl group sits on the second carbon from one end, bearing a methyl branch at that same carbon. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated groups; the only functional group is the single hydroxyl, and the substitution pattern is a simple one-carbon methyl branch next to it. The molecule lacks symmetry, since the two sides of the carbinol carbon differ in length and the chain can adopt many conformations, making it highly flexible. The hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen together provide one hydrogen-bond donor and one hydrogen-bond acceptor site, while the remaining carbon framework is nonpolar.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone built on a straight, unbranched chain. A carbonyl group (C=O) sits on the second carbon from one end, flanked by a methyl group on one side and a linear eight-carbon alkyl chain on the other, giving a methyl ketone scaffold. There are no rings, no fused systems, and no aromatic atoms, so the structure is entirely saturated apart from the single carbonyl. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two groups flanking the carbonyl differ in length. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a saturated six-membered oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydropyran-type ring bearing a hydroxymethyl group and three hydroxyl substituents. The ring oxygen closes a cyclic hemiacetal, since one ring carbon is bonded to both the ring oxygen and a hydroxyl group. Substitution is on three adjacent and nearby ring carbons: a hydroxymethyl group and hydroxyl groups at positions that give the ring a defined, stereochemically specified arrangement. The scaffold is a single ring with no fused or bridged systems, and it is conformationally constrained by its chair-like saturated framework, though the exocyclic hydroxymethyl group retains some rotational freedom. Overall the molecule has no internal symmetry, and it presents four hydroxyl oxygens and a ring oxygen, giving multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites and acceptor sites.

The molecule is an acyclic, four-carbon-backbone polyol bearing an aldehyde at one end and a primary alcohol at the other, with hydroxyl groups on the two interior stereogenic carbons. Its skeleton is a straight, unbranched chain with no rings, so it is highly conformationally flexible. The terminal aldehyde (C=O) and the three hydroxyl groups make it a strong hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The two adjacent secondary carbons carry defined stereochemistry, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the substitution pattern is asymmetric from end to end.

The molecule is built on a uracil-type pyrimidine-2,4-dione ring, a six-membered ring with two carbonyl groups and two nitrogen atoms, one of which is an N-H donor. This heterocycle is N-linked to a saturated five-membered oxolane (tetrahydrofuran) ring, forming a nucleoside-like scaffold with no ring fusion. The sugar-like ring carries a secondary hydroxyl group and a hydroxymethyl side chain, both of which can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. Two defined stereocentres on the saturated ring give the sugar portion a fixed three-dimensional shape, while the aromatic base is planar and rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry, and its carbonyl oxygens and ring nitrogen provide additional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

This molecule is built on a biphenyl scaffold, in which two benzene rings are joined by a single bond, with no fused ring system. One ring carries a dimethylamino group (N(CH3)2) at the position ortho to the biaryl bond, while the other ring carries a phosphorus atom at the adjacent ortho position, bearing two cyclohexyl substituents and a third connection to the phosphorus. The phosphine center is a trivalent phosphorus with lone-pair character, and the tertiary amine nitrogen likewise offers a lone pair. Because the biaryl axis is flanked by two ortho substituents, rotation about the central bond is hindered, giving the framework a somewhat restricted, twisted conformation, while the cyclohexyl groups add conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, but the nitrogen and phosphorus can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a biaryl scaffold: a benzene ring bearing two isopropoxy groups in a 1,3-relationship (meta to each other) is directly bonded to a second benzene ring that carries a dicyclohexylphosphino group at the position ortho to the biaryl bond. Both aromatic rings are simple unfused benzene rings, while the two cyclohexyl groups attached to phosphorus are saturated, non-planar rings. The two aryl rings are joined by a single bond and are twisted out of plane relative to each other, giving the framework a moderately rigid, sterically encumbered shape, with the bulky cyclohexyl groups and isopropoxy substituents flanking the phosphorus center. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two isopropoxy groups sit on one ring and the phosphine on the other. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two ether oxygens and the phosphorus lone pair, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a biaryl scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single bond, with the two rings positioned ortho to each other on the biphenyl axis. One ring carries a methyl group ortho to the biaryl bond, while the other carries a phosphorus atom ortho to that same bond. The phosphorus is trivalent and bears two cyclohexyl substituents, each saturated six-membered carbocycle attached through a single carbon. Because the aryl rings are twisted relative to each other around the central bond, the arrangement is non-planar and somewhat rigid. The phosphine center is a lone-pair-bearing donor site with no hydrogen-bond donors, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane due to the asymmetric placement of the methyl and phosphino groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placing them in an ortho relationship. One substituent is a dimethylamino group, in which a nitrogen atom carries two methyl groups and is attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a hydroxyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the two methyl groups and the acid group can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), whereas the tertiary amine nitrogen serves only as a weak acceptor since it has no hydrogen to donate. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the two substituents differ.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic methyl ketone with an unbranched chain. A straight carbon backbone of twelve carbons, with the carbonyl carbon sitting in the second position from one end, carries a single ketone functional group that bears a methyl group on one side and an eleven-carbon alkyl chain on the other. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no heteroatoms apart from the single carbonyl oxygen. The structure is symmetric only in a loose sense, since the two sides of the carbonyl differ in length. The long saturated chain is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a 1,2-dihydroquinoline scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring that contains one carbon-carbon double bond. The nitrogen is acylated by an ethyl carbamate group, so it carries a C(=O)O-ethyl substituent rather than an N-H. The carbon adjacent to the nitrogen bears an ethoxy group, giving an ether linkage at a stereogenic-capable position. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, while the two ethyl chains add conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity is absent because there are no N-H or O-H groups, whereas the carbamate carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one bond, which gives a flat, rigid aromatic core. An ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) is attached to one ring at a position next to the fusion area, while a formyl group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen, i.e., an aldehyde) sits directly beside it on the adjacent carbon. The aldehyde oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Apart from the flexible ethyl tail, the structure is largely planar and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically on one ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge. An ethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to an ethyl chain) sits on one ring at a position adjacent to the fusion carbon, while an acyl chloride group (a carbonyl bearing a chlorine atom) is attached directly to the neighboring carbon on the same ring. The two substituents are therefore ortho to each other, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, though the ethyl tail and the carbonyl-chloride group retain some rotational freedom. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl oxygen is a further acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, with two substituents placed on adjacent carbons (ortho substitution). The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two adjacent (ortho) substituents: an ethoxy group, meaning an oxygen atom bonded to an ethyl chain, and a carboxylic acid group attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The molecule is built on a cinnamic acid scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon side chain that ends in a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. This molecule is a small, flexible, acyclic ether-alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is simply a linear two-carbon chain bridging an ethyl group and a hydroxyl-terminated ethylene unit. A single ether oxygen sits in the middle of the chain, linking an ethyl terminus to a 2-hydroxyethyl terminus, and the terminal primary alcohol is the only other functional group. The molecule is a short, acyclic, fully saturated chain with no rings, so its skeleton is flexible and open, built from two-carbon segments linked by ether and ester oxygens. Because it has no hydrogen-bond donors, the oxygen atoms of the ester carbonyl and the two ether-type oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused together to share one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents on neighboring carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. The molecule is a small cyclic compound built on a five-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclopentane-1,3-dione core, with no fused or bridged ring systems. Two ketone carbonyl groups sit on the ring, separated by a single carbon, so the dione pattern is 1,3 rather than 1,2 or 1,4.
