This molecule is an acyclic saturated alcohol built on a flexible carbon chain with no rings. Its skeleton is a branched alkane: a two-carbon ethyl group and a two-carbon ethyl group attach to the same carbon, which bears a CH2 unit that terminates in a primary hydroxyl group. The branching point gives the molecule a degree of local symmetry, since the two ethyl arms are equivalent, but the overall structure remains conformationally flexible because all bonds are single bonds that rotate freely. This molecule is an acyclic, saturated aliphatic alcohol built on a branched carbon chain with no rings, so its skeleton is entirely open and flexible. The backbone consists of a six-carbon main chain with a two-carbon ethyl branch attached to the second carbon, and a terminal hydroxymethyl group bearing the single oxygen. Because the molecule lacks any ring or symmetry-enforcing element, it has no meaningful internal symmetry and many accessible conformations arising from rotation about its numerous single bonds.

The molecule is built on a single quaternary carbon that carries an ethyl group and three hydroxymethyl arms, giving it a compact, branched, fully saturated acyclic scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. Each of the three hydroxymethyl groups terminates in a primary alcohol, so the molecule contains three hydroxyl functional groups and no other heteroatoms or unsaturation. The central carbon is bonded to four different substituents on one side and three identical arms, so the three hydroxymethyl branches are symmetrically related around a single axis. Because the molecule has only single bonds and is highly branched, its conformational freedom is substantial, though it is not conjugated or rigid. All three hydroxyl oxygens can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle, a 2-oxazoline (4,5-dihydrooxazole) ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom. The ring has a single carbon-nitrogen double bond, which makes the nitrogen sp2-hybridized and part of an imine-like C=N unit, while the remaining ring atoms form saturated CH2 units. An ethyl group is attached to the carbon that sits between the nitrogen and the oxygen, so the substitution pattern is a single alkyl group on the ring carbon at position 2. The ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond through its lone pair, and the ring oxygen can act as a weaker acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, specifically an imidazole ring bearing two alkyl substituents. The molecule lacks any symmetry, since the two substituents occupy distinct positions on the asymmetric ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on six carbons, giving a single aromatic ring with no fused partners. The molecule is built on a benzene scaffold, a single six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The molecule is built on an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in a linear arrangement, with two carbonyl groups sitting on the central ring at positions opposite each other. The molecule is a short, saturated carboxylic acid built on a straight-chain backbone with no rings and no aromatic systems. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The molecule is a phenylboronic acid, with a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to one ring carbon. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a fluorine atom. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrile nitrogen and the fluorine serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The two aromatic rings are unfused and connected only through the sp2 carbonyl carbon, so the scaffold is non-symmetric and moderately flexible about the two aryl-carbonyl bonds. The phenolic hydroxyl serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atom act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a carboxylic acid, and a fluorine atom. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, forming a single aromatic core with no fused rings. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring systems. The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents, with no fused rings. Its core is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle that is fully planar and rigid. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a fluorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the acid, and a nitro group located para to the carboxylic acid. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no fused or additional ring systems. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple monocyclic aromatic compound with no fused rings. This molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (CH2OH), a fluorine atom, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a boronic acid group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a fluorine atom. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a fluorine atom on the carbon adjacent to it, and a trifluoromethyl group positioned meta to the acid on the opposite side of the ring. The molecule is a cinnamic-acid-type structure: a benzene ring bearing a trans-configured acrylic acid side chain, with the carboxylic acid joined to the ring through a C=C double bond. The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen), a fluorine atom, and a boronic acid group. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) sits on one ring carbon, with a fluorine atom on the adjacent carbon, ortho to it. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy different positions. Only the methoxy group's methyl and the amide's NH2 contribute much conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions: a methoxy group, a fluorine atom, and a carboxylic acid group. The molecule is a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, bearing three substituents on adjacent carbons. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits at one position, a fluorine atom sits on the carbon next to it, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 carrying a bromine) sits on the carbon at the other side of the methoxy-bearing carbon, creating a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and bromomethyl groups add some rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The oxygen of the methoxy group can accept a hydrogen bond, the fluorine is a weak acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substitution pattern is 1,2,3-trisubstituted: a nitro group sits on one ring carbon, a bromomethyl group (a CH2 bearing bromine) on the adjacent carbon, and a fluorine atom on the carbon on the other side of the bromomethyl-bearing carbon. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorine adds a further polar, weakly accepting site. The bromomethyl group is a flexible, reactive side chain with a rotatable bond, whereas the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the three substituents are all different and placed asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions. A nitro group (–NO2) sits at one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group (–OH) on the carbon next to it, and a fluorine atom on the carbon two positions further around the ring, giving a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors and the fluorine as a weak acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, whereas the substituents are small and largely free to rotate about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a diaryl ether, with two benzene rings joined through a single oxygen atom. One ring carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) at one position adjacent to the ether linkage and a fluorine atom at the neighboring position, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern on that ring. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. Both aromatic rings are planar and fully conjugated, while the ether oxygen provides a degree of rotational flexibility about the two C–O bonds. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry, since the substituted and unsubstituted rings differ. The nitrile nitrogen and the ether oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acetanilide, built on a single benzene ring with an acetamide group attached to one carbon. The acetamide consists of a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl carbon, which is linked through an amide nitrogen to the aromatic ring. A fluorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the amide-bearing carbon, giving an ortho-substitution pattern on the ring. The structure lacks symmetry because the two substituents are unlike and placed asymmetrically. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is rigid, though the amide bond gives the molecule some conformational flexibility at the side chain.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Two substituents are attached to adjacent carbons on that ring: an amino group (–NH2), which is a primary aromatic amine, and a fluorine atom. This ortho substitution pattern places the two groups next to each other, which breaks any higher symmetry and leaves the ring with a lower-symmetry, roughly planar shape. The core is rigid and flat, with only the N–H bonds free to rotate. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and as a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two adjacent substituents on neighboring carbons, making it a disubstituted aromatic compound with no ring fusion. One substituent is a methoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group and to the ring, and the other is a single fluorine atom attached directly to the aromatic carbon next to it. The 1,2-ortho arrangement of these groups gives the molecule a planar, rigid scaffold with a relatively compact shape and only one plane of approximate symmetry through the two substituents. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine is a weak acceptor and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a formyl group, an aldehyde carbon double-bonded to oxygen and attached directly to the ring, while the other is a fluorine atom. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has a flat, largely two-dimensional shape with a mirror plane through the ring, so its overall symmetry is limited by the unsymmetrical substitution. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are on the aromatic carbons and the aldehyde carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to both the ring and an NH2 group. The other substituent is a fluorine atom sitting directly next to the amide-bearing carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The amide group supplies both hydrogen-bond donor capability (through its two N-H bonds) and acceptor capability (through the carbonyl oxygen), while the fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a phenylboronic acid bearing a single fluorine substituent on the benzene ring. The aromatic core is a simple, unfused six-membered benzene ring, which is planar and rigid. A boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bonded to two hydroxyl groups, is attached directly to one ring carbon. The fluorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern, so the molecule has no symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. The two B–OH groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the oxygen and fluorine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and single-bonded to a chlorine atom and to the ring carbon. The other substituent is a fluorine atom attached to the neighboring ring carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with limited conformational flexibility beyond rotation about the sulfur-carbon bond. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane that would make the two ortho positions equivalent, so it is asymmetric. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a fluorine atom and a carbohydrazide group, meaning a carbonyl carbon attached to the ring that is further bonded to a hydrazine unit (–C(=O)–NH–NH2). The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings, giving a flat and largely rigid scaffold, while the hydrazide side chain offers some rotational freedom about the bond to the ring and within the N–N linkage. The ortho arrangement of the fluorine and carbonyl places the two substituents next to each other, so the molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the ring plane. The hydrazide group contributes multiple hydrogen-bond donors through its N–H bonds and hydrogen-bond acceptors through the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs, while the fluorine acts as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which forms a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group, consisting of a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and a fluorine atom sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The two substituents differ in character, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the fluorine acts only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a fluorine atom on one ring carbon and a trichloromethyl-bearing carbon on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the core is rigid, while rotation about the bond joining the ring to the carbon bearing three chlorines is relatively free. The carbon atom carrying the three chlorine substituents is sp3-hybridized, forming a bulky, tetrahedral group that breaks any overall symmetry of the molecule. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. Its only potential hydrogen-bond acceptors are the electronegative halogen atoms, which are weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho substitution pattern: one is a fluorine atom directly bonded to the ring, and the other is a trifluoromethyl group (a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the trifluoromethyl group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local threefold arrangement of the CF3 group, because the two substituents are different. Fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups at all.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen (double bond) and a chlorine atom, which makes it a reactive electrophilic center. The other substituent is a fluorine atom attached directly to the ring carbon next to the carbonyl-bearing carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the acyl chloride carbon lying roughly in the plane of the ring and the fluorine contributing only a small steric and electronic influence. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks any element of rotational symmetry beyond the ring plane, so its shape is effectively asymmetric in the two substituent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atom can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is 2-fluorobiphenyl, built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between adjacent positions on each ring. Each ring is an aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused ring systems, and the two rings can rotate about the central bond, giving the scaffold moderate conformational flexibility. A single fluorine atom sits on the ortho position of one ring, adjacent to the linkage, which breaks the symmetry of the molecule so the two halves are not equivalent. The compound contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only hydrogen-bond acceptor character comes from the weakly basic fluorine atom.

This molecule is a boronic acid built on a benzene ring, with a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups attached directly to one carbon of the ring. The ring carries a phenyl group, a second benzene ring, at the position para to the boronic acid, and a fluorine atom on the carbon adjacent to that phenyl substituent, so the substitution pattern is a 1,2,4-arrangement on the central ring. The biaryl linkage between the two rings is a single bond that allows some rotation, giving the scaffold moderate flexibility, while each aromatic ring is rigid and planar. The two B–OH groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, the fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the fluorine breaks the pattern of the substituents.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a three-carbon chain, with a chiral alpha carbon bearing a primary amino group and a carboxylic acid. The side chain is a benzyl group, a benzene ring attached through a CH2 linker to the alpha carbon, and that benzene ring carries a single fluorine atom on one position adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern with no internal symmetry across the ring. The molecule has no fused ring systems, and its only ring is the aromatic benzene, which is planar and rigid. The rotatable bonds in the side chain and the backbone give moderate conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes from the amine and the carboxylic acid OH, while the carbonyl oxygen, hydroxyl oxygen, amine nitrogen, and fluorine can act as acceptors.

The molecule is a two-carbon chain with a hydroxyl group on one terminal carbon and a fluorine atom on the other, so it is an acyclic, fully saturated scaffold with no rings or ring fusion. The hydroxyl group is an alcohol functional group, and the carbon-fluorine bond places a single halogen substituent at the opposite end of the chain. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond a lack of any mirror plane through the carbon backbone, and its two carbons can rotate freely about the central single bond, so it is flexible. The hydroxyl oxygen-bound hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the oxygen and the fluorine can each serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a two-carbon acid backbone: a carboxylic acid group sits at one end, followed by a tetrahedral carbon bearing a hydroxyl group, which is attached directly to a benzene ring. That ring is a single, unfused aromatic six-membered system with no additional rings. A fluorine atom occupies the position adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho substitution pattern on the phenyl ring. The molecule has one stereogenic center at the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group, so it lacks internal mirror symmetry and the phenyl ring can rotate relative to the side chain. Its hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the fluorine offers only weak acceptor capability.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a hydroxyl group, which makes the molecule a phenol, and the other is a fluorine atom attached to the neighboring ring carbon. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with no rotatable bonds in the ring itself. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, while the fluorine is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has a lower-symmetry, asymmetric arrangement because the two different substituents break the mirror symmetry of the parent benzene ring.

The molecule is built on a phenylacetic acid scaffold, consisting of a single benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain that ends in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted at one position by the CH2-COOH unit and carries a fluorine atom on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho substitution pattern with no symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, and it is connected to the carboxyl-bearing methylene by a single rotatable bond, so the overall structure is only moderately flexible. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine atom acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a boronic acid group and a fluorine atom on adjacent carbons, with the boron-bearing carbon sitting meta to the ring nitrogen. The boronic acid, B(OH)2, is attached directly to the aromatic ring and provides two hydroxyl groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen atoms that can act as acceptors. The fluorine substituent sits ortho to the boron and adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical. The single six-membered aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with only the two B–OH bonds offering rotational freedom. The pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached at one ring carbon, and a fluorine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, giving a 2-fluoro, 4-carboxylic acid substitution pattern. The planar, fully conjugated ring and the directly attached carboxyl group make the scaffold rigid, with only limited rotation about the bond to the acid. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local geometry of the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and two acceptor oxygens, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a methyl group and a fluorine atom, placing them in an ortho relationship to each other. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methyl group rotates freely around its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no functional groups beyond these two substituents, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The fluorine atom can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ring's pi system offers only limited additional acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached to the ring via carbon), and the neighboring substituent is a boronic acid group, a boron atom bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the overall structure is rigid apart from rotation about the single bonds connecting the two substituents to the ring. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the molecule lacks the high symmetry of a para- or meta-substituted analog. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the aldehyde oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a furan ring, with one oxygen atom in the ring and four carbon atoms. Attached to one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen is a formyl group, meaning a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen, so the substitution pattern is a monosubstituted furan at the 2-position. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because every ring and carbonyl hydrogen is bonded to carbon. The structure is small, planar, and rigid, with the aldehyde group able to rotate only slightly about its bond to the ring, and it lacks any stereocenters or meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic furan ring, which contains one oxygen atom in the ring and no fused rings. Attached directly to a carbon adjacent to that ring oxygen is a carboxamide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a nitrogen bearing two hydrogen atoms. The substitution pattern is therefore monosubstituted at the 2-position of the furan, leaving the remaining ring carbons unsubstituted. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a rotatable bond between the ring and the amide carbonyl, so its overall framework is largely planar and fairly rigid. The amide group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites on the nitrogen, while the carbonyl oxygen and the furan ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is 2-furoic acid, a small aromatic compound built on a single five-membered furan ring. The furan is an oxygen-containing heteroaromatic ring with four carbons and one oxygen, and it is fully planar and conjugated. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which defines the substitution pattern at the 2-position. The molecule is compact and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the carboxyl group's C–C bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the furan oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic furan ring bearing a carbohydrazide group at the 2-position, with no other substituents on the ring. The furan contains one oxygen atom within an unfused, planar heteroaromatic system. Attached directly to the ring carbon is a carbonyl group forming an amide-type linkage to a terminal hydrazine unit, meaning two adjacent nitrogen atoms with one bearing two hydrogens. The structure is fairly compact and conformationally flexible only around the single bonds linking the carbonyl to the ring and to the hydrazine. Its hydrogen-bonding character is rich: the terminal NH2 and the amide NH serve as donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the furan oxygen act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic furan ring containing one oxygen atom, with no ring fusion present. Attached to one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen (the 2-position) is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a chlorine atom, which is the sole functional group on the scaffold. The ring is otherwise unsubstituted, giving a simple monosubstituted pattern with no stereocenters. The planar aromatic ring and the nearly linear carbonyl-chlorine arrangement make the structure rigid, with only limited rotational freedom about the bond linking the carbonyl to the ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a furan ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one oxygen atom, with no ring fusion. It carries a ketone attached directly to the 2-position of the furan, and that carbonyl is linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen). The linkage between the furan and the nitrile-bearing chain is flexible, though the furan ring itself is planar and rigid. The ketone oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, the furan oxygen is a weaker acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent sits at only one position on the ring.

The molecule is a bicyclic heterocycle built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring that contains an oxygen and a nitrogen atom. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so the fused system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The saturated-looking portion is a lactam: a carbonyl group sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which is bonded directly to the fused aromatic carbon, forming an amide. The ring oxygen connects the other fused aromatic carbon to a methylene group that links to the carbonyl. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a straight-chain scaffold of six carbons plus a terminal methyl group, giving a seven-carbon backbone. The carbonyl carbon sits on the chain at the second-from-end position, bonded to a methyl group on one side and a pentyl chain on the other, so the substitution is simple and unbranched. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom substituents beyond the single oxygen of the ketone. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two alkyl groups flanking the carbonyl differ in length. It is highly flexible, with free rotation about its many single bonds. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a straight-chain scaffold of six carbons, bearing a carbonyl group at the second carbon position. The carbonyl carbon is flanked by a methyl group on one side and a linear n-butyl chain on the other, so there are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems. The molecule lacks any substitution pattern beyond this simple unbranched arrangement and has no symmetry element other than the local mirror-like placement of the terminal groups. Its chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds along the alkyl portion and only the planar carbonyl group imposing local rigidity. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a six-carbon straight-chain alkyne, hex-2-yne, with the triple bond between the second and third carbons counting from one end. It has no rings, no ring fusion, and no heteroatoms or functional groups beyond the alkyne itself. The carbon skeleton is linear and unbranched, and the alkyne unit imposes a rigid, straight geometry on the two carbons it links, while the two terminal alkyl segments remain flexible. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry that would make its two halves identical, since one end carries a methyl group and the other a propyl chain. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, because it is made up only of carbon and hydrogen.

This molecule is a short, unbranched carbon chain built from a propyl group attached to an alkyne, followed by a carboxylic acid terminus. The triple bond between the second and third carbons from the carboxyl end makes that region linear and rigid, while the saturated propyl tail remains flexible. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely acyclic, and the molecule has no symmetry. The carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites at its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic lactam. A six-membered aromatic pyridine ring is fused through a shared edge to a six-membered saturated-looking oxazine-type ring containing an oxygen atom, a methylene carbon, and a carbonyl-bearing amide nitrogen. The pyridine nitrogen sits adjacent to the ring-fusion carbon bonded to the amide nitrogen, so the system is planar and largely rigid, with only minor flexibility in the non-aromatic ring. Functional groups include a cyclic amide (lactam), an aryl ether oxygen, and the pyridine nitrogen. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, ether oxygen, and pyridine nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry and no stereocenters.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and fully aromatic, which makes the framework rigid. At the 2-position of the thiazole ring sits a hydrazine group (–NH–NH2), a flexible substituent with two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The hydrazinyl nitrogens and the thiazole ring nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar framework, and the benzo ring carries no additional substituents.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached at one carbon adjacent to the ring fusion, and a hydroxyl group sits on the neighboring carbon, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The fused aromatic system is rigid with no rotatable bonds in the core, though the aldehyde can rotate slightly about its single bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry element because the two substituents occupy positions on one ring only. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carries three substituents: a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, and two nitro groups, one on the carbon directly next to the hydroxylated carbon and another on the carbon meta to the nitrogen across the ring. There is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially flat and rigid, with the substituents lying in the plane of the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The hydroxyl group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the two nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings and no additional ring systems. Substituents sit around the ring: a methyl group on one carbon, a hydroxyl group on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and an iodine atom on the adjacent carbon, giving a contiguous, unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a low degree of conformational flexibility, mainly from the rotation of the hydroxyl and methyl groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a substituted aromatic aldehyde with a single six-membered carbocyclic core and no ring fusion. Reading around the ring, a methoxy group sits next to a hydroxyl group, a formyl (aldehyde) group occupies the position flanked by the hydroxyl, and a nitro group is positioned meta to the aldehyde on the opposite side. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core and the directly attached groups are rigid, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups retain some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aldehyde, nitro, and methoxy oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions: a methoxy group (an ether, -OCH3), an aldehyde (a formyl group, -CHO), and a hydroxyl group (a phenolic -OH) that sits between the other two. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple substituted benzene. The 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern places the methoxy and hydroxyl groups on neighboring carbons and the aldehyde on the carbon beside the hydroxyl, which makes the molecule asymmetric. The aromatic ring and the planar carbonyl are rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom. The phenolic hydrogen is a hydrogen-bond donor, and the oxygens of the hydroxyl, methoxy, and aldehyde groups all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions, forming a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group is attached to one carbon, a hydroxyl group sits on the neighboring carbon, and a methoxy group occupies the carbon on the other side of the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,3-substitution pattern with no molecular symmetry. The planar aromatic core and the directly attached carboxyl group make the framework fairly rigid, while the methoxy group adds some conformational freedom. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl both act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the methoxy oxygen and carbonyl oxygen serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a nitro group, and a hydroxyl group, arranged so that the hydroxyl sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen and the methyl sits on the neighboring carbon, while the nitro group occupies a meta-like position relative to the nitrogen. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, planar moiety, and the hydroxyl group can tautomerize toward a pyridone form. The overall scaffold is rigid and essentially planar, with only the methyl and hydroxyl rotors allowing limited flexibility. The molecule lacks symmetry because of its asymmetric substitution pattern. The hydroxyl group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a carbohydrazide group (a carbonyl attached to a hydrazine, -C(=O)NHNH2). The methyl and hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, and the carbohydrazide sits on the carbon next to the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with no symmetry. The single aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydrazide side chain has some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The hydroxyl group and the amide N-H and terminal NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms and nitrogen atoms serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned para to each other across the ring. A methyl group is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to a nitrogen, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the neighboring carbon, giving an ortho-substituted pattern on the ring. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and hydroxyl substituents, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while both ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions: a formyl (aldehyde) group, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The aldehyde and hydroxyl groups sit on neighboring carbons, while the nitro group occupies the position on the opposite side of the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with the hydroxyl flanked by the other two groups. The single six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the substituents are largely coplanar with it, which limits conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the oxygen atoms of the aldehyde, hydroxyl, and nitro groups can all accept hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the three substituents differ from one another.

The molecule is built from a benzophenone core, in which a carbonyl bridges two aromatic rings. One ring is a simple unsubstituted phenyl group, while the other is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: the ketone bridge, a hydroxyl group ortho to that ketone, and a methacrylate ester oxygen para to the ketone. The ortho-hydroxyl group can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl oxygen, which stiffens that region of the structure. The ester contributes a terminal alkene conjugated to its carbonyl, giving the molecule a reactive vinyl site. Overall it has no symmetry, offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the phenolic OH) and several acceptors (the two carbonyl oxygens, the ester oxygens, and the hydroxyl oxygen), and is moderately rigid due to its aromatic rings.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring bearing two substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and in its tautomeric lactam-like form this hydroxyl can be drawn as a carbonyl with an N-H, making the ring behave as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. A trifluoromethyl group is attached at the position meta to the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, on the opposite side of the ring from the nitrogen's immediate neighborhood, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The rigid, planar aromatic core has no rotatable bonds beyond the substituents, and the trifluoromethyl group adds a compact, strongly electron-withdrawing feature.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing five substituents: two methoxy groups, one hydroxyl group, and one acetyl group, with the remaining positions occupied by aromatic hydrogens. The acetyl (C(=O)CH3) group sits ortho to the hydroxyl, and the other methoxy group sits ortho to the acetyl on the opposite side, so the substitution pattern is unsymmetrical and the molecule has no mirror plane or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and acetyl groups can rotate about their single bonds, giving modest conformational flexibility at the periphery. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and also as an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The carbonyl oxygen of the acetyl group and the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups are additional hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the phenolic OH is positioned to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent carbonyl oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on six carbons, giving a substituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group and a hydroxyl group sit on adjacent positions, and two methoxy (O-methyl ether) groups are placed elsewhere on the ring, with one methoxy group flanking the carboxylic acid. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups and the carboxylic acid add some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic compound built on a single six-membered pyrimidinone ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship. The ring is partially unsaturated and bears a carbonyl group on the carbon between the two nitrogens, making it a cyclic urea-like lactam. Two methyl groups are attached at separate carbon positions, one on a ring carbon adjacent to nitrogen and one on a second ring carbon, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. There are no fused rings, and the flat ring system is rigid, with the methyl groups as the only rotatable elements. The ring NH and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the other ring nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl bridging two benzene rings. The first ring carries a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent positions, with the hydroxyl ortho to the carbonyl, so an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the phenolic OH and the ketone oxygen is structurally possible. The second ring bears a single methyl group para to the carbonyl attachment, giving it a simple substitution pattern. The two aromatic rings are not coplanar with the carbonyl and can rotate about their single bonds, so the scaffold is moderately flexible. The phenolic OH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ketone oxygen and methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, an acetyl group, and a hydroxyl group. The acetyl group is a ketone attached directly to the ring, and the hydroxyl sits on the carbon adjacent to it, so the two form an ortho arrangement. The methoxy group is located para to the acetyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The single fused-free aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and acetyl groups can rotate about their single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen and the ketone oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the hydroxyl hydrogen can serve as a hydrogen-bond donor, with the ortho placement allowing an intramolecular interaction between them.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one carbon, an aldehyde (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen) sits on the carbon directly opposite the methoxy's neighbor, and a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon between the aldehyde and the methoxy-bearing side. The result is a trisubstituted aromatic ring with no ring fusion. The hydroxyl group is ortho to the aldehyde, which allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between them. The methoxy oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl serves as both a donor and an acceptor. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups offering limited rotation, and it lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions.

This molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, with two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group. One ring carries a hydroxyl group ortho to the carbonyl, which can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the ketone oxygen, and a methoxy group positioned para to the carbonyl on the same ring. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. The structure has no fused ring systems and lacks any rotational symmetry across the whole molecule, since the two rings differ in substitution. The aryl-ketone linkage gives moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The molecule offers one hydrogen-bond donor from the phenolic OH, while the ketone oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the methoxy oxygen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A methyl group sits on one carbon of the ring, a hydroxyl group on another carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a nitro group on a third carbon next to the methyl-bearing position, giving a crowded, unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic core and the nitro group are essentially planar, so the molecule is rigid with little conformational flexibility, and it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no additional fused rings. A ring nitrogen sits in the core, and the ring carries two substituents: a methyl group and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl is attached to the carbon next to the nitrogen, while the methyl is on the carbon that is one position further around the ring, so the two groups are not adjacent. Because the ring is flat and aromatic, the scaffold is rigid, with only the methyl and hydroxyl rotating freely. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, and the ring nitrogen can accept one.

This molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine-type ring that shares two adjacent carbons. The heteroaromatic ring contains a ring nitrogen, and a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon next to that nitrogen, which allows tautomeric equivalence with a lactam-type carbonyl form. A methyl group is attached to the carbon at the opposite end of the pyridine-type ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern across the fused system. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond the small rotation of the methyl group. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl carbon, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a hydroxyl group ortho to the ketone, which can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the carbonyl oxygen, and the other ring is unsubstituted. The phenol ring bears a linear n-octyl ether chain para to the ketone, giving it an asymmetric substitution pattern with no overall molecular symmetry. The flexible octyl tail contrasts with the more rigid diaryl ketone core. The hydroxyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond donor and the carbonyl and ether oxygens act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold. An acetyl group (a ketone attached through a methyl) sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, so the two are ortho to each other and can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond. A trifluoromethoxy group, an ether oxygen bearing a CF3 unit, is located meta to the acetyl group and para to the hydroxyl group. The ring has no fused systems, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no symmetry beyond local planarity. The aromatic core and the carbonyl make it fairly rigid, with only the acetyl methyl and the trifluoromethoxy group offering rotational freedom. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ketone oxygen and the ether oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, attached directly to the ring), a hydroxyl group, and a trifluoromethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a carbon carrying three fluorine atoms). The aldehyde and hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, while the trifluoromethoxy group is placed meta to the aldehyde and para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and fully fused-free, with no additional ring systems, and the compound lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The aromatic core and the directly attached carbonyl make the scaffold fairly rigid, though the trifluoromethoxy group offers some rotational freedom about its ring-oxygen bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen and the ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving a single aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A nitrile group (carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) sits on one ring carbon, flanked on the adjacent position by a hydroxyl group, so the nitrile and phenol are ortho to each other. A trifluoromethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a carbon bearing three fluorines) is attached at the position meta to the nitrile and para to the hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a potential planar arrangement of the ring. Its rigidity comes from the planar aromatic core, while the trifluoromethoxy group offers some rotational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen and nitrogen atoms serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying four substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached directly to the ring), a hydroxyl group, a methoxy group, and an iodine atom. Reading around the ring, the hydroxyl sits between the methoxy and the aldehyde, so the aldehyde and hydroxyl are ortho to each other, and the iodine sits meta to the aldehyde on the far side of the ring. This substitution pattern leaves the molecule without any mirror or rotational symmetry, since the four groups differ from one another. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups have some rotational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl can donate a hydrogen bond, and the oxygen atoms of the aldehyde, methoxy, and hydroxyl groups can each accept one.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle, bearing two substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and an iodine atom is attached at the position para to that hydroxyl-bearing carbon, which places it meta to the nitrogen on the far side of the ring. Because the ring is fully aromatic and carries no additional fused rings, the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen having any rotational freedom. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational axis beyond the trivial. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and accept one at its oxygen, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a hydroxyl group, and an acetyl group (a ketone with a methyl). The hydroxyl and acetyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, so they are ortho to one another, while the methoxy group sits on the opposite side of the ring, para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is flat and rigid, and the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen are positioned to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond. The molecule has one hydrogen-bond donor (the phenolic OH) and three acceptor sites (the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the carbonyl oxygen). Its substitution pattern is asymmetric, so it has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring in its planar conformation. Only the methoxy and acetyl methyl groups add conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. One ring carbon carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), another carries a hydroxyl group, and an adjacent carbon carries an aldehyde (a carbonyl with a hydrogen). The hydroxyl and aldehyde sit next to each other, so they are ortho to one another, while the methoxy group sits para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy methyl and the aldehyde able to rotate. The molecule has no symmetry, since the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically on the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen and methoxy oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid, a hydroxyl group, and a methoxy group, arranged on adjacent and meta-related positions. The carboxylic acid and the hydroxyl sit next to each other on the ring, which gives an ortho relationship, while the methoxy group is placed further around the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single planar aromatic core, so its overall shape is largely flat and rigid, with some rotational freedom in the methoxy and carboxyl groups. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the oxygen atoms of the carbonyl, hydroxyl, and methoxy groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying four substituents: an acetyl group (a ketone with a methyl), a methyl group, a nitro group, and a hydroxyl group. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon with the nitro group adjacent to it and the acetyl group on the other side, giving a crowded, contiguous 1,2,3-substitution pattern around that carbon, while the methyl group sits meta to the acetyl group on the opposite side of the ring. The ring is a single fused-free aromatic system, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the acetyl methyl rotating freely. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the four substituents are all different. The phenolic hydroxyl is a hydrogen-bond donor and can also accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygen, and the carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens are additional acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons: a hydroxyl group and an acetamido group, the latter being an N-acetyl amide attached to the ring through its nitrogen. A methyl group occupies a position on the ring that is meta to the amide nitrogen and para to the hydroxyl group. The molecule is largely planar and fairly rigid across the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom around the amide C–N and C–O bonds. It has no internal symmetry. The hydroxyl and the amide N–H both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. An acetyl group (a ketone with a methyl) is attached to one ring carbon, a hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, and a methyl group is located on the ring carbon meta to the acetyl group and para to the hydroxyl. The hydroxyl and the acetyl carbonyl are positioned ortho to each other, which allows an intramolecular hydrogen bond between the phenolic oxygen-bound hydrogen and the carbonyl oxygen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group has a little rotational freedom around its bond to the ring. The phenolic OH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring, bearing two substituents. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is that of a 2-hydroxy-5-methyl pyridine scaffold. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, and the only rotatable bond is the one linking the methyl group to the ring, so the framework is essentially rigid. The hydroxyl oxygen can donate a hydrogen bond, while the ring nitrogen can accept one, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the planar ring itself.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an attached hydrogen), a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. The aldehyde and hydroxyl sit on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho relationship, while the nitro group is positioned meta to the aldehyde and para to the hydroxyl. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule as a whole is largely planar and rigid, with only limited rotation about the aldehyde and nitro bonds. The phenolic OH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen, nitro oxygens, and phenolic oxygen can all act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The arrangement lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are distinct and unevenly placed around the ring.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A carboxylic acid group is attached at one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a nitro group occupies the position meta to the acid on the opposite side of the ring. Because the ring is fully aromatic, the core is planar and rigid, with only the carboxyl and nitro groups able to rotate slightly. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the three substituents are placed at different positions around the ring. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, and together with the nitro oxygens and the ring nitrogen they supply several hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings, carrying two substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a nitro group (an N-oxide-free, formally charged nitro moiety) is attached at the position meta to that nitrogen on the opposite side of the ring. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, with the two groups placed so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the flat ring framework. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the nitro and hydroxyl groups are rotationally free only about their single bonds to the ring. The hydroxyl group provides a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on adjacent and nearby ring positions: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a hydroxyl group, and an acetyl group (a carbonyl attached to a methyl). The hydroxyl and acetyl groups sit next to each other, so they can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, which locks them into a planar, rigid arrangement. The molecule has a single phenyl core with an asymmetric substitution pattern, so it lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. It offers one hydrogen-bond donor from the hydroxyl oxygen and three acceptors from the ether oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions, giving a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Reading around the ring, a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one carbon, a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon two positions away, and a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O bonded to hydrogen) occupies the carbon between them. The aldehyde and the hydroxyl are ortho to each other, which allows an intramolecular interaction across the adjacent groups. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that maps it onto itself, and its aromatic core is rigid while the methoxy and aldehyde groups have limited rotational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aldehyde and methoxy oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while a hydroxyl group occupies the carbon on the other side of that nitrogen, and a nitro group is attached at the position beside the methyl-bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore fully asymmetric, with three different groups distributed around the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the methyl group contributing rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitro group provides additional acceptor sites through its oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, a carboxylic acid group on the carbon two positions away from that methyl-bearing carbon, and a hydroxyl group on the carbon flanked by the nitrogen and the carboxylic acid bearing carbon. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, leaving the ring without any internal symmetry. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the carboxylic acid group offering rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, while the carboxyl oxygens, hydroxyl oxygen, and ring nitrogen can accept them.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring, with no fused ring systems. A methyl group sits on one carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon on the other side of that nitrogen, so the two substituents flank the nitrogen at the 2 and 6 positions. The hydroxyl oxygen can donate a hydrogen bond and the ring nitrogen can accept one, while the methyl group contributes only nonpolar bulk. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the free rotation of the methyl group, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric because the two flanking groups differ.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons (ortho pattern): an acetyl group, a carbonyl attached to a methyl group, and a hydroxyl group bonded directly to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the phenolic hydroxyl supplies one hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule is essentially planar and relatively rigid, with only limited rotation around the bond linking the acetyl group to the ring, and it lacks a mirror-symmetric arrangement because the two substituents differ.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups, and the other is a phenolic hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with the two polar groups held in a fixed relative geometry. Both the boronic acid and the phenol can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H bonds and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that maps the two substituents onto each other, so it is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a phenolic hydroxyl group, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond. The other is a carbohydrazide unit, a carbonyl bonded to a hydrazine group with an NH–NH₂ terminus, which supplies several additional hydrogen-bond donor sites and a carbonyl oxygen acceptor. The only ring present is the single aromatic six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational freedom, while the hydrazide side chain retains some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole-type ring, giving a benzimidazole scaffold. The fused rings are planar and fully conjugated, so the framework is rigid, with no rotatable bonds. The five-membered ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon between the two nitrogen atoms, and one ring nitrogen bears a hydrogen, while the other is an unprotonated sp2 nitrogen. The four benzo positions are unsubstituted, so the substitution pattern is minimal, and the molecule has an overall approximate planar symmetry. The NH and the hydroxyl group act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the pyridine-like nitrogen and the oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons (ortho positioning). One substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, which is linear and strongly electron-withdrawing. The other is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, making it a phenolic OH. The scaffold is flat and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the hydroxyl hydrogen, and the molecule has a plane of symmetry running through the substituent axis. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single carbonyl carbon, giving a diaryl ketone scaffold. Each aromatic ring is a simple six-membered carbon ring with three hydrogen-bearing positions, and one ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl attachment, so the substitution pattern is ortho on that ring. The ketone oxygen and the phenolic hydroxyl oxygen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. The two rings are not symmetric because only one carries the hydroxyl, and the central carbonyl linkage gives moderate rotational flexibility between the aromatic systems.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen, giving a benzothiazole scaffold. The hydroxyl group sits on the carbon between the sulfur and the nitrogen in the thiazole ring, and this carbon-oxygen bond allows the structure to exist in a lactam-like tautomeric form with an N-H group and a carbonyl. The four unsubstituted positions on the benzo ring are all hydrogen-bearing, so the substitution pattern is simple and the fused framework is planar and rigid. Overall, the molecule has a single hydrogen-bond donor (the N-H or O-H) and acceptor sites at the ring nitrogen and oxygen.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound with no fused rings. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, and the other is a hydroxymethyl group, a methylene carbon bonded to a terminal hydroxyl. Both oxygen-bearing groups are polar, and each contributes one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor site. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm adds a degree of rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that maps the two substituents onto each other, so it has no internal symmetry beyond the ring's local planarity.

This molecule is a carbazole, a tricyclic scaffold in which two benzene rings are fused on either side of a central five-membered pyrrole ring containing an NH group. The hydroxyl group sits on one of the outer benzene rings, para-like to the ring fusion, giving a single substituent on an otherwise unsubstituted aromatic framework. The fused ring system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the molecule has an approximately mirror-symmetric arrangement about the central ring with the hydroxyl breaking that symmetry. The indole-type nitrogen and the phenolic oxygen each provide a hydrogen-bond donor site, and the oxygen and the ring nitrogen can also act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a chalcone-type scaffold: a two-carbon enone bridge joins two aromatic rings. One side is an unsubstituted phenyl ring attached to the alkene through a trans (E) double bond, which keeps that half of the molecule extended and fairly rigid. The other side is a benzoyl ring carrying a hydroxyl group at the ortho position relative to the carbonyl, which creates an intramolecular hydrogen-bonding arrangement with the ketone oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and little overall symmetry, since the two aryl ends differ in substitution. The hydroxyl group acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic ester built on a single three-carbon-chain scaffold with no ring systems. Its core is a methacrylate unit: a terminal vinyl group bearing a methyl substituent on the carbon that is attached to a carbonyl. The carbonyl is esterified to a two-carbon chain that ends in a primary alcohol, so the structure carries both a carbonyl oxygen and a free hydroxyl group. Because the molecule is open-chained and lacks any branching beyond the single methyl group, it has no meaningful internal symmetry and retains considerable conformational flexibility around its single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ester carbonyl and ester oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a three-carbon chain: a central quaternary carbon carries two methyl groups, a hydroxyl group, and a terminal carboxyl group. Because the central carbon is bonded to two identical methyl groups, the skeleton has a local mirror-plane symmetry, and the molecule carries no stereocenter. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups together supply two hydrogen-bond donors (the O–H of each group) and three acceptor oxygen atoms. The tertiary alcohol and the carboxyl group sit on the same carbon, giving a compact, branched arrangement.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a carboxylic acid group attached at the 3-position and a hydroxyl group attached at the 2-position, next to the ring nitrogen. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no additional ring fusion or stereocenters, and the only flexibility comes from rotation of the acid and hydroxyl groups. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (its OH) and acceptor (its carbonyl oxygen), the hydroxyl contributes another donor and acceptor, and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic carboxylic acid with a seven-carbon backbone and no rings or fused ring systems. The terminal carboxyl group (-COOH) sits at one end of the chain, and a hydroxyl group (-OH) is attached to the carbon immediately next to it, making the hydroxyl the alpha position relative to the acid. The rest of the carbon chain is saturated and unbranched, with a flexible n-alkyl tail that gives the molecule considerable rotational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond the trivial, since the two ends are chemically distinct. Both functional groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, with the carboxylic acid providing the strongest hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents: a hydroxyl group and an oxyacetic acid side chain, meaning a two-carbon unit ending in a carboxylic acid joined to the ring through an ether oxygen. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and its substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted, which gives the molecule no rotational symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The ether linkage and the CH2 group give the side chain some conformational flexibility, while the ring itself stays rigid and planar. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the phenolic OH and the carboxylic acid OH can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the two oxygens of the carboxyl group, the ether oxygen, and the phenolic oxygen can all accept one.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to the ring are two substituents on adjacent carbons, which gives an ortho substitution pattern: a hydroxyl group bearing an oxygen-linked hydrogen, and a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid. The side chain contains a flexible methylene linker between the ring and the carboxyl group, so the carboxylic acid can rotate relative to the planar aromatic core. The phenolic hydroxyl and the carboxylic acid both act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the remaining ring carbons are nonpolar. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane, because the two substituents differ in character.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion and no additional rings. A hydroxyl group is attached to the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho to the nitrogen, and the remaining four ring carbons carry hydrogens. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the O–H bond. Its symmetry is limited to a single mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.
