The molecule is built on a quinolin-2(1H)-one scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring. The second ring carries a carbonyl group adjacent to the ring nitrogen, forming a cyclic amide (lactam) that gives a conjugated, planar framework. The nitrogen bears a hydrogen, so it can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen can accept one. The fully aromatic benzo portion is unsubstituted, so the molecule has no substituents to break its shape, and the rigid fused rings make it largely flexible-free and close to planar.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered saturated ring, giving an indane skeleton. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, while the non-aromatic five-membered ring carries a single hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the benzylic CH2 that sits beside the fused ring junction. Because the fused system is largely planar and rigid, with only modest puckering in the saturated ring, the overall shape is well defined, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the hydroxyl breaks the mirror relationship. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic and aliphatic carbon framework contributes only nonpolar, hydrophobic surface.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is joined to a five-membered carbocyclic ring, creating an indanone framework. The five-membered ring contains a ketone carbonyl group that sits in the non-aromatic portion, with a methylene carbon linking it to the fused aromatic system. The benzene ring is unsubstituted, so there are no additional substituents and the ring fusion is the only structural modification of the aromatic core. The bicyclic system is largely planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility beyond minor puckering of the five-membered ring. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a para-toluenesulfonate (tosylate) ester. A p-tolyl ring, bearing a methyl group para to the sulfonyl group, is attached through a sulfonyl unit (S(=O)(=O)) to an oxygen that links to a 2-indanyl group. The indane is a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle, with the ester oxygen sitting on the saturated carbon at the 2-position. The two aromatic rings are unfused and connected only through this sulfonate ester linkage, which gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility around the S–O and C–O bonds. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an indane scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered carbocycle that carries a CH2 bridge. Its fused bicyclic core is fully aromatic on the benzene side and saturated on the cyclopentane side, which makes the ring system fairly rigid. A two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group hangs from the saturated ring. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the aromatic ring and the hydrocarbon framework contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, with the side chain attached at a single saturated carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold, with no ring fusion and no heteroatoms. Three methyl groups and one iodine atom are attached to the ring, giving a substitution pattern in which the iodine sits flanked by two methyl groups and the remaining methyl groups occupy the meta-related positions. The arrangement has a mirror plane through the iodine and the opposite ring carbon, so the molecule is symmetric in that sense. The aromatic ring and the small substituents make the structure rigid, with only the methyl rotations adding minor flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the iodine and the carbon framework do not provide suitable polar sites.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring, bearing a methyl group on one ring nitrogen and an iodine atom on the carbon between the two nitrogens. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, with the two nitrogens in a 1,3-relationship, one being an N-substituted pyrrole-type nitrogen and the other a pyridine-type nitrogen that can accept a hydrogen bond. Because the ring is not fused to any other ring and carries only two small substituents, the scaffold is compact and rigid, with essentially no rotatable bonds apart from the methyl group. The substitution pattern is asymmetric: the methyl and iodo groups occupy different positions relative to the nitrogens, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis beyond the ring plane. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited, since there is no N–H or O–H donor and the only acceptor is the unsubstituted ring nitrogen.

This molecule is a small acyclic alkane skeleton built around a single quaternary carbon. That central carbon bears three methyl groups and one iodine atom, giving it a tert-butyl-type framework with the iodine occupying the fourth position. There are no rings, ring fusions, or additional functional groups beyond the carbon-iodine bond. The arrangement has approximate threefold symmetry about the C–I axis, and the molecule is conformationally flexible only through rotation of the methyl groups. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors, since the iodine is a weak, polarizable halogen rather than a conventional acceptor.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Two substituents are attached to the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and an iodine atom, placed on adjacent carbons next to the ring nitrogen, which gives a 2-iodo-3-methoxy substitution pattern. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the methyl of the methoxy group providing rotational flexibility. The nitrogen of the ring and the oxygen of the methoxy group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. It lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ in type and position.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near-adjacent positions: a methyl group, a carboxylic acid, and an iodine atom. The carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the ring, and the iodine sits ortho to it, flanked by the carboxyl group on one side and the methyl group on the other, which creates a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the methyl and iodine groups are hydrophobic and contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, with only the carboxyl and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, a trifluoromethyl group is located para to it on the opposite side of the ring, and an iodine atom occupies the carbon adjacent to the amino group, giving an ortho-iodoaniline pattern. The trifluoromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky moiety composed of a carbon bonded to three fluorine atoms. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site, while the fluorine atoms can only weakly act as acceptors. The ring is rigid and planar, with only the amine and trifluoromethyl groups capable of rotation, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local pseudo-mirror relationship.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Four of its six ring positions carry substituents: two methyl groups, one amino group, and one iodine atom. Reading around the ring, the methyl groups sit meta to each other, the amino group sits between one methyl and the iodine, and the iodine is flanked by the amino group and a ring carbon bearing hydrogen. The arrangement lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. The primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor through its lone pair, whereas the methyl groups and iodine contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents. A nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) is attached at the carbon meta to the ring nitrogen, while an iodine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring itself is flat and fully aromatic, with no fused rings or additional stereocenters, so the scaffold is rigid and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen atoms, and the ring nitrogen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring systems. Reading the SMILES, a methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a nitro group [N+](=O)[O-] sits on a carbon meta to the methyl, and an iodine atom sits on the carbon adjacent to the methyl, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern. The scaffold is fully aromatic and planar, and the ring is rigid, while the methyl group is the only freely rotating part. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the three substituents onto one another, so it is asymmetric. The nitro group offers two oxygen atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since all ring positions beyond the substituents are occupied by C–H bonds that are not polar enough to donate meaningfully.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a primary amino group, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the other is an iodine atom, a heavy halogen that is a weak hydrogen-bond participant. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the substitution pattern is ortho, which removes any mirror symmetry beyond the planar framework and gives the molecule a lower-symmetry, asymmetric footprint. The core is rigid and planar, with the ring fixed in place, while the amino and iodo groups add only limited rotational freedom around their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bonded to one hydrogen), attached directly to the ring, and the other is an iodine atom on the neighboring carbon. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds within the core. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring, because the two substituents differ in identity. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, which carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The other substituent is an iodine atom attached directly to the ring, which contributes a large, polarizable halogen but no hydrogen-bonding capability. The aromatic scaffold is a single planar six-membered ring with no fused systems, and the substitution pattern gives the molecule only a mirror plane through the two substituents, so it has no stereocenters. The ring and the directly attached carboxyl group are rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid's C–O bonds offer limited rotational freedom.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen (double bond) and a chlorine atom, which is a strongly electrophilic, reactive functional group. The other substituent is an iodine atom attached directly to the ring at the position next to the carbonyl group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the carbonyl carbon lying in the ring plane, and the molecule has only a single rotatable bond connecting the acyl group to the ring, so conformational flexibility is minimal. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, since the two substituents differ in identity. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placing it in the ortho-disubstituted benzene family. One ring position carries a hydroxymethyl group, a methylene unit bonded to a terminal hydroxyl, which makes it a primary alcohol and a benzylic alcohol. The neighboring position carries a single iodine atom attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with no additional rings, and the molecule has no stereocenters. The flexible hydroxymethyl arm can rotate about its single bonds, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the iodine is a weak acceptor only.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two halogen-containing substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a bromomethyl group, a CH2 unit linked to the ring and terminated by a bromine atom, while the other is a directly attached iodine atom. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional rings, so the scaffold is compact and essentially planar. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, and the halogen atoms can only act as weak acceptors. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry because the two substituents differ in type and attachment, and its flexibility is limited to rotation about the single bond joining the CH2 group to the ring.

The molecule is a four-carbon acyclic alkane skeleton, specifically a butane chain bearing a single iodine atom on a secondary carbon. The carbon chain is branched at the second position, giving it a sec-butyl framework with no rings and no ring fusion. The only functional group is a carbon-iodine bond, which is a halide substituent rather than a polar heteroatom group. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the iodine sits on an asymmetric carbon bearing an ethyl and a methyl group, making it chiral with two possible configurations. It is flexible, since rotation about its single bonds is essentially free, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, as the iodine is a weak halogen acceptor rather than a conventional one.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, specifically an imidazole ring bearing a single iodine atom on the carbon between the two nitrogen atoms. The ring contains two nitrogens separated by one carbon, with one nitrogen bearing a hydrogen (an N-H) and the other as a pyridine-like nitrogen lacking one. The iodine substituent sits at the 2-position, flanked by both nitrogens, and no other substituents are present, so the skeleton is small, planar, and essentially rigid. Because the N-H can donate a hydrogen bond while the unprotonated nitrogen can accept one, the compound offers both donor and acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One ring carbon carries a hydroxyl group, so the structure contains a phenolic OH that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The neighboring ring carbon carries an iodine atom, a large, polarizable halogen that adds bulk and can participate in halogen bonding. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, and the substitution pattern leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry. Overall, it is a small, flat scaffold whose main polar feature is the single hydroxyl group.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is an isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit attached directly to the ring through nitrogen, which functions as an electrophilic carbon center and a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor at its nitrogen and sulfur atoms. The neighboring substituent is a single iodine atom, a large, polarizable halogen that contributes steric bulk and can act as a halogen-bond donor. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the overall scaffold has no hydrogen-bond donors and only a few weak acceptor sites, with limited conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the isothiocyanate group.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group attached through a methylene (CH2) spacer, which gives the side chain some rotational flexibility. The other substituent is an iodine atom directly bonded to the aromatic ring, placed next to the CH2 linker. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the iodine contributes a large, polarizable halogen atom but no hydrogen-bonding capability. Apart from the flexible CH2-COOH arm, the aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is a small saturated alkyl halide built on a three-carbon propane-type skeleton. A central carbon bears two methyl groups and a single iodine atom, so the iodine sits on a secondary carbon at the middle of the chain. There are no rings, no fused ring systems, and no other functional groups, and the molecule contains only sp3-hybridized carbons. The two methyl groups are equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror-plane symmetry through the C–I bond. Its flexibility is limited to rotation about single bonds, so it lacks any rigid framework. It has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the iodine can act only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, carrying two substituents. A primary carboxamide group (-C(=O)NH2) is attached at the carbon three positions around the ring from the nitrogen, and an iodine atom is attached at the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core. The carboxamide offers both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its NH2 group and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen, while the pyridine nitrogen serves as an additional acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is 2-iodothiophene, built on a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom. The ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with two carbon-carbon double bonds conjugated through the ring. An iodine atom is attached to a carbon directly adjacent to the sulfur, which is the only substituent and defines a monosubstituted pattern at that alpha position. The structure is small, rigid, and essentially flat, with no rotatable bonds and no symmetry beyond the local ring geometry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom is only a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a small, acyclic ether-alcohol with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple flexible chain. A two-carbon ethylene unit links an isopropyl group, attached through an ether oxygen, to a terminal hydroxyl group. The isopropyl fragment is branched, with a central carbon bearing two methyl groups, and the ether oxygen sits between that branch and the chain. There are no aromatic or fused ring systems, and the molecule is not symmetric because its two ends differ, one bearing a hydroxyl and the other a branched alkyl group. Rotation about its many single bonds makes it highly flexible. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen can act only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is an acetanilide-type compound built on a benzene ring, with an acetamide group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group and attached through its nitrogen to the ring) on one carbon. Directly adjacent to it, on the neighboring ring carbon, sits an isopropyl group, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, while the isopropyl and acetamide substituents add some conformational flexibility around their single bonds. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent positions. One substituent is an isopropyl group, attached through its central carbon, which bears two methyl branches. The neighboring position carries a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom is bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the isopropyl group adds some steric bulk beside the boron center. Because the two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, the molecule has no symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and also accept one through their oxygen atoms.

The molecule is a 2-isopropyl-substituted benzimidazole, consisting of a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imidazole ring that shares two adjacent carbons with it. The isopropyl group (a central carbon bearing two methyl groups) is attached to the carbon between the two nitrogens of the imidazole ring, giving a simple substitution pattern at that single position. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the isopropyl branch as the only flexible, non-aromatic element. One imidazole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so it acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other, unprotonated nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry axis beyond the local mirror plane of the aromatic system, because the isopropyl group is attached at a single asymmetric position.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring, bearing a single isopropyl group on one of the ring carbons. The two nitrogen atoms sit in a 1,3-relationship within the ring: one is a pyrrole-type nitrogen carrying an N-H, and the other is a pyridine-type nitrogen with a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet. The isopropyl substituent, attached through its central carbon, is a branched, flexible alkyl group, while the fused-free ring itself is planar and rigid. Because the molecule has only one substituent and the ring is unsymmetrical, the overall structure has no internal symmetry beyond the ring's own constraints. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the sp2 nitrogen lone pair serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A single isopropyl group, attached through its central carbon, is bonded to one of the carbons on the outer ring, placing the substituent at a beta position relative to the ring fusion. The molecule has no heteroatoms or polar functional groups, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl group adds a small amount of conformational freedom through rotation about its single bond to the ring. Overall the structure is asymmetric because the substituent sits on only one side of the fused system.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, giving a phenol-type functionality, while the other is an isopropyl group, a branched three-carbon alkyl unit attached through its central carbon. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the isopropyl group contributes some conformational flexibility around the ring-to-carbon bond. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane that would render all positions equivalent, since the two substituents are different in nature and placement.

This molecule is a straight-chain, saturated five-carbon dicarboxylic acid bearing a ketone. Its backbone is a flexible, acyclic chain with no ring systems or fusion, so the scaffold is fully open and rotatable. One terminal carbon carries a carboxylic acid group, and the other terminus is an alpha-keto acid unit, where a ketone sits directly adjacent to a second carboxylic acid group. The molecule has no symmetry, because the two ends differ in their functionalization. Its hydrogen-bond capability is high: both carboxyl groups can donate hydrogen bonds through their hydroxyl oxygens and accept them through their carbonyl oxygens, and the ketone oxygen provides an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is a small five-membered heteroaromatic ring built on a 1,3,4-thiadiazole scaffold, containing one sulfur and two adjacent nitrogen atoms in a planar, fully conjugated arrangement. It carries a single thiol (sulfanyl) group attached to one of the carbon atoms, and it has no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is minimal. The ring is rigid and flat, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only trivial symmetry, with the two nitrogens being the principal hydrogen-bond acceptors. The thiol hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the sulfur on the ring contributes to the electron-rich character of the aromatic system.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic imidazole ring, with no additional rings fused to it. A methyl group sits on one ring nitrogen, which makes that nitrogen a tertiary, non-hydrogen-bonding site, while the other ring nitrogen remains a pyridine-type acceptor. The carbon adjacent to the methylated nitrogen carries a thiol (sulfanyl) group, giving the molecule a thione/thiol functionality that can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and a sulfur-based acceptor. The structure is small, planar, and rigid, with only the methyl and thiol substituents able to rotate, and it lacks any symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions on the ring.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom, which places it in the thiazole family. The ring carries a single methyl group on one carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, and a thiol (sulfanyl) group on the carbon lying between the sulfur and nitrogen. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, though the methyl and thiol substituents are small and freely positioned. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiazole ring bearing a thiol group on the carbon between the sulfur and nitrogen atoms, which makes it a 2-mercaptothiazole scaffold. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon at the 4-position of the thiazole, so the two rings are joined by a single bond and can rotate relative to each other, giving moderate flexibility. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, with the thiol and the phenyl group on opposite sides of the heterocycle. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the thiazole ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall framework is largely planar and aromatic, with no stereocenters.

This molecule is a small bicyclic heteroaromatic system made of a pyridine-like six-membered ring fused to an imidazole-like five-membered ring, so it is an imidazopyridine scaffold with two nitrogen atoms in the fused core. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on the six-membered ring, and a thiol group (SH) is attached to the carbon between the two ring nitrogens in the five-membered ring. One ring nitrogen bears a hydrogen, giving a tautomeric NH that can donate a hydrogen bond, while the other ring nitrogens and the methoxy oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds. The fully aromatic, planar fused framework is rigid, with only the methoxy and thiol groups contributing rotational flexibility, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to an imidazole ring, forming a benzimidazole core. The fused rings are fully planar and aromatic, making the scaffold rigid. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) is attached to the benzene ring, and a thiol group (a sulfur bearing a hydrogen) sits at the carbon between the two imidazole nitrogens. The ring nitrogen bearing a hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other ring nitrogen and the oxygen of the methoxy group can act as acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational freedom, apart from rotation of the methoxy and thiol groups.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The benzene portion carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl group) at a position on the fused ring system, giving the molecule an aryl ether character. At the carbon between the nitrogen and sulfur of the thiazole ring sits a thiol group, which can exist in tautomeric thione form. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy methyl group contributing conformational flexibility. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen, the methoxy oxygen, and the sulfur atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom, a 1,3,4-thiadiazole scaffold. It is not fused to any other ring, so the core is a simple monocyclic heteroaromatic system. A methyl group is attached to one of the ring carbons, and a thiol (sulfanyl, -SH) group is attached to the other ring carbon, giving a 2,5-disubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the small methyl and thiol groups able to rotate. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyrimidine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms at the 1 and 3 positions, making it a diazine heterocycle. A linear propyl chain is attached to one of the ring carbons, placed meta to one ring nitrogen and para to the other. A thiol group (–SH) is bonded to the carbon sitting between the two ring nitrogens, the position typically called C2. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, apart from free rotation of the propyl chain, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two ring nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. The fused aromatic system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. A thiol group (–SH) is attached at the 2-position of the thiazole ring, between the sulfur and nitrogen atoms. A nitro group (–NO2) sits on the benzene ring, placed on the carbon that is meta to the ring fusion on the side away from the sulfur. Overall the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are at different positions. The thiol contributes a hydrogen-bond donor site, while the nitro oxygens and the thiazole nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic compound built on a quinoline scaffold, with a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring sharing a C–C bond. A methoxy group (–OCH3) sits on the benzenoid ring at a position para-like to the ring fusion, while a methyl group is attached to the pyridine-side carbon adjacent to the fusion. A thiol (–SH) group is positioned on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, giving a thiol/thione-capable heteroaromatic center. The fused system is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and thiol groups contributing limited rotational freedom. The molecule lacks symmetry because the substituents occupy different positions on the two rings. The thiol provides a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring nitrogen and methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold: a benzene ring ortho-fused to a five-membered imidazole-type ring, giving a planar benzimidazole core. The five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen (an N-H) and the other is a pyridine-like imine nitrogen. A thiol group (–SH) is attached at the carbon between the two nitrogens, located at the 2-position of the ring. Because the thiol can tautomerize with the adjacent ring nitrogen, the molecule can also be represented as a thione form. The fused system is rigid and flat, with no rotatable bonds, and the benzene ring is unsubstituted. The N-H and the thiol group serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the imine nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring sharing one carbon-carbon bond. The thiazole portion contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom, with the carbon between them bearing a thiol group, which gives the compound a free -SH substituent at the 2-position. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the thiol hydrogen. The thiol group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall the structure has only limited symmetry because the substituent sits on one side of the fused system.

This molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a benzene ring fused to a five-membered ring containing both nitrogen and oxygen, giving a benzoxazole scaffold. The two rings share an edge, making the whole framework planar, rigid, and fully aromatic. At the 2-position of the five-membered ring sits a thiol group (–SH), which is attached to the carbon flanked by the ring nitrogen and oxygen. The thiol can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen and oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single substituent on an otherwise unsubstituted benzo ring, so its overall shape is essentially two-dimensional and it is largely unbranched.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other): a hydroxymethyl group (a benzylic CH2 bearing an OH) and a thiol group (an SH attached directly to the ring). The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2-disubstituted, and the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a potential mirror plane through the ring. Its rotatable bonds around the CH2 and C–S linkages give it moderate flexibility, while the aromatic core remains rigid and planar. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the thiol contributes a weaker donor and a sulfur acceptor.

This molecule is a short, acyclic, saturated chain of two carbons bearing a hydroxyl group at one end and a thiol group at the other, so it has no rings and no fused scaffold. Its backbone is a flexible ethane-type unit, with an –OH on one carbon and an –SH on the second carbon, giving a simple linear substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two terminal groups differ, and its single-bond chain allows free rotation around each carbon–carbon and carbon–heteroatom bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thiol contributes a weaker hydrogen-bond donor capability and a modest acceptor character at sulfur.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring, bearing a thiol group. The ring contains two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, one of which carries a hydrogen and acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the other nitrogen is a pyridine-like acceptor. The thiol substituent sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens, so it is a single substituent on an otherwise unsubstituted ring. The scaffold is small, planar, and rigid, with very little conformational flexibility. Its donor and acceptor sites are located on adjacent positions of the ring, giving it a compact, polar character.

The molecule is a short, acyclic three-carbon-backbone compound: a propanoic acid chain bearing a thiol group on the alpha carbon, which is the carbon directly next to the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid (-COOH) sits at one end of the chain, and the sulfhydryl (-SH) group is attached to the adjacent carbon, which also carries a methyl group. There are no rings, so the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The molecule contains a stereocenter at the alpha carbon, so it can exist as distinct enantiomers. The carboxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thiol contributes a weaker hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or extra ring systems. A thiol (sulfanyl, –SH) group is attached directly to a ring carbon located adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is a 2-substituted pyridine. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only flexible element is the small S–H bond, giving the molecule no meaningful conformational freedom. Lacking any internal symmetry beyond the local ring geometry, the molecule has no symmetry elements that map substituents onto one another. The thiol hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen's lone pair serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the sulfur can also contribute weak acceptor character.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine-type ring in which the nitrogen atom carries a positive charge and an attached oxygen bearing a negative charge, forming an N-oxide. A sulfur-containing thiol group sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the nitrogen, giving a 2-substituted pattern with no additional fused rings. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, so the scaffold is rigid, with only the small S–H group free to rotate. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local planar arrangement of the ring.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a thiazole ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom separated by a carbon. It carries a single thiol group (–SH) attached to the carbon sitting between the sulfur and nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted at the 2-position. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat geometry with no rotatable bonds beyond the S–H bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the trivial planar mirror plane through the ring. The thiol hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom in the ring, with the carbon between them bearing an exocyclic thiocarbonyl group (C=S), which makes it a cyclic thiourea-type scaffold. The ring is saturated apart from that thiocarbonyl, and its two methylene carbons form a simple ethylene bridge linking the nitrogen to the second sulfur. There is a single ring system with no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the molecule is nearly planar and conformationally rigid. The N–H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the thiocarbonyl sulfur serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The ring sulfur is a thioether-type atom with weaker acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings or heteroatoms in the core. Three methyl groups sit on the ring at positions that leave the ring with a 2,4,6-trimethyl-type arrangement relative to the side chain, which occupies the position between two methyl groups. The side chain is a two-carbon ethyl linker terminating in a primary hydroxyl group, so the only functional group is a primary alcohol. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethanol tail retains rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic ring contributes only weak, non-polar interaction capacity.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a bicyclic aromatic system of two fused benzene rings that share a common edge. A methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) sits on one ring, and an aldehyde (formyl) group sits on the adjacent carbon of the same ring, so the two substituents are positioned next to each other. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups offering rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond its planar framework because the two substituents are not interchangeable. The ether oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) attached at the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, and the other is a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) on the neighboring carbon. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and can rotate relative to the ring, while the methoxy group adds modest conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro and methoxy groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one ring carbon, flanked by a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) on the neighboring carbon, giving an ortho relationship between these two groups. A trifluoromethoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a CF3 unit) is attached on the opposite side of the ring, meta to the methoxy. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the substituents have limited rotational freedom beyond the methyl and trifluoromethyl ends. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry plane because the three substituents are distinct. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ether oxygens and nitrile nitrogen can act as weak acceptors, while no hydrogen-bond donors are present.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a methyl group, and a sulfonamide group. The sulfonamide sits directly on the ring, and the methoxy group is on the carbon adjacent to it, so the two are ortho to each other, while the methyl group is positioned meta to the methoxy and para to the sulfonamide. The sulfonamide consists of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a free NH2 group, which provides two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptors through the oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The methoxy oxygen adds a further acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonamide and methoxy groups can rotate about their single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because of its asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring bearing three groups: a methoxy group, a methyl group, and a sulfonyl chloride group. The sulfonyl chloride sits directly on the ring, with the methoxy group positioned ortho to it and the methyl group located para to the sulfonyl group, relative to the methoxy-bearing carbon's neighbors. The aromatic core is a single rigid six-membered ring, and the sulfonyl group contributes two sulfur-oxygen double bonds and a reactive sulfur-chlorine bond. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a rough planarity of the ring, and its only rotatable bonds are the C–O bond of the methoxy group and the C–S bond to the sulfonyl group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy and sulfonyl groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group on adjacent carbons, plus a methyl group positioned para to the hydroxyl. The methoxy and hydroxyl groups sit ortho to each other, while the methyl group occupies the position across the ring from the hydroxyl, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no molecular symmetry axis beyond a local planar arrangement. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and only the methoxy methyl and the hydroxyl hydrogen provide rotational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an amino group, a methoxy group, and a nitro group, arranged so that the amino and nitro groups sit para to one another. The methoxy group is ortho to the amino group and meta to the nitro group, giving an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis beyond the flat aromatic plane. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, rigid and planar, while the methoxy oxygen-methyl bond and the nitro and amino groups can rotate modestly. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and an acceptor lone pair, the methoxy oxygen and nitro oxygens serve as acceptors, and the nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and separated positions: a methoxy group, a nitro group, and a sulfonyl chloride group. The methoxy ether sits ortho to the sulfonyl chloride, while the nitro group is positioned para to the sulfonyl chloride, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic core. The sulfonyl chloride (-SO2Cl) is a strongly electron-withdrawing, reactive functional group, and the nitro group adds further electron withdrawal to the ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational freedom, mainly around the C-O and C-S bonds. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy, nitro, and sulfonyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern: a methoxy group, a nitro group, and a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid sits directly on the ring, with the methoxy group adjacent to it and the nitro group in the meta position relative to the methoxy group and para to the acid. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion and no stereocenters. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and an acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the methoxy ether oxygen and the nitro oxygens serve as additional acceptors. The lack of symmetry makes the three substituents chemically distinct.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a nitro group, and a nitrile (cyano) group. The nitrile carbon is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the methoxy group sits on the carbon immediately adjacent to it, so these two groups are ortho to each other. The nitro group is positioned meta to the methoxy group and para to the nitrile, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the nitro and nitrile groups are both strongly electron-withdrawing, while the methoxy group is electron-donating through its oxygen. The molecule is essentially rigid, with only the methoxy methyl group providing limited rotational freedom. It has no internal symmetry, since the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The nitro oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with substituents at four positions. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one ring carbon and is adjacent to an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S), which is attached to the ring carbon next to it. A nitro group (–NO2) sits on the ring carbon that is para to the isothiocyanate. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,4-trisubstituted, with no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The aromatic core is fully rigid, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom. The nitro oxygens and the methoxy oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a trisubstituted aromatic compound with a single six-membered ring and no ring fusion. One substituent is a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond attached directly to the ring), which adds a small planar unsaturated appendage. The other two ring positions carry a hydroxyl group and a methoxy group on adjacent carbons, creating an ortho-disubstituted phenol ether pattern. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the methoxy oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited conformational flexibility, mostly from rotation of the methoxy and vinyl groups, so it is largely rigid and planar.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: a methoxy group, a trifluoromethoxy group, and an acetyl group. The acetyl group (a ketone with a methyl) is attached directly to the ring and sits ortho to the methoxy group, so the two substituents are neighbors on the aromatic core. The trifluoromethoxy group is para to the methoxy group and carries three fluorine atoms on a single carbon bridging to the ring through oxygen. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methyl and methoxy rotors add modest flexibility. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the local arrangement of its substituents. The ketone oxygen and the ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 pattern. Relative to the aldehyde carbon, a methoxy group sits at the ortho position and a trifluoromethoxy group sits at the para position on the opposite side of the ring. The aldehyde (formyl) group is an electron-withdrawing carbonyl that can accept hydrogen bonds at its oxygen, while the ether oxygens of the methoxy and trifluoromethoxy groups provide weaker acceptor sites. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups offering modest rotational freedom, and the molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond its flat ring plane.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a trifluoromethoxy group, and a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methoxy group sits adjacent to it at the ortho position, while the trifluoromethoxy group sits para to the methoxy, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The ether oxygens of the methoxy and trifluoromethoxy groups serve as additional, weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the three fluorine atoms make the trifluoromethoxy group bulky and electron-poor.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group), a primary amine group, and a trifluoromethyl group, which carries three fluorine atoms on one carbon. The amine and methoxy groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the trifluoromethyl group is positioned para to the methoxy group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only the methoxy methyl rotating. The amine group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the oxygen of the methoxy group as an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, making it a simple aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. An aldehyde group (C=O attached to a CH) sits on one ring carbon, a methoxy group (O-CH3) occupies the ortho position relative to it, and a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) sits para to the methoxy group. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,4 across the ring, which leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde groups can rotate about their single bonds to a modest degree. The oxygen atoms of the aldehyde and methoxy groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a carboxylic acid. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methoxy group sits on the carbon adjacent to it, making the arrangement ortho to the acid. The trifluoromethyl group is located para to the methoxy group and meta to the acid, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and carboxyl groups rotate with some freedom. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ether oxygen of the methoxy group acts as an acceptor, and the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group are weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a nitrile. The ring is a single, unfused aromatic six-membered system, so the scaffold is planar and rigid. The nitrile carbon is directly attached to the ring, and the methoxy oxygen sits ortho to it, while the trifluoromethyl group is positioned para to the methoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-substitution pattern. The aryl ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Its overall shape has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ and are arranged asymmetrically on the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group (an ether, -OCH3), a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3), and a bromomethyl group (-CH2Br), arranged so the methoxy and bromomethyl groups sit on adjacent carbons and the trifluoromethyl group is positioned para to the methoxy group. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the structure is essentially planar at the ring with flexible rotation around the benzylic CH2–Br and ether bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different. The oxygen of the methoxy group can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are attached to carbon.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a methyl group, and a hydroxyl group, arranged on a single six-membered aromatic ring with no fused rings. The hydroxyl group sits ortho to the methoxy group, and the methyl group sits para to the methoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. Because the three substituents are not all alike, the molecule has no symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring, which passes through the substituent positions. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyl and methoxy groups can accept them. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group and hydroxyl group can rotate somewhat about their bonds to the ring.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on the ring in a 1,2,4-pattern: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), a primary amino group on the carbon directly beside it, and a nitro group located across the ring from the amine. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing, while the amino and methoxy groups are electron-donating, so the ring carries contrasting electronic character. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane because the three substituents are all different, and the aromatic core is rigid while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, and the oxygens of the nitro and methoxy groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a methoxy group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methoxy group sits on the carbon adjacent to it, so the two are ortho to each other. The nitro group is positioned para to the methoxy group, giving the ring a trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and methoxy groups have limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, the nitro group and methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors beyond the acidic hydroxyl.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and a nitro group located para to the methoxy group. This gives a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion and no stereocenters. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group contributes a small degree of rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the methoxy oxygen is a weaker acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a plane through the ring, since the three substituents are distinct.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group and to the ring. The other is a formyl group, a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and attached to a hydrogen, placing an aldehyde at the position next to the ether oxygen. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, while the molecule as a whole is fairly rigid with only modest rotational freedom around the bonds connecting the substituents to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the two substituents onto each other, since they differ in identity. Its hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the oxygen atoms can act as acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group), attached through the oxygen as an ether linkage to the ring. The other is a carboxamide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a primary amine nitrogen. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, while the methoxy methyl and amide nitrogen contribute modest conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring. The amide group provides two hydrogen-bond donors (the N–H bonds) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the ether oxygen offers an additional weak acceptor site.

The molecule is a phenyl ring bearing two adjacent substituents, making it a 1,2-disubstituted benzene. One position carries a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group), and the neighboring position carries a boronic acid group, in which a boron atom is bonded to two hydroxyl groups. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the scaffold is rigid, while the methoxy and boronic acid groups have some rotational freedom around their single bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ortho arrangement of its two substituents. Its hydrogen-bond capability is dual: the two hydroxyl hydrogens can act as donors, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the methoxy ether can act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), and the other is a carbohydrazide-type acyl group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to an amide nitrogen that carries a free terminal amino group. The aryl ring is fully aromatic and planar, while the hydrazide chain is flexible and can rotate around its single bonds. The amide N–H and the terminal NH2 act as hydrogen-bond donors, whereas the carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ in both size and chemical character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent (ortho) substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings, giving the scaffold a flat, rigid core. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two substituents are not symmetrically placed, so the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the local arrangement. The methoxy and carboxyl groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds, adding modest flexibility to an otherwise planar aromatic framework.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two separate benzene rings. One ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) on the carbon directly adjacent to the carbonyl attachment point, placing it at the ortho position. The other ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the methoxy oxygen can also act as a weak acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Because the two aromatic rings are joined through a single sp2 carbonyl carbon, the scaffold is non-fused and moderately flexible, with rotation possible around the bonds linking the rings to the ketone. The molecule lacks any symmetry because of the single substituent on one ring.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a 2-methoxybiphenyl scaffold. One ring carries a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on the carbon adjacent to the inter-ring bond, so the substitution is ortho to the linkage on that ring, while the second ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are not fused; they are connected by a rotatable single bond, and steric crowding from the ortho methoxy group restricts that rotation and favors a twisted, non-coplanar arrangement. The molecule has no stereocenters and lacks a plane of symmetry through the whole structure because of the single substituent. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small, open-chain organic acid built on a four-carbon backbone with no rings and no fused systems. A carboxylic acid group sits at one end, providing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen). The central carbon carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen acting as an additional acceptor), and it is joined to the terminal carbon by a carbon-carbon double bond with a defined (E/Z) geometry, which makes the chain rigid at that point. The remaining single bonds allow some conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic ether with a linear, two-carbon-unit backbone: a methyl group bonded to oxygen, followed by a two-carbon chain, another oxygen, and a terminal two-carbon ethyl segment. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated centers, so the scaffold is simply a flexible chain of single bonds. The two ether oxygens are the only functional groups, and the substitution pattern is symmetric about the central ethylene unit, with the two terminal methyl groups mirroring each other. Because all bonds are freely rotatable, the molecule is highly flexible and adopts multiple conformers. Each ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, flexible structure built on a two-carbon ethylene chain. One terminus bears a methyl ether group, forming a methoxy substituent, while the other terminus carries a primary amine. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic systems, so the scaffold is simply a linear chain with a single heteroatom ether oxygen positioned between the methyl group and the ethyl backbone. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry aside from the near-linear arrangement, and its many rotatable single bonds give it considerable conformational flexibility. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair for acceptance, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group and two hydroxyl groups, arranged as a 1,2,4-pattern, which is a trisubstituted aromatic scaffold with a single six-membered ring and no ring fusion. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, so the core is rigid, while the methoxy group adds a small, rotatable ether linkage. The two phenolic hydroxyl groups, one adjacent to the methoxy group and one para to the other hydroxyl, make the structure asymmetric, since the three substituents are not equivalent. Each hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings fused together by sharing a common edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A single methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one of the outer carbons of the ring system, placing the substituent at a beta position rather than at the fusion point. The fused rings are rigid and planar, while the methoxy group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The oxygen atom of the ether can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure has only a loose approximation of symmetry, since the substituent breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent naphthalene skeleton.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) attached to the carbon directly next to the ring nitrogen, while the other is a carboxylic acid group attached to the neighboring carbon. The ortho arrangement of these groups places them close together, so the carboxylic acid and methoxy groups can interact through their oxygen atoms. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (its oxygen atoms), while the ring nitrogen and methoxy oxygen serve as additional acceptors. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid because of its aromatic core, with only the methoxy and carboxyl groups offering rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents on neighboring carbons, which makes it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a hydroxyl group attached directly to the ring, giving it a phenolic character, and the other is a methoxy group, an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group, which is an ether linkage to the ring. The benzene core is a single fused-free aromatic ring with no additional ring fusion, so the scaffold is compact and planar. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group can only accept one. Overall, the structure is fairly rigid, with only the rotatable bonds of the two substituents providing flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent oxygen substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), and the other is an ether oxygen linked to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the oxyacetic acid side chain provides rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens. The ether and methoxy oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because of the asymmetric arrangement of its two different oxygenated substituents.

The molecule is an aryl ester built from two benzene rings joined through a carboxylate linkage. One ring is a benzoyl group, with the carbonyl carbon attached directly to the phenyl ring, and the other is a phenyl ring bearing a methoxy group at the position ortho to the ester oxygen. The ester functionality, a carbonyl bonded to a bridging oxygen, is the central connecting unit and gives the molecule a rigid, extended shape with two aromatic faces. Because the two rings are not fused, the scaffold is flexible about the ester and ether linkages, though the planar aromatic rings limit overall conformational freedom. The molecule has no overall symmetry, since the two aryl groups carry different substituents. For hydrogen bonding, it has no donor groups, while the carbonyl oxygen, the ester oxygen, and the methoxy oxygen can each act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, forming an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), which contributes an ether oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other is a two-carbon side chain ending in a carboxylic acid, which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and a strong acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl groups. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker and the methoxy group add some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen atom bonded to a methyl group) attached directly to the ring, which contributes an ether functional group. The other is a cyanomethyl chain, a methylene linker ending in a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond). The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methylene linker and methoxy group provide some rotational flexibility. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the position next to the ring nitrogen, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on the neighboring carbon. The aromatic pyridine core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is flat and rigid, with the substituents adding only limited conformational freedom around their single bonds. The ring nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid serve as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a possible planar arrangement of its atoms.

This molecule is a naphthoquinone-type scaffold: a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered ring bearing two carbonyl groups. The two carbonyls sit on adjacent carbons of the non-aromatic ring, forming a 1,4-dione arrangement across a C=C double bond, and a methyl group is attached to one of the alkene carbons. The fused ring system is planar and rigid, with the aromatic benzo portion contributing extended conjugation with the enedione unit. Because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the ring, the molecule has no internal mirror plane through the substituted side. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small, acyclic hydrocarbon built on a four-carbon chain with no rings. It contains a terminal alkyne (a carbon-carbon triple bond at one end) and a terminal alkene bearing a methyl group on the same internal carbon, so the central carbon is sp2-hybridized and carries both an exocyclic double bond and a methyl branch. The molecule has no heteroatoms, no hydrogen-bond donors, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors. Its structure is essentially linear around the alkyne with a planar, branched region at the alkene, giving it limited conformational flexibility and no meaningful symmetry.

The molecule is an acyclic five-carbon alkene built on a linear chain with no rings and no heteroatoms, so its scaffold is purely aliphatic hydrocarbon. A terminal carbon-carbon double bond sits at one end, and the second carbon of that double bond carries a methyl branch, giving the skeleton a 2-methyl-1-butene pattern. Because the molecule contains only carbon and hydrogen with no polar functional groups beyond the alkene, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. Its chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and the structure lacks any internal symmetry because the branch sits on one end of the double bond only.

The molecule is a short, unbranched-chain alkene built on a six-carbon backbone with no rings. A terminal double bond (C=C) sits at one end, and the second carbon of that double bond carries a methyl branch, so the skeleton is a 2-methyl-substituted hex-1-ene framework. The chain is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds along the saturated segment, while the alkene carbon restricts rotation at one terminus. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it cannot act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor either, and it lacks any symmetry beyond trivial local features.

The molecule is built on a simple acyclic chain with a single benzene ring attached. A quaternary-type carbon bears two methyl groups and one hydroxyl group, making it a tertiary alcohol, and it connects through a methylene linker to a phenyl ring. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted, a plain monosubstituted benzene with no fused rings and no additional heteroatoms. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic ring offers only weak pi-based interactions. The chain has several rotatable single bonds, so the molecule is fairly flexible, and it lacks any element of symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the two equivalent methyl groups.

The molecule is built around a six-membered morpholine ring, a saturated heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by carbon atoms. At the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen sits a quaternary center bearing both a methyl group and a para-tolyl ring, a benzene ring carrying a methyl substituent opposite the point of attachment. The ring nitrogen is a secondary amine, providing one hydrogen-bond donor and a basic lone pair that also acts as an acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring and the fused-like geometry of the quaternary carbon give the scaffold a moderately rigid core, though the saturated morpholine ring retains some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the quaternary carbon is stereogenic and the substituents differ.

This molecule is a small, acyclic, saturated aliphatic diol built on a five-carbon chain. A methyl-bearing secondary carbon carries one hydroxyl group, and a quaternary carbon at the far end carries a second hydroxyl group flanked by two methyl groups, giving a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern on one terminus. Because the backbone is fully saturated and contains no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems, the structure is flexible with rotatable single bonds along the chain. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond local rotational freedom, since the two hydroxyl-bearing carbons sit in different environments. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two can potentially interact with one another intramolecularly.

This molecule is a tricyclic saturated hydrocarbon cage, specifically an adamantane-type framework with a single methyl group and a tertiary hydroxyl group attached to one bridgehead-adjacent carbon. The skeleton is built from three fused cyclohexane-like rings sharing bridging carbons, giving a rigid, strain-free three-dimensional scaffold with no double bonds or aromatic rings. The only functional group is the hydroxyl, which sits on a quaternary carbon also bearing the methyl group, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry. The rigid cage limits conformational flexibility to very little. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs, while the remaining hydrocarbon framework contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a small, fully saturated acyclic alcohol built on a linear chain of carbon atoms, with no ring systems or fused scaffolds. A hydroxyl group sits on a tertiary carbon, which carries two methyl groups and an ethyl group, so the substitution pattern is branched and the oxygen-bearing carbon is quaternary-like in its connectivity.
