The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis of note, though the two methyl groups on the central carbon are equivalent. Its single-bonded framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility around the carbon-carbon bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is built on a simple, acyclic four-carbon chain with no rings and no heteroatoms, so its scaffold is purely hydrocarbon. A carbon-carbon double bond sits near the middle of the chain, with a methyl group on each end of that double bond, giving a fully substituted alkene in which both sides of the double bond carry two carbons. Because the molecule contains no functional groups beyond this alkene, it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors. The structure is flexible, since the single bonds along the chain can rotate, while the double bond holds the immediate carbon framework rigidly planar. The arrangement is symmetric about the central double bond, which lends the molecule a near-mirror-plane character.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,3-relationship, with a saturated ethylene bridge (two CH2 groups) joining them, forming a 2-imidazoline scaffold. A methyl group is attached to the carbon that sits between the two nitrogens, and that carbon is double-bonded to one of the ring nitrogens, creating a cyclic amidine-type C=N unit. The ring has no fused partners and no stereocenters, so the structure is compact, nearly planar in its unsaturated part, and relatively rigid. The imine-type nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the ring NH is an available donor, giving the molecule both donor and acceptor capability.

The molecule is built on a small acyclic carbon skeleton: a central quaternary carbon bearing a methyl group, two hydroxymethyl arms, and a nitro group. There are no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system, and the molecule is flexible about its single bonds. The nitro group is attached directly to the central carbon and is drawn as a charge-separated N-oxide-type unit, while each hydroxymethyl arm carries a terminal primary alcohol. The two hydroxyl groups make the molecule a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitro oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two CH2OH arms are chemically equivalent, giving the molecule a local mirror-type symmetry about the C–CH3 and C–NO2 axis.

This molecule is a small, acyclic tertiary alcohol with a fully saturated carbon skeleton and no ring systems. The central carbon bears a hydroxyl group along with two methyl substituents and a n-propyl chain, so it can be read as a pentane-type chain with the hydroxyl on the second carbon. Because there are no double bonds or rings, the molecule is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. It contains one hydroxyl group that can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and lone pairs, while the hydrocarbon portions are nonpolar. The branching at the carbinol carbon gives it a compact, asymmetric shape lacking any element of rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built around a six-membered morpholine-type ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom at positions separated by two carbons on each side. A quaternary carbon sits adjacent to the ring oxygen, bearing both a methyl group and a phenyl ring, which creates a stereocenter and a bulky, three-dimensional substitution pattern. The phenyl group is a simple unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to that carbon, contributing aromatic character and conformational bulk. The secondary amine nitrogen in the ring can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only. The saturated ring gives the core moderate conformational flexibility, with the bulky aryl and methyl groups favoring a defined local geometry.

The molecule is a small five-membered heterocycle built around a single ring containing one sulfur atom and one nitrogen atom. The nitrogen is part of a carbon-nitrogen double bond within the ring, forming an imine-type (C=N) unit, and the carbon bearing this double bond carries a methyl substituent. The remaining two ring carbons are saturated methylene groups linking the nitrogen to the sulfur, so the ring is a non-aromatic thiazoline-type system with no fused rings. The molecule has no stereocenters and no meaningful symmetry beyond the planar ring, and its small, largely rigid ring offers little conformational flexibility. The imine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors since it contains no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a methyl group, a primary amino group, and a trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, so the scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with the methyl and trifluoromethyl groups flanking the ring carbon that bears the amine. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a weak acceptor through its lone pair, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl group can act only as weak acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial local symmetry of the methyl and CF3 groups. Overall it is a compact, relatively rigid aromatic structure with limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group, a nitrile group, and a trifluoromethyl group, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The nitrile (C≡N) is a linear, strongly polar group that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen, while the trifluoromethyl group is a bulky, electron-withdrawing group with three fluorine atoms that are weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the only hydrogens are aromatic C–H and methyl C–H. Its skeleton is largely planar and rigid, with only the methyl and trifluoromethyl rotors providing limited conformational freedom, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents in a fully substituted pattern: a methyl group, a carboxylic acid, two nitro groups, and one remaining aromatic C–H. Reading around the ring, the methyl and carboxylic acid sit on adjacent carbons, a nitro group occupies the position meta to the acid, and the second nitro group sits ortho to the methyl on the other side. The scaffold is therefore a single planar aromatic ring with no fused rings and no stereocenters, giving it a rigid, flat framework with only limited rotational freedom in the carboxyl and nitro groups. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the ring, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the two nitro groups act as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule has a short, acyclic carbon skeleton built from a terminal vinyl group attached to a single quaternary carbon that bears two methyl substituents. That same quaternary carbon also carries a hydroxyl group, making it a tertiary alcohol with a carbon-carbon double bond at the chain end. There are no ring systems or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and branched at one center. The molecule has a simple substitution pattern with the two methyls being equivalent, giving it local symmetry around the quaternary carbon. Its low number of heavy atoms and rotatable bonds means it is quite flexible and conformationally unconstrained. The single hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the alkene contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a small, acyclic tertiary propargylic alcohol built around a three-carbon chain. A terminal alkyne (carbon-carbon triple bond at one end) is directly bonded to a quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups and a hydroxyl group. The molecule contains no rings, so its scaffold is entirely open-chain and fairly compact. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the alkyne's terminal C–H is a weak donor and the triple bond offers a region of electron density. The gem-dimethyl substitution makes the molecule highly symmetric about the axis running through the carbinol carbon, and the rigid linear alkyne limits conformational flexibility at one end.

The molecule is a small aromatic heterocycle built on a five-membered furan ring, with a methyl group on one ring carbon and a carboxylic acid group on the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents sit next to each other. The furan core is planar and fully unsaturated, containing one oxygen atom in the ring, and the only rotatable bond is the one linking the carboxylic acid to the ring, which gives the molecule modest flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring oxygen acts as a weak additional acceptor. The structure has no symmetry elements beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, because the substituents are not identical and are arranged asymmetrically.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a primary amino group on the carbon next to it, and a nitro group on the carbon adjacent to the methyl on the other side, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl group is the only freely rotating part. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept through its lone pair, whereas the nitro group contributes two oxygen atoms that act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. Moving around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) sits on one carbon, a methyl group sits on the immediate neighbor, and a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, one charge-separated) sits on the carbon adjacent to the methyl on the other side. This gives a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern across the aromatic ring. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond beyond the methyl groups, so it is essentially rigid and planar, with limited conformational flexibility. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy and nitro groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a methyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and a nitro group. The carboxylic acid is attached to the ring at one position, with the methyl group on the neighboring carbon and the nitro group on the carbon on the other side of the methyl, so the three substituents sit together in a crowded cluster. The nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing group with two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (its oxygen atoms). The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl group is a small nonpolar substituent with no hydrogen-bonding capability, and the molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent positions: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a nitro group. Reading the SMILES, the methyl group sits at one carbon, the hydroxyl at the neighboring carbon, and the nitro group at the carbon flanking the methyl on the other side, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern with no additional rings or fused systems. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, though the methyl and hydroxyl groups can rotate about their bonds. Because the substituents are all on one side of the ring with no symmetry element through the molecule, the structure is asymmetric. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, while the oxygens of the nitro group are hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions: a methyl group, an isocyanate group (–N=C=O), and a nitro group (–NO2). Reading the SMILES, the methyl carbon sits at one ring position, the isocyanate is on the adjacent carbon, and the nitro group is on the carbon next to the methyl on the opposite side, giving a contiguous 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional ring systems, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only limited rotational freedom about the substituent bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three different groups occupy non-equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro and isocyanate groups and the isocyanate nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring carrying three substituents: an acetamide group (an acetyl group bonded through nitrogen to the ring), a nitro group, and a methyl group. The acetamide nitrogen is attached at one ring carbon, the nitro group sits para to it on the opposite side of the ring, and the methyl group occupies the position ortho to the acetamide. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is essentially planar apart from the rotatable amide and nitro linkages. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. A methyl group and an amino group sit on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-toluidine-type arrangement, while a nitro group is placed on the ring carbon that is meta to the methyl and para to the amino group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional ring systems. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N–H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, whereas the nitro group contributes two strong oxygen acceptor sites and no donor capability. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are all different, and its only meaningful flexibility comes from the rotation of the nitro group and the amino group about their bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a nitro group, and a carboxylic acid, arranged on the aromatic core. The carboxylic acid sits at one position, with the methyl group on the adjacent carbon, and the nitro group located on the opposite side of the ring relative to the carboxyl. This gives a substitution pattern in which the acid and the nitro group are para-like to one another across the ring. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational symmetry beyond the simple rotation of the methyl and carboxyl groups. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro group contributes two oxygen acceptor sites.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a nitro group, and an isocyanate group (N=C=O). The ring is aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion. The methyl and isocyanate groups sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other), while the nitro group is positioned meta to the methyl and para to the isocyanate, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid, though the isocyanate linear geometry and the rotatable bonds to the methyl and nitro groups add limited flexibility. The nitro group is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the isocyanate nitrogen carries no hydrogen.

The molecule is a substituted thiazole: a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. A methyl group sits on the carbon between the sulfur and the nitrogen, while a phenyl ring is attached to the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, making the two rings directly bonded, with a single rotatable bond between them that allows some conformational flexibility. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted and planar, and the overall scaffold is largely flat and aromatic, with no stereocenters and no chiral features. The thiazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. Overall the structure is a compact, asymmetric biaryl-type heteroaromatic system.

The molecule is a substituted aniline built on a single benzene ring, with an amino group, a methyl group, and a trifluoromethyl group attached around the ring. The amino group sits on one carbon, the methyl group on the adjacent carbon, and the trifluoromethyl group on the carbon para to the methyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstitution pattern. The trifluoromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky, three-fluorine substituent that is conformationally fixed relative to the ring. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair that can act as an acceptor, while the fluorine atoms contribute weak acceptor character. Overall the scaffold is a rigid, planar aromatic core with only limited flexibility, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are in different positions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a carboxylic acid, which together make it a substituted benzoic acid. The carboxylic acid carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the methyl group sits on the adjacent (ortho) position relative to it. The trifluoromethyl group is located para to the methyl group and meta to the carboxylic acid, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, whereas the trifluoromethyl group is a weak acceptor and the methyl group contributes no hydrogen bonding.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered pyrazole-type ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving an indazole scaffold. The nitrogen at position 1 of the five-membered ring carries a methyl group, so the fused system is an N-methylated indazole. A nitro group sits on the benzene ring, para to the ring-fusion carbon bearing the pyrazole nitrogen, which places it on the carbocyclic side of the fused framework. The fully aromatic, planar fused rings make the core rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, single-axis orientation of the nitro group. The nitro group's oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the remaining ring nitrogen can also accept hydrogen bonds, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors because the only nitrogen bearing a hydrogen position has been methylated.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a primary amino group, and a nitro group, arranged so the amine sits ortho to the methyl and the nitro group sits para to the methyl and meta to the amine, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any rotational symmetry, so it has no symmetry element beyond the planar ring itself. Its scaffold is essentially rigid and planar, with only the bond rotations of the methyl and nitro groups adding minor flexibility. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and its nitrogen lone pair acts as an acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a nitro group, and a sulfonyl chloride group. The sulfonyl chloride is attached to the ring through a sulfur atom that is doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, creating a tetrahedral sulfur centre. The nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formal positive charge on the nitrogen and one negative charge on an oxygen, sits para to the methyl group relative to the sulfonyl attachment. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,4 on the aromatic ring, which lacks any molecular symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the substituents add limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the two sulfonyl oxygens and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents, arranged in a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one drawn as charge-separated) sits para to the methyl, and a carboxylic acid group sits ortho to the methyl on the adjacent carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the substituents rotate only modestly around their single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents on adjacent and separated positions. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing a formal positive charge and two oxygens, one negatively charged) sits para to the methyl, and a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) sits ortho to the methyl on the adjacent carbon. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is planar and rigid. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three substituents differ and are placed asymmetrically. The nitro and nitrile groups are both strong electron-withdrawing acceptors, and the nitrogen of the nitrile and the oxygens of the nitro group can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered thiazole ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving a benzothiazole scaffold. The thiazole ring contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom, with a methyl group attached to the carbon between them at the 2-position. A nitro group is attached to the benzene ring, positioned on the carbon meta to the ring fusion nitrogen side, which places it on the far side of the fused system. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and nitro substituents. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitro oxygens also serve as acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a nitro group, and a hydroxyl group. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. The hydroxyl group sits directly beside the methyl group, while the nitro group occupies the position para to the methyl group, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitro group, with its two oxygens, is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond what the ring geometry imposes.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying three substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern: a methyl group, a nitro group, and an isocyanate group. The methyl and isocyanate groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the nitro group is positioned para to the methyl group. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the isocyanate group (N=C=O) is linear and attached through nitrogen, so the molecule has no internal rotational symmetry and little conformational flexibility. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing feature, and the isocyanate carbon is an electrophilic site. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group and the isocyanate group, along with the isocyanate nitrogen, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic furan ring, which is a single oxygen-containing heterocycle. Attached to the furan is a phenyl ring connected directly to one carbon of the furan, giving a biaryl-type linkage with no bridging atoms, so the two aromatic rings are conjugated and largely planar. The furan also carries a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen and a carboxylic acid group on the carbon next to the methyl, producing a contiguous substitution pattern on one side of the ring. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the furan oxygen acts as a weak acceptor. Overall the structure is rigid and largely flat, with the only notable flexibility arising from rotation about the single bond joining the two rings.

This molecule is a biaryl compound built from two aromatic rings joined by a single bond. One ring is a five-membered thiophene containing a sulfur atom, bearing a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the sulfur. The other ring is a simple unsubstituted benzene ring attached at the thiophene carbon opposite the methyl group, giving a 2,5-disubstituted thiophene pattern. Both rings are fully aromatic and planar, and the bond linking them is rotatable, so the molecule is largely rigid with modest conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the thiophene sulfur is at most a weak acceptor, so overall hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and nearby carbons, giving it a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methyl group and an amino group sit next to each other, and a nitro group sits on the carbon flanking the amino group on the other side, so the amino group is flanked by the methyl and nitro groups. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing, and the arrangement places it in conjugation with the ring. The overall shape is essentially flat and rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the methyl group and the nitro and amino groups. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and near positions. A methyl group and a carboxylic acid group sit ortho to each other, and a nitro group is positioned ortho to the carboxylic acid on the other side, giving a crowded, fully substituted aromatic core. The ring itself is planar and aromatic with no ring fusion, and the bulky neighboring groups restrict rotation around their bonds, so the scaffold is fairly rigid. The molecule lacks symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro group and the carbonyl oxygen contribute additional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites.

The molecule is a benzoxazole, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered oxazole ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom. A methyl group sits on the carbon of the oxazole ring between the oxygen and the nitrogen, at the 2-position. A nitro group is attached to the benzene ring, para to the ring nitrogen's fusion position on the carbocyclic side, giving a single substitution on the fused aromatic system. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl and nitro groups. The molecule lacks symmetry because the nitro group breaks the mirror relationship of the bicycle. The ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic aromatic heterocycle built on a quinoline scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge that contains the nitrogen-adjacent carbon. A methyl group sits on the pyridine ring adjacent to the nitrogen, and a nitro group is attached to the benzenoid ring at a position remote from the fusion. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds apart from the nitro and methyl substituents. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The nitro group contributes additional acceptor oxygens, and the substitution pattern leaves the molecule without any internal symmetry.

This molecule is a quinoline, a bicyclic aromatic scaffold made of a benzene ring fused to a pyridine ring through a shared edge. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen in the pyridine-type ring, which makes the nitrogen-bearing ring the site of that substitution. A nitro group is attached to the benzo-fused ring at the position next to the ring-fusion carbon that is bonded to the nitrogen, so the two substituents lie close together on opposite sides of the fused system. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the core. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygens are additional acceptor sites and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically across the bicycle.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: an acetamido group (an acetyl group bonded through nitrogen to the ring, giving a secondary amide) and a methyl group. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the substitution pattern is ortho, and the ring has no internal symmetry plane that would make the two groups equivalent. The amide N-H can donate a hydrogen bond, while the amide carbonyl oxygen can accept one. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, though the single bonds to the amide and methyl groups allow some rotation.

The molecule is built on an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused six-membered rings in a linear arrangement, with the central ring bearing two carbonyl groups at the 9 and 10 positions. One outer benzene ring carries a single methyl substituent positioned meta to the ring fusion, breaking the otherwise symmetric framework. The fused aromatic system is essentially planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility. The two ketone oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens are aromatic C–H or methyl C–H.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings, carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a methyl group, and the other is a boronic acid group, meaning a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. Because the methyl and boronic acid groups sit next to each other on the ring, the substitution pattern is ortho. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid unit can rotate about the bond to the ring, giving the molecule modest flexibility. Its two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and also accept one, so the molecule offers two hydrogen-bond donors and two acceptors in total, though it lacks any overall symmetry.

The molecule is a diarylmethanol, built from a central tetrahedral carbon that bears a hydroxyl group and is bonded to two separate benzene rings. One ring carries a methyl group on the carbon directly adjacent to the attachment point, placing it at the ortho position, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are not fused and connect to the sp3 carbon by single bonds, so the framework is non-planar and has considerable conformational flexibility around those bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic pi systems offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered imidazole ring through two adjacent carbon atoms. The imidazole portion contains one pyridine-like nitrogen, which has a lone pair available for hydrogen-bond acceptance, and one pyrrole-like nitrogen bearing a hydrogen, which can act as a hydrogen-bond donor. A methyl group sits on the carbon between the two imidazole nitrogens, giving the molecule a single substituent with no additional functional groups on the fused benzo ring. The bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with essentially no rotatable bonds apart from the methyl group. Its overall arrangement lacks any symmetry because the methyl group and the NH sit on different sides of the imidazole ring.

This molecule is a benzothiophene, a bicyclic aromatic system in which a five-membered thiophene ring is fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. The sulfur atom sits in the five-membered ring, and the carbon bearing the methyl group is adjacent to that sulfur, placing the substituent at the 2-position of the thiophene portion. The only functional group is this single methyl substituent on an otherwise unsubstituted fused framework. The fully aromatic, planar skeleton is essentially rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group's free rotation. The molecule lacks hydrogen-bond donors, and its sulfur atom provides only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone built from two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group, giving a benzophenone-type scaffold with no fused or bridged ring systems. One ring carries a single methyl substituent at the position adjacent to the carbonyl-bearing carbon, so the substitution pattern is ortho on that ring and unsubstituted on the other. Because the two aryl rings are not symmetric about the ketone, the molecule has no overall mirror or rotational symmetry beyond local planarity of each ring. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The two aryl rings can rotate about their bonds to the carbonyl carbon, so the framework is moderately flexible rather than rigid.

The molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a five-membered thiazole ring is fused to a benzene ring, giving a flat, fully conjugated benzothiazole scaffold. The thiazole ring carries a methyl group on the carbon between the nitrogen and sulfur atoms, while a hydroxyl group sits on the benzene ring, para-related to the ring nitrogen's attachment side. Because the fused framework is rigid and planar, the molecule has little conformational flexibility and only the small rotation of the hydroxyl group and methyl group. Its hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the thiazole nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall structure lacks any symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of the substituents.

The molecule is a 2-methylbenzothiazole, built from a bicyclic fused scaffold in which a benzene ring is joined to a five-membered thiazole ring that contains one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. The two rings share a common edge, making the system flat and fully aromatic, so the framework is rigid with essentially no rotatable bonds. A single methyl group is attached to the carbon sitting between the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the thiazole ring, which is the only substituent and gives the molecule no internal symmetry beyond its planar outline. The ring nitrogen has a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups because it carries no N–H or O–H bonds.

The molecule is a 2-methylbenzoxazole, built from a benzene ring fused to a five-membered oxazole ring. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the benzene portion bearing four unsubstituted aromatic CH positions. The oxazole ring contains an oxygen atom and a nitrogen atom separated by the carbon that carries a methyl group, which sits at the 2-position between them. The ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the ring oxygen contributes weaker acceptor character and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any stereocenters or rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group, giving it a compact, flat geometry with only partial symmetry across the fused ring plane.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which is a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. Two groups are attached to adjacent carbons of that ring, making the substitution pattern ortho: a methyl group on one carbon and a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 bearing an OH) on the next. The hydroxyl group is the only functional group present, so the molecule behaves as a primary alcohol with one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the CH2–OH arm has rotational freedom around its single bonds. The overall structure lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused partners. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, which makes the substitution pattern ortho: one is a methyl group and the other is a bromomethyl group, a CH2 linker carrying a bromine atom. The ring is fully planar and rigid, while the bromomethyl arm offers some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two substituents differ. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only polar feature is the carbon–bromine bond, so it offers essentially no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability in the classic sense.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which is a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A methyl group and a chloromethyl group, the latter bearing a chlorine atom on a CH2 unit, are attached to adjacent carbons of the ring, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The chloromethyl carbon is sp3-hybridized and freely rotatable, so the molecule is only modestly flexible, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The structure has no stereocenters and no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the two substituents. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only heteroatom is the chlorine, which can act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and a phosphonomethyl group on adjacent (ortho) carbons, giving a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ring is a single, unfused six-membered aromatic system with no additional rings. The phosphorus center is a phosphonic acid unit, bearing a double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups, attached to the ring through a flexible one-carbon CH2 linker. The two hydroxyl groups and the P=O oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the aromatic ring and methyl group contribute only hydrophobic character. Apart from rotation about the single bonds of the linker and the acidic hydroxyls, the framework is largely rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the two ring substituents differ.

This molecule is 2-methylbiphenyl, built from two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond, giving a biphenyl scaffold. Each ring is a fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fusion, and the two rings are linked at one carbon apiece. A methyl group sits on the ortho position of one ring, adjacent to the biaryl bond, which creates steric crowding around that linkage. The molecule has no heteroatoms and no functional groups beyond the alkyl substituent, so it offers no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The biaryl bond allows rotation between the rings, though the ortho methyl restricts that rotation and favors a twisted, non-coplanar arrangement. Overall the structure is aromatic, nonpolar, and lacks any symmetry that would make the two rings equivalent.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane skeleton in which two carbons are oxidized to ketone carbonyls, making it a cyclic 1,3-dione arrangement with the two C=O groups separated by a single intervening carbon. A methyl group is attached to the ring carbon that sits between the two carbonyls, so that carbon is the substituted position and it bears one hydrogen. The ring is saturated apart from the two carbonyl double bonds, which gives it moderate conformational flexibility, with the chair-like ring able to interconvert. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the ring. The two ketone oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single saturated six-membered carbocyclic ring, with no fused or bridged ring systems. The ring carries a ketone group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to two ring carbons, which makes the molecule a cyclic ketone. A methyl group is attached to a ring carbon directly adjacent to the carbonyl carbon, so the substitution pattern is an alpha-methyl substituent on the ketone. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the ring. The ring is conformationally flexible and can interconvert between chair-like forms. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a small, saturated five-membered carbocycle, a cyclopentane-1,3-dione core with no fused or bridged rings. Two ketone carbonyl groups sit at ring positions 1 and 3 of the cyclopentane skeleton, separated by a single methylene carbon, and a methyl group is attached to the carbon between them at position 2. Because the ring carries two carbonyls flanked by an sp3 carbon bearing a methyl substituent, the scaffold is conformationally flexible in the sense of puckering. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry and lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the methyl group breaks the symmetry of the dione. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups, but its two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused rings, and carries two substituents on adjacent (ortho) carbons. One substituent is a methyl group, and the other is a secondary amide nitrogen bearing a formyl group, so the nitrogen is an N-H amide attached directly to the aromatic ring. The amide carbonyl is an acceptor of hydrogen bonds, while the N-H provides one donor site. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, though the N-formyl and methyl groups can rotate, giving the molecule modest conformational flexibility. It has no symmetry element beyond the mirror plane of the ring framework.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a furan ring bearing one methyl group on a carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which places it at the 2-position. The ring contains four carbons and one oxygen atom, and its conjugated double bonds give it a flat, rigid framework with no fused rings. The oxygen atom's lone pairs contribute to the aromatic system, so the ring oxygen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The methyl substituent is the only non-ring group and is a simple alkyl branch with no additional polar functionality. Because the ring is unsymmetrical once substituted, the molecule lacks a mirror plane, and its overall structure is compact and largely inflexible apart from rotation of the methyl group.

The molecule is a short saturated dicarboxylic acid built on a linear five-carbon chain, with a methyl branch on the second carbon. Both terminal ends carry carboxylic acid groups, one at each end of the chain, so the scaffold is acyclic and contains no ring systems or ring fusion. The branching methyl group sits adjacent to one carboxyl group, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry, and the sp3 carbon framework gives the chain moderate conformational flexibility. Each carboxylic acid contributes a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, giving the molecule two donor sites and four acceptor sites in total.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two hydroxyl groups are attached directly to the ring, and they sit para to one another, which gives a symmetric 1,4-pattern. A methyl group occupies a position adjacent to one of the hydroxyls, so the ring carries three substituents in total. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with the methyl and hydroxyl groups forming only small, local rotational freedom. Each hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the methyl group contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a fused bicyclic heteroaromatic system: a five-membered imidazole ring is fused to a six-membered pyridine ring, forming an imidazopyridine scaffold. The imidazole portion carries a methyl group on the carbon between its two nitrogen atoms, and one of its nitrogens bears a hydrogen, giving a pyrrole-type N-H. The six-membered ring contains a single pyridine-type nitrogen positioned on the fused ring framework. The whole structure is planar and fully aromatic, so it is rigid with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group. The N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the asymmetric placement of its nitrogens.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an imidazole ring bearing one methyl group on a carbon atom. The ring contains two nitrogen atoms separated by one carbon, with the pyridine-type nitrogen (no hydrogen) sitting next to the carbon that carries the methyl group, and the pyrrole-type nitrogen (bearing a hydrogen) on the opposite side. There is no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a simple, planar, rigid unit with no stereocenters and no meaningful conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the methyl group. The ring is substituted at only one position, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make its two ring nitrogens equivalent. The N–H group is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. A methyl group is attached to the carbon at the 2-position of the pyrrole ring, adjacent to the nitrogen. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, with the aromatic system spanning both rings. The pyrrole nitrogen carries a hydrogen atom, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while its lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system and makes it a weak acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single small substituent, so its structure is largely unbranched and achiral.

The molecule is a small acyclic dicarboxamide built on a three-carbon chain: a central carbon bearing a methyl group, flanked by two carbon atoms that each carry a primary amide group (-C(=O)NH2). Its scaffold contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion, and the only functional groups are the two terminal primary carboxamides. The substitution pattern is a 2-methylsuccinamide-type arrangement, with the methyl branch on the central carbon between the two amide groups. The two amide ends are not identical in a mirror sense because the central carbon is a stereocentre, but the connectivity is symmetric about that centre. The chain is flexible due to free rotation about its single bonds. Each primary amide provides two hydrogen-bond donors and one hydrogen-bond acceptor, so the molecule has four donor sites and two acceptor sites in total.

This molecule is a tricyclic fused aromatic system in which a thiazole ring is fused onto a naphthalene-type framework, giving a planar, fully conjugated skeleton. The thiazole contains a sulfur atom and a nitrogen atom, and a methyl group sits on the carbon between them, which is the only substituent on the ring system. The fused rings are rigid and flat, so the molecule has little conformational flexibility and essentially no rotatable bonds. Its overall shape is largely asymmetric because the sulfur and nitrogen sit on opposite sides of the fused core, and the nitrogen lone pair can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated hydrocarbon built on a single continuous chain of carbon atoms with one methyl branch, giving a branched alkane skeleton with no rings and no ring fusion. It contains no functional groups, no heteroatoms, and no double or triple bonds, so every carbon is sp3-hybridized and bonded only to other carbons and hydrogens. The branching point sits on the second carbon from one end of the longest chain, producing an asymmetric pattern in which the two terminal ends are not equivalent. Because all bonds are single and rotatable, the structure is highly flexible and can adopt many conformations. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability, since there are no electronegative heteroatoms or polarized X-H bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and an ether oxygen at adjacent (ortho) positions, giving a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The ether oxygen links the ring to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, so the structure is an aryloxyacetic acid. The carboxylic acid group carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygen serves as an additional weak acceptor. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the oxyacetic side chain contains rotatable single bonds that give it conformational flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring and substituents.

The molecule is a saturated six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, a piperidine ring, carrying a single methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen (the 2-position). It contains no fused or additional rings and no unsaturation, so the scaffold is entirely sp3-hybridized and lacks any aromatic character. The only functional group is the secondary amine within the ring, whose N–H is both a hydrogen-bond donor and whose lone pair is a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The methyl substituent breaks any mirror symmetry the parent ring might have, making the carbon bearing it a stereocenter, and the ring can adopt chair-like conformations, giving moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle with a single methyl group attached to one ring carbon. The ring contains two nitrogen atoms positioned para to each other, which makes it a pyrazine-type scaffold, and the carbon-based skeleton is fully planar and fused to nothing else. The methyl substituent sits adjacent to one ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any rotational symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. There are no polar functional groups other than the two ring nitrogens, which can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors but cannot donate hydrogen bonds. The ring is rigid, and only the methyl group offers any conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyrazine ring, a benzene-like scaffold in which two nitrogen atoms sit para to each other across the ring. A methyl group is attached to one ring carbon, and a carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to a carbon adjacent to one of the ring nitrogens, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is fully planar and conjugated, so the core is rigid, while the carboxyl group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen), and the two ring nitrogens act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and a methyl group, making it a substituted phenol scaffold with a single six-membered aromatic ring and no additional ring fusion. The two hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other), while the methyl group occupies the carbon next to one of them, giving a contiguous three-substituent pattern on the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry plane that maps the substituents onto one another because the methyl group breaks the symmetry. Each hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, so the molecule is capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding in multiple directions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent substituents, placed on neighboring carbons (an ortho arrangement). One substituent is a vinyl group, a two-carbon unit with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond, and the other is a simple methyl group. The aromatic six-membered ring is planar and rigid, while the vinyl group offers a small degree of rotational flexibility about its bond to the ring. The structure contains no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, and its only sites of unsaturation are the aromatic ring and the terminal alkene. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a mirror plane through the ring that is roughly preserved by the substituents' positions.

The molecule is a single saturated five-membered oxygen heterocycle, a tetrahydrofuran ring. The ring contains one oxygen atom, which acts as an ether linkage and can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability. A methyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, giving a 2-substituted pattern with a stereogenic center at that position. The ring is fully saturated and non-aromatic, with no additional functional groups, so the scaffold is flexible and capable of puckering rather than being rigid or planar.

This molecule is 2-methylthiophene, built on a single five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. The sulfur heteroatom sits in the ring, and a methyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to it, which defines the substitution pattern at the 2-position. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, making the scaffold rigid, while the methyl group contributes only minor flexibility through rotation. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single ring system with no ring fusion, so it lacks any polar functional groups. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the sulfur atom is a very weak hydrogen-bond acceptor at most.

This molecule is an aliphatic aldehyde with no rings, so its scaffold is a straight-chain carbon skeleton. The main chain runs from a terminal methyl group through two methylene units to a branch point, where a methyl group is attached to the second carbon counting from the aldehyde end. The aldehyde carbonyl sits at one terminus, giving the molecule a single polar functional group at that end. The molecule has no symmetry, is fairly flexible because of its unbranched alkyl segments and single bonds, and carries no stereocenter. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a straight-chain skeleton of six carbons, with a methyl branch on the alpha carbon next to the acid group. The carboxyl group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to a hydroxyl) sits at one end of the chain, and the branch makes the alpha position a stereocenter. Because there are no rings, the structure is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms. The rest of the molecule is nonpolar alkyl carbon, so hydrogen-bonding capability is concentrated at that single functional end.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene rings fused together by sharing one edge, forming a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. Attached to one of the outer carbons of the ring system is an aldehyde group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen, which makes this a single substitution on an otherwise unsubstituted fused framework. The aldehyde sits at a position beta to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond what the planar core itself provides. The rigid aromatic system contributes little conformational flexibility, with the aldehyde oxygen acting as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the molecule offering no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a bicyclic aromatic system of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with the substituent attached at the 2-position of one ring. A boronic acid group, -B(OH)2, is bonded directly to that carbon, so the boron atom carries two hydroxyl groups and is trigonal planar. The fused aromatic framework is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since only one ring bears the group and the two hydroxyls are distinct from the aromatic carbons around them. The two hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and their oxygen atoms can accept one, giving the boronic acid group strong hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a planar and rigid aromatic core. A carboxylic acid group (a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl) is attached to one of the carbons on the outer ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is a single substituent on the naphthalene system. The carboxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms. Apart from the flat fused rings, the molecule has few rotational degrees of freedom, and its only notable flexibility comes from rotation about the bond joining the carboxyl group to the ring.

The molecule is a naphthalene-based hydrazide: a two-ring aromatic system made of two fused benzene rings, with a carbonyl group bearing a hydrazine (–NH–NH2) substituent attached at the 2-position of the naphthalene core. The fused bicyclic scaffold is planar and rigid, while the acyl hydrazide tail adds a degree of rotational freedom around its C–C and C–N bonds. The molecule has no symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring system. Hydrogen-bond capability is strong: the terminal NH2 and the adjacent NH act as donors, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as an acceptor, with the remaining hydrazide nitrogen offering additional weak acceptor character.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two benzene-type rings sharing a fused edge to form a flat, bicyclic aromatic system. A single hydroxyl group (–OH) is attached to one of the carbons on the outer ring, at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, so the substitution pattern is not symmetric. The fused aromatic core is essentially rigid and planar, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen free to rotate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The rest of the framework offers only π-electron density and no additional polar sites.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic system of two benzene-type rings sharing one edge, with an aryloxy substituent attached at the 2-position. That ether oxygen links the aromatic core to a two-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid group, giving an –O–CH2–COOH side chain. The aromatic framework is rigid and planar, while the oxyacetic acid tail adds rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks symmetry because the substituent sits on only one ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the ether oxygen serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat, rigid, fully aromatic framework. A carbonyl group bearing a chlorine atom, an acyl chloride, is attached to one ring at a carbon adjacent to the fusion region, so the substitution is on a single position of the bicyclic system. The unsubstituted remainder of the naphthalene core contributes no further functional groups. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited, planar symmetry in its skeleton. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor site is the carbonyl oxygen.

This molecule is an acetate ester of a naphthol, built on a fused bicyclic naphthalene scaffold made of two benzene rings sharing one edge. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone bonded through an oxygen) is attached to one of the carbons on the naphthalene ring system, at the 2-position relative to the fusion. The ring system is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with only the ester side chain free to rotate. Apart from the ester oxygen and carbonyl oxygen, which can accept hydrogen bonds, the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry beyond its planar aromatic core.

This molecule is an aryl ester built from two aromatic units joined through a carboxylate linkage. One side is a benzoyl group, a single benzene ring bearing no substituents other than the carbonyl. The other side is a naphthalene scaffold, two fused benzene rings, attached through an oxygen at the 2-position of the naphthalene system. The ester carbonyl and the ether-type oxygen form the central linking unit, which gives the molecule a fairly extended, planar, and rigid shape. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused together along a shared edge to form a planar bicyclic aromatic system. A single isocyanate group (–N=C=O) is attached to one of the carbons on the fused ring system, at a position one step away from the ring fusion. The isocyanate is a linear, cumulated group whose central carbon is electrophilic, and its nitrogen and oxygen atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Apart from the isocyanate, the molecule carries no other substituents, so it lacks any internal symmetry beyond the mirror-like outline of the naphthalene core. The fused aromatic system is rigid and flat, with the isocyanate group projecting roughly in the plane of the rings.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system of two six-membered rings sharing an edge. A two-carbon chain bearing a terminal carboxylic acid group is attached at the 2-position of one ring through a methylene linker, so the substituent is a carboxymethyl group. The aromatic core is largely rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker gives the side chain a degree of rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry in the substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused together to share a pair of adjacent carbon atoms, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A cyanomethyl group (a methylene bridge bearing a terminal nitrile, -CH2-C≡N) is attached at the 2-position of the naphthalene ring system, making it a monosubstituted derivative with no other ring substituents. The nitrile carbon is linear and sp-hybridized, and the methylene linker gives the side chain some rotational freedom while the fused ring core stays rigid. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is largely planar and asymmetric, with the substituent breaking the local symmetry of the naphthalene core.

This molecule is an acyclic, linear chain with no rings, built from a four-carbon n-butyl group joined through an ether oxygen to a two-carbon ethyl unit. Its only functional groups are an ether linkage and a terminal primary alcohol, with the hydroxyl sitting at the far end of the chain. Because there is no ring system or branching, the skeleton is fully flexible and can adopt many conformations around its single bonds. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond the trivial one-dimensional mirror of the unbranched chain. Its hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a saturated, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a single linear-branched carbon chain. A carboxyl group (-C(=O)OH) sits at one end, and the carbon immediately adjacent to it carries a long alkyl substituent, so the backbone is an eight-carbon chain with a six-carbon arm branching from the alpha position. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or heteroatom functionality beyond the carboxylic acid. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because of the asymmetric alpha branching. The carboxylic acid group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the hydrocarbon portion contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an amino group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a nitro group. The amino group and the nitro group sit on adjacent carbons, so the nitro group is ortho to the amine, and the trifluoromethyl group is located para to the amine on the opposite side of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the molecule has no internal flexibility beyond rotation of the nitro and trifluoromethyl groups. The arrangement lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are all different. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the nitro oxygens and the amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a sulfonyl chloride group. The sulfonyl chloride is attached directly to one ring carbon, with the nitro group on the adjacent carbon, which makes the arrangement ortho to each other. The trifluoromethyl group sits on the carbon meta to the nitro group and para to the sulfonyl chloride, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three groups differ. Oxygen atoms in the nitro and sulfonyl groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4 arrangement. One ring carbon carries a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen), which is linear and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The adjacent carbon carries a nitro group, a planar, strongly electron-withdrawing unit whose oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring carbon across from the nitrile is substituted with a trifluoromethyl group, a bulky, bulky-looking unit with three fluorine atoms that accepts but does not donate hydrogen bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its aromatic core is rigid and flat, with only modest rotational freedom at the nitro group.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitro group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a hydroxymethyl group. The nitro group and the hydroxymethyl group sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other), while the trifluoromethyl group is meta to the nitro group and para to the hydroxymethyl group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion and the scaffold is essentially planar and rigid. The hydroxymethyl group contributes a flexible, rotatable CH2–OH arm, and the nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing acceptor. The hydroxyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can donate one. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane due to the asymmetric substitution.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving it a single aromatic ring with no fused rings. Going around the ring, a nitro group sits at one position, a bromomethyl group (a CH2 carrying a bromine) sits on the carbon directly beside it, and a trifluoromethyl group is placed meta to the nitro group on the opposite side. The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The trifluoromethyl group adds a compact, highly electronegative fluorinated region, and the bromomethyl group provides a flexible sp3 linker with a reactive carbon-bromine bond. The overall framework is largely planar and rigid apart from the rotatable bonds of the side chains, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on adjacent and meta-related positions: a nitro group, a trifluoromethyl group, and a chloromethyl group. The nitro group sits ortho to the chloromethyl group, while the trifluoromethyl group is positioned meta to the nitro group and para to the chloromethyl group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the chloromethyl carbon providing rotational flexibility. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing acceptor with two oxygen atoms capable of accepting hydrogen bonds, while the trifluoromethyl group contributes three fluorine atoms that are weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents. A cyanomethyl group (a CH2 attached to a nitrile, C≡N) sits at one position, a nitro group (NO2) is on the adjacent carbon, and a trifluoromethyl group (CF3) is located para to the cyanomethyl substituent. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene with no ring fusion. The nitrile and nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry, and its rigid aromatic ring contrasts with the freely rotating CH2 linker.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a nitro group, a piperidine ring attached through its nitrogen, and a hydroxyl group. The nitro group sits para to the piperidine nitrogen, while the hydroxyl group is ortho to the nitro group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic core. The piperidine is a saturated six-membered ring with a flexible chair-like conformation, whereas the benzene ring and the attached nitro group are planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically on the ring. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens and the tertiary amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring: an amino group (-NH2), a nitro group (-NO2), and a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3). The amino and nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, while the trifluoromethyl group is positioned meta to the amino group and para to the nitro group, giving the ring an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the nitro and trifluoromethyl groups able to rotate about their single bonds to the ring. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two adjacent substituents, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded to a nitrogen attached directly to the ring, while the neighboring position bears a nitro group with its nitrogen bonded to two oxygens. The amide N-H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with the flexible acetamido side chain able to rotate about its bonds, and the molecule lacks any symmetry because the two substituents differ.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon attached to a methyl group, which makes the ketone a hydrogen-bond acceptor at its oxygen. The other substituent is a nitro group, attached through nitrogen and carrying two oxygen atoms in a charge-separated arrangement; it is strongly electron-withdrawing and also acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The scaffold is a single planar aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks N-H or O-H groups. Its overall shape is largely flat and rigid, with only modest flexibility around the single bonds linking the two substituents to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two adjacent (ortho) carbons on that ring each carry a substituent: one bears a primary amino group (-NH2), which is an electron-donating group, and the neighboring carbon bears a nitro group (-NO2), which is strongly electron-withdrawing and drawn with a formal positive nitrogen and two oxygens, one negatively charged. Because the two substituents sit next to each other, the substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the amino and nitro groups have limited rotational freedom about their bonds to the ring. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds, and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons, making this an ortho-disubstituted pattern: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and a nitro group (a nitrogen bearing two oxygens, drawn as one charged and one neutral oxygen). The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing, and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group is electron-donating, so the two groups interact across the ring. The overall framework is essentially planar and rigid, with only the methyl and the nitro oxygens able to rotate, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror relationship between the two substituents. The methoxy oxygen and the nitro oxygens can each accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is 2-nitrobenzaldehyde, built on a single benzene ring with two substituents on adjacent carbons. The aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen) and the nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, drawn with a formal positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on one oxygen) occupy the ortho positions, giving a 1,2-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the two substituents are small and fairly rigid as well, so the molecule has limited conformational flexibility, though the aldehyde and nitro groups can rotate somewhat. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring and its substituents. The oxygen atoms of the carbonyl and nitro groups are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons (ortho substitution). One substituent is a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, attached directly to the aromatic ring. The other is an oxime-bearing side chain, a carbon double-bonded to nitrogen that bears a hydroxyl group, attached to the ring through that carbon. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the oxime and nitro groups add modest rotational freedom around their single bonds to the ring. The nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the oxime hydroxyl can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, with the oxime nitrogen also acting as an acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a possible planar arrangement, because the two substituents differ in character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent (ortho) carbons: a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) and a nitro group (–NO2), which carries a formal positive charge on nitrogen balanced by a negative charge on one oxygen. The ring is therefore 1,2-disubstituted, giving the molecule little rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the two groups. The aromatic ring and the planar amide and nitro groups make the scaffold fairly rigid, with only modest rotation about the bonds connecting the substituents to the ring. The amide group offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH2 hydrogens) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Attached to one carbon of this ring is a boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. On the adjacent carbon, a nitro group is present, with a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens in a formal charge-separated arrangement.
