Because the two substituents sit on neighboring positions, the substitution pattern is ortho, and the aromatic ring is planar and rigid. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that would make it highly symmetric, since the two substituents differ. The hydroxyl groups on boron can donate hydrogen bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group and the hydroxyl oxygens can accept them.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents on adjacent carbons. One is a nitro group, with a nitrogen bearing a positive formal charge and two oxygens, one of them negatively charged, which makes it a strongly electron-withdrawing, planar, conjugated group. The other is a sulfenyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is bonded to both the aromatic carbon and a chlorine atom. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the substitution pattern is ortho, and the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the S–Cl bond allows some rotation around the C–S bond. The nitro oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a primary sulfonamide group, in which a sulfur atom with two double-bonded oxygens is attached to an NH2 group. The other is a nitro group, with a nitrogen bearing two oxygens in a charge-separated arrangement. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal rotational symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The sulfonamide NH2 provides two hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl and nitro oxygens serve as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, which makes it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one formally charged, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other is a sulfonyl chloride group, a sulfur doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, which is also a strong electron-withdrawing group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygens. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its aromatic core is planar and rigid, with only modest rotational freedom around the two bonds linking the substituents to the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a hydrazide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a nitrogen that carries a free terminal amino group, giving a flexible, polar, planar-capable linkage. The other substituent is a nitro group attached directly to the ring at the position next to the carbonyl, creating an ortho substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring with no additional rings, so the overall scaffold is compact and essentially planar. The hydrazide offers multiple hydrogen-bond donors through its NH and NH2 groups and acceptors at its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitro group provides two oxygen acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, which makes the substitution pattern ortho. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydroxyl, attached directly to the ring. The other is a nitro group, with a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens in a charge-separated arrangement. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the substituents, and its ring and directly attached groups are largely rigid, with rotation possible mainly around the bonds to the carboxyl and nitro groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons, which makes the substitution pattern ortho. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptors are the nitrogen of the nitrile and the oxygens of the nitro group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure has a mirror plane through the two substituents, giving it a degree of symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons, which makes it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a nitro group, where a nitrogen bears a formal positive charge and is bonded to two oxygens, one of them charged negatively. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm retains some rotational freedom around its bonds. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, and the nitro oxygens serve as strong hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local arrangement of its two substituents.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbon ring with no fused rings. Two groups are attached to adjacent carbons of that ring, making the substitution pattern ortho. One substituent is a nitro group, a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens with one of them charge-separated, which acts as a strong electron-withdrawing group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall framework is rigid in its aromatic core, with some rotational freedom at the benzylic CH2 and the nitro bond. The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic compound. One substituent is a nitro group, in which a nitrogen is bonded to two oxygens with one formal positive and one formal negative charge, and this group is strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the chloromethyl arm adds a small degree of rotational flexibility around the bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the substituents, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the nitro oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a chalcone-type scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a three-carbon unit consisting of a ketone carbonyl flanked by a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond. One ring is unsubstituted phenyl attached directly to the carbonyl, while the other is attached to the alkene and bears a nitro group on the adjacent (ortho) carbon, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern. The molecule has no fused ring systems and no stereocenters, and the conjugated enone linker keeps it fairly planar and rigid, though the single bonds allow some rotation of the rings. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors; the carbonyl oxygen and the two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. There is no internal symmetry, since the two aromatic ends differ in substitution.

The molecule is a short, acyclic two-carbon chain, with no rings and no ring fusion, so its scaffold is a simple linear ethane-type backbone. One terminal carbon carries a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one of which is formally charged and the other double-bonded), while the other terminal carbon carries a hydroxyl group, giving a 1,2-disubstituted pattern with the two functional groups at opposite ends of the chain. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the nitro and hydroxyl groups differ, and its single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methyl groups and one nitro group. The nitro group (-NO2, written as a charge-separated N+ with an O- and a double-bonded O) is attached to one ring carbon, and the two methyl groups sit on the carbons flanking it, so the nitro group is positioned between them, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted pattern. Because the nitro group is surrounded on both sides by methyl groups, the molecule has a clear mirror plane through the nitro group and the ring carbon opposite it, so it is symmetric about that axis. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the nitro and methyl groups add only limited flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N-H or O-H groups. Its two nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitro oxygens are good hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the mirror plane of the planar ring framework.

The molecule is built on a phenyl ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-disubstituted benzene scaffold. One substituent is a nitro group, which carries a formally charged nitrogen bonded to two oxygens and is strongly electron-withdrawing. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two-atom ether-methylene linker provides some conformational flexibility to the carboxylic acid end. Overall the molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the trivial one because the two substituents differ. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens, and the nitro and ether oxygens add further acceptor capacity.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two groups are attached to adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted benzene. One substituent is a nitro group, which is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes two oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds. The other is an isothiocyanate group, a linear N=C=S unit that is also electron-withdrawing and can accept hydrogen bonds through its nitrogen and sulfur atoms. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the arrangement lacks any symmetry because the two groups differ. Its core is rigid and planar, while the nitro and isothiocyanate groups are comparatively compact and add little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a phenylacetic acid scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon side chain ending in a carboxylic acid group. A nitro group is attached to the ortho position of the ring, directly adjacent to the CH2 linker, so the substitution pattern is 1,2-disubstituted. The carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens) capability, and the nitro group contributes strong hydrogen-bond acceptor sites through its oxygens. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ring substituents are different.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a cyanomethyl group, a methylene carbon bonded to a terminal nitrile, which contributes a linear, rod-like C≡N unit. The aromatic core is fully unsaturated and rigid, while only the CH2 linker between the ring and the nitrile offers rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement around the ring. Its nitrogen and oxygen atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Three hydroxyl groups (–OH) are attached to the ring at positions that are meta or ortho to one another, and a nitro group (–NO2) occupies one of the remaining positions, adjacent to a hydroxyl. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make all ring positions equivalent. The ring is rigid and planar, and the only flexibility comes from rotation about the bonds linking the hydroxyl oxygens and the nitro group to the ring. The three hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and one nitro group on adjacent-to-one-another positions around the aromatic core. The six-membered carbon ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no additional rings fused to it. The nitro group sits on one carbon, flanked on both sides by hydroxyl substituents, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,3 across three neighboring carbons. This arrangement lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, since the two hydroxyl groups occupy different environments relative to the nitro group. The scaffold is rigid, with only the hydroxyl and nitro groups able to rotate about their bonds to the ring. Both hydroxyl groups can donate hydrogen bonds and accept them through their oxygen atoms, while the nitro oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,2,4-pattern. One position carries a methyl ester (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to an O-methyl group), another carries a free carboxylic acid, and the third, adjacent to the ester, carries a nitro group. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional rings. The ester and carboxylic acid groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, though only the acid supplies a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitro group serves as a strong acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different and unevenly placed around the ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents. A methyl ester group (a carbonyl bearing an OCH3 unit) and a free carboxylic acid sit at positions para to each other, while a nitro group sits ortho to the carboxylic acid, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic scaffold. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has no internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the ester carbonyl and ether-type oxygen act as acceptors, and the nitro group contributes further acceptor oxygens.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom, bearing one nitro group on a carbon adjacent to that sulfur. The nitro group is attached as a substituent, with its nitrogen bonded to two oxygen atoms, one formally charged and one double-bonded, so it is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold a rigid, flat shape with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, while the nitro group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and the nitro group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every ring and substituent carbon is bonded only to other carbons, hydrogens, or heteroatoms without an attached hydrogen. Its hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the two nitro oxygens and, more weakly, the ring sulfur.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents: a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on one ring carbon and a nitro group (a nitrogen bonded to two oxygens, one formally charged) on the carbon adjacent to the sulfur. Because the two groups sit at positions separated by one carbon atom on the ring, the substitution pattern is meta-like across the thiophene. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with the strongly electron-withdrawing nitrile and nitro groups conjugated with the aromatic system. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry. The nitro oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a five-membered thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing aromatic heterocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on that ring: a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO) attached at the 3-position, and a nitro group (NO2) attached at the 2-position, adjacent to the sulfur atom. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen and the nitro oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The planar aromatic core and the conjugated substituents give the structure considerable rigidity with little conformational flexibility, and the asymmetric 2,3-disubstitution pattern means the molecule lacks any meaningful symmetry.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no ring fusion. A carboxylic acid group is attached at one carbon of the ring, and a nitro group sits on a carbon adjacent to the sulfur, giving a 1,3-substitution pattern across the ring. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and the hydroxyl oxygen), while the nitro group contributes two strong oxygen acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons, giving an ortho substitution pattern: a methyl group (CH3) and a nitro group (NO2). The nitro group is strongly electron-withdrawing and planar, with two oxygen atoms that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the methyl group is a small nonpolar alkyl substituent with no donor or acceptor capability. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites and lacks any stereocenters. Its overall shape is rigid and largely planar, with only limited rotational freedom about the bonds connecting the two substituents to the ring.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched aliphatic chain with no rings, aromatic systems, or heteroatoms other than the single carbonyl oxygen. The carbon skeleton is one continuous saturated run of methylene units ending in a methyl group on one side, with the ketone carbonyl placed near the far end of the chain, so the scaffold is essentially a long linear alkyl backbone. The only functional group is the ketone, which is a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbon substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and asymmetric with no internal symmetry axis. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen can serve as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is an acyclic saturated alcohol built on a straight-chain carbon skeleton with no rings and no fused systems. A hydroxyl group sits on the second carbon of a ten-carbon chain, which carries a methyl branch at that same position, so the hydroxyl is attached to a secondary carbon. The chain is fully saturated with single bonds, giving it considerable conformational flexibility with many freely rotatable bonds. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is asymmetric, with the long alkyl tail on one side and the methyl group on the other. The single oxygen atom acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

This molecule is an open-chain aliphatic ketone with no rings, so its scaffold is a simple linear carbon chain. A single carbonyl group sits at the second carbon from one end of an eight-carbon backbone, flanked by a methyl group on one side and a seven-carbon alkyl chain on the other. Because there are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic rings, the substitution pattern is limited to the terminal methyl and the chain itself. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry, and its many rotatable single bonds make it highly flexible. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and a propyl chain, giving a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The two phenolic OH groups sit on adjacent carbons (ortho to each other), and the n-propyl group occupies the carbon next to one of them, creating a trisubstituted pattern on the ring. Because the substituents are not arranged symmetrically, the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry in its substitution. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the propyl chain adds some conformational flexibility. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its oxygen-bound hydrogen and lone pairs.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic ketone with a straight-chain scaffold of nine carbon atoms, consisting of a seven-carbon alkyl chain attached to a methyl group through a carbonyl carbon. There are no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic groups, so the structure is entirely open-chained. The single functional group is a ketone, in which the carbonyl oxygen is double-bonded to a carbon flanked by two alkyl groups. The molecule is flexible, since its sp3-hybridized chain can rotate freely about its single bonds, and it lacks any molecular symmetry because the two sides of the carbonyl differ in length. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a single hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a five-membered saturated heterocycle built from a ring of one oxygen, one nitrogen, and three carbons, with the oxygen and nitrogen separated by a single carbon on one side and a two-carbon chain on the other. The carbon adjacent to both the ring nitrogen and ring oxygen carries an exocyclic double-bonded oxygen, making it a cyclic carbamate lactone–type carbonyl, which gives the ring a fused-free, single-ring scaffold with no substituents beyond this carbonyl. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ring is compact and largely rigid, with little conformational flexibility and no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror-like arrangement of the heteroatoms.

The molecule is built around a cyclopentanone core, a five-membered saturated carbocycle bearing a ketone (C=O) on one ring carbon. A carboxylic acid group is attached through a single methylene linker (CH2) to the adjacent ring carbon, so the acid and the ketone sit on neighboring positions of the ring. The ring is fully saturated and non-aromatic, and it carries no fused or bridged ring systems. The molecule is achiral in the sense that its only stereocenter-bearing carbon is the ring carbon bearing the side chain, which is a single stereogenic center. Both the ketone oxygen and the carboxylic acid oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the carboxylic acid OH provides one hydrogen-bond donor site. The side chain gives moderate conformational flexibility, while the cyclopentane ring itself is relatively puckered rather than rigid.

The molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic methyl ketone: a fifteen-carbon backbone in which the carbonyl carbon sits at the second position from one end, bonded to a terminal methyl group and to a long unbranched alkyl chain. It contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no heteroatoms other than the single oxygen of the ketone. The substitution pattern is entirely linear, with no branching along the chain, so the molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane-free but essentially unsymmetrical arrangement dominated by the extended hydrocarbon tail. Its backbone is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds that allow numerous conformations. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a short, acyclic aliphatic ketone built from a straight chain of five carbons, with the carbonyl carbon sitting at the second position from one end. Its scaffold is entirely open-chained, so it contains no ring systems or ring fusion, and it has no aromatic character. The single functional group is a ketone, a carbon-oxygen double bond flanked on both sides by alkyl carbons, which makes the carbonyl oxygen a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure is flexible, with freely rotating single bonds along the chain, and it lacks any symmetry because the two alkyl groups on either side of the carbonyl differ in length.

This molecule is a small acyclic alkyne built on a straight four-carbon chain, with the triple bond located between the second and third carbons, giving a 2-pentyne-type skeleton. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion or fused scaffold to consider. Its only functional group is the carbon-carbon triple bond, which is linear at the two alkyne carbons, and the molecule has no substituents beyond the two terminal methyl groups. Because the structure is symmetric about the middle of the triple bond, the two halves are mirror-equivalent, and the molecule is fairly rigid along the alkyne axis while the terminal ethyl segment retains some conformational freedom. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it offers no hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is a short, unbranched carbon chain with a terminal ethyl group, an internal carbon-carbon triple bond, and a carboxylic acid at the opposite end, giving an open-chain scaffold with no rings. The triple bond places two adjacent sp-hybridized carbons in a linear, rigid segment, so the carbon framework is largely extended and stiff near the unsaturation while the ethyl end retains rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl, is the sole polar functional group and sits directly beside the alkyne. The molecule has no stereocenters and no internal symmetry, and it can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

This molecule is a phenoxyacetamide: a benzene ring bearing a single ether-linked substituent, with the phenyl oxygen connected through a methylene carbon to a primary amide group. The aromatic ring is a monosubstituted benzene with no fused rings, so the scaffold is a simple, unfused six-membered aromatic system. The ether oxygen links the ring to a flexible CH2 spacer, which gives the chain moderate rotational freedom around its single bonds, while the planar aromatic ring stays rigid. The terminal carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) offers two hydrogen-bond donors from the NH2 group and an acceptor from the carbonyl oxygen, and the ether oxygen provides an additional weak acceptor site. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the local mirror plane of the phenyl ring.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single ether oxygen, giving a diaryl ether scaffold with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a primary amino group on the carbon adjacent to the ether linkage, so the substitution pattern is ortho on that ring, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The C–O–C linkage lets the two aromatic rings rotate relative to each other, so the molecule is moderately flexible rather than fully rigid. It has no internal symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its N–H bonds and accept them at its lone pair, while the ether oxygen can only act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a diaryl ether in which two benzene rings are joined through a single oxygen atom, with one ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at the position ortho to the ether linkage. The carboxylic acid is a planar C(=O)OH unit that can both donate one hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The ether oxygen serves as an additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two aromatic rings are unfused and attached through the flexible C–O–C linkage, so the scaffold can adopt a range of twisted, non-coplanar conformations. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because of the single substituent on one ring.

The molecule is a diaryl ether built from three benzene rings: two phenyl rings joined through an oxygen bridge, and a third phenyl ring attached directly to one of those rings, forming a biphenyl unit. The central ring is ortho-disubstituted, carrying the ether oxygen and the second phenyl ring on adjacent carbons. There are no heteroatoms other than the single ether oxygen, so the compound has no hydrogen-bond donors and only a weak acceptor at that oxygen. The overall framework is aromatic and largely planar within each ring, though rotation about the C–O and biaryl C–C bonds gives it moderate conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry because of the asymmetric ortho substitution pattern.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying a single substituent: a 2-hydroxyethoxy group attached through an ether oxygen. The aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered system with only one substituent, so it shows no substitution pattern beyond monosubstitution and retains a plane of symmetry through the ring and substituent. The side chain is a flexible two-carbon linker ending in a primary alcohol, which gives the molecule rotational freedom along the chain. The ether oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the terminal hydroxyl group can serve as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single substituent, so it is a monosubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Attached to the ring through an oxygen atom is a two-carbon chain ending in a bromine atom, giving an aryl ether linked to a primary alkyl bromide. The ether oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, whereas the ethyl linker adds conformational flexibility. The structure has no internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane of the phenyl ring.

The molecule is built from a benzene ring bearing a single substituent: an aryl ether oxygen attached to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is fully unsubstituted otherwise, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted with no fused rings or stereocenters present. The aryl ether oxygen and the terminal alkyl chloride are the only functional features, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the chloro group contributes modest polarity without accepting hydrogen bonds strongly. The two-carbon linker gives the molecule moderate conformational flexibility, whereas the phenyl ring remains planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on a pyridine ring bearing a carboxylic acid group at one carbon and an aryl ether at the adjacent carbon, so the carboxyl and ether substituents sit ortho to each other. The ether oxygen links the pyridine to an unsubstituted phenyl ring, giving a diaryl ether scaffold in which the two aromatic rings are connected through a single flexible C–O–C linkage. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the pyridine nitrogen and the ether oxygen serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The phenyl ring is monosubstituted and has no symmetry relationship with the more heavily substituted pyridine ring, so the molecule lacks any overall symmetry. Its two aromatic systems are rigid, but the ether linkage permits rotation about its bonds, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility.

This molecule is 2-phenoxypropanoic acid, built from a three-carbon propanoic acid backbone with a phenoxy group attached at the alpha carbon, which bears a methyl group and creates a stereocenter. The phenyl ring is a single unfused benzene ring connected to the alpha carbon through an ether oxygen, giving the molecule a flexible linkage that allows rotation about the C–O bonds. The terminal carboxylic acid group is the main functional group, containing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted with no symmetry-enforcing pattern, and the molecule as a whole lacks any internal symmetry because of the chiral alpha carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a tertiary alcohol group attached directly to one ring carbon through a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted apart from this one side chain, so it has no fused rings and no other functional groups on the ring, and it lacks any ring-based symmetry beyond the local freedom of rotation about the single bond linking the ring to the side chain. The 2-hydroxypropan-2-yl group is bulky and branched, with the central carbon carrying two identical methyl groups, which gives the side chain a degree of conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs, while the aromatic ring contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability of its own.

This molecule is a small tertiary propargylic alcohol built around a single benzene ring. A quaternary carbon bears a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, a phenyl ring, and a terminal alkyne (ethynyl) group, so the central sp3 carbon is a stereocenter and the structure is achiral only if the two substituents are considered identically placed, which they are not. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, with no ring fusion, and it contributes aromatic planarity. The ethynyl group is linear and rigid, while the rest of the molecule around the quaternary carbon has some rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the alkyne's terminal C–H can weakly donate a hydrogen bond, while the pi systems of the ring and alkyne offer additional acceptor character.

The molecule is a five-membered oxazolidinone-type ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen, with the carbonyl carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, forming a cyclic carbamate-like lactone scaffold. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the ring carbon that sits between the nitrogen and the oxygen, giving a single, non-fused aryl substituent at that position. The ring is saturated apart from the carbonyl, so it is fairly compact and conformationally constrained, while the bond to the phenyl group allows some rotational freedom. The amide-like N-H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no stereochemical symmetry through the ring, since the substituted carbon is a stereocenter that breaks any mirror plane.

The molecule is a 2-phenylanthraquinone-type scaffold: three fused rings in a linear arrangement, with the central ring bearing two carbonyl groups at opposite positions. The two outer benzene rings are fused to the central six-membered ring, giving a flat, fully conjugated, rigid tricyclic core. A phenyl ring is attached as a substituent on one of the outer rings, at a position that breaks the overall mirror symmetry of the core. The biaryl bond to the phenyl group allows some rotation, but the fused framework is essentially planar. The two ketone oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a benzimidazole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to an imidazole ring through two adjacent carbon atoms. The five-membered ring contains two nitrogen atoms: one is a pyridine-like nitrogen that accepts hydrogen bonds, and the other is a pyrrole-like NH that donates one. At the carbon between the two imidazole nitrogens, a phenyl ring is attached as a single substituent, giving a 2-phenyl substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core and the directly bonded phenyl ring are fully aromatic and essentially planar, so the molecule is rigid with only the bond between the rings able to rotate. Overall, the structure is a flat, largely unsymmetrical aromatic framework with one donor and one acceptor site.

The molecule is built from a benzothiazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered thiazole ring containing both sulfur and nitrogen. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon at position 2 of the thiazole, the carbon that sits between the sulfur and the nitrogen. Apart from that single connection, the structure has no other substituents, so the substitution pattern is simple and the whole framework is aromatic and planar. Because the phenyl and benzothiazole units are joined by a single bond, they can rotate relative to each other, though conjugation favors a near-coplanar arrangement. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a benzoxazole core, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered ring containing one nitrogen and one oxygen atom. A second benzene ring is attached directly to the carbon between the nitrogen and oxygen at the 2-position of the oxazole, with no linker between them. The two aromatic systems are fully conjugated and essentially planar, giving the structure a rigid, flat shape with little conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters, and its overall arrangement is nearly symmetric about the long axis through the biaryl bond. The ring nitrogen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built from a six-membered saturated carbocycle bearing a ketone, with a phenyl ring attached directly to the carbon adjacent to that carbonyl, giving a 2-substituted cyclohexanone scaffold. The cyclohexanone ring is non-aromatic and adopts flexible chair-like conformations, while the attached benzene ring is planar and aromatic, so the molecule combines one flexible aliphatic ring with one rigid aromatic ring joined by a single C–C bond. There is no ring fusion; the two rings are separate and connected only through one stereogenic center at the substituted carbon, so the molecule is chiral and has no internal symmetry plane. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single two-carbon side chain, so its scaffold is a monosubstituted aromatic ring. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, with no ring fusion or additional rings present. The side chain is an ethyl linker terminated by a primary alcohol group, which is the only functional group in the structure. Because the ring carries just one substituent, the molecule has no positional isomers to distinguish and shows a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring and the side chain. The two saturated carbons of the chain give it moderate flexibility, while the aromatic ring remains rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic ring contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is an ester built from a two-carbon acetyl unit linked through an oxygen to a flexible ethyl chain that terminates in a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single unsubstituted benzene, so it carries no substituent pattern beyond the attachment point, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a mild overall symmetry, with the phenyl ring providing the main rigid element. The ester carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the ester ether oxygen can also accept hydrogen bonds, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors. The two methylene groups between the ring and the ester oxygen give the chain considerable rotational freedom, making the overall structure fairly flexible.

The molecule is built on a two-carbon ethyl chain linked to a single benzene ring, giving a simple phenethyl scaffold with no ring fusion. The aromatic ring is unsubstituted apart from the ethyl attachment, so its substitution pattern is monosubstituted and it carries a mirror plane through the ring and chain, giving the molecule overall high symmetry. The only functional group is a primary amine at the terminus of the flexible ethyl chain, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The benzene ring itself is rigid and planar while the ethylene linker permits considerable conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two hydroxyl groups in a 1,4 (para) relationship, with a phenyl ring attached directly to the carbon between one of the hydroxyl-bearing positions. This gives a biphenyl-type scaffold: two six-membered aromatic rings joined by a single C–C bond, with no additional ring fusion. The hydroxyl groups are phenolic and can each act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The substitution pattern on the diol-bearing ring is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational axis through the whole structure. The biaryl bond allows some rotation, making the molecule moderately flexible around that linkage, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and planar.

The molecule is a 2-phenylimidazole, consisting of a benzene ring directly bonded at one carbon to the C2 position of an imidazole ring. The imidazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3, with the N1 position bearing a hydrogen atom and the N3 position acting as a pyridine-like nitrogen. The two rings are joined by a single bond, so they are not fused, and the connection allows a degree of rotation between them, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The unsubstituted phenyl ring and the imidazole together form a largely planar aromatic framework with no stereocenters. The N–H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated sp2 nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on an indole core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered pyrrole ring that carries an N-H group. A phenyl ring is attached directly to the carbon at the 2-position of the pyrrole portion, giving a 2-arylindole arrangement. The fused bicyclic system is planar and aromatic, while the single bond linking the two aromatic systems allows some rotational freedom, so the molecule is largely rigid with limited flexibility. The indole N-H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyrrole nitrogen's lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic system and makes it a poor acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a modest, asymmetric substitution pattern on its aromatic framework.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a benzene ring fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl bonded to a hydrogen) is attached at the 3-position of the five-membered ring, and a phenyl ring is attached directly to the 2-position, next to the nitrogen. The indole N–H is a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aldehyde oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused bicyclic core is rigid and planar, and the pendant phenyl ring can rotate relative to it, giving limited flexibility. The molecule has no internal symmetry.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between adjacent positions. One ring carries a hydroxyl group on the carbon directly bonded to the other ring, so the two aromatic rings are attached at ortho positions relative to that hydroxyl. Each ring is fully aromatic and unfused, with no additional substituents on the second ring. The single inter-ring bond allows rotation, so the two rings can adopt twisted conformations relative to one another. The hydroxyl group acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the aromatic pi systems contribute weak acceptor character. The overall shape is asymmetric because only one ring bears the polar substituent.

The molecule is built around a six-membered saturated piperazine ring, which contains two nitrogen atoms positioned at opposite (1,4) locations and bears no double bonds. One ring carbon is directly bonded to a benzene ring, so the phenyl group is a simple monosubstituted aromatic unit attached to the piperazine skeleton. Both nitrogens are secondary amines, each carrying a hydrogen, which makes them hydrogen-bond donors as well as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their lone pairs. The piperazine ring is non-planar and can flip between chair-like conformations, while the phenyl-piperazine bond allows rotation, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any overall mirror or rotational symmetry because the phenyl group sits on only one carbon of the ring, so the attached carbon is a stereocenter.

This molecule is built from a single benzene ring bearing one substituent, with no fused or additional ring systems. The substituent is a two-carbon chain: a branched carbon carrying a methyl group and a terminal carboxylic acid group, which is attached directly to the phenyl ring. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted, so there is no regiochemical substitution pattern to consider, and the molecule has a single stereocenter at the carbon bearing the methyl group, which means it lacks any internal mirror symmetry. The carboxylic acid group provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the aromatic ring contributes a flat, rigid region. The overall structure is only moderately flexible because rotation about the single bonds linking the chain to the ring and to the carboxyl group is allowed.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined directly by a single carbon-carbon bond, forming a biaryl scaffold. One ring is a benzene ring with no substituents, while the other is a pyridine ring in which a ring nitrogen sits directly adjacent to the carbon that forms the linkage. Neither ring is fused to the other, so the two rings are connected only through a single rotatable bond, which allows some conformational flexibility around the linkage. The molecule has no stereocenters and no functional groups beyond the pyridine nitrogen, which acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens are aromatic C-H positions.

The molecule is built on a quinoline core, a bicyclic scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring, and a phenyl group is attached at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, placing it at the 2-position. Its ring system is fully aromatic and planar, with the two fused rings sharing one edge, and the biaryl bond to the phenyl ring allows only limited rotation, so the overall framework is rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and no functional groups beyond the aromatic nitrogen, which is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and cannot act as a donor, since there are no N-H or O-H bonds. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, because the phenyl group sits on only one side of the nitrogen, giving the molecule a non-symmetric shape overall.

The molecule is built on a quinoline scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyridine ring through a shared C–C bond. A phenyl group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position of the quinoline core. A carboxylic acid group sits at the 4-position on the pyridine-containing ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The fused aromatic system is fully planar and rigid, while the biaryl bond to the phenyl ring allows some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a short, acyclic aliphatic chain built on a two-carbon backbone bearing both a carboxylic acid and a phosphonic acid group on adjacent carbons. There are no rings or ring fusions, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The terminal carboxyl group (-C(=O)OH) and the two hydroxyl groups on the phosphorus atom each carry acidic hydrogens, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl and phosphoryl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The ethyl substituent on the carbon bearing the phosphorus group adds a small saturated alkyl branch, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two acidic functional groups occupy different positions along the chain.

The molecule is a short aliphatic chain built around a two-carbon backbone bearing a methyl group, a carboxylic acid, and a phosphonic acid group on the same carbon. It contains no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is entirely open-chain and acyclic. The carboxylic acid (a carbonyl bearing a hydroxyl) and the phosphorus center carrying a double-bonded oxygen and two hydroxyl groups are the principal functional groups. The substitution pattern is branched at the alpha carbon, which is a stereogenic center, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. Its single-bond framework gives it considerable conformational flexibility. Together, the three acidic hydroxyl groups and the carbonyl and phosphoryl oxygens provide multiple hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a phthalimide scaffold, meaning a benzene ring fused to a five-membered imide ring that carries two carbonyl groups flanking a nitrogen. The nitrogen is substituted by a secondary carbon bearing a methyl group and a terminal carboxylic acid, so the side chain is a propanoic acid unit attached at its alpha position. The fused bicyclic core is planar and rigid, while the side chain adds a single rotatable bond region that gives some conformational flexibility. The two imide carbonyls and the carboxylic acid act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the acid's hydroxyl provides one hydrogen-bond donor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the alpha carbon is a stereocenter, leaving the side chain asymmetric relative to the planar core.

This molecule is a single six-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyridine ring, bearing one methyl group attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which places it at the 2-position. The ring is fully conjugated and planar, with no fused rings, so the scaffold is compact and rigid, and the only conformational freedom comes from rotation of the methyl group. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the nitrogen and the methyl-bearing carbon. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that is oriented outward in the ring plane, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the only N–H or O–H positions are absent.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring bearing a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The ring nitrogen is oxidized and carries a formal positive charge with a bonded oxygen atom bearing a negative charge, giving an N-oxide functional group. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl group, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl substituent breaks the mirror relationship of the ring. The N-oxide oxygen is a strong hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the methyl hydrogens are not polar.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing two nitrogen atoms placed at 1,4-positions, forming a piperazine-type scaffold with one ring carbon converted to a carbonyl. The ring carbonyl sits adjacent to one nitrogen, making that nitrogen part of a lactam (amide) linkage, while the other nitrogen remains a secondary amine. Because the ring contains only single bonds apart from the carbonyl, it is fairly rigid in its chair-like or boat-like conformations yet lacks any stereocenters or symmetry-defining substituents. The amide N-H and the secondary amine N-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the amine nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an isopropyl-substituted sulfonyl chloride: a central sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygen atoms, a single chlorine atom, and a secondary carbon group. That carbon group is an isopropyl unit, a carbon bonded to two methyl groups, which attaches directly to the sulfur. There are no rings and no ring fusion, so the scaffold is a small, acyclic, fully saturated alkyl chain connected to a tetrahedral sulfonyl center. The sulfonyl group is the sole functional group and is strongly electron-withdrawing, while the sulfur-chlorine bond is a reactive site. The isopropyl group is symmetric about its C-S axis, with the two methyl groups being equivalent. The molecule is fairly flexible around the carbon-sulfur bond. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a small acyclic thiol built on a short carbon skeleton. Its core is a propane-type chain whose central carbon is bonded to two methyl groups and a sulfur-bearing carbon, giving a branched, sterically compact arrangement. The sole functional group is a terminal sulfhydryl (thiol) group attached to the secondary carbon, so the substitution pattern is a single heteroatom substituent on an isopropyl-like framework. The molecule has no rings or ring fusion, and its two methyl groups are equivalent, providing local rotational symmetry about the central carbon. Because it contains only single bonds with free rotation, it is highly flexible. The thiol hydrogen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor, while the sulfur atom can serve as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is isopropanol, a small acyclic alcohol built on a three-carbon propane skeleton with no ring systems or ring fusion. The hydroxyl group sits on the central carbon, which carries two methyl groups, so the two terminal methyls are chemically equivalent and the molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry through the C–O bond. The only functional group is a secondary alcohol, with the oxygen-bound hydrogen able to act as a hydrogen-bond donor while the oxygen lone pairs can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Its single C–C and C–O bonds are freely rotatable, so the structure is flexible rather than rigid.

This molecule is a small aromatic ketone built around a five-membered furan ring, an oxygen-containing heteroaromatic system. A propanoyl group, consisting of a three-carbon chain ending in a carbonyl, is attached directly to one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, which is the 2-position of the furan. The rest of the furan ring carries only hydrogens, so the substitution pattern is simple and monosubstituted. The molecule is essentially planar across the ring and carbonyl, with a flexible ethyl tail. The carbonyl oxygen and the furan oxygen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a pyrrole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing a propanoyl group (an ethyl ketone, C(=O)CH2CH3) attached at the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen. The ring nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so the pyrrole N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the ketone oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The substitution pattern is a single acyl group on the 2-position, with no ring fusion and no additional substituents. The molecule has no stereocenters and a roughly planar, largely rigid aromatic core, with the ethyl chain providing modest conformational flexibility around the ketone.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a two-carbon side chain at the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho to nitrogen. The aromatic six-membered pyridine core is a single unfused ring with no additional ring systems. Attached to the methylene linker is a primary amide group, a carbonyl bonded to an NH2 unit, which provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability. The pyridine nitrogen adds a further hydrogen-bond acceptor site. The molecule is largely planar in its aromatic region but has a rotatable CH2 linker, giving moderate conformational flexibility, and it lacks any internal symmetry because of the single asymmetric substitution.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, and it is unfused, so no additional rings share bonds with it. A cyanomethyl group (a methylene carbon bearing a terminal nitrile, C≡N) is attached to one of the carbons adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which places the substituent at the 2-position. The nitrile is a linear, rod-like functional group, while the aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the single CH2 linker gives only limited conformational freedom. Because the substituent sits on one side of the ring, the molecule lacks any rotational or mirror symmetry beyond the ring's own local pattern. The pyridine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can both accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring bearing a single hydroxymethyl group, so it is a monosubstituted six-membered aromatic heterocycle with one nitrogen atom in the ring. The hydroxymethyl substituent sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring nitrogen, which is the 2-position of the pyridine, giving an ortho relationship between the ring nitrogen and the side chain. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the CH2–OH arm can rotate freely about its single bonds, adding some conformational flexibility. The primary alcohol group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen, and the pyridine nitrogen provides an additional acceptor site. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring in its idealized planar geometry.

The molecule is built around a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no additional ring fusion. At the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen sits a sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom bearing two double-bonded oxygens, which links the ring to a two-carbon chain. That chain ends in a nitrile group, a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen, giving a linear terminal unit. The pyridine nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The sulfonyl oxygens provide further acceptor sites, and the overall framework is largely rigid aromatic with a single rotatable bond along the sulfur-carbon linkage.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered lactam ring, a pyrrolidin-2-one (gamma-lactam) scaffold containing one nitrogen atom. The ring carbonyl sits directly adjacent to the nitrogen, forming a cyclic amide, and the remaining three methylene carbons form a saturated chain closing the ring. There are no substituents on the ring, so the substitution pattern is unsubstituted and the molecule has no stereocenters. The structure is compact and highly symmetric about a mirror plane passing through the carbonyl and nitrogen atoms, and the small ring confers limited conformational flexibility. The amide nitrogen bears one hydrogen, making it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries two substituents on adjacent (ortho) positions: a hydroxyl group directly attached to the ring, making it a phenol, and a sec-butyl group, a four-carbon branched alkyl chain attached through its secondary carbon. The sec-butyl chain contains a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral and not symmetric, though the ring itself is planar and rigid while the alkyl chain adds conformational flexibility. The phenolic oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs, while the rest of the structure is largely hydrophobic hydrocarbon.

The molecule is a bicyclic, fully fused system in which a benzene ring is joined through a shared edge to a five-membered heterocycle containing a sulfur atom and a carbonyl carbon. The five-membered ring is a cyclic sulfonate ester (a sultone-type lactone), so the sulfur bears two S=O groups and is bonded to an ester oxygen that connects to the carbonyl carbon. The carbonyl oxygen and both sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The benzene ring carries four aromatic hydrogens on its unfused carbons, with no further substituents, and the overall framework is planar and rigid. Apart from the fused benzene ring, the molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond that imposed by the ring arrangement.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Around this ring there are three substituents: a methyl group, a hydroxyl group, and a tert-butyl group, the last being a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups. The hydroxyl sits directly beside the bulky tert-butyl group, so the two are adjacent, while the methyl group occupies a position across the ring from the hydroxyl, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the three substituents are different. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl group contributes a bulky, non-polar, three-dimensional region. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered thiazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing one sulfur and one nitrogen atom. The ring carries a methyl group on one carbon adjacent to the nitrogen and a tert-butyl group on the carbon between nitrogen and sulfur, which together create a bulky, asymmetric substitution pattern. A carboxylic acid group is attached to the remaining ring carbon next to sulfur, adding a polar, planar functional handle. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the tert-butyl group contributes steric bulk but little conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ring nitrogen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a methyl group, a bulky tert-butyl group, and an isocyanate group (N=C=O) attached directly to the ring. The methyl and tert-butyl groups sit on carbons that flank the isocyanate-bearing carbon, so the isocyanate is shielded on both sides, giving a 1,2,3-trisubstituted (contiguous) substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no fused rings. The tert-butyl group adds a compact, highly symmetric quaternary carbon, while the isocyanate is linear and electrophilic at its central carbon but has no hydrogen-bond donor capability, and its oxygen and nitrogen can act only as weak acceptors. Overall the framework is rigid and planar, apart from rotation of the tert-butyl group.

The molecule is built on an anthraquinone scaffold: three fused six-membered rings, with the central ring bearing two ketone carbonyl groups at positions opposite each other. The two outer rings are benzene rings, so the central ring is fused to both. One outer ring carries a single tert-butyl group, a bulky branched alkyl substituent attached through a quaternary carbon. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds steric bulk but no flexibility to the core. The molecule has no overall symmetry because the tert-butyl group sits on only one ring. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons: a hydroxyl group and a tert-butyl group, making it an ortho-disubstituted phenol. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings attached. The tert-butyl group is a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups, giving it a bulky, three-fold symmetric shape that sits beside the phenolic oxygen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs. The overall scaffold is largely rigid because of the aromatic ring, with only limited rotational freedom around the bonds joining the substituents to the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic aliphatic diol built on a short carbon skeleton. A quaternary tert-butyl carbon, bearing three methyl groups, is bonded to a central tertiary carbon that carries two hydroxymethyl arms, so the scaffold is branched and contains no rings or aromatic systems. Its only functional groups are two primary alcohols, which can each act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The bulky tert-butyl group makes the framework fairly compact, while the two terminal hydroxyl-bearing arms give it considerable conformational flexibility around the single bonds. The arrangement is not symmetric overall, since one side is a fully alkylated tert-butyl unit and the other side carries the polar hydroxymethyl groups.

The molecule is a bicyclic compound built from a benzene ring fused to a six-membered carbocyclic ring that contains a ketone. The aromatic ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group, so the fusion is ortho, creating a tetralone-type scaffold where the saturated ring carries two CH2 units alongside the carbonyl carbon. The ketone sits on the saturated ring, adjacent to a methylene that connects toward the fused aromatic carbon, and this carbonyl is the only functional group present. The fused system is fairly rigid because of the aromatic ring, while the saturated portion retains some conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-like plane of symmetry in its planar aromatic portion. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, consisting of two fused benzene rings that share one edge, giving a flat, fully aromatic bicyclic core. A single thiol group (–SH) is attached to one ring at a position beta to the ring fusion, which makes it a 2-substituted naphthalene. The rigid, planar framework has no rotatable bonds apart from the S–H bond, so its shape is essentially fixed. The thiol sulfur can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S–H group and a weak acceptor through its lone pairs, while the aromatic system offers no strong hydrogen-bonding sites. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through its long axis, since the substituent breaks the symmetry of the parent naphthalene.

This molecule is built from a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, with a two-carbon side chain attached at the 2-position. That side chain is an acetamide unit: a methylene group linking the ring to a primary amide, which carries a carbonyl oxygen and a free NH2 group. The aromatic thiophene core is planar and rigid, while the CH2 linker gives the amide portion some rotational freedom. The sulfur atom is not a hydrogen-bond acceptor in any meaningful sense, so the main hydrogen-bonding capacity comes from the amide, where the two NH2 hydrogens act as donors and the carbonyl oxygen acts as an acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the substituent sits on only one side of the ring.

This molecule is built from a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom, with no fused rings. A two-carbon chain is attached at the 2-position of the ring, ending in a carboxylic acid group (a carbonyl bearing a hydroxyl), so the skeleton is a simple aryl-acetic acid scaffold. The ring is unsubstituted elsewhere, giving a single, non-symmetric substitution pattern. The methylene linker provides some rotational flexibility, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), and the sulfur atom in the ring can act as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is a simple monosubstituted thiophene, a single five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom and four carbon atoms. Attached to one of the carbons adjacent to the sulfur is a hydroxymethyl group, meaning a methylene carbon bonded to a terminal hydroxyl. The ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is rigid while the CH2–OH arm retains some rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the sulfur of the ring is a weak acceptor only.

The molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic alcohol with no ring systems and no aromatic rings. Its backbone is a long, unbranched carbon chain of saturated sp3 carbons, with a single methyl branch (a one-carbon side arm) located on the carbon that carries the hydroxyl group, making the hydroxyl sit on a secondary carbon. The only functional group is that one hydroxyl, which gives the molecule one hydrogen-bond donor and one hydrogen-bond acceptor. The chain is highly flexible, with many freely rotating single bonds, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the branch and the hydroxyl break the symmetry of the carbon skeleton.

This molecule is an acyclic methyl ketone: a straight, unbranched chain of twelve carbons with a ketone carbonyl group at one end, so the carbonyl carbon bears a terminal methyl group and a long saturated alkyl tail. The skeleton contains no rings and no ring fusion, and there are no heteroatoms other than the single oxygen of the carbonyl. Because the chain is fully saturated and unbranched, it is highly flexible, with many rotatable bonds that allow it to adopt numerous conformations. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry, since the two ends of the carbonyl differ markedly in length and substitution. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a saturated six-membered 1,3-dithiane ring, in which two sulfur atoms occupy positions separated by a single carbon, and the remaining three ring carbons are CH2 groups. At the carbon between the two sulfurs, a triisopropylsilyl group is attached, meaning a silicon atom bearing three branched isopropyl substituents. The ring is fully saturated and contains no double bonds or aromatic character, so it adopts a flexible chair-like conformation, with the bulky silyl group likely preferring an equatorial orientation. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it contains no N–H or O–H groups, and its sulfur atoms can act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the structure is a sterically encumbered, non-polar, sulfur-containing heterocycle with a single silicon-based substituent.

This molecule is a straight, unbranched saturated carbon chain with no rings, double bonds, or aromatic systems, so its scaffold is entirely acyclic and aliphatic. The chain contains twelve carbons in total, with a single secondary alcohol group located on the second carbon from one end, where a methyl branch also sits, giving the hydroxyl carbon a 1-methyl substitution pattern. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the hydroxyl-bearing terminus is distinct from the other end of the chain. Its flexible alkyl framework allows many conformations through free rotation about single bonds, so it is conformationally mobile rather than rigid. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the rest of the molecule is nonpolar hydrocarbon.

This molecule is a straight-chain aliphatic ketone, consisting of a ten-carbon backbone with the carbonyl group positioned at the second carbon from one end, so the skeleton is an unbranched alkyl chain with no rings or aromatic systems. The carbonyl carbon is bonded to a methyl group on one side and a nonyl chain on the other, giving a single functional group and no substitution beyond the chain itself. The molecule has no symmetry because the two flanking chains differ in length, and its extended, unbranched chain gives it considerable conformational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions: a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond, C=C) and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached to the aromatic carbon. The benzene ring is a single planar six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion, and the ortho-disubstitution pattern gives the molecule a modest, asymmetric shape with no internal symmetry axis beyond the local plane. The vinyl group is conjugated with the aromatic ring, which adds some rigidity to that side, while the B–C and B–O bonds allow rotation of the boronic acid group. The two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors and their oxygen atoms as acceptors, whereas the vinyl group contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons, making it an ortho-disubstituted aromatic system. One substituent is a vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond attached directly to the ring), and the other is a carboxylic acid group, which contains a carbonyl and a hydroxyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the vinyl and carboxyl groups add some rotational flexibility about their single bonds to the ring. Because the two groups sit next to each other, the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry in its overall arrangement. The carboxylic acid offers one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the rest of the framework is largely hydrophobic.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, which is two benzene rings fused along a shared edge to form a flat, rigid bicyclic aromatic core. A vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond, CH2=CH–) is attached at one of the outer positions, giving a single substituent on the fused system and no additional stereocenters. Overall the structure is planar and largely rigid, with only the vinyl group offering limited rotational freedom. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen sits on carbon, and no hydrogen-bond acceptors such as heteroatoms or polar carbonyl groups. Its symmetry is low, because the single vinyl substituent breaks the mirror symmetry of the parent naphthalene core.

This molecule is 2-vinylpyridine, built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring containing one nitrogen atom in place of a carbon. A vinyl group (a carbon-carbon double bond terminated by a CH2) is attached to the carbon immediately adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the substitution pattern is ortho to the nitrogen. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, with no fused rings, and the vinyl substituent adds a small amount of conformational freedom through rotation about the single bond linking it to the ring. The molecule lacks any symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring. The ring nitrogen, with its lone pair held in the plane of the ring, serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a meta-substituted aniline in which the benzene ring carries a primary amino group on one carbon and a 1H-tetrazol-5-yl group on the carbon three positions away. The tetrazole is a five-membered aromatic ring containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, and it is joined to the benzene ring by a single bond, so the two ring systems are not fused. The structure is largely planar and rigid, with limited rotation about the biaryl bond. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor and the tetrazole N-H is a further donor, while the ring nitrogens of both the tetrazole and the aniline nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks a symmetry axis because the two substituents sit at different positions on the benzene ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents at meta positions, giving a 1,3-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. One substituent is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bearing a hydroxyl that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other is a five-membered aromatic tetrazole ring attached directly through a carbon-carbon bond, containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, with an N-H proton on one nitrogen. Both aromatic rings are planar and conjugated, making the framework rigid, while the single bond joining the two rings permits some rotation. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond a local mirror plane through the aromatic system. Overall, it offers multiple hydrogen-bond donor sites from the acid and tetrazole N-H groups and several acceptor sites from the oxygen and nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH attached to the ring), which provides a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its hydroxyl oxygen. The other is a 1H-tetrazol-5-yl group, a five-membered aromatic ring containing four nitrogen atoms and one carbon, joined to the benzene by a single C–C bond. The tetrazole ring carries an N–H proton, so it can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. Because the two rings are connected by a single bond, they can rotate relative to each other, giving the overall scaffold moderate flexibility, while the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and planar. The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond a possible mirror plane through the substitution axis, so its two ends are chemically distinct.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, meaning two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with a substituent at the alpha (1-) position. Attached to that position is a short two-carbon chain containing a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which connects the aromatic system to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The fused bicyclic core is fully aromatic and planar, while the conjugated alkene linker keeps the side chain largely extended and rigid. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor (the O-H) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens) capability, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substitution is at a single asymmetric position.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a 1,2-benzisoxazole core, with the fusion occurring at adjacent carbons of the five-membered ring. Attached at the 3-position of the isoxazole ring is a piperazine group, a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms positioned opposite one another. The unsubstituted secondary amine nitrogen of the piperazine serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the tertiary nitrogen bonded to the aromatic system and the ring oxygen and nitrogen of the isoxazole act as acceptors. The fused aromatic core is planar and rigid, whereas the piperazine ring can adopt flexible chair conformations. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the local symmetry of the benzo ring and the piperazine ring.
