This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle, bearing two substituents at meta positions relative to each other. One substituent is a hydroxyl group, which makes the ring a phenol. The other is a piperazine ring attached through one of its nitrogen atoms, leaving the second nitrogen as a secondary amine with an N-H group. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogens opposite each other, and it adopts a flexible chair-like conformation. The phenol O-H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the free piperazine N-H and the lone pairs on both nitrogens add further donor and acceptor capacity. Overall, the molecule has a rigid aromatic portion joined to a more flexible saturated heterocycle, with no internal symmetry beyond the ring's local symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a meta relationship: a hydroxyl group directly on the ring and a piperidinylmethyl group, meaning a CH2 linker attached to the nitrogen of a six-membered saturated piperidine ring. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the piperidine ring is fully saturated and flexible, adopting chair-like conformations, and it is connected to the aryl system through a single rotatable methylene bond. The phenolic oxygen can donate a hydrogen bond through its OH group and accept one through its lone pairs. The tertiary amine nitrogen in the piperidine ring has a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor but carries no hydrogen-bond donor capability. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local symmetry of the piperidine ring.

The molecule is a phenylpropanoic acid, built from a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is monocyclic with no ring fusion, and it carries two chlorine atoms at positions 2 and 4 relative to the side chain, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The chain is flexible, with rotatable single bonds linking the ring to the carboxyl terminus. The carboxylic acid functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors and contribute no donor capability.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two chlorine atoms and one propargyl ether group. The ether oxygen links the aromatic ring to a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal alkyne (a carbon-carbon triple bond at the chain's end). The two chlorine atoms sit on the carbons flanking the ether-bearing carbon, giving a symmetric 2,6-disubstituted pattern around the ring. Overall the structure is fairly rigid at the aromatic core and halogenated ring, with a more flexible ether-alkyne tail. The ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on an isoxazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, bearing a methyl group on one carbon and a carboxylic acid on the adjacent carbon. At the remaining ring carbon sits a phenyl ring carrying chlorine atoms at both positions flanking the attachment point, giving a 2,6-dichloro substitution pattern. The aryl and isoxazole rings are joined by a single bond, so they are not fused, but steric crowding from the ortho chlorines restricts rotation and makes the connection relatively rigid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogen and oxygen serve as additional acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis because the two aromatic rings carry different substituents.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a trans-configured acrylic acid unit, meaning an alkene directly bonded to the ring and terminated by a carboxylic acid group. The other is a boronic acid group, which is a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the E-configured double bond further restricts conformational freedom, though the carboxylic acid and boronic acid groups retain some rotational flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the two substituents are different. Both the carboxylic acid and the boronic acid provide hydrogen-bond donor sites through their hydroxyl groups, and their oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered isoxazole ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. A methyl group sits on one carbon of the ring, while a second carbon carries a phenyl ring bearing both a chlorine and a fluorine atom at its ortho and meta positions relative to the attachment point. The remaining ring carbon is bonded to an acyl chloride group, a reactive carbonyl functionality that serves as a strong electrophile. The aryl-isoxazole bond permits some rotation, so the molecule has moderate conformational flexibility, though the ortho-chloro substituent restricts that motion. The molecule lacks internal symmetry, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen, ring oxygen, and carbonyl oxygen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered isoxazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. A methyl group sits on one carbon of this ring, while the adjacent carbon carries a carboxylic acid group, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The opposite side of the ring is attached to a phenyl ring bearing a fluorine and a chlorine atom on adjacent positions, with the chlorine flanking the bond to the isoxazole. This ortho-substitution pattern creates steric crowding that twists the phenyl ring out of the plane of the isoxazole, giving the molecule a non-planar, moderately rigid shape with no internal symmetry. The isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carboxylic acid hydroxyl provides a donor site.

The molecule is built around a five-membered isoxazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, which carries a methyl group on one carbon. A second carbon of the isoxazole bears a phenyl ring, and that phenyl ring has a chlorine atom on the carbon directly adjacent to the point of attachment, giving an ortho-substitution pattern. The remaining carbon of the isoxazole carries an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl bonded to chlorine, which is a highly reactive electrophilic functional group. The aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, though rotation about the bond linking the two rings is possible and the ortho chlorine introduces steric hindrance that restricts it. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen and the carbonyl oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a five-membered isoxazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The ring carries a methyl group on one carbon and a carboxylic acid group on the adjacent carbon, which together define its substitution pattern. The third ring position bears a phenyl ring that is ortho-substituted with a chlorine atom, so the two aromatic rings are joined by a single bond and can twist relative to each other, giving moderate conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the isoxazole nitrogen and oxygen serve as additional acceptor sites. Overall the structure is largely planar and aromatic, with the carboxylic acid as its most polar, interaction-capable feature.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain, with a carboxylic acid group at one terminus and a benzene ring at the other. The benzene ring is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and a chlorine atom sits on the carbon directly adjacent to the point where the chain attaches, giving an ortho substitution pattern. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen. The two-carbon linker between the ring and the acid is flexible, allowing rotation about its single bonds, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis or mirror plane because the chlorine breaks the symmetry of the ring substitution.

The molecule is an α-aryl α,β-unsaturated aldehyde: an aldehyde carbonyl is attached to a tetrasubstituted-looking alkene carbon bearing a phenyl ring, with the alkene's other carbon linked to a furan ring through a single C=C double bond. The phenyl ring is unsubstituted, and the furan is a five-membered oxygen heterocycle attached at its 2-position, so the two aromatic rings are not fused to each other. The conjugated chain of carbonyl, alkene, and two aromatic rings makes the framework largely planar and rigid, with restricted rotation about the connecting bonds. The aldehyde oxygen and the furan ring oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a small, open-chain α,β-unsaturated aldehyde built on a furan scaffold. A furan ring, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, is attached directly to a two-carbon vinyl linker whose carbon-carbon double bond adopts the trans (E) geometry. That linker terminates in an aldehyde group, a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen, which is conjugated through the double bond to the aromatic ring. The substitution pattern is monosubstituted at the furan's 2-position, leaving the rest of the ring unsubstituted, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis beyond the planar conjugated arrangement. The conjugated system is largely rigid and planar, with only limited rotation about the single bond linking the ring to the alkene. The carbonyl oxygen and the furan oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a short, conjugated carboxylic acid built around a furan ring. A furan, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, is attached at its 2-position to a two-carbon chain that bears a terminal carboxylic acid group. The chain contains a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which makes the scaffold largely planar and rigid, and the conjugation extends across the ring and the alkene into the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the furan oxygen acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local planarity of its conjugated framework.

The molecule is a short carboxylic acid chain attached to a five-membered aromatic heterocycle. A three-carbon chain ends in a terminal carboxylic acid group, and the first carbon of that chain is joined to the 2-position of a furan ring, an aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom and four carbons with two double bonds. The furan is unsubstituted apart from this single attachment, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted at one carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. The molecule has no stereocenters and little internal symmetry beyond the planar ring, and its saturated chain gives it moderate conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the furan oxygen acts only as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in an ortho (1,2) arrangement. One substituent is a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, consisting of a saturated two-carbon linker attached to a carboxyl group. The other substituent is a hydroxyl group directly on the aromatic ring, adjacent to the propanoic side chain. The structure contains no fused or bridged ring systems, and the aromatic ring is planar and rigid while the side chain is flexible through its sp3 carbons. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the phenolic hydroxyl can likewise act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry elements beyond a local mirror plane through the ring, since the two substituents differ.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent oxygen substituents: a methoxy group (an aryl methyl ether) and an ether linkage to a three-carbon chain, making it a 1,2-disubstituted, ortho-patterned aromatic scaffold. The side chain is a flexible glycerol-derived unit, OCH2–CH(OH)–CH2OH, containing a secondary hydroxyl and a primary hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the propane-1,2-diol tail adds conformational flexibility through its rotatable single bonds. The molecule has no stereocenter-driven symmetry beyond the ring, and its asymmetric side chain lacks any mirror plane. Overall, the two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the two ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents at adjacent (ortho) positions: a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) and a three-carbon chain. That chain runs through two methylene units and ends in a carboxylic acid group, so the side chain is flexible while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. There is no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and the substitution pattern lacks any symmetry axis that would make the two sides identical. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen provides an additional weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic imidazole ring bearing two nitrogen atoms at non-adjacent positions. A methyl group sits on the carbon between the two nitrogens, while a nitro group, a nitrogen-bound oxygen-containing substituent, is attached to one ring carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ring nitrogen opposite the nitro-bearing side carries a two-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group, which adds a linear, rod-like extension to the otherwise compact aromatic core. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ethyl-nitrile side chain provides some conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the nitrile and nitro oxygens and the unsubstituted imidazole nitrogen can accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methyl group, making it a toluene-derived aromatic scaffold with the methyl and the ether oxygen positioned ortho to each other on the same ring. The ether oxygen links the ring to a three-carbon chain, which terminates in a 2,3-dihydroxypropyl unit featuring a secondary hydroxyl and a primary hydroxyl. Together these form a 1,2-diol motif attached through an aryl ether. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the ether linkage and propyl chain add conformational flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ether oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substitution pattern on the ring and the diol side chain are distinct.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene core, two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, with the thioether substituent attached at the 2-position of that bicyclic system. A three-carbon chain runs from the sulfur atom and terminates in a carboxylic acid group, so the molecule contains a flexible, sp3-rich linker between the rigid aromatic scaffold and the polar acid end. The sulfur bridges the ring and the chain as a thioether, and the aromatic system is largely planar and rigid, while the propanoic acid tail rotates freely. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens, and the sulfur can act as a weak acceptor. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituent sits at only one position on the naphthalene ring.

The molecule is built from a phenol ring bearing a single substituent at the meta position relative to the hydroxyl group, giving a 1,3-disubstituted benzene core. That substituent is a piperazine ring attached through one of its carbon atoms (a 2-piperazinyl group), so the two ring systems are joined by a single C–C bond with no ring fusion. The piperazine is a saturated six-membered ring containing two nitrogen atoms in a 1,4-relationship, and it carries a secondary amine N–H on each nitrogen. The phenolic hydroxyl and the two amine N–H groups together provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the oxygen and both nitrogen lone pairs serve as acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element of note because the attachment point on the piperazine breaks its internal symmetry, and it has moderate flexibility from rotation about the aryl–piperazine bond.

The molecule is a chalcone-type scaffold: a para-tolyl ketone (a benzene ring bearing a methyl group para to the carbonyl) linked through an α,β-unsaturated enone bridge to a thiophene ring. The enone C=C bridge is conjugated with both aromatic rings and is largely planar, giving the molecule a rigid, extended shape. The five-membered thiophene ring is attached at its 2-position, and the two aromatic rings are not fused to each other. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the tolyl ring. Its only hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since it has no N–H or O–H groups, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the thiophene sulfur provides weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups on adjacent carbons, forming a trimethoxy-substituted aromatic scaffold. A three-carbon chain terminating in a carboxylic acid is attached to the ring at the position opposite the central methoxy group, giving the ring a symmetric substitution pattern across its meta positions. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the propanoic acid side chain adds conformational flexibility through its rotatable single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the three ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a substituted urea built around a central carbonyl flanked by a dimethylamino group and an aryl-NH group. The aromatic portion is a benzene ring carrying two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, placed meta and para relative to the urea nitrogen, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, while the N,N-dimethyl terminus adds some local bulk but relatively few rotatable bonds overall. The single N-H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two chlorine atoms contribute electron-withdrawing character and additional lipophilic bulk to the aromatic ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon chain: a propanoic acid unit attached directly to the ring, with the carboxylic acid terminus at the far end of a two-carbon linker. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, placing them ortho to each other and meta and para to the alkyl chain, which gives an asymmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the saturated CH2-CH2 linker and the carboxyl group add conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one through its carbonyl oxygen. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors on the ring itself.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, and two adjacent hydroxyl groups forming a catechol unit. The substitution pattern places the propanoic acid side chain at one position and the two phenolic oxygens on neighboring carbons, which gives the aromatic core an asymmetric arrangement with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The single aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated CH2–CH2 linker and the carboxyl group provide some conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the carboxylic acid and the two phenolic hydroxyls can each donate a hydrogen bond, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens can accept them.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups, placing them ortho to each other on the aromatic core. A four-carbon chain attaches to the ring at the position para to one methoxy group; this chain contains a ketone carbonyl and terminates in a carboxylic acid, giving a 4-aryl-4-oxobutanoic acid framework. The aromatic ring is the only ring system, with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the benzene core. The chain is flexible through its two methylene units, while the aromatic ring is rigid and planar. Hydrogen-bond capability is concentrated at the carboxylic acid, which can both donate and accept, while the ketone and the two ether oxygens serve only as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon chain terminated in a carboxylic acid, with two methoxy groups attached to the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, and the two adjacent methoxy substituents sit at positions that make the substitution pattern 1,2,4 relative to the propanoic acid side chain. Because the ring is unfused, the scaffold is a simple monocyclic aromatic system with a flexible saturated linker between the ring and the acid. The side chain contains two methylene units, allowing rotation about several single bonds, so the molecule is fairly flexible. Overall, the structure has no symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane in the ring framework. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the two ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built around a five-membered 1H-pyrazole ring bearing a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O attached to a ring carbon) at one position. Adjacent to the formyl-bearing carbon, the pyrazole carries a phenyl ring directly attached by a single C–C bond, so the two aromatic rings are biaryl-linked and largely planar, giving the scaffold a fairly rigid character with limited conformational freedom. The phenyl ring is substituted with two fluorine atoms in a 3,5-pattern, meaning they sit meta to the point of attachment and to each other, which creates a symmetric substitution pattern across the benzene ring. The pyrazole N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyrazole ring nitrogen and the aldehyde oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a simple benzene-based compound: a single six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on the ring in a meta relationship (1,3-disubstitution). One is a primary amino group attached directly to the ring, making it an aniline-type unit. The other is a three-carbon chain (a propanoic acid side chain) bearing a terminal carboxylic acid group. The flexible saturated linker between the ring and the acid gives the molecule considerable conformational freedom, while the aromatic core is rigid and planar. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the carboxylic acid provides both donor (O–H) and acceptor (C=O and O) capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta arrangement: a bromine atom on one ring carbon and a three-carbon chain on another, with the chain terminating in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unfused, so the core scaffold is a single six-membered aromatic ring with no additional ring systems. The 3-(bromophenyl)propanoic acid framework contains a flexible saturated two-carbon linker between the ring and the carboxyl carbon, giving the molecule moderate rotational freedom. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond the local symmetry of the ring, because the two substituents differ. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group, a fluorine atom, and a 4-oxobutanoic acid chain (a ketone carbonyl followed by a two-carbon linker ending in a carboxylic acid). The methoxy and fluorine sit on adjacent ring carbons, and the acyl chain is attached para to the methoxy group, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the saturated CH2–CH2 linker and the rotatable C–O bonds add conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, the ketone carbonyl and the ether oxygen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the fluorine provides a weak acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring, with a terminal carboxylic acid group at one end, so the scaffold is an aryl-propanoic acid. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused benzene ring carrying one fluorine atom at the meta position relative to the propanoic acid side chain, which gives it an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry plane through the whole molecule. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the fluorine atom is a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor only. The two saturated CH2 linkers give the chain moderate conformational flexibility, whereas the benzene ring itself is rigid and planar.

The molecule is an acrylic acid derivative in which a carboxylic acid group is joined to a furan ring through a trans carbon-carbon double bond, giving an extended, conjugated, and fairly rigid backbone. The furan is a five-membered aromatic ring containing one oxygen atom, and it is attached at its 3-position, so the ring oxygen sits away from the point of attachment. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two oxygens). The furan oxygen can also act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the molecule is essentially planar with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local geometry of its rings and double bond.

The molecule is built on a three-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring, with a terminal carboxylic acid group at one end of the chain. The aromatic ring is a single benzene ring with no fused rings, and a hydroxyl group sits on the ring at the meta position relative to the chain, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror plane through the ring and chain in its planar average, so its symmetry is limited. The chain provides modest flexibility, while the ring is rigid. Both the carboxylic acid and the phenolic hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carboxyl oxygens add further acceptor capacity.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying two substituents at the meta positions relative to each other. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group and the ring), which acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor. The other is a three-carbon chain ending in a terminal carboxylic acid, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated propanoic-acid side chain adds rotational flexibility. The molecule has no fused rings and no internal symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement around the ring.

The molecule is built from a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle, bearing a three-carbon side chain at the 3-position (meta to the nitrogen). That side chain ends in a carboxylic acid group, attached through two methylene units, so the overall scaffold is a flexible propanoic acid tail on a flat, rigid aromatic core. There are no fused ring systems, and the molecule lacks any stereocenters or internal symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring. The carboxylic acid supplies both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the pyridine nitrogen provides an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring with two substituents placed para to each other, meaning they sit at opposite positions on the ring. One substituent is a primary amino group attached directly to the aromatic ring, which can donate hydrogen bonds and acts as an electron-donating group. The other substituent is a two-carbon saturated chain ending in a carboxylic acid, which provides both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the ethylene linker introduces some conformational flexibility. The structure has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the para pattern on the ring, and it contains no stereocenters.

The molecule is a 4-aryl-4-oxobutanoic acid built from a para-disubstituted benzene ring. One end of the benzene carries a bromine atom, and the other carries a ketone that links through a two-carbon chain to a terminal carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated CH2–CH2 linker gives the chain some flexibility. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local mirror plane of the ring, since its two substituents differ. The carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ketone carbonyl and the carbonyl oxygen of the acid serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement: a bromine atom on one side and a three-carbon chain on the other. That chain is a saturated two-carbon linker ending in a terminal carboxylic acid group, giving a 3-arylpropanoic acid scaffold. The benzene ring is flat and aromatic with no ring fusion, and the molecule has a degree of symmetry about the long axis through the ring. The side chain contributes some rotational flexibility, while the aromatic core is rigid. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, and the bromine is a weak halogen acceptor.

The molecule consists of a benzene ring bearing a bromine atom at the position para to a sulfur-linked side chain, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. The side chain is a thioether: a sulfur atom bonded directly to the ring and to a two-carbon chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid group. The aryl ring is planar and rigid, while the S–CH2–CH2–COOH tail provides rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the sulfur and oxygen atoms can act as weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry axis beyond the local pseudo-symmetry of the para-substituted ring.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One side bears a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, a propanoic acid group attached through a CH2–CH2 linker, while the opposite side bears a directly attached carboxylic acid group. The benzene core is fully aromatic and planar, giving the molecule a rigid central scaffold, while the two-carbon linker adds some rotational flexibility on one side. The overall structure has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the ring, though the two acid groups differ in their chain lengths. Both carboxylic acid groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their O–H groups and as hydrogen-bond acceptors through their carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is built from a para-chlorophenyl ring attached directly to a ketone carbonyl, which connects to a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond that terminates in a free carboxylic acid. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, carrying a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the ketone, giving it a simple para substitution pattern with a two-fold axis of symmetry through the ring. The conjugated enone linkage, with the C=C flanked by the ketone and the acid carbonyl, is rigid and essentially planar, so the overall framework is extended and fairly stiff. The carboxylic acid OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ketone and acid carbonyl oxygens act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chlorine adds a weak halogen-bond capability but contributes no donor functionality.

This molecule is built on a straight four-carbon chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid at one end and a ketone at the other, with the ketone carbon bonded to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single unfused six-membered benzene system bearing one chlorine atom at the position para to the ketone attachment, giving a 1,4-disubstituted pattern with a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the ring axis. The chain itself is flexible, with two rotatable methylene units separating the polar carbonyl groups from the rigid aromatic core. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and an acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built from a three-carbon glycerol-type chain bearing two terminal hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons, with the third carbon linked through an ether oxygen to a benzene ring. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered carbocycle carrying a chlorine atom para to the ether linkage, giving a 1,4-disubstitution pattern. The arrangement has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local symmetry of the para-substituted ring, and the flexible alkyl chain allows considerable conformational freedom. Two secondary and primary hydroxyl groups act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the ether oxygen serves only as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the chlorine contributes weak polarity without donor capacity.

The molecule is a flexible, acyclic dicarboxylic acid built around a central carbon that bears a para-chlorophenyl group. Two carboxylic acid groups sit at the ends of two-carbon chains branching from that central carbon, so the structure is a 3-aryl pentanedioic acid skeleton. The benzene ring carries a single chlorine atom at the position opposite the point of attachment, giving a para substitution pattern. The molecule lacks rotational symmetry because the aryl group sits on only one side of the central carbon, though the two acid-bearing arms are chemically similar. Each carboxylic acid group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, giving the molecule four hydrogen-bond acceptor sites and two donor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a chlorine atom on one side and a three-carbon chain on the other. That chain is a propanoic acid unit, with two saturated carbons linking the ring to a terminal carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the two-carbon linker gives the molecule modest flexibility around its single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygen atoms. The overall shape is elongated and roughly linear, with no stereocenters and no symmetry element beyond the local flat symmetry of the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring carrying two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One side bears an ethyl group, while the other has a four-carbon chain containing a ketone (aryl carbonyl) and a terminal carboxylic acid, so the chain is a 4-oxobutanoic acid unit attached to the ring. The aromatic core is planar and fully unsaturated, and it is the only ring system, with no fused rings present. The para arrangement gives the ring a two-fold symmetry axis through its substituents, though the flexible chain and ethyl group reduce overall molecular symmetry. The acyl chain contributes conformational flexibility via its sp3 methylene units, while the aromatic ring remains rigid. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (O–H) and acceptor (C=O), and the ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a 4-aryl-4-oxobutanoic acid built on a straight four-carbon chain. A single benzene ring carries a fluorine atom at the position opposite the ketone, giving a para-disubstituted, planar aromatic scaffold. The aryl ketone links that ring to a saturated CH2–CH2 spacer that terminates in a carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid can both donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its two oxygens, while the ketone oxygen and the fluorine act as additional acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, whereas the two-carbon chain between the ketone and the acid gives the molecule some conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is fused to a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring. The indole nitrogen carries an isopropyl group, a branched alkyl substituent attached through a single bond. At the 3-position of the five-membered ring sits a phenyl group, which in turn bears a fluorine atom at the para position relative to the point of attachment. The aromatic framework is largely planar and rigid, though the biaryl bond between the indole and the phenyl ring allows some rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since the indole nitrogen is fully substituted, but the fluorine and the aromatic nitrogen's lone pair can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a 3-(4-fluorophenyl)propanoic acid, built on a flexible three-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring with a fluorine atom at the position para to the propyl linkage, giving a symmetric 1,4-substitution pattern across the ring. The terminal carboxylic acid group, which contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), sits at the end of the saturated chain. The two methylene units between the ring and the acid group provide conformational flexibility, while the phenyl ring itself remains rigid and planar. The fluorine atom acts as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor and an electron-withdrawing substituent on the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents: a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons, and a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid at the position opposite the hydroxyl. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system with no additional rings. The methoxy and hydroxyl groups make it a phenol-ether with ortho-relationship, while the propanoic acid chain adds a flexible, rotatable tail. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents differ, and the aromatic core is rigid while the side chain gives conformational freedom. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups each contribute hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the ether oxygen acts as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship. One substituent is a hydroxyl group directly attached to the ring, making it a phenol. The other is a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, so the aromatic ring is connected to a two-carbon linker (CH2CH2) that terminates in a –COOH group. The ring is flat and rigid, while the saturated linker gives the carboxylic acid end some conformational freedom. The molecule is not symmetric overall, though the para pattern gives the ring a local two-fold arrangement. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, making the molecule capable of forming multiple hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings. It carries two substituents placed para to each other, meaning they sit at opposite positions on the ring. One substituent is a hydroxyl group, so the ring bears a phenolic OH. The other is a three-carbon chain ending in a nitrile group, a carbon-nitrogen triple bond. The alkyl linker between the ring and the nitrile adds some conformational flexibility, while the aromatic core remains rigid and planar. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a methoxy group (an oxygen linked to a methyl) at one position and a carbonyl-containing side chain at the para position, giving a 1,4-disubstituted aromatic core. The side chain is an aryl ketone connected through a carbon-carbon double bond with an E (trans) geometry to a terminal carboxylic acid, forming a conjugated, largely planar and rigid linker. The aromatic ring is unfused and carries no stereocenters, and the overall shape is elongated and extended across the molecule. The methoxy oxygen, the ketone oxygen, and the two carboxylic acid oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the carboxylic acid hydroxyl provides one hydrogen-bond donor site.

The molecule is a para-substituted benzene ring bearing two groups on opposite sides: a methoxy group (an aryl ether, O-CH3) and a four-carbon chain attached through a ketone. That chain runs from the ring carbonyl through two methylene units to a terminal carboxylic acid, so the aryl ketone and the carboxyl group are separated by a flexible CH2-CH2 linker. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aliphatic chain and methoxy group add conformational flexibility. The structure has no stereocenters and only a single mirror-plane-like symmetry axis through the ring, reflecting the para arrangement. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from the carboxylic acid, which can donate one hydrogen and accept two, and from the ketone and ether oxygens, which act as acceptors only.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) arrangement. One substituent is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group and the ring), and the other is a three-carbon chain ending in a carboxylic acid, with two methylene units separating the ring from the carbonyl carbon. The aromatic ring is flat and rigid, while the propanoic acid side chain is flexible and can rotate freely around its single bonds. The para substitution gives the molecule a degree of local symmetry across the ring axis. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and hydrogen-bond acceptors (the two oxygens), while the ether oxygen of the methoxy group serves as an additional acceptor.

The molecule is built on a para-disubstituted benzene ring carrying a methyl group on one side and a carbonyl-bearing side chain on the other. That side chain is an aryl ketone attached to a trans (E) carbon-carbon double bond, which terminates in a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic ring and the conjugated enone-acid unit form a largely planar, rigid framework with limited conformational flexibility. The ketone oxygen and both carboxylic acid oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the acid hydroxyl provides one hydrogen-bond donor site. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local two-fold axis of the para-substituted ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a para (1,4) relationship: a methyl group and a three-carbon chain. The chain runs from the ring through two methylene units and ends in a carboxylic acid group, so the overall scaffold is a 3-arylpropanoic acid. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and there are no fused or additional ring systems. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry through the long axis of the ring, though the flexible propanoic acid tail breaks it somewhat. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the rest of the structure contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta relationship: a hydroxyl group and a morpholine ring attached through its nitrogen atom. The morpholine is a saturated six-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen separated by two carbons on each side, adopting a flexible chair-like conformation that is not fused to the aromatic ring. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the morpholine oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and the tertiary amine nitrogen, being conjugated with the aryl ring, is a weak acceptor. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single rotatable bond connecting the nitrogen to the ring, giving it moderate rigidity overall with limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings. A primary aminomethyl group (–CH2–NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, placed meta to the ring nitrogen, which gives a 3-substituted pyridine pattern without any internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the aminomethyl side chain has rotational freedom about its single bonds. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and an acceptor site on its lone pair, and the pyridine nitrogen adds a further hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a Boc-protected beta-amino acid: a tert-butyl carbamate (tert-butoxycarbonyl) group is attached to the nitrogen of a three-carbon chain that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The stereocenter at the beta-carbon carries a phenyl ring bearing a single fluorine atom at the ortho position, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The molecule contains one benzene ring and no fused ring systems, and its bulky tert-butyl group adds steric bulk while the chain remains conformationally flexible. The carbamate N-H and the carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygens and the fluorine serve as acceptors.

The molecule is a Boc-protected beta-amino acid: a tert-butyl carbamate (CC(C)(C)OC(=O)N-) is attached to the nitrogen-bearing carbon of a three-carbon chain that terminates in a free carboxylic acid. That carbon also carries a phenyl ring bearing a single fluorine atom at the meta position relative to the attachment point. The molecule has no ring fusion, and its only ring is the monosubstituted benzene. The tert-butyl group contributes local symmetry, while the stereocentre and flexible chain make the overall shape fairly flexible. The carbamate N-H and carboxylic acid O-H act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygens, ether oxygen, and fluorine act as acceptors.

This molecule is a phenylpropanoic acid derivative built around a single benzene ring bearing a methoxy group at the meta position relative to the side chain. The side chain runs from the ring to a carboxylic acid through a stereogenic carbon that also carries a carbamate nitrogen, which is protected by a tert-butoxycarbonyl group. The aromatic ring is the only ring system, so the scaffold is non-fused and the substitution pattern is meta-disubstituted. Flexibility comes mainly from the saturated three-carbon chain and the bulky tert-butyl group, while the aromatic ring and carbamate remain relatively planar. The carboxylic acid OH and carbamate NH act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygens and the methoxy oxygen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to the ring, which contributes two hydroxyl groups that can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The other substituent is a bromomethyl group, CH2Br, attached through a flexible sp3 carbon, adding a reactive carbon-bromine bond at the benzylic position. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid and bromomethyl arms have limited rotational freedom around their single bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring, since the two substituents differ.

This molecule is a diarylmethanol: a central sp3 carbon bearing one hydroxyl group and two identical aryl rings. Each aryl ring is a benzene ring carrying two trifluoromethyl groups in the 3 and 5 positions relative to the point of attachment, giving a symmetric meta,meta'-substitution pattern. The two halves are mirror-related about the central carbon, so the molecule has overall C2-like symmetry with the carbinol carbon as a stereogenic center bearing an H, OH, and two aryl groups that are equivalent. The aromatic rings are unfused and connected only through the flexible single bond to the central carbon, so conformational freedom is moderate. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl groups are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl group bridges two identical phenyl rings. Each phenyl ring is a benzene ring attached to the carbonyl carbon at one position and carrying two trifluoromethyl groups at the meta positions (3 and 5) relative to that attachment, giving a symmetric 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl pattern on both sides. The molecule has approximately two-fold symmetry through the carbonyl, and the aromatic rings are rigid while the bonds to the carbonyl allow some rotation. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a biphenyl scaffold: two benzene rings joined by a single C–C bond between their para-positions relative to each other's linkage. Each ring carries an amino group and two methyl groups, arranged symmetrically so that the two halves are mirror-related. The amino groups sit ortho to one methyl on each ring, creating a crowded, hindered environment around the nitrogen atoms. Each aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, while the central biaryl bond allows some rotation, though the flanking methyl groups restrict it. The two primary amine groups can act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the aromatic system offers additional weak interaction sites.

The molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond, giving a 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbiphenyl scaffold. Each ring carries three methyl groups in a symmetric 1,3,5 pattern, with the two rings bearing identical substitution, so the molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the central biaryl bond. There are no ring fusions, heteroatoms, or other functional groups. The methyl groups are nonpolar alkyl substituents, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor sites. The aromatic rings are rigid, while rotation about the central biaryl bond remains relatively free, allowing a range of twisted conformations.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone: two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group (C=O), giving a planar, conjugated backbone. Each aromatic ring carries a single trifluoromethyl group (-CF3) at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment point, so the two substituents sit symmetrically on opposite sides of the molecule. The overall structure has approximately two-fold symmetry about the carbonyl axis. The aryl-carbonyl bonds allow some rotation, so the molecule is moderately flexible, though conjugation favors near-planar arrangements. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all remaining hydrogens are aromatic C-H bonds.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone built from two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group, giving a benzophenone-type scaffold. Each aromatic ring carries a primary amino group placed meta to the carbonyl attachment point, so the two substituents sit symmetrically on opposite rings. The two phenyl rings are unfused and connected by a single sp2 carbon, which gives a fairly planar but somewhat twisted overall shape around the ketone. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis running through the carbonyl carbon and oxygen. The two amino groups can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pairs can accept them.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined through a single methylene (CH2) bridge, giving a diarylmethane scaffold with no fused ring systems. Each aromatic ring is a simple six-membered benzene ring that carries one primary amino group (-NH2). The two amino groups sit at the meta position relative to the bridging carbon on their respective rings, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the central CH2 group. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the methylene carbon. Its rigidity comes from the aromatic rings, while the CH2 linker permits some rotational freedom between them. Each amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bonded directly to two separate benzene rings. Each ring carries a single fluorine atom at the meta position, meaning two carbons away from the point where it attaches to the carbonyl carbon. The two aromatic rings are symmetrically substituted, so the overall structure has a mirror-type symmetry running through the carbonyl group. The C=O unit is an electron-withdrawing acceptor that can take part in hydrogen bonding, while the fluorine atoms add weak acceptor capability and no donor sites are present. The two rings can rotate about the single bonds linking them to the carbonyl, giving moderate conformational flexibility around the central ketone.

This molecule is a biaryl built from two benzene rings joined by a single carbon-carbon bond between their ring carbons, with no fused ring system. Each ring carries one fluorine atom at the meta position relative to that biaryl bond, so the two substituents sit on opposite sides and are mirror-related, giving the molecule an approximate C2 or mirror symmetry. The aromatic rings are flat and the central bond allows only limited twisting, so the scaffold is fairly rigid. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen is on carbon. The fluorine atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds, while the pi-electron faces of the rings offer additional weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built from two identical benzene rings joined by a 1,2-diketone bridge, giving a symmetric benzil-type scaffold. Each aromatic ring carries a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) at the meta position relative to the carbonyl attachment point, so the two substituents sit on the same side pattern of the molecule. The central C(=O)–C(=O) unit is a rigid, planar-leaning linker that connects the two rings, while the methoxy groups add modest conformational flexibility through their C–O bonds. The two carbonyl oxygens and the two ether oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a small acyclic aliphatic diol built on a four-carbon chain. Its skeleton features a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, a tert-butyl-type unit, attached to a carbon that carries a hydroxyl group and then a terminal hydroxymethyl group. There are no rings, no ring fusion, and no aromatic or unsaturated systems. The two hydroxyl groups are primary and secondary alcohols located on adjacent carbons, and the bulky tert-butyl group creates a branched, asymmetric arrangement with a stereogenic center at the carbinol carbon. Because the chain is unbranched beyond the tert-butyl group and has no rings, it is fairly flexible, while both hydroxyls can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors.

The molecule has a linear four-carbon chain with a terminal primary alcohol, and it contains no rings or aromatic systems. The carbon skeleton is a neopentyl-type unit: a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups is attached to a two-carbon chain that ends in a hydroxyl group on the terminal carbon. The only functional group is that primary alcohol, which is the single site of substitution on an otherwise saturated alkyl framework. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry element beyond the equivalent methyl groups on the quaternary carbon, and the sp3 chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

This molecule is a short, fully saturated-except-for-one-bond hydrocarbon built on a branched chain rather than any ring system. Its skeleton consists of a terminal vinyl group (CH2=CH–) attached to a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl substituents, giving a 3,3-dimethyl-substituted butene-type framework. There are no heteroatoms, no ring fusion, and no functional groups beyond the single carbon-carbon double bond, so it has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability. The quaternary center makes the two methyl groups equivalent, lending a partial local symmetry, while the molecule remains small and largely rigid around the double bond with only limited rotational freedom about the single bonds.

The molecule is built on a short acyclic carbon skeleton with no rings. A terminal alkyne group, a carbon-carbon triple bond bearing a hydrogen at one end, forms one end of the chain. The triple-bonded carbon is attached to a quaternary carbon that carries two methyl groups, giving a tert-butyl-like branched arrangement at the other end. There are no heteroatoms, so no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors are present, and the molecule is nonpolar in its functional character. Its only notable feature is the rigid, linear geometry around the alkyne, with the bulky branched end providing a compact, roughly symmetric terminus.

The molecule is a small, saturated, acyclic alcohol built on a branched carbon skeleton. Its backbone is a six-carbon chain containing a secondary hydroxyl group on one end, with a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups located adjacent to the carbinol carbon. There are no rings, no double or triple bonds, and no aromatic systems, so the structure is entirely sp3-hybridized and conformationally flexible about its single bonds. The only functional group is the hydroxyl, which can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The molecule lacks any overall symmetry because the hydroxyl-bearing carbon is a stereocenter with an asymmetric substitution pattern.

The molecule is a short, unsaturated carboxylic acid built on a linear four-carbon-plus-methyl chain with no rings. A terminal carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) sits at one end, and the carbon-carbon double bond adjacent to it (an α,β-unsaturation) places a conjugated alkene next to the carbonyl. The other end of the skeleton carries two methyl groups on the same alkene carbon, giving a trisubstituted double bond with a branched, compact substitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited rotational freedom, so it is relatively rigid around the double bond. The carboxylic acid group provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens).

The molecule is a short, acyclic carboxylic acid built on a straight chain with no rings and no aromatic groups. A quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, the tert-butyl unit, sits at one end and is joined by a methylene linker to a carboxyl group at the other end. Its single carboxylic acid functionality can both donate one hydrogen bond through the hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens. The tert-butyl group is bulky and symmetric about its central carbon, while the chain between it and the acid has some rotational freedom, so the overall structure is compact but moderately flexible.

The molecule is built on a short, acyclic carbon chain with no rings. At its center sits a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, which gives the backbone a branched, bulky shape. Two identical carboxylic acid groups sit at the ends of the two arms, each attached through a single methylene unit, so the molecule has approximate two-fold symmetry about the central carbon. Each carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total. The chain is fairly flexible because of its single bonds, though the gem-dimethyl group restricts some rotations.

This molecule is a symmetric acyclic dianhydride-type structure built from two 3,3-dimethylglutaric-derived halves linked through a central mixed anhydride. Each end carries a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, a methylene spacer, and a terminal carboxylic acid, giving a gem-dimethyl substitution pattern on both arms. The central C(=O)–O–C(=O) unit joins the two halves, creating an anhydride functional group flanked by two free carboxylic acids. Because there are no rings, the chain has considerable conformational flexibility, though the gem-dimethyl groups impose some local steric restriction. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the two free carboxylic acids can act as both donors and acceptors, while the anhydride oxygens serve as acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a straight-chain-like acyclic alkane skeleton with no rings, so there is no ring fusion or aromatic system to describe. Its carbon framework consists of a central quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups and two ethyl-type branches, giving a compact, highly branched arrangement. There are no functional groups, heteroatoms, or substituents beyond carbon and hydrogen, so the substitution pattern is entirely alkyl. The structure has a reasonable degree of symmetry around the central carbon, and because all bonds are single and rotatable, it is fairly flexible. It has no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone: a central carbonyl carbon bonded to two separate benzene rings, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Each benzene ring carries one nitro group (–NO2) attached at the meta position relative to the carbonyl linkage, so the two rings are substituted identically. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the nitro oxygens provide additional acceptor sites, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry axis passing through the carbonyl group. The two aryl rings can rotate about their bonds to the carbonyl carbon, so the scaffold is moderately flexible rather than rigid.

The molecule is a primary amine built on a three-carbon chain in which the central carbon bears two phenyl rings, so the scaffold is a 1,1-diphenylpropane core with the amino group at the terminal carbon. Both aromatic rings are unsubstituted benzene rings, attached to the same carbon, and they are not fused to each other or to any other ring system. The only functional group is the primary amino group (-NH2), which acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. The structure has a sp3 carbon framework with rotatable single bonds, giving it considerable conformational flexibility, and the central carbon is a stereocenter, so the molecule is chiral with no internal mirror symmetry overall.

This molecule is a symmetric, acyclic disulfide built from two identical three-carbon chains joined through a central S–S bond. Each half consists of a terminal carboxylic acid group attached to a two-carbon methylene linker that leads to the disulfide bridge, so the two arms mirror each other across the sulfur–sulfur axis. There are no rings or ring fusions, and the scaffold is entirely flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds. Each carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, giving the molecule two donor and four acceptor sites in total, while the sulfur atoms serve only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a cyclopentane ring whose single quaternary carbon, C1, carries two identical acetic acid side chains, making it a 1,1-disubstituted cyclopentane with a geminal substitution pattern. The ring itself is saturated and unfused, so there are no aromatic or unsaturated rings present. Each side chain ends in a carboxylic acid group, giving two C=O acceptor sites and two O-H donor sites, so the structure can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds at each terminus. The two arms are attached at the same carbon, which gives the molecule an approximate mirror symmetry through that carbon and the ring. The core is fairly flexible because of the saturated ring and the rotatable methylene linkers, though the quaternary center limits how freely the arms can move relative to each other.

This molecule is an acyclic dicarboxylic acid with a flexible, linear skeleton built from two propanoic acid units joined through a central thioether sulfur atom. Each terminal end carries a carboxylic acid group (–COOH), so the molecule has two identical functional groups arranged in a mirror-symmetric pattern about the central sulfur. There are no rings and no ring fusion, and the chain's many single bonds allow considerable conformational flexibility. Each carboxylic acid can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the sulfur atom contributes a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a five-membered 1,3-dioxole ring, making it a benzodioxole (methylenedioxybenzene) scaffold. The fused dioxole ring contains two ether oxygens bridged by a methylene carbon, which together give the ring system a flat, rigid character. A hydroxymethyl group (a primary alcohol, CH2OH) is attached to the aromatic ring at a position meta to one of the ring oxygens, creating an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror symmetry beyond the planar framework. The hydroxyl group can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the two dioxole oxygens act only as hydrogen-bond acceptors. Overall, the molecule is compact and largely rigid, with conformational flexibility limited to rotation about the single bond linking the hydroxymethyl group to the ring.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with a nitrogen atom at one position among the carbons. A carboxylic acid group is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, so the acid and the nitrogen sit side by side. The remaining four ring carbons each carry a chlorine atom, making the substitution pattern dense and asymmetric. The ring is flat and rigid, while the carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and several acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen, the other acid oxygen, and the ring nitrogen).

This molecule is a flavone, built on a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring. A second benzene ring is attached through a single bond at the 2-position of the pyranone, giving a largely planar, rigid, conjugated framework. The fused benzo ring carries two methoxy groups, and the pendant phenyl ring carries two adjacent methoxy groups at its 3- and 4-positions. The carbonyl oxygen and the ring ether oxygen, together with the four methoxy oxygens, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen, making it a pyrazole core. Three bromine atoms are attached directly to the ring carbons, occupying every carbon position, so the substitution pattern is fully halogenated and there is no remaining C-H on the carbon framework. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the bromines lie in the ring plane, giving the molecule only a low degree of symmetry. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated pyridine-like nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom and five carbon atoms, with no fused ring systems. Three bromine atoms are attached as substituents to three of the ring carbons, and they sit at positions that are not all adjacent to one another, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern on the ring. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the carbon-bromine bonds. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that makes it a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substitution pattern places one primary amino group on the ring with three chlorine atoms attached at the remaining positions, three of which are adjacent to each other, giving a trisubstituted aniline-type arrangement with an asymmetric distribution of substituents. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the amino and chloro groups lie in its plane and add no meaningful conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. The chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and contribute to the electron-poor character of the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a trifluoromethyl group and three chlorine atoms. The trifluoromethyl group sits at one position on the ring, and the three chlorines occupy three contiguous carbons on the opposite side, giving a 1,2,3-trichloro-5-(trifluoromethyl) substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system. Overall the molecule has only a mirror-plane symmetry through the ring, with no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors beyond the weakly electronegative halogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom and five carbon atoms. Three chlorine atoms are attached as substituents to the ring carbons, placed at positions that cluster together on one side of the nitrogen, giving a crowded, asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and it contains no fused rings, so the scaffold is rigid with essentially no conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydroxyl, amine, carbonyl, or other classic hydrogen-bond donor groups, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds. Its only acceptor site is the lone pair on the ring nitrogen, which is weakly basic because the electron-withdrawing chlorines pull electron density away from it.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, which contains one sulfur atom in place of carbon. The ring carries four substituents: an acyl chloride group (a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine) at one carbon adjacent to the sulfur, and three chlorine atoms on the remaining ring carbons, with two of them flanking each other. The substitution pattern is fully crowded, with no ring hydrogens remaining. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring, and it has no internal symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the sulfur atom can act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle, bearing a carboxylic acid group on one ring carbon adjacent to the sulfur. Three chlorine atoms occupy the remaining ring positions, with two on adjacent carbons and one on the carbon next to the sulfur, so the substitution pattern is fully crowded around the ring and no hydrogens remain on the core. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the carboxylic acid and the three chlorines sit at distinct positions. Its rigid, planar aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxylic acid group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the sulfur and chlorine atoms contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, which serves as the main functional group and sets the scaffold as a benzoic acid derivative. Three ethoxy groups (–OCH2CH3) are attached to the ring at positions that place two of them flanking the carboxylic acid-bearing carbon's meta positions and the third adjacent to one of them, giving a 3,4,5-trisubstituted pattern with the acid at position 1. The aromatic ring is fully conjugated and planar, so it is rigid, while the three ethoxy chains add conformational flexibility at their terminal ends. The molecule has an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the carboxyl carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the central ethoxy-bearing carbon. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl hydrogen and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the three ether oxygens can act only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and three fluorine atoms occupy the next three carbons around the ring, with the remaining ring positions bearing hydrogen. The fluorine atoms are placed on adjacent carbons, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no more than a single mirror plane through the ring. The rigid aromatic framework gives the molecule little conformational flexibility, with only the amino hydrogens free to rotate. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) is attached to one ring carbon, and three fluorine atoms occupy three adjacent ring positions, leaving the remaining two ring carbons bearing hydrogen. The fluorines sit contiguously, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, with the methoxy group positioned meta to the cluster of fluorines. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group retains some rotational freedom about its C–O bonds. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a single aldehyde group, with three fluorine atoms attached to adjacent ring carbons, so the fluorines sit together on one side of the ring. The aldehyde carbonyl is conjugated with the aromatic system and is the only polar functional group other than the carbon-fluorine bonds. The aromatic core is a flat, fully rigid six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the ring carbons carry three fluorines and one formyl group in a 1,3,4,5-type pattern, leaving two ring hydrogens. The overall framework has no symmetry relating the two ring hydrogens, so the molecule is asymmetric. The aldehyde oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine atoms offer only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a boronic acid built on a single benzene ring, with the boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups attached directly to the aromatic carbon. The ring carries three fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons located at the positions meta and para relative to the boronic acid group, giving a 3,4,5-trifluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the B(OH)2 group can rotate about its carbon-boron bond. The molecule has a mirror plane through the boron and the para carbon, so it has a degree of symmetry, although the fluorine atoms break the symmetry of the ring's lower half. The two hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fusion to other rings. A carboxylic acid group (–C(=O)OH) is attached to one ring carbon, and three fluorine atoms occupy the three ring positions adjacent or meta to it, specifically on carbons 3, 4, and 5 relative to the acid group, so the three fluorines sit contiguously on one side of the ring. The fluorines are strongly electron-withdrawing substituents bonded directly to the aromatic framework, while the carboxyl group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor oxygens. The ring is planar and rigid, with only the carboxyl group capable of rotation, and the overall substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis passing through the carboxyl carbon.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three adjacent fluorine atoms and a nitrile group, so it is a trisubstituted benzonitrile. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no sp3 carbons. The nitrile (cyano, -C≡N) group sits at one position, and three fluorines occupy three consecutive carbons, leaving two aromatic C-H positions. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a single plane of the ring. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorines are only weak acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic-acid-type structure: a benzene ring bearing a trans-configured acrylic acid side chain, meaning a carboxylic acid group joined to the ring through a two-carbon alkene linker. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered benzene core with no fused rings. Three fluorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, creating a 3,4,5-trifluoro substitution pattern relative to the vinyl attachment, which gives the ring a mirror-plane symmetry through the attachment point and the opposite carbon. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond from its OH and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen, while the ring fluorines act only as weak acceptors. The rigid planar alkene and aromatic system limit conformational flexibility, leaving only rotation around the bond to the carboxyl group.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, bearing one hydroxyl group and three fluorine atoms. The hydroxyl sits on one ring carbon, and the three fluorines occupy three adjacent carbons on the opposite side of the ring, giving a contiguous trifluoro substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that maps the substituents onto themselves, so it is asymmetric.
