The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms serve only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile, C≡N) at one position. Three fluorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, forming a contiguous trifluorinated stretch on the aromatic core, while the remaining two ring positions carry hydrogens. The benzene ring is planar and rigid, and the nitrile is linear, so the scaffold is largely flat with only the CH2 linker providing rotational freedom. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry across the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups (–OCH3) on adjacent-to-one-another positions, namely at three consecutive carbons of the ring, with the remaining two ring positions bearing hydrogen. An acetyl group (–C(=O)CH3) is attached at the position across from the central methoxy substituent, making the ring a 1,3,4,5-substituted pattern when counted around the ring. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the methyl rotations and the carbonyl-bearing side chain adding flexibility. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the central methoxy group and the acetyl-bearing carbon. The ketone oxygen and the three ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, fully aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent and alternating positions around the ring, forming a three-ether substitution pattern that makes the ring electron-rich. A primary amino group (–NH2) sits on the ring at the position opposite the central methoxy group, so the aromatic core carries one amine and three ether oxygens. The substituents are arranged with a degree of local symmetry about the axis running through the amine and the central methoxy carbon, though the two outer methoxy groups differ slightly in their environment. The ring itself is rigid, while the methoxy groups add modest rotational flexibility. The amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat aromatic scaffold with six carbons. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent ring positions, forming a contiguous cluster of ether substituents, while a carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) sits on the position opposite the middle methoxy group, so the substitution pattern is 3,4,5-trisubstituted with respect to the amide. The three methoxy oxygens and the amide carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the two amide N–H hydrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The ring carries no fused rings, and its rotatable bonds, mainly around the methoxy and amide groups, give limited conformational flexibility. The arrangement lacks a full mirror or rotational symmetry because the amide group differs from the three ether groups.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups and one boronic acid group, arranged on adjacent and meta-related positions. The three methoxy substituents sit on three consecutive carbons, while the B(OH)2 group occupies the position para to the central methoxy, giving a 3,4,5-trimethoxy-type substitution pattern on a single aromatic scaffold. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring and the para axis, so its symmetry is relatively high, although the methoxy methyl groups can rotate. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the ether and boronic acid substituents add some conformational flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the oxygen atoms of the three methoxy groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. A carboxylic acid group sits at one position on the ring, and three methoxy groups occupy the remaining positions, with two flanking the acid and one adjacent to it, giving a symmetric 3,4,5-trisubstituted pattern. The carboxylic acid can donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept one through its carbonyl oxygen, while the three ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can only act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The methoxy substituents add modest conformational freedom through rotation about their C–O bonds, but the core remains largely planar and rigid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent ring carbons in a contiguous 1,2,3 pattern, and a nitrile group (–C≡N) sits on the carbon opposite the central methoxy group, giving a 3,4,5-trimethoxy-substituted arrangement relative to the nitrile. The structure has a local mirror plane passing through the nitrile carbon and the central methoxy-bearing carbon, so the two flanking methoxy groups are equivalent. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups add modest rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. Oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three methoxy groups (–OCH3) on adjacent positions at one end of the ring, forming a 3,4,5-trimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the acyl group. The remaining ring position bears an acyl chloride group (–C(=O)Cl), which is the sole reactive functional group in the molecule. The six-membered aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, while the three methoxy substituents add modest conformational flexibility through rotation about their C–O bonds. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis passing through the acyl carbon and the carbon opposite it on the ring, since the two outer methoxy groups are equivalent. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its three ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a cinnamic acid scaffold: a benzene ring carrying a three-carbon chain that ends in an alpha,beta-unsaturated carboxylic acid. The aromatic ring bears three methoxy groups, placed at the 3, 4, and 5 positions relative to the side chain, which gives it a symmetric substitution pattern. The alkene linking the ring to the acid is conjugated with both the aromatic system and the carbonyl. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the three ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only. The planar, conjugated framework is fairly rigid, though the methoxy groups add some conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached at adjacent positions, and a hydroxyl group (–OH) sits on the ring two positions away from the first methoxy, with the remaining two ring carbons bearing hydrogens. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, since the hydroxyl breaks the threefold arrangement of the methoxy groups. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the three methoxy groups have some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups and one isocyanate group. The three methoxy (–OCH3) substituents sit on adjacent carbons at one side of the ring, while the isocyanate (–N=C=O) group is placed on the carbon opposite that cluster, giving a 1,3,5-type relationship with respect to the methoxy-bearing positions. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is compact and planar, with the methoxy oxygens and the linear N=C=O unit able to rotate about their bonds. Hydrogen-bond acceptor capability comes from the oxygen atoms of the three ethers and the carbonyl oxygen, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make all three methoxy groups equivalent.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups and one isothiocyanate group. The three methoxy substituents sit on adjacent carbons, forming a contiguous trimethoxy pattern, while the isothiocyanate group occupies the position meta to the central methoxy and para to the first methoxy group. The aromatic core is a single fused-free benzene ring, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, with the methoxy ethers adding modest conformational flexibility through rotation about the C–O bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that includes all substituents, since the isothiocyanate breaks the mirror relationship. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule carries no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups on adjacent-to-one-another positions, forming a 1,2,3-trimethoxy pattern on one side of the ring with the remaining substituent placed meta to the central methoxy group. A two-carbon chain attached to that position ends in a carboxylic acid, so the acetic acid side chain is the principal polar feature. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the three methoxy ethers and the CH2-C(=O)OH linker add conformational flexibility at their single bonds. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a possible local two-fold arrangement of the methoxy groups.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three methoxy groups (–OCH3) on adjacent positions, forming a 1,2,3-trimethoxy arrangement, and a cyanomethyl group (–CH2–C≡N) attached at the position opposite the central methoxy group. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the rest of the structure is rigid aside from rotation about the single bonds of the methoxy and cyanomethyl substituents. The substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis through the central methoxy carbon and the carbon bearing the cyanomethyl group, so the two flanking methoxy groups are chemically equivalent. The ether oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three methyl groups occupy three adjacent positions on the ring, creating a crowded, contiguous substitution pattern, while a single hydroxyl group sits on the carbon meta to the nearest methyl groups. The hydroxyl oxygen can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, whereas the methyl groups contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability. The molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. Its rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the hydroxyl hydrogen and the methyl C–H bonds free to rotate.

This molecule is built on a single six-membered oxygen-containing ring with one carbon-carbon double bond, a dihydropyran-type scaffold that is partially unsaturated and therefore somewhat rigid. Three acetyl ester groups are attached to the ring, two directly on ring carbons and one on a hydroxymethyl-type side arm, so the substitution pattern is contiguous and not symmetric. The molecule contains stereocenters that give it defined three-dimensional geometry, and the ester oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups present.

The molecule is built on a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one core (a chromone) carrying a phenyl ring at the 2-position. The chromone is a fused bicyclic system in which a benzene ring is joined to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring, giving a largely planar, rigid framework. Three methoxy groups are attached to the aromatic rings, two on the fused benzo portion and two on the pendant phenyl ring, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring-carbonyl oxygen and the ether oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a chromone (benzopyran-4-one) scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyranone ring. A catechol-bearing phenyl group is attached at the 3-position of the pyranone ring, giving the molecule a biaryl-like extension. The benzo ring carries a single hydroxyl group, and the phenyl ring carries two adjacent hydroxyl groups at its 3- and 4-positions. The fused core is largely planar and rigid, with the aryl substituent able to rotate only modestly about its single bond. Together, the four phenolic hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ketone carbonyl and the ring ether oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring carries a trifluoromethyl group at the para position relative to the carbonyl, while the other carries a trifluoromethyl group at the meta position. Each aromatic ring is a simple, unfused six-membered system, so the scaffold has no fused ring systems. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two aryl rings are attached through a single sp2 carbon, giving the molecule a moderately flexible, non-planar overall shape, and it lacks any symmetry because the two trifluoromethyl substituents sit at different positions.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents, with a planar aromatic core as its scaffold. Two acetamido groups (N-acetyl amide linkages) are attached at adjacent ring positions, while a carboxylic acid group sits on the ring carbon para to one of them, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the two amide groups are positioned differently relative to the acid. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the amide and carboxyl groups have some rotational freedom. Each acetamido group offers an N–H donor and a C=O acceptor, and the carboxylic acid contributes both a donor and two acceptor oxygens, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bonding sites.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydrazide group (-C(=O)NHNH2) on one carbon and two adjacent primary amino groups (-NH2) on the neighboring carbons, giving a 1,2-diamino-4-substituted aromatic scaffold. The central ring is a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and its substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The hydrazide carbonyl and the terminal hydrazine nitrogen are both conjugated with the ring to varying degrees, while the aromatic and hydrazide bonds contribute some rotational restriction, so the molecule is moderately rigid with a flexible hydrazide tail. Hydrogen-bond capability is high: the three amino and hydrazide NH groups act as donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and the amine nitrogens act as acceptors.

This molecule is a benzophenone scaffold, consisting of two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl group, so the carbonyl is a diaryl ketone. One ring carries two amino groups on adjacent carbons, giving an ortho-diamine substitution pattern, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The two aromatic rings are not fused to each other, and the central C=O linkage allows a twisted, moderately flexible geometry with no internal symmetry between the two halves. The amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and both the amines and the carbonyl oxygen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The ring contains one nitrogen atom, and two primary amine groups are attached to adjacent carbon atoms, placing them in an ortho relationship to each other on one side of the ring nitrogen's neighborhood. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the molecule has only minimal conformational flexibility, since the amine groups can rotate but have no other rotatable bonds. Overall the structure has a rough mirror-plane symmetry through the ring. Both amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, each offering two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the amine nitrogens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent amino groups and one methyl group, giving a simple aromatic diamine scaffold with no fused rings. The two amino substituents sit on neighboring carbons (an ortho-diamine arrangement), while the methyl group is placed on the ring meta to one amine and para to the other, creating an unsymmetrical substitution pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The benzene core is planar and rigid, while the amino and methyl groups add only limited conformational freedom through rotation about their bonds to the ring. Each primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites and a lone pair that can act as an acceptor, so the molecule as a whole can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds. The adjacent amines are also positioned to chelate or cyclize with appropriate partners.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. It carries three halogen substituents: a fluorine on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and two bromine atoms, one on the carbon directly beside that fluorine and another on the carbon two positions away across the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar with no fused ring systems, and the substituent pattern leaves the molecule without any rotatable bonds, so it is rigid. The ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all remaining ring positions bear only aromatic C–H hydrogens.

The molecule is a benzaldehyde, meaning a single benzene ring bearing a formyl group (–CHO) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two bromine atoms occupy adjacent ring positions, giving a 3,4-dibromo substitution pattern relative to the aldehyde, which breaks any mirror or rotational symmetry in the ring. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and it is essentially planar and rigid, with only the aldehyde carbonyl able to rotate about its bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle with no fused rings attached. Two bromine atoms are substituted onto the carbon atoms of the ring at adjacent positions, which places them on the 3- and 4-positions relative to the sulfur, giving a 3,4-dibromo substitution pattern. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, and it has a two-fold axis of symmetry through the sulfur atom and the midpoint of the opposite C–H bond. Because the ring carries no hydrogen-bond donor groups, its only hydrogen-bond character comes from the weak acceptor capacity of the sulfur atom, while the bromine atoms contribute halogen-bonding potential rather than classical hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three substituents. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms occupy two adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-dibromo arrangement with the methyl placed meta to the nearer bromine and para to the farther one. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar framework. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with the methyl and bromine groups attached in-plane and essentially free of rotational flexibility beyond the methyl rotor. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors, since the only heteroatoms are the bromines, which are weak halogen contributors rather than classical hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring carrying an acetyl group, that is, a two-carbon ketone in which a methyl group is bonded to a carbonyl carbon attached directly to the ring. Two chlorine atoms are bonded to adjacent ring carbons, positioned meta and para to the acetyl group, giving a 1,2-dichloro substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, and the substituents are fixed in place, so the scaffold is rigid apart from limited rotation of the acetyl group. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no O–H or N–H groups, but the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. Overall, the structure has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local arrangement of its substituents, which make it asymmetric.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The ring carries a primary amine group (-NH2) at one position and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, located on the carbons directly next to each other and on the opposite side of the ring from the amine's neighbors, giving a 1,2-dichloro arrangement with the amine para to one chlorine. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amine's C-N bond. The molecule lacks symmetry because the amine and the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions. The amine's two hydrogens make it a hydrogen-bond donor, while the nitrogen lone pair can accept hydrogen bonds; the chlorines contribute only weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen linked to a methyl group) and two chlorine atoms on adjacent ring carbons. The two chlorines sit next to each other, and the methoxy group is positioned meta to one chlorine and para to the other, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern on an aromatic core. The molecule contains no stereocenters and has no internal symmetry beyond a possible rotation of the methoxy methyl group, so the aromatic framework itself is planar and rigid. The ether oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the methoxy group and the aromatic carbons carry only hydrogens or substituents without acidic protons.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a formyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen) on one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms on adjacent ring carbons. Taking the aldehyde carbon as position 1, the chlorines sit at positions 3 and 4, so the substitution pattern is 1,3,4 on a single aromatic ring with no additional ring systems or ring fusion. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the aldehyde is the only rotatable linkage, with the two chlorines contributing steric and electronic bulk on one side. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane coinciding with all substituents, so it is asymmetric overall. The aldehyde oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing an oxime group, which is a carbon-nitrogen double bond attached to a hydroxyl group (C=N-OH). The aromatic ring is substituted at the 1-position with this oxime-bearing carbon and carries two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, at the 3- and 4-positions relative to the oxime group. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, with no fused ring systems. The oxime hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its O-H and as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through both its oxygen and nitrogen lone pairs. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis due to the asymmetric chlorine pattern, and its rigidity is limited mainly by the aromatic core, with some rotational freedom about the bond linking the oxime to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, positioned at the para and meta relationship relative to the amide, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused ring systems, so the scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The amide group contains both a carbonyl oxygen acceptor and two N–H groups that can act as hydrogen-bond donors. The chlorine substituents are electron-withdrawing and lipophilic but are not hydrogen-bond participants. The aromatic ring and the planar amide are rigid, while the molecule as a whole has no stereocenters and only limited conformational flexibility around the single bond joining the amide to the ring. It has no internal symmetry beyond the plane of the aromatic ring.

The molecule is a phenylboronic acid, with a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to one carbon of the ring. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons of the same ring, para and meta to the boron-bearing carbon, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern on the aromatic scaffold. The core is a single fused-free aromatic ring with no additional ring systems, so the framework is planar and rigid, and the only rotatable bond is the one linking boron to the ring. The molecule lacks any mirror-symmetry axis that passes through the whole structure because the chlorines break the symmetry of the ring. The boronic acid contributes two hydroxyl groups that act as hydrogen-bond donors and oxygen lone pairs that act as acceptors, while the chlorine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, which consists of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom. The aromatic ring is substituted at the carbon position opposite to the first substituent and adjacent carbons, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the sulfonyl group. The core is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with the sulfonyl group and the two ring chlorines lying in the ring plane. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the sulfonyl axis that is broken by the asymmetric chlorine placement. The sulfonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two chlorine atoms. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the two chlorines sit on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-dichloro arrangement that is meta and para to the carboxyl group. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the carboxylic acid group able to rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that maps the substituents onto themselves, so it is asymmetric. The carboxylic acid contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the chlorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, and it contains no fused ring systems. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) sits on one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms occupy adjacent ring carbons, placed para and meta relative to the nitrile in a 3,4-dichloro pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the linear nitrile adds further rigidity with almost no conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor, since it has no N-H or O-H groups. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are poor acceptors. Overall the structure has no rotational symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring, reflecting the asymmetric placement of the chlorines relative to the nitrile.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent chlorine atoms and one trifluoromethyl group. The aromatic six-membered ring forms a flat, rigid scaffold with no ring fusion. The trifluoromethyl group sits at one ring position, while the two chlorine substituents occupy the adjacent positions on the opposite side, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single mirror plane of symmetry through the ring, so it is essentially rigid apart from rotation of the trifluoromethyl group. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor-like sites are the electronegative halogen atoms, which are weak acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries an acyl chloride group, which is a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen and a chlorine atom. The ring also bears two chlorine substituents on adjacent carbons, placed meta and para relative to the acyl chloride, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and fully rigid, with no fused rings and no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, though the carbonyl group can rotate relative to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern, with the two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons and the remaining ring position linked to a ketone. A three-carbon chain extends from the carbonyl, ending in a nitrile group at the terminus, so the scaffold contains an aryl ketone flanked by an aliphatic cyanomethyl unit. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the saturated carbon between the carbonyl and nitrile provides some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks internal symmetry because the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions relative to the ketone. The carbonyl oxygen and nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a substituted benzyl alcohol built on a single benzene ring, with no ring fusion. A hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached to one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms occupy the adjacent positions two and three relative to that carbon, on the side of the ring opposite the hydroxymethyl group's neighbors. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm retains some rotational freedom about its single bonds. The molecule lacks any symmetry element that maps the ring onto itself beyond a single mirror plane through the ring. The primary alcohol provides one hydrogen-bond donor and one acceptor through its oxygen, while the chlorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four chlorine-containing substituents: a chloromethyl group (a CH2 carrying a chlorine) on one ring carbon and three directly bonded chlorine atoms on the others. Looking at the substitution pattern around the ring, the chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, forming a 1,2-dichloro unit, while the chloromethyl group occupies a position meta to one chlorine and para to the other, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted arrangement. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the chloromethyl arm providing a small degree of rotational freedom around its single bond to the ring. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the three ring substituents are not equivalent. It contains no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen is bonded to carbon, and its chlorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors at most.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a single benzylic side chain, with the aromatic ring carrying two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-dichloro substitution pattern that is meta/para-related to the side chain. The side chain is a methylene group bonded to an isothiocyanate group, in which a carbon is double-bonded to both nitrogen and sulfur in a linear N=C=S arrangement. The aromatic core is a fused-free, single six-membered ring, so the scaffold is flat and rigid, while the CH2-N=C=S linker adds some rotational freedom at the benzylic position. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the local ring symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the nitrogen and sulfur atoms of the isothiocyanate group provide weak hydrogen-bond acceptor capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrovinyl group on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 3,4-dichlorophenyl substitution pattern. The side chain is a two-carbon unit joined by a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, and its terminal carbon carries a nitro group, which makes the alkene an electron-poor, conjugated Michael-acceptor-type linkage. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the conjugation extends from the ring through the alkene into the nitro group, so the whole framework is largely flat and inflexible apart from rotation of the nitro group. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a limited local symmetry defined by the substitution pattern. Hydrogen-bond donor capability is absent, since there are no N-H or O-H groups, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro group serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a cinnamic acid-type scaffold: a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon unsaturated side chain ending in a carboxylic acid. The side chain contains a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which keeps the chain largely planar and rigid. The aromatic ring carries two chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the vinyl attachment, so the ring is not symmetric. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen. Overall, the molecule has one aromatic ring, one conjugated acid side chain, and limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a phenol: a single benzene ring carrying one hydroxyl group directly attached to the aromatic carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, placed meta and para relative to the hydroxyl group, so the substitution pattern is 3,4-dichloro on the phenol core. The aromatic ring is fully planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters. The molecule has no symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the hydroxyl oxygen and the ring axis. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing an isocyanate group (–N=C=O) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent ring carbons, positioned para and meta relative to the isocyanate, giving a 1,2-dichloro, 4-isocyanato substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no rotatable bonds within the ring system, though the linear isocyanate group extends the molecule along one axis. The molecule lacks any mirror-symmetry axis that passes through all substituents because the two chlorines break the ring's symmetry. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since every hydrogen is aromatic C–H. The isocyanate oxygen and nitrogen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a two-carbon acetic acid side chain, meaning a carboxylic acid group attached through a single methylene unit to the aromatic core. The ring is substituted at the position para to that side chain and at the adjacent meta position by two chlorine atoms, so the two halogens sit next to one another on one edge of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and fully unsaturated, and it is fused to nothing else, giving a single six-membered ring system. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl and acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen, while the chlorine atoms serve only as weak acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry across the ring because the substitution pattern is asymmetric, and its flexibility is limited to rotation about the single bonds of the side chain.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a cyanomethyl group, with two chlorine atoms on adjacent ring carbons. The scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so it is planar and rigid. The nitrile group, a carbon-nitrogen triple bond, is attached to the ring through a flexible methylene linker, which allows some rotational freedom. The two chlorine substituents sit ortho to each other on the ring, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the side chain, which breaks any potential mirror or rotational symmetry of the core. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built on a benzene ring that carries a chlorine atom at the position opposite the carbonyl attachment, giving a para-disubstituted pattern. The carbonyl carbon links the aromatic ring to a short two-carbon chain ending in a chloromethyl-type terminus, so the chlorine sits on the terminal carbon of an aliphatic tail. The benzene ring is planar and aromatic, while the saturated chain provides some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The structure has no internal symmetry axis because the two substituents differ in size and character. The ketone oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a three-carbon ketone side chain, specifically a propanoyl group (CH3CH2C(=O)-) attached directly to one ring carbon, making it an aryl ketone. Two chlorine atoms occupy adjacent ring positions, which are meta and para relative to the ketone carbonyl attachment, giving a 3,4-dichloro substitution pattern on the aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, a rigid scaffold, while the ethyl portion of the side chain offers modest conformational flexibility. The molecule has no stereocenters and only a single plane of approximate symmetry that is broken by the asymmetric chlorine placement. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a methyl group and two chlorine atoms, giving a 3,4-dichlorotoluene scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, so the framework is planar and rigid. The two chlorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons, forming a vicinal dihalogen pattern, while the methyl group occupies a position meta to one chlorine and para to the other. Because the substituents are not symmetrically placed, the molecule lacks any mirror plane or rotational symmetry beyond the trivial one. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the chlorine atoms can act only as weak acceptors, so its hydrogen-bonding capacity is minimal.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two ethoxy groups (each an oxygen attached to an ethyl chain). The ring is a single, unfused aromatic six-membered system, so the scaffold is a simple benzoic acid core. The two ethoxy groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, next to each other, while the carboxylic acid is positioned on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the substituents are not arranged in a mirror-symmetric way. Rotation is possible around the ethyl chains and the C–O bonds, so the molecule is moderately flexible, while the planar aromatic core is rigid. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the ether oxygens serve only as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted benzoic acid built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group (C(=O)OH) sits on one ring carbon, flanked on one side by a methoxy group (an oxygen bearing a methyl) and on the other by a hydrogen-bearing carbon, while a fluorine occupies the position para to the acid and another fluorine sits adjacent to the methoxy-bearing carbon. The ring substitution is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar aromatic core. Its rigidity comes from the aromatic ring, though the carboxylic acid and methoxy groups can rotate about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the methoxy oxygen and the fluorine atoms can serve as weaker hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, with no fused rings, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered ring. Going around the ring, a methyl group sits next to a carboxylic acid group, followed by two adjacent fluorine atoms on the remaining carbons, leaving one ring position as an unsubstituted C–H. The carboxylic acid is the most polar feature, providing both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens. The fluorine atoms are weak acceptors, while the methyl group contributes only hydrophobic bulk. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the carboxylic acid group capable of rotation, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing five substituents. Starting from one carbon, a methyl group is attached, followed by a nitrile (cyano) group on the adjacent carbon, and then a fluorine on the carbon two positions along, with a second fluorine on the next carbon, so the ring carries a methyl, a cyano group, and two adjacent fluorines in a contiguous arrangement with the remaining positions bearing hydrogen. The scaffold is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused or additional rings. The cyano group contributes a linear C≡N unit that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorines are weak acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the ring plane. Rotation is restricted to the methyl group, and the overall framework is rigid.

This molecule is an acetophenone derivative: a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, positioned meta and para to the acetyl group, giving a 3,4-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a planar, rigid six-membered ring with no fused rings, while the acetyl group has limited rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure has no symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the acetyl group and ring axis.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it an aromatic compound with no fused or additional ring systems. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one carbon of the ring, serving as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair and N-H bonds. Two fluorine atoms occupy adjacent ring positions, one para and one meta to the amine, giving a 3,4-difluoro substitution pattern on the aniline scaffold. The ring is planar and rigid, with the amino group able to rotate slightly about its C-N bond, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are unequally placed.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group on one carbon and two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons located para and meta to that amide, giving a 3,4-difluorobenzamide-type substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is flat and rigid, with the fluorines and amide lying in the same plane as the ring. The amide group (–C(=O)NH2) provides two hydrogen-bond donors through its N–H bonds and one hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The two adjacent fluorine substituents are electron-withdrawing and act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane that includes the full set of substituents, since the two fluorines are not equivalent to each other relative to the amide, and the only conformational freedom lies in rotation of the amide group about its bond to the ring.

The molecule is a benzoic acid core, meaning a single benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group. The ring is a flat, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the carboxyl group is attached at one ring position. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, one position removed from the carboxyl-bearing carbon, giving a 3,4-disubstituted pattern. The molecule has no internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane through the ring. The aromatic core and carboxyl group are rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached at one position. Two fluorine atoms sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, placed para and meta relative to the nitrile, giving a 3,4-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a mirror-plane symmetry along the axis through the nitrile and the ring. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two benzene rings. One ring is unsubstituted, while the other carries two adjacent fluorine atoms at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, giving a 3,4-difluorophenyl group. The two aromatic rings are planar and conjugated through the carbonyl, which makes the scaffold fairly rigid, though the rings can rotate somewhat about the bonds to the carbonyl carbon. The molecule has no fused ring systems and lacks any symmetry because the two rings differ in substitution. The carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent fluorine atoms at the 3 and 4 positions, relative to the vinyl linkage. A carboxylic acid group, which can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, is attached through a trans-configured carbon-carbon double bond, giving the molecule an extended, nearly planar conjugated skeleton. Aside from the aromatic ring and the alkene, there are no additional ring systems or ring fusions. The 3,4-difluoro substitution pattern breaks any mirror symmetry along the long axis, while the rigid conjugated linker limits conformational flexibility. The carboxyl oxygens and the hydroxyl hydrogen provide hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capacity, and the fluorine atoms act only as weak acceptors.

This molecule is an alpha-amino acid built on a single stereogenic carbon bearing a free primary amine, a carboxylic acid, a hydrogen atom, and a benzylic CH2 linker. The aromatic portion is a benzene ring carrying two adjacent fluorine substituents at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the attachment point, giving a 3,4-difluorophenyl group with no fused ring system. The flexible CH2 linker allows rotation about several single bonds, while the aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar. The amine group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and the carboxylic acid as both a donor and acceptor, and the two fluorines are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry because of its chiral center and asymmetric substitution pattern.

This molecule is a mandelic acid derivative built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent fluorine atoms at the 3 and 4 positions, which together form a 3,4-difluorophenyl group. The aromatic ring is attached to an alpha-hydroxy carboxylic acid side chain, where a stereogenic carbon carries both a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group. The scaffold is compact and has no fused rings, and the side chain provides some rotational flexibility around its single bonds. Functionally, the carboxylic acid and the secondary alcohol can each donate a hydrogen bond and accept one, while the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror plane.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Attached to the ring is one hydroxyl group, which makes it a phenol, and two fluorine atoms on adjacent carbons, which together form a 1,2-difluoro pattern on the ring. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry because the substituents are not evenly placed around the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on adjacent and nearby positions. A carboxylic acid group is attached to one carbon of the ring, with a hydroxyl group on the neighboring carbon, so the acid and phenol are ortho to each other. Two fluorine atoms sit on the adjacent carbons opposite to the hydroxyl side, creating a 2,3-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with no molecular symmetry, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl both act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms can only weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a seven-membered 1,5-dioxepine-type ring, so it is a bicyclic benzo-fused cyclic bis-ether. The aromatic ring carries a single primary amine group (an aniline-type NH2) on one carbon, positioned meta to one of the ring oxygen attachments and para to the other, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The saturated three-carbon bridge between the two oxygens adds conformational flexibility, while the fused aromatic portion stays rigid and planar. The amino group can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring fused to a seven-membered 1,5-dioxepine-type ring containing two oxygen atoms, giving a bicyclic benzodioxepine scaffold. The aromatic ring carries a single carboxylic acid group, which is attached directly to one of the benzene carbons and sits meta to one of the ring oxygens, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The saturated three-carbon chain bridging the two oxygens gives the seven-membered ring a degree of conformational flexibility, while the fused benzene ring remains planar and rigid. The carboxylic acid acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl group and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, and the two ether oxygens in the ring can each accept hydrogen bonds.

This molecule is a six-membered saturated heterocycle containing one oxygen atom, whose ring carbons include a single carbon-carbon double bond, placing it within the dihydropyran family. The ring is not fused to any other ring and carries no substituents, so the scaffold is unadorned and the molecule has no stereocenters. Its ring is partially flexible: the sp3 carbons allow puckering, while the enol-ether double bond locally constrains the geometry. The ether oxygen is the only heteroatom and can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, but there are no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzothiazine scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered ring containing both a sulfur and a nitrogen atom, with the lactam carbonyl sitting on the nitrogen-adjacent carbon. The sulfur-bearing carbon is also substituted by an acetic acid side chain, giving the molecule a carboxylic acid functional group attached through a single methylene linker. The lactam amide (a cyclic carbonyl bonded to the ring nitrogen) provides a further carbonyl and an N-H group. The fused bicyclic core is largely rigid and planar, while the acetic acid arm adds conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond donor capability comes from the carboxylic acid O-H and the lactam N-H, and hydrogen-bond acceptor sites come from the two carbonyl oxygens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents sit on that ring: an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing one hydrogen and attached directly to the ring) and two adjacent hydroxyl groups on neighboring carbons, forming a catechol unit. Because the two hydroxyls are ortho to each other and the aldehyde is positioned meta to one hydroxyl and para to the other, the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the molecule has no internal mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring. The aromatic core is rigid and flat, while the aldehyde and hydroxyl groups can rotate only modestly about their single bonds to the ring. Each hydroxyl contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site, and the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is built on a flavonol scaffold, a benzopyranone (chromone) core in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered pyran-4-one ring that contains the ring oxygen. The carbonyl sits on the pyranone ring, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the adjacent carbon of the five-atom ring. A 4-hydroxyphenyl group is bonded to the carbon at the 2-position, making the aryl ring para-substituted with a single hydroxyl. The fused bicyclic core is largely planar and rigid, with the pendant phenyl ring able to rotate only modestly about its connecting bond. Overall the molecule has no true symmetry beyond a local pseudo-planar arrangement. It offers several hydrogen-bond donors from its two phenolic-type hydroxyl groups and multiple acceptors from the carbonyl oxygen, the ring oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygens.

This molecule is a flavone, built on a planar bicyclic benzopyranone scaffold in which a benzene ring is fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing pyranone ring bearing a ketone at the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen. Attached at the carbon opposite the ketone is a separate phenyl ring carrying two adjacent hydroxyl groups at its meta and para positions, forming a catechol-type pattern. The fused core and the pendant ring are largely coplanar, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with limited rotational freedom. The two phenolic hydroxyls serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ketone oxygen, the ring ether oxygen, and the hydroxyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis because the hydroxylated ring is substituted asymmetrically.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) attached at one position, and two adjacent hydroxyl groups on neighboring ring carbons, giving a catechol motif. The substitution pattern is 1,3,4 around the ring, so the two hydroxyls sit ortho to each other and the side chain is meta to one hydroxyl and para to the other. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2-COOH side chain provides a single rotatable bond that adds some conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents are all distinct in position. Hydrogen-bonding capacity is high: the two phenolic OH groups and the carboxylic acid OH each act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens of the acid serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a propanoyl (ethyl ketone) group and two adjacent hydroxyl groups on the ring, arranged so that the ketone sits para to one hydroxyl and meta to the other. The two neighboring phenolic hydroxyls form a catechol motif, while the carbonyl oxygen of the ketone provides an additional acceptor site. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the ethyl chain of the ketone adds a small degree of conformational flexibility. The two hydroxyl groups can each act as both hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ketone oxygen acts as an acceptor, giving the molecule several hydrogen-bonding sites. The overall structure lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is built around a four-membered cyclobutene-dione core, a small strained carbocycle bearing two adjacent ketone carbonyls on the ring. Two methoxy groups are attached to the two sp2 carbons of the C=C double bond, giving an ether-substituted, symmetrical scaffold with a two-fold axis through the midpoints of the ring. The ring is essentially rigid and planar, with little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the two methyl groups. The two carbonyl oxygens are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent ring carbons, creating a 1,2-dimethoxy pattern, and an acetyl group (–C(=O)CH3) sits on the ring carbon para to one of the methoxy groups, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted arrangement. The ketone carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core and the carbonyl are rigid and planar, whereas the methoxy and acetyl side chains retain some rotational freedom. The substitution pattern lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule is asymmetric overall.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, so it has no fused ring system and is fully aromatic. Three substituents are attached around the ring: two adjacent methoxy groups (O-CH3 ethers) and one primary amino group (NH2). The two methoxy groups sit next to each other, and the amine is positioned para to one of them, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ether oxygens and the nitrogen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two N-H bonds of the amine can act as hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is rigid, with only the methyl and amino groups providing limited conformational freedom.

This molecule is a substituted phenylboronic acid built on a single benzene ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. The boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups, is attached directly to the aromatic ring. Two methoxy groups, each an oxygen bonded to a methyl group, sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, giving a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the boron. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and hydroxyl groups add some rotational freedom. The two boronic acid hydroxyls can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyl and methoxy groups can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a sulfonyl chloride group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to chlorine) and two adjacent methoxy groups (each an oxygen bonded to a methyl). The sulfonyl chloride sits para to one methoxy group and meta to the other, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted aromatic pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the methoxy and sulfonyl substituents rotate about their single bonds, adding modest flexibility. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy and sulfonyl groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carbohydrazide group (a carbonyl attached to a hydrazine, C(=O)NN) and two adjacent methoxy groups (OCH3) on the ring, giving a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the carbonyl. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the planar benzene system is conjugated with the carbonyl. The molecule has no stereocenters and only partial symmetry, since the two methoxy groups are not equivalent to each other. Its rigidity comes mainly from the aromatic ring, while the methoxy and hydrazide groups add some rotational flexibility. The hydrazide unit contributes multiple hydrogen-bond donors (the NH and NH2 groups) and acceptors (the carbonyl oxygen and nitrogen atoms), and the methoxy oxygens serve as additional weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two adjacent methoxy substituents, making it a dimethoxy-substituted benzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern places the two ether oxygens at adjacent positions, with the carboxyl group on the ring carbon opposite the first methoxy group. The molecule is largely planar and rigid because of the aromatic ring, while the methoxy and carboxyl groups have some rotational freedom. It has no internal symmetry axis that maps the full structure onto itself, since the two methoxy groups sit in different environments. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the two ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, forming a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two adjacent methoxy groups (O-CH3 ethers) sit at positions that make the ring electron-rich on one side, while a nitrile group (C#N) occupies the position across from the first methoxy group, giving a linear, electron-withdrawing substituent. The substitution pattern is 1,2,4 (trisubstituted), so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry and is asymmetric overall. Its core is rigid and planar, with only the two methoxy methyl groups providing limited rotational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no O-H or N-H groups, but the two ether oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an acyl chloride group and two adjacent methoxy substituents. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings, giving it a flat, rigid scaffold. The acyl chloride (–C(=O)Cl) sits at one position, and two methoxy groups (–OCH3) occupy the adjacent positions, forming a 1,2-dimethoxy pattern that is not symmetric across the ring. The methoxy oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall, the structure is rigid and planar apart from the rotatable methyl groups of the methoxy substituents.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, forming a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Two adjacent positions carry methoxy groups (–OCH3), each an ether oxygen that can accept a hydrogen bond, and a third substituent is a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) positioned para to one of the methoxy groups. The hydroxyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond donor and also acts as an acceptor, giving the molecule one donor and three acceptor sites overall. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl and methoxy side chains add modest rotational flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a nitrostyrene-type compound built from a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups on the ring, placed meta and para relative to a two-carbon vinyl linker. The aromatic ring is a single benzene ring with a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern relative to the side chain, which gives the ring an asymmetric arrangement with no mirror symmetry through the side chain. The side chain is an E-configured alkene (trans double bond) conjugated directly to the aromatic ring and terminated by a nitro group, creating a planar, rigid conjugated system. Each methoxy oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the nitro group's oxygens provide additional acceptor sites, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the structure is largely planar and rigid, with only the two methoxy methyl groups offering rotational freedom.

The molecule is built from two aromatic rings joined by a three-carbon linker containing a trans carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to a ketone, giving a chalcone-type scaffold. One ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached directly to the carbonyl carbon. The other is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups at the 3- and 4-positions, relative to the vinyl attachment. The α,β-unsaturated ketone is largely planar and conjugated across both aromatic rings, which makes the core fairly rigid, while the two methoxy groups add modest rotational freedom. The molecule has no symmetry element that maps one half onto the other, since the two rings differ in substitution. The carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core, with its benzo ring fused to a six-membered pyranone ring that carries a ketone at one position. Attached at the 2-position of the pyranone is a separate phenyl ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups at its 3- and 4-positions, giving a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern. The fused bicyclic core and the directly bonded aryl ring are largely planar, making the framework fairly rigid, with only the two methoxy groups providing rotational flexibility. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the two ether oxygens and the ring oxygen add further acceptor sites. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, so it has no fused ring systems and only one aromatic core. Three substituents are attached to that ring: two adjacent methoxy groups (each an oxygen bonded to a methyl carbon) and one hydroxyl group sitting para to the first methoxy. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,2,4 across the ring, which gives the molecule no internal symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the two methoxy groups and the hydroxyl can rotate fairly freely about their single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on adjacent ring carbons, creating a 1,2-dimethoxy substitution pattern, while an isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) occupies the position para to one of the methoxy groups, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted arene. The ring and its substituents are largely planar, and apart from the rotatable methyl ether bonds the scaffold is quite rigid. The molecule has no stereocenters and only approximate local symmetry, since the methoxy groups are not equivalent to each other. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups and the sulfur of the isothiocyanate act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a phenyl ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups at positions that make it a 3,4-dimethoxy substitution pattern, with a carboxymethyl (acetic acid) side chain attached at the position para to one methoxy group. The aromatic benzene ring is a single, unfused six-membered ring, flat and rigid, while the CH2–C(=O)OH chain provides a degree of conformational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The two ether oxygens of the methoxy groups serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methoxy groups (a 3,4-dimethoxy pattern) at one edge, with a para-substituted two-carbon chain. That chain is a methylene linker leading to a carbonyl, forming an amide-type carbonyl attached to a hydrazine (NH-NH2) terminus. The aromatic core is a single unfused six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule is largely planar in its aryl region. The methoxy and hydrazide groups are relatively flexible, with rotatable bonds in the linker. The hydrazide unit offers hydrogen-bond donors through its NH and NH2 groups and acceptors at the carbonyl oxygen and the methoxy oxygens. The lack of symmetry arises from the unequal substitution around the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to adjacent carbons on the ring, giving a 1,2-dimethoxy substitution pattern, and a cyanomethyl group (–CH2–C≡N) sits on the carbon para to one of the methoxy groups. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and cyanomethyl side chains have some rotational freedom around their single bonds. The nitrile nitrogen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. It lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry overall because the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one methyl group. The two methoxy groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, creating an ortho-dimethoxy arrangement, while the methyl group occupies the position para to one of the methoxy groups, giving a 1,2,4-trisubstituted pattern. The benzene core is a single aromatic ring with no fused rings, and the molecule is largely planar and rigid, with only the methoxy and methyl groups providing limited rotational freedom. It has no obvious mirror or rotational symmetry because the substituents are not arranged identically around the ring. The oxygen atoms of the two ether linkages can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is an acetanilide-type compound built on a single benzene ring. The ring carries an acetamide group, with a carbonyl flanked by a methyl group on one side and an NH linked directly to the ring on the other. Two adjacent methyl substituents sit on the ring at positions that are meta and para to the amide nitrogen, giving a 1,2-dimethyl pattern across part of the aromatic core. The molecule has no fused rings and no stereocenters, and its overall shape is largely planar, with the amide bond restricting rotation and the methyl groups adding minimal flexibility. The amide N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent methyl groups and one primary amino group, making it a dimethyl-substituted aniline. The six-membered aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion present. The amino group sits para to one methyl group and meta to the other, giving a 3,4-dimethyl substitution pattern relative to the nitrogen. The molecule lacks any true rotational symmetry beyond a single mirror plane through the ring and its substituents, and its overall shape is rigid because the aromatic core restricts flexibility, with only the methyl and amino rotors providing minor motion. The primary amine offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites through its N–H bonds and one acceptor site through the nitrogen lone pair, while the aromatic ring contributes weak pi-electron acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two adjacent methyl groups and one carboxamide group, giving a 3,4-dimethylbenzamide scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, and it is not fused to any other ring system. The primary amide group, attached directly to the ring, provides two N-H hydrogen-bond donors and a carbonyl oxygen that acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The two methyl substituents sit on adjacent carbons, creating an unsymmetrical substitution pattern, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond a local planar arrangement. The overall structure is largely rigid, with only the amide C-N and C-C bonds to the ring allowing limited rotation.

This molecule is a substituted phenyl ring, a single benzene core with no ring fusion or additional rings. Two adjacent methyl groups sit on the ring, and a boronic acid group, consisting of a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups, is attached at the position para to one of the methyl groups. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the boronic acid group can rotate somewhat about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks a mirror-symmetric axis through the full structure because the substituents are placed asymmetrically, and the two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the boron and oxygen atoms can also accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two adjacent methyl groups, arranged so the acid sits para to one methyl and meta to the other. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the methyl groups adding minor steric bulk but no additional ring systems or ring fusion. The carboxylic acid functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen, while the methyl groups contribute only nonpolar hydrophobic character. The substitution pattern lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry, so the molecule has no stereocenters and no chiral elements.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two adjacent methyl groups and one nitrile group, with the nitrile placed para to one of the methyl groups. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion, giving a planar, rigid scaffold. The cyano group is a linear, strongly electron-withdrawing functional group, while the two methyl groups are small, nonpolar alkyl substituents on adjacent carbons. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planarity of the ring. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, and only the nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzophenone-type diaryl ketone, built from two benzene rings joined through a central carbonyl carbon. One ring is a 3,4-dimethylphenyl unit, carrying two adjacent methyl groups para and meta to the carbonyl attachment, while the other is an unsubstituted phenyl ring. Neither ring is fused to another, so the scaffold is a simple, non-bridged bis-aryl arrangement. The ketone oxygen is the only heteroatom and serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, with no donor groups present. The two aromatic rings are non-coplanar about the carbonyl, giving a moderately flexible, asymmetric structure because the methyl substitution breaks any mirror symmetry between the two halves.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, making it a monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Two adjacent methyl groups sit on the ring at the 3 and 4 positions relative to the hydroxymethyl substituent, creating a 1,2-dimethyl substitution pattern on one side. The third substituent is a hydroxymethyl group, a primary alcohol attached to the ring through a CH2 linker. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl arm retains some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the aromatic ring and methyl groups contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with no fused ring systems. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent carbons of the ring, giving a 1,2-dimethyl substitution pattern, and a hydroxyl group is attached to the ring at a position para to one of the methyls, making it a phenol-type aromatic alcohol. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methyl groups are small, nonpolar substituents with free rotation. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydrogen and an acceptor through its lone pairs. The overall arrangement is asymmetric, since the three substituents are not evenly distributed around the ring.

The molecule is an aryloxyacetic acid built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. The benzene carries two methyl groups on adjacent carbons, giving a 1,2-dimethyl pattern, and an oxyacetic acid side chain on the carbon para to one of those methyls. The ether oxygen links the ring to a flexible CH2 group that terminates in a carboxylic acid. The carboxyl group contributes one hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ether oxygen adds a further acceptor. The overall shape is largely planar around the aromatic ring, with rotational freedom about the ether and CH2 linkages, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, containing one sulfur atom and four carbon atoms. Two methyl groups occupy adjacent carbons on one side of the ring, while two nitrile groups, each a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, are attached at the remaining two ring positions flanking the sulfur. The ring is fully substituted and has no fused rings, so the core is compact and rigid. The arrangement is roughly symmetric about an axis through the sulfur atom, although the two methyl groups differ slightly from the two nitriles. The nitrile nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with two nitro groups on adjacent ring carbons. The carboxylic acid sits at one position on the ring, and the two nitro groups occupy the carbons next to each other, para and meta to the acid, giving a 3,4-dinitro substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring itself, though the carboxyl and nitro groups can rotate about their attachment bonds. The molecule lacks symmetry because the acid and the two nitro groups are arranged asymmetrically around the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (its hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (its carbonyl oxygen), while the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile (cyano, C≡N) group and two nitro groups.
