The two nitro groups sit on adjacent carbons, ortho to each other, while the nitrile is positioned para to one of them, so the substitution pattern is 1,2,4 across the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, and the substituents are essentially rigid and linear or planar in orientation, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility. The molecule lacks any hydrogen-bond donor groups, since none of its atoms bears an N–H or O–H bond. Its acceptor capability comes from the nitrogen of the nitrile and the oxygens of the two nitro groups, and it has no meaningful symmetry because the three substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing one methyl group and two adjacent nitro groups, making it a substituted nitroaromatic. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbon ring with no fused rings, so the scaffold is flat and rigid. The methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and the two nitro groups occupy neighboring positions on the ring, creating an ortho pattern with the methyl placed meta to one nitro group and para to the other. Each nitro group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, planar substituent with oxygen atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The structure lacks any internal symmetry that would make its substitution pattern equivalent at all positions.

This molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic compound built from a straight six-carbon chain containing two adjacent carbonyl groups at the center, making it a 1,2-dione (an alpha-diketone). Each carbonyl is flanked by an ethyl group, so the structure is symmetric about the central C–C bond. It contains no rings, no aromatic systems, and no heteroatoms other than the two oxygens of the carbonyls. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, though the planar dicarbonyl unit introduces some local rigidity. Neither carbonyl oxygen carries a hydrogen, so the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites, but both oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. Two methyl groups are attached to adjacent ring carbons, one at the position next to the carbon bearing the ring nitrogen's neighbor and one on the adjacent carbon, giving a 3,4-disubstituted pattern with no other functional groups. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that is not part of the aromatic sextet, so it can accept a hydrogen bond, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The structure is planar and rigid, with only the two methyl rotors providing minor conformational freedom, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond the ring's local arrangement because the two methyl groups sit at different positions.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered saturated ring containing one oxygen atom and a quaternary carbon bearing two methyl groups, which together form an acetonide-type cyclic ketal. The ring is fully saturated, so it has no double bonds and is conformationally fairly constrained. Two adjacent ring carbons each carry a side chain, and each side chain ends in a secondary alcohol followed by a primary alcohol, giving two 1,2-diol units. The molecule has an approximate two-fold symmetry because the two side chains are chemically similar, though they carry distinct stereocenters. Its hydroxyl groups can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, while the ring oxygen can only accept them.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two adjacent thiol groups and a single methyl group, giving it a substituted aromatic scaffold with a single six-membered ring and no ring fusion. The two sulfhydryl (-SH) substituents sit on neighboring carbons, forming an ortho-dithiol arrangement, while the methyl group occupies a position that breaks any mirror symmetry through the ring, leaving the overall framework asymmetric. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has few rotatable bonds, with only the thiol and methyl hydrogens able to orient freely. Each thiol group can act as a weak hydrogen-bond donor through its S-H bond and a weak acceptor through the sulfur lone pairs, while the methyl group contributes only nonpolar, hydrophobic character.

This molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring, a cyclohexane-based scaffold bearing three methyl substituents on the ring carbons. Two adjacent ring carbons are both ketones, forming an α-diketone (1,2-dione) unit, while a third ring carbonyl sits one position away, giving a cyclohexanetrione-type arrangement. The gem-dimethyl group on one carbon and the single methyl on the neighboring carbon make the substitution pattern asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The saturated ring framework gives moderate conformational flexibility, though the carbonyl groups and substituents restrict some ring motion. The three carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites since it contains no N–H or O–H groups.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated carboxylic acid built on a branched carbon chain. A terminal carboxyl group (-COOH) sits at one end, and a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups sits at the other, with a methyl-substituted carbon between them. There are no rings, no aromatic systems, and no double bonds other than the carbonyl within the acid group. The chain is flexible, with free rotation about its single bonds, and it lacks any symmetry element beyond a local tert-butyl-like terminus. The carboxylic acid provides one hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the hydrocarbon portion contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a five-membered heterocycle containing one nitrogen and one oxygen in the ring, placing it in the oxazolidinedione family. The nitrogen carries a methyl group, and the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen bears two methyl substituents, giving a gem-dimethyl pattern. The ring contains two carbonyl groups: one is a carbamate-type carbonyl flanked by the nitrogen and oxygen, and the other is an imide-type carbonyl adjacent to the nitrogen. The scaffold is a compact, fully saturated, non-aromatic ring with limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the nitrogen is fully substituted, while the two carbonyl oxygens and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid, a hydroxyl group, and three chlorine atoms, making it a salicylic acid scaffold. The carboxylic acid and the adjacent phenolic hydroxyl sit on neighboring ring carbons, giving an ortho relationship between them. The three chlorine atoms occupy the remaining positions, so the ring is heavily and asymmetrically substituted with no mirror or rotational symmetry. The single aromatic ring is planar and rigid, although the carboxylic acid can rotate about its bond to the ring. Both the carboxylic acid and the phenol can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the chlorines contribute only weak halogen-type interactions.

This molecule is a flavanone, built on a benzopyran-4-one (chromanone) core in which a saturated heterocyclic ring is fused to a benzene ring bearing two hydroxyl groups. Attached at the stereogenic carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen is a second benzene ring carrying a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent positions. The fused bicyclic core contains a ketone carbonyl, and the aromatic A-ring has hydroxyls at both meta-positions relative to the carbonyl-bearing carbon. The molecule has one stereocenter, and the two aromatic rings give it a moderately rigid framework with some flexibility at the pendant ring linkage. Hydroxyl groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring oxygen, and methoxy oxygen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is built on a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core fused to a second benzene ring, with a phenyl group attached at the 2-position of the pyranone ring. The fused bicyclic chromone system is largely planar and rigid, and the attached phenyl ring can rotate only modestly about its single bond to the core. Three hydroxyl groups decorate the structure, two on the fused benzo ring at meta-related positions and one on the central pyranone ring adjacent to the carbonyl, while the ketone oxygen serves as an additional acceptor. The molecule has no internal symmetry because the hydroxyl substitution pattern is asymmetric across the bicyclic core. Together, the three hydroxyls act as hydrogen-bond donors and the carbonyl and ring oxygen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an acetamide group, with the nitrogen attached directly to the aromatic carbon, so it is an anilide built on a single six-membered aromatic scaffold. The acetyl carbonyl and the amide N-H form a secondary amide linkage, which can both donate one hydrogen bond through the N-H and accept one through the carbonyl oxygen. On the ring, two trifluoromethyl groups sit at the meta positions relative to the amide nitrogen, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern with a mirror plane through the amide substituent and the ring carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, while the amide and the two CF3 groups add limited conformational freedom at their single bonds. The trifluoromethyl groups contribute strong electron-withdrawing character but no hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor capability of their own.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold, bearing three substituents. A primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) sits at one position, and two trifluoromethyl groups (–CF3) occupy the two meta positions relative to it, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstituted pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxamide can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The amide nitrogen carries two hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability of their own.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, on one carbon. Two trifluoromethyl groups, CF3, sit on the ring at positions meta to each other and meta to the boronic acid, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstituted pattern across the aromatic core. The ring is a single, fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, so the scaffold is planar and rigid. The two CF3 groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and bulky, while the boronic acid is a Lewis-acidic group with two hydroxyl hydrogens that can donate hydrogen bonds and oxygen atoms that can accept them. Overall the molecule has a mirror-symmetric arrangement about the axis through the boron-bearing carbon and the ring carbon opposite it.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with the sulfur atom double-bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine. Two trifluoromethyl groups are attached to the ring at the meta positions relative to the sulfonyl chloride and to each other, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern with a two-fold symmetry axis through the sulfonyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the sulfonyl chloride and trifluoromethyl groups add polar, electron-withdrawing character. Oxygen atoms of the sulfonyl group can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a carbohydrazide group, meaning a carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring on one side and to a hydrazine unit (two linked nitrogens, one of them bearing a free NH2) on the other. Two trifluoromethyl groups sit on the ring at the meta positions relative to the carbonyl, at the 3 and 5 positions, giving the aromatic core a symmetric substitution pattern across its mirror axis. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, while the hydrazide side chain offers some rotational freedom around its single bonds. The NH and NH2 groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms serve as acceptors, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two trifluoromethyl groups. The carboxylic acid sits at one position, and the two CF3 groups occupy the two positions meta to it and to each other, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern about the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no fused rings or flexible linkers, while the three substituents are attached as single bonds that allow only limited rotation. The carboxylic acid group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its O–H and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its carbonyl oxygen. The fluorine atoms of the CF3 groups are weak acceptors, and the aromatic ring offers a pi-electron face that can take part in non-covalent stacking interactions.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a nitrile group (-C≡N) and two trifluoromethyl groups (-CF3). The two trifluoromethyl groups sit at the meta positions relative to each other, both meta to the nitrile, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern around the aromatic core. The aromatic ring is planar and fully unsaturated, with no ring fusion, and the substituents are essentially rigid with little conformational freedom. The nitrile nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2 bearing an OH) at one position, and two trifluoromethyl groups (each a carbon bearing three fluorines) at the two meta positions relative to it, giving a 1,3,5 substitution pattern. The arrangement has approximate threefold symmetry around the ring axis, with the two CF3 groups equivalent. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxymethyl arm adds some rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a flat six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two trifluoromethyl groups (-CF3) are attached at positions 1 and 3 of the ring, giving a meta substitution pattern, and a chloromethyl group (-CH2Cl) sits at position 5, so the three substituents are spaced evenly around the ring. The molecule has approximate threefold symmetry across the ring's axis, though the chloromethyl group breaks it slightly because it differs from the two CF3 groups. The aromatic core is rigid, while the chloromethyl group has a single rotatable bond that gives modest flexibility. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and only the fluorine and chlorine atoms can weakly accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. An aminomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a primary amine) sits at one position, and two trifluoromethyl groups occupy the two meta positions relative to it, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a planar, rigid six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and are fully fluorinated, so they contribute no hydrogen-bond capability. The primary amine supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one lone pair acceptor, and the molecule's only real flexibility comes from rotation about the single bond linking the methylene carbon to the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a conjugated side chain: a trans-configured vinyl unit terminating in a nitrile group (a C≡N triple bond). The aromatic ring carries two trifluoromethyl (–CF3) groups placed meta to each other, both on carbons flanking the point of attachment, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstituted pattern across the ring. The structure is essentially planar and rigid because of the aromatic ring and the conjugated, double-bonded linker, with only the trifluoromethyl groups able to rotate freely. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it lacks N–H or O–H groups. Its only hydrogen-bond acceptor sites are the lone pair on the nitrile nitrogen, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors at best.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: one hydroxyl group and two trifluoromethyl groups. The hydroxyl sits at one ring carbon, and the two CF3 groups occupy the positions meta to it and to each other, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern with a mirror plane through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so the scaffold is fully planar and rigid, while the C-CF3 bonds allow only limited rotation. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine atoms in the CF3 groups are weak acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing a carboxymethyl group, meaning a CH2 linked to a terminal carboxylic acid, attached at one carbon of the ring. Two trifluoromethyl groups sit on the ring at the 3 and 5 positions relative to that side chain, giving a symmetric meta,meta' substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The scaffold is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic ring, so it is rigid, while the CH2 linker and the carboxyl group add modest rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen. The fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the trifluoromethyl groups are strongly electron-withdrawing and bulky.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a hydrazine group (two linked nitrogen atoms, with one nitrogen attached to the ring) at one position. Two trifluoromethyl groups are attached to the ring at the two meta positions relative to the hydrazine, giving a symmetric 1,3,5-substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The ring itself is planar, fully aromatic, and rigid, with no fused rings and only a small amount of conformational flexibility around the hydrazine's N–N and C–N bonds. The terminal NH2 groups of the hydrazine act as hydrogen-bond donors and the lone pairs on the nitrogens can serve as acceptors, while the fluorine atoms of the trifluoromethyl groups are weak acceptors only.

This molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two trifluoromethyl groups. The substitution pattern places one CF3 group on the carbon directly adjacent to the ring carbon that neighbors the nitrogen, and the second CF3 group on the meta position relative to the nitrogen, giving a 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl) arrangement around the ring. The molecule has no ring fusion and no stereocenters, and its structure is largely rigid, since the aromatic core is planar and the CF3 groups rotate only about single bonds. Each trifluoromethyl group is strongly electron-withdrawing and contributes no hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the pyridine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The arrangement gives the molecule an approximate two-fold symmetry axis through the nitrogen and the opposite ring carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a vinyl group (a two-carbon chain with a terminal carbon-carbon double bond) on one ring carbon, with two trifluoromethyl groups attached at the two meta positions relative to that vinyl group. Because the substituents occupy positions 1, 3, and 5 around the ring, the aromatic core is fully substituted at three alternating sites and has a mirror-plane symmetry passing through the vinyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring itself is a single aromatic six-membered system with no fusion, so the scaffold is rigid and planar, while the vinyl group offers limited rotational freedom. Each trifluoromethyl group is a strongly electron-withdrawing, sterically compact group with three fluorine atoms that can accept weak hydrogen bonds, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and its only acceptor sites are the fluorine atoms and the pi-electron system of the ring and alkene.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with three substituents arranged in a 1,3,5 pattern around it. Two of the substituents are acetate ester groups, each formed by an oxygen linking the ring to an acetyl unit, and the third is a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the ester side chains have some rotational freedom around their single bonds. The ring carries a threefold-related arrangement of substituents, giving the molecule an approximate mirror-plane symmetry through the carboxylic acid carbon and the ring carbon opposite it. Hydrogen-bond capability comes from the carboxylic acid, which can both donate and accept a hydrogen bond, while the four ester and acid oxygens serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is built on an acetophenone scaffold: a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) at one position. Two benzyloxy groups (–O–CH2–phenyl) are attached to the ring at the two positions meta to the acetyl group, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted benzene core. The molecule therefore has three aromatic rings linked through flexible ether and methylene bridges, and it has a rough two-fold symmetry axis through the acetyl group and the central ring carbon opposite it. The ketone carbonyl oxygen and the two ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring, one on the carbon directly adjacent to the nitrogen and one on the carbon two positions away, while two bromine atoms occupy the remaining ring positions, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the methoxy groups add only limited conformational flexibility through rotation about their C–O bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since it carries no N–H or O–H groups. Its ring nitrogen and the two ether oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetyl group (a two-carbon ketone, CH3–C(=O)–), a hydroxyl group, and two bromine atoms. The hydroxyl and acetyl groups sit on adjacent carbons, which creates a ring-adjacent ortho arrangement, while the two bromines are placed meta to one another on the opposite side of the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry axis. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and only the acetyl methyl rotates freely. The hydroxyl oxygen-bearing hydrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the adjacent hydroxyl.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom. A hydroxyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and it can exist in tautomeric equilibrium with the corresponding pyridone form, which makes the ring carbonyl-like character relevant. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring at positions meta to each other across the ring, one on the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group's neighbor and one on the carbon further around, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The molecule is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with a nitrogen atom in the ring and no additional ring fusion. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring at adjacent carbon positions, flanking one side of the nitrogen, while a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached to the carbon between them. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The rigid aromatic framework is essentially planar and inflexible, with only the nitrile group lying in line with the ring. The ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen can both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with a hydrogen) and two bromine atoms, along with a hydroxyl group on the ring. The aldehyde and the hydroxyl sit at positions para to each other relative to the ring carbon bearing the aldehyde, while the two bromines flank the hydroxyl, giving a symmetric 3,5-dibromo-4-hydroxy substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, and only the aldehyde carbonyl rotates freely about its single bond to the ring. The phenolic OH acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The two bromine atoms add steric bulk on either side of the hydroxyl group.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a rigid, planar aromatic scaffold. A carboxylic acid group is attached to the ring and functions as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Two bromine atoms and one hydroxyl group occupy the remaining ring positions, with the hydroxyl flanked by the two halogens, giving a substitution pattern that is symmetric about an axis passing through the hydroxyl carbon and the carboxyl-bearing carbon. The phenolic hydroxyl adds a further donor and acceptor site. Because the ring is fully aromatic and the only flexible element is the carboxyl rotation, the overall framework is largely rigid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a methyl group and three halogen substituents. Its six-membered aromatic core is fully unsaturated and planar, giving it a rigid, flat scaffold with no ring fusion. The methyl group sits on one ring carbon, while bromine atoms occupy two positions and an iodine atom occupies the position between them, so the substitution pattern is 1,3,5-type with the halogens clustered on one side. Because the two bromines flank the iodine, the arrangement has a mirror plane passing through the iodine and the methyl-bearing carbon, giving the molecule local symmetry. The ring carries no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors, so hydrogen-bonding capability is minimal.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two bromine atoms and a methyl group are attached to the ring, with the bromines sitting meta to each other and the methyl group positioned between one bromine and the amino group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The primary amine (-NH2) is the only polar functional group: it can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept one, while the bromines and methyl group contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability. Overall the structure is compact and largely rigid, with only the amino group and the methyl group offering minor rotational freedom around their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a substituted benzoic acid. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring carbon, which serves as the principal functional group, and that carboxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Two bromine atoms are attached at positions meta to the carboxyl group on opposite sides of the ring, and a methyl group sits adjacent to one of them, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar ring itself. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the carboxyl and methyl groups offering limited rotational freedom. The bromines contribute steric bulk and polarizability but no hydrogen-bonding capability.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying six substituents, with no fused or additional rings. Going around the ring, it bears a methyl group, a bromine atom, a hydroxyl group, and a second bromine, with the remaining positions occupied by hydrogen; the pattern gives a 2,6-dibromo-3-methylphenol-type arrangement in which the two bromines flank the methyl and the carbon bearing the hydroxyl sits para to the methyl group. The hydroxyl group is the sole hydrogen-bond donor and also acts as an acceptor through its oxygen lone pairs, while the bromines are weak halogen-bond-capable acceptors. The scaffold is essentially planar and rigid, with only the methyl and hydroxyl groups able to rotate, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom among its five carbons, so it is a planar, fully conjugated heteroaromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Two bromine atoms are attached to the ring at positions adjacent to the carbon framework, while a methyl group occupies a third ring carbon, giving a trisubstituted pattern in which the substituents are not arranged symmetrically. Because the ring is rigid and the substituents are directly bonded without rotatable linkers, the molecule is conformationally rigid and lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that makes it a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since the ring carbons and the methyl group bear no acidic hydrogens.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, with two bromine atoms attached to the same ring at positions meta to each other and both meta to the formyl group, giving a 3,5-dibromo substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is compact and rigid, with all atoms lying in one plane. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because the aldehyde C–H and the aromatic C–H positions do not carry acidic hydrogens. The two bromine substituents are symmetrically placed on opposite sides of the aldehyde, giving the molecule an approximate mirror plane that passes through the formyl carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the carbon opposite it. Apart from the rotation of the aldehyde group, the structure has little conformational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary carboxamide group, with two bromine atoms attached at the meta positions relative to it, giving a 3,5-dibromo substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the amide carbonyl and C–Br bonds lie in the same plane as the ring. Because the two bromines sit symmetrically on either side of the carboxamide, the molecule has a local mirror plane running through the amide carbon and the ring carbon bearing it. The carboxamide offers two hydrogen-bond donors (the NH₂ group) and one acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), while the bromines contribute only weak halogen-bonding capability. The scaffold is largely rigid, with only the amide C–N bond showing restricted rotation.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group and two bromine atoms, arranged as a 3,5-dibromobenzoic acid scaffold. The aromatic ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving it a rigid, flat framework with no sp3 stereocenters or rotatable bonds beyond the carboxyl group. The two bromine substituents sit meta to each other and both meta to the carboxylic acid, creating a symmetric substitution pattern across a mirror plane passing through the carboxyl carbon and the ring carbon opposite it. The carboxylic acid contributes both hydrogen-bond donor capability through its hydroxyl hydrogen and hydrogen-bond acceptor capability through its carbonyl oxygen. The bromine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors and add considerable steric bulk and polarizability along the ring periphery.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) is attached at one ring position, giving it a primary alcohol functional group. Two bromine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to each other and meta to the hydroxymethyl substituent, creating a 3,5-disubstituted pattern. The arrangement has approximate mirror symmetry through the axis running from the CH2OH carbon through the ring. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the CH2–OH bond allowing rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen and its hydrogen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the bromine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Three bromine atoms are attached directly to the ring at the 1, 3 and 5 positions, giving a symmetric meta-substitution pattern. A bromomethyl group (a CH2 carrying one bromine) is attached to one of the ring carbons, so the compound contains both aryl and benzylic-type carbon-bromine bonds. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatom acceptors beyond the halogens. Its rigid aromatic core, with only one rotatable bond at the benzylic CH2, makes it structurally compact and largely planar.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a single benzene-like ring containing one nitrogen atom in place of a carbon. Two bromine atoms are attached as substituents at the 3 and 5 positions relative to the nitrogen, which places them meta to each other on opposite sides of the ring nitrogen. This substitution pattern gives the molecule a two-fold axis of symmetry passing through the nitrogen and the carbon opposite it. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the bromine atoms lie in the plane of the ring. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a substituted benzaldehyde built on a single benzene ring with no fused rings. The aldehyde group (CHO) is attached to one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, so the aldehyde and phenol are ortho to each other. Two bromine atoms occupy the remaining meta positions relative to the aldehyde, leaving the ring with a 1,2,3,5-substitution pattern and no internal symmetry. The aromatic core and the aldehyde carbonyl are rigid and planar, while the molecule has little conformational flexibility. The phenolic OH can donate a hydrogen bond, and the phenol oxygen, carbonyl oxygen, and bromine atoms can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with the ortho arrangement allowing an intramolecular interaction between the OH and the carbonyl.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which serves as the central scaffold. A carboxylic acid group (-COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group (-OH) sits on the adjacent carbon, giving an ortho arrangement of the acid and phenol functions. Two bromine atoms occupy the remaining meta positions relative to the carboxylic acid, creating a substitution pattern on the ring that lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl together offer two hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen, hydroxyl oxygen, and carboxyl oxygen provide several acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no fused rings present. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two bromine atoms occupy the positions meta to each other, both meta to the methyl group, giving a 3,5-dibromo-substituted toluene-type arrangement. The molecule has a plane of symmetry running through the methyl carbon and the carbon opposite it, since the two bromines are equivalent. It has no hydrogen-bond donors and no hydrogen-bond acceptors, because the only substituents are carbon-based alkyl and halogen groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with the nitrogen atom occupying one ring position. Five of the remaining ring carbons each carry a halogen substituent, so the scaffold is fully substituted with fluorine and chlorine atoms, with no free C-H positions. The rigid, planar aromatic framework leaves little conformational flexibility. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl carbon bridging two separate benzene rings and no fused ring systems. One ring carries two methyl groups in a 2,4-relationship relative to the carbonyl attachment point, so the methyls sit ortho and para to the ketone-bearing carbon on that side of the molecule. The other ring carries two chlorine atoms at the meta positions relative to the carbonyl. The arrangement is asymmetric, since the two aryl rings differ in their substitution pattern. The two aryl rings can rotate about their bonds to the carbonyl, giving moderate conformational flexibility, though ortho-methyl substitution restricts that rotation somewhat. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom among its ring carbons, with no additional fused rings. A nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) is attached directly to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, at the 2-position. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at the 3- and 5-positions relative to that nitrile, leaving a single unsubstituted ring carbon between them and the ring nitrogen. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the nitrile orientation, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two chlorines occupy non-equivalent positions. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a single pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries three halogen substituents: a fluorine on the carbon directly adjacent to the nitrogen, and two chlorines on the ring carbons at the 3- and 5-positions relative to that fluorine-bearing carbon. The ring has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring positions are occupied by halogens except for two aromatic C–H positions. The ring nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the halogens contribute only weak acceptor character. The scaffold is planar and rigid, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric, lacking any mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework, with no fused rings. An acetyl group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl) is attached to one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group sits on the adjacent carbon, so the ketone and phenol sit side by side. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at the positions meta to the acetyl group, one on each side of the carbon that carries it, giving a symmetric 3,5-dichloro substitution pattern relative to the acetyl group. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the carbonyl oxygen and hydroxyl oxygen can both accept hydrogen bonds. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group retains some rotational freedom.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, C=O with an H), a hydroxyl group, and two chlorine atoms. The aldehyde and hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, so the hydroxyl is ortho to the formyl group, while the two chlorines occupy the remaining positions meta to one another and flank the ring. The scaffold is a single fully aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the molecule is essentially planar and rigid. The substitution pattern lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry axis that would make the two chlorines equivalent with respect to the hydroxyl and aldehyde, so the molecule is asymmetric overall. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, the aldehyde oxygen is an acceptor, and the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type acceptor character.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a sulfonyl chloride group (a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to a chlorine), a hydroxyl group, and two chlorine atoms. The sulfonyl chloride sits at one ring position, the hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and the two chlorines on the ring carbons meta to the sulfonyl group, giving a trisubstituted-plus-halogen pattern that is asymmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with the sulfonyl and hydroxyl groups free to rotate only slightly about their single bonds. The hydroxyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring, so it has a simple monocyclic aromatic scaffold with no ring fusion. Starting from a methyl-bearing carbon, the ring carries three halogen substituents at the remaining positions: two chlorine atoms and one iodine atom, arranged asymmetrically so that the iodine sits ortho to the methyl group. Because the substitution pattern is not symmetric, the molecule has no internal mirror plane or rotational symmetry axis that maps the ring onto itself. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methyl group offers only minor rotational freedom. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors, and its halogen atoms can act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyridone ring, with a ring nitrogen bearing a hydrogen and a carbonyl carbon adjacent to it, making it a 2-pyridone scaffold. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring carbons at positions 3 and 5 relative to the carbonyl, giving a symmetric-looking but asymmetric substitution pattern because the ring is not fully symmetric around its nitrogen and carbonyl. The ring is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds, and the carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor while the ring N–H serves as a hydrogen-bond donor. The chlorine substituents add electron-withdrawing character to the ring but contribute no hydrogen-bonding capability of their own.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) pattern relative to the sulfonyl group. The sulfur atom is part of a sulfonyl chloride group, with two S=O double bonds and a single S–Cl bond attached directly to the aromatic ring. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions flanking a hydroxyl group, which occupies the position para to the sulfonyl group. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the substituents are rigid, giving the molecule little conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the sulfonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has a pseudo-mirror symmetry along the axis through the sulfonyl carbon and the hydroxyl carbon.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, which is the principal functional group and sits on the ring at one position. Two chlorine atoms and one hydroxyl group occupy other ring positions, with the hydroxyl flanked on both sides by the chlorines, giving a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no additional fused ring systems, so the core scaffold is rigid, while the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups can rotate slightly about their bonds. The carboxylic acid and the phenolic hydroxyl each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the chlorine atoms serve as weak halogen-type acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom and a carbonyl group, making it a pyridone-type scaffold in which the ring carbon bearing the oxygen is double-bonded to it. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions flanking the carbonyl carbon on one side and at a position separated from the nitrogen by one carbon on the other, giving a substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring is planar and fully rigid, with the only flexibility coming from none, as there are no rotatable bonds. A single N-H group on the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the exocyclic carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: one primary amino group and two chlorine atoms. Reading the SMILES, the amino group sits on one ring carbon, and the two chlorines occupy carbons that are both meta to it and to each other, giving a 1,3,5-substitution pattern with threefold symmetry about an axis through the amino carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion and no rotatable bonds beyond the C–N bond to the amine. The amino group is the only hydrogen-bond donor, offering two N–H hydrogens, while the nitrogen lone pair can also act as an acceptor; the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type polarity and are not meaningful hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) and two chlorine atoms. The chlorines sit at positions meta to each other and both meta to the methoxy group, giving a symmetric 3,5-dichloro-1-methoxy substitution pattern across a single aromatic ring with no fused ring systems. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy methyl group adds limited rotational flexibility. The molecule has a mirror plane passing through the methoxy carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the ring carbon opposite it. The oxygen of the ether can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a formyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen) on one ring carbon and two chlorine atoms on the ring carbons that are meta to it and to each other, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern around the aromatic core. The benzene ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. The symmetric placement of the two chlorines makes the molecule roughly mirror-symmetric across an axis running through the aldehyde carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aldehyde group is rigid in conjugation with the ring, so the overall scaffold is largely rigid with only the C–C bond to the formyl group allowing limited rotation. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a primary carboxamide group (a carbonyl bearing an NH2 group) attached to one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to the amide and meta to each other, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern that lends the molecule a mirror-symmetric arrangement about an axis running through the amide carbon and the ring carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, while the amide group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The amide offers two hydrogen-bond donors from its NH2 group and one hydrogen-bond acceptor at its carbonyl oxygen. The chlorine atoms are weak halogen acceptors and contribute no hydrogen-bond donor capacity.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with two chlorine atoms attached to the ring. The sulfonyl group, a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom, is attached directly to one carbon of the aromatic ring. Two chlorine substituents sit at the meta positions relative to the sulfonyl group, one on each side, giving a symmetric 3,5-substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl chloride unit is a polar, electron-withdrawing functional group. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, but the two sulfonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydrazide group, with a carbonyl carbon bonded to the ring and to a hydrazine unit (–C(=O)–NH–NH2). The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings, and it carries two chlorine atoms on the meta positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstitution pattern across the ring. The planar aromatic core and the amide-like carbonyl make the scaffold fairly rigid, while the terminal N–N bond allows some conformational freedom. The hydrazide unit provides hydrogen-bond donors through its two NH groups and hydrogen-bond acceptors through the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, and two chlorine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to the acid and to each other, creating a symmetric 3,5-disubstitution pattern. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the chlorine atoms are weak halogen-type acceptors and add lipophilic bulk without donating hydrogen bonds. The overall structure has a mirror plane through the carboxyl carbon and the ring carbon bearing it, and its limited rotational freedom comes mainly from the single bond linking the carboxyl group to the ring.

This molecule is a benzene ring carrying three substituents: a nitrile (cyano, C≡N) group on one carbon and two chlorine atoms on carbons meta to each other and to the nitrile, giving a 3,5-disubstituted benzonitrile pattern. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the bond to the nitrile carbon. The arrangement has a mirror plane running through the nitrile carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the carbon opposite it, so the two chlorines are symmetrically placed. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups, since all ring positions not bearing substituents carry only aromatic hydrogens.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents arranged in a 1,3,5 pattern. One substituent is an acyl chloride group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to both an oxygen (double bond) and a chlorine atom, positioned directly on the ring. The other two substituents are chlorine atoms attached to the ring at positions meta to the acyl chloride and to each other, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis running through the acyl carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with the carbonyl carbon sitting roughly in the ring plane. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydroxymethyl group (a primary alcohol, CH2OH, attached directly to the aromatic ring) and two chlorine atoms. The ring is fully aromatic and planar with no fused ring systems. The two chlorines sit at positions meta to each other and both meta to the hydroxymethyl carbon, giving a 3,5-disubstitution pattern on the ring, which gives the molecule a mirror-symmetric arrangement with respect to the axis through the CH2OH group and the carbon opposite it. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors only. The core scaffold is rigid, with the single CH2 linkage providing the only significant rotational freedom.

The molecule is a phenol: a benzene ring bearing one hydroxyl group on a single carbon, with two chlorine atoms on the same ring. The ring is a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, so the scaffold is simple and fully planar. The chlorines sit at positions meta to each other and both meta to the hydroxyl group, giving the substitution pattern 3,5-dichloro relative to the OH at position 1. This arrangement gives the molecule a two-fold symmetry axis running through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the hydroxyl hydrogen can rotate slightly around the C–O bond. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, and the chlorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. The ether oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The flexible CH2 linker gives the side chain some rotational freedom, whereas the ring itself remains rigid.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. A thiocyanate-type isothiocyanate group (N=C=S) is attached to one ring carbon, giving a linear, cumulene-like functional group that projects away from the ring. The molecule is essentially planar and conformationally rigid, with little flexibility beyond the orientation of the isothiocyanate group. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfur and nitrogen atoms of the isothiocyanate group, along with the chlorine atoms, can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a hydrazino group (-NH-NH2) on one carbon, with two chlorine atoms attached at the positions meta to it on either side of the ring, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern with the hydrazine at position 1. The hydrazine group is a strong hydrogen-bond donor through its N-H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its nitrogen lone pairs, whereas the chlorines act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom and five carbon atoms, with no fused rings or additional substituents beyond two chlorine atoms. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, making the scaffold rigid with no rotatable bonds. The ring nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two halogen atoms add electron-withdrawing character to the ring but do not provide hydrogen-bonding functionality of their own.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and two chlorine atoms. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl sit next to each other on the ring, forming an ortho arrangement, while the two chlorines occupy meta positions relative to the carboxyl group and sit on opposite sides of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry axis because the substituents are not all equivalent. The carboxylic acid and phenol groups each provide a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor site, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weak halogen-type interactions.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3), a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms. The two fluorines occupy meta positions relative to each other and are placed symmetrically with respect to the acetyl-bearing carbon, giving the ring a substitution pattern with partial but not full mirror symmetry. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group has a single rotatable bond connecting it to the ring. The phenolic oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the carbonyl oxygen, the hydroxyl oxygen, and the fluorine atoms act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, which together define its scaffold: a boronic acid group (-B(OH)2), a methoxy group (-OCH3), and two fluorine atoms. The boronic acid carbon is adjacent to the methoxy group, and the two fluorines sit meta to each other on the opposite side of the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no molecular symmetry. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and boronic acid groups can rotate somewhat around their single bonds. The two hydroxyl groups of the boronic acid act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the hydroxyls and the methoxy ether act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorines contribute weak acceptor character.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a rigid, planar aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Going around the ring, a methoxy group (an ether oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits on one carbon, flanked on one side by a fluorine atom and, on the other side, by a nitrile (cyano) group, with a second fluorine located on the opposite side of the ring. This gives a substitution pattern in which the ring carries four substituents in total, two of them fluorines, arranged without any internal symmetry axis, so the molecule is asymmetric. The nitrile nitrogen and the methoxy oxygen are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the fluorines are weak acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with the nitrogen atom at one position of the ring. Two fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions that give a nonsymmetric substitution pattern, and a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) is attached adjacent to the ring nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the methoxy group has limited rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the ether oxygen of the methoxy group can also accept hydrogen bonds, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The overall arrangement is compact and contains no stereocenters.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group (a formyl group, CHO) on one carbon, with two fluorine atoms and one hydroxyl group attached to the other ring positions. The aldehyde and hydroxyl are placed at positions that give the ring a symmetric substitution pattern: the two fluorines flank the hydroxyl group, so the molecule has a mirror plane passing through the aldehyde carbon, the ring carbon bearing the hydroxyl, and the ring carbon opposite them. The aromatic ring is planar and rigid, and the aldehyde is the only group with notable rotational freedom. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen and the fluorine atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. There are no additional fused rings in the structure.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing a propanoyl (ethyl ketone) group, making it an aryl ketone. The aromatic core carries three additional substituents: a hydroxyl group and two fluorine atoms. The fluorines sit at the two positions flanking the hydroxyl group, which sets up a symmetric substitution pattern across the ring, with the ketone located para to the hydroxyl. The scaffold is a single, fully aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the ketone side chain adds some conformational flexibility. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the fluorine atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single fully aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. It carries five substituents around the ring: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl), two fluorine atoms, and a primary amino group. The two fluorines sit ortho to the methoxy group and meta to each other, while the amine is positioned para to the methoxy carbon, giving a 1,2,4,6-type substitution pattern without any internal symmetry axis. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, the ether oxygen and the fluorines can accept them, and the aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy methyl group providing rotational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing six substituents in a single, non-fused aromatic core. Going around the ring, there is a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on one carbon, with fluorine atoms on the two carbons flanking it, so the methoxy sits between two halogens. The remaining position opposite the methoxy carries an aldehyde group, with the carbonyl carbon attached directly to the ring. The substitution pattern is therefore 1,3,5-type relative to the aldehyde, with the methoxy-bearing carbon flanked by fluorines. The scaffold is rigid and planar, with only the methoxy methyl and the aldehyde C=O able to rotate. The oxygens of the methoxy and carbonyl groups are hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a methoxy group, and two fluorine atoms, with no fused ring systems. The carboxylic acid sits on the ring with the methoxy group and fluorines distributed around it in a 2,6-difluoro-3-methoxy pattern relative to the acid, so the substitution is asymmetric and the ring is not symmetric about the acid position. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the carboxylic acid and methoxy groups add only limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its hydroxyl and accept one at its carbonyl oxygen. The methoxy oxygen and the two fluorine atoms act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors, though the fluorines are weak ones.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two fluorine atoms sit ortho to a central methoxy group, creating a 2,6-difluoro-substitution pattern flanking the ether oxygen, while a nitrile (cyano) group occupies the position para to the methoxy group on the opposite side of the ring. The methoxy oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, whereas the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core and the rigid, linear cyano group make the scaffold largely planar and conformationally restricted, with only the methyl of the methoxy group offering rotational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Four of the six ring positions carry substituents: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) on one carbon, fluorine atoms on the two carbons flanking it, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 bearing a bromine) on the carbon opposite the methoxy. The arrangement is fairly symmetric, with the two fluorines related by a mirror plane through the methoxy and bromomethyl positions. The aromatic ring itself is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and bromomethyl groups add some rotational flexibility. The ether oxygen can act as a weak hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing five substituents, with no fused rings, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle. Going around the ring, a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) sits between two fluorine atoms that are adjacent to each other, and a hydroxyl group sits on the opposite side of the ring, with a lone hydrogen on the remaining positions. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, since the methoxy and hydroxyl groups are not placed to create any mirror or rotational symmetry. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy group adds only limited conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the ether oxygen and the two fluorine atoms can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group, which is a methyl ketone (a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group and to the aromatic ring). Two fluorine atoms are attached to the ring at the meta positions relative to the acetyl group, sitting at positions 3 and 5 so that the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the carbonyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. The ketone oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the acetyl group offering limited rotational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, and two fluorine atoms are attached to two other ring carbons, placing them meta to each other and both meta to the amine, in a 3,5-disubstitution pattern relative to the amino group. This arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane passing through the amino-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, so the structure is symmetric. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, with only the amino hydrogens offering limited conformational freedom. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor (through its N-H bonds) and a hydrogen-bond acceptor (through the nitrogen lone pair), while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a primary sulfonamide group, with two fluorine atoms attached to the ring at positions meta to each other and meta to the sulfonamide carbon, giving a 3,5-difluoro substitution pattern. The aromatic ring is a single, unfused six-membered system, so the scaffold is fully planar and rigid, and the only flexible element is the rotation of the sulfonamide group around the carbon-sulfur bond. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the sulfonamide substituent and the carbon opposite it, so the two fluorine atoms are related by symmetry. The sulfonamide contributes two N-H hydrogens that can act as hydrogen-bond donors and two sulfonyl oxygens that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fluorine atoms are weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing a sulfonyl chloride group, with two fluorine atoms attached to the ring. The sulfonyl chloride, consisting of a sulfur atom doubly bonded to two oxygens and singly bonded to a chlorine, is the principal functional group and is attached directly to one ring carbon. The two fluorine substituents sit at the meta positions relative to the sulfonyl group, on carbons separated from one another by a single ring carbon, giving the aromatic ring a symmetric 3,5-disubstitution pattern. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the sulfonyl chloride group offers limited rotational freedom about the carbon-sulfur bond. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, and the two sulfonyl oxygens and the fluorine atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a carboxylic acid group, with two fluorine atoms attached at the 3 and 5 positions relative to it, giving a meta-disubstituted, symmetrical pattern across the aromatic core. The benzene ring is a single fused-free six-membered aromatic system, so the scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds in the ring itself. The carboxylic acid group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptors (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The two fluorine substituents are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors and strongly electron-withdrawing, which shapes the electronic character of the ring while leaving the overall framework compact and flat.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) on one ring carbon, with two fluorine atoms attached to the ring. The two fluorines sit at the meta positions relative to the nitrile, separated from it by one carbon on each side, so the substitution pattern is 1,3,5 across the ring. This arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the nitrile carbon, the ring carbon bearing it, and the carbon opposite it, so it has effective C2v symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with the linear nitrile group extending directly from the ring. The nitrogen of the nitrile can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorine atoms are weak acceptors. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a diaryl ketone, with a central carbonyl group bridging two aromatic rings. One ring is an unsubstituted benzene ring, while the other is a benzene ring carrying two fluorine atoms at the meta positions relative to the carbonyl attachment, giving a symmetric 3,5-difluoro substitution pattern. The carbonyl carbon is sp2-hybridized, so the two aryl rings are linked in a planar-leaning but twist-capable arrangement that offers moderate conformational flexibility around the single bonds to the carbonyl. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The fluorine atoms also contribute weak acceptor character.

The molecule is a cinnamic acid derivative built on a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms at the meta positions relative to the side chain. The side chain is an acrylic acid unit attached to the ring through a carbon-carbon double bond with trans (E) geometry, which makes the chain rigid and planar. The terminal carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond from its hydroxyl and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl oxygen. The two fluorine atoms are electron-withdrawing substituents that create a 3,5-disubstitution pattern, giving the aromatic ring a symmetric arrangement along its axis through the side chain. Overall the scaffold is largely flat and conjugated, with only the carboxyl group offering polar interaction sites.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms in a meta relationship, with a 2-hydroxy-2-carboxyethyl-type side chain attached at the remaining ring position. That side chain is a two-carbon unit: a carbon bearing a hydroxyl group that is bonded to a carboxylic acid group. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no fusion, so the scaffold is compact and largely planar. The fluorine substituents are symmetrically placed on the ring at positions 3 and 5 relative to the side chain, giving the aryl portion a mirror-like symmetry, while the stereocenter at the hydroxyl-bearing carbon breaks overall symmetry. The side chain adds some rotational flexibility. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid groups can each donate a hydrogen bond, and their oxygen atoms, along with the fluorines, can accept hydrogen bonds.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents around that ring: a hydroxyl group (–OH) on one carbon and two fluorine atoms on carbons that sit meta to the hydroxyl and to each other, giving a symmetric 3,5-difluoro substitution pattern. The molecule has a mirror plane running through the hydroxyl-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, so it is highly symmetric and has no stereocenters. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the hydroxyl group can rotate about its C–O bond. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, whereas the fluorine atoms are only weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a phenylacetic acid derivative, built from a single benzene ring with a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a COOH) attached to one carbon of the ring. Two fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to each other and meta to the side chain, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstitution pattern across the aromatic core. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, while the CH2 linker adds a degree of rotational flexibility. The carboxylic acid group contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), whereas the fluorine atoms act only as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two fluorine atoms and a cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile, C≡N). The ring is fully aromatic and planar, and the fluorines sit at the 3 and 5 positions relative to the side chain, giving a symmetric meta,meta' substitution pattern with a mirror plane running through the ring. The side chain is short and fairly flexible about its single bond to the ring. The nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the fluorines are weak acceptors and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. Overall the scaffold is compact, rigid in its ring core, and carries a polarized, electron-poor aromatic system.

The molecule is an aryl ketone built on a benzene ring, with a three-carbon propanoyl chain (ethyl group attached to a carbonyl) bonded directly to one ring carbon. Two fluorine atoms sit on the ring at positions meta to each other and both meta to the ketone attachment, giving a symmetric 3,5-difluoro substitution pattern about the carbonyl axis. The benzene ring is aromatic and planar, and the rest of the structure is quite rigid, with only the ethyl group offering limited rotational freedom. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The two fluorine atoms can also act as weak acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms, giving it a fully aromatic, planar, six-membered carbon scaffold with no fused rings. The carboxylic acid and the hydroxyl sit on adjacent carbons, so the hydroxyl is ortho to the acid, while the two fluorines occupy the meta positions relative to the acid and are arranged symmetrically across the ring. The substitution pattern therefore has a mirror-like symmetry axis passing through the carbon bearing the acid and the carbon bearing the hydroxyl. The ring and its directly attached groups are rigid, with only the hydroxyl and carboxyl bonds able to rotate. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (its OH) and acceptors (its carbonyl oxygen), and the phenolic hydroxyl adds a further donor and acceptor site, while the fluorines act only as weak acceptors.

The molecule is built on a flavone-type scaffold: a benzopyran-4-one (chromone) core fused to a benzene ring, with a second benzene ring attached at the 2-position of the pyranone. That phenyl ring carries a methoxy group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons, giving a 3-hydroxy-4-methoxy substitution pattern. The chromone portion bears a free hydroxyl at the 5-position, adjacent to the carbonyl, which can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, plus two methoxy groups on the fused benzo ring. The fused tricyclic-plus-pendant framework is largely planar and conjugated, which makes the molecule rigid with restricted rotation apart from the methoxy groups. Hydrogen-bond donor capacity comes from the two phenolic hydroxyl groups, while the carbonyl oxygen, ring oxygen, and methoxy oxygens serve as acceptors.

This molecule is an acetophenone, a benzene ring bearing an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two hydroxyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to the acetyl group and to each other, giving a symmetric 3,5-dihydroxy substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl group has limited rotational freedom about its ring bond. The two phenolic OH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the ketone carbonyl oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. An aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached to one ring carbon, and two hydroxyl groups sit on ring carbons separated from the aldehyde and from each other by one carbon each, giving a 1,3,5 substitution pattern. Because the aldehyde and the two hydroxyls are placed symmetrically around the ring, the molecule has a mirror plane passing through the aldehyde carbon and the carbon opposite it. The ring and the aldehyde are essentially rigid and planar, while the hydroxyl groups can rotate about their bonds. The two phenolic hydroxyls can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, and the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 pattern, making it a meta-disubstituted aromatic scaffold with an extra hydroxyl group at the 5-position. One substituent is a carbohydrazide group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to an amine-substituted nitrogen that carries a free terminal NH2, giving a hydrazide function. The two phenolic hydroxyl groups sit symmetrically on either side of the carboxyl-derived carbon, so the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through that carbon and the ring's para position. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the hydrazide side chain has some rotational freedom about its single bonds. Overall, the molecule has multiple hydrogen-bond donors from the hydroxyl and hydrazide NH groups and several acceptors from the oxygens and nitrogens.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, with a nitrile group (a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen) attached to one ring carbon. Two hydroxyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to each other and also meta to the nitrile, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted, symmetric substitution pattern. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the hydroxyl O–H bonds. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the nitrogen of the nitrile serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two hydroxyl groups are attached at the carbons meta to one another and meta to the methyl group, giving a 1,3,5-trisubstituted pattern. The phenolic hydroxyls can each act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the aromatic ring and methyl group are hydrophobic. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, with only the methyl and hydroxyl rotors offering limited flexibility. The substitution pattern gives the molecule an approximate mirror plane passing through the methyl-bearing carbon and the carbon opposite it.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO), and two iodine atoms and one hydroxyl group on the ring. The aldehyde and the hydroxyl sit para to each other, with an iodine flanking the hydroxyl on each side, giving a symmetric 3,5-diiodo-4-hydroxy substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so it is rigid and planar, with the substituents lying in the ring plane and only the aldehyde C=O and the phenolic O–H rotating minimally. The molecule has a mirror plane through the aldehyde and hydroxyl carbons, giving it approximate C2v symmetry. The phenolic OH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the aldehyde oxygen is an acceptor only, and the iodines contribute halogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a nitrile group (C≡N) on one carbon, two iodine atoms, and a hydroxyl group.
