The hydroxyl sits between the two iodines, which occupy positions flanking it, while the nitrile sits opposite the hydroxyl carbon, giving a symmetric 3,5-diiodo-4-hydroxy substitution pattern. The aromatic core is a single fused-free six-membered ring, so there is no ring fusion, and the molecule is essentially planar and rigid apart from rotation of the hydroxyl hydrogen. The phenolic OH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor and oxygen as an acceptor, while the nitrile nitrogen is an additional acceptor site.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an aldehyde group (a formyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen), a hydroxyl group, and two iodine atoms. The aldehyde and hydroxyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, so the phenol and carbonyl functions are ortho to each other, while the two iodine atoms occupy the remaining meta positions relative to the aldehyde, giving a symmetric 3,5-substitution pattern across the ring. The aromatic core is fully planar and rigid, with no ring fusion or additional rings. The aldehyde oxygen and the phenolic oxygen can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the phenolic hydrogen can donate one, with the ortho arrangement enabling an intramolecular hydrogen bond between them. The molecule has a single hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group on the carbon directly adjacent to it, and two iodine atoms. The carboxylic acid and phenol hydroxyl sit on neighboring ring carbons, forming an ortho-hydroxy acid arrangement. The two iodine atoms occupy the meta positions relative to the carboxyl group, placed symmetrically on either side of the ring axis that passes through the carboxyl and hydroxyl carbons. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and hydroxyl groups can rotate only slightly out of plane. The carboxyl group offers both a hydrogen-bond donor and two acceptor oxygens, and the phenolic hydroxyl adds a further donor and acceptor site.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substituents are arranged around that ring: two isopropyl groups, a carboxylic acid group, and a hydroxyl group sitting directly on the ring. The hydroxyl and carboxylic acid are adjacent to each other, while the two bulky isopropyl groups flank the hydroxyl on the opposite side, giving a crowded, unsymmetrical substitution pattern. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors and several acceptor sites on the oxygen atoms. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the isopropyl groups add some steric bulk with limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Three substituents are attached around the ring: two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) and one hydroxyl group sitting between them, plus an acetyl group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl) at the position opposite the hydroxyl. This gives a 1,3,5-type pattern on the ring with the phenolic OH flanked by the two methoxy groups, so the arrangement is symmetric about an axis through the hydroxyl and acetyl carbons. The ring is rigid, while the methoxy and acetyl side chains retain some rotational flexibility. The phenolic OH and the carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two methoxy oxygens serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carbohydrazide group (C(=O)NN) at one position, and two methoxy groups and one hydroxyl group on the remaining positions. The aromatic core is a single six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion, and the ring is planar and rigid. The carbohydrazide unit contributes a carbonyl oxygen acceptor and a hydrazine NH–NH2 segment that provides multiple hydrogen-bond donors and an additional nitrogen acceptor. The phenolic hydroxyl group adds a further donor and acceptor site, while the two ether oxygens on the methoxy groups act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern places the two methoxy groups symmetrically flanking the phenolic hydroxyl, giving the ring an approximate mirror-plane arrangement, while the flexible hydrazide and methoxy side chains add some conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three oxygen-containing substituents and a carboxymethyl side chain. Its aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, with no additional rings attached. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) flank a free hydroxyl group on one side of the ring, and a –CH2–COOH acetic acid arm sits on the opposite side, giving a 3,5-dimethoxy-4-hydroxy substitution pattern. The molecule is roughly symmetric about an axis passing through the hydroxyl and the carbon bearing the side chain, with the two methoxy groups in equivalent positions. The aromatic ring is rigid, while the methylene linker and methoxy groups add some conformational flexibility. Hydrogen-bond capability is strong: the phenolic OH and carboxylic acid OH serve as donors, while the ether oxygens, the phenolic oxygen, and the carbonyl oxygen act as acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a fully substituted aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group sits on one ring carbon, which serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Two methoxy groups occupy positions flanking the ring, and a methyl group sits on the carbon between one methoxy and the carboxylic acid, creating a crowded substitution pattern. The arrangement is roughly symmetric across the ring's axis through the carboxylic acid and the methyl-bearing carbon, while the rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, with only the methoxy and carboxyl groups able to rotate.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with alternating double bonds. Two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) are attached to the ring at positions meta to one another, and a third substituent, an acetyl group (a carbonyl bonded to a methyl), sits on the ring between them, making the pattern 3,5-dimethoxy with an acetyl at position 1. The ring is planar and rigid, while the methoxy and acetyl groups have some rotational freedom about their single bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the acetyl carbon, the ring carbon it attaches to, and the opposite ring carbon, so it shows local symmetry across the two methoxy groups. The ketone oxygen and the two ether oxygens can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as its scaffold, with no ring fusion. It carries three substituents: two methoxy groups (each an oxygen bonded to a methyl group) and one primary amine group, arranged in a 1,3,5 pattern around the ring, so the two methoxy groups sit meta to each other and the amine sits between them on the opposite side. The arrangement gives the molecule a mirror-like symmetry through the amine and the ring carbon opposite it. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy groups add modest conformational freedom. The amine nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the oxygen atoms of the methoxy groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on the ring at positions meta to each other, flanking one carbon that bears a formyl group (–CHO), so the substitution pattern is 1,3,5 across the ring. This arrangement gives the molecule a mirror plane running through the formyl carbon and the carbon opposite it, so it is symmetric. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and aldehyde substituents have some rotational freedom. The aldehyde oxygen and the two ether oxygens can each accept hydrogen bonds, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: two methoxy groups and one carboxamide group. The ring is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The two methoxy groups (–OCH3, attached through oxygen) sit at positions meta to one another, and the primary carboxamide (–C(=O)NH2) occupies the position between them, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstituted pattern about the ring axis through the amide carbon. The methoxy oxygens and the amide carbonyl oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two amide N–H bonds serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The aromatic core and the amide make the scaffold largely planar and fairly rigid, with the methoxy groups providing modest rotational flexibility.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 pattern: a carboxylic acid group and two methoxy groups, with the carboxylic acid flanked symmetrically by the two ether oxygens at the meta positions. The aromatic core is a single, unfused six-membered ring, giving a flat, rigid scaffold, while the two methoxy and one carboxyl group each add some conformational freedom about their single bonds. The carboxylic acid carries both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the two ether oxygens serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The arrangement has approximate mirror symmetry through the carboxyl carbon and the ring carbon bearing it, and the two methoxy groups are equivalent.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) arrangement: two methoxy groups and one nitrile group. The aromatic core is a single, fully unfused six-membered ring, which is planar and rigid, while the two methoxy ether oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen each carry lone pairs that can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, with no hydrogen-bond donors present. The nitrile is a linear carbon-nitrogen triple bond extending from the ring, and the methoxy groups are attached through ether linkages with flexible methyl ends. The substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis passing through the nitrile-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon, giving the molecule an overall mirror-symmetric framework.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta, meta) arrangement. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on carbons separated by one ring carbon, and an acyl chloride group (–C(=O)Cl) occupies the remaining position between them, giving the ring a symmetrical, C2v-like substitution pattern. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings, and its rigidity is limited only by the rotation of the ether and carbonyl bonds. The two ether oxygens and the carbonyl oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The acyl chloride carbon is strongly electrophilic, which makes this a highly reactive scaffold for acylation chemistry.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at positions meta to each other, and a hydroxymethyl group (–CH2OH) sits on the ring between them, giving a symmetrical 3,5-substitution pattern. The ring is rigid and planar, while the methoxy and hydroxymethyl arms add some conformational flexibility. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the two ether oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors only.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring at alternating positions: two methoxy groups (oxygen atoms bonded to methyl groups) and one hydroxyl group, which gives the arrangement a 1,3,5 pattern and a mirror-symmetric outline. The methoxy ether oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, while the phenolic hydroxyl can both donate and accept them. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the two methyl groups on the ether oxygens add only modest conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at positions meta to each other, with the isothiocyanate group (–N=C=S) sitting between them at the position meta to both ether oxygens, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about an axis through that carbon and its opposite ring carbon. The isothiocyanate is a linear, cumulated heterocumulene, which makes that end of the molecule rigid and planar with the ring. The methoxy groups have some rotational freedom around their C–O bonds. The oxygen atoms can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) pattern. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) sit on two of the ring positions, flanking a third position that carries a –CH2–COOH (acetic acid) side chain. The benzene core is aromatic and planar, while the carboxylic acid side chain adds rotational flexibility around its single bonds. The molecule has an approximate mirror plane passing through the ring carbon bearing the side chain and the carbon opposite it, giving it a symmetric substitution pattern. The carboxylic acid group can both donate a hydrogen bond through its O–H and accept hydrogen bonds at its carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens, while the two ether oxygens of the methoxy groups can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methoxy groups (–OCH3) are attached to the ring at positions meta to one another, flanking a third ring position that carries a cyanomethyl substituent (–CH2–C≡N), so the substitution pattern is 1,3,5 with the cyanomethyl group opposite the carbon bearing a methoxy group. The arrangement gives the molecule a local mirror-type symmetry through the cyanomethyl carbon and the ring carbon para to it. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methylene linker and the methoxy groups add modest conformational flexibility. The ether oxygens and the nitrile nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrazole ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, with two methyl groups attached to carbon atoms of the ring. One methyl sits on a carbon adjacent to the nitrogen that bears the hydrogen, and the other sits on the carbon next to the unsubstituted nitrogen, giving a 3,5-dimethyl substitution pattern on the ring. The scaffold is planar and fully conjugated, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the structure is rigid apart from free rotation of the two methyl groups. Because of the placement of the methyls, the molecule has an approximate mirror plane through the ring. The N-H group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine-like nitrogen lacking a hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a pyrazole ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle with two adjacent nitrogen atoms, bearing two methyl substituents on the carbon atoms. The methyl groups sit at the 3- and 5-positions relative to one another, which makes the substitution pattern symmetric about the ring. The nitrogen atom adjacent to the ring junction carries a carboxamide group, a urea-like unit in which a carbonyl is bonded to a terminal NH2. The core is rigid and planar, while the carboxamide adds a small degree of conformational freedom. The amide NH2 group can donate hydrogen bonds, and the carbonyl oxygen and the unsubstituted ring nitrogen can accept them.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms within a planar, fully conjugated scaffold. Two methyl groups sit on the carbon atoms of the ring, one on a carbon flanking the nitrogen with a free lone pair and one at the opposite carbon position, giving a 3,5-dimethyl substitution pattern. The second ring nitrogen, the one bearing the substituent, carries a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH unit), which adds a flexible rotatable linkage and a primary alcohol functional group. The ring itself is unfused and rigid, while the hydroxymethyl arm provides the only significant conformational freedom. The hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the unsubstituted pyridine-like nitrogen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on a single six-membered aromatic scaffold, with no ring fusion. A methyl group and a hydroxyl group sit ortho to each other, and a second methyl group is placed meta to the hydroxyl on the opposite side, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric and the ring is not symmetric about any axis through the hydroxyl carbon. A nitrile (cyano) group occupies the position para to the hydroxyl. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the methyl and hydroxyl groups contribute only minimal conformational freedom. The phenolic hydroxyl acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle built on a pyrazole scaffold, containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms within the ring. Its ring carries three substituents: a methyl group on one carbon adjacent to the sp2 nitrogen, a second methyl group on the carbon next to the NH nitrogen, and an iodine atom on the remaining ring carbon between them. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion, so the core is rigid while the methyl groups add only minor rotational freedom. The molecule lacks any symmetry because the three substituents occupy distinct positions. Regarding hydrogen bonding, the ring NH serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine-like nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, an isoxazole ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom adjacent to each other. Two methyl groups sit on the ring carbons flanking the heteroatoms, one next to the nitrogen and one next to the oxygen, while a single iodine atom occupies the remaining carbon position between them. The ring is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds or stereocenters, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the iodine breaks the pattern of the substituents. It has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all hydrogens are on carbon, but the ring nitrogen and oxygen can act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups and one iodine atom are attached to the ring at positions flanking one another, while a hydroxyl group sits on the carbon across from the iodine-bearing position, giving a 1,3,5-type arrangement of substituents around the ring. The phenolic hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the iodine contributes a bulky, polarizable halogen substituent. The ring itself is rigid and planar, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond an approximate mirror plane through the hydroxyl carbon and the iodine-bearing carbon.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents on a single six-membered aromatic core, with no fused rings and no stereocenters. A carboxylic acid group sits para to one methyl group, and the remaining two substituents are a methyl group and a nitro group positioned ortho to each other, with the nitro group flanked by a methyl on one side and the carboxylic acid's meta position on the other. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry beyond a mirror plane running through the aromatic ring's substituent axis. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxyl and nitro groups can rotate modestly around their bonds to the ring. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl) and acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen), and the nitro group contributes two strong hydrogen-bond acceptor oxygens.

This molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic nitrogen heterocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group at one position, a hydroxymethyl group adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a nitro group sitting next to the methyl-bearing carbon, which places it in a crowded, ortho-flanked arrangement. The nitro group is a strong electron-withdrawing functionality, and the hydroxymethyl group contributes a primary alcohol. Because the ring is aromatic and planar, with the nitro group likely twisted somewhat out of plane due to steric crowding, the scaffold is fairly rigid apart from rotation of the hydroxymethyl and nitro groups. The molecule lacks symmetry. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ring nitrogen and the nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is an aromatic ketone built on a single benzene ring, with an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) attached directly to one ring carbon. Two methyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to the acetyl group and to each other, giving a 3,5-disubstituted pattern. Because the two methyl groups are equivalent, the molecule has a mirror plane running through the acetyl group and the ring carbons opposite it. The benzene core is rigid and planar, while the acetyl group has modest rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on an adamantane cage, a rigid, diamond-like scaffold made of three fused cyclohexane rings sharing a compact tricyclic framework. It carries two methyl groups at bridgehead positions and a carboxylic acid group at a third bridgehead carbon, so the substitution pattern is 1,3,5-type across the cage. The cage has high symmetry and very little conformational flexibility, with the three substituents held in fixed spatial orientations. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two hydrogen-bond acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the hydrocarbon cage itself contributes no hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents spaced around the ring: two methyl groups and one primary amino group. Taking the amino group as position 1, the two methyl groups sit at positions 3 and 5, so the pattern is meta-disubstituted on both sides and the molecule has a mirror plane passing through the amino-bearing carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the methyl groups rotate freely and contribute little to conformational flexibility. The amino group is an aniline-type nitrogen that can donate two hydrogen bonds and accept one, and the aromatic ring itself offers only weak pi-based interactions.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no fused rings. Two methyl groups occupy the meta positions relative to each other, and an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) is attached at the position between them, giving a 1,3,5 substitution pattern with threefold symmetry about the ring. The aldehyde carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks any N–H or O–H bonds. The aromatic ring and the planar aldehyde group keep the structure largely rigid, with only the rotation of the aldehyde about its bond to the ring and the methyl groups contributing modest flexibility.

This molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to each other, and a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, is attached at the position flanked by them, making the arrangement symmetric about an axis running through that carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, since the aromatic ring constrains its geometry and the substituents have little conformational freedom. The boronic acid hydroxyl groups can each donate a hydrogen bond and also accept one through their oxygen atoms, giving the molecule two donor sites and two acceptor sites overall.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving it a 3,5-dimethylbenzenesulfonyl chloride scaffold. The aromatic ring is a single, fully unsaturated six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit meta to each other and flank the sulfonyl group on either side, so the substitution pattern is symmetric about the axis running through the sulfonyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The sulfonyl chloride group, with its sulfur doubly bonded to two oxygens and bonded to chlorine, is a strongly electron-withdrawing functional group. The molecule is largely rigid, apart from rotation of the methyl groups and the sulfonyl group, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors, with the sulfonyl oxygens acting as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no additional fused rings. Two methyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to each other, flanking a carboxylic acid group attached at the position between them on the opposite side, giving a symmetric 3,5-disubstituted pattern about one axis. The carboxylic acid is the only functional group and contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens). The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid group can rotate slightly about its bond to the ring. The methyl groups are nonpolar and add steric bulk without contributing hydrogen-bonding capability.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two methyl groups sit on the ring at positions meta to one another, and a bromomethyl group (a CH2 bearing a bromine atom) occupies the remaining position, giving the ring a 1,3,5-trisubstituted pattern. The arrangement is roughly symmetric about an axis passing through the bromomethyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon, with the two methyl groups equivalent. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the benzylic CH2–Br bond gives the only notable conformational freedom. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors, since its only heteroatom is the halogen, which is a weak acceptor at best.

This molecule is a small aromatic heterocycle built on a five-membered isoxazole ring, which contains adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms within a planar, fully conjugated scaffold. The ring carries two methyl substituents, one on a carbon next to the nitrogen and one on a carbon next to the oxygen, leaving the remaining ring carbon bearing a boronic acid group, B(OH)2, attached directly to the ring. The substitution pattern is therefore asymmetric, with no internal symmetry axis or mirror plane in the molecule. The core is rigid and flat, while the boronic acid group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. Two hydroxyl groups on boron act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the ring nitrogen and oxygen atoms, along with the oxygens of the boronic acid, act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic isoxazole ring, which contains one oxygen and one nitrogen atom adjacent to each other. Two methyl groups sit on the ring carbons flanking the heteroatoms, while the remaining ring carbon carries a carboxylic acid group. Because the ring is the only ring present and the acid group is attached directly to it, the scaffold is compact, planar, and fairly rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation of the carboxyl group. The carboxylic acid provides both a hydrogen-bond donor through its hydroxyl and hydrogen-bond acceptors through its carbonyl oxygen, and the ring nitrogen can also accept a hydrogen bond. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the methyl and carboxyl substituents occupy different positions on the ring.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic isoxazole ring, a heterocycle containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms, bearing a methyl group on each of the two carbons flanking the oxygen. The third ring carbon, positioned between the two methylated carbons, carries a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygens and single-bonded to a chlorine atom. The ring itself is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, while the sulfonyl chloride group is a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent attached to the ring. The nitrogen of the ring can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the sulfonyl oxygens are also acceptors, but the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry.

The molecule is a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion, bearing three substituents. A hydroxyl group sits on one ring carbon, and two methyl groups occupy the positions meta to it. Because the two methyl groups are placed symmetrically about the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, the molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry through the hydroxyl carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and an acceptor, while the aromatic ring is planar and rigid with only the small rotational freedom of the O–H and the two methyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents in a 1,3,5 (meta) arrangement: two methyl groups and one acetic acid side chain, making it a substituted phenylacetic acid. The aromatic ring is a single six-membered unit with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid group (–CH2–COOH) is attached through a flexible methylene linker, which allows some rotational freedom. The two methyl groups sit symmetrically flanking the ring, giving the aromatic core a pseudo-mirror symmetry along the axis through the side chain. The carboxyl group contains both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens, while the aromatic ring and methyl groups contribute only nonpolar, hydrophobic character.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group (–COOH) is attached to one ring carbon, and two nitro groups (–NO2) sit on carbons flanking a central hydroxyl group (–OH), giving a 1,3-dinitro substitution pattern around the phenol. The arrangement of substituents is symmetric about an axis running through the carboxylic acid carbon and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon, so the two nitro groups are chemically equivalent. The rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the carboxylic acid and nitro groups can rotate slightly out of the ring plane. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups serve as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents on a single six-membered aromatic scaffold, with no additional ring fusion. A carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) sits at one position, while two nitro groups flank a central hydroxyl group at the meta-related positions on the opposite side of the ring, giving a 1,3,5-type arrangement of the three substituent sites. The ring's substitution pattern makes the molecule asymmetric overall, though the nitro-hydroxyl portion is roughly symmetric about the axis through the hydroxyl carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the CH2 linker gives the acid group some rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the oxygen atoms of the carboxyl and both nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group and two nitro groups. The carboxylic acid is attached to one ring carbon, and the two nitro groups sit at the positions meta to it and meta to each other, giving a symmetric 1,3,5 substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no additional fused or saturated rings. The carboxyl group offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability through its hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens, while the nitro groups are strong hydrogen-bond acceptors through their oxygen atoms. Overall the scaffold is rigid, with the only notable flexibility coming from rotation about the single bonds connecting the substituents to the ring.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as the scaffold. The ring carries a nitrile group (a carbon triply bonded to nitrogen) on one carbon, and two nitro groups on the carbons that sit meta to each other and to the nitrile, giving a symmetric 1,3,5 substitution pattern. Because the ring is fully aromatic and planar, the framework is rigid, with the nitro and nitrile groups extending outward from the ring plane. The molecule has a mirror-plane symmetry through the nitrile carbon and the opposite ring carbon. The nitrogen atoms of the nitrile and the oxygen atoms of the nitro groups can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving it a symmetric meta-substitution pattern. Two of the substituents are nitro groups (-NO2), each attached through a carbon-nitrogen bond with the nitrogen carrying a formal positive charge and two oxygen atoms, one of them negatively charged. The third substituent is a trifluoromethyl group (-CF3), a carbon bearing three fluorine atoms. The aromatic core is a single planar six-membered ring with no ring fusion, so the scaffold is rigid and flat. The nitro oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all ring positions not bearing substituents carry only aromatic hydrogens bonded to carbon.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: an aldehyde group (CHO), two nitro groups (NO2), and a hydroxyl group (OH). The aldehyde and hydroxyl sit on adjacent carbons, so the ring carries an ortho hydroxy-aldehyde arrangement, while the two nitro groups occupy the meta positions relative to each other and flank the ring at the remaining sites. This gives a fully planar, rigid aromatic scaffold with no stereocenters and an asymmetric pattern of substitution. The hydroxyl group can donate a hydrogen bond, while the aldehyde oxygen and the oxygens of the nitro groups serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aldehyde and hydroxyl groups can also form an intramolecular hydrogen bond across their adjacent positions.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a phenolic hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and two nitro groups placed meta to one another on the opposite side of the ring. The ring is a single fused-free aromatic system with no additional rings, so the scaffold is a simple substituted benzene. The carboxylic acid and hydroxyl groups sit on neighboring carbons, giving an ortho arrangement that allows intramolecular hydrogen bonding between them. The two nitro groups are electron-withdrawing and contribute strong acceptor character through their oxygen atoms. Overall the molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with the carboxylic acid and hydroxyl acting as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the nitro groups serve as additional acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyrazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen (an N-H). Two phenyl rings are attached to this core, one at each carbon adjacent to the nitrogens, giving a 3,5-diphenyl substitution pattern on the pyrazole. The two phenyl groups are unsubstituted and connected by single bonds, so the aromatic system is extended and largely planar, though the rings can rotate about those bonds. Overall the structure is rigid and flat in its core. The N-H group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the unprotonated pyrazole nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. It carries three substituents: a formyl group (an aldehyde, CHO), a hydroxyl group on the adjacent carbon, and two tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls. The aldehyde and hydroxyl sit next to each other, so the hydroxyl can form an intramolecular hydrogen bond with the carbonyl oxygen, and the bulky tert-butyl groups flank the hydroxyl position. The two tert-butyl groups occupy positions on either side of the hydroxyl, and the ring has no internal symmetry beyond a rough mirror through the substituents. The aromatic core is rigid, while the tert-butyl groups are sterically bulky but rotationally fixed. The hydroxyl acts as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the aldehyde oxygen serves as an acceptor only.

This molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents, making it a substituted aromatic ketone. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone) sits on one ring carbon, and a hydroxyl group is present on the ring as a phenol. Two bulky tert-butyl groups flank the hydroxyl on both sides, creating a crowded, sterically shielded environment around the phenolic oxygen. The substitution pattern is 1,3,5-related for the acetyl and the two tert-butyl groups, with the hydroxyl positioned between the two tert-butyl groups. The phenolic hydroxyl can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the ketone oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only. The rigid aromatic core contrasts with the freely rotating tert-butyl and acetyl groups.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a methoxy group (OCH3), a hydroxyl group (OH), and two tert-butyl groups. The ring is fully aromatic and carries no fused rings, so the scaffold is a single six-membered carbocycle. The substitution pattern is 1,3,5 relative to the methoxy group for one tert-butyl, with the hydroxyl flanked by the other tert-butyl on the adjacent carbon, giving a crowded, asymmetric arrangement overall. Both bulky tert-butyl groups sterically shield the phenolic oxygen, which limits its accessibility. The methoxy and tert-butyl groups are non-polar, while the hydroxyl oxygen can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the methoxy oxygen can serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The rigid aromatic core with bulky side groups gives the molecule limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two bulky tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls, flank a hydroxyl group on adjacent positions, while a formyl (aldehyde, C=O with H) group sits at the position para to the hydroxyl. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis running through the hydroxyl carbon and the formyl carbon, so the two tert-butyl groups are chemically equivalent. The aromatic core is fully rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl groups add steric bulk that restricts rotation near the phenol. The phenolic OH can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the aldehyde oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor only.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group, and two tert-butyl groups. The carboxylic acid sits at one position, with the hydroxyl flanked on both sides by bulky tert-butyl groups, creating a 3,5-di-tert-butyl-4-hydroxy substitution pattern across the ring. The arrangement is symmetric about an axis passing through the carboxyl carbon and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the tert-butyl groups add steric bulk and conformational rigidity around the phenolic oxygen. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl together provide two hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single benzene ring bearing four substituents. Two tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyls, sit flanking a phenolic hydroxyl group on adjacent ring positions, creating a sterically crowded environment around the oxygen. A nitrile (cyano) group occupies the position para to the hydroxyl, so the ring is 1,3,5-trisubstituted relative to the nitrile and bears the hydroxyl between the two bulky alkyl groups. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl groups are bulky but rotationally fixed in their attachment. The phenolic OH serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, though the flanking tert-butyl groups hinder access to the hydroxyl.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework. Three substituents sit on the ring: a hydroxyl group that is flanked on both sides by bulky tert-butyl groups, a third tert-butyl group on the opposite side, and a hydroxymethyl group (a CH2OH unit) at the position para to the hydroxyl. Because of the two ortho tert-butyl groups, the phenolic OH is sterically shielded. The ring has no fused partners, so the core is a simple monocyclic scaffold. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, though the two tert-butyl groups flanking the hydroxyl are mirror-related. The bulky tert-butyl groups restrict rotation, making the ring-bound portion fairly rigid. The phenol and the primary alcohol each carry an O-H that can donate a hydrogen bond, and their oxygens can accept one.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two bulky tert-butyl groups flank a phenolic hydroxyl at positions 2 and 6, which sterically shields the OH, and a carboxymethyl group (a CH2 linked to a carboxylic acid) sits at the position para to that hydroxyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the CH2-COOH arm adds some rotational flexibility. Along with the phenol OH, the carboxylic acid provides both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, whereas the bulky tert-butyl groups limit access to the phenolic oxygen. The substitution pattern is asymmetric overall, though the two tert-butyl groups are related by a mirror plane through the ring.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents. Two bulky tert-butyl groups sit on carbons flanking a hydroxyl group, so the phenol oxygen is sterically shielded on both sides. A cyanomethyl group (a CH2 linked to a nitrile) is attached at the position opposite the hydroxyl, giving a 1,3,5-type pattern around the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl groups add substantial three-dimensional bulk. The phenolic OH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the nitrile nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule lacks an element of symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring and the hydroxyl.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. Two bulky tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls, are attached at positions 1 and 3 of the ring, meta to each other, while a primary amino group sits at position 5, placing the three substituents in a symmetric 1,3,5 pattern. The molecule therefore has approximate threefold-type symmetry about the ring axis, though the two tert-butyl groups are equivalent and the amine is unique. The amino group is the only hydrogen-bond donor and also a weak acceptor through its nitrogen lone pair, while the aromatic ring offers limited π-acceptor character. The bulky alkyl groups add steric shielding around the ring, and their rotation is restricted, leaving the overall framework relatively compact and rigid.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents arranged in a 1,3,5 pattern: a carboxylic acid group at one position and two tert-butyl groups at the other two meta positions. The aromatic core is a single six-membered ring with no ring fusion. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and two acceptor oxygens. The two bulky tert-butyl groups are quadruply branched alkyl substituents that add steric bulk and lipophilic character, while the aromatic ring and carbonyl bond keep the core largely rigid. The molecule has an approximate mirror symmetry through the carboxyl carbon and the para carbon of the ring, which makes the two tert-butyl groups chemically equivalent.

This molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring bearing two adjacent carbonyl groups, making it a 1,2-dione (an ortho-quinone-type scaffold) with one ring C=C double bond conjugated to the diketone. Two bulky tert-butyl groups sit on the ring at positions flanking the dione unit, one on each side of the quinone-like core, creating a substitution pattern that is roughly symmetric across the ring's central axis. The ring is essentially planar and rigid because of its conjugated enedione system, while the tert-butyl groups are sterically bulky and rotationally restricted. The molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors, since all its hydrogens are on carbon, but its two carbonyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Its substitution pattern is 1,3,5 (meta on both sides): one methyl group sits at one position, and two tert-butyl groups, each a quaternary carbon bearing three methyls, occupy the other two positions that are separated from it by one carbon each. There are no heteroatoms and no classical functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, or amine. The aromatic ring is rigid and planar, while the bulky tert-butyl groups add steric bulk but only limited conformational flexibility. The molecule has an approximate threefold axis of symmetry through the ring, and it has no hydrogen-bond donors or acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, which is a pyridine scaffold. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring carbons, placed at positions that give a 3,5-dimethyl substitution pattern relative to the nitrogen, so the two substituents sit symmetrically on either side of the ring. The ring is fully aromatic and planar, with no fused rings and no rotatable bonds beyond the methyl groups, making the structure rigid. The pyridine nitrogen carries a lone pair that can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The overall arrangement retains a mirror plane through the nitrogen and the para carbon, giving the molecule a high degree of symmetry.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries two bromine atoms and one methyl group. The methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, while the two bromines occupy the carbon adjacent to the nitrogen on the opposite side and a carbon one position further around the ring, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, and the only conformational freedom is rotation of the methyl group. The ring nitrogen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a pyridazine core. Two chlorine atoms are attached to carbons flanking the ring nitrogens, and a methyl group sits on a carbon adjacent to one of those chlorinated carbons, so the substitution pattern is asymmetric. The ring is planar and fully conjugated, giving the scaffold considerable rigidity, while the methyl group is the only freely rotating part. There are no hydrogen-bond donors, since no N–H or O–H groups are present. The two ring nitrogens act as weak hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the chlorine atoms contribute only weak, non-classical halogen interactions.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic compound built on a single six-membered ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which is the pyridazine scaffold. It is fully aromatic and planar, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Two chlorine substituents are attached to the ring, one on a carbon adjacent to a nitrogen and one on the opposite side of the ring at a carbon next to the other nitrogen, giving a symmetric 3,6-disubstitution pattern. The molecule has no stereocenters, its rigid framework allows essentially no conformational flexibility, and it has no hydrogen-bond donor sites. The two ring nitrogens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the chlorine atoms contribute only weakly polar, non-hydrogen-bonding character.

The molecule is built on a six-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which makes it a pyridazine-type scaffold, and it carries a carboxylic acid group on one ring carbon. Two chlorine atoms are attached to the ring at positions flanking the nitrogen atoms, and a single aromatic hydrogen remains on the ring carbon between the acid and one of the chlorines. The fused-ring picture is simple: there is one ring and no ring fusion, and the fully aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens), while the ring nitrogens act as additional hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no meaningful symmetry beyond the planar framework.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing an aldehyde group, a hydroxyl group, and two fluorine atoms, making it a substituted benzaldehyde with a single six-membered aromatic ring and no ring fusion. The aldehyde carbon is attached directly to the ring, and the hydroxyl sits on the adjacent carbon, so the two groups are ortho to each other. One fluorine is also ortho to the aldehyde, while the second fluorine sits para to the hydroxyl, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The ring and the aldehyde are essentially planar and rigid, with limited conformational freedom beyond rotation of the formyl and hydroxyl groups. The hydroxyl acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the aldehyde oxygen and the fluorines serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing four substituents: a carboxylic acid group, a hydroxyl group on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl, and two fluorine atoms. The carboxylic acid and the neighboring hydroxyl sit at ortho positions, while one fluorine is ortho to the carboxyl on the other side and the second fluorine is located para to the hydroxyl group, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern with no internal symmetry. The aromatic core is fully flat and rigid, with only the carboxyl and hydroxyl bonds offering rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid and phenolic hydroxyl groups can each act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, while the fluorine atoms are weak hydrogen-bond acceptors. Together these features make the scaffold a compact, polyfunctional, planar aromatic system.

The molecule is a small fused-free heterocycle built on a single six-membered 2-pyranone ring, with the lactone oxygen and carbonyl forming the core of an α-pyrone scaffold. A methyl group sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, and a second methyl group occupies a carbon next to the carbonyl carbon, while a hydroxyl group is positioned on the ring carbon between them. The ring is essentially planar and rigid, with conjugated double bonds throughout and little conformational flexibility beyond rotation of the two methyl groups and the hydroxyl hydrogen. The hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no internal symmetry, since the substituents are arranged asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is an acyclic, fully saturated-except-for-one-triple-bond chain of eight carbons, arranged as a central alkyne flanked on each side by a quaternary carbon bearing a hydroxyl group and an ethyl group. It contains no rings, so there is no ring fusion to consider. Its only functional groups are two tertiary alcohols and one internal carbon-carbon triple bond. The substitution pattern is mirror-symmetric about the central C≡C unit, with each end carrying identical methyl and ethyl substituents. The carbon framework is rigid around the alkyne, which is linear, while the terminal ethyl and methyl groups rotate freely. Each hydroxyl group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the alkyne offers only weak pi-electron character.

The molecule is built on a 9H-fluorene scaffold, a tricyclic system in which two benzene rings are fused to a central five-membered ring that carries a CH2 bridge. Each of the two outer benzene rings bears one tert-butyl group, a bulky tetrahedral substituent consisting of a quaternary carbon bonded to three methyl groups. The two tert-butyl groups sit on the rings in a symmetric, mirror-related arrangement, so the molecule has an overall two-fold symmetry through the central CH2. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl groups add steric bulk and lipophilic character at their attachment points. The molecule contains no hydrogen-bond donors and no heteroatoms, so it has no hydrogen-bond acceptor sites either.

The molecule is a fused tricyclic aromatic system built on a phenanthridine-type scaffold, with a central pyridine-like ring fused between two benzene rings. A phenyl group is attached to the carbon at the 6-position of the central ring. Two primary amino groups sit on the outer benzo rings, one on each side, giving the molecule a roughly symmetric substitution pattern. The fully aromatic, planar framework is rigid, with only the phenyl ring able to rotate about its single bond. The two amino groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a fused bicyclic aromatic system made of two six-membered rings sharing one edge. Attached to the ring is an aldehyde group (a carbonyl carbon bearing a hydrogen) and two methoxy groups, each an oxygen bonded to a methyl. One methoxy sits on the same ring as the aldehyde, adjacent to it, while the other sits on the opposite side of the fused system, at a peri-like position relative to the ring fusion. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid because of its aromatic core, with only the methoxy and aldehyde groups offering limited rotation. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks a mirror or rotational symmetry. The oxygen atoms of the methoxy and carbonyl groups can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a spiro-fused bicyclic core of two six-membered oxygen heterocycles sharing a single quaternary carbon, which gives it a rigid, three-dimensional scaffold. Each ring is a tetrahydropyran-type ether, and the two acetal-like carbons adjacent to ring oxygens are attached to bulky 2,2-dimethyl-substituted hydroxymethyl side chains. Each of these side chains terminates in a primary alcohol, so the molecule carries two hydroxyl groups, which can act as hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors. The four ether oxygens in the rings provide additional hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The structure is approximately symmetric about the central spiro carbon, though the rings are fairly constrained, leaving limited conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built from a biphenyl core, with one ring bearing a methoxy group at the para position and the other ring carrying a sulfonamide at its para position. The sulfonyl group links to the nitrogen of an aniline-type ring, which is substituted with a carboxylic acid at the meta position relative to the nitrogen. Overall the structure contains three benzene rings in a linear, extended arrangement with no fused ring systems. The sulfonamide N–H and the carboxylic acid O–H serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sulfonyl oxygens, the carboxyl oxygens, and the methoxy oxygen act as acceptors. The biaryl linkage and sulfonamide allow some rotational freedom, though the aromatic rings themselves are rigid and planar.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a meta relationship, one carbon apart. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which a nitrogen bearing a hydrogen is bonded to an acetyl carbonyl, creating a secondary amide. The other is an acetyl group, a ketone attached directly to the ring. Both carbonyl oxygens can accept hydrogen bonds, and the amide N–H can donate one. The molecule has no stereocenters and only modest flexibility, mainly from rotation about the bonds linking the side chains to the ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetamido group, a nitrogen attached to the ring and to an acetyl carbonyl, which forms an amide. The other is a carboxylic acid group, a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, so the molecule has no chiral centers and only limited conformational flexibility around the single bonds of the two side chains. Both functional groups can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N–H and O–H bonds and as acceptors through their carbonyl oxygens, giving the structure several sites for intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetamido group, in which an acetyl carbonyl is bonded to a nitrogen that is attached directly to the ring. The other is a hydroxyl group sitting on the ring carbon two positions away from the amide nitrogen. The aromatic core is planar and fully conjugated, while the acetamido side chain offers some rotational freedom around the ring-nitrogen and nitrogen-carbonyl bonds. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis beyond the local mirror plane through the ring. Both the amide N-H and the phenolic O-H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, and the amide carbonyl oxygen and the phenolic oxygen can each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no fused ring systems. The ring carries three substituents: a carboxylic acid group, an acetyl ester group (an acetoxy linkage bearing a methyl-carbonyl), and a methyl group sitting between the carboxylic acid and the ester on adjacent carbons. This crowded 1,2,3-trisubstitution pattern makes the arrangement asymmetric, with no internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The ring and its directly attached groups are fairly rigid, while the ester and acid bonds allow some rotation. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the ester oxygens and carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: an acetyl ester (CC(=O)O–, an acetate group attached through its oxygen to the ring), an acyl chloride (C(=O)Cl), and a methyl group. The aromatic ring is fully substituted at a 1,2,3-pattern, with the methyl group sitting between the ester oxygen and the acyl chloride carbon, so the substituents crowd one face of the ring. The scaffold is a single, planar, rigid six-membered aromatic ring with no ring fusion and no internal symmetry, since the three different groups occupy unequal positions. The ester and acyl chloride carbonyls can each accept hydrogen bonds through their oxygen atoms, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors because it lacks N–H or O–H groups.

This molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which contains one nitrogen atom bearing a hydrogen. The ring is fully substituted: a carboxylate ester (an ethyl ester) sits on the carbon next to the nitrogen, while the remaining positions carry two methyl groups and one acetyl group (a ketone). The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry. The pyrrole core is planar and rigid, though the ethyl ester and acetyl side chains retain some rotational freedom. Hydrogen-bond capability is mixed: the ring N–H acts as a donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens of the ester and ketone act as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a thiophene scaffold, a five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to the sulfur, and the two remaining free ring positions each carry a chlorine substituent, one at the other carbon flanking the sulfur and one at the position adjacent to the acetyl-bearing carbon. The arrangement is fully substituted on the ring except for a single aromatic C–H, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry. Because the ring is planar and the acetyl group is nearly conjugated with it, the structure is quite rigid, with only limited rotation about the bond joining the carbonyl to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built around a single five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, which contains one sulfur atom. Attached to this ring is a methyl group at the carbon adjacent to sulfur, and an acetyl group (a ketone bearing a methyl) on the neighboring carbon at the opposite side of the ring. At the remaining open position on the ring sits a phenyl group, a simple six-membered benzene ring, linked directly by a single bond, so the two aromatic rings are unfused. The ketone carbonyl oxygen is the only hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The biaryl linkage allows some rotation about the single bond between the two rings, making the scaffold moderately flexible overall, though the aromatic rings themselves are planar and rigid. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal symmetry.

This molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom. An acetyl group, a ketone bearing a methyl substituent, is attached to one ring carbon, and a bromine atom sits on a carbon that is meta to the acetyl group and also meta to the nitrogen across the ring. Because the ring is fully aromatic and carries only single substituents at two positions, the structure is planar and rigid, with the only notable flexibility coming from rotation of the acetyl group. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the two substituents occupy non-equivalent positions. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited: the ring nitrogen and the carbonyl oxygen can act as acceptors, while there are no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is an acyclic four-carbon chain built on a but-2-enedioic-type backbone, with no ring systems and no ring fusion. Its skeleton carries a methyl group at one end, followed by a ketone carbonyl, then a carbon-carbon double bond joining two sp2 carbons, and finally a terminal carboxylic acid group. The double bond is locked in the trans (E) configuration, which keeps the molecule rigid and largely planar along the central unit. Because the two terminal groups sit at opposite ends of this rigid linker, the overall shape is elongated and asymmetric, with no internal symmetry element. The ketone oxygen and the carboxylic acid group each act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the acid's hydroxyl hydrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond donor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents at the meta position (positions 1 and 3). One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon attached to a methyl group, which contributes a ketone functional group. The other substituent is a boronic acid group, a boron atom bearing two hydroxyl groups. The ring is aromatic and planar, and the molecule has limited rotational freedom, with only the acetyl and boronic acid groups able to rotate about their bonds to the ring. The molecule has no symmetry axis that maps it onto itself, since the two substituents differ. The ketone oxygen and the two boronic acid hydroxyl oxygens can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two hydroxyl groups on boron can act as hydrogen-bond donors.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon attached to a methyl group and directly bonded to the aromatic ring. The other is a sulfonyl chloride group, in which a sulfur atom is doubly bonded to two oxygen atoms and singly bonded to a chlorine atom and to the ring. The scaffold is a single planar, fully aromatic six-membered ring with no fused rings, and the molecule is rigid apart from rotation of the two substituents. Its symmetry is low because the two substituents differ, so it has no rotational symmetry axis beyond a possible local mirror plane through the ring. The carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the sulfonyl oxygens can also accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on a benzothiophene scaffold, in which a five-membered thiophene ring containing one sulfur atom is fused to a benzene ring through a shared carbon-carbon bond. This bicyclic aromatic system is essentially planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the core. An acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) is attached to the carbon at the 3-position of the thiophene ring, which is the only substituent. The carbonyl oxygen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The structure lacks any meaningful symmetry because the single substituent breaks the symmetry of the fused ring system.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) arrangement. One substituent is an acetyl group, a ketone with a carbonyl attached to a methyl carbon. The other is a carboxylic acid group directly bonded to the ring. The aromatic core is a single six-membered fully conjugated ring with no ring fusion, and the substitution pattern leaves the molecule without a mirror plane that maps the two groups onto each other, so it has no rotational symmetry axis either. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid through the ring, with the two side chains having limited rotational freedom. The carboxylic acid OH can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the two carbonyl oxygens serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group and attached directly to the ring, which places a ketone functional group on the aromatic core. The other substituent is a nitrile group, a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, positioned on the ring carbon two atoms away from the acetyl attachment. The structure contains no fused or additional ring systems, and the aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the acetyl methyl provides only minor rotational freedom. Overall the molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis that maps the two substituents onto each other, although the ring positions give it a pseudo-symmetric outline. The carbonyl oxygen and the nitrile nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, and the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

This molecule is a coumarin-type scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered oxygen-containing lactone ring, specifically a 2H-chromen-2-one (benzopyran-2-one) core. The fused bicyclic system is fully aromatic on the benzene side and largely planar across both rings, giving the molecule a rigid, flat framework with little conformational flexibility. An acetyl group (a ketone bearing a methyl) is attached at the 3-position of the pyranone ring, adjacent to the lactone carbonyl. The structure has no internal symmetry axis because the acetyl substituent breaks the symmetry of the scaffold. Hydrogen-bond capability is limited to acceptors: the lactone carbonyl oxygen, the ring ester oxygen, and the acetyl carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups.

The molecule is built on an indole scaffold, a bicyclic system in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing pyrrole ring is fused to a benzene ring along a shared carbon-carbon bond. An acetyl group, a ketone bearing a methyl substituent, is attached to the carbon at the 3-position of the five-membered ring, which is the carbon adjacent to the ring fusion on the side away from nitrogen. The indole nitrogen carries a hydrogen, so it can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen of the acetyl group can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The fused aromatic framework is essentially planar and rigid, with only the acetyl group offering limited rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle, with no ring fusion. It carries two substituents placed meta to each other: an acetyl group (a methyl ketone, C(=O)CH3) and an isothiocyanate group (N=C=S), which is a linear, heterocumulene unit. The acetyl carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the isothiocyanate contributes electrophilic carbon and nitrogen and sulfur atoms that can accept hydrogen bonds, while neither group provides a hydrogen-bond donor. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, and the acetyl group has limited rotational freedom about its single bond to the ring. Overall the molecule has a lower-symmetry, asymmetric arrangement, since the two substituents are not identical.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused ring systems. An acetyl group, a carbonyl bonded to a methyl group, is attached directly to one ring carbon, and that carbon sits adjacent to the ring nitrogen's neighboring position, placing the substituent at the 3-position relative to nitrogen. The ketone carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the aromatic ring nitrogen provides a second acceptor site, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donor groups. The planar, rigid aromatic core limits conformational flexibility, though the acetyl group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The overall structure lacks any rotational symmetry beyond a local mirror plane through the ring.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrrole ring, which contains one nitrogen atom bearing a hydrogen. An acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, is attached to one of the ring carbons, so the ring carries a ketone functional group. The ring is flat and rigid, and the acetyl group has only a small amount of rotational freedom about its bond to the ring. The pyrrole N–H can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen can act as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The structure has no internal symmetry plane beyond the local ring geometry, because the substituent sits at a single, asymmetric position on the ring.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic ring containing one sulfur atom, a thiophene core, with no fused rings. An acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon bonded to a methyl group, is attached to a carbon adjacent to the ring sulfur's neighboring position, at the 3-position of the ring. The ketone carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only rotatable bond is between the ring and the carbonyl carbon, giving the molecule limited flexibility. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule lacks any mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the planar framework.

The molecule is built around a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The ring carries a primary amino group (-NH2) on one carbon, making it a 3-aminopyrazole, and the second nitrogen is substituted by a phenyl ring rather than bearing a hydrogen. That phenyl ring is para-substituted with a chlorine atom, so the two rings are joined by a single N-aryl bond and are not fused. The overall scaffold is planar and largely rigid, with only a single rotatable bond between the two aromatic systems. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyrazole nitrogen and the chlorine atom provide acceptor character.

The molecule is built from a para-substituted benzene ring bearing a methoxy group on one side and a five-membered pyrazole ring on the other, with the two rings joined directly through a nitrogen-carbon bond. The pyrazole is an aromatic, fully unsaturated heterocycle with two adjacent nitrogen atoms, and an amino group sits on one carbon of this ring. The methoxy ether oxygen and the primary amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the two NH2 hydrogens serve as hydrogen-bond donors. The overall framework is largely planar and conjugated across the two aromatic rings, with a single rotatable bond linking them, giving limited flexibility. The substitution pattern is asymmetric because the amino group and the aryl linkage occupy different positions on the pyrazole.

The molecule is a single five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing three nitrogen atoms and two carbon atoms, forming a 1,2,4-triazole ring with no fused rings. An amino group is attached to one of the ring carbons, which places it at the substitution site adjacent to two ring nitrogens. The ring nitrogen bearing a hydrogen atom makes the scaffold a tautomer-capable NH-azole, and the molecule is small, planar, and rigid with no rotatable bonds. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, giving the structure substantial hydrogen-bonding capability. Overall, the molecule lacks any internal symmetry beyond the planar ring framework.

The molecule is a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which places it in the pyrazole family. The ring is fully unsaturated and planar, with one nitrogen bearing a hydrogen atom and the other acting as a pyridine-like nitrogen. A single primary amino group is attached to a carbon atom of the ring, giving a simple monosubstituted scaffold with no ring fusion. The molecule is small and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amino group. Its hydrogen-bond capability is notable: the ring N–H and the amino group serve as hydrogen-bond donors, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen serve as acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of them bearing an N-H hydrogen. The ring is fully unsaturated and planar, so the scaffold is rigid with no rotatable bonds. Two substituents sit on the carbon atoms of the ring: a primary amino group on one carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, and a nitrile (carbon-nitrogen triple bond) group on the neighboring carbon. The arrangement lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents occupy different positions. The amino group and the ring N-H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the free ring nitrogen and the nitrile nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a simple acyclic-chain amine built on a benzene scaffold. A single unsubstituted benzene ring carries a two-carbon saturated linker that terminates in a branched carbon bearing a primary amine group, so the amine sits on a secondary carbon one position removed from the aromatic-linked chain. The aromatic ring is monosubstituted with no fused ring systems and has no additional functional groups. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry element beyond the free rotation of the flexible alkyl chain, which gives it considerable conformational flexibility, while the phenyl ring itself is rigid and planar. The nitrogen of the primary amine can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair.

This molecule is an acyclic, straight-chain aliphatic compound with a three-carbon backbone, so it has no ring systems, no ring fusion, and no aromatic character. It carries two functional groups at opposite ends of the chain: a primary amine on one terminus and a primary alcohol on the other. Because the two groups are placed symmetrically at the ends of a flexible propyl linker, the overall shape is unsymmetrical in terms of its functional groups but without any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. The chain is highly flexible, with free rotation about its single carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bonds. Both the amine and the hydroxyl group can act as hydrogen-bond donors through their N-H and O-H bonds, and each can also serve as a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pairs.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a primary amino group (–NH2) attached to the ring carbon next to the one that carries the second substituent, a trifluoromethyl group (–CF3). The trifluoromethyl carbon bears three fluorine atoms, making it a strongly electron-withdrawing, bulky group, and the ortho arrangement of the two groups creates a crowded local environment. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents are unlike. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

This molecule is a small, acyclic aliphatic compound built on a single quaternary carbon center, with no rings and no aromatic systems. That central carbon bears two methyl groups, a primary aminomethyl arm (CH2NH2), and a hydroxymethyl arm (CH2OH), so the substitution pattern is fully branched at one position. The molecule carries two functional groups: a primary amine and a primary alcohol, each capable of acting as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. Because the scaffold is saturated and the carbon-carbon bonds allow free rotation, the structure is flexible rather than rigid. It also lacks any internal symmetry, since the amine and hydroxyl ends are chemically distinct.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Attached to the ring are an amino group, a carboxylic acid group, and three fluorine atoms, which sit at positions that create a densely substituted, asymmetric pattern around the ring. The carboxylic acid and amino groups both act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carboxyl oxygens and the nitrogen serve as acceptors. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, though the carboxylic acid group can rotate somewhat about its bond to the ring. Overall, the structure has no internal symmetry, since the substituents are arranged unevenly around the ring.
