The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, containing one nitrogen atom within the ring. Two methyl groups are attached to the ring, one on a carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen and one on a neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-disubstitution pattern relative to the nitrogen. An amino group sits on the ring carbon at the position between the methyl-bearing carbon and the remaining unsubstituted ring carbons, so the ring carries three substituents in total. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring system, while the methyl groups add minor local flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, and the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, a fully aromatic nitrogen-containing heterocycle with no fused rings. The ring carries three substituents: a methyl group, a bromine atom on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a primary amino group on the neighboring carbon, leaving the remaining ring position unsubstituted. The aryl bromide and the free amine sit next to each other, making this an ortho-substitution pattern, while the methyl group occupies a position across the ring. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the methyl rotation and the amine's limited motion adding conformational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the amine nitrogen both serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom, bearing two substituents on adjacent carbons. A primary amino group (-NH2) sits at one ring carbon, and a bromine atom sits on the neighboring carbon that lies next to the ring nitrogen, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, with no fused rings and no stereocenters, which makes the scaffold rigid. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond the trivial one, because the amino and bromo groups occupy different positions relative to the nitrogen. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds and as an acceptor through its lone pair, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is a substituted pyridine, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, with no fused rings. It carries three substituents around the ring: a methyl group, a chlorine atom adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a primary amino group on the carbon next to the methyl-bearing position. The substitution pattern is unsymmetrical, so the molecule has no internal symmetry beyond its planar framework. Its rigidity comes from the aromatic ring, with only the single bonds to the substituents permitting rotation of the amino and methyl groups. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with a fully conjugated, planar scaffold. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons next to the ring nitrogen: a primary amino group (-NH2) and a chlorine atom, giving a 2,3-disubstituted substitution pattern with no symmetry. The ring is rigid and flat, and the molecule has essentially no rotatable bonds beyond the amino group's orientation. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a six-membered carbocyclic ring with a single endocyclic double bond conjugated to a ketone, forming an enaminone-type scaffold. One ring carbon bears a primary amino group attached directly to an sp2 carbon of the C=C bond, so the nitrogen is conjugated with the carbonyl through the alkene. The ring is non-aromatic and only partially unsaturated, with the remaining ring carbons saturated and giving it some conformational flexibility. The amino group supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pair act as acceptors. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the substituents sit at non-equivalent positions on the ring.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring that carries three substituents on adjacent and nearby positions: a methyl group, an amino group, and a carboxylic acid group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methyl and carboxyl groups sit on neighboring carbons, which creates a crowded, ortho-disubstituted arrangement. The amino group is placed on the carbon next to the methyl-bearing carbon, so the three substituents occupy a contiguous stretch around the ring. Because the ring is aromatic and planar and the substituents are attached directly to it, the core is rigid, though the carboxylic acid group can rotate about its bond to the ring. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry, since the three different substituents occupy unequal positions. The amino and carboxylic acid groups together provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the carbonyl and hydroxyl oxygens and the amino nitrogen act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a methyl group on the carbon next to the ring nitrogen and a primary amino group on the neighboring carbon, giving a 2,3-disubstituted pyridine pattern. The ring is planar and rigid, and the molecule has only a single rotatable bond (the C–NH2 bond), so it is conformationally limited and lacks any internal symmetry. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a naphthalene scaffold, a bicyclic aromatic system of two fused benzene rings sharing one edge, giving a flat and rigid framework. An amino group sits on one ring at a position adjacent to a hydroxyl group, so the two substituents are ortho to each other on the same six-membered ring. This arrangement makes the structure asymmetric, since the two substituents occupy positions that break any mirror or rotational symmetry. The amino group serves as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, while the hydroxyl group can donate and accept hydrogen bonds as well. Overall, the aromatic core is rigid, with only the polar substituents offering limited conformational freedom.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered pyridine ring, an aromatic heterocycle containing one nitrogen atom in the ring. Two substituents sit on adjacent carbons next to that ring nitrogen: an amino group (-NH2) and a nitro group (-NO2). The nitro group is planar and strongly electron-withdrawing, while the amino group is a donor, so the two neighboring substituents create a push-pull electronic arrangement on the ring. Because the scaffold is fully flat and aromatic with only a small number of rotatable bonds, the structure is rigid and lacks any internal symmetry. The amino group supplies two hydrogen-bond donor sites, and the ring nitrogen and the oxygens of the nitro group act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on an indenone-type scaffold: a five-membered ring containing a ketone carbonyl, fused to a benzene ring, so the bicyclic core is planar and rigid. The five-membered ring also carries an amino group on one sp2 carbon and a phenyl ring on the adjacent carbon, giving a 2-phenyl-3-amino substitution pattern across the double bond. The second phenyl ring is attached as a pendant aromatic group that can rotate about its single bond, adding some conformational flexibility. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pair serve as acceptors. The molecule has no symmetry axis because the amino and phenyl substituents sit on different positions of the core.

The molecule is built on a five-membered heterocyclic core containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, a pyrazoline ring that is partially saturated with one sp3-hybridized CH2 group. An amino group (NH2) is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, forming an amidine-like arrangement with the C=N double bond. The second ring nitrogen carries a phenyl substituent, an unsubstituted benzene ring attached directly to the nitrogen. Because the ring is only partly saturated and the phenyl is attached through a single bond, the scaffold is fairly compact and semi-rigid, with limited conformational freedom. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the imine nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms within the ring alongside three carbons. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one carbon adjacent to a ring nitrogen, and a bromine atom is attached to the neighboring ring carbon, giving a contiguous substitution pattern on the heterocycle. The ring is planar and fully aromatic, so the scaffold is rigid with no rotatable bonds, and it has no internal symmetry because the two substituents sit on different positions. The amino group and the ring N-H can act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the unprotonated ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, a pyrazole ring with two adjacent nitrogen atoms. The ring nitrogen bearing the methyl group sits at position 1, which removes the N-H tautomerism present in unsubstituted pyrazoles and fixes the substitution pattern. A bromine atom is attached to a carbon on the ring, and an amino group occupies the adjacent carbon, so the two substituents are ortho to each other. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the exocyclic methyl and amino groups. The primary amine contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the unsubstituted pyridine-like ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a five-membered isoxazole ring, a heteroaromatic system containing adjacent oxygen and nitrogen atoms within the ring. Three substituents decorate this core: a methyl group on one ring carbon, a bromine atom on a neighboring carbon, and a primary amino group on the carbon sitting between the nitrogen and the bromine-bearing carbon. The ring itself is planar and rigid, with only the methyl group contributing any rotational freedom. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds, while the ring nitrogen and oxygen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The substitution pattern is fully asymmetric, so the molecule has no internal symmetry elements beyond the trivial one.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one bearing a hydrogen on the ring nitrogen. A primary amino group is attached to one carbon of the pyrazole, and a bromine atom sits on the neighboring carbon, giving a contiguous substitution pattern. The other ring carbon carries a phenyl group, a flat benzene ring with no fused rings, connected by a single bond that allows some rotational freedom. The amino group and the ring NH act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the sp2 ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The overall scaffold is largely planar and rigid, with no stereocenters and no internal symmetry beyond the local arrangement of the rings.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which forms the central aromatic scaffold. A carboxamide group (a carbonyl bonded to an NH2 nitrogen) sits on one ring carbon, while a chlorine atom and a primary amino group occupy two adjacent positions on the ring, giving a 1,2,4-type substitution pattern. Because the ring is planar and aromatic, the molecule is rigid, with no rotatable bonds within the ring core, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ. The amide and amino groups each supply N–H hydrogen-bond donors, and the carbonyl oxygen and amide and amino nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The chlorine is a halogen substituent that adds electron-withdrawing character to the aromatic system.

The molecule is a substituted benzene ring, a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no fused rings. A carboxylic acid group sits on the ring, and an amino group and a chlorine atom are attached at positions that are ortho to one another, with the amino group meta to the carboxyl group. The structure is rigid and planar apart from the rotatable carboxyl and amino bonds, and it lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents occupy different positions. The amino group and the carboxylic acid together provide hydrogen-bond donors, while the carboxyl oxygens and the amino nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a pyridine scaffold, a six-membered aromatic ring containing one nitrogen atom, so it is a fully conjugated, planar, and rigid core with no rotatable bonds. Two substituents sit on adjacent ring carbons: an amino group (–NH2) and a chlorine atom, placing them ortho to each other. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and, together with the ring nitrogen, provides hydrogen-bond acceptor sites. The chlorine is a halogen substituent that adds lipophilic character and is a weak acceptor. The overall arrangement is asymmetric, since the two substituents differ in identity and the ring nitrogen sits at a position that breaks any mirror symmetry through the substituted carbons.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a hydrazide group (a carbonyl attached to an NH-NH2 unit), a primary amine, and a hydroxyl group. The amine and hydroxyl sit on adjacent ring carbons, while the hydrazide carbonyl is placed on the carbon farthest along the ring from the hydroxyl, giving a 1,3,4-type substitution pattern across the aromatic core. The ring itself is fully aromatic and planar, and it is unfused, so the scaffold is a single six-membered ring with no additional ring systems. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents differ in identity and position. Its flexibility is limited to rotation around the bond linking the hydrazide carbonyl to the ring and the bonds within the hydrazide chain. The hydrazide, amine, and hydroxyl groups each provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity, and the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen and oxygen atoms can act as acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused rings or side chains beyond the two substituents attached to it. One ring carbon bears a primary amino group (-NH2), and the adjacent carbon bears an iodine atom, so the two substituents sit on neighboring positions and are ortho to each other. The ring nitrogen is positioned meta to the amino group and para to the iodine-bearing carbon. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the amino hydrogens able to rotate. The molecule has no meaningful symmetry because the two substituents are different. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H hydrogens, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around it: a methoxy group (an oxygen bonded to a methyl) on one carbon, a primary carboxamide (a carbonyl bearing an NH2 group) on the carbon para to the methoxy, and a free primary amine on the carbon adjacent to the methoxy. The amine and carboxamide each carry N–H bonds that can donate hydrogen bonds, while the carbonyl oxygen, methoxy oxygen, and amine nitrogen can accept them. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond its planar aromatic core. Only the rotatable bonds to the methoxy and carboxamide groups add some conformational freedom, so overall the scaffold is fairly rigid.

The molecule is a benzanilide, built from two benzene rings joined by a secondary amide linker, C(=O)NH. The first ring is a para-substituted benzoyl unit, carrying a methoxy group on one side of the ring and a primary amino group on the adjacent position, so the two substituents sit ortho to each other. The second ring is an unsubstituted phenyl group attached to the amide nitrogen. Both aromatic rings are planar and conjugated with the amide, giving the scaffold a fairly rigid, extended shape with limited conformational flexibility. The amide N-H and the primary amine provide hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the amide carbonyl oxygen, the methoxy oxygen, and the amine nitrogen serve as acceptors.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, with no fused ring systems. The amino group is a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds, while the oxygen atoms of the methoxy and sulfonyl groups, and the sulfonyl fluoride fluorine, can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a benzene ring, which serves as a flat, rigid aromatic scaffold. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any internal mirror or rotational symmetry. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents, giving it a simple single-ring aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. A methyl group and an amino group sit on adjacent carbons, while a carboxamide group is positioned para to the methyl. The primary aromatic amine and the primary carboxamide each contribute two N–H hydrogen-bond donors, and their nitrogen and oxygen atoms serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, though the amide and amine groups can rotate about their bonds to some degree. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule lacks any meaningful internal symmetry.

This molecule is a benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a boronic acid group, and an amino group, so its scaffold is a single aromatic six-membered carbocycle with no ring fusion. The boronic acid group, written as B(O)O, carries two hydroxyl groups on a trigonal boron atom attached directly to the ring. The rigid aromatic core is flanked by small rotatable bonds, so overall flexibility is limited. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents: a methyl group, a carboxylic acid group, and an amino group. The carboxylic acid is attached directly to the ring, and the methyl and amino groups occupy adjacent positions, forming an ortho-disubstituted pattern on one side of the ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, while the substituents rotate relatively freely around their single bonds. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the three substituents are different. The amino group and the carboxylic acid each contribute hydrogen-bond donor capability, and the carboxyl oxygens and the amino nitrogen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, a nitrogen-containing heterocycle with one ring nitrogen. It carries two substituents on adjacent carbons: a methyl group and a primary amino group, placing them in an ortho relationship to each other and one carbon away from the ring nitrogen. The ring is fully planar and rigid, and the molecule has no stereocenters and only a slight conformational freedom from the rotation of the methyl and amino groups. The amino group contributes two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the pyridine nitrogen and the amino nitrogen both act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is built on a pyrazole core, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, with an amino group attached to one ring carbon adjacent to a nitrogen. A phenyl ring is bonded directly to the adjacent carbon of the pyrazole through a single bond, forming a biaryl-type arrangement with no ring fusion. The amino group and the ring NH provide hydrogen-bond donor capability, while the pyridine-like ring nitrogen serves as an acceptor. The molecule is essentially planar and rigid, with a single rotatable bond linking the two aromatic rings, and it lacks any notable molecular symmetry.

The molecule is a small heteroaromatic compound built on a five-membered pyrazole ring bearing a primary amino group on one carbon. A furan ring is attached directly to a carbon of the pyrazole through a single bond, forming a biaryl-type linkage between two five-membered aromatic rings with no fusion between them. The pyrazole carries an N-H on one nitrogen, which makes the ring a protic tautomer, and the amino group sits at a position adjacent to the pyrazole nitrogen framework. The planar, fully conjugated system is largely rigid, with only rotation about the single bond joining the two rings. The amino and pyrazole N-H groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the pyrazole nitrogen and the furan oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

This molecule is a bicyclic heteroaromatic compound built on an indazole scaffold, in which a benzene ring is fused to a pyrazole ring through a shared C–C bond. The five-membered ring carries an exocyclic amino group on the carbon adjacent to the fused junction, while the NH of the pyrazole sits at the nitrogen next to the benzo ring. A trifluoromethyl group is attached to the benzene portion, placed para-like to the ring fusion on the far side from the pyrazole nitrogen. The fused framework is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds beyond the amino and trifluoromethyl substituents. This molecule is built on a benzene ring, a single six-membered aromatic scaffold with no fused rings. Three substituents are attached around the ring in a 1,3,5 pattern: an amino group, a carboxylic acid, and a trifluoromethyl group, so the substitution is symmetric about one axis with the amino group opposite the carbon bearing the trifluoromethyl group. The carboxylic acid can both donate and accept hydrogen bonds, the amino group can donate hydrogen bonds and accept them at its nitrogen lone pair, and the trifluoromethyl group is a poor hydrogen-bond participant. The aromatic core is rigid and planar, while the carboxylic acid and trifluoromethyl groups have limited rotational freedom about their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is a small, fully aromatic six-membered heterocycle containing three ring nitrogen atoms, forming a 1,2,4-triazine scaffold. Two methyl groups sit on adjacent ring carbons, and a primary amino group is attached to the carbon between two ring nitrogens, giving a clearly asymmetric substitution pattern with no meaningful symmetry. The ring is planar and rigid, and the only conformational freedom comes from rotation of the small methyl and amino substituents. The exocyclic amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor positions, while the ring nitrogens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule is a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no ring fusion and no additional rings. Ring atoms carry a nitrogen in the ring, an amino group (-NH2) on one ring carbon, a chlorine atom on the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen, and a bromine atom on a carbon further around the ring, giving a trisubstituted, unsymmetrical substitution pattern. Because the ring is planar and the substituents are attached directly to it, the scaffold is essentially rigid, with little conformational flexibility. The amino group can act as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N-H bonds, while the ring nitrogen serves as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The halogens contribute polarizability and can participate in weak halogen-bonding interactions.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no additional fused rings. A nitrogen atom sits within the ring, and an amino group (-NH2) is attached to one ring carbon, giving it hydrogen-bond donor capability through its two N-H bonds. A chlorine substituent occupies a carbon position meta to the amino group on the same side of the ring, while the ring nitrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor. The scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the amino group's hydrogens free to rotate, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents are placed asymmetrically around the ring.

The molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, which is a pyrazole ring. A methyl group sits on one ring carbon, and an amino group is attached to the carbon adjacent to the ring nitrogen that is not bearing a hydrogen. The ring nitrogen bearing a hydrogen acts as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine-type nitrogen and the amino nitrogen can serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The fused-free, single-ring scaffold is compact and essentially rigid, with only the methyl and amino groups contributing small rotational freedom, and the substitution pattern is asymmetric.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of them bearing a hydrogen. The ring is fully substituted and carries three groups: a methylthio (S-methyl) group on one ring carbon, a primary amino group on the other ring carbon adjacent to the NH nitrogen, and a nitrile (cyano) group on the carbon between them. Because the scaffold is a single flat aromatic ring with no fused rings and only a small rotatable methyl group, the overall structure is rigid and essentially planar, with no stereocentres or internal symmetry beyond that of the ring itself.

This molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic scaffold with three substituents. An amino group sits on one ring carbon, a carboxylic acid group sits on the carbon directly across from it in a 1,3,5 (meta) arrangement, and a nitro group occupies the remaining position, giving a symmetric-looking but fully planar and rigid framework. The carboxylic acid contributes both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the amino group serves as a donor and the nitro group as a strong acceptor. Because the ring is fused to nothing and the substituents are single bonds rotating only at the ring attachments, the molecule is largely rigid, with limited conformational flexibility overall.

The molecule is a substituted pyrazole, a five-membered aromatic ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms. It bears a free amino group on one carbon of the ring, which acts as a hydrogen-bond donor through its two N–H bonds and a hydrogen-bond acceptor through its lone pair. A phenyl ring is attached directly to a neighboring ring carbon, so the molecule is a biaryl-type scaffold with a single rotatable bond linking the two aromatic systems. The ring NH provides an additional hydrogen-bond donor, while the pyridine-like sp2 nitrogen serves as an acceptor. The overall structure is largely planar and rigid, with limited conformational flexibility beyond rotation about the inter-ring bond, and it lacks any internal symmetry.

The molecule is built on a five-membered aromatic pyrazole ring, which contains two adjacent nitrogen atoms, one of which carries a hydrogen. A tert-butyl group, a quaternary carbon bearing three methyl groups, is attached to one ring carbon, giving a bulky, nonpolar substituent that dominates one side of the scaffold. An primary amino group sits on the other ring carbon adjacent to the nitrogen, providing an additional polar site. The core is fully planar and rigid, while the tert-butyl group adds only local three-dimensional bulk. Hydrogen-bond capability is present: the ring NH and the amino group act as donors, and the unprotonated ring nitrogen and the amino nitrogen act as acceptors.

This molecule is a small five-membered aromatic heterocycle, specifically an isoxazole ring containing one oxygen and one nitrogen atom adjacent to each other. A tert-butyl group, consisting of a central carbon bearing three methyl groups, is attached to one ring carbon adjacent to the oxygen, giving a bulky, nonpolar substituent. An amino group is bonded to the carbon next to the ring nitrogen, providing a primary amine functionality. The scaffold is fully planar and rigid, with only the bulky tert-butyl group rotating freely about its single bond to the ring. The amino group can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds, while the ring nitrogen and oxygen can accept them.

The molecule is built on a carbazole scaffold, a tricyclic system in which a five-membered nitrogen-containing ring is fused between two benzene rings. The nitrogen of the central pyrrole-type ring carries an N-ethyl substituent, so the ring nitrogen is tertiary and contributes no N-H donor. An amino group sits on one of the outer benzene rings, at a position para-like to the ring-fusion carbon, giving an asymmetric substitution pattern. The fused aromatic framework is planar and rigid, with only the ethyl chain offering conformational flexibility. The primary amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites and one acceptor site, while the ring nitrogen can act only as a weak acceptor.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing two substituents in a meta (1,3) relationship. One substituent is an acetyl group, a carbonyl carbon attached to the ring and to a methyl group, which contributes a ketone functional group. The other substituent is a primary amino group attached directly to the aromatic ring. The aromatic core is planar and rigid, with no ring fusion, while the acetyl group can rotate about its single bond to the ring. The carbonyl oxygen acts as a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the amino group offers two hydrogen-bond donor sites along with an acceptor capability at the nitrogen. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond the local planar arrangement of the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no ring fusion. Two substituents sit on the ring in a meta relationship, separated by one carbon: a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) and a primary amino group (–NH2). The molecule has no internal symmetry element beyond the planar ring framework because the two substituents differ.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings. Two substituents sit on the ring in a meta relationship: a primary amino group (-NH2) and a primary sulfonamide group (-SO2NH2). The sulfonamide carries a tetrahedral sulfur bearing two double-bonded oxygens and an NH2 group. The core is largely rigid and planar, with only the bonds to the two substituents allowing rotation. This molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents at the meta positions (1 and 3). One substituent is a carbohydrazide group, in which a carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrazine (–NH–NH2) unit, and the other is a primary amino group attached directly to the ring. The carbohydrazide group can rotate about its single bond to the ring, giving modest flexibility to that side. The amide-like carbonyl and the hydrazine NH groups act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen atoms act as acceptors. The molecule lacks any symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the aromatic ring.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent-but-one positions, specifically at meta positions relative to each other. One substituent is a primary amino group (–NH2) attached directly to the aromatic ring, and the other is a carboxylic acid group (–COOH) attached through its carbonyl carbon. The molecule has no internal symmetry plane coinciding with both substituents, so its substitution pattern is asymmetric. The molecule is a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbocycle with no fused rings, so its scaffold is a simple monocyclic arene. The amino group provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites on its nitrogen, and both the nitrile nitrogen and the amine nitrogen can act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is a benzophenone scaffold: two benzene rings joined through a single carbonyl carbon, with no fused ring systems. One ring carries a primary amino group (–NH2) at the meta position relative to the carbonyl bridge, while the other ring is unsubstituted. The ketone carbonyl is a hydrogen-bond acceptor, and the amino group supplies two N–H donors plus a lone pair that can accept hydrogen bonds. The two aryl rings are not coplanar with the carbonyl, giving the molecule moderate conformational flexibility around the two C–C single bonds. It has no internal symmetry plane because the amino substituent breaks the symmetry between the two rings.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent positions relative to one another, specifically an amino group and a hydroxymethyl group placed meta to each other (1,3-disubstitution). The aromatic ring is a single six-membered carbon ring with no fused ring systems, giving a flat, rigid core. The molecule is built on a single benzene ring bearing three substituents at the 1, 3, and 5 positions, giving a meta-substituted, roughly symmetric arrangement. One substituent is a primary carboxamide (-C(=O)NH2), another is a carboxylic acid (-COOH), and the third is a nitro group (-NO2) attached to the ring. Because the ring is fully aromatic and carries no fused rings, the scaffold is planar and rigid, with only the substituents able to rotate. The amide and acid groups each supply hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor sites, while the nitro group contributes two strong oxygen acceptor sites.

The molecule is built on a benzopyranone (coumarin-type) scaffold: a benzene ring fused to a six-membered lactone-containing pyranone ring. The fused bicyclic system is planar and largely rigid, with the aromatic benzo ring sharing an edge with the unsaturated oxygen-containing ring. An exocyclic carbonyl (C=O) sits on the carbon adjacent to the ring oxygen, forming the lactone, and a primary amino group (–NH2) is attached to the adjacent carbon of the pyranone ring. The amine provides two hydrogen-bond donor sites, while the carbonyl oxygen and ring oxygen serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors. The molecule has no meaningful internal symmetry and only minimal conformational flexibility, since the amino group is the sole substituent that can rotate.

The molecule is a benzene ring bearing two substituents on adjacent-spaced positions: an amino group (-NH2) and a hydroxyl group (-OH) attached at positions meta to each other, giving a 1,3-disubstituted aromatic scaffold. The benzene ring is fully aromatic, planar, and rigid, with no fused ring systems. The substitution pattern is asymmetric, so the molecule has no mirror or rotational symmetry beyond the local planar geometry of the ring, and only the two polar groups provide conformational variation at their single bonds to the ring.

The molecule is built on a single benzene ring, a six-membered aromatic carbon framework with no ring fusion. Attached to one ring carbon is a terminal ethynyl group, a carbon-carbon triple bond with one hydrogen on the far carbon, which makes the chain linear and rigid. A primary amine group sits on a ring carbon located meta to the ethynyl substituent, giving a 1,3-disubstituted pattern. The amine nitrogen can donate hydrogen bonds through its two N-H bonds and accept one through its lone pair, while the terminal alkyne C-H is a weak donor.

The molecule is built on a bicyclic fused scaffold in which a benzene ring is ortho-fused to a six-membered diazine-type ring containing two adjacent nitrogen atoms, both bearing hydrogens, and two carbonyl groups. An amino group is attached to the benzene ring at a position adjacent to the ring fusion, giving a single substituent that breaks the symmetry of the framework. The fused core is planar and largely rigid, with little conformational flexibility beyond the amino group. The two ring N–H groups and the amino N–H functions act as hydrogen-bond donors, while the two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a single six-membered aromatic pyridine ring, with no fused or additional ring systems. An amino group (-NH2) is attached to one of the ring carbons adjacent to the nitrogen atom, so the substitution pattern is a 3-amino arrangement relative to the ring nitrogen. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry axis because the amino substituent breaks the symmetry of the ring. The molecule is built on a fused bicyclic scaffold in which a pyridine ring is joined to a benzene ring, forming a quinoline-type framework. The six-membered nitrogen-containing ring shares an edge with the benzenoid ring, so the system is planar and rigid, with no rotatable bonds. A primary amino group sits on the nitrogen-containing ring, at a carbon adjacent to the fused junction, and this is the only substituent present. The molecule is a five-membered aromatic thiophene ring, a sulfur-containing heterocycle, carrying two substituents on adjacent carbons. One substituent is a primary carboxamide group (–C(=O)NH2) attached directly to the ring carbon next to the sulfur, and the other is a primary amino group (–NH2) on the neighboring carbon. The ring is planar and rigid, and the amide bond gives limited rotational freedom at the attachment point. The molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two substituents sit at different positions on the ring. The amino and amide groups together provide hydrogen-bond donor capacity through their N–H bonds and acceptor capacity through the amide oxygen and the ring nitrogen-free sulfur environment.

The molecule is built on a six-membered carbocyclic ring containing a ketone and a carbon-carbon double bond conjugated to it, forming an α,β-unsaturated cyclohexenone scaffold. A secondary amine bridges the ring at the β-carbon, with its nitrogen attached to a phenyl ring, so the core is an enaminone-type arrangement in which the nitrogen lone pair conjugates into the enone system. The phenyl group is unsubstituted and monocyclic, giving the molecule two separate ring systems joined through the NH linker. Aside from the ring double bond and the aromatic ring, the cyclohexanone portion is largely saturated, so the molecule is fairly rigid overall with some flexibility at the N–phenyl bond. The NH group serves as a hydrogen-bond donor, while the carbonyl oxygen and the nitrogen lone pair act as hydrogen-bond acceptors.

The molecule is built on a four-carbon chain bearing a ketone at each end of a short linker, with a phenyl ring attached to one carbonyl carbon. The aromatic ring is a simple, unfused benzene ring with no substituents, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted. At the other end of the chain sits a trifluoromethyl group adjacent to a second ketone, which makes that portion strongly electron-withdrawing. The two carbonyl oxygens act as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors. The central methylene unit gives the chain some conformational flexibility, and the molecule lacks any internal symmetry because the two ends differ.

This molecule is a benzoic acid bearing a benzoyl group at the meta position, giving a diaryl ketone scaffold. Two benzene rings are linked through a single carbonyl carbon, so the ketone bridge is the central connecting unit. The carboxylic acid group sits on one ring and is attached directly to the aromatic carbon, while the other ring is unsubstituted and carries only the carbonyl link. The meta substitution pattern on the first ring breaks any mirror or rotational symmetry across the whole molecule, leaving it asymmetric. The aryl ketone and the carboxylic acid each contribute hydrogen-bond acceptor sites, and the acid's hydroxyl also provides a hydrogen-bond donor. The two rings can rotate about their single bonds to the carbonyl, so the molecule has moderate conformational flexibility.

The molecule is built from a linear four-carbon chain that carries a terminal carboxylic acid at one end and a ketone at the other, with the ketone bonded directly to a benzene ring. The benzene ring is a single unfused six-membered aromatic ring with no substituents besides this acyl group, so the substitution pattern is monosubstituted and the ring has no fusion. Apart from the flat aromatic ring, the chain is flexible, with two rotatable methylene units separating the two carbonyl-bearing ends. The carboxylic acid offers both a hydrogen-bond donor (the hydroxyl hydrogen) and acceptor sites (the oxygens), while the aryl ketone oxygen serves as an additional hydrogen-bond acceptor. The molecule has no symmetry element beyond a local mirror plane through the aromatic ring.

The molecule is a diaryl ketone built from two aromatic rings joined through a single central carbonyl group. One ring is a plain benzene ring bearing no substituents, while the other is a pyridine ring, a six-membered aromatic system in which one ring carbon is replaced by nitrogen, with the carbonyl attached at the meta position relative to that nitrogen. Both aromatic rings are unfused, planar, and largely unsubstituted, so the scaffold is rigid apart from rotation about the two bonds linking the carbonyl carbon to the rings. The molecule has no stereocenters and only limited symmetry, since the two rings differ in their heteroatom content. The ketone oxygen and the pyridine nitrogen both serve as hydrogen-bond acceptors, while the molecule has no hydrogen-bond donors.

This molecule is built on a thiophene ring, a five-membered aromatic heterocycle containing one sulfur atom. Attached to the carbon next to the sulfur is a carboxylic acid group, and at the adjacent position on the ring sits a benzoyl group, meaning a carbonyl linked directly to a phenyl ring. The benzoyl carbonyl and the phenyl ring are conjugated with the thiophene, giving a largely planar, rigid framework with limited flexibility apart from rotation around the single bonds joining the rings. The molecule has no internal symmetry axis, because the two substituents are different and sit at distinct positions on the thiophene. The carboxylic acid offers both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor capability, while the ketone carbonyl and the ring sulfur serve as additional acceptor sites.

The molecule is built from two benzene rings joined by a single methylene (CH2) bridge, so there is no fused ring system; the scaffold is a diarylmethane. One ring carries a primary amino group (-NH2) at the meta position relative to the bridging carbon, while the other ring is unsubstituted. Both aromatic rings are planar and rigid, but the single sp3 CH2 linker gives the molecule a degree of conformational flexibility around the two C-C bonds. The amino group can act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, and the aromatic rings provide weak pi-based interaction sites. The molecule has no symmetry axis that maps the two halves onto each other, since only one ring is substituted.
